en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory. Victorious is Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and the delighter of Satyavatī’s heart.
Victory has been won by that Blessed One, Hari, the sustainer of the world— the unborn, universal-formed, quality-less Great Soul, from whose lotus-mouth the world drinks the nectar of speech.
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, and has four arms,
with a serene countenance, for the sake of pacifying all obstacles.
Janamejaya said:
Having heard that Devavrata— whose peerless was his being, vigor, strength, heroism, and prowess— had been slain by Śikhaṇḍin of the Pañcālas,
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s mind was then overwhelmed with grief.
"O brahmin-sage, what did that valiant man do when his father was slain?
For his son, O Blessed One, having defeated the great archers— the Pāṇḍavas— led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, desired the kingdom."
"O Blessed One, O best of the twice-born, tell me what the Kaurava did after that Ketu, the foremost of all archers, had been slain. Vaiśampāyana said:

Having heard that his father had been slain, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men and descendant of Kuru, found no peace, being wholly devoted to anxiety and grief. As that king brooded over that sorrow incessantly, [it increased].
Then the pure-souled son of Gavalgaṇa returned;
at that time, the king sat with his head bowed, lost in thought and sighing deeply.
When the sun had set, the night had fallen, and the son of Gavalgaṇa was there.
With a distressed mind, he went to Hastināpura,
having learned through the grace of Vyāsa the entire and most excellent account of all the soldiers of both armies at that time.
When Sañjaya arrived at the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura) from the camp during the night,
O Great King, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, questioned him;
for having heard of the death of Bhīṣma, his mind was exceedingly dejected.
Desiring victory for his sons, he lamented like one who is distressed:
"O Sañjaya, I consider all the Dhārtarāṣṭras already dead in battle.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Having overcome the high-souled Bhīṣma of terrible prowess,
what did the Kurus, impelled by Time, do next, O dear one?
And having heard that my son was slain, what did he do, Sañjaya?
When that invincible hero of great prowess had been slain,
what indeed did the Kurus do, submerged as they were in an ocean of grief? Having encountered him in battle, which of those scorchers of foes remained standing there?
O Sañjaya, what man among the Kauravas could advance against that great, surging army— even if it belonged to the three worlds—
and cause intense fear to arise in the high-souled Pāṇḍavas?
"Who indeed was the great car-warrior (*mahāratha*) in Duryodhana’s army who,
having encountered that [Arjuna] in that great and most terrifying battle, [survived]? Tell us that,
since Devavrata, the bull among the Kurus, has been slain."
"Tell me, Sañjaya, what those kings did.
Sañjaya said:
"Listen with an attentive mind, O King, to my words as I speak them."
When Devavrata had been slain in battle, your sons did then what they had resolved;
and when Bhīṣma, whose prowess was truth, had been struck down, O King,
your men and the Pāṇḍavas each reflected separately.
Having observed the duty of the Kṣatriyas, they were both amazed and delighted; yet,
O Lord of the People, they felt great revulsion for that supreme Kṣatriya deed and,
censuring their own dharma, they prostrated themselves before the Great-Souled One.
O tiger among men, they prepared a bed for Bhīṣma of immeasurable splendor using arrows with smooth joints as its pillows;
having thus arranged the protection for Bhīṣma, they addressed one another.
Having paid homage to the son of Gaṅgā and circumambulated him,
those kṣatriyas, their eyes bloodshot with rage, looked at one another and went forth once more for battle, impelled by Time.
Then, with the sounding of trumpets and the great roar of kettledrums,
O king of kings, as the day turned and the son of Jahnavi had fallen, your armies and those of the enemy marched forth.
Overcome by indignation and with their minds struck down by fate,
those best of the Bharatas disregarded the beneficial words of the high-souled son of Gaṅgā and went forth, taking up all their weapons.
"Because of your delusion, and because of the slaughter of your son and of the son of Śantanu,
the Kauravas, together with all the kings, have fallen into the power of death,
like goats and sheep without a shepherd in a forest teeming with beasts of prey."

"Karna! Karna! the remaining kings of the earth cried out, O Bhārata, their minds deeply agitated, now that they were deprived of Devavrata. When that best of the Bharatas had fallen, the Kuru army was utterly despondent.
Like the sky stripped of its stars, like the atmosphere devoid of wind,
like the earth with its crops ruined, or like speech that is unrefined;
it was like the army of the Asuras when Bala had been captured in ancient times.
Like a widow of noble form, like a river whose waters have dried up,
like the goddess Lakṣmī abandoned by the gods, or like Brahmins deprived of the Vedas;
she was like a female deer whose leader of the herd has been slain and who is hemmed in by wolves in the forest.
O best of the Bharatas, when the son of Jahnavi had fallen, the great voice of Bharata became as unassailable as a mountain cave whose lion has been slain;
it was like a shattered ship on the great ocean, tossed by winds from every direction.
Then that army, severely afflicted by the powerful Pāṇḍava heroes who had attained their mark, became utterly distressed; with its horses, chariots, and elephants thrown into confusion,
and the majority of its men despondent, it appeared truly pitiable to behold.
In that situation, the kings and various kinds of soldiers were terrified;
deprived of Devavrata, they felt as if they were sinking into the underworld.
Indeed, the Kurus remembered Karṇa, for he was equal to Devavrata.
To him, the best among all wielders of weapons, who shone like a guest, their minds turned as if toward a kinsman come to their aid in distress;
O Bhārata, the kings there cried out, "Karna! Karna!"

The son of Rādhā, the charioteer’s son who is devoted to our welfare and ready to sacrifice his life— he, the highly illustrious Karṇa, did not fight for ten days along with his ministers and kinsmen; therefore, summon him without delay.
For while all the kṣatriyas looked on, as the chariot-warriors endowed with strength and prowess were being enumerated by Bhīṣma,
that bull among men, Karṇa— who was actually twice the merit of an ordinary warrior— was reckoned as only half a ratha.
He who was the foremost in the reckoning of chariot-warriors and atiratha-warriors, esteemed as a hero,
and who would venture to fight even his father, his wealth, the waters, and the lords of the gods— he,
O King, spoke to the son of Gaṅgā out of that very anger.
"O Kauravya, as long as you live, I shall not fight under any circumstances.
But once the sons of Pāṇḍu have been slain by you in the great battle,
O Kaurava, I shall take leave of Duryodhana and go to the forest."
"O Great King, whether Bhīṣma has been slain by the Pāṇḍavas or you yourself have ascended to heaven,
I shall slay with a single chariot alone all those whom you consider to be great car-warriors.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, the highly illustrious one [remained] for ten days.
Then, O King, with your son’s consent, Karṇa did not fight; instead,
Bhīṣma, who is valiant in battle and possesses immeasurable prowess, struck down the warriors of the Pāṇḍavas in the fray.
When that hero, true to his promise and possessed of great prowess, had been slain, your sons remembered Karṇa like those desiring to cross [the ocean] remember a boat;
so did your men and your sons, united with all the kings.
"Alas, Karṇa! they cried out, saying, "This is the end!
Thus did those mighty warriors, gathered together here and there, lament for Rādheya, the Sūta’s son, who had cast away his body.
Our minds turned toward Karṇa as toward a kinsman in times of extreme peril— he who, authorized by the son of Jamadagni, possesses irresistible prowess in the use of weapons;
for he alone, O King, is capable of protecting us from great danger in battle.
Just as Govinda always protects the thirty gods from great fear,
and just as Viṣṇu protects the gods from great danger;
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, his eyes agitated with grief, hissing like a venomous serpent, spoke these words to Sañjaya, the son of Gavalgaṇa, who was repeatedly praising Karṇa as the best in battle.

When your minds then turned toward Karṇa, the son of Vikartana, did you also behold that son of Rādhā, the Sūta’s son, who is ready to sacrifice his life? Did he of true prowess not make those words false in battle?
Then, for those who were bewildered, afflicted, and terrified, and who desired protection,
that best of archers fulfilled their wish in battle—
that which had been opened up for the Kauravas when Bhīṣma was slain.
He filled that division, instilling fear in his enemies;
for indeed, O Sañjaya, he is called a tiger among men in this world,
especially toward afflicted kinsmen and those who are crying out in distress.
Having sacrificed his life in battle for their protection and for the sake of their welfare,
he made my sons' hope for victory bear fruit.
Sañjaya said:
Having learned that Bhīṣma was slain—
like a shattered boat in the bottomless depths of the Kurus—
the son of the Sūta, like a brother, [acted] out of the calamity.
Hearing that the son of Śantanu, the great car-warrior and lord of men, the infallible Karna, had been struck down, he [Duryodhana] intended to rescue your son’s army.
Then Vṛṣa, the crusher of enemies and the foremost of archers, arrived swiftly;
for Bhīṣma, the best of car-warriors, had been slain by his foes.
Then, like a father hastening toward his sons, he rushed forward to rescue your son’s army, which was sinking like a ship in the ocean.
Having polished that divine bow with its string drawn, he—
the slayer of hosts of enemies— took up arrows equal in power to the fire of cosmic destruction, which had been given by Rāma.
Shaking his head, he spoke these words.
Karṇa said:
"In whom there is steadfastness, intelligence, prowess, and vigor..."
Self-restraint, truthfulness, all the virtues of a hero, celestial weapons, as well as humility, modesty,
and pleasant speech— these qualities never departed from Bhīṣma.
He who constantly slays those who hate the Brahmins and is ever-grateful— he,
that slayer of enemy heroes, is as eternally tranquil as the moon with its spot.
I consider all warriors already slain,
for nothing here is ever certain; in this world, everything is subject to the impermanence of action.
At sunrise, who indeed, free from doubt,
would maintain confidence today now that the one of great vows has been slain—
he who possessed the splendor of wealth and was born of the potency of wealth?
Now that the lord of the earth has departed for the Vasus,
you must grieve for your wealth, your sons, the earth itself, the Kurus, and this army.
Saṃjaya said:
When that one of great majesty, the granter of boons,
the best in the world, the son of Śantanu, and possessed of great energy, had been struck down;
When the Bharatas had been defeated, Karṇa, dejected in spirit, sighed deeply and shed tears;
having heard these words of the son of Rādhā, they [the others]—
And your sons, O King, and your soldiers as well,
cried out to one another intensely with cries of distress; indeed, they shed tears from their eyes accompanied by loud sounds.
But as that great battle proceeded and the armies were being plunged into by the kings, he then spoke these words, which inspired courage:
Karna, the bull among all great chariot-warriors, said to those bulls among chariot-warriors: "In this transient world that is constantly rushing along;"
Reflecting deeply, I perceive today that while you all remain here, this bull among the Kurus, who resembles a mountain, has been struck down in battle— how can this be?
When the great car-warrior Śāntanava had been struck down,
like the sun descended to the surface of the earth,
the kings were not able to withstand Dhanañjaya.
Like trees facing a wind that would uproot a mountain,
this army today appears distressed, its leaders slain, its enthusiasm destroyed by the enemy, and truly left without a protector.
I must protect the Kurus in battle,
just as that high-souled one did;
likewise, such a burden has been placed upon me by him with full concentration.
I perceive this world to be thus impermanent,
and that one who was once fierce in battle has been struck down in the fray;
how then could I feel fear in battle?
But I, moving through the battle, shall dispatch those bulls of the Kuru race to the abode of Yama with my straight-flying arrows;
having manifested supreme glory in the world, I shall conduct myself [in this way].
Yudhiṣṭhira, who possesses fortitude, intelligence, and the essence of dharma, may lie slain by others in battle,
as may Vṛkodara, whose prowess is equal to that of a hundred elephants.
Likewise, since Arjuna— the son of the foremost of the thirty gods— is present,
that force cannot be easily conquered even by the immortals;
and where the twins, equal to Yama in strength, are in battle;
Where Sātyaki and the son of Devakī were,
no coward could approach that army;
he would repeatedly turn back as if from the very jaws of death.
Excessive asceticism is countered by asceticism alone, and likewise strength by strength, by those possessed of mental fortitude;
and my mind is certainly resolved upon repelling the enemy.
And he remained as immovable as a mountain in protecting himself.
Then the son of the Sūta spoke to his own charioteer:
"I shall slay the Pāṇḍavas and the Somakas!"
"O charioteer, having understood their power in this way,
I shall go and conquer them today;
this betrayal of my friends cannot be forgiven by me."
He who is a helper when the army is broken is a true friend; I shall perform this noble deed of a virtuous man,
and having cast off my life, I will follow Bhīṣma.
"I shall slay all the hosts of enemies in battle;
either I will kill them, or, slain by them, I will go to the world of heroes," he said while the women and children were crying out in lamentation.
O Sūta, I know that when the manliness of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son has been defeated, my duty must be performed;
therefore, I shall conquer the enemies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
Protecting the Kurus and desiring to slay the sons of Pāṇḍu,
he has cast away his life in this battle of terrible form,
having struck down all the hosts of enemies in the fray.
"I shall give the kingdom to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
let my wonderful golden armor, bright and radiant with jewels and gems, be fastened upon me."
Let them prepare a helmet with a brilliance equal to the sun,
as well as a bow and arrows like venomous serpents,
and sixteen quivers.
Let them likewise bring celestial bows,
swords, spears, heavy maces,
and a conch shell that shines with the variegated luster of gold.
Bring this golden elephant-girth, which brings victory,
and my victorious banner that has the luster of a blue lotus,
having wiped them clean with smooth cloths.
Having tied a variegated garland with a net upon them,
he [prepared] the foremost horses, which shone like white clouds,
well-fed and bathed with water purified by mantras.
"Bring here quickly, very quickly, the son of the Sūta with his swift horses and equipped with heated golden vessels;
and bring the preeminent chariot covered with a network of gold."
"Quickly bring back the chariot, adorned with jewels as bright as the sun and moon,
equipped with all necessary implements for combat,
and yoked with draft animals."
Variegated and powerful bows, excellent bowstrings fitted with sturdy frames,
and great quivers filled with arrows;
Having put on their body-coverings,
they quickly brought all the provisions for the journey,
as well as full vessels of gold and hero-bronze for the maidens.
"Having brought the garland and fastened it upon his body,
let them quickly sound the kettledrums for victory!
O charioteer, proceed swiftly to where Kirīṭin is!"
Vṛkodara, the son of Dharma, and the twins—
either I shall slay them all upon meeting them in battle,
or I shall go to my death slain by my enemies for Bhīṣma’s sake.
In which [army] King Yudhiṣṭhira, firm in truth,
is stationed, along with Bhīmasena and Arjuna,
Vāsudeva, Sātyaki, and the Sṛñjayas.
I consider that strength to be invincible even for lords of the earth,
if Death himself— the destroyer of all— were to protect that Diademed One in battle, ever remaining vigilant.
Nevertheless, having encountered them in battle, I shall either slay them or go to Yama by the path of Bhīṣma; indeed,
I shall certainly not fail to go among them.
I speak thus among the brave:
those who betray their friends, who are disloyal,
and who are evil-minded— these are not my allies.
Saṃjaya said:
He [ascended] that excellent, firm chariot,
which was equipped with a pole, adorned with gold, and auspicious.
Mounting a chariot adorned with banners and yoked to excellent horses swift as the wind, that high-souled one set forth for victory,
being honored by the Kurus.
Then that bull among chariot-warriors, with his white horses and formidable bow, proceeded to the battlefield where the bull of the Bharatas lay.
Karna [advanced] in a great chariot provided with a protective fender and a banner,
adorned with gold, pearls, gems, and diamonds,
and yoked with excellent horses.
Like the sun with its thundering clouds, he of immeasurable luster—
resembling fire and possessing the brilliance of fire—
the auspicious archer stood upon his own auspicious chariot.
Standing there, the great car-warrior Adhirathi shone resplendent,
like the King of the Gods himself stationed upon his celestial chariot.
Sañjaya said:
The high-souled one of immeasurable splendor lay upon a bed of arrows,
like an ocean dried up by a great mass of wind;
he who had raised up the heavy earth was now struck down by Savyasācin.
Or even if Mount Meru were lifted up and playfully hurled into the waters,
or if the entire earth were destroyed by that great archer, the preceptor who was the end of all the kṣatriyas,
and brought down by Savyasācin with his divine weapons— [even so, you would not be able to protect him].
The hope for victory of your sons has been shattered, along with their refuge and their armor—
like an island sought by those wishing for a foothold in the bottomless deep,
or like one swept away by the flood of the Yamunā’s current amidst a torrent of arrows.
Like the great Maināka mountain, unbearable, cast down upon the earth;
like the sun fallen from the sky onto the surface of the ground;
like the inconceivable defeat of Śatakratu by Vṛtra in ancient times.
The stunning of the entire army and the felling of Bhīṣma in battle;
the preeminent leader of all forces and the emblem of all archers—
your father, observer of great vows, was covered by the arrows of Dhanañjaya.
Seeing Bhīṣma, that bull among men and the peerless leader of the Bharatas, lying upon the hero’s bed, the son of Adhiratha descended from his chariot, distressed,
his voice choked with tears.
Overwhelmed by grief and delusion, he went on foot in his distress;
having offered salutations with joined palms, he spoke while paying homage.
"I am Karṇa; may it be well with you. O Bhārata, do not speak to me today;
look instead with your eyes and address me with auspicious and peaceful words.
Surely no one here partakes of the fruit of their own good deeds."

O best of the Kurus, since you, who are devoted to dharma and advanced in years, lie here upon the ground, I see no other protector for the Kurus in matters of raising revenue, in counsel, or in the deployment of troops and weapons.
"Endowed with pure intelligence, he who would have delivered the Kurus from fear—
you, having abandoned your warriors in the absence of a boat, shall go to the world of the ancestors.
From this day forward, they will be as enraged as tigers toward a slaughter-ground of deer."
O best of the Bharatas, today the Pāṇḍavas will bring about the destruction of the Kurus; for now the Kurus, knowing the prowess of Savyasācin and the roar of the Gāṇḍīva,
will tremble like the Asuras before the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Today, the sound of arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, like that of thunderbolts,
will terrify the Kurus and other kings in battle;
just as a kindled fire with great flames, O hero, would consume trees.
The arrows of Kirīṭin will consume the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
for wherever wind and fire advance together in the forest,
those two blessed ones burn everything therein according to their will.
Just as a fire is when fully kindled, so indeed is Pārtha; of this there is no doubt.
For Kaunteya is exactly like a forest fire on a mountain.
And just as Vāyu is, O tiger among men, so is Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.
Janārdana will advance,
consuming the enemy ranks; O Bhārata, upon hearing the roar of the Pāñcajanya conch and the twang of the Gāṇḍīva bow, all the armies will fall into terror.
"O hero, except for you, the kings will not be able to endure the sound of the chariot of the one who bears the monkey-banner and who crushes his enemies.
For what other king besides you is worthy to fight Arjuna in battle?"
The wise proclaim his divine deeds; he fought an unearthly battle with the wise Tryambaka,
and from him he obtained a boon that is difficult for those of unrefined souls to attain.

Who else is capable of conquering him in battle, he who was previously unconquerable even by the gods? By you, O hero endowed with prowess, Rāma— the terrible destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, worshipped by gods and Dānavas— has been defeated in combat.
The son of Pāṇḍu, who boasted of his strength and was protected by Mādhava,
now lies slain, pierced by the arrows of Śikhaṇḍin.
Today I shall [slay] that Pāṇḍava, who is skilled in battle.
Unable to endure this, though instructed by you,
I shall place before me a most terrible, sight-killing venomous serpent,
and seek either death or victory.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard him thus lamenting, the aged grandfather of the Kurus,
with a pleased mind, spoke these words appropriate to the time and place.
Having observed that the chariot was empty and having cleared away the guards, the son of Gaṅgā embraced him with one arm like a father embracing a son, saying:
"Come, come, O son of a Sūta! You indeed challenge me."
If you had not found me, your welfare would certainly not have been secured.
You are the son of Kuntī, not the son of Rādhā; Adhiratha is not your father.
O mighty-armed one, you were known to me through Nārada as being born from the Sun.
From Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana and from Keśava as well, there is no doubt;
be the destroyer of the pride of your enemies and the remover of the grief of your friends.
And through the splendor of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, there is indeed no doubt.

"O Karṇa, I have no hatred for you; I tell you this truly. However, I spoke harshly for the purpose of suppressing your arrogance, for it was my conviction that you were harboring enmity toward the Pāṇḍavas without cause."
Therefore, you were repeatedly addressed with harsh words in the assembly of the Kurus:
"O destroyer of the enemy faction, you shall slay the heroes in battle! You possess devotion to the Brahmins, heroism, and are a supreme treasury of generosity."
Out of fear of causing a rift within the family, O hero, I have always spoken harshly to you regarding your mastery of the bow, your aim, your swiftness, and the power of your weapons;
yet you are the equal of Phalguna and even equal to Krishna in strength.
Be as the ocean is to rivers, as the sun is to lights,
as the virtuous are to truth, and as fertile soil is to seeds; be as the rain-cloud is to living beings— be thus the refuge of your friends.
May your kinsmen depend upon you, as the immortals depend upon the thousand-eyed Indra.
Be the destroyer of the pride of your enemies and the increaser of the joy of your friends. Be the refuge of the Kauravas, just as Viṣṇu is the refuge of the dwellers of heaven.
O Karṇa, desiring to do what was pleasing to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, you went to Rājapura by the strength and prowess of your own arms and slew the Kambojas;
you also defeated the kings dwelling in Girivraja, headed by Nagnajit.
The Ambaṣṭhas, the Videhas, and the Gāndhāras have been conquered by you;
likewise, the exceedingly powerful King Jarāsaṃdha,
who was like a marvel and who boasted of his prowess in battle, has not surpassed you in combat.
O Karṇa, in the past you brought under Duryodhana’s control the Kirātas, who dwell in the fastnesses of the Himavat and are fierce in battle;
as well as the Utkalas, Mekalas, Pauṇḍras, Kaliṅgas, and Andhras in combat.
The Niṣādas, the Trigartas, and the Bāhlīkas were conquered by you in various battles by Duryodhana’s well-wisher;
and many other heroes were defeated by you, O Karṇa of great prowess.
Devoted to Brahman and truthful in speech, he is the sun in his splendor; of this there is no doubt.
A son of the gods, unconquerable in battle, he is superior to men in combat. Today my anger toward you, which was previously harbored, has been dispelled.
Fate cannot be overcome by human effort.
O hero, slayer of enemies, the Pāṇḍavas are your uterine brothers;
go to them in unity, O mighty-armed one, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me.
"O son of the Sun, let my enmity come to an end;
today let all kings on earth be free from affliction.
Karṇa said:

"O mighty-armed one, I know this: I am the son of Kuntī, not born of a charioteer. Though abandoned by Kuntī and raised by a charioteer, having enjoyed the sovereignty of Duryodhana, I cannot bring myself to act falsely."
"O giver of many sacrificial fees, for the sake of Duryodhana, I have renounced my wealth, my body, my sons, my wife, and likewise my fame; all this,
O Kaurava, shall lead to the disease of death for a kṣatriya."
The Pāṇḍavas have been constantly provoked by me through my reliance on Suyodhana.
Those outcomes that are irreversible cannot be turned back;
who would venture to turn back destiny by means of human effort?
O Bhārata, these omens here portend the destruction of the earth;
indeed, they were seen by you in the past and described in the assembly, saying,
"They cannot be conquered by other men," and thus we take heart against them.
"Father, grant me leave for battle with a joyful heart;
O hero, it is my resolve that I shall fight only when permitted by you. [I have endured] harsh words spoken out of agitation or even out of rashness."
"O bull of the Bharatas, abandon whatever I have done for you;
O dear one, so that Duryodhana, along with his kinsmen, family, and relatives,
may find security everywhere and achieve the destruction of his enemies."
In that same way, may you also become the refuge for all the Kauravas.
I bid you farewell with auspicious wishes; go and fight the enemies. Rule the Kurus in battle and bestow victory upon Duryodhana.
Act in such a way, O lord of men, that victory may be achieved over Duryodhana;
for you are like a grandson to us as Duryodhana is,
and according to dharma, we are all yours just as we are his.
"O best of men, the wise declare that association with the virtuous in this world is superior to the bond of kinship; therefore,
having become true to your promise, you must resolve that 'this is mine.'"
Protect the army of the Kurus just as Duryodhana does;
for in this way the Pāṇḍavas will surely conquer the Kauravas in battle,
and they will attain the worlds earned through the duty of a kṣatriya— of this there is no doubt.
"Fight without ego, relying upon your own strength and prowess;
for indeed, there exists no duty greater for a Kṣatriya than battle.
Sañjaya said:
Thus addressed by Bhīṣma,
having resolved upon battle and having heard these words regarding how the Kurus fought the Pāṇḍavas in war, he then paid homage at his feet.
Vaikartana Karṇa quickly went toward the battlefield;
then, there, that great archer assigned the best of chariot-warriors and,
immediately thereafter, arranged the elephants in their respective positions.
Just as Bṛhaspati stationed horsemen and foot soldiers according to the scriptures,
so did he, who was fond of victory, station your sons.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, having arranged the wings and the flanks, he set out.
At the tip of the wing, moreover, surrounded by two [divisions] on each flank and two [divisions] of friends;
thus was this array previously formed by me and Karṇa,
which the kings along with the Kurus considered a sight to behold.
Seeing that battle array— which seemed as if it were dancing and as if it were eager to consume its enemies—
constructed according to the doctrine of Bṛhaspati by the wise Karṇa,
the two armies, the very core of the body of the formation, faced one another.
Beholding that incomparable and vast array of men,
with their broad chests protected by armor, he strengthened that army;
all the Kurus, led by Duryodhana, were filled with joy.
Seeing that mighty-armed Karna, the great archer, who stood at the head of his entire army and was stationed for battle,
they greeted him with the sounds of lion-roars and the slapping of arms.
And with various cries of "Bravo! Bravo!", the Kurus honored him.
Sañjaya said:
Having seen that tiger among men, Karṇa, stationed upon his chariot, [the Kurus cheered].
O King, Duryodhana, being delighted, spoke these words:
"This army is exceedingly well-protected and has found its protector in you.
However, I believe it is necessary to deliberate upon what is capable and what is beneficial."
Karna said:
"Speak that, O tiger among men, for you, O King, are the wisest;
for a lord of wealth perceives what ought to be done in a way that no other does."
"O lord of men, they are all desirous of hearing your words;
for it is my conviction that you would never speak an unjust word.
Duryodhana said:

Bhīṣma was the leader of the army, endowed with both age and prowess, as well as great learning and all the qualities of a warrior. By him, O Karṇa, my hosts of enemies were slain, he who possessed exceeding fame.
For ten days we have been protected by that high-souled one through his skillful fighting;
now that he, having performed deeds difficult to accomplish, has ascended to heaven,
whom do you consider to be the leader of the army after him?
An army does not remain standing for even a moment without a leader,
especially in battles— like collyrium fallen from the eyes—
or like a boat in the water deprived of a helmsman, O best of warriors.
For just as a ship without a helmsman, or a chariot without a driver,
would drift at will, so too would an army be without a commander;
and just as a caravan without a guide meets with every kind of misfortune.
Just as an army without a leader encounters every kind of calamity, so it is with this host.
Therefore, having observed all these great-souled men of mine,
look for a commander here who is worthy to succeed the son of Śantanu.
"O noble one, whomever you shall name as the leader of the army in battle,
all of us together will follow him.
Karna said:

All these great-souled ones, the best among men, are worthy of the command of the army; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. They excel in lineage, physical build, knowledge, strength, prowess, and intelligence.
They are disciplined, grateful, modest, and do not retreat in battles;
yet it is not possible for all of them to be made leaders at once.
Only one person should be appointed here, in whom exceptional qualities reside.
"O Bhārata, if you show favor to only one among those who are vying with one another, the rest will clearly become dejected and will not fight. Moreover,
this man is the teacher, the elder, and the preceptor of all the warriors."
Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons, is fit to be the commander;
for who else could stand as commander against the invincible Droṇa, the supreme knower of Brahman,
were it not for the example of Śukra of the Aṅgirasa lineage?
O Bhārata, there is indeed no warrior among all those kings who will not follow Drona as he advances in battle;
for he is the foremost of army leaders and the greatest among those who bear arms.
"O King, he is the foremost among the wise and is your preceptor;
therefore, quickly appoint Duryodhana’s teacher as the commander-in-chief,
just as the immortals appointed Kārttikeya when they desired to conquer the Asuras in battle."
07,005.021 Saṃjaya said:
07,005.021a Having heard the words of Karṇa, King Duryodhana then 07,005.021c spoke these words to Droṇa, who was situated in the midst of the army.
By virtue of his excellence in caste, noble birth, sacred learning, age, and intellect;
by heroism, skill, invincibility, knowledge of worldly affairs, policy, and victory;
and by asceticism and gratitude—he was aged in every quality.

"O best of the twice-born, there is no other protector found who is as fit for kings as you are. May you protect us all, just as Vāsava protects the gods; with you as our leader, O most excellent of brahmins, we desire to conquer our enemies."
Like Kapālin among the Rudras, like Pāvaka among the Vasus, like Kubera among the Yakṣas, like Vāsava among the Maruts,
like Vasiṣṭha among the Brahmins, and like Bhāskara among the luminaries.
He was like Dharma among the ancestors, like the Lord of Waters among the Ādityas,
like the Moon among the stars, and like Uśanas among the sons of Diti;
he was indeed like the refuge of all the worlds and of the entire universe.
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, is supreme in the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the universe;
he is the foremost of all commanders of armies—may you become our general. O sinless one, let eleven akṣauhiṇīs of troops be under your command.
Having arrayed the enemy with them, slay them as Indra slew the Dānavas. May you go before us, like Pāvaki at the head of the gods;
we shall follow you in battle, like bulls following the leader of the herd.
Seeing you at our head, Arjuna— the fierce bowman, the great archer who draws his celestial bow—
will not prevail over Yudhiṣṭhira in battle, along with his followers and kinsmen; this is certain.
"O tiger among men, I shall conquer [the enemy] if you become our commander. When this was said, Drona, the lords of men cried out "Victory! with a great lion-roar, gladdening your son.
And the soldiers, filled with joy, honored the best of the twice-born while placing Duryodhana at their head, seeking great glory;
they considered the sons of Pṛthā as already defeated and regarded their own fame as supreme.
Then, O King, Droṇa spoke these words to Duryodhana.
Droṇa said:
"I know the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs, as well as the science of statecraft (arthavidyā) composed by Manu."
I shall employ the Traiyambaka weapon, as well as the Īśvastra and various other weapons;
and I will fight the Pāṇḍavas, desiring to make true those qualities which you, seeking victory, have attributed to me.
"O King, I shall not slay the son of Pṛṣata in battle by any means whatsoever;
for he was created specifically for my destruction, O bull among men. I, however, will fight the armies, destroying all the Somakas."
"And the Pāṇḍavas will not joyfully challenge me to battle.
Saṃjaya said:
Having been thus authorized, he then appointed [Droṇa] as the commander of the army.
O King, your son [Duryodhana], according to the prescribed rites,
then consecrated Droṇa; and the kings, headed by Duryodhana, bathed Droṇa with benedictions, other gentle words, and auspicious, delightful hymns.
Just as in ancient times the gods, headed by Śakra, appointed Skanda to the generalship, so then,
upon Drona being made the commander-in-chief, there arose a great joy accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and the loud shouts of men.
Then, with the sound of the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the resonance of benedictions (*svastivāda*),
the praises and songs of the *sūtas*, *māgadhas*,
and bards, the cries of "Victory! from the foremost of the twice-born, and likewise the graceful dancing of beautiful women—
When the twice-born Drona had been appointed as the commander-in-chief, a great roar arose;
with joyful hearts,
they all honored the high-souled Drona according to tradition and considered the Pandavas already conquered.
Saṃjaya said:
Having obtained the command of the army, the great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja,
desiring to fight, arrayed the troops and set out together with your sons.
Saindhava, Kaliṅga, and your son Vikarṇa,
clad in armor, took their positions on the right flank.
Śakuni was their wing, accompanied by the most excellent horse-riders.
He advanced together with the Gāndhāra warriors who fought with bright lances;
while Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, Citrasena, and Viviṃśati,
led by Duḥśāsana, vigilantly protected his left flank.
Their flank was formed by the Kambojas led by Sudakṣiṇa,
who advanced with horses of great speed, together with the Śakas and Yavanas;
as did the Madras, Trigartas, Sāmbaṣṭhas, and those dwelling in the western and northern regions.
The Śibis, the Śūrasenas, and the Śūdras along with the Maladas; the Sauvīras, the Kitavas, and all those from the East and the South— all these,
placing your son at their head, followed behind the Sūta’s son.
Gladdening all the troops and instilling strength within the forces,
Karna Vaikartana went forth at the head of all the archers;
his great-bodied chariot, blazing with light, gladdened his own ranks.
With the great banner of the elephant’s girth, he shone with a splendor equal to the sun.
Upon seeing Karṇa, no one thought any longer of the calamity that was Bhīṣma;
all the kings, together with the Kurus, became free from grief.
And many warriors, gathered there, spoke joyfully:
"Indeed, having seen Karṇa in battle, the Pāṇḍavas will not stand their ground in the fight;
for Karṇa is capable of conquering even the gods led by Vāsava in combat."
How much more so the sons of Pāṇḍu, whose strength and prowess are inferior in battle?
For the sons of Pṛthā were protected in combat by Bhīṣma, who is mighty of arm;
but Karṇa will undoubtedly destroy them with his sharp arrows.
O lord of the people, speaking thus to one another with joyful countenances, honoring and praising the son of Rādhā, they went forth. Our array of wagons had been formed by Droṇa.
O King, O Bhārata, the array of those high-souled enemies was in the form of a *krauñca* (crane), arranged by Dharmarāja as he took pleasure in it;
at the head of that array stood those two bulls among men.
Having raised the monkey-banner, Viṣvaksena and Dhanañjaya—
the pre-eminent peak of all armies and the mark of all archers—
became the banner of Pārtha of immeasurable splendor, reaching even to the path of the sun.
He set that army of the high-souled Pāṇḍava ablaze,
just as the blazing sun at the end of an eon scorches the earth;
likewise, O King, the Bharata host was tormented by Arjuna.
For thus the banner of the wise one would be seen blazing everywhere. Arjuna, the best of archers, wields the Gāṇḍīva, the foremost of bows;
and Vāsudeva is the supreme among beings, and the Sudarśana among discs.
Bearing these four fires, the chariot with its white horses stood before the enemies like the uplifted wheel of Time;
thus did those two great-souled ones stand at the head of their respective armies.
Karna was the leader of your men’s faces, and Dhananjaya was the leader of the enemies’. Then, filled with intense fury and each desiring the other's death,
Karna and the son of Pandu glared at one another in that battle.
Desiring to consume one another in battle, the two enraged heroes, possessed of great prowess, cast their eyes upon each other while brandishing their firm bows;
that best of chariot-warriors stood with his banner raised high, its pennons fluttering.
The preceptor of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas stood at the head of the battle.
Then, as the great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, suddenly advanced,
the earth trembled with a terrible internal roar.
Then a thick dust, stirred up by the wind and resembling a mass of silk, arose and covered the sky along with the sun in a tumultuous roar.
And though the heavens were cloudless, they rained down flesh, bones, and blood.
O King, vultures, hawks, *baḍas*, herons, and crows by the thousands then flew directly over your army;
and jackals howled with terrifying and dreadful cries.
They repeatedly moved counter-clockwise around your army,
desiring to devour its flesh and thirsting for its blood;
and a blazing meteor fell, accompanied by thunder and causing the earth to tremble.

A blazing meteor, O King, appeared in the battle, enveloping everything with its tail; there was also a great halo around the sun, accompanied by lightning and thunder, when the commander of the army set forth.
These and many other most dreadful portents appeared,
foreboding the destruction of the lives of the heroes in battle;
then the combat commenced between those who sought to slay one another.
The sound of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies made the world resound. Highly incensed with one another, those strikers— the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas—
eager for victory, struck each other with sharpened arrows.

That great archer of immense splendor rushed with speed toward the vast army of the Pāṇḍavas, scattering hundreds of sharp arrows. Seeing Droṇa thus advancing, the Pāṇḍavas together with the Sṛñjayas [prepared for battle].
O King, they then received those [attacks] with their own showers of arrows, each individually.
That great army, being agitated by Droṇa and torn asunder,
was scattered along with the Pāñcālas, like clouds by the wind.
Displaying many divine weapons in that battle,
Droṇa afflicted the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas in an instant.
Being slaughtered by Droṇa like the Dānavas by Vāsava, they were overcome.
The Pāñcālas, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, trembled;
then the heroic great car-warrior Yājñaseni, skilled in divine weapons,
pierced Drona’s army in many places with a shower of arrows.

Having warded off Droṇa’s showers of arrows with his own showers of arrows, part by part, the mighty one then began to slay the Kuru army. Then Droṇa, having withdrawn and steadied himself in the battle, [proceeded].
The mighty-armed one rushed against the son of Pṛṣata with his own division;
he unleashed a vast shower of arrows toward the son of Pṛṣata,
like the enraged Maghavan suddenly attacking the Dānavas.
Shaken by Droṇa’s arrows, those Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas were broken again and again, like other animals before a lion. Then the mighty Droṇa rushed about, scattering the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
O King, it was like a whirling circle of fire and appeared as something marvelous—
a city fashioned according to the vision of the scriptures,
with banners fluttering in the moving wind, resounding, and with horses leaping about.
Mounted upon his excellent chariot, which had a banner as pure as crystal and which scorched his enemies, he struck down the hostile army. Sañjaya said:
Seeing Droṇa thus slaughtering horses, charioteers, chariots, and elephants, the Pāṇḍavas were distressed and could not check him. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira [addressed] Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Dhanañjaya.
The Pot-born (Droṇa) said: "Let him be warded off by all of you, exerting yourselves on every side.
Then all those great car-warriors—Arjuna, the son of Pṛṣata (Dhṛṣṭadyumna), and his followers—surrounded him as he approached.
The Kekayas, Bhīmasena, the son of Subhadrā, and Ghaṭotkaca;
Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins, the Matsyas, and the sons of Drupada;
as well as the sons of Draupadī, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Sātyaki—all were filled with joy.
And Cekitāna, enraged, and the great car-warrior Yuyutsu,
O King, as well as the other kings who were followers of the Pāṇḍava,
performed numerous deeds worthy of their lineage and prowess.

Seeing that army being rallied by the Pāṇḍavas in battle, the son of Bharadvāja turned his eyes in anger and gazed upon them. Taking up a fierce rage, he, who was difficult to vanquish in combat, stood upon his chariot.
Like the wind dispersing the clouds, he scattered the Pāṇḍava army;
charging here and there against chariots, horses, men, and elephants,
Droṇa, though old, moved like one who was young and mad.

O King, those well-bred horses, swift as the wind, their limbs smeared with blood and crimson in hue, bore him in undaunted splendor. As he approached like the wrathful God of Death himself, firm in his vows—
Seeing him, the warriors of the Pāṇḍava fled here and there; as they were fleeing,
and even as some turned back again,
looking on and standing their ground, there arose a most dreadful clamor.
Producing joy for the brave and increasing the fear of the timid,
it filled the space between heaven and earth on all sides.
Then, once again in that battle, Droṇa proclaimed his own name.
He made himself fierce, scattering hundreds of arrows at his enemies;
thus Drona, though aged, slew those divisions of the wise son of Pandu like Death himself, as powerful as a youth.

Having severed heads and even arms still adorned with ornaments, that fierce great car-warrior, having left the seats of his chariot empty, let out a loud shout. O Lord, by the sound of his joy and the force of his arrows, [the enemy was overwhelmed].
The warriors trembled in battle like cows afflicted by the cold;
from the rattling of Droṇa’s chariot, the friction of his bowstring,
and the sound of his bow, a great noise arose in the sky.
Then, his arrows issuing forth by the thousands in great numbers,
they fell, pervading all directions, upon the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
That [bow] possessed the great momentum of a bow and had the fire of weapons blazing from it.
The Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, assailed Droṇa; Droṇa,
however, dispatched them— along with their chariots, elephants, and horses— to the abode of Yama,
and in a short time he turned the earth into a mire of blood.
As Droṇa deployed supreme weapons and discharged arrows incessantly, a web of shafts was seen spread in all directions among the foot soldiers,
chariots, horses, and elephants on every side.
His banner, moving like lightning among the clouds,
became visible as he crushed the five foremost of the Kekayas and the king of the Pañcālas with his arrows.
Droṇa, whose warriors were undaunted, advanced against Yudhiṣṭhira’s army with bow and arrows in hand; Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya [also advanced] against him.
The grandson of Śini, the son of Drupada, the son of Śaibya, the lord of Kāśī, and Śibi—
delighted and roaring, they scattered showers of arrows.
In battle, their impetuous force was rendered futile as they were arrayed in ranks like *kāśarohā* reeds on an island in the rivers;
then, arrows released from Droṇa’s bow struck them.
Feathered arrows with variegated golden shafts,
having pierced the bodies of elephants and young horses,
entered the earth with their feathers smeared with blood.
The earth became covered with fallen throngs of warriors, chariots,
and elephants and horses pierced by arrows.
On all sides, like the sky with dark clouds,
were the armies of Śaineya, Bhīma, Arjuna, Vāhinīpa,
Śaibya, Abhimanyu, and the King of Kāśi.
And Drona, desiring the prosperity of your sons, crushed other heroes in battle;
these and other such deeds, O Indra among the Kauravas.
O King, having performed deeds in battle like the sun at the end of time scorching the worlds, the high-souled Droṇa has indeed departed from here to heaven.
Having performed great deeds, that hero Drona,
the crusher of enemy forces and possessor of the golden chariot, was struck down by the son of Prishata after he had slain hundreds of thousands of Pandava warriors in battle.
Having slain more than an *akṣauhiṇī* of heroes who never retreated, the resolute one subsequently attained the supreme goal,
along with the Pāṇḍavas, the Pañcālas, and those of inauspicious and cruel deeds.
"O King, Rukmaratha was slain after having performed a most difficult feat.
Then, O King, a great clamor arose among all beings in the sky and among the troops, now that the Preceptor had been killed in battle."
Making the heavens, the earth, the sky, the cardinal points, the waters, and the intermediate directions resound, a great cry of "Alas! Woe! arose from all living beings;
so too did the gods, the ancestors, and those who were his former kinsmen.
They beheld the great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, slain there;
but the Pāṇḍavas, having achieved victory, let out lion-like roars,
and by that great sound the earth trembled.
Having heard that the great chariot, the golden chariot with its banner adorned with various kinds of Jāmbūnada gold, had been struck down, no one indeed experienced any joy.
"Except for Drupada’s son, the descendant of Sṛñjaya, in the midst of battle.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"What was Droṇa doing in the fight when the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas slew him?"
Though he was so skilled in weapons among all wielders of arms,
his chariot broke while he was shooting, or his bow shattered as he discharged arrows; or perhaps Drona became distracted, and thus he met his death.
"How indeed, O dear one, did the son of Pṛṣata [Dhṛṣṭadyumna] overcome him who was invincible to enemies,
who scattered multitudes of gold-feathered arrows many times over,
that best of the twice-born, swift-handed, skillful, and a versatile warrior?"

The son of the Pañcāla king has slain that self-controlled great car-warrior, who was an expert in the science of weapons, capable of shooting arrows at long distances, and who, though striving in battle, performed terrible deeds— by good fortune, he has struck down that excellent and unshakable hero.
It is clear that destiny is indeed more powerful than human effort; this is my conviction,
since the heroic Drona has been slain by the high-souled son of Prishata,
in whom the fourfold weapons were firmly established.

You tell me that Drona, the preeminent teacher of archery, has been slain. Having heard that he— whose chariot was adorned with gold, whose vehicle was covered in tiger-skins, and whose equipment was made of refined gold— is killed, I cannot today dispel my grief.

"Surely no one dies from the sorrow of another, O Saṃjaya, since I still live and do not die even after hearing that Droṇa has been slain. I consider destiny alone to be supreme, neither good policy nor human effort."
"Wherein my leader, the most excellent in virtues, has been slain by enemies—
surely my heart is made of the essence of stone, very firm,
since it does not shatter into a hundred pieces upon hearing that Droṇa has been killed."

How could he— who was worshipped by Brahmins and princes seeking merit for his mastery of the Veda of Brahmā as well as the science of archery— be slain by death? It is like the drying up of the ocean or the shifting of Mount Meru.
I cannot endure the fall of Droṇa, which is like the falling of the sun;
he who was the restrainer of the arrogant and the protector of the righteous,
that scorcher of foes who even cast away his life for the sake of a miserable man.
How was he slain— he in whose prowess my dull-witted sons placed their hope for victory, who was equal to Bṛhaspati and Uśanas in intelligence, and who,
possessed of great splendor, stood as the very embodiment of all the warriors' virtues?
How could he, who stands subject to the power of death, be slain by death?
And those large, crimson horses from the Sindhu region, adorned with golden garlands, were yoked to his chariot; they possessed the speed of the wind and could outstrip all sounds in battle.
Were the Sindh horses— powerful, loud-neighing, well-tamed, and excellent at drawing the chariot—
firm in the midst of battles and never overwhelmed? And as for the elephants, massive in combat, [did they endure] the sound of conchs and drums?
Enduring the strikes of bowstrings, showers of arrows, and various weapons,
those swift and fleet horses carrying the chariot of Bhāradvāja’s son were intent on conquering the enemy, having mastered their breath and overcome all pain.
07,008.019a Those [warriors], yoked to the golden chariot and concentrated by that hero among men,
07,008.019c— how was it, O dear one, that they did not overcome the army of the Pāṇḍavas?
07,008.019d Seeing that golden chariot, the enemies indeed fled.
As he was manifesting divine weapons, his enemies gathered from all sides; what did the heroic Bhāradvāja do, that roaring warrior in battle, as he stood upon his supreme chariot adorned with gold?
He upon whose knowledge all the archers of the world depend—
that truthful and powerful Droṇa, the foremost among great bowmen, who was like Śakra in heaven— what did he do in battle?
Who were the chariot-warriors that advanced against that man of fierce deeds in battle? Surely the Pāṇḍavas would flee upon seeing the one with the golden chariot,
as he displayed divine weapons and inexhaustibly decimated the army.

Or perhaps the King of Dharma, together with his younger brothers and supported by the Pāñcālya forces, surrounded Droṇa on all sides with his entire army? Surely Pārtha held back the other chariot-warriors with his straight-flying arrows.
Then the son of Pṛṣata, that doer of evil deeds, mounted Drona;
for I see no one else capable of slaying that fierce warrior,
except for the terrible Dhṛṣṭadyumna while he is protected by Kirīṭin.
Leaving behind all his troops, he rushed toward Drona alone. Then,
surrounded on all sides by those heroes— the Kekayas, the Cedis, the Karushas, the Matsyas, and other kings— that lowest of the Panchalas was hemmed in by them.
"It is my conviction that he struck down the preceptor while he was distracted by ants, like a snake, and thus engaged in a difficult task— [the preceptor] who,
having studied all four Vedas with the Purāṇas as the fifth,"

He was the foundation for the Brahmins, as the ocean is for rivers; that scorcher of foes maintained both the Kshatriya power and the spiritual authority (brahman) in this world. He was the restrainer of the arrogant and the eye for those who were sightless.
Impatient with the arrogant, yet righteous toward the righteous—
how did that aged Brahmin meet his death by the sword? Though he was intolerant, he remained patient even while being constantly tormented by me.
How could that son of Kuntī— who is unworthy of such a fate,
whose deeds all archers in the world live upon,
who is true to his promise and virtuous— have been slain by those who lust for power?
Like Śakra in heaven, that most excellent one, a great being of immense strength—
how was he slain by the sons of Pṛthā, like a timingila fish by small fish?
He was swift-handed, powerful, firm with his bow, and a crusher of enemies.
How was that bull among brahmins slain by the wicked in battle— he,
upon reaching whose territory no one desiring life could survive,
and whom two sounds never left while he lived?
The Vedic chanting of those desiring the Vedas and the twang of the bowstrings of archers [resounded].
O tiger among men, I cannot endure that Drona— undaunted, modest, and unconquered, possessing the prowess of a lion or an elephant— has been slain.
While those lords of men were looking on in battle, the son of Pṛṣata slew them. Who fought in front, protecting Droṇa from close by?
And who indeed followed behind as he proceeded upon that difficult path?

O Sañjaya, how did he— who was as invincible as Brahmā in the Brahminical way of life and like Nārāyaṇa in the Kṣatriya way of life, whose fame and strength were unassailable— become one who resembled a pillar,
with both the Brahmins and the Kṣatriyas remaining under his control?

"For we consider all the Kurus in battle— along with their horses, chariots, and elephants— to have been slain by the ascetic power of Yudhiṣṭhira. Who protected the right wheel and who protected the left wheel of that high-souled one?"
Who were those who stood before the hero as he fought in the encounter?
And who there, having cast off their bodies, advanced against death? Which heroes displayed supreme fortitude in the battle against Droṇa?
I hope that the dull-witted Kṣatriyas did not abandon him in battle out of fear;
I hope that he was not slain by his enemies alone while his protectors were away from the empty field. Out of valor, he would never show his back to the enemy in battle out of terror.
Having encountered even the greatest calamity, how was he slain by his enemies—
he, Drona, who was capable of conquering the gods along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas? How was he slain by his enemies?
"O Sañjaya, this is what a noble man must do in times of dire calamity:
he should exert his prowess to the best of his ability, for that is established as his duty.
I trust that base men did not surrender him to the sons of Pṛthā out of fear in battle?"
"Has he not been slain by others, having been abandoned by those protectors?
For I see Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O dear one, as if slaughtering a Brahmin while being restrained in battle by the son of Droṇa, who possesses immeasurable splendor."

"My mind is bewildered, dear father; let this story be stopped for a moment. O Sūta, I shall not be able to speak for a single instant, but once I have regained my composure, Sañjaya, I will question you further."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus questioned the son of the Sūta,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, severely afflicted by heartache and despairing of his sons' victory, fell to the ground.
The attendants sprinkled him, who had fallen unconscious,
with exceedingly cold water while fanning him with fragrant incense.
And perceiving that he had fallen, the women of Bharata’s household gathered from all sides.
They surrounded the great king and touched him with their hands;
then, having slowly raised the king from the surface of the earth,
those beautiful women, their throats choked with tears, led him to his seat.
Having reached his seat, the king, overwhelmed by a swoon,
remained motionless while being fanned on all sides. Then,
gradually regaining consciousness, the lord of the earth began to tremble.
Again, he questioned the charioteer Gāvalgaṇi for the truth of what had happened:
"When Ajātaśatru arrived like the rising sun dispelling darkness with its light, who indeed held him back from Droṇa?"
Like a rutting elephant, furious and swift,
with a mind fixed on his goal, blazing and slaying rival elephants— just as such a beast is invincible by other leaders of the herd when united with a female in heat.
That hero, the best of men, surpasses all other warriors in battle— he who,
mighty-armed, resolute, and true to his promise, could alone consume the entire army of Duryodhana with his terrible gaze.
Who were the heroes that surrounded Cakṣuḥhaṇa, who was intent on victory, protected by the best of archers, self-controlled, and highly esteemed in the world;
who surrounded that invincible king, the foremost of archers, who never wavered?
Then my men, O tiger among men, approached the son of Kuntī there;
having rushed forward with great speed, he who indeed attacked Droṇa was that one of mighty strength who performs great deeds against his enemies.
With a massive body and great energy, equal in strength to ten thousand elephants—
what heroes could hold back that Bhīmasena as he advanced,
when his chariot, resembling a rain-cloud and possessed of supreme valor, came charging forward?
Like Parjanya discharging a tumultuous thunderbolt,
he who bore the foremost of monkeys upon his banner rained down showers of arrows like Maghavan raining during the monsoon; he filled the sky with a dense mass of shafts.
Resounding in all directions with the noise of his palms and the rims of his wheels,
that terrible cloud of a chariot-army— with the bow as its lightning-flash,
the clatter of the chariot-rims as its thunder, and the sound of arrows as its deep rumbling— appeared.
With clouds conquered by his wrath, swift as the movement of the mind,
that tumultuous torrent of arrows pierced the vital organs; with blood for its water,
it then flooded the entire earth and strewn it with men.
Resounding with the clashing of maces, fierce, and exerting itself by Duryodhana,
that battle— thick with the lightning-flashes of maces and swords and terrifying to the enemies—
was drenched in blood by Vijaya with stone-sharpened arrows fletched with vulture feathers.
O wise ones, what was the state of your minds then when he arrived, wielding the Gāṇḍīva? How did you feel upon seeing Pārtha?
Did his strength not utterly destroy yours with the roar of the Gāṇḍīva?
When Arjuna approached you most fiercely, creating that terrible spectacle,
did Dhananjaya not drive you away from Droṇa with his arrows—
just as the mighty wind drives the clouds away from the sun, or as it scatters the dust?
Like a wind scattering the clouds, the wind from the forest of arrows blew forward;
for what man is able to conquer Pārtha in battle, even by looking at him?
For what man is worthy to withstand the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow in combat?
Upon hearing which, all the people at the head of the army were shattered;
at which the armies trembled and fear touched the heroes— who among them did not abandon Droṇa there, and who were the cowards that fled in fear?
Who there, having cast off their bodies, will go against Death himself—
Dhanañjaya, the conqueror of non-human beings even in battles? And my men here will not be able to withstand the impetuosity of him who possesses white horses.
And the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow, like the sound of clouds in the rainy season—
he whose charioteer is Viṣvaksena and whose warrior is Dhanañjaya—
that chariot is, I believe, impossible to conquer even by the gods and asuras combined.
The Pāṇḍava is delicate, young, heroic, and handsome;
he is intelligent, skillful, wise, and possesses true prowess in battle.
Uttering a great roar, he causes all the Kauravas to tremble.
When the wise Nakula arrived, who were the heroes that surrounded him—
that hero, the best of chariot-warriors, ever intoxicated with pride in battles,
Nakula, the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas? Who were the warriors that hemmed him in?
When Sahadeva advanced like an enraged venomous serpent— Sahadeva, who comes charging forward, the destroyer of enemy armies,
performing slaughter among his foes, a victor difficult to defeat in battle— [the king spoke].
He whose arrows are never in vain, whose shafts are perfected, who is invincible by enemies in battle— [Arjuna],
who observes the noble vow, whose arrows are unfailing, who is modest and unconquered,
raising a tumultuous roar and causing terror in the fray.
Which heroes surrounded him as he advanced toward Droṇa—
he who, having crushed the vast army of the Sauvīra king, seized his queen, the daughter of the Bhojas, who was desirable and beautiful in every limb?
Truth, fortitude, heroism, and absolute celibacy—
all these qualities reside eternally in this bull among men, Yuyudhāna,
who is powerful, true to his word, undepressed, and unconquered.
Equal to Vāsudeva in battle, second only to Vāsudeva,
devoted to serving Dhanañjaya, a hero in the duties of a preceptor,
and preeminent in the science of archery through the instruction of Dhanañjaya.
Who could have restrained from Droṇa that hero equal to Pārtha in weapons—
the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, a hero among all archers—
who was equal to Rāma in weapons, fame, and prowess?
Truth, fortitude, self-restraint, heroism, and unsurpassed celibacy—
all these qualities reside in the Sātvata just as the three worlds reside in Keśava;
for they are eternally present in that hero of true prowess.
Having encountered that great archer, who was endowed with such qualities and difficult even for the gods to resist, which heroes stood to oppose him—
that foremost hero among the Pāñcālas, beloved of his noble lineage?
He who is always engaged in the highest deeds and possesses supreme energy in battle, who is devoted to the welfare of Dhanañjaya and intent on my ruin,
and who is like Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, Āditya, Mahendra, and Varuṇa— [him I have slain].

Which heroes held back Drona as he advanced in battle, renowned as a great car-warrior (*mahāratha*), exerting himself in the fray and casting away his life in the tumult? He who, having departed alone from the Chedis, sought refuge with the Pandavas— [who held him back]?
Who held back Dhṛṣṭaketu as he advanced from Droṇa— he,
the heroic Ketumān, who slew the prince Sudarśana? Who at the western mountain pass restrained him from Droṇa?
That tiger among men who was previously a woman— he alone knows virtues and faults; he knows Śikhaṇḍin, the son of Yajñasena, whose mind does not falter in battle,
and who was the cause of the high-souled Devavrata’s death in combat.
Which heroes surrounded him as he advanced toward Droṇa—
he in whom all virtues surpassed those of Dhanañjaya,
and in whom weapons, truth, and celibacy were ever present?
Equal to Vāsudeva in heroism, equal to Dhanañjaya in strength,
like the sun in splendor, and equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect—
[they beheld] the high-souled Abhimanyu, who was like Death with its mouth wide open.
Which heroes surrounded him as he advanced toward Droṇa?
When the youthful son of Subhadrā, who resembles Aruṇa and slays the enemies' heroes,
rushed against Droṇa, what was the state of your minds then?

Those sons of Draupadī, tigers among men, rushed toward Droṇa in battle like rivers to the ocean— who were the heroes that held them back? Those boys who, for twelve years, had abandoned all play— [who could withstand them]?
07,009.048c For the sake of weapons, they dwelt with Bhīṣma, observing the highest vow.
07,009.049a Kṣatrañjaya, Kṣatradeva, and the proud Kṣatradharman—
those heroic sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna— who kept them away from Droṇa?
Whom did the Vṛṣṇis behold in battle as superior even to a hundred— the great archer Cekitāna? Who held him back from Droṇa—
he who, the son of Vṛddhakṣema, seized the maiden of the Kaliṅgas in combat?
Who held back Anādhṛṣṭi— the undepressed-souled one— from Droṇa?
And the five Kaikeya brothers, righteous and of true prowess,
who were the color of indragopaka insects, with red armor, weapons, and banners?
Who were the heroes that held back those heroic sons of their maternal aunt, the Pāṇḍavas, who had arrived seeking victory and desiring to slay Droṇa—
those whom the kings could not defeat even when fighting them at Vāraṇāvata?
For six months, they were intent on attacking and seeking to slay the Lord of Warriors—
the best among archers, a hero true to his word and possessed of great strength— who tiger among men, desiring to fight, was with Drona; who then held him back?
He who, with a broad-headed arrow, struck down from his chariot the son of the King of Kāśī— a great car-warrior who was lusting after women in battle—
that great archer Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the preserver of the counsel of the Pārthas.

Which heroes restrained him as he advanced toward Droṇa— him who was intent on Duryodhana’s ruin and created for the sake of slaying Droṇa, who was consuming the warriors in battle and tearing them apart on all sides?
Who held back Śikhaṇḍin— that best of weapon-knowers, who grew up like a child in the lap of Drupada and was himself a god among warriors— from Droṇa,
he who enveloped this entire earth like a piece of leather?
That great chariot-warrior, the slayer of foremost enemies,
performed ten horse-sacrifices with abundant food, drink, and liberal sacrificial fees; he also performed unobstructed *sarvamedha* sacrifices while protecting his subjects like his own children.
Drinking his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), they drank as it were the stream of the Gaṅgā; indeed,
the sacrificial fee bestowed by him was so vast that it even obstructed the flow of the Gaṅgā’s waters, reaching as far as every single grain of sand in her current.
The heroic son of Uśīnara gave away as many cows at that sacrifice;
"Neither those of old nor any others among men have ever done this," the gods cried out when that difficult task was accomplished.
We do not see anyone in the three worlds— among things stationary or moving—
who has been born, will be born, or even exists at present,
as a second bearer of the yoke like Śibi, the son of Uśīnara.
Who held back Śaibya, the grandson of that man whose path no inhabitants of the human world can follow,
as he advanced toward Droṇa like Death himself with gaping jaws?
Which heroes held back the chariot-force of Virāṭa, the Matsya king and slayer of enemies, as he sought to seize Droṇa in battle—
he who was born immediately from Vṛkodara and possesses great strength and prowess?
Who held back from Droṇa that mighty-armed Ghaṭotkaca— the illusory and terrible Rākṣasa from whom I have great fear, who desired victory for the Pārthas, and who was a thorn in the side of my sons?

O Sañjaya, that very Kṛṣṇa, whom the twice-born call Vāsudeva— the father of his father— is now firmly resolved for the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son when disaster has befallen Dhanañjaya; he is now preparing for battle.
I find no steadfast opponent of great prowess;
neither Saṃkarṣaṇa nor Gada, nor both Pradyumna and Viḍūraka,
nor Āśāvaha and Sāmba— these Vṛṣṇi heroes are all skilled strikers.
These men have indeed been appointed there for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, desiring victory;
wherever Keśava is, there they are, and wherever they are, there is Keśava. Arjuna is the self of Keśava, and Kṛṣṇa is the self of the Diademed One (Kirīṭin).
Victory is ever with Arjuna, and eternal glory is with Kṛṣṇa;
yet, because of his preeminence, the immeasurable virtues of Keśava are even more abundant.
But out of delusion, not everyone recognizes Mādhava, who is the self-controlled Kṛṣṇa.
Deluded by the snare of the gods and placed before the noose of death,
he did not recognize Kṛṣṇa of the Daśārhas nor Arjuna, the best among victors—
both of whom are the high-souled primordial deities, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

For even with their minds alone, these two powerful heroes could have destroyed this army had they so desired; yet, because of their human nature, they did not wish to do so. It was like the overturning of an age, or the delusion of all living beings.
This fall of Bhīṣma and Droṇa appears to me thus:
that the two heroes, the elders of the world, who were knowers of counsel and upholders of secret plans,
having been slain in battle, will cause delusion among men.
That prosperity which I formerly envied upon seeing it in Yudhiṣṭhira,
I now acknowledge as my own, since Bhīṣma and Droṇa have been slain;
or rather, this destruction of the Kurus has come about on my account.

O Sūta, for when the ripened [enemies] are slain, even blades of grass act like thunderbolts. O Sañjaya, what is there that remains unconquered in battle for these and many others who have renounced their lives in the fray for their sake?
How could there be defeat for those who have that tiger among men as their refuge— the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
who seeks the welfare of the sons of Pṛthā?
He is the eternal Lord of the worlds, the supreme teacher of the world.
Nārāyaṇa is the lord in battle, divine and possessing a divine self,
the sovereign whose divine deeds the wise proclaim;
those I shall now glorify with devotion for the sake of my own steadfastness.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Listen, Sañjaya, to the divine deeds of Vāsudeva,
which Govinda has performed— deeds such as no other man anywhere has ever done."
While being reared in the family of cowherds, that high-souled one, even as a mere child,
killed Śakaṭa and Pūtanā and broke the twin Arjuna trees; thus,
O Sañjaya, his strength of arms was made famous throughout the three worlds.
He who slew the king of horses dwelling in the forests of the Yamunā— a horse equal in strength to Uccaiḥśravas and like the wind in speed—
was a Dānava of terrible deeds who had arisen like Death itself for the cattle.
In his youth, he struck down Pralamba with his two arms;
the lotus-eyed one also slew Naraka, Jambha, the great asura Pīṭha, and Muru, who resembled a mountain.
Having slain Pūtanā and Śakuni, as well as the horse Keśin, and having likewise killed Ṛṣabha, Dhenuka, and the mighty Ariṣṭa,
the long-armed one slew Vṛka and held up Mount Govardhana.
Having slain both Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika in the midst of the arena,
the highly resplendent Kaṃsa— who was protected by Jarāsaṃdha—
was likewise struck down in battle along with his followers by Kṛṣṇa through his prowess alone.
Sunāman by name was a valiant hero, the commander of a complete akṣauhiṇī;
he was the powerful brother of Kaṃsa, standing in the midst of the Bhoja king's host. [He was slain] by Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemies, accompanied by Baladeva.
The swift king of the Śūrasenas was consumed in battle along with his army.
Likewise, the brahmin seer named Durvāsas, who was exceedingly prone to anger,
was propitiated by him together with his wife, and he granted him boons.
Likewise, at the svayaṃvara, the heroic lotus-eyed one, having conquered the lords of the earth, carried off the daughter of the king of Gāndhāra;
those kings who could not endure him were like horses of noble breed.
On the wedding chariot, the horses had been wounded by the goad;
Janārdana, by means of a superior stratagem, caused the mighty-armed Jarāsaṃdha—
the lord of a separate akṣauhiṇī— to be slain.

Then the powerful one slew the valiant King of Cedi, the commander of the royal army, who was disputing over the guest-offering like an animal; he also destroyed Saubha, the well-established city of the Daityas, protected by Śālva and difficult to assail.
Mādhava, having displayed his prowess upon the shore of the ocean, struck them down;
he conquered the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Māgadhas, Kāśis, Kosalas,
Vatsas, Gargas, Karūṣas, and Puṇḍras in battle.
The Āvantyas, the Dākṣiṇātyas, the Pārvatīyas, and the Daśerakas;
the Kāśmīrakas, the Aurasakas, and the Piśācas along with the Samandarās;
the Kāmbojas, the Vāṭadhānas, the Colas, and the Pāṇḍyas, O Sañjaya.

The lotus-eyed one conquered the Trigartas, the Mālavas, and the very difficult-to-vanquish Daradas; he also defeated the various tribes who had arrived from all directions, including the Aśvaka-Śakas and the Yavanas along with their followers.
In ancient times, having entered the abode of the sea-monsters, which was crowded with aquatic creatures, he conquered Varuṇa in battle while he was within the depths of the waters;
and having slain Pañcajana, who dwelt in the bottom of the netherworld, in combat.
Hṛṣīkeśa obtained the divine conch Pāñcajanya after satisfying the Fire-god at Khāṇḍava together with Pārtha;
and the one of great strength received the invincible discus, the fiery weapon.
Having mounted Vainateya and terrified Amarāvatī,
the hero brought the Pārijāta tree from the palace of Mahendra.
And Śakra endured that, knowing his prowess.
Having learned of Govardhana’s lifting, he indeed engaged in battle;
nor have we heard of any king here who was not conquered by Kṛṣṇa.
And as for that great marvel which occurred in my assembly hall, O Saṃjaya—
What other person here is worthy of performing such deeds as the lotus-eyed Lord has done?
And that I, having approached with devotion, beheld Kṛṣṇa the Lord—
all that is well known to me and has come before me as if it were directly perceived.
"O Sañjaya, it is impossible to reach the end of the deeds of Hṛṣīkeśa, whether they be endowed with valor or endowed with wisdom.
Likewise, there are Gada, Sāmba, Pradyumna, and Vidūratha."
Āgāvaha, Aniruddha, Cārudeṣṇa, Sāraṇa, Ulmuka, Niśaṭha, Jhallī, the heroic Babhru,
Pṛthu, Vipṛthu, Samīka, and Arimejaya.
These Vṛṣṇi heroes are indeed powerful strikers; if they,
standing firm in battle, were somehow summoned by the high-souled Vṛṣṇi hero Keśava, they would surely join the Pāṇḍava army.
Therefore, it is my opinion that everything will become uncertain;
for where Janārdana is, there is the heroic Rāma, who possesses the strength of ten thousand elephants, who resembles the peak of Mount Kailāsa, and who wears a forest garland and wields the plow.
He who is truly one has become twofold and is seen by men on earth; he whom the twice-born call Vāsudeva, the father of all,
and who is recited in the Vedas as even prior to the ancestors.
Or rather, O Sañjaya, he will indeed fight for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas. When Keśava, dear one, arms himself for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas,
then there shall be no one at all to stand against him in the opposing ranks.
If all the Kurus were to defeat all the Pāṇḍavas,
Vārṣṇeya would surely take up his supreme weapon for their sake;
then that tiger among men, having slain all those kings in battle, [would prevail].
The mighty-armed one shall give the earth to Kuntī and the Kauravas;
for what chariot could stand as an adversary in battle against that chariot whose driver is Hṛṣīkeśa and whose warrior is Dhanañjaya?
"By no means whatsoever is victory seen for the Kurus.
Therefore, tell me everything about how the battle proceeded. Arjuna is the very self of Keśava, and Kṛṣṇa is also the self of the Diademed One (Arjuna)."

Victory is ever with Arjuna, and eternal fame is with Kṛṣṇa; indeed, in all the worlds, Bībhatsu is unconquered. For it is preeminently and in great measure that immeasurable virtues reside in Keśava.
Out of delusion, O Kṛṣṇa, Duryodhana does not recognize Mādhava here;
bewildered by the power of fate and standing at the very throat of the noose of death,
he knows neither Kṛṣṇa of the Daśārhas nor Arjuna the Pāṇḍava.
The two high-souled ancient gods, Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
who are one soul appearing as two, are seen on earth by men;
for those two illustrious ones are difficult even to withstand in thought, let alone this army.
Though they desired to destroy them here, they did not wish to do so because of their human nature;
it was like the overturning of a yuga, like the delusion of the worlds,
and like the slaying of Bhīṣma and the high-souled Droṇa, O dear one.
For indeed, no one is ever liberated from death by celibacy, nor by the study of the Vedas, nor by ritual acts, nor by weapons.
[Yet here are] two heroes honored by the world, skilled in weaponry and fierce in battle.
"Having heard that Bhīṣma and Droṇa have been slain, O Sañjaya, why indeed do I still live? That prosperity which we formerly envied in Yudhiṣṭhira,
today we acknowledge it as his due to the slaughter of Bhīṣma and Droṇa."
And thus, for my sake, this destruction of the Kurus has been brought about;
for when those who are ripe for death are to be slain, O Sūta, even blades of grass act like thunderbolts.
Yudhiṣṭhira has attained a sovereignty in this world that is without rival.
Through whose wrath those great archers Bhīṣma and Droṇa have been struck down, dharma has returned to its natural state for human beings, and unrighteousness no longer prevails;
cruel Time now moves forward for the destruction of all.
"For objects intended in one way by wise men, dear one, turn out quite otherwise through fate; this is my conviction. Therefore, when an unavoidable matter has arrived in its most difficult form,"
"Explain to me, as it truly is, that which is unfathomable and difficult to conceive.
Saṃjaya said:
"Listen attentively and remain steadfast, O Bhārata, as I speak to you."
"Come now, I shall describe to you everything as one who has seen it with his own eyes—
how that Drona, the great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, having attained the command of the army, was struck down and slain by the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas."
In the midst of the entire army, he spoke these words to your son:
