"O King, since today you have honored me with the command of the army immediately after that bull among the Kauravas, the son of the River (Bhīṣma)."
"May you receive a fruit corresponding to that action;
O King, obtain a result befitting that deed.
What desire of yours shall I fulfill today? Choose whatever you wish."
Then Duryodhana, having deliberated with Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and the others,
spoke to that invincible preceptor, the best among victors:
"If you grant me a boon, let Yudhiṣṭhira be captured alive in battle."
"O twice-born one, seize that best of chariot-warriors and bring him here to my presence;
for I truly desire to capture the high-souled and righteous Yudhiṣṭhira alive, even as his brothers look on."
"By this deed, I, along with my friends and kinsmen, shall find joy.
Then the preceptor of the Kurus, having heard these words of your son,
spoke these words, gladdening the entire army.
"Blessed is King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, for whose capture you desire this boon today, O invincible one, and not his death.
And for what reason, O tiger among men, do you not wish for his slaughter?"
O Duryodhana, you certainly do not expect this action from me;
or rather, perhaps your hater does not exist,
since you wish him to remain alive and seek to protect your own lineage.

Or else, O best of the Bharatas, having conquered the Pāṇḍavas in battle and returned their share of the kingdom, you wish to establish brotherly affection. Blessed is King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, and well-born is this wise man.

"His state of being 'Ajātaśatru' (one whose enemy is unborn) is true, since you feel such affection for him. O Bhārata, when your son had been addressed thus by Droṇa, his inner disposition— which always manifests within him— suddenly emerged.
"Even those equal to Bṛhaspati cannot conceal their true intentions.
Therefore, O King, your son spoke these words with great joy:
'O Teacher, there can be no victory for me in battle without the slaughter of Kuntī’s son.'"
If Yudhiṣṭhira were killed, Pārtha would surely slay all of us;
moreover, he cannot be slain in battle even by all the immortals.
Yet, if all the Pāṇḍavas, along with their sons, were to be killed in the fray—
Then, having brought the entire circle of kings under his absolute control and having conquered this prosperous earth with its oceans and forests,
Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, will bestow it upon Kṛṣṇā or Kuntī.
Whatever portion remains of them would leave nothing remaining for us. But when he who is true to his promise has been brought back and defeated again at dice—
if he is brought back alive despite many stratagems having been employed— then [the situation changes].
"The sons of Kuntī, devoted to him, will once again go to the forest;
therefore, this victory of mine will clearly endure for a long time. For this reason, I do not desire the death of Dharmarāja at any time."
Knowing his crooked intention, the wise Droṇa, who understood the true nature of things, reflected and granted him that boon with a hidden condition.
Droṇa said:
O hero, if Arjuna does not protect Yudhiṣṭhira in battle,
consider the eldest Pāṇḍava already brought under your control;
for Pārtha cannot be overcome in combat even by the gods and asuras led by Indra.
"While Pārtha stands there, Dharmarāja cannot be opposed by me in battle;
therefore, my dear son, I cannot endure this. Without doubt, he is my disciple and was taught by me first in the practice of weapons."
He is young, endowed with fame, and has reached a singular path;
he has acquired many weapons from Indra and Rudra.
O King, because of that, he is provoked by you, and for that reason I am not provoked.
And let him be removed from the battle by whatever means possible;
once Pārtha has been withdrawn from there, Dharmarāja will be conquered by you.
O bull among men, if you consider his capture to be victory, [then act accordingly].
By this means, he will certainly be captured. Having seized the king, who is devoted to truth and righteousness, I shall bring him under your control today, O King; of this there is no doubt.
If he should stand before me in battle for even a moment—
now that Dhananjaya, that tiger among men, the son of Kuntī, has been led away—
then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pṛthā, would not remain in the presence of Phalguna.
"He could not have been captured in battle even by the gods and asuras led by Indra.
Sañjaya said:
"When this had been spoken at that time in that battle, which was like the war between the gods and the asuras..."
When Droṇa had promised the capture of the king with certain conditions attached,
your very foolish sons considered him already captured;
for your son knew that Droṇa felt partiality toward the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, for the sake of ensuring the firmness of his vow, that counsel was expanded.
Subsequently, O noble one, Duryodhana also ordered the capture of the Pāṇḍava throughout all the military camps,
each in its respective location.
"O subduer of enemies, this was proclaimed throughout all the military encampments.
Sañjaya said:
"Then those soldiers, having heard of that capture of Yudhiṣṭhira..."
They let out lion-like roars along with the sounds of arrows and conchs.
O Bhārata, all that had occurred, as well as what the son of Bharadvāja intended to do, was quickly learned by the King of Dharma through his trusted spies.
Then, having summoned all his brothers and his troops from every side,
Dharmarāja spoke these words to Dhanañjaya:
"O tiger among men, you have heard what Droṇa intends to do today."
Let such a policy be adopted so that this [plan] may not come true. For a loophole was indeed promised by Droṇa, O crusher of foes;
and that loophole has been placed by him upon you, whose arrows are never in vain.
"Therefore, O mighty-armed one, fight today at my side,
so that Duryodhana may not obtain this desire from Droṇa.
Arjuna said:
"Just as it is not my wish that my preceptor be slain by me under any circumstances,
O King, so too is your abandonment not what I intend to do.
Even so, O Pāṇḍava, I would rather give up my life in battle."

"I would never disregard my teacher, nor would I ever abandon you in any way. O King, that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra whom he desires to capture in battle shall by no means attain his wish in this world of the living."
The sky with its stars might fall, and the earth might shatter into pieces;
yet, as long as I am alive, Drona could never certainly capture you,
even if the wielder of the thunderbolt himself were to provide him assistance in battle.
"O Indra among kings, even if joined by the gods or the Daityas, he shall not overcome you in battle while I live; therefore, you need have no fear of Drona,
the best among wielders of weapons and the foremost of all those who bear arms."
Furthermore, O Indra among kings, I shall state my constant vow:
I do not recall ever speaking an untruth, nor do I recall ever suffering defeat;
nor do I recall having promised anything and failed to fulfill it.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O great king, conchs, kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas, and ānakas were sounded together in the camp of the Pāṇḍavas.
A lion’s roar arose from the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
and the sound of their bowstrings and palms was most terrifying, reaching the very heavens.
Hearing that blare of the conch of the high-souled Pāṇḍava, [the enemy trembled].
Even among your own ranks, musical instruments were struck;
then, O Bhārata, the arrayed forces of yours and theirs slowly approached one another, eager to fight in the encounter.
Then there commenced a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end,
between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus, and also between Droṇa and the Pañcāla prince,
as they strove with great effort to shatter Droṇa’s army.
O King, the Sṛñjayas were unable [to prevail], for that army was protected by Droṇa;
likewise, the noble car-warriors and strikers of your son's side were unable to overcome the Pāṇḍava host, which was being protected by Kirīṭin.
Those two armies remained motionless, guarding one another,
like two flowering forest ranges fast asleep at night.
Then, O King, the one with the golden chariot shone like the sun.
Rushing forth with his protective armor, he roamed through the midst of the enemy ranks. Seeing him alone on his chariot, swift in action in battle,
the Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas, out of terror, perceived him as if he were many.
The terrible arrows released by him coursed in every direction,
O great king, terrifying the army of the son of Pāṇḍu,
like the sun reaching midday, enveloped by hundreds of rays.
Just as the sun was seen, so too was Droṇa seen;
and no one among the sons of Pāṇḍu, O noble one,
was able to even look at him when he was enraged in battle, just as the Dānavas cannot look upon Mahendra.
Then the powerful son of Bharadvāja, having confounded the army,
swiftly shattered Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s forces with sharpened arrows;
obstructing all directions and covering the sky with his straight-flying shafts.
Wherever the son of Pṛṣata went, there he crushed the Pandava host.
Sañjaya said:
Then, he created a great and tumultuous uproar within the Pandava army.
Droṇa moved among the Pāṇḍavas like a fire consuming dry undergrowth;
seeing him with his golden chariot in battle, consuming the armies like Agni himself risen in person, the Sṛñjayas trembled.
As he draws his bow continuously,
that swift-acting warrior’s twang of the bowstring is heard excessively, like the crash of a thunderbolt;
[it strikes] chariot-warriors, riders, elephants, horses, and infantry alike.
The fierce arrows released by the wielder of the hand (the mace) crushed [the enemy],
while Parjanya, roaring with the wind at the end of the summer heat,
rained down as if a shower of stones, bringing fear to his foes.
O King, that lord then moved about, agitating the army and increasing the superhuman terror of his enemies;
his gold-adorned bow appeared like lightning among the clouds.
As that cloud-like chariot whirled about, that hero Satyavān was seen again and again— wise, ever-devoted to dharma, yet most formidable,
like Yama at the end of a yuga as he causes the river of destruction to overflow.
[He saw] that river arising from the force of indignation, teeming with throngs of flesh-eating creatures, filled on all sides by floods of troops, sweeping away the trees that were the heroes,
with blood for its water, chariots for its eddies, and elephants and horses for its banks.
It was filled with armor and helmets as its rafts, thick with the mud of flesh,
choked with hair for its moss, and reddened by the mire of blood and flesh; it had fat,
marrow, and bones for its sands, and excellent turbans for its froth.
Filled with the waters of battle, teeming with spears for its fish,
born of men, elephants, and horses, flowing with the current of the force of arrows,
having bodies for its wooden crossroads and arms for its serpents;

With heads for its bedrock, inhabited by the fish of swords, possessing the deep pools of chariots and elephants, with various ornaments for its lotuses, having hundreds of great chariots for its whirlpools, and garlanded with waves of earthly dust— [the river of battle].
In battle, it was exceedingly difficult for cowards to cross, yet easily traversed by those of great heroism;
crowded with hundreds of bodies, frequented by vultures and herons,
it led thousands of great chariot-warriors to the abode of Yama.
It was crowded with heroes like fierce serpents and frequented by those who trade in living beings;
its great swans were shattered umbrellas, it teemed with birds that were crowns,
its tortoises were discuses, its crocodiles were maces, and it was filled with small fish that were arrows.
Droṇa caused a river to flow, infested by terrible throngs of vultures and jackals, with hair for its moss and grassy weeds;
it was a river of living beings slain in battle by the arrows of the mighty Droṇa.
O best of kings, it carried [the dead] by the hundreds to the world of the ancestors; O King,
it bore that river to the world of the ancestors,
crowded with hundreds of bodies, where hair was the moss and water-grass.
O King, he caused a river to flow that increased the fear of the timid.
O Bhārata, as Drona was thus conquering those various divisions,
the troops led by Yudhiṣṭhira rushed against him from all sides.

As those heroes were charging forward, your warriors, firm with their bows, received them from all sides; that was hair-raising. Śatamāya, however, rushed against Sahadeva, while Śakuni rushed against Sahadeva.

Saniyan pierced the chariot bearing the banner with sharp arrows. The son of Mādrī, not excessively enraged, cut down his uncle’s standard, bow, charioteer, and horses with his shafts, and then pierced him with sixty more.
Having pierced him with a shower of arrows, he held Śakuni at bay.
Then Saubala, seizing a mace, leaped down from his excellent chariot;
with that mace, O King, he struck down the other's charioteer from the vehicle.
Then, O King, those two mighty heroes, deprived of their chariots and with maces in hand,
sported in battle like two peaked mountains.
Drona, having pierced the king of the Panchalas with ten swift arrows, [continued the fight].
O Great King, O Bull among Men, there the sky was illuminated by the showers of arrows from those two, like the sky at night with fireflies;
and he, having practiced extensively, pierced him with more than a hundred shafts.
Having pierced Vivimśati with twenty sharpened arrows, the heroic Bhīmasena could not make him tremble; that was like a marvel.
But Vivimśati, by force, deprived him of his horses, standard, and bow.
O great king, he made it terrifying, and then the troops honored him;
all the armies, being greatly delighted, worshipped that wheel.
That hero could not endure the victory of his enemy in battle.

Then, with his mace, he struck down all of his well-trained horses. O King, from that chariot whose horses had been slain, the mighty warrior took up a shield and rushed toward Bhīmasena, like one rutting elephant charging another.
But the heroic Śalya, laughing as if fondling and provoking him, pierced Nakula— his own dear sister’s son— with arrows;
he struck down his horses, his parasol, his standard, his charioteer, and his bow.

Having struck him down in battle, the powerful Nakula blew his conch; and he [the opponent], being diligent in the encounter, cut [Nakula's bow] and desisted from the fight. Dhṛṣṭaketu, having severed the various kinds of arrows discharged by Kṛpa—
He pierced Kṛpa with seventy arrows and struck off his standard with three;
Kṛpa then overwhelmed him with a great shower of shafts,
and having warded him off in battle, the Brahmin fought against Dhṛṣṭaketu.
Satyaki, having pierced Kritavarman between the breasts with a steel arrow,
struck him again with seventy others as if smiling;
then the Bhoja warrior, having pierced him with seventy-seven sharpened shafts.
As a swift wind cannot shake a mountain, he could not shake the descendant of Śini; meanwhile,
the commander Suśarman quickly struck him in his vital parts,
and he in turn struck him in the region of the collarbone with a *tomara* spear.
In that battle, Virāṭa, together with the highly heroic Matsyas, held back the son of Vikartana; it was like a marvel. Therein, the prowess of the Sūta’s son was formidable.
With straight-jointed arrows, he held back the army; meanwhile,
King Drupada himself encountered Bhagadatta,
and their battle, O great king, was like a wondrous spectacle.
But Bhagadatta, that bull among men, pierced King Drupada— along with his charioteer, banner, and chariot— with straight-knotted arrows.
Thereupon, Drupada, filled with rage, [assailed] the great car-warrior Bhagadatta.
With a swift, straight-knotted arrow, he quickly struck him in the chest;
Śikhaṇḍin and the son of Somadatta, those two foremost warriors in the world and masters of weapons, engaged in a battle that struck terror into all living beings.
O King, in that battle which caused delusion for both those who heard of it and those who witnessed it,
the heroic Bhūriśravas covered the great car-warrior Yājñaseni with a vast shower of arrows.
Then, O lord of the people, Śikhaṇḍin, filled with rage, made the son of Somadatta tremble with ninety arrows, O Bhārata;
he covered him with iron shafts and cried out, "Stay! Stay!"
Clad in bear-skins, those two illustrious and high-souled warriors, leaping over the outer and inner tracks,
appeared like two winged mountains.
Yoked with flesh-eating steeds that fell upon their arrows,
the two quivers— bearing great banners, terrible in form, and fearsome—
were like two clouds of doom, threatening the worlds with their roars.
With a great roar of chariots, those two supreme car-warriors stood ready;
their banners were vast, they were equipped with quivers, and they were joined by Pishacha mounts—
those two Rakshasas of terrible deeds, the son of Hidimba and Alambusa.
Desirous of slaying one another, they waged a most wonderful battle; proud and creating hundreds of illusions, they moved about, concealed by their magic,
causing great amazement.
Cekitāna fought most terrifyingly with Anuvinda;
a battle took place between those two as they sought each other's death,
while King Yudhiṣṭhira himself fought Duryodhana.
Those two invincible sons of yours fought with one another,
like the mighty Bala and Śakra in the war between the gods and the asuras;
Lakṣmaṇa waged a fierce struggle against Kṣatradeva.
O King, just as Viṣṇu did of old in his encounter with Hiraṇyākṣa,
Paurava then rushed toward the son of Subhadrā, roaring loudly from his chariot which was properly equipped and drawn by swift horses.
Then, having approached in haste, desiring battle, the mighty Abhimanyu, the tamer of foes, engaged him in a great combat; meanwhile,
Paurava covered the son of Subhadrā with showers of arrows.
Arjuna’s son struck down his [the opponent's] banner, umbrella, and bow to the earth; meanwhile,
the son of Subhadrā, having pierced Paurava with seven swift arrows,
struck his horses and charioteer with five shafts.
Then, cheering his army and roaring repeatedly like a lion,
the son of Arjuna quickly took up an arrow capable of ending the Paurava.
Perceiving that he had fixed that terrible-looking shaft, [the enemy prepared for battle].
With two arrows, the son of Hṛdika cut through his bow along with the arrow fixed upon it.
Abandoning that severed bow, the son of Subhadrā, slayer of enemy heroes,
drew a bright sword and took up a shield.
With that sword of many blades, like one skilled with a shield, he whirled his blade while moving through the paths, displaying his own prowess; it was spun,
whirled upward again, brandished, and raised once more.
O King, no difference could be seen between the shield and the sword.
Leaping suddenly upon the shaft of Paurava’s chariot while roaring aloud,
he mounted Paurava’s chariot and seized him by the hair.
He struck down his charioteer with his foot and felled his standard with his sword;
having agitated the ocean, he cast him aside like Tārkṣya casting a serpent.
All the kings beheld him with the ends of his hair grasped.
Seeing the Paurava fallen, like a senseless bull being struck down by a lion,
having come under the power of Arjuna’s son and being dragged along like one who is helpless,
Jayadratha could not endure it.
Taking up a shield adorned with peacock feathers and great bells, and equipped with a network of hundreds of small tinkling bells, as well as a sword, he leaped from his chariot while roaring.
Then, beholding the ruler of the Sindhus, the son of Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna) released the Paurava.
He leapt swiftly from his chariot and swooped down like a hawk; then,
with his sword, the son of Kṛṣṇa cut down the spears, javelins, and scimitars hurled by his enemies, and he warded them off with his shield.
Having displayed the strength of his own arms to the troops, that powerful and great chariot-warrior then raised his massive sword and shield; once more,
he suddenly brandished both the sword and the shield.
The hero advanced toward Vṛddhakṣatra’s heir, his father’s mortal enemy, like a tiger toward an elephant. Having encountered one another, they were armed with swords as their teeth and claws.
They struck each other with joy, like a tiger and a lion;
in their collisions, their charges, and the falling of their swords and shields,
no one could perceive any opening between those two lions among men.
The downward thrust, the whizzing sound of the sword, the display of various weapons,
and the striking of both external and internal targets appeared indistinguishable from one another as they moved along the supreme path, both externally and internally.
Those two high-souled ones appeared like two mountains with wings.
Then, as the illustrious son of Subhadra was brandishing his sword,
Jayadratha struck him at the edge of his armor and wing-guard.
Stuck within the golden-winged [quiver] upon that radiant shield,
that great sword, shaken by the force of the King of Sindhu’s army, broke apart. Realizing his sword was broken, he leaped back six steps.
In the blink of an eye, he was seen once again mounted upon his own chariot.
All the kings together surrounded from every side that son of Kṛṣṇa, who had emerged from the battle and was seated upon his excellent chariot.
Then, raising both his shield and sword, the mighty heir of Arjuna, the son of Subhadrā and slayer of enemy heroes, let out a roar as he looked toward Jayadratha,
having left the King of Sindhu behind.
He scorched that army just as the sun scorches the world. Then Śalya hurled at him in battle a terrible spear made entirely of iron, adorned with gold, blazing like a flame of fire.
Leaping up, he seized him along with his sword-case and drew the blade,
just as the son of Vinatā [Garuḍa] seized the falling king of serpents for the sake of the son of Kṛṣṇa [Arjuna].
Recognizing the dexterity and the courage of that hero of immeasurable splendor, [he was amazed].
Then all the kings together let out a lion’s roar. Thereupon, Saubhadra, the slayer of enemy heroes,
by the strength of his arms, released that very [spear] of Śalya, whose surface was inlaid with lapis lazuli.
Approaching his chariot, which resembled a sloughed-off serpent,
she struck Śalya’s charioteer and felled him from the vehicle. Then Virāṭa, Drupada, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Yudhiṣṭhira [advanced].
Sātyaki, the Kekayas, Bhīma, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, the twins, and the sons of Draupadī cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
There were various sounds of arrows and abundant lion-roars.
Appearing to gladden the son of Subhadrā as he did not flee,
all those great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas surrounded him,
cheering on Saubhadra and inciting your sons to wrath.
Your sons could not endure that sign of victory belonging to the enemy;
then, O great king, they all suddenly overwhelmed him from every side with sharpened arrows, like clouds covering a mountain.
Seeking to please them and enraged by the defeat of his charioteer,
the slayer of enemies, Ārtāyani, rushed against the son of Subhadrā. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, having heard you describe so many diverse duels, I envy those who possess eyes;
for a battle such as this would not occur even between the gods and the asuras."
And I reflect, O Saṃjaya, having heard of these terrible battles;
men in the worlds will speak of it as a marvel—
the battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, which was like that between the gods and the asuras.
"For I have no satiety here in hearing of this supreme battle;
therefore, tell me of the combat between Ārtāyani and the son of Subhadrā.
Sañjaya said:
Seeing his charioteer struck down, Śalya, raising his mace made entirely of iron,
leaped from his excellent chariot,
roaring in rage like the blazing fire of time or like Death himself with staff in hand.

Seizing his great mace, Bhīma rushed forward with speed; and the son of Subhadrā also, seizing his great mace which resembled a thunderbolt, cried out, "Come! Come! though he was being strenuously restrained by Bhīma from attacking Śalya.
Having held back the son of Subhadrā, the powerful Bhīmasena approached Śalya in battle and stood firm like an immovable mountain.
Likewise, the King of Madra, seeing the mighty Bhīma, [stood his ground].
He rushed swiftly toward the enemy like a tiger toward an elephant;
then there arose the sounds of trumpets and thousands of conchs,
along with lion-roars and the great resonance of kettledrums.
As the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus, hundreds in number and of like minds, looked on, there arose the cry, "Excellent! Excellent!
For among all the kings, O Bhārata, there was none other than the lord of Madra [who could do so].
In battle, he is able to withstand the force of Bhīmasena;
likewise, in this world, who other than Vṛkodara is able to withstand the force of the mace of the high-souled lord of Madra in combat?
Bound with bands of Jāmbūnada gold, that great mace, which delighted the people,
blazed forth when wielded by Bhīma; thus,
like a great and fierce meteor flaming with fire, that mace shone resplendent at that time.
As they moved along their paths and through their circular maneuvers in due order,
Śalya’s mace shone like a great flash of lightning.
Roaring like two bulls, the two of them moved in circles.
Both Śalya and Vṛkodara, their mace-ends braced for combat,
were heroes with eyes copper-red with rage, crushers of enemy hosts,
great chariot-warriors of immense energy, and experts in the art of mace-fighting.
In their circular maneuvers and in the brandishing of their maces,
the battle between those two lions among men was indistinguishable.
The great mace of Śalya was struck down by Bhīmasena.
That extremely fierce mace, blazing with fire, was shattered into fragments;
likewise, Bhīmasena’s mace, struck by his enemy,
shone like a tree covered with fireflies at the onset of the rainy season.
O Bhārata, the mace hurled in battle by the King of Madra illuminated the sky and emitted a great deal of fire;
likewise, the mace dispatched by Bhīmasena against his enemy did the same.

Fearsome in form and possessed of great speed, that mace drove Śalya back in battle; it scorched that army like a great meteor falling from the sky. And those two excellent maces, having encountered one another—
Sighing like two daughters of the Nāgas, they emitted fire;
again, from the point of Bhīma’s mace struck by Śalya’s mace,
fire arose from the friction and set the earth ablaze.
And again, O King, Bhīmasena suddenly struck Śalya’s great mace,
which then emitted fire like two great tigers with their claws or two great elephants with their tusks.
Having encountered one another, the two of them moved about, striking each other with their maces.
Then, struck by the tips of the maces, those two great-souled ones, drenched in blood in an instant, appeared like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
The sound of the clash of the maces of those two lions among men was heard in all directions, resembling the roar of Śakra’s thunderbolt;
struck on both the left and the right with the mace by the King of Madra, [he was assailed].
Then Bhīma did not waver, like a mountain being split asunder;
likewise, though struck by the force of Bhīma’s mace,
the mighty lord of the Madras stood firm through his fortitude, like a mountain struck by thunderbolts.
Possessing great speed and with their massive weapons raised high, they charged at one another;
then, stationed on the intervening path, they moved in circular maneuvers. Then, leaping forward eight paces, they collided like two elephants.
Suddenly, they struck each other with their iron clubs;
violently wounded by one another’s momentum and by the maces,
those two heroes fell simultaneously upon the earth like two Indra-poles.
Then, O great king, seeing him agitated and sighing again and again,
the great car-warrior Kṛtavarman quickly rushed toward Śalya,
who was being oppressed by the mace.
Like a serpent writhing, overwhelmed by a swoon,
the lord of the Madras was then placed upon his chariot with his mace;
the great car-warrior Kṛtavarman quickly bore him away from the battlefield.
Like one intoxicated, the hero was dazed, yet in the blink of an eye he rose again;
Bhīma too, the mighty-armed, was seen with mace in hand.
Then, seeing the lord of Madra turned away, your sons—
O noble one, the chariots, elephants, infantry, and horses trembled;
being oppressed by the Pāṇḍavas who appeared victorious,
your men fled in fear in all directions like clouds driven by the wind.
Having utterly defeated the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O King, the illustrious great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas shone resplendently on the battlefield;
filled with joy, they uttered loud lion-roars and blew their conchs.
They sounded kettledrums along with clay drums and *ānaka* drums; then there were *maḍḍuka*, *bherī*, and great *muraja* drums,
together with *paṇava*, *ānaka*, *dundubhi*, and *jharjhari* drums.
They cry out loudly along with the sounds of conchs and various lion-like roars, O best of men. Sañjaya said:
Seeing that vast army of yours shattered,
the heroic Vṛṣasena alone held back the Pāṇḍavas in battle through his mastery of weapons.
O noble one, arrows were released by Vṛṣasena toward the ten directions.
Piercing through men, horses, chariots, and elephants,
his blazing great arrows issued forth by the thousands,
O mighty-armed one, like the rays of the sun in the summer season.
Afflicted by him, O great king, chariot-warriors and horsemen alike suddenly fell upon the earth like trees blown down by the wind;
and masses of horses, masses of chariots, and masses of elephants [were scattered] on all sides.
O King, he struck them down in battle by the hundreds and thousands.
Seeing him thus moving fearlessly through the fray,
all the kings united together surrounded him on every side.
Śatānīka, the son of Nakula, rushed against Vṛṣasena and pierced him with ten iron arrows that penetrate the vital organs.
The son of Karṇa, having cut his bow, felled his standard.

Desiring to rescue their brother, the sons of Draupadī rushed forward and quickly rendered Karna’s son invisible with volleys of arrows. Roaring, the chariot-warriors led by Drona’s son charged at them.
O great king, quickly covering the great car-warriors, the sons of Draupadī, with various kinds of arrows like clouds shrouding mountains,
the Pāṇḍavas, longing for their son, swiftly countered them.
The Pāñcālas, Kekayas, Matsyas, and Sṛñjayas, with weapons raised,
engaged in that battle which was terrible, tumultuous, and hair-raising—
your men against the sons of Pāṇḍu, like the Dānavas against the gods.
Thus, with the utmost fury, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas fought,
glaring at one another, each having committed offenses against the other.
The bodies of those men of immeasurable splendor were seen to be ablaze with rage.
Like eagles and great serpents eager to fight in the sky,
that battlefield shone with Bhīma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, the son of Pṛṣata, and Sātyaki, who appeared like suns risen at the end of time.
Just as the rising of the sun occurs at the terrible destruction of living beings,
so too did that bull among men arise for the sake of the heroes;
then there was a tumultuous battle as they struck one another down.
Just as the mighty gods [overcame] the powerful Dānavas,
so did [the enemy] strike down Yudhiṣṭhira’s army, which roared like the surging ocean,
while your own host fled with its great chariot-warriors scattered.
Seeing that army broken and severely afflicted by the enemies,
Droṇa addressed them, saying, "O heroes, enough of this fleeing!
Then both indignation and valor took possession of the son of Bharadvāja.
Having drawn [the bow] from its quiver and wiped the string of the great bow,
he, with the great bow and arrow in hand, spoke thus to the charioteer:
"O charioteer, go where this [man], shining with his white [garment], is."
With the royal parasol held over him, the King, the Lord of Dharma, stands firm;
yet this army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons is being shattered in many ways. I shall rally them by holding Yudhiṣṭhira in check in battle.
For the Pāṇḍavas, O dear one, nor all the kings of the Matsyas and Pañcālas together with the Somakas, can withstand me as I rain down [arrows] in battle; indeed,
it is by my grace that Arjuna has acquired these great weapons.
"Neither my father, nor Bhīma, nor Sātyaki dares to face me, dear son;
for by my grace, Bībhatsu has attained the status of a supreme archer,
and even Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, knows my weapons alone."
"This is not the time for one who desires victory, O dear one, to protect his life.
Sañjaya said:
"Go forth, placing heaven before you, as well as glory and victory."
Thus urged, the charioteer then drove Droṇa forward;
having consecrated the horses with the "Heart of Horses" mantra, he quickly gladdened them as they moved in a radiant, shining chariot equipped with a protective fender.
The Karūṣas, the Matsyas, the Cedis along with the Sātvatas,
and the Pāṇḍavas together with the Pañcālas, all united, surrounded him.
Then, like an enraged four-tusked elephant, he whose horses are ruddy [Droṇa] advanced in fury.
Having entered the Pāṇḍava host, he rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
Yudhi�ṣṭhira pierced him with sharp, heron-feathered arrows;
Droṇa, having cut his bow, quickly charged at him.
But the prince Cakrarakṣa, the bringer of glory to the Pāñcālas,
held back the advancing Droṇa as the shore holds back the lord of rivers.
Seeing that Droṇa, the bull among the twice-born, had been repelled by the prince, [the troops were filled with joy].
A lion’s roar indeed arose from those crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
Then, in that great battle, the prince, filled with rage, pierced Droṇa in the chest with an arrow and roared repeatedly like a lion.
Having checked the prince in battle, the mighty Droṇa—
skilled of hand and free from fatigue— assailed him with many thousands of arrows; he who was a hero, devoted to noble vows, and who had exerted himself in the mastery of weapons.
The best of the twice-born crushed the wheel-protector Kumāra,
warding him off with arrows while all the archers looked on.
Having reached the center of the army, he ranged through all directions.
Bhāradvāja, that bull among chariot-warriors, was the protector of your army;
having pierced Śikhaṇḍin with twelve arrows, Uttamaujas with twenty, Nakula with five, and Sahadeva with seven.
Having pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with twelve arrows, each of the sons of Draupadī with three,
Sātyaki with five, and the Matsya king with ten shafts,
he agitated the warriors in battle as he rushed against the foremost leaders.
Desiring to seize Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, he turned back;
then, O King, Yugandhara checked the enraged great chariot-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, like the ocean tossed by the wind.
Having pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with straight-jointed arrows,
he struck Yugaṃdhara from the seat of his chariot with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla).
Having thus conquered him, the high-minded Bhāradvāja, possessed of great splendor, [proceeded].
Then Virāṭa, Drupada, the Kekayas, Sātyaki, Śibi, Vyāghradatta the Pāñcālya, and the heroic Siṃhasena—
these and many others, desiring to protect Yudhiṣṭhira in battle— [advanced].
Scattering many arrows, they blocked his path;
then Vyāghradatta of the Pañcālas pierced Droṇa with fifty sharp shafts,
O King, and the people raised a great shout.
Then Siṃhasena, having swiftly pierced the great car-warrior Droṇa,
suddenly laughed in joy, terrifying the one of firm vows. Then,
widening his eyes and wiping his bowstring, he—
Making a great sound with his palms, Droṇa rushed toward him;
then the mighty one, attacking Siṃhasena and Vyāghradatta, severed their heads— complete with earrings— from their bodies with two broad-headed arrows.
Having crushed those great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas with volleys of arrows,
he stood in the vicinity of Yudhiṣṭhira like Death the Destroyer himself. Then, O King, a great clamor arose in Yudhiṣṭhira’s army.
When the one of firm vows was near, the warriors cried out, "The king has been captured! Seeing Drona’s prowess, the soldiers there said,
"Today King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son will surely have his purpose fulfilled."
"In this very moment, Droṇa, having seized the Pāṇḍava,
will surely come to us in the battle against the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
While your men were thus conversing, the great chariot-warrior [arrived].
The son of Kuntī advanced with speed, making the earth resound with the roar of his chariot;
saying "Do not fear," he warded off Droṇa with his arrows,
creating a river of blood with its whirlpools of chariots in that slaughter.

Having crossed that river— which was strewn with heaps of heroes' bones, which swept away the corpses of the dead, which had showers of arrows for its great foam and spears for its fish— the Pāṇḍava swiftly routed the Kurus.
Then Kirīṭin suddenly rushed toward Droṇa’s army,
shrouding it with a great net of arrows as if to bewilder it,
while swiftly discharging and incessantly aiming his shafts.
No one could perceive any opening in the illustrious son of Kuntī;
neither the cardinal directions, nor the intermediate space, nor the sky, nor even the earth could be seen, O great king, for everything seemed to have become composed of arrows.
O King, nothing at all could be seen there in that battle when a great darkness of arrows was created by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva;
for the sun had set and everything was shrouded in dust.
At that time, neither enemy nor friend, nor anything at all, could be distinguished.
Then Drona, Duryodhana, and the others withdrew their forces,
perceiving that the enemies were utterly terrified and had no desire for further combat.
Bībhatsu slowly withdrew his own divisions;
then the delighted Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas,
as well as the Pañcālas, praised Pārtha with pleasing words, just as the Ṛṣis praise the sun.

Thus, having conquered his enemies, Dhanañjaya returned to his own camp at the rear of the entire army, joyful and accompanied by Keśava. [He was adorned] with cat’s-eye gems, emeralds, gold, and silver.
In a variegated chariot adorned with the finest diamonds, coral, and crystal, the son of Pāṇḍu shone like the moon in a sky decorated with stars.
Saṃjaya said:
O lord of the people, having gone to their camp, those two armies settled down according to their respective shares, according to the rules, and according to their divisions in every respect.
Having withdrawn his troops, Droṇa, being deeply dejected, looked toward Duryodhana and spoke these words with shame:
"I said this previously: as long as Dhanañjaya is not present,"

"Yudhiṣṭhira could even be captured in battle by the gods themselves," O Yudhiṣṭhira—this which was said has now been accomplished by Pārtha against you in combat. Do not doubt my words: Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava are invincible.
But when Śvetavāhana has been drawn away by some stratagem,
then today, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, he shall come under your control in battle. Let someone else challenge him in the fray and draw him to another place.

The son of Kuntī would not turn back under any circumstances without having conquered him. In the meantime, O King, while this space is empty, I shall break through the army and seize Dharmarāja while Dhr̥ṣṭadyumna looks on.
"But if, deprived of Arjuna, he does not abandon the battle,
know that upon seeing me approaching, he will consider himself captured. Thus, O King, [you shall seize] Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, by force."
Having shaken the strength of those high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
I shall today bring them, along with their hosts, under my control; of this there is no doubt,
provided that the Pāṇḍava remains in battle for even a moment.
"Rather than remaining in battle, it is better to depart; that is superior to victory.
Having heard these words of Droṇa, O King, the lord of the Trigartas, together with his brothers, then spoke these words.

"O King, we have always been treated with contempt by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow; O bull of the Bharatas, he has committed offenses against us even though we were innocent. Remembering those various insults, we [have come here]."
Burning with the fire of anger, we could not sleep at night; now that he,
endowed with divine weapons, has come within the range of our vision,
we shall accomplish everything that we desire in our hearts.
"That which would be pleasing to you and bring glory to us—
we shall slay him by dragging him out from the field of battle.
Today let the earth be either Arjuna-less or devoid of the Atrigartas."
"We promise you the truth; this shall not be false.
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, Satyaratha, Satyadharman, Satyavarma, Satyeṣu, and likewise Satyakarman, [departed].
Together with their five brothers and ten thousand chariots,
O great king, they returned after having sworn an oath in battle;
so too did the Mālavas and Tuṇḍikeras with thirty thousand chariots.
And Suśarman, that tiger among men, the Trigarta king and lord of Prasthala, accompanied by the Mācellakas, the Lalitthas, and the Madrakas,
together with his brothers, cursed [the enemy] with ten thousand chariots.
The Maladas, the Karūśas, and the Daradas— all great chariot-warriors—
as well as the Taṅkaṇas and the Parādās, gathered there simultaneously;
furthermore, from various regions, ten thousand chariots arrived.
Having arisen for the purpose of taking a solemn oath among those distinguished men,
they then took fire and, having each offered oblations individually, they donned garments of kusha grass and variegated armor.
And those heroes, having donned their armor, anointed with ghee, clad in kusha-grass garments, and girded with bowstrings, were givers of hundreds and thousands in sacrificial fees;
they were performers of sacrifices, possessed of sons, world-winners, who had fulfilled their duties and were ready to cast off their bodies.
Desiring to yoke themselves then with glory and victory,
through the practice of celibacy, the study of the Vedas, and sacrifices accompanied by liberal gifts,
they sought to attain the celestial realms and were eager to depart swiftly by means of a righteous battle.
Having gratified the Brahmins and given them gold coins individually,
as well as cows and garments, and having addressed one another,
they were granted blessings and rites for success by the assembled leaders of the twice-born.
Joyful and exultant, having touched the pure water and kindled the fire, they approached the vow in battle; with firm resolve, they then made their pledge before that fire.
They spoke these words loudly so that all beings might hear them,
and they made a vow to slay Dhanañjaya, saying:
"Whatever worlds await those who speak falsehoods, and those who kill Brahmins— "
The worlds of those who drink intoxicants, those who take pleasure in the wives of their gurus,

those who steal the property of Brahmins, those who misappropriate the sustenance of kings, those who abandon one who has sought refuge, and likewise those who strike one who is begging; [go to those worlds].
And those worlds that belong to house-burners, and those who kill cows,
and those who act improperly, and even those who hate the Veda,
and those who out of delusion approach their wives during their courses— [may I not go to those worlds].
And for those who associate with those performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), those who take their own lives,
those who misappropriate deposits, those who destroy what they have heard [the sacred texts], those who fight out of anger, and those who follow the base; [for all these, there is no fruit].
May we reach those worlds of the nihilists, those of those who abandon the *agnihotra* fire and their ancestors, those who urinate facing the sun,
and even those of the evildoers.
If we were to turn back from the battle without having slain Dhanañjaya,
we would surely become disheartened and flee in terror, being overwhelmed by him.
But if we perform a deed in this conflict that is difficult for anyone in the world to accomplish—
"We shall undoubtedly attain the desired worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds.
Having spoken thus, O King, those heroes then turned back in battle toward Arjuna, calling out as they advanced toward the quarter favored by the ancestors.
Summoned by those tigers among men, Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities,
immediately addressed these words to Dharmarāja:
"It is my established vow that once summoned, I shall not turn back."
"O King, the Saṃśaptakas are challenging me again and again;
and here Suśarman, together with his brothers, challenges me in battle. You ought to grant me permission to slay him along with his host."
"O bull among men, I cannot endure this challenge;
I promise you truly: know that the enemies shall be slain in battle. For Arjuna, O King, will never speak anything false in combat."
"Behold the Trigartas already slain; let no dejection come upon you.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, you have heard what Droṇa intends to do."
Act in such a way that his [promise] may become a falsehood;
for Drona is powerful, heroic, skilled in weapons, and has conquered all fatigue, and he has made this vow, O great chariot-warrior: "I shall capture him."
Arjuna said:
"O scorcher of the foe, having been challenged, I shall by no means turn back;
that Trigarta, together with his brothers, is summoning me most urgently."
"O lord of men, protection has indeed been provided for you in battle by me;
yet, regardless of that, I shall go forth to slay these evil-minded ones.
O King, this Satyajit shall indeed be your protector in the fight today."
For as long as the Pāñcālya remains alive, the Preceptor will not achieve his desire; but once that tiger among men, Satyajit, has been slain in battle, O Lord,
none of us together should remain standing under any circumstances.
Saṃjaya said: Then,
having been granted leave by the king, embraced, and gazed upon with affection from many sides, Phalguna was bestowed with blessings.
Leaving him there, the powerful Pārtha then advanced against the Trigartas,
like a hungry lion seeking to satisfy its hunger upon a herd of deer;
thereafter, the army of Duryodhana was filled with the highest joy.
When Arjuna had departed, [Duryodhana] was intensely incensed at the thought of subduing the King of Dharma;
he exerted himself in the great battle with the intent of capturing the King of Dharma.
Then those two armies clashed against one another with great force.
With speed, they blew their conchs amidst a great sound filled with joy,
like the Ganges and Sarayu rivers surging with turbulent waters during the rainy season.
Sañjaya said:
Then, O King, the Saṃśaptakas,
stationed on level ground and filled with joy, drew up their army in a formation called the "Half-Moon" using only chariots.
Seeing Kirīṭin approaching, O noble one, they were overcome with delight.
Beholding Dhanañjaya, those tigers among men were exceedingly delighted; they then raised a great shout with a mighty sound.
That noise filled all the intermediate directions, the cardinal points, and the sky.
And because the world was covered over, there was no echo there.
Perceiving them to be exceedingly joyful, Dhanañjaya,
smiling slightly, spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa.

"Behold these Trigarta brothers, O mother Devakī, who are about to die today in battle; though they ought to weep, they are instead filled with joy. Or rather, this is undoubtedly a time for the Trigartas to rejoice."
"For they shall attain those unsurpassed worlds that are difficult for others to reach;
indeed, slain by me in battle, they shall attain abundant worlds.
Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, the mighty-armed Arjuna [then addressed him].
He encountered the battle-arrayed army of the Trigartas in combat. Taking up his gold-adorned conch, Devadatta,
Phalguna blew it with great force, filling all the quarters.
Terrified by that sound, the army of the Saṃśaptakas stood motionless in the battle,
as if made of solid stone;
O best of the Bharatas, that motionless host then shone resplendent.
Just as figures are depicted on a variegated cloth by skilled artisans, so too,
by that sound of the armies which then enveloped the heavens, the entire earth and the great ocean resounded with that noise.
With all those troops arrayed in battle formation upon the earth— that ocean of combat— the ears of all the soldiers were deafened by the roar;
their mounts’ eyes rolled back, and their ears and necks became rigid.
With their legs paralyzed, they discharged urine and blood.
Then the clamor ceased, and they became overjoyed;
having regained consciousness, they steadied the army.
Simultaneously, they hurled arrows feathered with heron plumes at the son of Pāṇḍu;
Arjuna, of swift prowess, cut down those fifteen thousand shafts with his own arrows even before they had reached him.
Then, with ten sharp arrows each, they pierced Arjuna once more;
thereupon Pārtha pierced them back with three arrows each.
Then, O King, each one of them in turn pierced Pārtha with five arrows.
And that valiant warrior pierced each of them in return with two shafts.
But they, becoming even more enraged, overwhelmed Arjuna along with Keśava with sharp arrows, like rain showers filling a lake.
Then thousands of arrows fell upon Arjuna like swarms of bees upon a forest of flowering trees. Then Subāhu [struck him] with thirty firm arrows made of the essence of stone.
He pierced Savyasācin deeply with arrows in his diadem;
with those straight-flying, gold-feathered shafts fixed in his crown, Kirīṭin shone like a lofty sacrificial post adorned with a golden fillet.

In that battle, the Pāṇḍava cut off the hand-guard of Subāhu with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla) and then once more overwhelmed him with showers of shafts. Then Suśarman and Suratha struck Kirīṭin with ten arrows each.
Sudharmā, Sudhanus, and Subāhu each discharged their arrows;
however, he whose banner bore the foremost of monkeys pierced all of them individually with his own shafts and cut down their golden banners with broad-headed arrows.
Having severed Sudhanvan’s bow, he indeed struck down his horses with arrows;
then he struck off from his body his head, which was protected by a helmet. Pārtha then carried away two thousand warriors among the troops.
When that hero had fallen, his followers were terrified;
those illustrious men, for the most part obstructed by slain warriors,
fled in fear toward the army of Duryodhana.

Then, filled with rage, the son of Vāsava struck that great army with unceasing nets of arrows, just as the sun destroys darkness with its rays. Then, when that force was broken, it fled in every direction.
When Savyasācin was enraged, fear entered the hearts of the Trigartas.
Being slaughtered by Pārtha with his straight-knotted arrows,
they became bewildered right where they stood, like herds of deer struck with terror.
Then the King of Trigarta, enraged, spoke to those great car-warriors:
"O heroes, enough of this fleeing! You ought not to give way to fear.
Having sworn terrible oaths in the sight of the entire army, he continued:

"Having gone to Duryodhana’s army, what indeed will you say when you have reached the leaders? How shall we not become objects of ridicule in the world because of this deed in battle? Let us all return together according to our strength."
Thus addressed, O King, those heroes cried out again and again and blew their conchs, gladdening one another. Then those hosts of Saṃśaptakas turned back once more.
And the Nārāyaṇa cowherds, having made death their means of retreat.
Saṃjaya said:
But having seen those hosts of Saṃśaptakas returning once again,
Arjuna addressed the high-souled Vāsudeva:
"Urge the horses forward, O Hṛṣīkeśa, toward the hosts of Saṃśaptakas;
it is my conviction that they will not abandon the battle as long as they live."
"Behold my terrible power of weapons, as well as the strength of my arms and bow;
today I shall strike them down in my wrath, like Rudra striking down animals.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having smiled, greeted him with auspicious words.
To Bibhatsu who was speaking thus, the invincible Keśava led him into the enemy host wherever Arjuna desired. Then that chariot shone exceedingly as it was being driven through the battle.
Like a celestial chariot being carried through the sky by white horses,
he then performed circular maneuvers, advancing and retreating,
just like the chariot of Śakra in the ancient battle between the gods and the asuras, O King.
Then the Nārāyaṇas, enraged and with various weapons in their hands,
surrounded Dhanañjaya, covering him with volleys of arrows. O bull of the Bharatas, in a mere moment they made him invisible.
In the battle against Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī who was accompanied by Kṛṣṇa,
the enraged Phalguna, his prowess redoubled in the conflict,
wiped the Gāṇḍīva bow and swiftly grasped it for the fray.
Knitting his brows upon his face as a sign of his wrath,
the Pāṇḍava blew the great conch Devadatta;
then Arjuna discharged the Tvaṣṭra weapon, which destroys the hosts of enemies.
Then thousands of forms appeared individually;
deluded by those various forms which were reflections of themselves,
they mistook one another for Arjuna and struck down their own selves.
"This is Arjuna! This is Govinda! These two are the Yādava and the Pāṇḍava!"—saying this, the bewildered men slaughtered one another in the battle;
O bull of the Bharatas, your warriors struck each other down in that conflict.
Deluded by that supreme weapon, they went to their destruction at one another's hands.
With their limbs drenched in blood, those warriors, gazing at one another in battle, shone like *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
With blood flowing from their wounds, they were drenched in gore;
on the field of battle, they shone as if sprinkled with the juice of sandalwood.
Then, laughing, Bībhatsu drew his Gāṇḍīva bow with great force.

He struck them down with sharp arrows, as the sun destroys darkness with its rays. Those who remained after being slain surrounded Dhanañjaya once more and, along with his horses, standard, and chariot, made him invisible with showers of arrows.
Then, having reduced to ashes those thousands of arrows released by them,
that weapon sent those heroes to the abode of Yama. Then Bībhatsu, laughing, [attacked] the Lalitthas and the Mālavas as well.
He afflicted the Mācellakas, the Trigartas, and the Yaudheyas with his arrows. Being slaughtered by that hero, those Kṣatriyas, impelled by Time,
discharged various kinds of showers of arrows at the son of Pṛthā.
Then neither Arjuna, nor the chariot, nor Keśava could be seen there, as they were shrouded by that terrible shower of arrows. Thereupon,
having found their mark, they cried out to one another.
Thinking, "The two Kṛṣṇas have been slain," they were then filled with joy and shook their garments;
thousands of heroes blew kettledrums, clay drums,
and conchs, and let out fierce lion-roars there, O noble one.
Then Kṛṣṇa perspired and, feeling distressed, said to Arjuna:
"Where are you, Pārtha? I do not see you; are you still alive, O slayer of foes?
Recognizing that human emotion of his, the son of Pāṇḍu, who understands the inner state of others, [replied].
With the Vāyavya weapon, he warded off that shower of arrows discharged by them.
Then the blessed Lord Vāyu carried away the hosts of Saṃśaptakas, along with their horses, elephants, chariots, and weapons, like heaps of dry leaves.
Being carried away by the wind, O King, they appeared exceedingly beautiful,
like birds flying up from trees at the proper season, O noble one.
Having thus thrown them into confusion, Dhananjaya acted with haste.
With sharpened arrows he struck down hundreds and thousands;
with broad-headed shafts (bhalla) he severed heads and arms still grasping weapons,
and with his arrows he felled to the earth thighs resembling the trunks of elephants.
Dhananjaya rendered his enemies devoid of various limbs and members— some with their backs severed, some unable to move, others deprived of brains, eyes, or fingers—
and he [destroyed] the chariots, which were constructed according to rule and resembled cities of the Gandharvas.
Shattering them with his arrows, he deprived the chariots and elephants of their horses;
here and there, the heaps of severed standards and chariots shone like groves of palm trees stripped of their crowns, scattered in various places.
The elephants, equipped with superior weapons and adorned with banners, goads,
and armaments, fell like mountains covered in trees struck by Śakra’s thunderbolt;
their chowries, head-ornaments, and armor were shattered, and their entrails, eyes, and life-breaths spilled out.
Horses with their riders fell to the earth, struck down by the arrows of Pārtha;
with swords and claws scattered, armor torn asunder, and spears and pikes shattered,
the foot soldiers lay slain in a pitiful state, their coats of mail mangled.
With those slain and being slain, falling and having fallen,
as well as those wandering about and groaning, the field of battle appeared terrible;
and the great cloud of dust that had arisen was settled by showers of blood.
The earth also became impassable, crowded with hundreds of headless trunks;
that chariot of Bībhatsu appeared fierce and loathsome in battle,
like the playground of Rudra as he slaughters sacrificial animals at the end of time.
Being slaughtered by Pārtha, their horses, chariots, and elephants thrown into confusion, they—
exhausted and facing him alone— became guests of Śakra.
O best of the Bharatas, that ground was covered with those slain great car-warriors.
The entire field was strewn on all sides with those who had become like departed spirits.
Meanwhile, while Savyasācin was thus preoccupied,
Droṇa, having arrayed his troops, then rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
The strikers, with their ranks arrayed, quickly received him, desiring to seize Yudhiṣṭhira; at that time, there was a great and tumultuous uproar. Saṃjaya said:
Having passed that night, O King, the great car-warrior Bhāradvāja spoke at length to King Suyodhana and then arranged for Pārtha to engage with the hosts of Saṃśaptakas.
When Pārtha had departed from the battle to slay the Saṃśaptakas,
O best of the Bharatas, Droṇa then drew up his array and advanced against the great army of the Pāṇḍavas with the desire to capture Dharmarāja.
Then, having seen the Suparṇa array formed by the son of Bharadvāja,
Yudhiṣṭhira countered it with a half-moon array.
The great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, was at the mouth of that Suparṇa formation.
King Duryodhana, together with his uterine brothers and their followers, [protected] the head;
Kṛtavarman and Gautama, the best of archers, [protected] the two eyes;
and Bhūtavarmā, Kṣemaśarmā, and the heroic Karakarṣa [guarded the rest].
The Kaliṅgas, Siṃhalas, Easterners, Śūras, Ābhīras, Daśerakas, Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, and those who are Haṃsapadas;
and on the neck [of the earth], the Śūrasenas, Daradas, Madrakas, and Kekayas.
Multitudes of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry stood there by the hundreds of thousands.
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, Somadatta, and Bāhlika—
these heroes, surrounded by an *akṣauhiṇī*, took their positions on the right wing.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja,
taking their position on the left wing, stood with the son of Droṇa at their head;
behind them were the Kaliṅgas, the Ambaṣṭhas, the Māgadhas, the Pauṇḍras, and the Madrakas.
The Gāndhāras, the Śakunis, the Easterners, the Pārvatīyas, and the Vasātis [were stationed there]. At the tail stood Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, together with his sons, kinsmen, and relatives,
accompanied by a vast army from which various banners rose aloft.
Jayadratha, Bhīmaratha, Sāṃyātrikasabha, Jaya, Bhūmijaya, Vṛṣakrātha, and the mighty Naiṣadha—
surrounded by a great force and placing the world of Brahmā before them.
O King, those experts in warfare stood at the head of the array;
the formation designed by Droṇa, composed of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants,
appeared like an ocean tossed by the wind, as if it were actually surging forward.
From his wings and sub-wings, those eager for battle rushed forth,
like clouds accompanied by lightning and thunder emerging from all directions during the hot season.
In the midst of that army of Prāgjyotiṣa stood an elephant, duly equipped according to ritual.
Seated there, O King, he shone like the sun at its rising;
the monarch was graced by a white umbrella held over him and adorned with garlands of flowers,
like the moon on the night of the full moon joined with the constellation Kṛttikā.
Blinded by rut, the elephant shone like a mass of blue collyrium,
resembling a great mountain drenched by massive clouds;
it was surrounded by various heroic kings adorned with diverse weapons and ornaments.

Accompanied by the mountaineers, he was like Śakra surrounded by the hosts of gods. Then Yudhiṣṭhira, beholding that superhuman array which was invincible to enemies in battle, spoke these words to the son of Pṛṣata.
"O Lord, O you whose horses are the color of pigeons, let such a policy be ordained today that I do not fall under the power of this Brahmin. Dhṛṣṭadyumna said:
"O you of noble vows, you shall not fall under the power of Drona while he strives against you.
Today I shall hold back Drona along with his followers.
O Kauravya, as long as I am alive, you ought not to feel any anxiety."
"For Droṇa is not capable of defeating me in battle by any means whatsoever.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus, the powerful son of Drupada scattered arrows [at his opponent].
With horses the color of pigeons, he himself rushed toward Droṇa. Seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna standing there— an ominous sight—
Droṇa in an instant became as if his mind were no longer joyful.

For he was born exceedingly fierce with respect to the destruction of Droṇa; therefore, due to his mortal nature, the son of Bharadvāja became bewildered. Consequently, no one in the army was able even to look at him.
Then, scattering sharp arrows upon Drupada’s army,
the son of Bharadvāja advanced swiftly in battle, avoiding the son of Pṛṣata,
while the Brahmin held back Drupada’s great host.
But beholding him, your son Durmukha, the crusher of enemies,
desiring to do what was pleasing to Droṇa, checked Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
That tumultuous clash became as if equal on both sides.
O Bhārata,
having quickly covered Durmukha with a net of arrows, the son of Pṛṣata then held back the son of Bharadvāja with a great shower of shafts, while the heroic Pārṣata and Durmukha were engaged.
Seeing Droṇa thus obstructed, your son, greatly distressed,
confounded the son of Pṛṣata with volleys of arrows of various descriptions.
While those two, the prince of the Pañcālas and the leader of the Kurus, were locked in combat on the field, [the battle raged on].

A tumultuous battle ensued between those two who were intent on slaying each other. Droṇa scattered Yudhiṣṭhira’s army in many directions with his arrows, just as clouds are dispersed on all sides by the wind.
Thus the armies of the son of Pṛthā were scattered here and there;
for a moment that battle was sweet to behold,
but then, O King, it proceeded without restraint like a madness.
Neither the sky, nor the quarters, nor the earth, nor the sun shone;
O King, neither one's own people nor those of the enemy could be distinguished from one another,
and that battle proceeded by means of inference and designations.
Upon their crest-jewels, neck-ornaments, decorations, swords, and shields,
rays of light with the brilliance of the sun shone forth. This was from those chariots, elephants, and horses with their banners fluttering in the wind.
In that battle, a form resembling a flight of cranes amidst the clouds was seen;
men slew men, fierce horses slew horses,
chariot-warriors slew chariots, and elephants slew choice elephants.
In an instant, a tumultuous and terrible battle took place between the elephants with their banners raised and the supreme tuskers; as they grappled with one another,
their bodies became entangled as they dragged each other along.
From the friction of the clashing of their tusks, smoke-enshrouded fire was produced;
with their banners scattered and fires generated by their tusks,
they became like clouds reaching the sky accompanied by lightning.
With elephants streaming with ichor, trumpeting, and falling,
the earth became strewn over like the autumnal sky with clouds.
As they were being struck by showers of arrows and lances, [the field of battle was filled].
The roar of the elephants arose like the thundering of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Some of those supreme elephants, struck by iron javelins and arrows, were terrified;
others fled, making only a sound as they went, causing all living beings to tremble.
And there, some elephants struck by the tusks of other elephants let out a terrible cry of distress, like clouds at the time of a cosmic portent;
and those elephants were driven back by superior elephants.
Driven by supreme goads, they were struck down again; great elephant-drivers, beaten by other great drivers with arrows and *tomaras*,
fell from their elephants to the earth, dropping their weapons and goads.
Deprived of their drivers, the elephants, trumpeting here and there,
rushed about like scattered clouds as they collided with one another;
and being restrained by supreme weapons, they bore away those who had been slain.
Some great elephants fled in all directions like solitary wanderers;
struck and being struck by javelins, spears, and battle-axes,
those elephants then fell in the slaughter-ground, uttering cries of distress.
As their bodies, resembling mountains, fell down on all sides,
the earth was suddenly struck, shook, and roared;
it was overwhelmed everywhere by those [bodies] along with their elephant-riders and banners.
The earth shone with the fallen elephants as if strewn with mountains;
and the great elephant-drivers, standing upon their beasts, had their hearts pierced in battle and were crushed by the elephants' excellent limbs, while their tusks were cast down.
Struck down by chariot-warriors with broad-headed arrows, their hooks and lances scattered,
other elephants, pierced by iron shafts, trumpeted like cranes and fled in the ten directions, trampling both enemies and their own kin.
O King, the earth became covered with a flood of bodies from the multitudes of elephants, horses, and chariots, and was turned into a mire of flesh and blood;
and having been crushed by the tips of tusks and tossed up by the elephants, it lay scattered about.
Great car-warriors with their wheels intact and others with wheels shattered fled on their chariots;
chariots were left without their riders, horses were bereft of men,
and elephants whose drivers had been slain fled in all directions, tormented by arrows.
There, the father slew the son, and likewise the son slew the father;
thus there was a tumultuous battle in which nothing could be discerned. Men sank up to their ankles in the mire of blood.
Surrounded by those blazing [weapons], they resembled great trees encircled by forest fires;
the garments and armor being drenched with blood,
as well as the umbrellas and banners— everything appeared red.
Multitudes of horses, multitudes of chariots, and multitudes of men were struck down;
they were turned back and scattered in many directions by the rims of the chariot wheels.
That great torrent of elephants, with its powerful current, had the lifeless men for its moss.
The ocean of the army shone forth, with its tumultuous whirlpools formed by the multitude of chariots.
Desiring the wealth of victory, the warriors plunged into it upon the great ships that were their mounts; even as they were being submerged, they did not fall into confusion.
While the warriors, whose marks were unvanquished, were being rained upon by showers of arrows,
not a single man struck by those signs regained his composure;
for the battle continued in such a manner, terrible in form and fearsome.
Having confounded his enemies, Droṇa rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
Saṃjaya said:
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing that Droṇa had approached close by, [acted].
He fearlessly received that great shower of arrows;
then a tumultuous roar arose among Yudhiṣṭhira’s troops,
like that of a great lion wishing to seize the leader of a herd of elephants.
Then, seeing Droṇa, the hero Satyajit, whose prowess is truth,
rushed toward the preceptor who was seeking Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thereupon, the preceptor and the Pāñcālya fought with one another.
Agitating that army like Indra and Virocana,
Satyajit, whose prowess was truth, then pierced the great archer Droṇa with sharp-pointed arrows, displaying his supreme mastery of weapons.

Then he discharged five arrows at that charioteer, resembling the venom of snakes and like unto Death itself; the charioteer fainted from them. Then he suddenly pierced his horses with ten swift shafts.
Enraged, with ten [chariots] on each side and both his flank-drivers,
he moved about the front of the army, wheeling in circles;
and the destroyer of enemies, filled with wrath, cut down Drona’s banner.
But Droṇa, the subduer of enemies, having observed that conduct of his in battle, reflected in his mind upon what was appropriate for the occasion;
then he struck Satyajit with ten sharp arrows that pierce the vital organs.
The preceptor quickly pierced him, having severed his bow along with the arrow;
the preceptor indeed cut his bow with three swift shafts.
Taking up another bow even more swiftly, that powerful warrior—
He quickly struck Droṇa with twenty heron-feathered arrows.
Perceiving Droṇa as if being swallowed by Satyajit in the battle,
Vṛka, the Pāñcālya, afflicted Droṇa with hundreds of sharp shafts.
Seeing the great car-warrior Droṇa being overwhelmed in battle,
O King, the Pāṇḍavas cried out and waved their garments.
But Vṛka, extremely enraged, struck Droṇa between the breasts with sixty arrows.
O King, the powerful one pierced him, and that was like a marvel.
But the great car-warrior Droṇa, being covered by a shower of arrows,
exerted his great speed, rolling his eyes in rage.
Then Droṇa, having cut the bows of both Satyajit and Vṛka,
slew Vṛka along with his charioteer and horses with six arrows.
Thereupon, Satyajit took up another bow of even greater speed.
He pierced Droṇa, along with his horses, charioteer, banner, and arrows, with his own shafts. Droṇa could not endure that affliction by the Pāñcālya in battle;
thereupon, he swiftly discharged arrows for the sake of his destruction.
Then Drona covered his horses, his standard, his bow-grip, and both his flank-protecting charioteers with thousands of showers of arrows. Thus,
as his bows were being severed again and again, [he continued his assault].

The Pāñcālya, an expert in supreme weapons, fought against Śoṇāśva; he quickly covered the son of Bharadvāja with arrows from all sides. When his horses became entangled, he turned away from the battle.
Beholding Satyajit thus exulting in that great battle,
he crushed him with great force, like the wind uprooting a tall tree;
then, in that combat, [he struck] the son of the Pañcāla king, Satyajit.
With a crescent-shaped arrow, he severed the head of that great-souled one.
When that high minister, that bull among the chariot-warriors of the Pāñcālas, had been slain,
Yudhiṣṭhira, terrified of Droṇa, fled away on swift horses.
The Pāñcālas, Kekayas, Matsyas, Cedis, Kārūṣas, and Kosalas,
looking toward Yudhiṣṭhira with joy, rushed against Droṇa.
Then the Teacher, the slayer of enemy hosts, desiring to reach Yudhiṣṭhira, [advanced].
He scattered those armies like the wind dispersing a heap of cotton;
as Drona was repeatedly consuming those various divisions,
Śatānīka, the younger brother of the Matsya king, advanced against him.
With six arrows resembling the rays of the sun and polished by a smith, he pierced Droṇa along with his charioteer and horses, and roared loudly;
desiring to perform a difficult feat, he was intent upon a cruel deed.

He covered Bhāradvāja from all sides with hundreds of arrows. As he was roaring, Droṇa swiftly struck off his head, complete with earrings, from his body with a razor-sharp arrow; thereupon the Matsyas fled in all directions.

Having conquered the Matsyas, Bhāradvāja repeatedly defeated the Cedis, the Kārūṣas, and the Kekayas, as well as the Pañcālas, the Sṛñjayas, and the Pāṇḍus. He was consuming the armies like an enraged fire consuming a forest.
Seeing Rukmaratha enraged, the Sṛñjayas trembled;
for as that swift-acting warrior drew his supreme bow and struck down his enemies, the twang of his bowstring was heard in all directions.
The fierce arrows released by the skillful archer crushed the elephants, horses, infantry, chariot-warriors, and elephant-riders,
like a roaring rain-cloud accompanied by wind at the end of winter.
Like a rain of stones, he rained down [arrows], instilling fear in his enemies;
he roamed through all directions as if agitating the entire army—
he who was powerful, heroic, a great archer, and the granter of fearlessness to his friends.

O Bhārata, we beheld the gold-adorned bow of Drona, who possessed immeasurable splendor, appearing like lightning among the clouds in all directions; and upon his banner, we saw a beautiful sacrificial altar.
Moving violently in battle with the form of a Himalayan peak,
Droṇa wrought great carnage among the Pāṇḍava army,
just as Viṣṇu, who is honored by gods and asuras, did among the hosts of Daityas.
He was a hero, truthful in speech, wise, powerful, and of true valor;
possessed of great majesty, at the end of time he [wielded] that river which was fierce and terrifying to the timid,
with its waves of armor and its whirlpools of banners, carrying away the shores of mortals.
[The river] had elephants and horses for its great crocodiles, swords for its fish, and was difficult to approach;
it was fierce, with the bones of heroes for its gravel, and had drums and kettledrums for its tortoises;
it was terrible, with shields and armor for its rafts, and hair for its moss and aquatic plants.
The terrible river of the Kurus and Sṛñjayas flowed across the field of battle, with showers of arrows for its current, bows for its stream, and arms for its swarming serpents;
it had human heads for its stones, spears for its fish, and maces for its rafts.
With turbans for its foam and entrails for its crawling serpents,
fierce and carrying away heroes, it was a river with flesh and blood for its mud,
where elephants were the crocodiles, banners the trees, and where the *kṣatriyas* sank.
There, Droṇa set flowing a river leading to the abode of Death— a cruel confluence of bodies, with riders for its crocodiles and difficult to cross,
resounding with the cries of throngs of flesh-eating beasts and teeming with packs of dogs and jackals.
Attacked on all sides by fierce flesh-eaters,
that noble car-warrior Drona was burning through the ranks like the God of Death;
then, led by the sons of Kuntī, they rushed toward him from every direction.
Those heroes, united together, surrounded Droṇa on all sides,
just as the rays of the sun surround the sun as it blazes throughout the world.
Your warriors, with weapons raised, [assailed] those heroes who were great archers.
Kings and princes surrounded him from all sides. Then Śikhaṇḍin pierced Droṇa with five straight-jointed arrows,
Kṣatravarmā with twenty, and Vasudāna with five.
Uttamaujas pierced him with three arrows, Kṣatradeva with seven,
Sātyaki with a hundred in the battle, Yudhāmanyu likewise with eight,
and Yudhiṣṭhira pierced Droṇa with twelve shafts.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna struck him with ten arrows and Cekitāna with three;
then Droṇa, true to his promise, like an elephant in rut,
having bypassed the array of chariots, struck down Dṛḍhasena.
Then, approaching King Kṣema as he was striking fearlessly, he pierced him with nine arrows; slain, the king fell from his chariot.
Having reached the midst of the armies, he roamed through all directions.
For he had been the protector of others, and was not to be protected by anyone under any circumstances. With twelve arrows he struck Śikhaṇḍin, with twenty Uttamaujas,
and with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla) he sent Vasudāna to the abode of Yama.

With eighty arrows he struck Kṣatravarmā, with twenty-six Sudakṣiṇa, and with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla) he struck Kṣatradeva from the seat of his chariot. With sixty-four arrows he struck Yudhāmanyu, and with thirty, Sātyaki.

Having pierced him, Rukmaratha quickly rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira. Then Yudhiṣṭhira, that gambler and best of kings, swiftly retreated on his fleet-footed horses, while the Pāñcālya prince advanced against Droṇa.
Droṇa, however, destroyed him along with his bow, his horses, and his charioteer.
Struck down, he fell from his chariot to the earth like a celestial light falling from the sky.
Having slain him, Droṇa shone resplendent, surrounded by the Kurus.
When that prince, the glory of the Pañcālas, had been slain, a great and tumultuous outcry arose: "Slay Drona! Slay Drona!
[Seeing] those Pāñcālas, Matsyas, and Kekayas thus intensely enraged, [he advanced].
The mighty Droṇa agitated the Sṛñjayas and the Pāṇḍavas,
as well as Sātyaki, Cekitāna, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin,
Vārdhakṣemi, Citrasena, Senābindu, and Suvarcas.
Droṇa, surrounded by the Kurus, defeated these and many other lords of various realms in battle.
But your men, O great king, having gained victory in that great conflict—

They struck down the sons of Pāṇḍu as they fled in every direction on the battlefield. Then Vārṣṇeya Vārdhakṣemi, O protector of the earth, having pierced Droṇa with nine excellent arrows, struck him again with five more.
Then Citrasena, the Pāñcāla, afflicted Droṇa with arrows;
further enraged, Senābindu pierced him with five,
as did Suvarmā with five and Dhṛṣṭadyumna with five.
O King, Śikhaṇḍin pierced him with nine arrows, Cekitāna with five,
and Sātyaki with sixty-four shafts;
then the mighty Sucitra, having pierced Droṇa with ten arrows, uttered a loud roar.
O King, in that battle Droṇa covered him with showers of arrows;
then Droṇa struck down the highly brilliant one along with his charioteer.
O King, together with his horses, he fell indeed to the earth, slain in the encounter.

O Great King, as he was being struck down, he shone like a celestial light falling from the sky. O Bhārata, like those Dānavas being slain by the high-souled Indra, the Pañcālas, Kekayas, and Matsyas trembled.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When the Pāṇḍavas and all the Pañcālas had been broken by Bhāradvāja in that great battle, did anyone else advance against him?
Having resolved upon a noble course of action in battle that brings glory to Kṣatriyas—
a path not pursued by cowards but frequented by the bulls among men—
that man, O Sūta, is truly a hero who turns back when others have broken.
"Alas! Was there no man who, upon seeing Droṇa stationed there—
yawning like a tiger, like an elephant in rut,
ready to give up his life in battle, armored and a versatile warrior— could have stood against him?"

Having seen the son of Bharadvāja— the great archer, tiger among men, who increases the suffering of his enemies, grateful, devoted to truth, and seeking the welfare of Duryodhana— standing there as a hero in the army;
"Which heroes turned back [to fight], O Sañjaya? Tell me that.
Sañjaya said:
"Having seen them wavering in battle, driven away by Droṇa’s arrows..."
The Pāñcālas, Pāṇḍavas, Matsyas, Sṛñjayas, Cedis,
and Kekayas were carried away by the life-taking torrent of arrows released from Droṇa’s bow,
like rafts swept away by the great flood of a river.
The Kauravas, with lion-like roars and the sound of various musical instruments,
