surrounded him on all sides with chariots, elephants, men, and horses.
Seeing them, the king, standing in the midst of his army and surrounded by his own kin, [spoke].
Duryodhana, delighted and as if laughing, said to Karṇa:
"Behold, O son of Rādhā, the Pāñcālas driven away by Droṇa’s arrows,
like wild deer terrified by a lion with a firm bow."
"It is my conviction that these men will never again seek battle,
for they have been shattered by Droṇa like great trees by the wind,
and are now being tormented by the gold-tufted arrows of that high-souled one."
They do not proceed by a single path, reeling here and there;
hemmed in by the Kauravas and the high-souled Droṇa,
these others have formed circles like elephants surrounded by fire.
Pierced by Droṇa’s sharp arrows as if by swarms of bees,
they huddled together, intent on flight.
"Here is Bhīma, firm in his wrath, abandoned by the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas!"
Surrounded by my warriors, O Karṇa, he seems to be threatening me;
clearly, that evil-minded one beholds today a world consisting entirely of Droṇa. Surely the Pāṇḍava has now lost all hope for his life and his kingdom.
Karna said:
"This mighty-armed one will never abandon the battle while he lives,
nor, O tiger among men, will he be able to endure these lion-roars."
Furthermore, it is my conviction that the Pāṇḍavas will not be broken in battle;
for they are heroes, powerful, skilled in weapons, and fierce in combat. The Pāṇḍavas have endured the afflictions of poison, fire, and gambling, as well as exile in the forest.
It is my conviction that, remembering [his vow], they will not abandon the battle;
for the mighty-armed Vṛkodara of immeasurable energy has been humiliated,
and the son of Kuntī will surely slay the most excellent of the noble chariot-warriors.
With sword, bow, spear, horses, elephants, men, and chariots,
and with an iron mace, he will slay host after host;
and these chariot-warriors, headed by Sātyaki, follow after him.
The Pañcālas, Kekayas, Matsyas, and especially the Pāṇḍavas—
those heroes, powerful, valiant, and great car-warriors—
were particularly urged on by the enraged Bhīma.
And this mighty-armed one, as firm as the Himalayas,
O Great King, will slay [him] with his mace of terrible velocity;
those bulls among the Kurus are advancing against Droṇa from all sides.
Desiring to protect Vṛkodara, they were like masses of clouds surrounding the sun;
the Pāṇḍavas, kinsmen of Kṛṣṇa, were designated for battles—
modest, skilled in slaying enemies, and endowed with auspicious marks.
"O King, there are many earthly rulers who have fallen under their power in battle;
do not despise the Pāṇḍavas, who are led by Nārāyaṇa.
For they have entered upon a single path and would surely afflict one of such disciplined vows."
Just as moths seeking death swarm toward an unprotected lamp,
those skilled in weapons and capable of warding him off will undoubtedly attack;
yet I consider the burden placed upon the son of Bharadvāja to be excessive.
"Let us quickly follow them to where Droṇa is stationed;
let them not slay that man of firm vows, like crows attacking a great elephant.
Sañjaya said:
Having heard the words of the son of Rādhā, King Duryodhana,
accompanied by his brothers, O King, then proceeded toward Droṇa’s chariot.
A great clamor arose there from those who desired to slay Droṇa alone.
As the Pāṇḍavas returned with their excellent horses of various colors,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, tell me the chariot-standards of all of them."
"I wish to hear those [accounts] from you in detail, one by one.
My mind is distressed, O dear one, regarding Droṇa, O scorcher of foes;
having heard of Bhīṣma’s death, this [regarding Droṇa] will be likewise."
07.022.001 Those who, led by Bhīma, advanced against Droṇa in a rage—
07.022.002 Sañjaya said:
07.022.002a Seeing Vṛkodara striving with his antelope-colored horses, [Droṇa...]
Then the heroic Śaineya, whose horses were silver-colored, turned back;
and Yudhāmanyu, borne by excellent dappled steeds,
that invincible warrior, returned in a rage toward Droṇa’s chariot.
Dhrishtadyumna, the son of the king of the Panchalas, advanced with horses of great speed that were the color of pigeons and adorned with golden trappings;
he was Kshatradharman, firm in his vows, seeking to protect his father.
Desiring his supreme success, Śoṇākṣa turned back,
accompanied by horses adorned with eyes like jasmine flowers and resembling lotus petals;
Śikhaṇḍin and Kṣatradeva also went forth, urging him on themselves.
The handsome Kambojas, clad in coverings of parrot feathers,
swiftly bore Nakula as they charged against your troops. Then the dark horses, resembling clouds, bore Sahadeva with his weapon raised.
O Bhārata, having aimed at the invincible one, he drove his horses of supreme vigor against the enraged Durdharṣa;
likewise, his Tittiri and Kalmāṣa steeds were equal to the wind in speed.
In that tumultuous battle,
horses with the hue of ivory and black manes, possessing terrible speed and the swiftness of the wind, bore King Yudhiṣṭhira, that tiger among men.
Covered by excellent golden trappings, horses equal to the wind in speed brought all the armies toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
Immediately following the kings, however, was King Drupada of Pañcāla.
With a golden umbrella held over him and protected by all his own [attendants],
that great archer, free from fear, advanced into the midst of the kings on bay horses adorned with forehead-marks, which were capable of enduring every sound in battle.
Virāṭa followed behind him, accompanied by heroic great chariot-warriors;
the Kekayas, Śikhaṇḍin, and Dhṛṣṭaketu likewise followed the King of the Matsyas, each surrounded by his own respective troops.
Those excellent horses, possessing a color identical to that of *pāṭala* flowers,
shone brightly as they bore the Matsya king, the slayer of enemies. Furthermore, swift steeds with a hue like turmeric and adorned with golden garlands [followed].
They swiftly bore away the son of King Virāṭa; meanwhile,
the five Kekaya brothers, possessing the hue of indragopaka insects and all shining with the luster of gold, had red banners.
Wearing golden garlands, all those heroes skilled in battle appeared, clad in armor, like rain-showering clouds; they,
whose forms resembled unbaked earthen vessels, [advanced] against the Pāñcālya of immeasurable splendor.
Tamed, copper-red horses, well-trained, bore Śikhaṇḍin;
likewise, there were twelve thousand great car-warriors of the Pañcālas,
of whom six thousand followed Śikhaṇḍin.

O noble one, dappled horses, variegated like antelopes, bore the son of Śiśupāla, that lion among men, as they frolicked about. And Dhṛṣṭaketu, the bull among the Cedis, was impelled by his exceeding strength.
The invincible one advanced against Bṛhatkṣatra,
the prince of the Kaikeyas, with dappled horses from Kamboja; excellent steeds from Sindh, possessing the hue of smoke rising from straw, swiftly bore that delicate youth.
Well-adorned horses of the Bāhlīka breed, with eyes like jasmine and the color of lotuses,
bore Kṣatradeva, the son of Śikhaṇḍin, that hero;
those steeds were covered in golden trappings and resembled silk.
The patient horses born in Araṭṭa bore Saṃkhye in battle;
the excellent steeds, the color of curlews, bore the youthful Sukumāra, the great car-warrior and son of Abhibhū, the king of Kāśi, into the fray.
The white horses with black necks, swift as thought and obedient to the driver’s command, O King, bore that prince Prativindhya;
those steeds, acting as servants to their rider, carried the youth into battle.

The horses that bore him into battle were the color of *māṣa* flowers; they were like a thousand Soma sacrifices personified— those very steeds for which Pārtha had requested Sutasoma as a son from Dhaumya.
He was born in that city of the Kurus named Udayendu, amidst the moon and Indra;
therefore, he became known as Sutasoma.
Horses resembling the *soma* plant in hue, adorned with golden ornaments,
neighing on all sides, bore that hero in battle;
while horses resembling *śāla* flowers bore Śatānīka, the son of Nakula.
Resembling the young sun, they bore that praiseworthy youth;
with yokes like golden images and resembling the necks of peacocks,
they bore Śrutakarman, the son of Draupadī and tiger among men.
The excellent horses, resembling the feathers of blue jays, bore Śrutakīrti, the son of Draupadī and a treasury of sacred learning, who was equal to Pārtha in battle;
he whom they say possesses one-and-a-half times the qualities of both Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha in combat.
Tawny horses bore that youth Abhimanyu into the fray;
but Bṛhantas, those of massive body, bore Yuyutsu— who alone among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had sought refuge with the Pāṇḍavas— into the battle.
In that tumultuous battle, spirited and well-adorned horses, pale as stalks of straw, bore the swift Vārdhakṣemi;
while those with white feet bore Kumāra, who was clad in breastplates adorned with golden plates.
In battle, the horses, obedient to the driver's command, bore Sauvitri;
those patient steeds, adorned with golden saddles, covered in silk-like trappings,
and wearing golden garlands, carried Śreṇimat.
Wearing garlands of gold coins, heroic, golden-hued, and well-adorned,
those excellent horses bore the praiseworthy King of Kāśī,
who had reached the further shore of the science of weapons, the art of archery, and the Veda of Brahmā.
The ruddy steeds bore forward that Satyadhṛti as he approached—
he who, as the commander of the Pañcāla army, had assigned Droṇa as his portion.
Horses with the color of pigeons bore Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Satyadhṛti, the son of Sucitti, who was difficult to vanquish in battle, followed him,
as did Śreṇimān, Vasudāna, and the son of the King of Kāśī, O Lord—
each mounted on excellent Kamboja horses, swift and adorned with golden garlands.
Terrifying the enemy host like Yama and Vaiśravaṇa,
six thousand Prabhadrakas from the Pañcāla country stood with weapons raised,
mounted on excellent horses of various colors and adorned with chariots and banners of gold.
Shaking their enemies with showers of arrows and stretching their bows,
they followed Dhṛṣṭadyumna, having made death common to all;
they were the color of tawny silk and wore excellent golden garlands.
The best of horses, with unwearied minds,
bore Cekitāna. And Kuntibhoja, the maternal uncle of Savyasācin, arrived with excellent, well-trained, and victorious steeds that were the color of Indra’s bow.
The horses, colored like the intermediate space and appearing as if variegated with stars, bore the radiant king in battle; they were dappled, white-footed, and adorned with trappings of golden mesh.
The best of horses,
the color of lotus stalks,
swift as hawks and variegated, bore Sudāmā along with Sahadeva, the son of Jarāsaṃdha.
The horses, red as a hare's blood and marked with white rising streaks,
bore Siṃhasena, the son of Gopati and king of the Pañcālas—
that tiger among men who was renowned as Janamejaya among the Pañcālas.
His excellent horses were equal in color to mustard flowers;
swift, large, and adorned with golden garlands, they were the color of black beans.
With backs as white as curd and faces like the moon, they bore the prince of Pañcāla swiftly along.
Brave and auspicious steeds,
resembling the stalks of reeds and possessing the hue of lotus filaments, bore Daṇḍadhāra;
they were reddish-brown like donkeys and had the appearance of mice on their backs.
Leaping as if in combat, tawny steeds— black, dappled, and adorned with variegated garlands— carried Vyāghradanta.
O tiger among men, those horses bore Sudhanvan, the prince of the Pañcālas.

With a touch like Indra’s thunderbolt and resembling indragopaka insects, horses with variegated bellies and colorful inner trappings bore Citrāyudha; these steeds wore golden garlands and had the hue of ruddy geese.

The spirited horses bore Sukṣatra, the son of the lord of Kosala; while tall, magnificent, and well-trained dappled steeds, adorned with garlands of gold, bore Satyadhṛti, the son of Kṣema, into battle.
With everything of a single color— his banner, his armor,
his horses, and even his bow— all white, Śveta turned back.
But the son of Samudrasena, possessing the splendor of Rudra, was surrounded by ocean-born warriors.
Horses resembling the moon bore Candradeva;
and horses the color of blue lotuses, adorned with gold,
bore Śaibya Citraratha, who was resplendent with variegated garlands in battle.
Excellent horses, the color of *kalāya* flowers and marked with white and red stripes,
carried Rathasena, who was intoxicated by battle;
he was the king whom they declared to be the bravest among all men.
Excellent horses, the color of *kiṃśuka* flowers, bore that slayer of Pataccara— whose complexion was like a parrot’s,
who possessed variegated weapons, variegated garlands, and variegated armor, weapons,
and banners.
Nīla advanced with a standard, armor, bow, and chariot-steeds that were all entirely blue; likewise, others advanced with chariot-fenders, standards,
and bows variegated with jewels in various forms.
Variegated with horses, banners, and flags, the variegated [chariot] approached. Those excellent horses, whose color was like that of a lotus petal,
bore the gold-colored son of Rocamāna.
The *yodhas*, the *bhadrakāras*, and those born from the staffs and secondary staffs of Śara—
white-egg creatures with the appearance of cock’s eggs— carried the banner of Daṇḍa.
When their father, the lord of men, had been slain in battle by Keśava, [they fought on].
When the gates of the Pāṇḍyas were shattered and their kinsmen had fled,
he obtained weapons from Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Rāma, and Kṛpa; thus, through those weapons, he attained equality with Rukmin, Karṇa, Arjuna, and Acyuta.
He desired to destroy Dvārakā and to conquer the entire earth; however,
having been restrained by wise friends out of a desire for his welfare, he abandoned the persistence of enmity and ruled over his own kingdom.

The powerful Pāṇḍya king, Sāgaradhvaja, relying on his wealth of valor, rushed toward Droṇa while stretching his divine bow; he was accompanied by horses resembling moonbeams, covered with nets of lapis lazuli.
The horses of the followers of the Pāṇḍya king, possessing the hue of *āṭarūṣaka* flowers,
carried fourteen myriads of preeminent chariot-warriors;
those steeds were of various forms and colors, with faces of diverse shapes.
They bore the heroic Ghaṭotkaca, whose banner was a chariot wheel;
he who, disregarding the opinions of all the assembled Bharatas,
had gone out of devotion to Yudhiṣṭhira, abandoning everything he had striven for.

Red-eyed, long-armed, and massive, he stood upon a golden chariot with an excellent banner; those beings of great power and great bodies were accompanied by various flags and banners, and by various armored horses.

The excellent horses of various divine colors followed from all sides and from behind Yudhiṣṭhira— the best of kings, knower of dharma, and stationed at the head of the army— as they were golden-hued and of the finest breed.
The Prabhadrakas likewise followed with noble steeds of diverse and celestial colors.
Many of divine form turned back for battle;
joined by Bhīmasena, those warriors with golden banners appeared, O king of kings, like the inhabitants of heaven accompanied by Indra.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna outshone all those who had assembled there,
while the son of Bharadvāja outshone all the armies as well.
Sañjaya said:
His banner, topped with a black antelope skin, shone exceedingly;
O great king, it bore a beautiful water-pot made of gold. As for Bhīmasena’s banner, its crest was a lapis lazuli gem.
I beheld a shining great lion made of silver upon the banner of the Kuru king, the Pandava of mighty luster; and I saw a golden moon accompanied by the hosts of planets.
And here were two large, divine mṛdaṅga drums, Nanda and Upananda, which,
when struck by their mechanism, produced beautiful sounds that increased one's joy;
and the great banner of Nakula was a śarabha with a golden back.
We beheld him standing upon his chariot, exceedingly fierce and striking terror;
the glorious silver swan-standard, equipped with bells and banners,
was Sahadeva’s— unassailable and increasing the grief of his enemies.
The golden chariot of Abhimanyu, the prince, was adorned with the images of the five sons of Draupadī,
as well as those of Dharma, Māruta, Śakra, and the two high-souled Aśvins;
it was decorated with the feathers of the Śārṅga bird.

O king of kings, on Ghaṭotkaca’s chariot shone a supreme, victorious banner, brilliant with refined gold; upon that banner, a vulture gleamed like the one that once graced the chariot of Rāvaṇa, while his horses moved at will.
The divine Māhendra bow was given to Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma;
O King, the divine Vāyavya bow belonged to Bhīmasena.
This weapon was created by Brahmā for the purpose of protecting the three worlds.
That divine and undecaying bow was indeed for the sake of Phalguna;
then the Vaiṣṇava bow for Nakula, and the Aśvin-bow for Sahadeva;
and for Ghaṭotkaca, the divine and terrifying Paulastya bow.
O Bhārata, the five sons of Draupadī possessed five jewel-like bows: the Raudra, the Āgneya, the Kaubera, the Yāmya, and the Giriśa.
Among them, the son of Rohiṇī obtained the Raudra, the most excellent and supreme of bows.
Pleased, Rāma bestowed that [banner] upon the high-souled son of Subhadrā.
These and many other banners, adorned with gold,
were seen there, increasing the grief of his enemies who were heroes.
O great king, that army of Droṇa, crowded with banners and frequented by no cowards, appeared like a painting depicted on a canvas; and then,
in that battle, they heard the names and lineages of the heroes.
O King, as they rushed toward Droṇa in battle, it was like a svayaṃvara ceremony.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"These [warriors] would cause even the army of the gods to tremble in combat."
Those chariot-warriors headed by Vṛkodara who turned back in battle— indeed,
it is said that a man is impelled by destiny;
for within that very destiny, all various kinds of outcomes are seen to manifest.
Having lived for a long time in the forest with matted hair and clad in deerskins,
Yudhiṣṭhira wandered about unknown to the world;
yet it was he who now marshalled that great army for battle.
What else could have happened to my son other than through the conjunction of fate? For a man is surely born endowed with his own destiny;
he is dragged along by it in such a way that he does not wish for himself.
Having fallen into the calamity of gambling, Yudhiṣṭhira was indeed afflicted;
yet, by means of his good fortune, he has regained his allies. Half of my Kekayas have been won, as well as those from Kāśī and Kosala.
"The Cedis and other Vaṅgas have all taken refuge with me alone;
O dear one, the earth is more extensive for me than it is for Pārtha," so the foolish Duryodhana then said to me, O Sūta.

Droṇa, who was well-protected in the midst of that host of armies, has been slain in battle by the son of Pṛṣata; what else can this be but fate? [They saw] the mighty-armed one, who always delighted in battle, in the midst of the kings.

How did death come upon Droṇa, who had reached the further shore of all weapons? Having fallen into great distress and reaching a state of supreme delusion, I have heard that Bhīṣma and Droṇa are slain; I have no desire to live.
"O Sūta, that which the Kṣattṛ spoke to me, dear friend, while perceiving me to be longing for my son— all that has now been obtained by Duryodhana along with me. Yet,
it would have been a supreme act of cruelty had I abandoned Duryodhana."
"I wish to leave behind some remnant of my sons; let this be a hardship, not death.
For that man who abandons righteousness and becomes devoted solely to wealth is deprived of this world and falls into a state of wretchedness."

"And today, O Sañjaya, when the preeminent leader has been crushed, I see no remnant remaining for this kingdom whose energy has been destroyed. For how could there be a remnant when the two draft-oxen have passed away?"
Those two bulls among men, Droṇa and Bhīṣma, who were ever-forgiving and upon whom we constantly relied— now that they have been struck down, what else can this be but destiny?
Tell me clearly, indeed, how the battle proceeded.
Who fought, who retreated, and which base ones fled in fear?
Tell me of Dhananjaya and whatever that bull among chariot-warriors did;
for from him we have the greatest fear, especially from that rival.
O Sañjaya, tell me how there occurred that most terrible encounter between my remaining troops and the Pāṇḍavas when they had turned back;
and how, my dear son, did your minds behave once they had retreated?
"And which heroes among my own men held them back there?
Sañjaya said:
"A great and terrible tumult arose when the Pāṇḍavas had turned back."
Seeing Droṇa being shrouded by them like the sun by clouds,
and seeing the thick dust raised by them, it obscured your army;
then, our vision being lost, we thought Droṇa had been slain.
Seeing those heroes, great archers, desiring to perform a cruel deed,
Duryodhana quickly urged on his own army:
"O lords of men, act according to your strength, according to your energy, and according to your courage!"
"Restrain the army of the Pāṇḍavas as is appropriate.
Having spoken thus, your son himself advanced against Bhīma.
But seeing your son acting so cruelly, Bhīmasena rushed toward him.
Then your son Durmarṣaṇa approached Bhīma;
seeing him from afar, he scattered arrows, desiring the life of Droṇa.
Enraged, he covered him with arrows in that battle, like Death itself.

And Bhīma struck him with arrows; then there was a great tumult. Those wise and heroic strikers, commanded by their lord, disregarding the external fear of death, stood firm against the enemies in battle.
O lord of the people, Kṛtavarman intercepted the son of Śini as he approached— the hero who graces the assembly and was seeking to reach Droṇa.
Enraged, the grandson of Śini (Sātyaki) checked that enraged warrior with volleys of arrows.
Kṛtavarman [held back] the descendant of Śini, like one rutting elephant against another;
and Saindhava Kṣatradharman, with his formidable bow, exerted himself to ward off the great archer who was rushing toward him with a shower of arrows, having been drawn away from Droṇa.

Kṣatradharman, enraged, severed the standard and the bow of the Lord of Sindhu and struck him in all his vital parts with many iron arrows. Then the ruler of Sindhu took up another bow and, displaying great manual dexterity, [discharged shafts].

Subāhu, exerting himself, warded off his heroic brother from Drona, as he was striving for the sake of the Pandavas and piercing Kshatradharman in battle with arrows made entirely of iron. That great car-warrior Yuyutsu was being assailed by him.
As Subāhu was discharging arrows resembling iron clubs along with his bow,
Yuyutsu severed both his arms with two sharp, yellow-edged razor-headed shafts.
Meanwhile, Duḥśāsana [intercepted] Nakula as he was advancing toward Droṇa in the battle.
The hero checked the hero who was shooting with both his left and right hands—
the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, the best of the Pāṇḍavas and king—
just as the shore restrains the agitated ocean; so did the King of Madra hold him back.

Dharmarāja covered him with many arrows that pierce the vital organs; the Lord of Madra, having pierced him with sixty-four shafts, roared loudly. As he was roaring, Dharmarāja cut down his standard along with his bow.
Then, with two razor-sharp arrows, the best of the Pāṇḍavas [struck]; thereupon the people raised a great shout.
Likewise, King Bāhlīka, accompanied by his army, checked King Drupada as he was charging forward with his own troops.
That battle between the two aged warriors, each with his army, became terrible,
like that of two great leaders of elephant herds with temporal juice flowing.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti then assailed Virāṭa, the king of the Matsyas.
Accompanied by their armies and hosts, they were like Indra and Agni against Bali in ancient times.
That tumultuous battle was like the conflict between the gods and the asuras;
it was fought between the Matsyas and the Kekayas, featuring fearless horses, chariots, and elephants.

But Bhūtakarman, the lord of the assembly, checked Śatānīka, the son of Nakula, as he was discharging nets of arrows and advancing toward Droṇa. Then the heir of Nakula [struck him] with three well-sharpened broad-headed arrows.
In that battle, he rendered Bhūtakarman headless and armless.
Then, Viviṃśati checked the heroic Sutasoma as he was rushing toward Droṇa, displaying great prowess and discharging a flood of arrows.
But Sutasoma, filled with rage, pierced his own paternal uncle with straight-flying arrows in that battle;
he too roared again and again, yet, clad in armor,
he did not turn back after piercing Vivimshati with his shafts.
In that great battle, Śālva Bhīmaratha checked the heroic Śrutasena with a shower of arrows as he was advancing toward Droṇa.
Then Bhīmaratha [struck] Śālva with swift, sharp arrows made of iron.

With six [arrows], he sent Śrutakarman— along with his horses and charioteer— to the abode of Yama. O great king, as Śrutakarman approached on horses resembling peacocks, your grandson Caitraseni checked him.
The son of Arjuna (Abhimanyu) rendered his paternal uncle’s appearance shattered with arrows;
and Citrasena covered the son of Draupadī with arrows,
as he was scattering nets of shafts like an elephant in rut.
Dauḥśāsani beheld Śrutakarman approaching;
those two invincible grandsons of yours, each desiring the death of the other,
engaged in a supreme battle for the sake of accomplishing their fathers' purpose.
Seeing the son of Subhadrā, that great car-warrior skilled in all forms of combat, standing at the front in the fray, the son of Droṇa,
honoring his father’s reputation, checked him with his arrows.
Enraged, Prativindhya pierced him—
who bore the mark of a lion’s tail and stood firm for the sake of his father—
with sharp arrows, O bull among men, like one sowing seeds at the time of planting.
The son of Droṇa covered the son of Draupadī with a shower of arrows; likewise,
the son of Duḥśāsana held back the great car-warrior Śrutakīrti, the son of Arjuna and Draupadī, as he was advancing toward Droṇa.
O King, the son of Kṛṣṇa (Sātyaki),
who was considered the bravest among both armies, having severed his bow, standard, and charioteer with three well-sharpened broad-headed arrows, proceeded toward Droṇa.
Lakṣmaṇa checked that slayer of Paṭaccara;
having severed Lakṣmaṇa’s bow and his banner, O Bhārata,
he shone greatly as he discharged nets of arrows at Lakṣmaṇa.

Then Abhimanyu, the son of Arjuna, fought against the skillful and heroic Lakṣmaṇa, who was performing his deeds as a versatile warrior. But the highly wise Vikarṇa fought against Śikhaṇḍin, the son of Yajñasena.
The youth surrounded the advancing youth in battle;
then the son of Yajñasena covered him with a net of arrows, but your powerful son shone forth, having shaken off that mass of shafts.
In that battle, Aṅgada, facing forward, checked with calf-toothed arrows the heroic Uttamaujas as he was advancing toward Droṇa. That encounter between those two lions among men was tumultuous.
Increasing the joy of all the soldiers and of those two [heroes],
that scorcher of foes pierced Aṅgada with five arrows;
Aṅgada, in turn, covered him with ten arrows.
Then there arose a battle between them, one against the other,
among those heroes desiring victory, through their exceeding strength and prowess.
Then the mighty and great archer Durmukha [encountered] the hero Purujit.
He warded off Kuntibhoja as he was advancing toward Droṇa;
he struck Durmukha between the eyebrows with a steel arrow,
and his face shone like a lotus with its stalk.
Karna, however, with showers of arrows, held back the five Kekaya brothers— who bore crimson banners— as they advanced toward Drona.
Enraged, they in turn covered him with volleys of shafts.
And he repeatedly covered them with nets of arrows;
neither Karna nor those five could be seen, shrouded as they were by the shafts,
along with their horses, charioteers, standards, and chariots, all pierced by one another’s arrows.
Your sons Durjaya, Jaya,
and Vijaya— those three heroes— opposed Nīla, Kāśya, and Jaya respectively;
that battle was terrible, increasing the joy of the spectators.
Like lions, tigers, and hyenas against elephants, buffaloes, and bulls,
your sons— Bṛhaddhanu, Bṛhat, Jayamitra, Jaya,
and likewise Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s heroic sons— held them back.
Kṣemadhūrti and Bṛhanta, those two brothers, struck the Sātvata hero with sharp arrows as he advanced toward Droṇa in battle;
that combat between them and him was truly marvelous.
Just as a lion in the forest is resisted by two pre-eminent elephants with temporal juice flowing,
so did the King of Cedi, discharging arrows in a rage, hold back the single King Ambaṣṭha, who delighted in battle, from Droṇa.
Ambaṣṭha pierced him with a bone-shattering shaft;
he, casting aside his bow and arrow, then fell from his chariot to the ground.
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, [struck] Vārṣṇeya Vārdhakṣemi with arrows.
The noble Drona warded off the fierce form of the ignoble Kshudraka.
Those who beheld Kripa and the Varshneya fighting with such wonderful skill became so intent on that battle that their minds were fixed on the fight alone, and they perceived no other activity.

But the son of Somadatta, increasing the fame of Droṇa, quickly intercepted King Maṇimān as he approached with unwearied vigor; having swiftly severed the bow and the standard of the son of Somadatta, [he struck him].
Again, he struck down the banner, the charioteer, and the umbrella from the chariot.
Then, quickly leaping from his chariot, Yūpaketu, the slayer of enemies,
cut that [chariot]— along with its horses, charioteer, standard, and vehicle— with his excellent sword.
Mounting his own chariot and taking up another bow,
O King, he himself guided the horses and scattered the Pandava army,
like Indra approaching the Asuras to slay them, the Pandya king striking down his foes.
Capable with a flood of arrows, he covered [the enemy] like the ocean covering its island;
with maces, iron clubs, swords, spears, stones for battle,
straw-bundles, *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons, darts, lances, and shafts.
The heroic King of Pāṇḍya himself, enraged, struck down the horses of that Lord of Sindhu as he advanced toward Droṇa; meanwhile,
the furious Alambuṣa held back Ghaṭotkaca.
Standing in his chariot during the battle between the deer and the bear, that hero,
like an asura against the gods, covered that great Pāṇḍava army— which resembled the host of the gods— in battle with a flood of arrows from his chariot-bolts.
As Droṇa advanced against Pārtha like Indra himself, striking him down,
the King himself assailed him with a flood of arrows and warded him off. That slayer of enemies struck down the king, along with his horses and charioteer.
With a *pṛṣatka* arrow, he crushed that subduer of enemies, Duryodhana;
having struck the bowstring with that *pṛṣatka*, like a thunderbolt striking a tree,
the hero, causing amazement in the battle, advanced toward Droṇa.
But Alambusa, filled with rage, checked Ghaṭotkaca—
who stood upon his chariot yoked with wolves and bears— with excellent arrows,
maces, clubs, discuses, slings, and battle-axes.
Scattering dust, wind, fire, and water; crushing with ashes, clods, grass, and trees;
tearing asunder, shattering, breaking, striking down, routing, and hurling [his weapons], Ghaṭotkaca advanced, terrifying the army and seeking to reach Droṇa.
Then the enraged Rākṣasa Alambuṣa struck that Rākṣasa with various weapons and diverse modes of combat. Between those two foremost leaders of the Rākṣasas, there ensued a battle.

It was just like what occurred in the past between Śambara and the king of the immortals. But Bhāradvāja, O King, looking only at the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the commander of the army, bypassed many others.
O Great King, they warded off the enemy host as it showered a great net of arrows,
along with their ministers and foot-soldiers;
likewise, O King, there were other monarchs who, due to their great number, have not been mentioned by name.
They all engaged one another according to their rank and according to their strength; horses encountered horses, elephants encountered elephants,
foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers, and the best of chariot-warriors with chariots.
There, those bulls among men performed noble deeds,
consistent with their lineage and prowess, as they engaged one another in combat;
thus there were hundreds of duels between chariots, elephants, and horses.
Blessings to you; such a tumultuous clash between foot soldiers— yours and theirs— has never been seen before, nor has it ever been heard of,
as occurred when they were intent upon the presence or absence of Droṇa.
"This is terrible, this is wonderful, this is fierce"— thus, O Lord,
many extensive battles were seen there.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When they had thus returned and were arrayed in their respective divisions,
how did the sons of Pṛthā and my own energetic warriors fight?
And what did Arjuna do against the force of the Saṃśaptakas?
"O Sañjaya, what did the Saṃśaptakas do against the son of Pṛthā?
Sañjaya said:
"When they had thus returned and advanced against him in their respective divisions,"
Your son himself rushed against Bhīma with a division of elephants;
summoned by the king himself, he charged toward that elephant force like an elephant against an elephant, or a bull against a bull.
Skilled in battle and endowed with the strength of his arms, that son of Pṛthā, O noble one, shattered the elephant division in no time at all. There,
many fierce battles were witnessed.
Those elephants, resembling mountains and exuding rut from all sides,
were turned back and deprived of their pride by Bhīmasena’s iron arrows;
just as the wind disperses masses of clouds on every side.
The son of the Wind likewise scattered those armies;
Bhīma, discharging his arrows at those elephants,
shone like the risen sun casting its rays across all the worlds.
Pierced by the hundreds of Bhīma’s arrows, those elephants shone like various clouds in the sky pierced by the rays of the sun. Thus did the son of the Wind-god continue to slaughter the elephants.
Enraged, Duryodhana approached and pierced him back with sharp arrows.
Then, in an instant, Bhima— whose eyes resembled blood and who desired to lead the king to his destruction— pierced the lord of the earth with whetted feathered shafts.

With all his limbs pierced by arrows, he, filled with rage, struck the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena as if smiling, piercing him with iron shafts as brilliant as the rays of the sun. [He struck] the jewel-encrusted elephant that stood upon his banner, variegated with gems.

With two broad-headed arrows, the Pāṇḍava swiftly cut down Duryodhana’s bow. O sire, seeing Duryodhana being oppressed by Bhīma, Aṅga, mounted upon an elephant, approached, desiring to cause a disturbance.
As that elephant charged with a roar like a thundercloud,
Bhīmasena struck it violently between its frontal globes with a steel arrow (nārāca).
Having pierced through its body, the arrow sank deep into the surface of the earth.
Then the elephant fell like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt. As that Mleccha was about to fall, having lost control of his mount,
Vṛkodara, acting with swift precision, severed his head with a broad-headed arrow.
When that hero had fallen, that army fled in all directions,
with its horses, elephants, and chariots thrown into confusion, trampling the foot soldiers as it went;
and while all those divisions were fleeing on every side, [the battle continued].
Then the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa rushed against Bhīma on an elephant—
the very same elephant with which Maghavan had conquered the Daityas and Dānavas—
and he charged at Bhīmasena upon that elephant of his lineage.
That preeminent elephant rushed suddenly toward Bhīma with his two ears,
his feet, and his trunk contracted together;
with rolling eyes and filled with rage, he seemed to consume the Pāṇḍava.
He crushed Vṛkodara’s chariot along with its horses without distinction; then Bhīma, running on foot, hid himself within his limbs. Knowing the *añjalikāvedha* maneuver, the Pāṇḍava did not retreat.
Having entered within its body, he repeatedly struck it with his hand and fondled that elephant, who was seeking to kill him and remained unyielding;
then the elephant whirled rapidly like a potter’s wheel.
The glorious Kālayāna, possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, rushed toward Vṛkodara;
Bhīma also emerged from there and stood before Supratīka.
Bending down with his trunk, he threw Bhīma down upon his knees.
Having coiled himself around the elephant's neck, that beast sought to kill him;
Bhīmasena, by executing a whirlwind motion, loosened his grip on the trunk and freed himself.
Then Vṛkodara once again entered the body of the elephant.
As long as he observed his own forces stationed against the approaching enemy elephant,
Bhīma also emerged from the body of the beast and fled with speed;
then, a great roar arose from the entire army.
"Alas, alas! Bhīma has been struck down by the elephant!"— O Sire, at that cry, the army of the Pāṇḍavas was terrified and suddenly rushed, O King, toward the place where Vṛkodara stood.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, believing Vṛkodara to have been slain,
surrounded Bhagadatta on all sides along with the Pañcālas.
The powerful Bhīma, moreover, having crushed the lord of elephants with his two arms, released it.
Surrounding him on all sides with their chariots, those best of chariot-warriors showered him with sharp arrows by the hundreds and thousands. He, for his part,
countered that onslaught of shafts with his goad.

With his elephant, the lord of the mountains scattered the Pāṇḍus and Pāñcālas; O lord of the people, we beheld that wonderful feat of Bhagadatta in battle as he, though so aged, moved about with his elephant.

Then the king of the Daśārṇas rushed toward the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa with an elephant that moved swiftly like the wind, intoxicated and galloping obliquely. A battle then took place between those two elephants of terrifying form.
Just as in the past, when two rival kings of mountains, both possessing trees,
were at war, the elephant of the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, having approached and turned back,
went to the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa and awakened the elephant.
Then Bhagadatta,
with seven lances as radiant as the rays of the sun,
struck that enemy who was mounted upon an elephant whose seat had been shaken, piercing its flank and felling it.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing the lord of Daśārṇa slain,
charged toward the king of Prāgjyotiṣa with a great multitude of chariots.
Having approached King Bhagadatta, Yudhiṣṭhira—

With a great array of chariots, he surrounded him on all sides. Seated upon his elephant and encompassed by the chariot-warriors, he shone like a blazing fire situated in the midst of a forest on a mountain.
That elephant moved about, surrounded on all sides by a circle of chariot-warriors with fierce bows who were scattering showers of arrows;
then the King of Prāgjyotiṣa, having seized that bull among elephants, [proceeded].

He suddenly dispatched [his chariot] toward the chariot of Yuyudhāna. But seeing the elephant charging toward him, that bull among the Sātvatas pierced it with five sharp arrows resembling venomous serpents.
O lord of the people, having been deeply pierced by the powerful Sātyaki,
he— afflicted by arrows— turned away in terror, wheeling in circles; meanwhile,
that great elephant seized the chariot of Śini’s grandson.
Yuyudhāna hurled [the weapon] with great force, but he drew back;
however, the charioteer, having raised up the large Sindhu horses,
stood firm and brought the chariot back, having leaped over it once more toward Sātyaki.
But that Naga, having found an opening, quickly emerged from the circle of chariots and then scattered all the kings. Those bulls among men were terrified by him as he moved with such swift speed.
In that battle, the kings perceived that single elephant as if it were hundreds;
those Pāṇḍavas were driven away by Bhagadatta mounted upon his elephant,
just as the Dānavas were driven by the King of the Gods mounted upon Airāvata.
As those Pāñcālas fled here and there,
a tremendous roar arose from their elephants and horses;
for the Pāṇḍus were being driven back in battle by Bhagadatta.
Enraged, Bhīma once again advanced toward Prāgjyotiṣa.
As he was charging forward, the elephant drenched his horses with water discharged from its trunk; thus terrified, the beast then carried away the son of Pṛthā.
Then the son of Ruciparvan and Ākṛti quickly advanced against him,
standing upon his chariot like the Destroyer himself, drenching him with a shower of arrows.
Then, with a straight-knotted arrow, he struck Ruciparvan.
Suparvan, the lord of mountains, was led to the abode of Vaivasvata.
When that hero had fallen, the son of Subhadrā, the sons of Draupadī,
Cekitāna, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Yuyutsu began to afflict the elephant.
Desiring to kill him, they drenched him with showers of arrows like clouds with torrents of rain, uttering terrible roars;
then the elephant, urged by the skillful driver with his heels, hooks, and toes, [proceeded].
With his trunk extended and his ears and eyes fixed in a rigid stare, he rushed forward swiftly;
treading upon Yuyutsu’s horses with his feet, he crushed the charioteer and,
filled with rage, shattered the chariot like a fierce wind breaking a tree.
But Yuyutsu, O King, quickly alighted from his chariot;
then those Pāṇḍava warriors swiftly struck the king of elephants with arrows,
while your son, in great agitation, leaped onto the chariot of Subhadrā’s son.
Seated upon his elephant and discharging arrows at his enemies,
that king shone like the sun emitting its rays over the worlds;
then he was pressed down in many ways by Bhīma with his tusks.
The elephant, possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, was rescued by that warrior skilled in battle. Then the son of Arjuna, eager for combat, pierced him with twelve arrows,
while the sons of Draupadī and Dhṛṣṭaketu each struck him with three shafts.
Cekitāna, in turn, pierced all of them with sixty-four arrows, including his superior weapons; Bhagadatta then struck each of them back with three shafts.
Covered by those arrows discharged with great effort by his enemy, that elephant shone resplendent.
Like a great cloud pierced by the rays of the sun, that elephant—
afflicted by the enemy's arrows and driven by the skill and effort of its driver—
threw those foes to the left and to the right.
Just as a cowherd with his staff repeatedly drives his herds of cattle in the forest,
so did Bhagadatta repeatedly drive that army about.
The sound was like that of crows when suddenly attacked by a hawk.
O King, a vast cloud of dust covered the firmament;
that trail of dust shone in the sky like a raised staff,
towering as if it were the upraised arm of the army in its state of extreme distress.
"Chase after the son of Kuntī!"— as if urging Arjuna on,
such was the great outcry of the Pāṇḍavas as they fled in haste.
That king of elephants, struck by the excellent goad;
O King, like a great mountain with its wings intact in ancient times,
he instilled intense fear in his enemies,
just as a turbulent ocean terrifies groups of merchants.
Then, from the elephants, chariots, horses, and kings fleeing in terror, a most terrifying noise was produced,
filling the earth, the sky, the heavens, and likewise the intermediate and cardinal directions.
Then, O lord of kings, that ruler of the earth completely surrounded him on all sides in that battle with that preeminent elephant.
He plunged deeply into the army of his enemies—
which had previously been well-guarded by the gods— as Virocana once did against the celestial host in battle.
The wind, the friend of fire, blew fiercely, and dust repeatedly shrouded the sky as well as the soldiers;
[they surrounded] that single elephant with their troops, just as elephants surround a single elephant.
The people thought it was as if [the earth] were fleeing in every direction.
Sañjaya said:
"As for what you ask me regarding the deeds of Pārtha in battle—"
Listen to that, O Great King, which Pārtha did in the battle:
having seen the dust that had arisen and having heard the trumpeting of the elephants as they were being broken by Bhagadatta,
the son of Kuntī spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
"O Madhusūdana, this is surely the sound of the King of Prāgjyotiṣa as he hastens past us on his elephant;
for in battle he is not inferior to Indra himself and is highly skilled in the management of elephants."
Whether he be first or second on earth— such is my thought—
he is that best of elephants, who has no rival elephant in battle;
he transcends all sounds in combat, has accomplished his tasks, and has conquered fatigue.
O sinless one, he who withstands the falling of weapons and the touch of fire will clearly destroy the Pāṇḍava army alone today,
having let out a great lion’s roar along with the sounds of his bow and arrows.
Beholding my army being routed, its leaders for the most part slain, and seeing him suddenly roaring and crushing my forces,
there is no one other than the two of us capable of resisting him.
Therefore, proceed with haste to where the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa resides—
he who is amazed by his friendship with Śakra, his elephant forces, and his great age. Today I shall send him as a welcome guest to the slayer of Bala.
Then, at the word of Savyasācin, Kṛṣṇa proceeded to where the Pāṇḍava army was being torn apart by Bhagadatta. As he was thus advancing, the great car-warriors from behind called out to him.
Fourteen thousand Saṃśaptakas ascended [to battle],
O lord of men; ten thousand were from the Trigartas,
and four thousand were the followers of Vāsudeva.
O venerable one, seeing his army being shattered by Bhagadatta and being summoned by those [foes],
his heart was divided in two as he reflected,
"What action would truly be for my welfare?"

"Either I shall turn back from here, or I shall go to Yudhiṣṭhira. Having reflected upon this with his intellect, O bull of the Kurus, Arjuna’s mind became increasingly firm in its resolve to slay the Saṃśaptakas.
That son of Vāsava, whose banner bears the foremost of monkeys, suddenly returned alone to slay thousands of chariots in battle;
for such was the intention of both Duryodhana and Karṇa.
He devised a double stratagem for the means of Arjuna’s slaughter; however,
that son of Pāṇḍu, by means of his duplicity,
rendered that plan of those foremost of chariot-warriors futile with his own chariot.
Then, O King, the great car-warriors of the Saṃśaptakas discharged hundreds of thousands of straight-knotted arrows at Arjuna;
yet neither Pārtha, the son of Kuntī, nor Janārdana Kṛṣṇa was [overwhelmed].
O King, neither the horses nor the chariot could be seen, as they were covered by arrows.
Then, Arjuna, Upendra, and the chariot together with its horses and banner were no longer visible,
being completely shrouded by that powerful shower of shafts.
Then, completely covered by that great shower of arrows,
Bībhatsu was indeed unable to repel his enemies;
and Janārdana fell into a state of confusion and broke out in sweat.
Then Janārdana, as if smiling, replied to Pārtha:
"Fixing the Vajra weapon, slay the Saṃśaptakas here.
Thereupon, Pārtha struck them down for the most part with the Vajra weapon.
Hundreds of hands were severed, still clutching arrows, bowstrings, and bows;
standards, horses, charioteers, and car-warriors fell upon the earth.
Well-constructed and resembling trees, mountain peaks, or clouds, they lay scattered.

Struck by the arrows of Pārtha, elephants fell to the earth with their riders slain; their blankets and reins were scattered, their trappings torn away, and they were deprived of life. Horses, crushed by Pārtha’s shafts, fell along with their riders.
Severed by the broad-headed arrows of Kirīṭin, the arms of men— equipped with spears, shields, swords, and claws, as well as mallets and battle-axes— fell down,
O noble one, resembling the young sun, the lotus, and the moon.
Severed by Arjuna’s arrows, heads fell to the earth;
the army blazed with those feathered shafts, which were adorned and devourers of life,
as the enraged Phalguna struck his enemies with weapons of various forms.
Then, as he agitated that army like an elephant agitating a lotus pond, the hosts of beings honored Dhanañjaya, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
And beholding that feat of Pārtha, which was like that of Vāsava, Mādhava [was filled with joy].
Filled with supreme wonder, he struck his palms together in worship and said:
"O Pārtha, it is my conviction that this deed you have performed today in battle is difficult even for Śakra, Yama, or the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) to achieve."
And in that battle, I saw hundreds and thousands of great car-warriors among the Saṃśaptakas fallen all at once. Then,
having slain the majority of those Saṃśaptakas who remained stationed there...
"Go toward Bhagadatta," Pārtha urged Kṛṣṇa.
Sañjaya said:
Then, as Pārtha was desirous of going, Kṛṣṇa [urged] his horses, which were as swift as thought.
He dispatched white jars covered with gold for the army of Droṇa.
As that best of the Kurus set forth to protect his own men who were tormented by Droṇa,
Suśarman, seeking battle, followed behind him along with his brothers.
Then Jaya, whose horses are white, spoke to the unconquered Kṛṣṇa:
"O Acyuta, here is Suśarman challenging me along with my brothers;
O slayer of enemies, this army of ours is being torn asunder by the northern flank."
My mind is now divided by these Saṃśaptakas:
"Should I slay the Saṃśaptakas, or should I protect my own people who are afflicted by their enemies?
You know this thought of mine; what would be the best course of action in this matter?
Thus addressed, the descendant of Daśārha turned the chariot back toward where the lord of the Trigartas had challenged the Pāṇḍava. Then Arjuna pierced Suśarman with seven swift arrows.
With two razor-sharp arrows, he likewise cut down his standard and bow; then,
with six iron shafts, Pārtha swiftly dispatched the brother of the lord of Trigarta, along with his horses and charioteer, to the abode of Yama.
Then Suśarman, aiming at Arjuna, hurled an iron spear resembling a serpent, and at Vāsudeva, he cast a *tomara* lance. Having cut down the spear with three arrows and the *tomara* with three, Arjuna—
Having bewildered Suśarman with volleys of arrows, he turned back;
O King, no one among your troops could restrain him as he advanced like Vāsava, raining down a torrent of many showers of shafts.

Then Dhananjaya, from that very place, began striking down the great car-warriors among the Kauravas with his arrows, like a fire consuming dry undergrowth. Yet, the unbearable force of that wise son of Kuntī was difficult to withstand.

They were unable to endure him, just as living beings cannot endure the touch of fire. Enveloping the ranks with a shower of arrows, O King, the son of Pāṇḍu advanced toward Prāgjyotiṣa like the swoop of a Garuḍa.

O King, that very bow which was then the source of health for the victorious Bharatas who never retreated— a bow that ensured security in battle and caused the tears of enemies to flow— is now yours, whose son plays with such a disastrous dice-game.
Having resolved upon the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, Arjuna drew his bow;
thus agitated by Pārtha,
O great king, your army was shattered like a boat that has struck a mountain.
Then ten thousand archers turned back,
those heroes enraged in battle, having set their minds upon victory or defeat.
That chariot was free from fear in its heart and transcended the laws of calamity.
Pārtha, capable of bearing every burden in battle, took up that heavy weight;
like an enraged sixty-year-old elephant with temples rent open might trample a forest of reeds,
so did the exerted Pārtha crush your army.
When that army had been crushed, Bhagadatta, the lord of men,
suddenly rushed toward Dhanañjaya with that elephant.
That tiger among men received him fearlessly with his chariot.
A tumultuous encounter took place between that chariot and the elephant,
both equipped according to the scriptures;
in that battle, the two heroes Bhagadatta and Dhanañjaya moved about.

Then, like Indra overcoming the clouds, Bhagadatta, the subduer of foes, rained a shower of arrows upon Dhanañjaya from his elephant that resembled a mass of clouds. And Vāsavi, too, met that shower of arrows with a shower of his own.
The valiant son of Indra (Arjuna) cut down [the weapon] even before it had reached him;
by means of his swiftness, he quickly parried it. Then Dhananjaya once again rained down a shower of arrows.

Then, O Bhārata, the king of Prāgjyotiṣa, having warded off that shower of arrows, struck the mighty-armed Pārtha and Kṛṣṇa with his own shafts. Then, having overwhelmed those two with a vast net of arrows, he...
He urged that elephant forward for the slaughter of Acyuta and Pārtha.
Seeing that elephant charging like the enraged God of Death,
Janārdana swiftly turned his chariot to the right to avoid it.
Even when he had reached that great elephant,
Dhanañjaya, mindful of his duty (*dharma*), did not wish to deliver it— along with its rider— to death as it turned back.
But that elephant, O noble one, having crushed elephants, chariots, and horses, [rushed forward].
He dispatched him to the realm of death; thereupon Dhanañjaya became enraged.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Being thus provoked to anger, what did the Pāṇḍava do to Bhagadatta?"
"Tell me truly, was it the King of Prāgjyotiṣa or the son of Pṛthā [who encountered him]?
Sañjaya said:
"Both the descendant of Daśārha and the son of Pāṇḍu were engaged in combat with the King of Prāgjyotiṣa."

All living beings considered those two to have reached the very presence of Death itself; for thus, O Lord, Bhagadatta from the back of his elephant incessantly showered volleys of arrows upon the two Kṛṣṇas stationed on their chariot.
Then, with iron arrows released from a fully drawn bow—
gold-feathered, whetted on stone, sharp as the touch of fire, and impelled by Bhagadatta— he pierced the son of Devakī.
Then those arrows, having pierced through the son of Devakī, entered the earth.
Having cut his bow and destroyed his quiver, Pārtha fought with King Bhagadatta as if in sport.

Savyasācin discharged fourteen sharp javelins, glowing like the rays of the sun; he then cut each one of them into three pieces. Thereafter, the son of Pākaśāsana shattered the armor of that elephant.
With that net of arrows, he shone like the king of mountains when free from clouds;
that elephant, its armor shattered and severely afflicted by the shafts, fell to the surface of the earth in pieces.
Then the elephant on his head shone forth;
thereafter, the king of Prāgjyotiṣa hurled an iron spear with a golden shaft at Vāsudeva, but Arjuna cut it into two pieces.
Then Arjuna, smiling, quickly cut down the king’s parasol and banner with his arrows and pierced the lord of the mountains with ten shafts.
Deeply pierced by Arjuna’s well-feathered arrows with vulture plumes, he [fell].
Then Bhagadatta, enraged, hurled iron javelins at the head of the high-souled Pāṇḍava, who possessed white horses, and let out a loud roar;
by those [javelins], Arjuna’s diadem was displaced in the battle.
Adjusting his displaced crown, Phalguna said to the king, "Take a good look at this world. Thus addressed,
he became enraged and assailed the Pāṇḍava with a shower of arrows.
Taking up his radiant bow, he rained arrows upon Govinda.
O Bhārata, though they were pierced by Bhagadatta’s iron shafts, those two— Acyuta and Arjuna— neither fell into confusion nor were they shaken.
Pārtha, having cut his bow and destroyed his quivers, swiftly struck him in all his vital organs with seventy-two arrows. Though thus pierced, he remained unperturbed and invoked the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
Enraged, he consecrated a goad with mantras and hurled it at the chest of the Pāṇḍava.
Seeing that weapon raised, the powerful Vāsudeva placed Arjuna behind him and, full of valor, received the blow himself.
Keśava, shielding Pārtha, received with his own chest that all-slaying weapon discharged by Bhagadatta;
that weapon became the Vaijayantī garland upon Keśava’s breast.
Variegated with lotus buds and filled with flowers of every season,
rich with the colors of blazing fire, sun, and moon, and possessing the brilliance of shimmering stars;
by that [forest], which was beautified by lotuses and made restless by the wind—
Śauri shines most brilliantly, resembling an *atasī* flower;
Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and crusher of enemies,
is like the best of mountains shrouded by the clouds of twilight during the rainy season.
Then Arjuna, with a weary mind, addressed Keśava:
"O Janārdana, I am but a driver who does not fight;
having said this, O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, you do not keep your own promise."
"O son of Devakī, tiger among men, why did you yourself accept this weapon when it was offered to me by you after you had set it aside?
[This would have been so] if I were in distress or incapable of warding it off."
"Therefore, you must act in this manner; however, while I am present, this should not be done.
With my arrow and my bow, I am capable of conquering these worlds—including gods, asuras, and humans—and that too is known to you."
Then Vāsudeva replied to Arjuna with these meaningful words:
"Listen, O sinless Pārtha, to this secret as it occurred in the past. This goddess who is the supporter of the worlds, the supporter of all beings, is the Earth."
Her desire fulfilled, she approached Nārāyaṇa, the creator of the world. Having united with her, he was pleased and granted her a boon.
She chose a son equal to Viṣṇu and the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
And a son named Naraka was born of her, who became world-renowned;
and Nārāyaṇa himself bestowed upon him the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
That very weapon of Naraka was the destroyer of all enemies.
Therefore, the *prāgjyotiṣa* [weapon] has been obtained, which destroys all weapons.
O Arjuna, there is no one else in this world who cannot be slain by it except for me.
Sañjaya said:
"Therefore, this has indeed been done by me; let there be no other thought in your mind.
Having thus conciliated the Pāṇḍava, the descendant of Daśārha quickly said:
"Slay the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa swiftly, and hear the remainder of my words."

I am eternally fourfold in form, ever intent upon the protection of the worlds; dividing myself here, I bring about the welfare of the worlds. One form of mine, established on earth, performs ascetic penance.
One sees the world performing good and evil deeds; another, resorting to the world of men, performs action;
but a fourth lies in sleep for a thousand years.
At the end of a thousand years, that form of mine which arises bestows the most excellent boons upon those worthy of boons;
knowing then that that time had arrived, the Earth—
Listen to the boon he requested of me for the sake of Naraka:
"Let my son be unslayable by both gods and asuras;
let him be endowed with the Vaiṣṇava weapon—this you ought to grant me."
Having thus heard the boon from the daughter of the Earth at that time,
I then gave her that Vaiṣṇava weapon, which is never-failing; and I said, "Indeed,
let this weapon be unfailing upon the earth."
For the sake of protecting him from hell, no one shall slay him;
guarded by this weapon, your son, the crusher of enemy forces,
shall be invincible at all times throughout all the worlds.
Having said, "So be it," the wise goddess departed, her purpose accomplished.
Then the goddess Earth gave birth to a son, the youngest of a hundred sons. And he was the invincible Naraka, the scorcher of his enemies.

Therefore, O Pārtha, that weapon of mine has reached Prāgjyotiṣa. That weapon would slay all the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Pannagas, and Rākṣasas even if they were gathered together; how much more so you, Dhanañjaya?
"O Pārtha, I have given you this weapon, which is invincible even to the gods and asuras and cannot be withstood by those who possess wealth. Slay the King of Prāgjyotiṣa before he destroys us all;
O noble one, there is no one in the worlds, including Indra and Rudra, who is immune to it."
"Because of you, I have rendered this weapon useless; it has been deprived of its supreme power. O Pārtha, slay the great asura Bhagadatta, that enemy of the gods who is invincible in battle."
Just as I previously slew Naraka for the sake of the world's welfare,
so too is this Bhagadatta incapable of being slain by even the gods and asuras with their great weapons,
just as I formerly killed Naraka for the benefit of the world.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Keśava,
Pārtha then suddenly overwhelmed Bhagadatta with sharp arrows,
as well as his bell covered in gold and fashioned by Viśvakarman.
The Pāṇḍava severed the left [leg], which was bound with golden chains;
struck by the impact of his arrow, which resembled the crash of a thunderbolt,
it fell from a great distance, radiant as the orb of the moon.
O King, even the bell of Kirīṭin’s chariot was struck by arrows;
having traveled a great distance, it fell to the earth like the sun.
Supratīka also, released with great force by Bhagadatta, [fell].
Like Hanumān exerting himself to swallow the orb of the sun,
the mighty-armed Pārtha, unperturbed and high-minded,
struck the elephant between its two frontal globes with a steel arrow.
Then, having fixed an arrow that blazed like fire,
Arjuna pierced the elephant deeply between its two frontal globes.
Having reached that elephant, the arrow struck it like a thunderbolt hitting a mountain.
Like a serpent entering its ant-hill, it retreated along with the arrow;
though urged again and again by Bhagadatta,
that elephant did not obey his word, just as a poor man’s lover disregards his command.
Split in the middle, he stood there, and then he flowed again and again;
as the elephant was thus flowing, he prodded him with his two feet.
But the elephant, having stiffened his limbs, went toward the earth with his two tusks.
Crying out with a piteous sound, that great elephant gave up its life.
Then Keśava addressed the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow:
"O Pārtha, this one is even greater; he is completely covered in grey hair."
With eyes covered by wrinkles, the hero was exceedingly difficult to conquer; yet,
though that king always wore a cloth bandage for the purpose of keeping his eyes open,
Arjuna, acting upon the word of the gods, cut it away completely with an arrow.

As soon as that parrot was cut down, the powerful Bhagadatta closed his eyes; he perceived the entire world to be filled with darkness. Then, with a crescent-shaped arrow of smooth joints, [he struck].
His entire body was split asunder and became divided in two;
held up by his knees by that powerful king in the battle,
he did not remain suspended for long against Arjuna.
Thus did that battle take place then between the king and that evil-minded one;
and with a straight-knotted arrow having a crescent-shaped head, the Pāṇḍava Kirīṭin pierced the heart of King Bhagadatta.
With his heart pierced by the diadem-wearing Arjuna, King Bhagadatta, losing his life,
dropped both his bow and his arrows. His excellent goad fell away from his head as it slipped off.
Like a palāśa petal fallen from a lotus when its stalk is struck,
he— wearing a golden garland— fell from that mountain-like elephant which was adorned with golden trappings.
Like a *karṇikāra* tree in full bloom blown down by the force of the wind from the mountain peak,
he struck down that king who possessed the prowess of Indra.
Just as Indra’s companion, the son of Indra, [acts] in battle,
so then did he crush other men who desired victory for you,
like a powerful wind breaking trees.
Saṃjaya said:
Having slain the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa, who was a constant favorite of Indra and possessed of immeasurable energy, Pārtha circumambulated him.
The two Kṛṣṇas— the scion of the Daśārhas and Bibhatsu— slew in battle the former Daitya, the great hero Bhagadatta of immense strength, who was difficult to conquer,
possessed the power and vitality of ten thousand elephants, and was a hero who graced the field of combat.
Supratīka was also powerful, possessing strength equal to ten thousand elephants;
endowed with the Vaiṣṇava weapon and the goad, he was heroic. There, those three splendors were present together like the three sacrificial fires at a ritual.
"Who, other than Arjuna, could slay the heroic Bhagadatta in battle?
And even Arjuna, though possessed of great prowess, having slain his father’s friend in combat, reflected upon the duty of a Kshatriya and cried out, 'Fie! Fie! on the field."
Then, beholding him fallen from heaven to the earth like the sun in brilliance, yet shrouded by dust,
Pārtha [beheld] the two sons of the King of Gāndhāra, conquerors of enemy cities.
The two brothers, Vṛṣaka and Ācala, assailed Arjuna in battle. Those two heroic archers, meeting Arjuna from both the front and the rear,
pierced him violently with sharp, high-velocity arrows.
With sharp arrows, Pārtha shattered Vṛṣaka’s horses, charioteer, bow, umbrella, chariot, and standard into pieces as small as sesame seeds;
then Arjuna [assailed him] with showers of arrows and various other weapons.
He once again threw the Gāndhāras, led by the son of Subala, into utter confusion.
Then, filled with rage, Dhanañjaya dispatched five hundred heroic Gāndhāra warriors, who stood with weapons raised, to the realm of death with his arrows.
Quickly descending from the chariot whose horses had been slain, the mighty-armed one mounted his brother’s chariot and took up another bow.
Then those two brothers, Vṛṣaka and Acala, ascended a single chariot.
With a shower of arrows,
those two high-souled kings, your brothers-in-law Vṛṣaka and Ācala,
pierced Bībhatsu again and again; they struck Pārtha most fiercely, like Vṛtra and Bala striking Indra.
Having found their mark, the two Gāndhāra princes struck the Pāṇḍava again,
just as the summer and rainy months afflict the world with heat and rain.
Those two tigers among men, the kings Vṛṣaka and Ācala, stood upon their chariots.

O King, as those two stood with their limbs locked together, Arjuna struck them with a single arrow. Those two heroes, resembling lions, with red eyes and mighty arms— brothers of identical appearance— fell lifeless from their chariot.
The bodies of those two, who were dear to their kinsmen, fell from the chariot to the earth;
having caused their merit and fame to pervade the ten directions, they lay still. Seeing his two maternal uncles slain in battle, they had not fled.
O lord of the people, seeing their two brothers slain, your sons shed profuse tears; then Śakuni, who was skilled in a hundred illusions,
employed an illusion that bewildered the two Kṛṣṇas.
Clubs, iron balls, stones, *śataghnīs*, and spears;
maces, iron bars, swords, tridents, mallets, *paṭṭiśas*,
*kampanas*, *ṛṣṭis*, claws, pestles, and battle-axes.
Razors, razor-edged shafts, calf-toothed arrows, and those with three joints;
discuses, arrows, spears, and various other weapons fell from all directions and intermediate points toward Arjuna.
Donkeys, camels, buffaloes, lions, tigers, sṛmaras, chillas,
bears, jackals, vultures, monkeys, and reptiles,
as well as various kinds of hungry *rakṣas* [demons], rushed toward Arjuna.
Various birds, filled with rage, rushed toward him;
then the heroic Dhananjaya, son of Kuntī and skilled in divine weapons,
suddenly struck them down by discharging nets of arrows.
Being struck by that hero with excellent, firm arrows,
they perished on all sides, uttering great cries as they were slain.
Then, a darkness appeared toward Arjuna’s chariot.
And from that darkness, cruel voices reviled the son of Pṛthā.
That terrifying, formidable darkness, which caused fear in the great battle,
Arjuna destroyed with a mighty weapon of light.
When he was slain, terrifying floods of water appeared.
Then Arjuna, for the purpose of destroying that water, discharged the Āditya weapon;
by that weapon, the water was for the most part dried up.
Thus, as the son of Subala repeatedly employed various kinds of illusions, Arjuna, laughing, swiftly destroyed them all with the power of his weapons.
"O gambler, O son of Gandhāra, it is not dice that you cast; it is the Gāṇḍīva! he cried.
The Gāṇḍīva bow discharged blazing, whetted, and sharp arrows; thus,
when his illusions were destroyed and he was struck by Arjuna’s shafts,
Śakuni fled on swift horses like an ordinary man in terror.
Then Arjuna, the foremost of those skilled in weapons, displaying his own preeminence among his enemies,
rained down a flood of arrows upon the army of the Kauravas.
That host of your son was being slaughtered by Pārtha.
Split in two, O great king, like the Ganges upon reaching a mountain, some of those great car-warriors there followed Droṇa alone,
while others, O king, being harassed by Kirīṭin, followed Duryodhana.
Then we could no longer see this army, for it was indeed enveloped in darkness;
yet the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow was heard by me from the south,
along with the sound of conchs, drums, and the resonance of musical instruments.
And the roar of the Gāṇḍīva, transcending all, touched the very heavens.
Then, once again, there was a fierce battle on the right side between those who fight with diverse skills;
Arjuna fought a great battle, while I followed after Droṇa.
The armies of Yudhiṣṭhira were burning them on every side; O Bhārata, Arjuna scattered the various divisions of your sons at that time, just as the wind disperses clouds in the sky.
No one could restrain that fierce tiger among men, the great archer, as he approached like Vāsava himself, raining down a torrent of arrows;
being struck by Pārtha, your troops were deeply distressed.
Many of their own men were slain as they fled hither and thither.
Those arrows released by Arjuna— feathered with heron plumes and capable of piercing the body—
fell like locusts, shrouding the ten directions.
O noble one, having pierced through horse, chariot-warrior, elephant, and even foot-soldier,
they entered the earth like serpents entering an anthill;
he did not discharge a second arrow at those elephants, horses, or men.
Struck individually by single arrows, they fell down, deprived of life;
the ground was covered everywhere with slain men and horses,
and with elephants struck down by a rain of arrows.
Then the head of the battlefield became a wondrous sight, resounding with the cries of dogs, jackals, and crows;
fathers abandoned their sons, and friends their dearest friends.
Likewise, a son [abandoned] his father when afflicted by arrows; at that time, people, intent on self-preservation and tormented by the son of Pṛthā, even abandoned their mounts.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, when those armies had been broken by the son of Pāṇḍu,
what indeed was the state of mind of you who were shaken and fleeing?"
"O Sūta, since my troops were broken and could see no means of regrouping, what did my men do next in battle? Tell me, Sañjaya, how they performed that difficult task of reformation."
Saṃjaya said:
"Nevertheless, O lord of the people, desiring to do what was pleasing to your son and protecting their fame in the worlds, those great heroes followed Droṇa."
When weapons were raised and Yudhiṣṭhira had arrived,
those of immeasurable prowess performed noble deeds in that terrifying situation as if they were not afraid; they fell upon the opening of Bhīmasena.
O Lord, the cruel Pāñcālas urged on Droṇa, crying "Droṇa! Droṇa!", while your sons urged all the Kurus, crying "Do not [slay] Droṇa!"— [thus urging] the heroic Sātyaki and Dhṛṣṭadyumna as well.
"Kill Droṇa! Kill Droṇa! cried some, while others cried, "Do not kill Droṇa!
Thus did the game of dice unfold between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, as Droṇa assailed whichever cluster of Pāñcāla chariots he encountered.

Then, in that terrible battle where the distribution of roles was overturned, the Pāñcālya Dhṛṣṭadyumna was stationed here and there; the heroes encountered heroes, while the cowards fled to the enemy.
There, the Pāṇḍavas became unshakable by their enemies,
yet they caused the enemy ranks to tremble as they remembered their own past sufferings. Driven by their inner strength, though possessed of modesty, they fell under the sway of indignation.
Having cast away their lives, they turned back to strike Droṇa in that great battle;
it was like a clashing of iron and a falling of rocks,
as those of immeasurable splendor gambled with their very lives in that tumultuous combat.
But even the elders do not remember such a battle,
O Great King, whether previously seen or even heard of before;
indeed, the earth seemed to tremble during that slaughter of heroes.
As that great flood of troops set forth, oppressed by its own weight,
the roar of the surging host was as if it had paralyzed the very heavens;
such was the sound produced by your son Ajātaśatru as he marched in his wrath.
Having encountered the Pandava armies by the thousands,
they were shattered in battle by Drona as he moved about with his sharp arrows;
while they were being thus crushed by Drona of wondrous deeds.
Having approached Droṇa himself, the commander-in-chief surrounded him;
that battle between Droṇa and the Pāñcālya at that time was truly wonderful,
and it is my opinion that no comparison whatsoever could possibly exist for it.

Then Nīla, resembling a blazing fire, consumed the Kuru army— his arrows the sparks and his bow the flame, like a fire burning dry undergrowth. As he was thus consuming the ranks, the powerful son of Droṇa [advanced].
Addressing him first with gentle words and a smile, he said:
"O Nīla, what is the use of these many warriors of yours being consumed by the flames of my arrows? Fight alone with me; enraged, strike at me with your swift shafts."
Nīla pierced with his arrows that man who resembled a cluster of lotuses, whose eyes were like lotus petals, and whose face was like a full-blown lotus.
Suddenly, the son of Droṇa, having been deeply pierced by him, struck back with three sharp broad-headed shafts.
He cut down the bow, the banner, and the umbrella of his enemy. Then Nīla, leaping from that chariot and wielding an excellent sword and shield,
desired to sever the head of Droṇāyani from his body, like a bird of prey.
O sinless one, as he raised his sword, the son of Droṇa, as if smiling, struck off from the body that head with its beautiful nose and earrings using a broad-headed arrow—
his face resembling the full moon and his eyes like lotus petals.

Tall and resembling the interior of a blue lotus, he fell slain upon the earth. Then the Pāṇḍava army was deeply distressed and became utterly agitated when Nīla, blazing with splendor, was killed by the preceptor’s son.
And all those great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas thought, "O noble one, how shall Vāsavi protect us from our enemies? Meanwhile,
the mighty hero was causing a slaughter on the right flank of the army.
[Regarding] the remnants of the Saṃśaptakas and the Nārāyaṇa force,
Sañjaya said:
"Vṛkodara, however, could not endure the repulse of his army."
He pierced Bāhlīka with sixty arrows and Karṇa with ten.
Droṇa, seeking to bring about the end of his life, swiftly struck him in his vital organs with sharp, keen-edged iron shafts.
Seeking to achieve an act of immediate retribution, Karṇa struck him with twenty-six arrows,
and Aśvatthāman followed with twelve shafts whose touch was like fire and whose venom was like that of poisonous serpents, as well as seven more.
Then King Duryodhana covered him with sixty arrows;
the mighty Bhimasena also pierced all of them in return—
Droṇa with fifty arrows and Karṇa with ten shafts.
Striking Duryodhana with twelve swift arrows and the son of Droṇa with eight,
he advanced against them in battle, raising a tumultuous roar.
As he was thus casting off his life-breaths, having made himself common to death, [the enemy] attacked him.
Ajātaśatru urged those warriors, saying, "Protect Bhīma!
Then Yuyudhāna and the others, as well as the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī— those of immeasurable prowess— went to the side of Bhīmasena.
Having assembled together, those bulls among men, highly enraged and united,
desiring to break through Droṇa’s army which was protected by the foremost of great archers,
those car-warriors of immense prowess led by Bhīma, rushed forward.
Droṇa, the best of chariot-warriors, remained unperturbed and received them—
those mighty, great car-warriors (atiratha), heroes who adorn the battlefield;
casting aside the external fear of death, your men advanced against the Pāṇḍavas.
Horsemen struck down horsemen, and likewise chariot-warriors struck down chariot-warriors;
there was a clash of spears and swords, and the battle was fought with battle-axes.
There occurred a close-quarter sword-fight that resulted in bitter consequences.

A collision of elephants occurred, resulting in a bitter outcome; through the clashing of elephants, there was a most terrible battle. One fell from an elephant, while another fell headlong from a horse.
O noble one, another man was pierced by an arrow and cast from his chariot;
there, amidst the crush of men, an elephant, having stepped upon the chest of another who had fallen and was stripped of his armor, crushed his head.

Other elephants also struck down men who had fallen; descending to the earth with their tusks, they gored many chariot-warriors. Others, with human entrails dripping from their tusks, [dragged them along].
Hundreds of elephants wandered about, crushing hundreds of men; they trampled down men,
horses, chariots,
and elephants clad in bronze and iron armor who had fallen, as if they were thick stalks of reeds.
O King, at that time, it was difficult for the broken ranks, unable to see where they stood, to regroup upon the earth; the lords of men had their beds covered with vulture feathers.
Modest men, ripened by time, lie down amidst great sufferings;
here, a father kills his son as he passes him in a chariot,
and a son, out of delusion, acts without restraint toward his father.
The axle was broken, the banner severed, and the umbrella cast down upon the earth;
taking up a half-yoke that had been snapped, the horse likewise fled. An arm still clutching a sword fell, and a head adorned with earrings was cut off.
Having been seized by a powerful elephant, the chariot was crushed upon the earth;
struck by the charioteer with an iron shaft (nārāca), the elephant fell lifeless;
and the horse, along with its rider, fell down after being violently struck by the elephant.
A vast and most terrible battle, devoid of all restraint, took place:
"Alas, father! Alas, son! Friend, where are you? Stay! Where are you running?
"Strike! Seize! Slay him!"—thus they cried with laughter, shouts, and roars.
Thus various cries were heard being uttered:
"The blood of man, horse, and elephant mingled together;
the dust of the earth was laid, and despondency entered the hearts of the cowards."

In that battle, having encountered one hero with his wheel, the hero [Duryodhana], when the time for discharging arrows had passed, struck off the other's head with his mace. There was a seizing of the hair and a fierce struggle with fists.
With their claws and teeth, the heroes sought an island in that place where no island existed.
