There, the upraised arm of one hero was severed along with his sword; likewise, the arm of another was cut off together with his bow, his arrow, and his goad.
There, one cried out to another, while yet another fled with his back turned;
one struck off the head of another who had come within reach from his body,
and one rushed toward a sound while another fled violently from that very sound.
One slew his own kin, while another slew his enemies with sharpened arrows;
one, struck with fear, cried out, while another, terrified, fled away;
and another took the life of one who had not yet reached that spot.
There, a mountain-like elephant, struck down by an iron shaft,
fell to the earth like the bank of a river during the summer heat;
likewise, the elephant crushed the charioteer as if a mountain were being shattered while discharging its rut.
He trampled with his feet upon the ground the horses and the charioteers;
seeing many brave warriors— skilled in weapons and drenched in blood— striking out, a delusion overcame those who were cowardly and weak of heart.
Everything became agitated and nothing could be discerned;
as the army was obscured by dust, it fell into utter disorder.
Then the commander-in-chief, saying "This is the time," quickly [acted].
He constantly urged on the Pāṇḍavas with great haste;
carrying out his command, the illustrious sons of Pāṇḍu rushed toward Droṇa’s chariot like swans toward a lake, striking him down.
"Seize him! Run at one another! Do not be afraid! Cut him down!"—such was the tumultuous roar that arose near the chariot of the invincible one.
Then Drona, Kripa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, and King Jayadratha [advanced].
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, along with Śalya, held them back;
yet those Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, though afflicted by arrows, did not turn away from Droṇa, for they were enraged by their noble duty and were difficult to restrain or assail.
Then Drona, filled with great rage and discharging arrows by the hundreds,
wrought a great slaughter among the Chedis, Panchalas, and Pandavas.
O noble one, the sound of his bowstring and the slapping of his palms was heard in all directions.
Resembling a mass of thunderbolts and terrifying many of the Pāṇḍavas,
in that interval the mighty Jiṣṇu, having slain the Saṃśaptakas,
proceeded to the place where Droṇa was crushing the Pāṇḍus.

Having slain the Saṃśaptakas, Phalguna was seen again, having crossed that great lake whose waters were blood and whose great whirlpools were masses of arrows. The mark of that illustrious one, whose splendor was equal to the sun, [was visible].
We beheld the monkey-bannered one blazing with splendor;
having dried up that ocean of Saṃśaptakas with the rays of his weapons, he,
like the sun at the end of the age for the Pāṇḍavas, scorched even the Kurus.
Arjuna consumed all the Kurus with the fiery energy of his weapons,
like the risen comet at the end of an eon consuming all living beings.
By means of those floods of thousands of arrows, he [destroyed] the elephant-riders, horsemen, chariot-warriors, and combatants.
Struck down, they fell to the earth, their weapons dropped and tormented by arrows;
some uttered piteous cries, others wailed aloud,
and some, slain by Pārtha’s shafts, fell lifeless.
As they were fleeing, Arjuna did not strike some of those warriors who had fallen or were turning their backs, as he remained mindful of the code of conduct for combatants.
With their chariots, horses, and elephants shattered, they were for the most part turned away in retreat.
"O Karna! O Karna! and "Alas! Alas! cried out the Kurus.
Recognizing that cry of distress from those seeking refuge, the son of Adhiratha promised them, "Do not fear," and advanced toward Arjuna.
That best of Bharata chariot-warriors, who brings joy to all the Bharatas,
the mighty-armed disciple of Rāma and the constant destroyer of the pride of archers—
that foremost of those skilled in weapons— manifested that *Āgneya* weapon.
Against him who possessed a blazing mass of arrows and wielded a flaming bow,
Dhanañjaya dispersed his showers of shafts with a net of his own arrows;
likewise, the son of Adhiratha [warded off] his arrows of blazing splendor.
Having warded off that weapon with his own weapon, he roared while discharging arrows;
and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Bhīma, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki,
having approached Karṇa, pierced him each with three straight-flying shafts.
But the son of Rādhā, having warded off Arjuna’s weapon with showers of arrows,
severed the bows of those three with three shafts.
With their weapons cut away, those heroes were like venomless serpents.
Hurling their chariot-spears, they roared loudly like lions.
Released from the tips of their arms with great velocity, those blazing, serpent-like great spears sped toward the son of Adhiratha.
Having cut them down with three straight-flying, sharp arrows each,
the powerful Karṇa roared while discharging shafts at the son of Pṛthā;
and Arjuna, too, having pierced the son of Rādhā with seven swift arrows.
With three sharpened arrows, he struck the younger brother of Karṇa;
then, having slain Śatruñjaya with six straight-flying shafts, Pārtha immediately severed Vipāṭa’s head from his chariot with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla).
While the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked on, by Kirīṭin alone,
three uterine brothers were slain in the very presence of the Sūta’s son.
Then Bhīma, leaping up from his own chariot like Vainateya, [advanced].
With his excellent sword, he struck off fifteen of Karṇa’s flank-protectors.
Then, mounting his own chariot again and taking up another bow,
he pierced Karṇa with ten arrows, and the charioteer and horses with five.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, having taken up an excellent sword and a radiant shield,
struck Candravarman and Bṛhatkṣatra the Paurava.
Then the prince of the Pañcālas, mounting his own chariot, took up another bow.
Taking up [his bow], he pierced Karṇa with seventy-three arrows while roaring in the battle;
Śaineya, too, taking up another bow radiant as Indra’s weapon,
pierced the Sūta’s son with sixty-four arrows and roared like a lion.
Having severed Karṇa’s bow with two well-aimed bhalla-arrows,
he struck Karṇa again in the arms and chest with three shafts.
Then Duryodhana, Droṇa, and King Jayadratha [rushed forward].
As the son of Rādhā was sinking, they rescued him from the ocean that was Sātyaki;
hundreds of other foot-soldiers, cavalry, chariots, and elephants of your side,
though being terrified by the strikers, rushed toward Karṇa alone.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Bhīma, the son of Subhadrā, Arjuna,
Nakula, and Sahadeva protected Sātyaki in battle.
Thus did this most terrible conflict unfold for the destruction of all the archers.
A battle took place between your men and the enemy, in which they sacrificed their lives; foot-soldiers fought with chariots, elephants, and horses, while elephants, horses,
and chariots fought against infantry, and chariot-warriors against elephants, infantry, and horses, and chariots and infantry against chariots and elephants.

Horses were seen engaged with horses, elephants with elephants, chariot-warriors with chariot-warriors, and even foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers. Thus the battle became a dense melee, bringing joy to the flesh-eating beasts.

In that encounter between Droṇa and Arjuna, as the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas— fearless before those great warriors and intent on increasing the realm of Yama— rushed forward in fury and struck one another down.
Then, by means of men, chariots, horses, and elephants, numerous elephants, chariots, horses, and foot-soldiers were slain;
elephants were struck down by elephants, and chariots with their riders by those with uplifted weapons.
Horses by horses, infantrymen by groups of infantrymen;
elephants by chariots, great horses by the best of elephants;
men by horses, and swift steeds by excellent chariot-warriors.
With their tongues, teeth, and eyes forced out, they lay upon the earth,
their armor and ornaments crushed; likewise, by others with many implements and excellent weapons, they were brought to destruction.
Slain and fallen, they were terrifying to behold;
trampled by the feet of horses and elephants,
they lay utterly overwhelmed, struck down by the hooves of chariots and the rims of their wheels.
While that terrible destruction of people was occurring, causing joy to the beasts of prey, birds,
and rākṣasas, those mighty warriors became enraged with one another.
Destroying [the enemy] with their might, they advanced like a turbulent great ocean; desiring to become guests in the abode of Mahendra, those of great strength moved forward.
Then, as the two armies were violently agitated against one another, gazing at each other while drenched in floods of blood,
the sun slowly set behind the western mountain.
Both having set out for their camps, O Bhārata,
Sañjaya said:
"Previously, when we had been broken by Phalguna of immeasurable prowess..."
When Droṇa’s resolve had been frustrated and Yudhiṣṭhira was protected,
all your warriors were defeated in battle with their armor shattered;
covered in dust and deeply agitated, they gazed toward the ten directions.
Then, having withdrawn with the consent of Bhāradvāja,
they were mocked bitterly in battle by their enemies, who had achieved their aim;
while all beings were praising the immeasurable virtues of Phalguna.
As the friendship of Keśava toward Arjuna was being extolled,
they became as if cursed; they fell into a state of silent meditation,
devoid of luster, despondent, lacking in vigor, and bereft of prowess.
Those who were the foremost have been slain; relying upon dispassion,
Arjuna is not their equal in prowess, even though they praise him again and again—
all the kings and princes, Duryodhana and the rest.
Then, at the time of dawn, Duryodhana spoke to Droṇa.
Thereupon King Duryodhana, dejected, addressed Droṇa out of affection,
pride, and being ill-at-ease due to the prosperity of his enemies.
In the hearing of all beings, he who was skilled in speech,
provoked by the affectionate yet harsh words of Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the others,
said: "O best of those who know the Veda, we are surely on the side of those to be slain by you."
For thus you did not seize Yudhiṣṭhira today, though he was within reach; had you desired it, an enemy who has come within your sight in battle would not escape you,
even if he were being protected by the Pāṇḍavas along with the gods.
"Having joyfully granted me a boon, you have subsequently acted contrary to it.
Noble men never, under any circumstances, cause the frustration of the hopes of one devoted to them.
Thus addressed, Bhāradvāja, feeling displeased, spoke to the king.
"You ought not to think otherwise of me as I strive for your welfare; for the worlds—
including the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas—
are not capable of conquering in battle one who is protected by Kiritin."
Where Govinda, the creator of the universe, and Arjuna, the foe of hostile armies, are present—whose strength could prevail there, O Lord, other than that of the Three-Eyed One?
I tell you this truly today; it can never be otherwise.

First, I shall strike down their preeminent hero, that great car-warrior; and I shall arrange a formation that is impenetrable even by the gods themselves. However, O King, let Arjuna be drawn away by some stratagem.
For there was nothing in that battle unknown to him or impossible for him to achieve;
indeed, he had acquired from here and there all powerful knowledge.
When Droṇa had thus spoken, the hosts of the Saṃśaptakas once again [advanced].
Challenging Arjuna in battle toward the southern direction,
a combat then took place there between Arjuna and his enemies such as had never been heard of or seen anywhere else.
Then, O King, the battle array formed by Droṇa shone brilliantly,
like the sun scorching at midday, difficult to behold as it moved along.
And Abhimanyu, O Bhārata, [penetrated] that array at the command of his eldest father.
In battle, he shattered the impenetrable wheel-array (cakravyūha) in many ways. Having performed that difficult feat and slain thousands of heroes,
he killed a hundred princes and Bṛhadbala, the king of Kosala.
Engaged with six heroes— the great car-warrior son of Śalya and your beloved Lakṣmaṇa—
that tiger among men, the son of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, fell under the power of the son of Duḥśāsana and was slain.
O protector of the earth, O scorcher of foes, the son of Subhadrā gave up his life. We were exceedingly joyful, while the Pāṇḍavas were emaciated by grief;
when the son of Subhadrā was slain, O King, they called for the withdrawal of their forces.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Sañjaya, hearing that the son of that lion among men has been slain in battle before reaching his youth, my heart is deeply rent asunder.
Cruel indeed is this duty of the Kṣatriyas ordained by the makers of dharma,
wherein heroes desiring sovereignty have cast their weapons upon a child who was wandering about like one fearless and accustomed to extreme comfort.
"O Sañjaya, son of Gavalgaṇa, tell me how many skilled in weapons struck him;
tell me how the son of Subhadrā, possessed of immeasurable splendor, sported in battle while seeking to break through that array of chariots."
Saṃjaya said:
"O Indra among kings, as you ask me concerning the fall of Subhadrā’s son, I shall relate that to you in its entirety; listen, O King, with a concentrated mind."
07,032.025e The boy’s playful sport as he sought to break through the ranks, 07,032.025f And how the heroes were shattered, even those difficult to overcome in the upheaval;
07,032.026a [The state] of those surrounded by forest fires amidst many thickets, grasses, and trees.
"Like forest-dwellers in the wilderness, fear arose among those who were yours.
Sañjaya said:
"In battle, those of most fierce deeds had their exhaustion manifested through their actions."
The five Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇa, are difficult to overcome even by the gods; for in terms of their essential nature, deeds, lineage, intellect, disposition, fame, and splendor,
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a man whose virtues equal those of Kṛṣṇa.
Devoted to truth and righteousness, a donor, and endowed with virtues such as the worship of Brahmins,
King Yudhiṣṭhira indeed attained heaven forever. O King, at the end of the age, he became the Destroyer, as did the valiant son of Jamadagni.
Bhīmasena standing in the fray— these three are said to be equal;
yet, I find no fitting comparison on earth for Pārtha, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, who is so skilled in the performance of his vows in battle.
Excessive devotion to one's teacher, modesty, humility, self-restraint,
incomparable beauty, and valor— these six qualities are constant in Nakula.
He possesses the depth of learning, sweetness, goodness, heroism, and prowess.
The hero Sahadeva is indeed equal to the two divine Aśvins;
and those abundant virtues which exist in Kṛṣṇā and those virtues which exist in the Pāṇḍavas— indeed,
that entire collection of virtues is seen gathered together in Abhimanyu.
He was equal to Yudhiṣṭhira in steadfastness, to Kṛṣṇa in conduct,
and to Bhīmasena of terrible deeds in his actions;
he was equal to Dhanañjaya in beauty, prowess, and sacred learning.
In discipline, he was equal to Sahadeva and Nakula.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sūta, I [grieve for] Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadrā, who was unconquered."
"I wish to hear in its entirety how he was slain in battle.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having heard that Abhimanyu had been killed, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,"
07,033.011d *0251_02 In detail, O Great King, he questioned Saṃjaya.
07,033.012 Saṃjaya said:
07,033.012*0252_01 Be firm, O Great King; sustain this sorrow that is so difficult to bear.

"I shall tell you of a great destruction of kinsmen; listen to that. O Great King, the wheel-array (cakravyūha) has been designed by the Preceptor, and all the kings, who are like Śakra himself, have been stationed therein."

O Bhārata, the princes, possessing the splendor of the sun, were stationed upon the filaments of the lotus; and those delicate filaments of the lotus were like the princes of the royal world placed there as their counterparts.
O Great King, Duryodhana stood at the pericarp;
at that time, there was a gathering of all the princes,
all of whom had made their solemn vows and possessed banners adorned with gold.

All wore red garments, and all were adorned with red ornaments; all those excellent chariots and horses were likewise adorned with red ornaments. All bore red banners, and all indeed wore garlands of gold.
With their limbs smeared with sandalwood and aloe paste, wearing garlands and fine garments,
they ran together, desiring to fight against the son of Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna).
There were ten thousand of those firm bowmen.
Placing your handsome grandson Lakṣmaṇa at their head,
they— sharing one another’s sorrows, possessing equal courage for one another,
vying with one another, and devoted to one another’s welfare— [proceeded].
But Duryodhana, O king of kings, stationed in the midst of the army, surrounded by Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Kṛpa— those great car-warriors— the illustrious king,
resembling the lord of the gods, was covered by a white umbrella.
With the waving of yak-tail fans, Drona stood like the rising sun at the head of that army, its leader firmly stationed; likewise,
the illustrious King of Sindhu stood there like the immovable Mount Meru.
Standing at the side of the King of Sindhu, led by Aśvatthāman,
were your thirty sons, O great king, who resembled the gods;
as well as the gambler-king of the Gāndhāras, Śalya, and Bhūriśravas.
On both flanks of the King of the Sindhus, those great car-warriors shone resplendently.
Then there commenced a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end,
between your men and the enemy, with death as the only means of turning back.
Saṃjaya said:
The sons of Pṛthā, led by Bhīmasena, advanced against that invincible army protected by the son of Bharadvāja.
Sātyaki, Cekitāna, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata;
the valiant Kuntibhoja and the great car-warrior Drupada; the son of Arjuna, Kṣatradharman, and the heroic Bṛhatkṣatra.
Cedipa and Dhṛṣṭaketu, the two sons of Mādrī, Ghaṭotkaca,
the valiant Yudhāmanyu, the unconquered Śikhaṇḍin,
the invincible Uttamaujas, and the great car-warrior Virāṭa.
The sons of Draupadī were enraged, as was the heroic son of Śiśupāla; the Kekayas of great prowess and the Sṛñjayas by the thousands—
these and others, accompanied by their hosts, were masters of weapons and fierce in battle.
Desirous of battle, they suddenly rushed together against the son of Bharadvāja. But the valiant Bhāradvāja, remaining unperturbed, checked all those assembled warriors with a great shower of arrows.
Like great torrents of water hitting an impenetrable mountain, they could not overcome Droṇa, just as bodies of water cannot overstep the shore;
O King, they were tormented by the arrows released from Droṇa’s bow.
The Pāṇḍavas were unable to stand before the son of Bharadvāja;
we then beheld that wonderful strength of Droṇa’s arms,
in that the Pañcālas, together with the Sṛñjayas, could not overcome him.
Seeing Drona approaching in a great rage, Yudhishthira reflected in many ways on how to check Drona. However,
considering that Drona was impossible for anyone else to withstand, Yudhishthira—

He placed upon the son of Subhadrā an unbearable and heavy burden—one who was not inferior to Vāsudeva and possessed immeasurable energy like Phalguna—and spoke these words to Abhimanyu, the slayer of enemy heroes:
[He said: "O Abhimanyu, slayer of hostile warriors, [this is your task]."
"Come, O dear one, act in such a way that Arjuna does not reproach us.
We do not know by any means how to break the wheel-array;
only you, or Arjuna, or Kṛṣṇa, or indeed Pradyumna, could pierce it."
"O mighty-armed one, the wheel-array (*cakravyūha*) is the fifth; no other exists.
O Abhimanyu, my dear child, you ought to grant a boon to those who ask it—on behalf of your fathers, your maternal uncles, and all your troops."
"For Dhanañjaya, O dear one, will surely reproach us upon returning from the battle.
Therefore, quickly taking up your weapons, shatter Drona’s army.
Abhimanyu said:

"Listen, O King, mighty-armed one of noble vows, to my words. O Lord, O Indra among kings, I have heard from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa how, even while still in the womb, he entered the wheel-array (cakravyūha)."

Therefore, O best of kings, desiring victory for my ancestors, I shall enter the firm and unshakeable array called the *cakra*, the preeminent division of Droṇa in battle; I plunge into it and break through it.
"For my father taught me this yoga for breaking through an army;
yet, I do not venture to go out in any kind of calamity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Break through the enemy host in battle, O best of warriors; open a gateway for us.
We shall follow you, dear brother, by the path you take.
For in combat, O dear one, we regard you as equal to Dhanañjaya."
"Having made this vow, we shall follow you, protecting you from all sides.
Bhīma said:
"I shall follow you, as will Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Sātyaki."
The Pāñcālas, Kekayas, Matsyas, and all the Prabhadrakas—
once our array has been broken by you here and there again and again, we shall utterly destroy it, slaughtering the very best of warriors.
Abhimanyu said:
"O King, having been begotten by Arjuna upon Subhadrā,
behold my great manly prowess, which is equal to that of a mighty force."
"O lord of men, I shall slay all the Kurus, with Droṇa as their chief,
by whom evil deeds were committed against the high-souled Pāṇḍavas—
those by whom my eldest mother was dragged into the assembly hall by those who are so difficult to overcome."
O King of kings, whatever was done against the Pāñcālas by the wicked Duḥśāsana of evil deeds and by those who commit such malice— that I shall today display all in this array with great agility.
"I shall enter this unassailable army of Droṇa,
like an enraged moth entering a blazing fire.
Today I will perform that deed which is beneficial for both lineages."

The joy that my maternal uncle and my father will feel when all their armies, standing in a wretched state, are being driven away in groups by a single child in battle— [that joy shall be theirs]. My story [shall be told].
Today all beings shall behold the enemy armies by my hand;
neither could I have been born of Pārtha, nor born of Subhadrā,
had anyone escaped alive from me today in battle.
"And if, with a single chariot, I do not divide the entire circle of the Kṣatriyas into eight parts in battle, then may I not be the son of Arjuna. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Saubhadra, may your strength increase as you speak these words,
you who venture to pierce Drona’s army, so difficult to breach,
protected as it is by tigers among men, great archers, and mighty strikers.
[He was] like Sādhya, Rudra, and the Maruts, and possessed the prowess of the Vasus, Agni, and the Ādityas.
Sañjaya said:
Having heard those words of his, he urged on his charioteer.
"O Susharman, swiftly urge the horses toward Drona’s army in battle!
Sanjaya said:
"But the son of Subhadra, having heard the words of the wise Dharmaraja..."
O Bhārata, he urged his charioteer toward Droṇa’s division.
Being thus urged by him with the words "Go! Go!", O King, the charioteer then replied these words to Abhimanyu:
"O long-lived one, this is a very heavy burden that has been placed upon you by the Pāṇḍavas;
having deliberated with your intellect on what is appropriate, you should then engage in battle. For the preceptor Droṇa is skilled and has exerted himself in the supreme weapons."
You have been raised in extreme luxury and are skilled in battle;
for Droṇa, who has exerted himself and mastered the use of weapons and missiles, is indeed experienced.
But you are a youth, whereas he is powerful and unskilled in the ways of war.
Then Abhimanyu, smiling, spoke these words to his charioteer:
"O charioteer, who indeed is this Droṇa, or even the entire host of Kṣatriyas? For my resolve to fight has arisen from the joy of battle."
I would fight Śakra mounted upon Airāvata together with the hosts of gods,
or else Rudra the Lord surrounded by all the hosts of beings at the front of the battle; today I have no fear of the warrior class.

"O charioteer, this army of enemies that you see here, with its warriors, horses, chariots, and elephants— it does not equal even a sixteenth part of me. Although he was addressed in this way again and again, the charioteer—

"O hero, do not fight with him," he said to the son of Subhadrā. "O son of a Sūta, even having encountered Viṣṇu himself, the conqueror of all worlds, as your maternal uncle, and Arjuna as your father in battle, fear shall not come upon me."
Then Abhimanyu, disregarding those words of his charioteer, said to him, "Go! Proceed toward Drona's army without delay.
Thereupon, he urged on his three-year-old horses.

With minds not overly elated, the charioteer urged those horses, which were equipped with golden trappings, toward Droṇa’s army as dispatched by Sumitra; O King, those steeds of great speed and prowess charged against Droṇa.
Beholding him approaching in that manner, all the Kauravas led by Droṇa turned toward him, and the Pāṇḍavas followed after him. His banner, bearing a preeminent *karṇikāra* tree, stood high aloft.
Suvarṇavarmā, the son of Arjuna and superior even to Arjuna himself,
approached the great chariot-warriors headed by Droṇa with a desire for combat,
like a lion cub attacking elephants.
Prepared for battle on a space of twenty paces, they engaged in a fierce encounter;
for a moment, it was like a whirlpool in the Ganges or in the ocean,
as those heroes fought and struck one another down.
O King, a tumultuous and most dreadful battle commenced.
While that exceedingly terrifying battle was raging,
the son of Arjuna, having pierced the array even as Droṇa looked on, entered it.

Having pierced that impenetrable, unassailable, and most difficult-to-conquer army of Droṇa, the son of Arjuna, undaunted and possessed of inconceivable prowess, entered it. As that mighty warrior had entered and was slaying the enemies in the midst of the foe, [he proceeded].
Multitudes of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, with weapons raised, surrounded him amidst the sounds of various musical instruments, the shouting and roaring of battle cries,
the utterance of "huṃ," lion-like roars, and the shouts of "Stay! Stay!"

With terrible "halahala" cries, repeatedly shouting, "Do not go! Stay! Come to me! Here I am, over there!"—and with their bellows, tinkling ornaments, laughter, and even the sounds of their hooves and wheel-rims.
Making the earth resound, they rushed toward the son of Arjuna.
As they were charging forward, the hero— skilled in swift weapons, a knower of the vital points, and firm in his aim— quickly struck down their throngs with arrows that pierce the vitals.
Being thus struck by sharp arrows of various descriptions,
they fell upon him in battle like moths into a fire;
then, with their bodies and the limbs of their bodies, he—
He quickly covered the ground with kusha grass, as if preparing an altar for a sacrifice;
[he covered it with] those who wore leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, who carried quivers, bows,
swords, shields, goads, reins, javelins, and battle-axes.
[He saw] iron-headed darts smeared with molasses, spears,
*tomaras*, and *paṭṭiśas*; together with *bhiṇḍipālas* and iron clubs, *śaktis*, excellent *kampanas*, goads, great conchs, *kuntas*, and hair-seizing grips.

Arjuna’s son severed by the thousands the rounded arms of your men— arms that were capable of hurling mallets, slings, nooses, clubs, and stones; arms adorned with bracelets and armlets, and anointed with fragrant unguents.
O great king, with those quivering [heads] smeared with blood, the field shone,
O noble one, like the severed five-headed serpents by Garuḍa; they possessed beautiful noses,
faces, and hair-ends, were free from wounds, and adorned with lovely earrings.
With their lips bitten together in rage, they were shedding much blood;
they wore beautiful garlands, crowns, and turbans, resplendent with jewels and gems,
resembling lotuses without stalks and possessing the luster of the sun and the moon.
The son of Phalguna covered the earth with the heads of his enemies— heads that were pleasant to behold, spoke kindly at the proper time, and were fragrant with merit—
just as one covers the ground with chariots fashioned according to rule and appearing like cities of the Gandharvas.

The excellent warriors stood upon their chariots, which were drawn by well-trained horses and guided by skillful charioteers; yet these vehicles were now stripped of banners, standards, and umbrellas, devoid of quivers and weapons,
with their drivers, horses, and reins lost, and their crossbars, thongs, and poles shattered.
[He saw chariots] with their yokes shattered, their triple-pole frames split, and their poles and frames disarrayed;
[he saw those] with broken shafts, hubs, and axles, as well as those lacking rims,
spokes, and frames, and even those with their equipment and seats destroyed.
With his arrows, he was seen in all directions dismembering by the thousands those whose equipment had been stripped away and whose warriors were slain;
furthermore, he struck down elephants, their riders, banners, hooks, and standards.

With arrows whose tips were sharpened to a keen edge, he struck down the quivers, armor, girths, neck-ornaments, and blankets; as well as the bells, trunks, the tips of tusks, razor-edged blades, and the foot-followers of his enemies.
[He saw] horses from Vanāyu, the mountains, Kamboja, Araṭṭa, and Bāhlīka—
swift, well-trained, with steady tails, ears, and eyes, ridden by skilled warriors who fought with spears, swords, and lances.
With their yak-tail whisks and saddle-cloths shattered, their head-ornaments scattered about,
their tongues and eyes cast out, and their entrails and livers spilling forth;
with their riders slain and their trappings broken, they brought joy to the throngs of flesh-eating beasts.
Striking down your excellent horses— whose armor and mail were cut away and who were drenched in excrement, urine, and blood— he shone forth,
like the inconceivable Viṣṇu alone, having performed a difficult feat in the past.
In that manner, your great threefold army was crushed by him,
just as the formidable host of the Asuras was crushed by Tryambaka of immeasurable splendor;
having performed deeds in battle impossible for others to endure, the son of Arjuna prevailed in the fray.
O Bhārata, he struck down the throngs of your own foot soldiers;
thus, seeing that army being violently shattered by the son of Subhadrā alone with his sharp arrows, as if it were the army of the Asuras by Skanda himself.
Your men and your sons, looking toward the ten directions,
had parched mouths, rolling eyes, were perspiring, and their hair stood on end;
they were intent on flight and lacked any enthusiasm for conquering the enemy.
Crying out to one another by their lineages and names, seeking to save their lives,
they abandoned their slain sons, fathers, friends, relatives, and kinsmen,
and proceeded on while urging on their horses and elephants.
Saṃjaya said:
Seeing that army shattered by the son of Subhadrā, who possessed immeasurable splendor,
Duryodhana became violently incensed and personally advanced against the son of Subhadrā.
Then, seeing King [Jayadratha] turned back toward the son of Subhadrā in the encounter, Droṇa said to the warriors: "Protect the lord of men!
Before the heroic Abhimanyu destroys our target while we look on."
"Run toward him! Do not fear; quickly protect the Kaurava!
This hero Abhimanyu, whose prowess is equal to Viṣṇu’s, the son of Subhadrā and possessor of great strength, has arrived here to conquer us."
Then those grateful, powerful, and friendly warriors, who had already achieved victory,
surrounded your heroic son out of fear as he was being assailed.
Drona, the son of Drona, Kripa, Karṇa, Kṛtavarman, and the son of Subala [surrounded him].
Bṛhadbala, the king of the Madras, Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, Śala,
Paurava, and Vṛṣasena— discharging sharp arrows,
they completely covered the son of Subhadrā with a great shower of shafts.
Having utterly bewildered Duryodhana, they then released him;
the son of Arjuna could not endure that, as if a morsel had been snatched from his very mouth.
With a great torrent of arrows, he [struck] those great car-warriors along with their horses and charioteers.
Having turned them back, the son of Subhadrā then let out a lion’s roar.
Hearing that roar, which was like that of a lion seeking prey,
the chariot-warriors led by Droṇa, highly incensed, could not endure it.
O noble one, having hemmed him in with a multitude of chariots, they discharged masses of arrows of various kinds in great numbers. Your grandson cut those down in the sky with his sharp shafts.
He pierced them in return, and that was like a marvel. Then the chariots, throngs of infantry, elephants, and horsemen were provoked by him with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Desiring to slay him, they surrounded the son of Subhadrā, who did not flee;
Abhimanyu alone held back that ocean-like army of yours as it surged like the sea, just as the shore holds back the abode of sea-monsters.
Among the heroes fighting and striking one another,
neither Abhimanyu nor his enemies turned their backs.
While that terrible and fearsome battle was thus proceeding, [the warriors fought on].
Duḥsaha pierced Abhimanyu with nine arrows;
Duḥśāsana with twelve; Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, with three;
and Droṇa with seventeen arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Viviṃśati struck him with twenty arrows, Kṛtavarman with seven,
Bṛhadbala likewise with eight, Aśvatthāman with seven,
Bhūriśravas with three shafts, and the Lord of Madra with six swift arrows.
Śakuni pierced him with two arrows and King Duryodhana with three;
he, however, pierced them back with three straight-flying shafts each,
O great king, appearing as if dancing, the powerful hero with bow in hand.
Then Abhimanyu, enraged and being tormented by your sons,
displayed his truly great strength acquired through training and physical prowess,
with horses as swift as Garuḍa or the wind that obeyed the driver's word.
The lord of the Ashmakas, acting with haste, rushed toward that son of Kṛṣṇa;
urging on his well-trained horses,
he swiftly attacked the heir of the Ashmakas and pierced him with ten arrows, saying, "Stay!"
Smiling, Abhimanyu struck down his charioteer, horses, standard, arms, bow, and head to the earth with ten arrows. Then,
when that heroic lord of the Ashmakas had been slain by the son of Subhadra...
The entire army trembled, intent on flight.
Then Karna, Kṛpa, Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, the king of the Gāndhāras, Śala,
Śalya, Bhūriśravas, Krātha, Somadatta, and Vivimśati [advanced].
Vṛṣasena, Suṣeṇa, Kuṇḍabhedin, Pratardana, Vṛndāraka, Lalittha, Prabāhu, Dīrghalocana,
and the enraged Duryodhana covered him with showers of arrows.
Greatly incensed by those great archers with their straight-flying shafts, Abhimanyu took up an arrow capable of piercing the bodies of enemies for Karna.
That swift arrow, having shattered his armor, pierced right through his body.
O King, he entered the earth like a serpent entering its ant-hill. Agonized by that severe blow and as if overwhelmed,
Karṇa trembled in the battle like a mountain during an earthquake.
Then, filled with rage, the powerful one struck Suṣeṇa, Dīrghalocana, and Kuṇḍabhedin— those three— with three sharp arrows each;
Karna then struck him with twenty-five iron shafts.

Aśvatthāman struck him with twenty arrows and Kṛtavarman with seven. With all his limbs tormented by those shafts, the enraged grandson of Śakra was seen moving through the army like Death himself with a noose in hand.
And with a shower of arrows, he overwhelmed Śalya, who was standing nearby;
the mighty-armed one cried out aloud, terrifying your troops.
Then, pierced by that master of weapons with straight-flying shafts that struck his vital organs—
O King, Śalya sank down upon the seat of his chariot and lost consciousness. Seeing him thus pierced by the illustrious son of Subhadrā,
the entire army fled while the son of Bharadvāja looked on.
Beholding that mighty-armed one covered with gold-feathered arrows,
your men fled like deer tormented by a lion;
he alone swiftly struck down the many, like the Destroyer himself.
Equal to the fire of cosmic destruction in valor and like the wind-god Mātariśvan in speed, the mighty-armed one, whose prowess was equal to Śakra’s,
slaughtered in battle all those skilled in various weapons as they fought.
Thus, in that battle, the high-souled one,
possessed of great majesty and the most excellent among those who follow the path of policy,
[assailed] his enemies with great strength.
He rendered them all scorched by his arrows;
those warriors of godlike prowess were pierced in battle by the shafts of Subhadrā’s son.
Thus, O Bhārata, was Śalya crushed by your grandson.
He was being honored for his fame in battle by hosts of ancestors, gods, cāraṇas, siddhas, and yakṣas,
as well as by multitudes of beings dwelling upon the surface of the earth.
The consumer of oblations shone intensely, like a fire drenched with clarified butter.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"While that great archer was thus crushing [the enemy] with straight-flying arrows..."
"O Sañjaya, all my men [surrounded] the son of Arjuna; who were those that hemmed him in? Sañjaya said:
"Listen, O King, to the great prowess displayed by the prince in battle."
Seeing the lord of Madra struck down in battle by the son of Subhadrā with swift arrows while he was attempting to break through the chariot-array protected by the son of Bharadvāja,
Śalya’s younger brother, filled with rage, advanced against him scattering his shafts.
Having pierced the son of Arjuna along with his horses and charioteer with ten arrows, he raised a great shout and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Then the son of Arjuna [struck] his head, neck, hands, feet, bow, and horses.
With his arrows, he destroyed the parasol, the banner, the charioteer, the triple-pole, the pins and equipment, the wheels, the yoke, the shafts, the quivers,
the chariot-bottom, the pennon, the two wheel-protectors, and all the other implements.
He dispersed that [weapon] with such agility that no one could see it;
he fell to the earth, exhausted, his ornaments and garments scattered,
like a great shrine-tree shattered by a wind of immeasurable power.
His followers, terrified, fled in every direction; and seeing that deed of Arjuna’s son, O Bhārata, all living beings shouted "Excellent! Excellent! from all sides with a great roar.
When Śalya’s brother had been struck down, his soldiers, many of them,
incited by shouts of their lineages and names, rushed furiously toward the son of Arjuna with various weapons in hand.
Others, fierce in their might, arrived on chariots, horses, elephants, and on foot; with the great sound of arrows, the noise of hooves and wheel-rims,
and with the sounds of "hum," shouts, cries, and roaring lion-like bellows.
Others, roaring at the son of Arjuna with the sounds of bowstrings, palms, and armor,
cried out, "You shall not escape from us alive while we live!
Seeing them speaking thus, the son of Subhadrā seemed to laugh.
Whosoever struck first, him the heroic son of Arjuna pierced in return with feathered shafts;
displaying his various and swift weapons in battle,
he fought with initial gentleness.
Whatever weapon he had received from Vāsudeva and from Dhanañjaya, the son of Kṛṣṇā displayed it, making no distinction between himself and the two Kṛṣṇas;
casting that heavy burden to a great distance, he accomplished his task again and again.
As he took up his arrows and released them, he appeared indistinguishable from the bow itself; only the circle of his vibrating bow was seen in all directions,
like the disc of the brilliantly shining sun destroying the darkness.
The sound of his bowstring and the fierce sound of his palms were heard like the roar of a cloud discharging great thunderbolts at the appointed time.
Modest, indignant, observant of honor, and pleasing to behold was the son of Subhadrā.
Desiring to measure out his heroic archers, he fought;
having been mild, O great king, he became fierce,
like the divine sun at the end of the rainy season in autumn.
Enraged, he released hundreds of great, variegated arrows, whetted on stone and fletched with gold, like the sun emitting its rays;
the highly illustrious one [discharged them] with razor-sharp arrows, calf-toothed shafts, and *vipāṭha* bolts.

Seeing them thus fleeing, the son of Subhadrā, as if laughing, covered the chariot-force with iron shafts, half-iron shafts, crescent-headed arrows, and *añjalika* arrows, even as the son of Bharadvāja looked on.
Then that army, afflicted by arrows, turned its back in retreat.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, my mind is divided between shame and satisfaction."
That army of my son which the son of Subhadrā held in check—
my grandson now seeks to destroy it,
just as he did that very army.
"O son of Gavalgaṇa, tell me again in full how my grandson is repelling the army of my son, and describe in detail the youthful prowess of that boy,
who sports like Skanda against the Asuras."
Saṃjaya said:
"Behold, I shall describe to you that most terrible slaughter—
how that tumultuous battle took place between one man and many."
Abhimanyu, full of energy, standing upon his chariot, gladdened all your car-warriors— those subduers of enemies who were themselves filled with zeal—
including Droṇa, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, the son of Droṇa, Bhoja, and Bṛhadbala.
Moving like a whirling circle of fire with his arrows, he assailed Duryodhana, the son of Somadatta, the mighty Śakuni, various kings and princes, and diverse armies.

Slaying his enemies with supreme weapons, the powerful and radiant son of Subhadrā displayed his prowess in all directions, O Bhārata. Having seen that conduct of the son of Subhadrā, who possessed immeasurable energy, [the warriors were amazed].
Your troops trembled again and again.
Then the highly wise and powerful Bhāradvāja,
his eyes wide with joy, addressed Kṛpa in haste.

O noble one, as he beheld Abhimanyu, skilled in battle, in the midst of the fray, [Duryodhana] seemed to strike at the very vitals of your son. "There goes the youthful son of Subhadrā, standing at the forefront of the Pārthas."
Gladdening all his friends, King Yudhiṣṭhira,
Nakula, Sahadeva, and the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena,
as well as other kinsmen, relatives, and neutral allies.

"I do not consider any other archer to be his equal in battle; were he so inclined, he could destroy this army. Why then does he not wish to do so? Having heard these words of Droṇa, which were full of affection, your son [spoke].
Seeing Droṇa enraged against the son of Arjuna, Duryodhana, as if smiling, then spoke to Karṇa, Bāhlīka, Kṛpa,
Duḥśāsana, the King of Madra, and those various other great car-warriors.
The preceptor, the foremost knower of Brahman among all the consecrated kings,
praised the great-souled Abhimanyu like a panegyrist;
and while that wise teacher Droṇa was thus looking on, [the battle continued].
O fool, he does not wish to strike Arjuna’s son here; for even Antaka himself could not escape him in battle when he stands as an assailant—how much less any other mortal? I tell you this truly.
But he protects Arjuna’s son because of his status as a pupil;
for the virtuous, sons, pupils, and their offspring are dear.
Protected by Droṇa, he considers himself to possess great heroism.
"Crush that fool, who is puffed up with self-conceit, without delay!
Thus addressed by the king, they rushed toward the son of Sātvatī,
enraged and desiring to slay him, even as the son of Bharadvāja looked on.
Then Duḥśāsana, having heard those words of Duryodhana,
that tiger among the Kurus spoke these words to Duryodhana;
for Duḥśāsana, perceiving his elder brother to be agitated, [addressed him].
Having turned back those noble charioteers, he then spoke to his brother:
"O great king, I tell you this: I shall slay him while the sons of Pāṇḍu and the Pañcālas look on."
"Today I shall devour the son of Subhadrā, just as Rāhu devours the sun.
Having cried out thus, he spoke these words again to the Kuru king:
"Upon hearing that the two Kṛṣṇas have been devoured by me, let those who are excessively proud [be humbled]."
"Without a doubt, they will depart from the world of the living for the world of the departed;
and hearing that Pāṇḍu has clearly died, those sons born of his wives,
along with their circle of friends, will out of dejection give up their lives in a single day."
"Therefore, when this enemy is slain, all your adversaries are slain. Think of me with auspicious intent, O King; here I slay your foe.
Having spoken thus, O King, your son Duḥśāsana roared aloud.
Having been told "So be it" by his brother, your son Duḥśāsana then,
filled with rage, rushed toward the son of Subhadrā, covering him with showers of arrows.
As your son approached in a fury, that subduer of enemies—
Abhimanyu struck him with twenty-six sharp arrows;
then Duḥśāsana, enraged like an elephant in rut,
fought the son of Subhadrā, Abhimanyu, in that battle.

Those two, experts in the science of chariot warfare, fought while maneuvering their chariots in various wonderful circles, moving both to the left and to the right. Then, [the sound] of paṇavas, mṛdaṅgas, and dundubhis—
The men raised a most intense clamor of kṛkaras, mahānakas, bherīs, and jharjharas,
mingled with lion-like roars arising from the salt waters.
Saṃjaya said:
Then there occurred a battle between those two lions among men;
at that time, the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, the slayer of enemy heroes, [entered the fray].
Having severed the bow along with the arrow with great dexterity,
he struck Duḥśāsana on all sides with terrible shafts. With his limbs mangled by arrows, [Duḥśāsana] stood firm against his adversary.
Then the wise Abhimanyu, smiling, spoke to Duḥśāsana:
"By good fortune, I behold in battle this proud enemy arrived—
cruel, one who has abandoned dharma, and devoted to insults."
That which occurred in the assembly hall while King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was listening—
relying on fraudulent dice, the strength of Saubala’s power was displayed—
hear my words, dear one; you are my uncle, O high-minded one.
Casting friendship aside, all these wicked and deluded men, who have cast out every dharma, have enjoyed this kingdom;
yet a kingdom is enjoyed by friends, and happiness is enjoyed by friends.
Without friends, all enjoyments—both those of this world and the next—are false;
for when one is deprived of friends, all that is then unreal. You are addicted to distant gambling, most wicked and deceitful sinners.
O wicked one, you were the leader of those by whom that virtuous daughter of Drupada was brought into the assembly hall; this is the fruit of that deed,
which I shall show to all the Kurus and these evil-minded ones.
Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira was provoked by harsh words,
as was Bhīma, who was intoxicated by victory and spoke much that was incoherent,
while the evil-minded son of Subala relied upon fraudulent dice.
This which you have now encountered has come about through the wrath of that great-souled one,
on account of the theft of another's wealth, his unappeasable anger,
his greed, the destruction of his knowledge, and his most grievous malice.
"O you of wicked mind, this which has now come upon you— namely, the seizing of my kingdom from the Pitṛs who were fierce archers— is indeed the result of the wrath of those high-souled ones;
receive immediately the terrible fruit of your unrighteousness."
Today I have been chastised by your arrows while the entire army looks on; today,
in this battle, I shall be free from the debt of my anger toward the indignant Kṛṣṇā and of the desire of my father.
"O Kauravya, today in battle I shall become free of my debt to Bhīma.
For you shall not escape from me alive unless you abandon the fight. Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one [discharged] an arrow destined for Duḥśāsana's end.
The slayer of enemy heroes fixed [his arrow], which possessed the radiance of the fire of cosmic destruction and the wind;
having swiftly reached his chest and pierced him in the region of the collarbone,
that conqueror of hostile cities struck him indeed in the collarbone with it.
Like a serpent entering its anthill, it went forth along with the feathered shaft;
then he struck him again with twenty-five arrows,
whose touch was like fire and which were drawn back as far as his ear.

Deeply pierced and pained, O great king, Duḥśāsana sat down on the floor of his chariot and was overcome by a great faint. His charioteer, however, acting with haste, [prepared to carry away] the unconscious Duḥśāsana.
They carried him away from the midst of the battle, for he was tormented by the arrows of Subhadrā’s son.
Upon seeing him, the Pāṇḍavas, the sons of Draupadī, Virāṭa,
the Pañcālas, and the Kekayas then let out lion-like roars.
And there, the soldiers of the Pāṇḍavas, filled with joy, sounded all kinds of musical instruments of various types from every side,
beholding and smiling at the exploits of Subhadrā’s son.
Seeing their utterly hostile and arrogant enemy defeated,
the great chariot-warriors, the sons of Draupadī, bore upon the tips of their banners the images of Dharma, Maruta, Śakra, and likewise those of the Aśvins.
Sātyaki, Cekitāna, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and Śikhaṇḍin;
the Kekayas, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the Matsyas, Pañcālas, and Sṛñjayas;
and the Pāṇḍavas, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, were filled with joy.
United together, they advanced against Droṇa’s army, desiring to break through it.
Then a great battle took place between your men and the enemies—
those heroes who were longing for victory and would never retreat.
While that most terrifying battle was thus proceeding,
O great king, Duryodhana spoke these words to the son of Rādhā:
"Behold the heroic Duḥśāsana, who has fallen under the power of Abhimanyu!"
Scorching like the sun and slaughtering his enemies in battle,
the Pāṇḍavas— fierce with strength like lions and highly agitated— then rushed forward, intent on rescuing the son of Subhadrā.
Then, O King, Karṇa advanced with the intent to slay Abhimanyu, thinking:
"This boy is fighting; he desires to fight with me here.
I shall kill this enemy, just as the Lord of Śacī killed Vṛtra."
Having spoken thus, the great car-warrior Rādheya, that mighty hero, mounted his chariot and went forth to fight while the Kurus looked on,
having blown his conch shell which resounded like the roar of a mass of great clouds.
He rushed forward with speed on a chariot resembling the sun,
while his bow— adorned with a string of bowels—
was being drawn; he discharged arrows shaped like flames of fire and possessing a luster equal to venomous serpents.
Then Karṇa, your son’s well-wisher, being enraged, showered the invincible Abhimanyu with sharp arrows;
he also pierced his followers with excellent, keen shafts.
O King, on the field of battle,
the high-minded hero Abhimanyu, desiring to reach Droṇa, quickly pierced the son of Rādhā with seventy-three stone-tipped arrows, having previously treated him with contempt.

At that time, no one was able to restrain him from Droṇa in battle as he shattered the best of chariot-warriors, like the wielder of the thunderbolt against the Asuras. Then Karṇa, the proudest among all archers, desiring victory, [advanced].
Displaying his supreme weapons, he pierced the son of Subhadrā in hundreds of places.
That powerful disciple of Rāma, the best among those skilled in weapons,
afflicted Abhimanyu— who was difficult for enemies to overcome— in that battle with his own missiles.
Though thus afflicted in battle by the showers of weapons from the son of Rādhā, the son of Subhadrā, who resembled an immortal, did not waver.
Then, with sharp, straight-knotted *bhalla* arrows whetted on stone, he struck back.
Having severed the bows of the heroes, the son of Arjuna afflicted Karṇa with arrows resembling venomous serpents, released from his drawn bow-circles;
laughing, as it were, he swiftly struck him along with his umbrella, standard, charioteer, and horses.
Karna also discharged straight-knotted arrows at him,
but the son of Phalguna, remaining unperturbed, caught them all.
Then, after a moment, the heroic one [struck] Karna with a single arrow.
He discharged at him a sharpened arrow, most carefully aimed;
it severed both his standard and his bow and felled them to the ground.
Then, seeing Karṇa fallen into distress, Karṇa’s younger brother [attacked].
Raising his firm bow, he quickly rushed toward the son of Subhadrā;
then the Pārthas and their followers raised a loud shout,
struck their musical instruments, and praised the son of Subhadrā.
Saṃjaya said: Roaring, bow in hand, and repeatedly drawing the bowstring,
he quickly rushed into the space between the chariots of those two great-souled warriors.
Smiling as it were, he quickly pierced the unassailable Abhimanyu with ten arrows— along with his umbrella, standard, charioteer, and horses—
as he performed superhuman deeds worthy of his father and grandfather.

Seeing the son of Kṛṣṇa afflicted by arrows, your men were filled with joy. But Abhimanyu, drawing his bow, smilingly struck off his head with a single feathered shaft; he fell from his chariot to the earth.
Seeing Karṇa’s younger brother, who was like a *karṇikāra* tree blown down from the mountain by the wind, your men were struck with distress;
and seeing his brother slain, O King, Karṇa himself fell into deep anguish.
Again, Karṇa pierced him with arrows resembling venomous serpents;
the hero struck the mighty Abhimanyu with ten shafts, but he,
with great lightness of hand, cut down all of them before they could reach him.
Smiling, the mighty one severed the bow of Rādheya,
swiftly slew his horses, and struck down his standard along with his charioteer.
Having deprived the son of Rādhā of his chariot, the son of Subhadrā spoke these words:
"O son of Rādhā, you have been defeated by me; O high-minded one, you are now without a chariot. Ascend another chariot and fight, O one of great strength!"
"You are a servant, you are the son of a charioteer, and you have always acted like a cat-in-disguise. You have constantly practiced backbiting against the Pāṇḍavas;
having brought the princess of Pañcāla into the assembly hall, you caused her to be stripped of her clothes."
07,040.005d@006_0012 Many various forms and very many garments were seen there by you and by the evil-minded Kurus.
07,040.005d@006_0013 I shall now show you the fruit of that, if you do not venture into battle.
And today, by you wicked-souled ones, the *cakravyūha* has been formed;
yet those kings who are of noble birth, most righteous, and true to their vows,
do not form this array known as the *cakra*, which is the work of the most sinful.

The Krauñcas, Suparṇas, Haṃsāhvās, Muśalas, and Gāruḍas—these are the battle arrays of the heroic, most righteous, and high-souled ones. You all have been born from portions of the Daityas; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus,
that high-souled and mighty son of Subhadrā,
a hero among men, then desired to fight with the Kurus.
The mighty Saubhadra, the best among those who speak the truth,
having turned Karna away with his heron-feathered arrows,
swiftly rushed toward the other great archers as well.

Then the highly illustrious Abhimanyu shattered that extended net of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, like an enraged fish tearing through a net. Meanwhile, Karṇa was being afflicted by Abhimanyu with many arrows.
With swift horses, they broke through that army from the direction of the *apāya*.
"Stay, O Karṇa, great archer! O Kṛpa, O Duryodhana!"—as Droṇa cried out thus, O King, that army was shattered.
O King, when the sky was covered by Abhimanyu’s arrows as if by locusts or torrents of rain, nothing at all could be discerned;
yet your warriors were being slaughtered by those sharpened shafts.
O King, with the exception of Saindhava, no one remained standing;
then, O bull among men, the son of Subhadrā, that foremost of men, blew his conch and swiftly rushed toward the Bharata army, O best of the Bharatas.
Like a fire let loose in dry grass,
the son of Arjuna moved through the midst of the Bharata host,
swiftly consuming his enemies while afflicting the chariots, elephants, horses, and men with his sharpened arrows.
Having entered, he made the earth crowded with throngs of headless trunks;
severed by the supreme arrows produced from the bow of Subhadrā’s son,
those seeking to save their lives fled away, even as they struck down their own comrades who stood before them.
Those terrible, broad, and sharp Vipāṭhas, performers of fierce deeds,
swiftly fell to the earth, slaughtering chariots, elephants, and horses;
they were equipped with weapons, finger-guards, swords, and armlets in that battle.
Severed arms adorned with golden ornaments were seen,
as were arrows, bows, swords, bodies, and heads;
thousands of them, still wearing earrings and garlands, lay upon the ground.
With undercarriages, bases, and beautiful poles and shafts;
with axles crushed and chariots shattered in many ways;
and with spears, bows, weapons, and great fallen banners.
O lord of the people, strewn on all sides by those bearing shields and bows, and with slain Kṣatriyas, horses, and elephants,
the earth became almost impassable in an instant, most terrible to behold.
As the princes were being slain and were crying out to one another,
a great sound arose that increased the fear of cowards;
O best of the Bharatas, that sound made all the directions resound.
The son of Subhadrā rushed toward the army, slaughtering horses, chariots, and elephants;
he roamed through all the cardinal and intermediate directions, crushing his enemies,
while we could not see him then, as he was shrouded by the dust raised by the host.
O Bhārata, as he was taking away the lives of elephants, horses,
and men, we suddenly beheld Abhimanyu once more, O great king, scorching the hosts of his enemies like the sun at midday.
O great king, Abhimanyu, equal to Vāsava in battle and the grandson of Vāsava himself, shone in the midst of the army like the heroic son of Agni among the celestial hosts in ancient times.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
[He was] a youth, exceedingly happy, possessing irresistible strength and pride,
skilled in battles, a hero, a son of noble lineage, and one who would sacrifice his own body.
As he plunged into the ranks with his excellent three-year-old horses,
was there any chariot-warrior who followed after him from Yudhiṣṭhira’s army?
Saṃjaya said:
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Śikhaṇḍin, Sātyaki, the twins, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, Drupada along with the Kekayas,
and the enraged Dhṛṣṭaketu, as well as the Matsyas, pursued [the enemy] in battle.
Following that very same path, the Pitṛs, together with their maternal uncles,
rushed forward on chariots drawn up in battle array, seeking to rescue them as they fled.
Seeing those heroes fleeing, your warriors turned their faces away from the fight.
Then, O great king, seeing that the vast army of your son had turned its back,
your energetic son-in-law,
King Jayadratha, the son of the ruler of the Sindhus, rushed forward, desiring to rally them.
Ugradhanvan, the great archer, son of Vṛddhakṣatra, discharging divine weapons, held back the sons of Pṛthā and their armies— those who were greedy for their son—
just as one restrains elephants from a steep slope.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, I consider that an excessive burden was placed upon the King of the Sindhus,
in that he alone held back the enraged Pāṇḍavas who were eager for their son."
"I consider this strength and heroism of the ruler of the Sindhus to be most wonderful. Tell me, therefore, of the prowess and the preeminent deeds of that high-souled one;
what was given, what was offered in sacrifice, what was worshipped, or what severe austerity was performed?"
O Sūta, what is his self-restraint or his holy life,
and which deity— be it Viṣṇu, Īśāna, or Agni’s son— that he has propitiated,
by means of whom this best of men alone held back the enraged Pārthas, even as they were like the kings of rivers?
"Such a great deed was not performed by Bhīṣma; I did not realize it until the King of Sindhu’s son alone held back the Pārthas. Saṃjaya said:
Because he had been defeated by Bhīmasena during the abduction of Draupadī,
that king, out of pride and seeking a boon, performed very great austerities,
withdrawing his senses from their pleasant objects.
Enduring hunger, thirst, and heat, emaciated and covered with visible veins,
he propitiated Lord Śarva while chanting the eternal Brahman.
Then the Blessed One, who is compassionate toward his devotees, showed him mercy.
Then, even in a dream, Hara spoke to the son of the lord of Sindhu:
"Choose a boon; I am pleased, Jayadratha, what do you desire?
Thus addressed by Śarva, Jayadratha, the king of Sindhu, [replied].
Bowing down with joined palms and self-restrained, he spoke to Rudra:
"O Bhārata, I alone shall withstand in battle all the sons of Pāṇḍu, who possess terrible heroism and prowess."
And after he had been well-pleased by his disciplined observances in a short time, Maheśvara, being gratified, then granted him this boon:
"He chose as his boon there: 'In battle, I shall [slay] the sons of Pāṇḍu.'"
"I alone could hold them back with my chariot.
Thus addressed, the Lord of the Gods then spoke to Jayadratha:
"O gentle one, I grant you this boon: except for Pārtha Dhananjaya."
He whom they call unconquerable in battle, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace,
Viṣṇu of the thousand heads— that Kṛṣṇa protects Phālguna.
You shall hold the four sons of Pāṇḍu in battle.
Saying "So be it" to the Lord of the Gods, the king woke up. Addressed by him [Śarva], O Pārtha, Śarva granted him a boon;
saying "For one day," O Indra among kings, he vanished right there.
By virtue of that boon and the power of his divine weapons,
he alone held back the army of the Pāṇḍavas;
through the sound of his bowstring and the slap of his palm, fear entered the hearts of the kṣatriyas.

But among your troops, O King, there arose supreme joy upon seeing that the entire burden had been placed upon the ruler of the Sindhus; they raised a great shout and rushed toward the army of Yudhiṣṭhira.
Saṃjaya said: O Indra among kings, regarding the prowess of the King of the Sindhus about which you ask me—
listen, for I shall relate all of it to you, how he fought against the Pāṇḍavas.
Large, well-trained Saindhava horses, obedient to the charioteer and capable of excellent draught, carrying him with a speed like that of the wind, bore him along;
he was mounted upon a chariot fashioned according to rule, appearing like a city of the Gandharvas.
His great silver banner, shaped like a boar, shone brilliantly;
with its white umbrella, flags, and yak-tail fans,
he gleamed with those royal insignia like the Lord of Stars in the sky.
Adorned with pearls, diamonds, gems, and gold,
that iron chariot-fender shone like the sky covered with celestial lights.
Stretching his great bow and scattering many volleys of arrows, he [advanced].
He filled that gap which the son of Arjuna had torn open;
he struck Sātyaki with three arrows, Vṛkodara with eight,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna with sixty, and Virāṭa with ten shafts.
He struck Drupada with five sharp arrows and Śikhaṇḍin with ten;
he struck the Kekayas with twenty-five and each of the sons of Draupadī with three;
then, with seventy more, he repelled Yudhiṣṭhira and the rest.
With that great net of arrows, it was like a marvel. Then, aiming at his bow with a sharp, yellow-edged crescent-headed shaft,
the powerful King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, cut it asunder while laughing.

In the mere twinkling of an eye, he took up another bow and pierced Pārtha with ten arrows, and those others with three each. Recognizing that dexterity of his, Bhīma again struck him with three broad-headed shafts.
He swiftly cast the bow, the standard, and the umbrella down upon the earth.
Taking up another bow and stringing it, that powerful warrior,
O noble one, shattered Bhīma’s banner, his bow, and his horses.

Leaping down from his excellent chariot, whose horses were slain and whose bow was severed, he sprang onto the vehicle of Sātyaki like a lion onto a mountain peak. Then your men, filled with joy, cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Beholding that most incredible and supreme feat of the King of Sindhu,
those best of kings pierced him from all sides with a shower of arrows;
he was being covered by many great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas.
O Great King, relying upon his divine weapon, he did not waver;
having cut those arrows down with various showers of shafts, O King,
he covered them all, and that was hair-raising.
That all living beings honored that deed of his— how he alone, by the power of his weapons, held back the enraged Pāṇḍavas—
was due to the elephants previously slain by the son of Subhadrā along with their riders and weapons.
The path shown to the Pāṇḍavas was blocked by the ruler of the Sindhus; yet those heroes— the Matsyas, Pañcālas, Kekayas,
and the Pāṇḍavas— striving together, each one individually pursued the Saindhava.
"Whosoever among your enemies strove to break through Drona’s array,
that very person the ruler of the Sindhus held back by virtue of having obtained a boon from the gods.
Sanjaya said:

When the Pāṇḍavas, greedy for victory, were held back by Saindhava, a most terrible battle took place between your men and the enemy. Then the son of Arjuna, true to his promise, entered that army which was difficult to approach.
The radiant hero agitated [the enemy] like a sea-monster agitating the ocean. As that subduer of foes was thus causing agitation with a shower of arrows,
the foremost of the Kurus advanced against the son of Subhadrā according to their rank.
A fierce clash occurred between them and him as those warriors of immeasurable prowess incessantly discharged showers of arrows;
then the son of Arjuna was hemmed in by that multitude of chariots belonging to his enemies.
Having slain Vṛṣasena’s charioteer, he cut his bow asunder;
then the powerful one pierced his horses with straight-flying arrows.
Thereupon, carried away from the battle by those horses that moved like the wind, [Vṛṣasena departed].
In that interval, Abhimanyu’s charioteer drew the chariot away;
then the throngs of chariots, filled with joy, cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
as he, like an enraged lion, was crushing his enemies with his arrows.
As he was approaching from afar, Vasātīya rushed forward swiftly;
he covered Abhimanyu with sixty gold-feathered arrows and said,
"While I am alive, you shall not escape me alive in battle."
The son of Subhadrā pierced that man clad in iron armor in the heart with a swiftly falling arrow; he fell lifeless upon the earth.
Seeing Vasātīya slain, the bulls among the Kṣatriyas were filled with rage.
O King, desiring to slay your grandson, they then surrounded him,
repeatedly stretching their bows of various forms;
that battle between the son of Subhadrā and his enemies became fierce.
Enraged, the son of Phalguna severed their arrows along with their bows, as well as their bodies and heads— heads adorned with earrings and garlands—
and their swords, finger-guards, spears, and battle-axes.
Severed arms adorned with golden ornaments were seen there,
along with fallen garlands, jewelry, garments, and great banners;
as well as armor, shields, necklaces, crowns, parasols, and yak-tail whisks.
With undercarriages, bases, and curved poles;
with shattered axles, wheels broken in many ways, and yokes;
with chassis, banners, as well as charioteers and horses.
The earth became strewn with broken chariots and slain elephants;
covered with the fallen bodies of heroic kṣatriyas, the lords of various realms who were greedy for victory, the ground became truly dreadful.
As Abhimanyu roamed through all the directions and intermediate quarters in battle, his form, enraged as he was, became invisible; likewise,
whatever golden armor and ornaments he possessed vanished from sight.
We saw only his bow and his arrows; at that time,
no one was able to look upon him with their eyes as he stood like the sun in the midst of the warriors, striking down combatants with his shafts.
Saṃjaya said:
The son of Arjuna became like Death himself at the arrival of the appointed time, taking away the lives of heroes and the vital breaths of all beings.
Like Śakra himself in prowess, that mighty son of Śakra’s son,
Abhimanyu, shone brilliantly as he agitated that army.
Having entered it, O king of kings, he was like the Destroyer unto the lords of the Kṣatriyas.
Like a tiger seizing a fierce deer, he seized Satyaśravas;
and when Satyaśravas had been captured, the great car-warriors, acting with haste and grasping their massive weapons, rushed toward Abhimanyu.
"I first! I first!"—thus vying with one another, those bulls among Kṣatriyas arrived, desiring to slay the son of Arjuna. The hosts of Kṣatriyas rushed forward, charging toward him as he fled.
Having encountered him, he swallowed them like small fish in the ocean;
those who came near him and did not flee never returned,
just as rivers do not turn back from the sea.
Seized as if by a great sea-monster and afflicted by the fear of the wind's force,
that army trembled like a ship wrecked upon the ocean;
terrified, your host was like a boat in the great deep.
Then the powerful son of the lord of the Madras, named Rukmaratha, being himself undaunted, spoke these words to reassure the terrified army:
"Enough of your fear, O heroes! This is no one while I stand here."
"I shall capture him alive, without a doubt.
Having spoken thus, the heroic one rushed toward the son of Subhadrā,
borne upon a well-equipped and resplendent chariot.
Having pierced Abhimanyu in the chest with three arrows, he then roared;
and with three sharp shafts, he struck him on the right arm and three on the left.
Then the mighty Abhimanyu, having cut off those [arrows] of the roaring one, [acted].
Having severed his bow, Phālguni quickly struck down both his left and right arms, as well as his head with its beautiful eyes and eyebrows, onto the earth.
He beheld the proud son of Śalya, Rukmaratha, thus shattered.
O King, those princes, who were intoxicated with the pride of battle and skilled in striking, seeking to capture Saubhadra alive by force, were the companions of Śalya’s son,
their banners adorned with gold.
Drawing bows as long as palm trees, those great car-warriors surrounded the son of Arjuna on all sides with a shower of arrows—
heroes endowed with the strength of training, youthful, and exceedingly intolerant.
Seeing the lone, invincible hero, the son of Subhadrā,
being covered by showers of arrows in battle, Duryodhana was filled with joy;
he considered him as having already gone to the abode of Vaivasvata.
With three arrows each, gold-feathered and of various marks,
those princes made the son of Arjuna invisible in the twinkling of an eye,
O noble one, along with his chariot, horses, driver, and standard.
We beheld him covered all over, like a porcupine with its quills. Deeply pierced and enraged, like an elephant tormented by goads,
he invoked the Gāndharva weapon and employed the Ratha-māyā (the illusory chariot).

That which was obtained from the Gandharvas, headed by Tumburu, by Arjuna after he had performed austerities— by means of that, he bewildered his enemies. O King, though he was alone, he appeared as a hundredfold and even a thousandfold.
Displaying his weapons swiftly in battle like a whirling circle of fire,
that scorcher of foes bewildered his enemies with the illusions of his chariot maneuvers and weapons; O King, he then pierced the bodies of the monarchs into a hundred pieces.
With their ranks broken, disoriented, and their minds further terrified, they—
whose heads were severed by broad-headed arrows— then entered the next world;
the life-breaths of the living beings were dispatched in battle by sharpened shafts.
O King, they reached that world, while their bodies fell to the earth;
with sharp, broad-headed arrows, the son of Phalguna severed their bows, horses, drivers, banners, arms adorned with bracelets, and heads.
Just as a mango grove might be destroyed when it has reached its fifth year of fruiting,
so too did a hundred princes fall, slain by the son of Subhadrā— youths who were delicate, accustomed to comfort, and resembled enraged venomous serpents.
Seeing them destroyed by a single man, Duryodhana became terrified. Seeing the chariot-warriors, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers being crushed,
the indignant Duryodhana quickly advanced toward him.
The battle between those two continued for what seemed like a mere moment;
then your son, afflicted by hundreds of arrows, turned his face away from the fight.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Sūta, just as you have described to me the tumultuous and terrible battle of that high-souled one against many, and his victory—
this prowess of Subhadrā’s son is indeed wonderful and almost incredible.
But it is not at all surprising for those who have the Dharma as their refuge.
Now that Duryodhana has turned away and a hundred princes have been slain,
what course of action did my men take against the son of Subhadrā?
For he is the root of all dharmas and the deity of those dwelling in heaven; for those who have Kṛṣṇa as their deity, how could there be the arising of suffering?
When the purpose of actions has been undertaken and brought to fruition by time.
O King, what is this great anxiety? The dull-witted are afflicted by anxiety.
One who first undertakes action and then perceives its ultimate result finds happiness; O Great King, without renunciation, there is no peace of mind.
"O King, you are free from that; hear now the fruit of such conduct.
Saṃjaya said:
"Your men and your sons looked at one another."
With parched mouths, rolling eyes, perspiring, and their hair standing on end,
they were intent on flight and lacked the will to conquer their enemies;
desiring life, they called out to one another by their family names and personal names.
Abandoning again and again their slain brothers, fathers, sons, friends, relatives, and kinsmen,
they rushed forward, urging on their horses and elephants.
Seeing them thus broken, Droṇa, the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman), and Bṛhadbala [pressed on].
Kṛpa, Duryodhana, Karṇa, Kṛtavarman, and the son of Subala—
all of them likewise rushed forward and swiftly struck the son of Subhadrā. Thus they saw your army slaughtered like one who is protectorless.
O King, those highly enraged warriors rushed against the unconquered son of Subhadrā;
yet they too, O great king, were for the most part turned back by your grandson,
the son of Subhadrā, who possessed a splendor equal to that of Śakra.

But Lakṣmaṇa, who had been raised in luxury, fearless due to his youth and pride, skilled in archery and possessed of great splendor, advanced against the son of Arjuna. His father, out of longing for his son, followed immediately after him and turned back.
Other great car-warriors followed after Duryodhana;
they showered him with arrows, as clouds drench a mountain with water.
And he alone crushed them all, like a wind blowing in every direction scatters the clouds.
But your grandson Lakṣmaṇa— invincible, pleasing to behold,
standing near his father, a hero with bow raised,
raised in extreme luxury, and resembling the son of the Lord of Wealth— [beheld].
In the battle, the son of Kṛṣṇa (Abhimanyu) assailed him like one rutting elephant attacking another;
then Lakṣmaṇa, the master of weapons, spoke to the enraged son of Arjuna:
"Listen to my words, O mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful Abhimanyu!"
"Go quickly to the Pāṇḍavas; do not engage in battle, O observer of noble vows. Having heard those words of his, the powerful Abhimanyu, O Bhārata, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa while laughing as if in anger.
"O brother, having indeed slain all these Pāṇḍavas, I shall go away for a long time; I tell you this truly: even today. [He spoke thus] like a lion cub in the forest toward a young white lotus.
Having encountered Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Subhadrā, that slayer of enemy heroes,
was struck on his arms and chest with exceedingly sharp and keen arrows;
thereupon the mighty-armed one became enraged like a serpent struck by a staff.
"O great king, your grandson spoke to your own grandson:
'Take a final look at this world, for you shall go to the other world;
while your kinsmen look on, I shall lead you to the abode of Yama.'"
Seeing his transgression, O King, the wise Lakṣmaṇa, skilled in combat,
then engaged him in battle with various weapons and missiles;
the duel between those two was like that between Mercury and Mars.
Like the mighty Indra and Vāsava wishing to slay one another,
they pierced each other with most terrible nets of arrows;
and Lakṣmaṇa struck him in the middle of the chest with ten sharpened shafts.
He struck the son of Arjuna as well; thus pierced by Abhimanyu,
he in turn struck down the horses of the chariot with five arrows each,
slew the charioteer with one arrow, and struck down the standard with another single arrow.
Having severed the bow with three arrows, the son of Arjuna, possessed of great strength,
spoke thus; then the mighty-armed Saubhadra, the slayer of enemy heroes, drew forth a broad-headed shaft that resembled a snake freed from its slough.
Released from his arm, it struck off Lakṣmaṇa’s head—handsome to behold, with its fine nose, beautiful brows, and dark hair, adorned with earrings.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa slain, the people cried out, "Alas! Alas! in loud lamentation.
The son of Subhadrā slew with his arrows fourteen thousand brothers and princes who were followers of the Kumāra,
as well as eight thousand chariots and seven hundred elephants.
Then Duryodhana, that bull among Kṣatriyas, enraged because his beloved son had been struck down,
cried out to the Kṣatriyas, "Kill him!
Thereupon Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Bṛhadbala [advanced].
And Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, along with six chariot-warriors, surrounded him.
Having pierced them with sharp arrows and forced them to turn back, the son of Arjuna,
filled with rage, rushed with speed toward the great force of the ruler of the Sindhus.
Clad in armor, the Kalingas, the Niṣādas, and the heroic son of Krātha blocked his path with a division of elephants.
O lord of the people, that battle became exceedingly intense, as if it were continuous.
Then the son of Arjuna fearlessly scattered that elephant division,
just as the ever-moving wind disperses hundreds of clouds in the sky.
Thereupon Kratha covered the son of Arjuna with a multitude of arrows.
Then the other chariot-warriors, led by Droṇa,
returned once more and rushed toward the son of Subhadrā, brandishing their supreme weapons. Checking them with his arrows, the son of Arjuna then afflicted the son of Krātha.

Hurrying with the intent to slay him, he struck down his bow, his two arms adorned with arrows and bracelets, his head with its crown, his umbrella, his standard, his charioteer, and his horses, using an immeasurable flood of arrows.
When he— who was endowed with noble lineage, character, learning, strength, fame, and the power of weapons— was slain, the heroes for the most part turned their backs in retreat. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Thus did the youthful and unconquered son of Subhadrā enter,
acting in accordance with his lineage, never retreating in battles,
