and mounted upon three-year-old steeds of noble breed and great strength.
"Who were the heroes that held back him who was gliding, as it were, through the sky?
Sañjaya said:
"Abhimanyu, having entered your ranks, [assailed them] with sharpened arrows."
The son of Pāṇḍu turned all the kings away;
but Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, Bṛhadbala, and Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika— these six chariot-warriors— surrounded him.
O great king, seeing that an excessive burden had been placed upon the Saindhava,
your army rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira; meanwhile,
the others showered the heroic son of Subhadrā with a rain of arrows.
Drawing bows as long as palm trees, those great car-warriors were all mighty archers perfected in every branch of knowledge;
yet Saubhadra, the slayer of enemy heroes, paralyzed them all in battle with his arrows.
Having pierced Droṇa with fifty arrows and Bṛhadbala with twenty,
he struck Kṛtavarman with eighty and Kṛpa with sixty feathered shafts—
gold-tufted, high-velocity arrows drawn back to his ear.
The son of Arjuna pierced Aśvatthāman with ten arrows; then,
in the midst of his enemies, the son of Phalguna struck Karṇa on the ear with a sharp, yellow, barbed arrow of supreme quality.
Having struck down Kṛpa’s horses as well as both his flank-guards,
he then pierced him in the middle of the chest with ten arrows—
Vṛndāraka, the hero who increases the fame of the Kurus.
While your heroic sons were looking on, the mighty one slew him;
then the son of Droṇa struck that fearlessly crushing the best of his enemies with twenty-five small arrows.
But while the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked on, O noble one, the son of Arjuna swiftly pierced Aśvatthāman in return with sharp arrows;
the son of Droṇa then struck him with sixty shafts of keen edge and excellent temper.
Though pierced by those fierce arrows, he did not tremble, remaining like Mount Maināka.
Then that powerful and highly energetic warrior pierced the son of Droṇa, his wrongdoer, in return with seventy-three straight-flying shafts feathered in gold.
In that battle, Droṇa, longing for his son, discharged a hundred arrows;
likewise Aśvatthāman, seeking to protect his father in the fray, shot eight.
Karṇa loosed twenty-two broad-headed shafts, and Kṛtavarman fourteen.
Bṛhadbala had fifty, while Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, had ten;
he struck them all back with ten arrows each.
Thus afflicted on all sides by those sharp arrows, the son of Subhadrā—
The lord of the Kosalas struck him in the heart with a barbed arrow;
he [the Kosala king] felled his horses, standard, bow, and charioteer to the ground. Then the king of Kosala, deprived of his chariot, took up sword and shield.

He desired to sever from the body of Phālguni’s son the head adorned with earrings. He pierced Bṛhadbala, the prince and lord of the Kosalas, in the heart with an arrow; with his heart shattered, he fell.
O King, he shattered ten thousand high-souled warriors who were uttering inauspicious cries while wielding swords and bows;
having thus slain Bṛhadbala, the son of Subhadrā roamed through the battlefield.
Paralysing those great archers, your warriors, with his waters of arrows,
Sañjaya said:
"The son of Phalguna pierced Karṇa again in the ear with a barbed arrow."
Enraged, he pierced him with fifty arrows; then the son of Rādhā pierced him back with as many in return. With all his limbs covered by those shafts, O Bhārata, he shone most brilliantly.
And in his rage, he caused Karna to flow with a stream of blood;
yet the heroic Karna shone forth, variegated by arrows and drenched in gore,
like the sun at the end of autumn when its edges are touched by the twilight.
Both those great-souled ones, their limbs variegated by arrows and drenched in blood, appeared like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom. Then,
[he struck] the six heroic ministers of Karṇa, who were skilled in diverse modes of combat.
The son of Subhadrā indeed struck down [the enemies] along with their horses, charioteers, banners, and chariots; then,
remaining unperturbed, he pierced the other great archers with ten arrows each, and that was like a marvel.
Furthermore, having struck the son of the Magadha king with six straight-flying arrows,
he felled the youthful Aśvaketu along with his horses and charioteer. Then [he struck] the Bhoja from Mārtikāvata, whose banner bore the emblem of an elephant.
Having severed the head of Jayatsena, the lord of Magadha,
with a razor-sharp arrow while discharging other shafts, he let out a roar.
Duhshasana’s son, having pierced his four horses with four arrows, [struck him].
He pierced the charioteer with one arrow and Arjuna’s son with ten;
then the son of Kṛṣṇa, having struck the son of Duḥśāsana with seven swift shafts,
his eyes red with fury, spoke these words aloud.
"Your father has fled from this battle like a coward;
by good fortune you too know how to fight, but today you shall not escape.
Having spoken these words, [he drew] the sword polished by the smith.
He discharged an iron shaft (nārāca) at him, which the son of Droṇa cut into three pieces with three arrows.
Having severed his banner, Arjuna’s son struck Śalya with three arrows;
Śalya, in turn, struck him with nine vulture-feathered shafts.
O King, that appeared like a marvel, as if it were occurring calmly within his heart.
Arjuna’s son, having cut down his standard and both his flank-drivers,
pierced him with six iron arrows, and he fled to another chariot.
Having slain these five— Śatruñjaya, Candraketu, Meghavega, Suvarcas, and Sūryabhāsa— he pierced the son of Subala.
Having pierced him with three arrows, the son of Subala then spoke to Duryodhana.
"Let us all crush him before he slays one of us at a time.
Then the bull Karna Vaikartana said to Droṇa:
"Before he crushes us all, tell us quickly how we may slay him."
Then the great archer Droṇa addressed them all:
"Does anyone among you perceive any vulnerability in this youth?
For today he moves about in every direction, following in the footsteps of his father."
Behold the swiftness of that lion among men, the son of Pāṇḍu!
On the paths of his chariot, only the circle of his bow is visible,
like the orb of the brilliantly shining sun as it destroys the darkness.
As he fitted his arrows, released them with great speed,
and drew that excellent bow, no interval whatsoever could be seen; indeed,
with his shafts, he seemed to tear at my very life-breaths and to bewilder me.
The son of Subhadrā, the slayer of enemy heroes, gladdens me ever more; this son of Subhadrā brings me exceeding joy as he moves about the battlefield,
such that even the enraged great car-warriors cannot find his opening.
"As he shoots with such lightness of hand, filling all directions with his great arrows, I perceive no distinction [in prowess] in battle for the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva.
Then Karṇa, afflicted by the arrows of Arjuna’s son, spoke again to Droṇa."
Thinking "I must stand firm," I remain even while being tormented by Abhimanyu;
the most dreadful arrows of that radiant youth,
terrible and possessing the brilliance of fire, are piercing my heart today.
"O twice-born one, even as the kings look on today, because of my modesty,
not a single limb of mine is failing, nor does my voice falter,
despite being scorched by the excellent arrows of the noble prince."
By his arrows, released without being obstructed, and by his shafts that have entered within me,
my body cannot be discerned, as if they were searching for my very life-breaths.
What is that science of archery, and who is he, by whom we alone have been conquered?
The teacher spoke softly to Karṇa, as if smiling:
"His armor is impenetrable, and he is young with swift prowess; I have taught his father the method of wearing this armor."
The conqueror of enemy cities certainly knows all of this;
however, the characteristics of the bowstring have not been taught here by me to Phalguna.
Yet, it is possible to cut his bow and its string with well-aimed arrows.
The reins, the horses, and likewise both the outriders and the charioteer—
perform this, O great archer Rādheya, if it is possible;
then, having turned him away, strike him from behind.
"With his bow, he cannot be conquered even by the gods and asuras;
therefore, if you so desire, deprive him of his chariot and his bow,
or else render him devoid of his splendor."
O King,
as he was discharging that arrow which had been aimed at its mark, the son of Arjuna— his mind being slightly distracted by someone standing before him— was difficult for anyone to defeat.
Having heard those words of the preceptor, Karṇa Vaikartana, seeing the son of Subhadrā discharging his arrows, quickly raised a loud cry:
"This prince has missed his mark! Let him be slain! Let him be slain!"
While the high-souled Abhimanyu was thus reflecting and shooting arrows with light-handed skill, [Kṛtavarman] cut his bow with shafts;
Bhoja slew his horses, and Gautama killed his two flank-drivers.
The remaining six great car-warriors, acting with haste at a time that required speed,
being pitiless, overwhelmed the lone youth— who was now without a chariot— with showers of arrows as he stood with his bow broken.
With his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, that illustrious hero, upholding his own duty, leapt into the air wielding sword and shield;
he performed circles through his well-trained movements, advancing and retreating with skill.
With the Kaiśika and other maneuvers, and through both agility and strength,
the son of Arjuna moved through the sky like the king of birds.
With their eyes fixed upward, they thought, "He is falling upon me with his sword."

Seeing an opening in the battle, those great archers pierced him. Droṇa, the conqueror of enemies and possessor of great splendor, acting with haste, cut off his sword— which had a hilt adorned with jewels— from his fist using a razor-sharp arrow.
The son of Rādha pierced his excellent shield with sharpened arrows. With his shield shattered and his limbs covered by arrows, he descended from the sky back to the earth;
then, raising his discus, he rushed furiously toward Droṇa.
With his limbs resplendent with the dust of the wheels,
Abhimanyu appeared exceedingly noble in battle, like the moon on an auspicious night.
Emulating the likeness of Vāsudeva,
his face made singularly red by the flowing blood,
with a face distorted by a frown and a roar like that of a great lion, he—
The lord Abhimanyu, possessed of immeasurable strength in battle,
shone brilliantly as he stood in the midst of the foremost of kings.
Sañjaya said:
The brother of Viṣṇu, who brings joy and is adorned with the weapons of Viṣṇu,
shone in battle like another Janārdana,
that great chariot-warrior whose locks were tossed by the wind and who held raised the excellent weapons of his enemies.
Having beheld that form, difficult even for the gods to behold, the lords of the earth [thought]:
"If this discus were released from the palm of Phālguna's hand,
it would fall like the discus of Viṣṇu by virtue of his maternal uncle’s boon."
Greatly agitated, they shattered that wheel into many pieces.
Thereupon, the son of Kṛṣṇa, that great car-warrior, seized a massive mace, for he had been deprived of his bow, chariot,
sword, and wheel by those enemies.
Abhimanyu, mace in hand, rushed toward Aśvatthāman. Seeing that raised mace blazing like a thunderbolt,
that bull among men leaped down from the seat of his chariot and took three strides backward.
Having slain his horses with his mace as well as both his flank-drivers, the son of Subhadrā, his body covered with arrows, appeared like a porcupine. Then he crushed Kālakeya, the son of Subala.
He slew seventy-seven of his followers, the Gāndhāras;
furthermore, he killed ten chariot-warriors from Brahmavāsātīya,
having destroyed seven chariots of the Kekayas and ten elephants.
With his mace, he crushed the chariot of Duḥśāsana’s son, along with its horses.
Then, O noble one, the enraged son of Duḥśāsana raised his mace and rushed toward the son of Subhadrā, crying out, "Stay! Stay!"
Those two heroes, with maces raised and each desiring to slay the other,
struck one another like Tryambaka and Antaka in days of yore.
Having struck each other with the tips of their maces, they both fell to the earth.
Then, from the surface of the earth, the son of Kṛṣṇa (Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana), stumbling as if he had drunk poison,
rushed toward the son of Duḥśāsana on the ground with bitten lips;
he too, seizing his swift mace, raised it against the son of Arjuna.
The son of Subhadrā, however, struck the son of Duḥśāsana with a few breaths;
thus both those brothers went to the abode of Vaivasvata, like two banners of Indra cast down in the midst of battle, O scorcher of foes.
Then the son of Duḥśāsana, the enhancer of the Kurus' fame,
who was like a god, a great archer of immense renown, having consumed the warrior class,
rose up and struck the head of the advancing son of Subhadrā with his mace.
Stunned by the great force of the mace and by his own exertion,
he relied upon his manly strength and yet fell into a faint;
thus did that great hero, the enhancer of the Kuru lineage, then succumb.
While fighting, overcome by thirst, delicate yet possessed of great strength,
and tormented by hunger, O King, he fell into a slight faint;
his eyes were seen to be slightly rolling.
Then, having sat down for a moment, he spoke these words:
"Let all the Kauravas hear these words, which are consistent with dharma and worldly purpose.
[Of Arjuna’s...]"
I am the heir and nephew of that great-souled one;
yet I, dull-witted as a base man,
having become the son of Subhadrā, have accomplished nothing at all.
"All of you, while still alive, must remain devoted to our grandfather Droṇa!
Speaking thus, Abhimanyu,
though possessed of great prowess, was then lost in battle.
Seized by fortitude at that time, that great-souled one,
overcome by fainting, fell into a state of agitation;
looking toward all directions with wrath, he of great strength [roared].
On that very hero’s bed, the son of Subhadrā fell to the earth,
having slain those many heroes led by Lakṣmaṇa,
and likewise having destroyed ten million chariots and elephants.
A full hundred million horses and one hundred billion foot soldiers—
having crushed these in battle, Abhimanyu has gone to heaven. Thus, when the sun had set, these two departed together.
Deprived of his senses, Saubhadra, the slayer of enemy heroes, fell to the ground.
Thus, O King, was he alone slain by many in battle,
after having agitated the entire army like an elephant stirring a lotus pond.
Slain, the hero shone like a wild elephant struck down by hunters;
your men surrounded that fallen warrior just as people surround a fire at the end of winter after it has consumed a forest and grown quiet.
Like the wind that has subsided after crushing the mountain peaks,
like the sun that has set after scorching the Bharata host,
like the moon eclipsed, or like the ocean dried up.

Seeing him fallen on the ground— his face like the full moon, his eyes fringed by hair like a crow's wing, his locks adorned with side-locks, and known as a mere youth— those great car-warriors of yours [beheld him].
Filled with supreme joy, they repeatedly roared like lions. O lord of the people, there was the greatest delight among your men,
while from the eyes of the other heroes, tears fell.
O lord of the people, upon seeing that hero fallen like the moon dropped from the sky, beings in the intermediate space cried out in lamentation;
he had been struck down by six great car-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s side, headed by Droṇa and Karṇa.
"This man lies here alone, slain; for this is not considered righteous by us.
Yet, when that hero was struck down, the earth shone greatly, like the sky garlanded with hosts of stars and graced by the full moon.
It was strewn with gold-tufted arrows and drenched in floods of blood;
it was covered with the radiant heads of heroes adorned with earrings,
and filled with variegated elephant-hides and banners.
With fly-whisks and elephant-blankets scattered about, with the finest garments,
and with the radiant ornaments of chariots, horses, men, and elephants—
along with sharp, polished swords that resembled sloughed-off serpents.
The earth, strewn with broken bows and arrows, with spears, double-edged swords, javelins, and kampanas,
and with various other weapons,
shone as they groaned in extreme agony, vomiting streams of blood.
The earth shone even more intensely with men falling and those already fallen,
and also with lifeless horses drenched in blood;
the ground became uneven with their riders, all struck down by the son of Subhadrā.
With elephants that had tusks, along with their mahouts, and were equipped with armor, weapons, and banners— like shattered mountains uprooted by arrows—
and with horses, charioteers, and warriors strewn across the earth, [the field was covered].
With its excellent chariots whose elephants had been slain, resembling agitated lakes,
and with throngs of foot soldiers killed along with their various weapons and ornaments,
the earth assumed a terrible form that struck terror into the hearts of cowards.
Seeing him fallen upon the ground, possessing a splendor like that of the sun and moon,
your men felt supreme joy while the Pāṇḍavas were overcome with grief.
O King, this occurred when Abhimanyu, a mere child who had not yet reached his youth, was slain.
The entire army fled while Dharmarāja looked on;
seeing his forces being shattered after the son of Subhadrā had been struck down,
Ajātaśatru spoke these words to his own heroes:
"This jewel of the sky, possessed of great power, has set after having scorched [the world].
What has become of the son of Subhadrā, the subduer of enemies? We truly do not know.
Speaking thus, the king was surrounded by a vast army.
Having reached the gate of the array, his eyes were clouded with a flood of tears;
and having heard from the people all that had been told regarding the prowess of Abhimanyu and how his son had been slain by the deceitful Kauravas.
Having heard that the hero had been slain, he quickly summoned his fortitude; relying upon supreme courage, that best of warriors replied:
"This hero has gone to heaven, for he was slain while facing the enemy and not turning his back."

"Steady yourselves! Do not fear! We shall conquer our enemies in battle!"—thus did that king of great energy and supreme luster, the King of Dharma and best of warriors, dispel their sorrow by speaking these words to those who were grieving.
Having first slain many princes who resembled venomous serpents in battle during that conflict, the son of Arjuna followed after them;
having killed ten thousand warriors and the great car-warrior Kausalya as well.
The son of Kṛṣṇa, equal to Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, has surely gone to the abode of Śakra;
having slain chariots, horses, men, and elephants by the thousands,
that performer of meritorious deeds is not to be grieved for, as he remained unsated with battle.
He has gone to the radiant worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds, won by their merit. There is no other sorrow greater than grief for a son;
there is no other giver found who bestows such fruit both in this world and the next.
"My son has been slain today; I have no desire to live.
What purpose is there for me in living on this earth without the son of Subhadrā?
Having attained the inexhaustible goal, he has gone to eternal years."
But we, having slain their foremost leader and being afflicted by their arrows, returned toward our camp at sunset, drenched in blood. We and the enemy slowly surveyed the field of battle.
They retreated, O great king, overcome by exhaustion and deprived of their senses.
Then, at the junction of night and day, there occurred a wondrous and inauspicious occurrence marked by the howling of jackals.
When the sun, resembling a cluster of lotuses,
had reached the mountain of setting and was hanging low,
[the field was strewn] with excellent swords, spears, lances, chariot-fences, and shields.
Diminishing the luster of ornaments and as if bringing heaven and earth together,
the sun approaches its beloved form, the fire.
Resembling great peaks of mountains piled with massive clouds,
they were like many elephants struck down by the thunderbolt, equipped with victory banners, goads, armor, and riders.
The earth seemed to groan, strewn with fallen elephants trumpeting, with their masters slain and their foot-soldiers' equipment crushed,
and with horses and charioteers killed, their banners and standards cast down.
O lord of men, the earth shone with the crushed great chariot-warriors, like cities destroyed by enemies,
along with the multitudes of chariots and horses, including the slain drivers.
With various kinds of broken vessels and ornaments,
and with tongues, teeth, entrails, and eyes cast out,
the earth shone with a terrifying and hideous appearance.
Men whose armor and ornaments were cast away, though once possessed of excellent weapons,
and whose elephants, horses, chariots, and followers had perished—
men who were always accustomed to costly beds and coverings.
Slain, they lie upon the earth like those without a protector;
jackals, dogs, and crows are exceedingly delighted,
as are eagles, wolves, and hyenas.
Birds that drink blood, hosts of *rakṣasas*,
and most dreadful throngs of *piśācas* were present in the battle;
piercing through the skin, they drank fat and blood.
In that very same way, they ate marrow and flesh; they tore apart the fat, laughed, and sang,
dragging away corpses by the many.
Carrying heaps of bodies, with blood for its water, chariots for its rafts, crowded with elephants for its rocks, and human heads for its stones and flesh for its mud;
Then a river was set in motion by the best of warriors— a river garlanded with various kinds of discarded weapons, terrifying and as difficult to cross as the Vaitaraṇī.
It flowed fiercely through the middle of the battlefield,
terrifying and carrying away both the living and the dead; there, hideous creatures drank and devoured [the corpses].
Various hosts of piśācas, most terrifying,
were greatly delighted; they caused fear among living beings,
and dogs, jackals, and birds shared their food equally.
Thus, at the onset of night, the men gazed upon that battlefield of fierce appearance, which resembled the kingdom of the Lord of the Ancestors, and slowly departed.
Crowded with swarms of rising vultures,
stripped of its magnificent ornaments which were scattered and destroyed, that great chariot— once equal to Śakra— lay prostrate.
Then the people beheld Abhimanyu in battle,
like a sacrificial fire in the assembly hall when the oblations have been cast away.
Sañjaya said:
When that hero, the son of Subhadrā and leader of chariot-divisions, had been slain, all the kings— having cast off their chariots and armor and laid aside their bows—
sat down together, surrounding King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Meditating on that very sorrow, their minds fixed on the son of Subhadrā,
King Yudhiṣṭhira then lamented in great distress,
for the heroic Abhimanyu, his brother’s son and a great car-warrior, had been slain.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"This [arrow] shall strike Karṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and King Suyodhana,
as well as Droṇa, the son of Droṇa— that great archer— and likewise other great chariot-warriors."
Desiring to do what was pleasing to me, this hero lies fallen, having slain the enemy hosts and the unimpeded army of Droṇa—
those masters of weapons, skilled in battle, great archers, and possessed of great strength.

Those endowed with noble lineage, virtuous conduct, and excellent qualities—heroes of celebrated prowess—[were stationed]. Drona had formed an impenetrable array, which even the immortals could not breach;
it was a lotus-array (*padmavyūha*) never before seen by us, beloved of the wielder of the discus.
Having broken through the array, he entered it like a lion into the midst of a herd of cattle.
As he struck down the foremost of the enemy in battle, he sported there;
for even the heroic, great archers who stood against him in the fray [could not withstand him].
Even those skilled in weapons, intoxicated by battle, turn back in defeat;
for by him, our ultimate enemy Duḥśāsana was swiftly turned away from the field of battle, rendered unconscious by his arrows while facing him.
Having crossed that formidable and difficult-to-traverse great ocean of Droṇa’s army,

which was terrifying and teeming with heroes as its crocodiles, the heroic son of Kṛṣṇa (Sātyaki) passed through it fearlessly; and having reached the son of Duḥśāsana, he went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
How shall I behold Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, now that Subhadrā’s son has been slain?
Or how shall I see the highly fortunate Subhadrā, who no longer sees her beloved son—
she who looks up toward him with longing, like a cow whose calf has been killed?
"What indeed shall we say in reply to both Hṛṣīkeśa and Dhanañjaya when they speak words that are devoid of meaning, incoherent,
and improper? I alone [shall answer] for Subhadrā, and for Keśava and Arjuna as well."
Desiring what is pleasing and longing for victory, he has committed this unpleasant act. The greedy man does not perceive his faults; through delusion, greed prevails.
For in my desire for honey, I did not see such a precipice as this.
"He who was indeed to be placed at the forefront in matters of food, vehicles, beds,
and ornaments— that boy has been placed by us at the front in battle. For how can a mere youth, unskilled in wars, [be thus treated]?"
Like a fine horse in a narrow and treacherous place, he deserves safety;
for if we do not [protect him], we too shall lie upon the earth,
consumed by the fire of Bībhatsu’s wrath and his pitiful gaze.
Free from greed, wise, modest, patient, handsome, and strong; possessed of a noble form, respectful, heroic, beloved, and devoted to truth—
he whose deeds the gods praise, for he was one of mighty action.
The heroic one slew the Nivātakavacas and the Kālakeyas—
those enemies of Mahendra who dwelt in Hiraṇyapura; in the mere twinkling of an eye, he destroyed the Paulomas along with their hosts.
The Lord, who grants fearlessness even to others who seek it,
has today been unable to protect his own son from danger;
for a truly great fear has now befallen the vast army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons.

Enraged by the slaughter of his sons, Pārtha will wither the Kauravas. Seeing clearly that he is base, surrounded by base companions, and afflicted by the destruction of his own side, Duryodhana will grieve and give up his life.
Neither victory, nor sovereignty, nor immortality, nor even residence in the same world as the gods brings me joy,
when I behold this man of such matchless heroism and prowess.
"The son of the best of gods has been struck down.
Sañjaya said:
"While Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, was thus lamenting,"
Then the great seer Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana arrived there.
Having honored him according to custom, Yudhiṣṭhira,
tormented by grief over the slaughter of his brother’s sons, spoke to him as he sat down.
Surrounded by many great car-warriors who were joined with unrighteousness,
the son of Subhadrā, that slayer of enemy heroes, though a youth yet possessed of the intellect of an adult, was slain in battle by those mighty archers.

Fighting in battle without skillful means, he was destroyed. When I spoke to him in the midst of the fray, saying, "Open a passage for us," and he had entered among the enemies, we were held back by the ruler of the Sindhus.
"Indeed, those who live by war ought to desire a fair fight; yet this battle undertaken by our enemies is utterly unfair. Because of this, I am deeply distressed and overwhelmed by tears of grief."
Reflecting upon this again and again, I find no peace at all.
To him who was thus lamenting, overwhelmed by tears of grief,
the blessed Vyāsa spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O highly wise one, expert in all the scriptures! O bull among the Bharatas, those such as you do not lose their composure in times of calamity.
This hero has gone to heaven after slaying many enemies in battle.

Having performed deeds worthy of one who is not a child, O Yudhiṣṭhira, that Supreme Person is indeed beyond being transgressed; for this is the law, O Bhārata: Death carries away even the gods, Dānavas, and Gandharvas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"These protectors of the earth lie here upon the surface of the ground;
slain in the midst of the army, these mighty ones have lost their consciousness."
Others possess the strength of ten thousand elephants, and likewise the force of the wind;
I see no slayer of these beings anywhere in combat,
for they are endowed with prowess and possessed of fiery energy and strength.
And yet these wise men lie here slain, their lives departed;
the word "dead" is used for them as if its purpose were already fulfilled.
These lords of the earth, who for the most part possessed terrible prowess, are now dead.
The princes, filled with fury, have entered the mouth of Vaiśvānara.
Here a doubt has arisen in me: from where is the designation "the dead"?
Whose is death? From what does death arise? By whom are these creatures brought to death?
Saṃjaya said:
"O Grandfather, you who resemble an immortal, tell me that which carries [the soul] away.
To Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, who was thus questioning him, [the Grandfather spoke].
The Blessed One, the Seer, spoke these words of consolation:
"In this regard, O King, they cite this ancient history told long ago by Nārada concerning Akampana."

And that king, O Indra among kings, experienced the supreme calamity regarding his son— the most unbearable thing in the world— such is my conviction. Therefore, I shall fully describe that supreme origin of death.

Then you shall be released from suffering, which arises from the bond of affection. O dear one, listen as I recite this ancient account, which is auspicious, life-prolonging, a destroyer of grief, and a promoter of prosperity.
Long ago in the Kṛta age, O dear one, there was indeed a king named Akampana.
He fell under the power of his enemies in the midst of the front line of battle. His son, named Hari, possessed a splendor equal to that of Nārāyaṇa.
Glorious, skilled in weapons, intelligent, and as powerful as Śakra in battle,
he stood at the head of the fray surrounded by enemies on many sides,
discharging thousands of arrows upon both warriors and elephants.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having performed that difficult task in battle and scorched his enemies, he was slain by his foes in the midst of the army during the conflict; that king, overcome with grief,
performed the funeral rites for him.
Grieving by day and by night, he found no happiness for himself.
But perceiving his grief arising from the calamity that had befallen his son,
the celestial sage Nārada then approached him.

But that illustrious king, having beheld the best of divine sages and having honored him according to the prescribed rule, then related his story. O lord of men, he recounted everything exactly as it had happened.
Victory over enemies in battle and likewise the slaughter of my son— my son, possessed of great heroism and a splendor equal to Indra and Viṣṇu,
was slain by many foes in battle despite his prowess and strength.
"O Blessed One, who is this Death? What is his vigor, strength, and prowess?
O best among the wise, I desire to hear this in its true essence. Having heard those words of his, the lord Nārada, the granter of boons, [replied].
He related this great narrative that dispels the grief for one's son.
Nārada said:
"Listen, O King, O mighty-armed one, to this very extensive narrative."
O lord of the earth, I too have heard exactly what occurred:
at the time of the original creation, the Grandfather Brahmā,
the Lord of great splendor, having created all beings, beheld this world as it was not yet withdrawn.
O King, a thought concerning the dissolution of the world arose within him;
for even while reflecting upon it, O lord of the earth, he did not know how that dissolution would occur. Out of his wrath, O great king, fire issued forth from the pores of his skin.
Desiring to consume [all things] along with the intermediate regions, he pervaded all directions;
then the Lord, the Master, burnt the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, including heaven, earth, and the sky, which were enveloped by garlands of flames.
Then the heroic one, as if terrifying all beings— both moving and stationary— with the great force of his wrath, [struck them].
Then Hara, the matted-haired Sthāṇu, Śiva, the lord of night-stalkers, [remained firm].
He went for refuge to the god Brahmā, the supreme lord. When Sthāṇu had thus approached out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures,
the supreme god, blazing like a great sage, spoke.
"What shall we do for you, O you who are worthy of desires? You have been born from desire, my dear son.
Sthāṇu said:
"I shall do everything that is pleasing; tell me, Sthāṇu, what you wish."
O Lord, you indeed exerted effort for the sake of creating progeny;
by you the various multitudes of beings were created and brought to growth.
Yet now, through your wrath, those very progeny are being consumed on every side.
Brahmā said:
"Seeing them, compassion has arisen within me; be gracious, O Blessed One, O Lord.
I am not angry, nor is there any desire on my part that this should happen thus."
Out of a desire for the welfare of the earth, wrath then entered me; for this goddess, afflicted by her burden, constantly urged me on,
O Mahādeva, being overwhelmed by that weight for the sake of its destruction.
Then I could not find [the answer] and was distressed in many ways at that time.
Sthāṇu said:
"Then, because of my inability to comprehend the withdrawal of the immeasurable [power], wrath took possession of me."
Be gracious for the sake of withdrawal; do not be angry, O Lord of the gods! Let not the creatures, both stationary and moving, be destroyed.
By your grace, O Blessed One, may this threefold world continue to exist.
That which is future, that which is past, and that which exists at present—
the Blessed One, blazing with anger, emitted fire from his wrath. It burns the heaps of stones, the trees, and likewise the rivers.
All the ponds and all the grasses and reeds,
as well as the entire world— both stationary and moving— he reduces to nothingness;
thus this entire pure world has been turned to ashes.
"Be gracious, O Blessed One! Let there be no anger; this is my boon.
For all [these beings] have perished and will by no means lead you away, O God. Therefore, let your splendor turn back and be absorbed right here within you."
Out of a desire for the welfare of living beings, look for another means; act in such a way that all these creatures may turn back from this path,
so that these offspring do not go to their destruction here with their lineages utterly cut off.

"O Destroyer of worlds, I have been appointed by you among the worlds as a presiding deity over the celestial realm. O Lord of the universe, let not this world, with its mobile and immobile beings, come to ruin.
Nārada said:
Therefore, I speak thus to the Lord who is inclined toward grace; for having heard the words of Sthāṇu, whose sins have been destroyed,
the Lord indeed withdrew his splendor back into his own inner self.

Then, having withdrawn that fire, the Blessed One, honored by the world, the Lord, ordained both the path of worldly activity and the path of renunciation. As he was thus withdrawing that fire born of his wrath, [the world remained as it was].
From all the pores of the Great-Souled One, a woman appeared—
dark-complexioned, wearing crimson garments, with red tongues, face, and eyes,
and adorned, O King of kings, with two glowing earrings.
Emerging from those apertures, she took recourse in the southern direction;
as if smiling, she gazed upon both the gods, the lords of the universe.
Then the god, the lord of the origin and dissolution of the worlds, called out to her.
"O Death, O protector of the earth, destroy these subjects!
For you have appeared from my wrath with the intent of universal destruction; therefore, withdraw all these subjects, both the ignorant and the wise."
"By my command, you shall indeed attain what is for your highest good.
Thus addressed by him, that lotus-eyed Death,
the frail woman, reflected deeply and wept with a loud voice.
The Grandfather (Pitāmaha) received those tears with both his hands.
Nārada said:
"And then, for the sake of the welfare of all beings, he also consoled her."
Having suppressed her distress within herself, the weak woman, with palms joined in reverence, spoke again to Prajāpati like a creeper bending down,
O best of speakers: "How was such a woman as this created by you?"
Why would I, though wise, act like a fool and perform a cruel and harmful deed? For I am afraid of unrighteousness; be gracious, O Blessed Lord!
[I fear for] my beloved sons, friends, brothers, mothers, fathers, and husbands.
O Lord, I am afraid of those who, after death, will meditate upon me;
for from the drops of tears that fall from the wretched as they weep,
I am struck with great fear, and have therefore come to you for refuge.
"O God, O Supreme among Devas, may I not go to the abode of Yama; I propitiate you, O Giver of Boons, with my head and my upraised nails. I desire this wish from you, O Grandfather of the World."
"O Lord of Creatures, by your grace, I wish indeed to perform ascetic penance.
O God, O Blessed One, O Lord, grant this boon to me;
for, having been told by you, I shall go to the excellent Dhenukāśrama."
There I shall perform severe penance, devoted solely to your propitiation. For I am not able, O Lord of Gods, to abandon my life-breaths, which are dear to all living beings.
Brahmā said:
Protect me from unrighteousness as I lament for those being carried away. O Death, you were created for the purpose of destroying living beings;
go, destroy all creatures, and let there be no hesitation on your part.
"This shall indeed come to pass; it can never be otherwise.
Nārada said:
"Let her be blameless in the world; do as I say."
Thus addressed, she became afraid; with palms joined and facing the Blessed One’s face, she did not set her mind upon the destruction of creatures out of a desire for their welfare.
Then the God, the Lord of the lords of creatures, remained silent.
And the Grandfather quickly attained serenity within himself;
smiling, the Lord of the World gazed upon all the worlds,
and the worlds appeared as they were before, seen by him free from anger.
When that Blessed One Aparājita had ceased his wrath,
that maiden then departed from the presence of the wise one,
having withdrawn and not having promised to carry out the destruction of living beings.
Hurrying there, O king of kings, Death approached Dhenuka. There she performed a supreme, most intense, and excellent vow;
with her mind concentrated, she stood on one foot for sixteen padmas.
And out of compassion for her subjects, she who desired their fearlessness withdrew those five senses from their beloved objects;
then, with one foot [remaining], she again [withdrew] another seven.

O King, she stood upon six, seven, and one lotus; then, O dear one, she wandered with the deer for ten thousand years. Then, having gone again to the holy Nandā, whose waters are cool and pure, she dwelt there.
For eight thousand and one hundred years she performed austerities in the waters;
having maintained her vow at the Nandā, she was freed from all taint. Firmly resolved in her discipline, she first went to the holy Kauśikī.
There, subsisting on air and water, she practiced [austerities] for another million years;
at the holy Pañcagaṅgā and at the Vetasa grove,
that maiden emaciated her own body with many specific forms of penance.
Then, having gone to the great Gaṅgā and to Mount Mahāmeru alone,
she stood motionless like a stone, devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
at the summit of the Himavat where the gods formerly sacrificed.
There, that most auspicious woman stood upon her big toe for a *nikharva* of years;
then, at Puṣkara, Gokarṇa, Naimiṣa, and likewise Malaya,
she emaciated her own body through observances dear to the mind.

Constantly devoted to no other deity and possessing firm devotion toward the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), she remained steadfast and gratified the Grandfather through her righteous conduct. Then the imperishable Source of the worlds, being pleased, spoke to her.
"O Death, why do you perform such excessive austerities? Thus [asked].
Thereupon, Death spoke again to the venerable Grandfather:
"O Lord, I shall not slay the creatures when they are healthy and likewise crying out."
O Lord of all, O Master, I desire this boon from you:
I am terrified by the fear of unrighteousness, and for that reason I have undertaken these austerities. O Illustrious One, grant freedom from fear to me who am afraid; you are the imperishable one.
“I am a woman in distress and innocent; I entreat you, be my refuge.
Then the god, the knower of the past, present, and future, said to her:
“O Death, there is no unrighteousness in you for withdrawing these creatures.”
"O auspicious lady, what I have spoken shall by no means become false. Therefore, O virtuous one, withdraw all four kinds of living beings;
eternal Dharma shall enter into you in every way."
Yama, the guardian of the world, as well as the diseases that are his companions,
I, and the gods— these shall all grant you a boon once more, so that,
freed from sin, you shall attain stainless renown.
Having been addressed thus, O Great King, she, with palms joined in reverence,
spoke these words once more to the Lord, propitiating him by bowing her head:
"If this must indeed be done by me, O Lord, it cannot be without you."
"Your command has been placed upon my head; listen to what I shall say to you. Greed, anger, malice, envy, hostility, and delusion [are the enemies] of embodied beings.
Brahmā said:
"Shameless and harsh toward one another, they shall tear their bodies apart in various ways.
O Death, it shall be so; therefore, withdraw your destruction of living beings. No unrighteousness shall be yours, nor shall I harbor ill-will toward you, O auspicious one."
Those drops of tears that rest upon the hand are diseases born of one's own self for living beings;
they will kill men whose life-force has departed.
No unrighteousness shall be yours; do not fear. O Death, your duty is the slaying of living beings;
you are indeed Dharma, for you are the sovereign of Dharma.
Having become righteous, constant in dharma, and a supporter of the earth,
you must therefore restrain these vital breaths in every way;
for desire and anger exist in all living beings.
"Abandoning [them], you must withdraw the living beings here;
in this way, your dharma will become infinite,
while unrighteousness will slay those of false conduct."
Therefore, purify yourself by means of your own self;
for those who lack virtue will cause you to sink into sin. Therefore, you [should restrain] desire and even anger when they arise.
Nārada said:
"Therefore, abandon [them] and withdraw the living beings here.
She, indeed, became terrified at that instruction regarding the name of Death.
Terrified by the arrow, she said to him, "Certainly.
And at the time of death, she, casting off desire and anger, takes away the life-breaths of living beings without attachment.
Death is their end, and diseases are born from that; a disease is that by which a living being is afflicted with pain, occurring at the time of departure for all living creatures indeed.
The vital breaths, having departed, returned in that very same way;
that wind, terrible, with a fearsome roar and great power,
is all-pervading and the shatterer of the bodies of living beings.
The fierce one of infinite splendor, being preeminent, never encounters either obstruction or conformity;
all the gods are distinguished as those designated as mortals.
Therefore, O lion among kings, do not grieve for your son; having attained heaven, your offspring rejoices,
having reached the eternally delightful worlds of heroes.
Having abandoned suffering, he has united with those who perform meritorious deeds;
this death, ordained by the gods for all creatures,
duly withdraws them when their time has arrived.
This life-taking [weapon] was fashioned by himself for all living beings;
indeed, all creatures kill themselves,
and Death, staff in hand, does not strike them.
Therefore, the wise do not grieve for the dead.
Vyāsa said:
Having known the reality and the certainty of that which was created by Brahmā.
Having heard these meaningful words revealed by Nārada, King Akaṃpana then spoke to his friend Nārada:
"O Blessed One, O best of sages, my grief has departed; I am filled with joy."
"Having heard this history from you today, I have attained my purpose; I bid you farewell.
Thus addressed by that king, Nārada, the best of the foremost sages and a celestial seer of immeasurable self-control, quickly departed for the Nandana grove.

It is meritorious, conducive to fame, leading to heaven, auspicious, and even bestowing long life. O Pāṇḍava, by constantly hearing and reciting this history, and by understanding these words of its meaning, you shall attain [these benefits].

Having understood the duty of a warrior (*kṣatradharma*) and the supreme goal of heroes, that great car-warrior (*mahāratha*) of immense valor, Abhimanyu, having slain his enemies at the forefront of all archers, has attained the heavenly world.
That great archer, fighting face-to-face in battle, has been slain;
that great car-warrior was killed with sword, mace, spear, and bow.
Therefore, O Pāṇḍava, together with your brothers, summon the highest fortitude.
Saṃjaya said:
"Being vigilant and well-armored, quickly prepare for battle,
having heard of the origin of Death and her incomparable deeds."
Then Dharmarāja, having appeased him, spoke these words again:
"O Brahmin, how many royal sages of former times— teachers of meritorious deeds and possessing prowess equal to that of Śakra— were struck down by death?"
But further strengthen me with truthful words; console me by recounting the deeds of the ancient royal sages. How many sacrificial fees were given, and by which high-souled ones were they bestowed?
Vyāsa said:
"O you who perform meritorious deeds, may you tell me that which was [done] by the royal sages.
Śvitya’s son was a king named Sṛñjaya."
Both of his friends, the two sages Nārada and Parvata,
once entered his house out of a desire to see him. Honored by him according to the prescribed rites, they dwelt there happily, well-pleased.
Once, while he was sitting comfortably with those two,
the daughter of Sṛñjaya, a maiden of radiant complexion and pure smiles, approached him; so Nārada said.
"To whom does this woman belong, with her tremulous side-glances and endowed with every auspicious mark?
Or is she perhaps the radiant crest of the blazing sun?
Vyāsa said:
“Modesty, Prosperity, Fame, Fortitude, Nourishment, Success, and the Radiance of the Moon”—
when the celestial sage had spoken thus, King Sṛñjaya said to him:
“O Blessed One, this daughter of mine desires a boon from me.”

But Nārada said to him, "O King, give this woman to me for the sake of a wife, if you wish, O sinless one, to attain great spiritual merit. "I shall give her," Sṛñjaya replied to Nārada with great joy.
But Parvata, becoming greatly incensed, spoke these words to Nārada:
"O Brahmin, since you have chosen her whom I had previously chosen with my heart, do not go to heaven as you please."
Thus addressed, Nārada replied with these further words:
"The conversation of mind, speech, and intellect; truth; water; and the fires;
as well as the mantras recited at the taking of the hand—these are the celebrated characteristics of a bridegroom."
But this is not the final decision; the finality is said to be after the seven steps have been taken. Since the purpose of the rite had not yet been accomplished, you addressed me [in such a manner];
therefore, you too shall not go to heaven without me.

Having thus cursed one another, the two of them then remained there. Meanwhile, Sṛñjaya, desiring a son, being pure and striving with the utmost effort, served the Brahmins with drinks, clothing, and food.
Once, those foremost of Brahmins— devoted to austerity and the study of the Vedas, masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences— became pleased with him. Desiring a son,
they approached Nārada together and said, "Grant him the son he desires."
Having said "So be it" to the words spoken by the twice-born, Nārada spoke to Sṛñjaya:
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever kind of son you desire.
Thus addressed, the king, with palms joined in reverence, chose a son endowed with every virtue.
He was illustrious, renowned, radiant, and a subduer of enemies;
because his urine, feces, moisture, and sweat were all gold,
he was given the name Suvarṇaṣṭhīvin (Gold-Spitter).
While that immeasurable wealth increased through the granting of the boon,
the king caused everything desired to be made of gold:
houses, walls, fortresses, and even dwellings for the Brahmins.
His beds, seats, vehicles, cooking pots, pans, and vessels—
whatever that king’s residence contained, as well as all his external implements— were all made of gold and had increased over time.
Then the bands of Dasyus, having heard of and seen him in such a state,
gathered together and set about intending to do harm to that king.
Some among them there said, "Let us seize the king's son ourselves."
"He is the mine of that gold; let us exert ourselves for it.
Then those greedy bandits, having entered the king's palace, forcibly seized the prince who was vomiting gold.
Having seized him and, being ignorant of the means [of his power], led him away from there to the forest, those greedy men killed and dissected him, yet they did not see any wealth at all;
for when he was deprived of life, that boon-granting wealth vanished.
Then those Dasyus, foolish and senseless, slaughtered one another;
having killed each other, they perished, and that wonderful youth on earth—
who was beyond conception— those evildoers went to a terrible hell.
Seeing his son Varadatta slain, the king of great asceticism,
afflicted by intense grief, lamented piteously in many ways, O King. Then, hearing the king lamenting, struck by sorrow for his son—
The celestial sage Nārada appeared in the presence of the king; approaching Sṛñjaya, who was afflicted by grief, lamenting, and senseless,
Nārada spoke to him— listen to that, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O Sṛñjaya, unsated with desires, you shall die here— even you,
in whose house we, the exponents of the Veda,
have dwelt. O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that even Marutta, the son of Avikṣita, has died."
Saṃvarta officiated at the sacrifice for him out of rivalry with Bṛhaspati;
to that royal seer, the blessed Lord granted a boon,
as he desired to perform various sacrifices upon the golden foothills of the Himalayas.
The gods who create the universe, including Indra and the hosts of Maruts led by Bṛhaspati, all performed sacrifices for that Great-Souled One;
all the furnishings of his sacrificial enclosure were made of gold.
At that time, all food was pure and according to the mind's desire;
the Brahmins and all people seeking food ate as they wished,
enjoying milk, curds, ghee, honey, and excellent hard and soft foods.
In whose sacrifices garments and ornaments appeared at will for all those who had mastered the Vedas and were present there;
the Maruts became the attendants in his house.
The Viśvedevas were the courtiers of the royal sage Āvikṣita;
by that heroic king, the dwellers of heaven were properly gratified with well-prepared oblations, and through his excellent rain, there was an abundance of crops.
Toward the sages, the ancestors, and the gods who live in happiness,
he is free from debt through celibacy, sacred learning, sons, sacrifices, and giving;
even beds, seats, vehicles, and heaps of gold that are so difficult to relinquish [he has given].
Having given all that immeasurable wealth to the Brahmins according to his desire,
and having rendered the subjects free from disease, he was meditated upon by Śakra;
full of faith, he went to the imperishable worlds won through merit.
"If he has died, O Sṛñjaya— he who was four times more blessed than you and more meritorious than your son— do not grieve for your son.
Nārada said:
Regarding Śvaitya, who was a non-sacrificer and one who gave no priestly gifts, he spoke thus;
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that the king named Suhotra died—
he who was a peerless hero, invincible, and the crusher of enemy hosts.

Having obtained the kingdom, he who ruled according to dharma consulted his officiating priests, the Brahman, and the domestic chaplain regarding his own welfare; having questioned them, he remained steadfast in their counsel.
The protection of subjects, charity, sacrifice, and the conquest of enemies constitute his dharma.
Having understood this, Suhotra desired the acquisition of wealth through righteousness;
he propitiated the gods through righteousness, likewise conquered his enemies with arrows,
and delighted all living beings as well by means of his own virtues.
He who enjoyed this earth, free from barbarians and forest-dwellers; for whom the rain-cloud poured down gold for an entire year;
and for whom, the high-souled Suhotra, the rivers flowed with gold—[all these belonged to him].
In that place, the rain-cloud pours down tortoises, crabs, and many various kinds of fish,
as well as manifold objects of desire and immeasurable golden forms; there are also ponds measuring a *krośa* in extent.
There, seeing hundreds of thousands of crocodiles, sea-monsters,
and tortoises fallen down, made of gold, that guest indeed smiled;
that royal seer [had seen] such boundless gold in Kurujāṅgala.
While the sacrifice was being performed, he indeed resolved to give to the Brahmins;
with a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Rājasūyas,
and meritorious Kṣatriya sacrifices accompanied by abundant and excellent sacrificial fees.
O Sṛñjaya, if he has died— he who attained his desired goal through optional, occasional, and constant sacrifices, and who was more distinguished in the four virtues than you,
and more meritorious than your son— then do not grieve for your son.
"Nārada said:
'O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that the heroic Paurava king, Śvaitya, who performed no sacrifices and gave no sacrificial fees, has died.'"

When that royal seer released thousands upon thousands of white horses for his horse-sacrifice, there was no counting the wise men who gathered from every region— those who were experts in phonetics, syllables, and the rules of ritual procedure.
Those who have bathed after completing their vows of Vedic learning, who are generous and pleasant to behold; who possess excellent food, clothing, houses, fine beds, seats, and vehicles;
and who are accompanied by actors, dancers, musicians, *pūrṇaka* drums, and *vardhamānaka* drums.
He was greatly delighted there by the playful musicians;
at every sacrifice, he bestowed sacrificial fees at the proper time,
including ten thousand elephants and women with the luster of gold.
There were golden chariots equipped with excellent banners and flags; likewise,
there were thousands upon thousands of maidens adorned with gold,
accompanied by draft animals, horses, and elephants, along with houses, fields, and hundreds of cattle.
He bestowed as sacrificial gifts a hundred times a hundred thousand bulls adorned with golden garlands, followed by thousands of cows,
all possessing horns tipped with gold, hooves of silver, accompanied by their calves, and provided with bronze milking vessels.
He gave away female and male slaves, donkeys, camels, and many goats and sheep; various heaps of jewels and diverse mountains of food—
all this he bestowed as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) during that extensive sacrifice.
Regarding this, those people who are knowers of the ancient lore sing these verses:
"The auspicious sacrifices of Aṅga, the patron of the rite, were acquired through his own dharma; they were preeminent in quality and fulfilled all desires."
If he has died, O Sṛñjaya— he who was four times more blessed than you and more meritorious than your son— then do not grieve for your son.
Nārada said:
He cited the example of Śvaitreya, who was neither a performer of sacrifices nor a giver of sacrificial fees; and we have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that even Śibi Auśīnara died,
he who had encompassed this entire earth like a hide.
Making the mountains, islands, oceans, and forests resound with the roar of his chariot,
that conqueror of enemies constantly struck down the foremost of his foes in camp. By him, sacrifices of many kinds were performed, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
That king, heroic and wise, having acquired abundant wealth,
became esteemed above all consecrated monarchs in battle;
and having conquered this earth, he performed horse-sacrifices.

Śibi bestowed upon the Brahmins an earth filled with various things— unrestricted and yielding great fruit, including thousands of millions of gold coins, elephants, horses, cattle, grain, wild game, and likewise goats and sheep.
As many as are the drops of rain falling, as many as are the stars in heaven—
so many cows indeed did Śibi Auśīnara bestow at his sacrifice;
Prajāpati could find no other driver for his burden than him.
Whether past, present, or future, they found no one superior to that best of men.
For him there were various sacrifices provided with all desired objects;
their sacrificial posts, seats, and halls were of gold, as were their enclosures and gateways.

In his sacrificial enclosures, there were millions upon millions of Brahmins partaking of pure and delicious food and drink; there were banks heaped with various kinds of edibles, and lakes of milk, curd, and honey, as well as rivers and mountains of radiant food.

"Drink! Bathe! Eat!"—wherever these words are uttered by people, for him to whom Rudra, being pleased by his meritorious deed, granted this boon, there shall be inexhaustible wealth, faith, fame, and likewise ritual efficacy.
As has been stated, the highest heaven is dear to all living beings. Having obtained these desired boons, Śibi ascended to the celestial realm in due time.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya, who was four times more blessed than you;
"He is more meritorious than your son; do not grieve for your son," he declared regarding Śvaitya, who had neither performed sacrifices nor given sacrificial gifts. Nārada said:
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that even Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, has died—
he whom all creatures rejoiced in as a father rejoices in his own legitimate sons,
and in whom there were innumerable virtues due to his immeasurable splendor.
For fourteen years, that unswerving bull among men, following the command of his father, dwelt in the forest together with his wife and followed by Lakṣmaṇa; and there,
in Janasthāna, he slew the Rākṣasas.
For the sake of protecting the ascetics, fourteen thousand [monkeys] dwell right there. While he was living in that very place, a rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa,
having deluded him along with his younger brother, carried off his wife, Vaidehī.

Enraged in battle, he struck him down as Tryambaka once did Andhaka; that mighty-armed one slew in combat the descendant of Pulastya along with his hosts— him who was unslayable by gods or asuras and a thorn to the gods and brahmins.

Having duly obtained the kingdom, he who was compassionate toward all beings performed a great sacrifice while protecting his subjects according to dharma; the powerful lord offered a hundred horse-sacrifices, complete with the *jārūthya* ceremony and free from all restrictions.
He brought joy to the Lord of the Gods by offering oblations;
the king performed various other sacrifices of manifold merit. Rāma conquered hunger and thirst, as well as all diseases of embodied beings.
Constantly endowed with virtues and blazing with his own splendor,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, shone forth, surpassing all beings—
of sages, deities, and humans alike— in every respect.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, there was a dwelling together upon the earth;
at that time, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of living beings did not diminish, nor did it become otherwise.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *samāna* [breaths] functioned perfectly.
All creatures will then be long-lived, and no youth shall die;

delighted by the four Vedas, they shall attain the celestial realms through various offerings to the gods and ancestors, as well as through sacrifices performed with clarified butter and oblations duly completed.
The lands were free from gadflies and mosquitoes, and devoid of venomous serpents and reptiles;
there was no death for living beings in water, nor did fire burn out of season; at that time, there were none who delighted in unrighteousness, nor any who were greedy or foolish.
At that time, all the social orders (varṇas) became performers of the duties prescribed by the learned and the wise.
When Janasthāna had been destroyed by the Rākṣasas, the Lord, having slain those demons, bestowed *svadhā* and *ūrj* upon the ancestors and the gods.

Men had a thousand sons and lived for a thousand years; at that time, the elders did not perform funeral rites (*śrāddha*) for their juniors. [He was] dark-complexioned, youthful, with red eyes, and possessing the prowess of an elephant in rut.

With arms reaching to his knees, beautiful-armed, with shoulders like those of a lion and great strength, Rāma, beloved by the minds of all beings, ruled the kingdom for ten thousand and one thousand years.
"Rāma, Rāma, Rāma"—such was the talk among the subjects.
While Rāma governed the kingdom, the world became "Rāma from Rāma. Having led the fourfold classes of subjects to heaven, Rāma departed for the celestial realm.

Having firmly established his own royal lineage here in eight branches, O Sṛñjaya, he died— he who was fourfold more blessed than you and more meritorious than your son; therefore, do not grieve for your son.
"Regarding Śvaitya, who was neither a performer of sacrifices nor a giver of sacrificial fees," so he spoke.
Nārada said:
"O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that even King Bhagīratha died."
By him the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā was covered with altars of gold;
he bestowed upon the Brahmins a thousand times a thousand maidens adorned with golden ornaments, as well as kings and princes.
All the maidens were mounted on chariots, and every chariot was yoked to four horses. In each chariot there were a hundred elephants of the *padmin* breed, adorned with golden garlands;
and a thousand horses followed behind each of those elephants.
For every horse, there were a hundred cows, and behind the cows, goats and sheep;
with such a flood of people, he gave away even more sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). Distressed in that narrow space, she sat down upon his lap.
In ancient times, Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā and Urvaśī became the daughters of the king; at that time, she attained the status of his son. There, the Gandharvas, radiant as the sun, joyfully sang this verse:
While the ancestors, gods, and men were listening to those speaking sweetly,
Gaṅgā, the goddess who flows to the ocean, chose as her father the lord Bhagīratha, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, who was performing a sacrifice and bestowing abundant sacrificial fees.
His sacrifice was well-adorned by the gods, including Indra and Varuṇa;
it was properly undertaken, free from obstacles, and devoid of affliction.
Whatever a Brahmin might desire as dear to himself, wherever he may wish for it—

Then Bhagīratha, being self-controlled, was delighted and bestowed there whatever he possessed; there was no dear wealth that he would not give to the Brahmins. By the grace of the Brahmins, that king also went to the world of Brahmā.
"Those trees here, which followed him toward the various quarters at the commencement of his sacrifice,
desire to go and remain with that lordly king. If he has died, O Sṛñjaya, who was four times more blessed than you,"
"One more meritorious than your son—do not grieve for your son.
Nārada said:
"He spoke concerning Śvaitya, saying, 'He was one who did not perform sacrifices and gave no sacrificial fees.'"
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that Dilīpa, the son of Ilavila, died— he at whose hundreds of sacrifices there were millions and tens of thousands of twice-born ones,
who were perfected in the knowledge of reality, performers of sacrifice, and possessed of sons and grandsons.

A lord of the earth who, having performed sacrifices upon this earth filled with wealth, bestowed it all upon the Brahmins during the extended rite; for at the sacrifices of Dilīpa, a golden path was prepared.
Acting as if they were that very Dharma, the gods together with Indra assembled there;
on whose golden sacrificial post stood both the *caṣāla* and the *pracaṣāla*,
and where intoxicated women, draped in gold, lay upon the paths.
I consider this a marvel, unequaled by other kings:
that while he was fighting upon the waters, his two wheels did not sink.
[This was] King Dilīpa, the firm-bowed and truthful speaker.
Those men who beheld his abundant munificence were likewise conquerors of heaven. Three sounds never ceased in the residence of Khaṭvāṅga:
the sound of Vedic recitation, the twang of the bowstring, and "Eat! Drink! Feast!"
"If he has died, O Sṛñjaya— he who was four times more blessed than you and more meritorious than your son— then do not grieve for your son.
Nārada said:

He cited the case of Śvaitya, who was neither a performer of sacrifices nor a giver of sacrificial fees; and he spoke of Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva, the conqueror of the three worlds, who died even though the two divine Aśvins had drawn him from his father’s womb before his time.
While wandering on a hunt, the king, thirsty and with his mount exhausted, saw smoke and approached a sacrificial site; there he obtained the *pṛṣadājya* offering.
Seeing that [offering] had entered the belly of Yuvanāśva and become his son, [he rejoiced].
For the two divine Aśvins, the best of physicians, indeed drew [the child] from the womb. Seeing him lying on his father’s lap, possessing divine luster, Vāsava said: "Let him suckle me first."

Then, from Indra’s fingers, milk— ambrosia— manifested; because Indra, out of compassion, felt pity for him, thinking, "He shall suckle me," therefore that wonderful name Māndhātṛ was bestowed upon him.
Then, from the mouth of that great-souled son of Yuvanāśva, streams of milk and clarified butter flowed; Indra’s hand poured forth [the milk],
and he drank from Indra’s hand, and he grew by the day.
In twelve days, that energetic youth became equal to one twelve years of age;
and in a single day, he conquered this entire earth.
He was righteous-souled, steadfast, heroic, true to his promise, and a master of his senses.
Māndhātṛ, the son of Manu, conquered Janamejaya, Sudhanvan, Gaya, Pūru, Bṛhadratha, as well as Asita and Rāma.
He rose from where the sun rises and established himself where it sets.
All that is called the domain of Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva.
Having performed a hundred horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūyas,
O lord of the people, he gave red horses to the Brāhmaṇas.

People who eat food in excess of what is given to the Brahmins will decline, even if they consume golden mountains of various kinds of delicious foods and edibles, a hundred *yojanas* in length and one *yojana* in height.
Heaps of various foods and drinks shone like mountains of grain; there were lakes of ghee with soups for their mud and curds for their foam, with molasses for their waters.
Auspicious rivers flowing with honey and milk surrounded those mountain-like mounds.
Gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and birds were there; brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas had also arrived;
and among the brahmins and sages present, there was not one who was unlearned.
Having bestowed the earth, bounded by the oceans and filled everywhere with wealth,
upon the Brāhmaṇas, that king then set as the sun sets;
having pervaded the quarters with his own glory, he departed for the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds.
"If he has died, O Sṛñjaya— he who was four times more blessed than you,
and more meritorious than your son— then do not grieve for your son.
Nārada said:
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, died while living in a state of poverty, having failed to perform sacrifices or give sacrificial gifts—
despite having previously offered hundreds of Rājasūya and hundreds of Aśvamedha sacrifices.
With a thousand *puṇḍarīka* sacrifices, as well as a hundred *vājapeya*s;
with a thousand *atirātra*s and the *cāturmāsya* rites performed according to desire;
and with various *agniṣṭoma*s and sacrificial sessions (*satra*) accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Whatever wealth of non-Brāhmaṇas exists anywhere upon the earth, having calculated all of that, he makes it the property of the Brāhmaṇas;
for when the battle between the gods and the Asuras was arrayed, he rendered assistance to the gods.

Having performed various kinds of sacrifices and procreated excellent offspring in accordance with dharma— namely Devayānī, the daughter of Uśanas, and Śarmiṣṭhā— he divided this entire earth into four parts among his four sons.
In all the celestial groves of the gods, he, who was like an immortal,
wandered at his own will like a second Vāsava; yet,
though he was a knower of all the Vedas, he did not reach the end of desires.
Then, having sung this verse, he entered the forest together with his wife:
"Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women there are upon the earth—all that is not enough for even one person; realizing this, one should seek tranquility."
Having thus renounced sensual pleasures and attained steadfastness,
Yayāti, the lord, established Pūru upon the throne and departed for the forest.
Since even he died, O Sṛñjaya— who are superior to him in the four auspicious virtues— how could you not die?
"One more meritorious than your son—do not grieve for your son.
Nārada said:
"He spoke thus concerning Śvaiti, who was one who had not performed sacrifices and had not given sacrificial fees."
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that Nābhāga and Ambarīṣa died;
he who alone fought against a thousand times a thousand kings.
Desiring victory, his enemies assailed him from all sides in battle.
Those terrible warriors, skilled in the art of combat with weapons, uttered inauspicious cries;
yet, having brought them under control through the acquisition of strength and by the power of his own arms, he—
free from pain— cut down their umbrellas, weapons, banners, and chariots, as well as their spears.
Having cast off their armor and desiring to live,
they approached him, seeking refuge and saying, "We are yours for protection.
But he, having conquered this earth, brought them under his control.
O sinless one, he performed hundreds of desired sacrifices just as Śakra did;
at that time, other people enjoyed food endowed with every excellence. In his sacrifices, the foremost of Brahmins were highly honored and thoroughly satisfied.
Modakas, pūrikās, cakes, parched grains, vaṭakas, śaṣkulis, karambhas, flattened rice, stirred drinks, and other well-prepared delicacies;
soups, maireyaka wines, broths, meat gravies, and fruit sherbets.
There, the twice-born partake of refined foods that are well-prepared, soft, and fragrant;
likewise, ghee, honey, milk, water, and flavorful curds,
as well as sweet fruits and roots.
Knowing that intoxicating drinks would bring them pleasure,
the drinkers drank as they desired to the accompaniment of singing and instrumental music; there, being intoxicated and delighted, they sang songs and recited verses.

Accompanied by hymns of praise for Nābhāga, they danced by the thousands. In those sacrifices, Ambarīṣa bestowed sacrificial fees upon ten thousand kings, each of whom had performed ten million sacrifices.

He, performing the sacrifice with its rites fully extended, bestowed as sacrificial fees all those men clad in golden armor, adorned with white umbrellas and fans, mounted upon golden chariots, and accompanied by their retinues and attendants.
He bestowed upon the Brahmins the consecrated kings, hundreds of princes, and the accumulated treasuries along with the royal scepters—
things that neither people of the past ever did, nor will others do in the future.
"One more meritorious than your son—do not grieve for your son.
Nārada said:
"He spoke concerning Śvaitya, saying, 'He was one who had not performed sacrifices and had given no sacrificial fees.'"
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that King Śaśabindu also died;
he was illustrious and possessed of true prowess, and he performed various sacrifices.
That high-souled king had one hundred thousand wives.
And from each of his wives, a thousand sons were born;
those princes were all valiant, performers of a million sacrifices,
kings who had performed the principal rites and had mastered the Vedas.
All of them wore golden armor, and all were supreme archers;
all those princes, the sons of Śaśabindu, had performed the Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Their father, the lord of kings, bestowed them upon the Brāhmaṇas at the Aśvamedha.
A hundred chariots followed behind each one of them;
at that time, maidens beautifully adorned with gold followed behind the prince.
For every maiden there were a hundred elephants, and for every elephant there were a hundred chariots.
In every chariot there were a hundred powerful horses adorned with golden garlands;
for every horse, there were a thousand cows, and behind the cows, goats and sheep.
This was the boundless wealth [bestowed] at the great sacrifice of the Aśvamedha.
The illustrious Śaśabindu bestowed [wealth] upon the Brahmins;
indeed, as many wooden sacrificial posts as there were for the great Horse Sacrifice (*aśvamedha*),
so many others likewise became made of gold.
Mountains of heaps of food, snacks, and drinks rose to a height of one *krośa*.
When that king’s horse sacrifice was completed, thirteen [remnants] remained;
[the land] was crowded with contented and well-nourished people, free from obstacles and disease.

Śaśabindu, having enjoyed this earth for a long time, departed for heaven. If he died, O Sṛñjaya, though he was more distinguished in the four virtues than you and more meritorious than your son, do not grieve for your son.
Nārada said:
"O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that Śvaitya, though dead, was proclaimed as one who had performed no sacrifices and given no sacrificial fees; and likewise Gaya Āmūrtarayas, though dead."
Indeed, to that king who for a hundred years subsisted on the remnants of sacrificial offerings, Agni granted a boon; then Gaya chose a boon [saying]:
"By means of austerity, celibacy, vows, and self-restraint..."

And by the grace of my gurus, I wish to know the Vedas; and by following my own duty without harming others, I desire inexhaustible wealth; and may there always be faith in me as I give to the Brahmins.
May I have sons born to me from wives of equal caste who are not others';
may there be faith in my giving of food, and may my mind delight in dharma; O Purifier, may there always be freedom from obstacles for me in my religious duties.
Having said, "It shall be so," he vanished right there. Gaya, too, having obtained all that, conquered his enemies through righteousness.
He [performed] the Darśa and Paurṇamāsa sacrifices at the proper times, as well as the Āgrayaṇa.
With various *cāturmāsya* sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
the king performed worship with faith for a hundred years;
he offered ten thousand elephants and a hundred times a hundred horses.
Rising day after day for a full hundred years, he bestowed one hundred thousand *niṣkas* and sixty thousand cows;
and while giving gifts corresponding to the lunar mansions, he made offerings to all the constellations.
He performed various sacrifices, just as Soma and Aṅgiras did;
having fashioned this earth out of gold, studded with jewels and pebbles,
that king bestowed it upon the Brahmins at the great horse-sacrifice.
The sacrificial posts were made of Jāmbūnada gold, all adorned with jewels;
they belonged to Gaya, were magnificent, and were enchanting to all beings. And then Gaya bestowed those [sacrifices], which fulfilled every desire.
To the joyful brahmins and to all living beings alike—those who dwell upon the oceans, islands, and mountains; in the rivers, streams, and forests;
in cities and kingdoms; and those who reside in heaven and in the sky.
And the various hosts of beings were fully satisfied by the perfection of the sacrifice;
they declared, "There is no other sacrifice equal to that of Gaya. It was thirty-six *yojanas* in width and thirty *yojanas* in length.
Behind and before [the altar], there was indeed a twenty-fourfold sacrificial platform made of gold for Gaya the sacrificer, strewn with pearls, diamonds,
and gems; he then gave garments and ornaments to the Brahmins.
He, who gave profuse sacrificial fees, bestowed other gifts as prescribed upon the Brahmins; at that time, there were twenty-five mountains of leftover food,
and streams flowed with *kṛśara* and savory juices.
There were various heaps of garments, ornaments, and perfumes;
and by its power, Gaya became renowned throughout the three worlds,
as did the Banyan tree that grants imperishability and the holy Brahma-lake.
"If he has died, O Sṛñjaya— he who was four times more blessed than you,
more meritorious than your son— do not grieve for your son.
Nārada said:
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that Śvaitya, the son of Saṃkṛti, and Rantideva died because they were neither performers of sacrifices nor givers of sacrificial fees;
that great-souled one had two hundred thousand cooks.
To the Brahmins who had come to his house as guests,
the servers provided cooked and uncooked food, excellent fare like nectar by day and night; for he considered wealth acquired through righteous means to belong to the Brahmins.

Having studied the Vedas according to dharma, he brought his enemies under his control; and many who desired heaven approached him, who was firm in his vows, to perform the sacrificial session (sattra) according to the prescribed rules.
From that heap of hides from which the river Mahānasā issued forth,
the Carmaṇvatī first arose during the Agnihotra sacrifice in ancient times;
by his power, he gave golden *niṣkas* to the Brahmins.
"Gold for you! Gold for you! he would say;
"For you, for you," he gave thousands of gold coins.
Then, having comforted him once more, he presented him with yet more gold coins.

Thinking, "Only a small amount has been given by me today," he will give ten million *niṣkas* in a single day; who else could bestow such a gift? He will also give thousands of golden bulls, each followed by a hundred cows.
For one hundred years, he gave half-monthly rations to the Brahmins;
he provided the implements for the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the equipment for other sacrifices,
as well as water-pots, jars, cooking vessels, and pans to the sages.
He gave beds, seats, vehicles, palaces, and houses;
he gave various trees, food, and wealth;
for the wise Rantideva, everything was indeed made of gold.
Regarding this, those people who are knowers of ancient lore sing this verse,
having seen that superhuman prosperity of Rantideva:
"Never before has anything such as this been seen, even in the abodes of Kubera."
"Even our wealth is being replenished; how much more so among men!
they said there in amazement, "Clearly this is Vasvokasārī.
