On whatever night a guest might dwell in the house of Rantideva, the son of Saṃkṛti—
Then twenty-one thousand cows were slaughtered;
there the cooks, wearing polished jeweled earrings, cried out:
"Eat your soup in abundance today, for there is no meat as there was before!"
Whatever gold Rantideva possessed at that time,
he bestowed it all upon the Brahmins during his extensive sacrifice; indeed,
the deities accepted the sacrificial offerings from him before his very eyes.

Except for Vāsudeva or the eldest son of Pāṇḍu, there is no one else who,
in all circumstances, acts for the welfare of Arjuna and accords with his mind; out of great respect and affection, those two are worthy to speak to him.
Then the king spoke these words to that lotus-eyed one, who was enraged and whose mind was deeply afflicted by grief for his son.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O mighty-armed one, when you had gone against the force of the Saṃśaptakas,
the Preceptor made a strenuous effort to capture me.
We, having surrounded the army on all sides, chose Droṇa as our opponent."
Having arrayed his division of chariots and exerting himself thus in battle, though he was being held back by the chariot-warriors and by me as I protected them,
he quickly struck even us, afflicting us with sharpened arrows.
Being thus oppressed by Droṇa, we were not even able to look upon Droṇa’s army in battle, much less break through it;
yet we all consider the son of Subhadrā to be of incomparable heroism.
"O dear one, O Lord, we have said to you, 'Break through the army!
Then I spoke to that son of Subhadrā, who was a charioteer without rival:
'Break this army of Droṇa; create an opening for us.'"
Thus urged by us, like a spirited horse,
he began to bear that burden, even though it was unbearable;
for he is endowed with both the instruction in weapons and heroic prowess that you possess.
That boy entered that army like Suparṇa entering the ocean. We followed that hero, the son of Sātvatī, in battle, desiring to enter by the very same path through which he had entered the host.
Then, O dear one, the base King Jayadratha of Sindhu,
by virtue of a boon from Rudra, held all of us back.
Then Drona, Kripa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Bṛhadbala [did the same].
Kṛtavarman and six other chariot-warriors surrounded the son of Subhadrā. Having been hemmed in by all those great car-warriors in battle, the youth,
though striving with his utmost power, was deprived of his chariot by the many.
Then the son of Duḥśāsana, having quickly deprived him of his chariot in that manner and brought him to the brink of extreme peril,
dispatched him to the end ordained by fate;
mace in hand, he rushed swiftly, desiring to slay the unconquered one.

Then, seeing that [opponent] wielding a mace, the heroic grandson of Vāsava, who was skilled in mace-fighting, seized a mace. While all the kṣatriyas looked on, the two remained within the circular maneuvers of their maces.
Those two heroes, seeking each other's weak points,
struck one another; those two, intoxicated by battle, were struck by each other with the ends of their maces and fell to the earth, lifeless, like two uprooted banners of Indra.
Having slain thousands of elephant-riders, horsemen,
and chariot-warriors— eight thousand chariots, nine hundred elephants,
a hundred preeminent princes, and many unobserved heroes— he [prevailed].
Having dispatched King Bṛhadbala to heaven in battle,
the mighty [Arjuna] then slew Duryodhana’s son, Lakṣmaṇa;
he has gone to the worlds of the virtuous and those auspicious realms won by the conquerors of heaven.
Undaunted, he terrified his enemies and brought joy to his kinsmen;
having repeatedly proclaimed the names of his ancestors and his maternal uncle,
that supremely righteous soul then met his end.
The hero has met his end, causing grief to many kinsmen; therefore, we have gathered here today, tormented by sorrow. This much alone has transpired, increasing our lamentation.
And thus that tiger among men attained the heavenly world.
Sañjaya said:
Then Arjuna, having heard the words spoken by Dharmarāja, [acted accordingly].
"Alas, my son! he sighed, and overcome with grief, he fell to the ground;
afflicted by pain, he fell to the earth and lost consciousness.
All of them, their faces dejected, gathered around Dhanañjaya.
With unblinking eyes, they looked at one another in distress; then,
having regained consciousness, the son of Vāsava, overwhelmed with rage,
trembled as if with fever and sighed again and again.
Squeezing his hand against his hand, panting with tears in his eyes,
knitting his brows into three furrows and with eyes bloodshot with rage,
he looked about like one mad and spoke these words:
I promise you truly: tomorrow I shall slay Jayadratha,
unless— fearing death— he abandons the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and seeks refuge with us or with Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person.
"O Great King, tomorrow I shall slay you or Jayadratha—
him who does what is pleasing to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and has forgotten his friendship with me;
him who has forgotten his benevolence toward me and is devoted to the welfare of Duryodhana."

"The slaughter of a child is the cause of my sin; tomorrow I shall slay Jayadratha. And whosoever shall fight against me in battle while protecting him—even if they be the heroic Droṇa and Kṛpa—I shall shroud them with my arrows."
"O King, I shall ward off those various warriors headed by Droṇa with my arrows. If I do not do this in battle, O bulls among men,
may I never attain the worlds of the merit-makers esteemed by heroes."

Whatever worlds belong to those who kill their mothers, and those who kill their fathers; whatever worlds belong to those who violate the bed of their preceptors, and likewise to those who are slanderers; and whatever worlds belong to those who envy the virtuous, and those who are backbiters—[may you not go there].
And those worlds which belong to those who steal deposits, those who betray trust,
those who revile women previously enjoyed by others, those who proclaim their own sins, those who slay Brahmins, and even those who kill cows— [may I not go there].
Whether it be milk-rice, barley-food, vegetables, or even *kṛsara*,
or *saṃyāva*, cakes, and meats— whatever worlds belong to those who eat in vain,
who consume meat without having given [it away], that indeed shall be my destination.
"May I attain those very regions this very day if I do not slay Jayadratha—
those who, out of contempt, pass by the best of the twice-born who are excessively devoted to Vedic study and strictly observant of vows, as well as by the aged, the virtuous, and their teachers."
May I go to that terrible destination which awaits those who touch a Brahmin, a cow, or fire with their foot,
or those who discharge phlegm, excrement, or urine into the water—
if I do not slay Jayadratha.
If I do not slay Jayadratha, I shall go to the destination of those Brahmins who are afraid of the cold, and of those Kṣatriyas who are afraid of battle;
and I shall go to the destination of one who bathes while naked, and of one whose guest departs empty-handed.
The destination of those who take bribes, those who speak falsehoods, and those who are deceivers; the destination of those who betray their own souls, and that of those who bring false accusations;
and likewise, the destination of those who are watched over by servants, children, wives, and dependents.
The destination of those base people who eat delicacies without sharing them,
and the destination of that Brahmin who has fallen from his status and does not practice renunciation again,
and the destination of one who becomes pure through penance— [all these are the same].

I shall go to that terrible destination if I do not slay Jayadratha— that cruel-souled man who, having sought refuge with me, abandons a virtuous person devoted to his word, neither upholds him nor censures his benefactor.
Likewise, those deluded ones who constantly feed *devalakas*— who corrupt the row— at a *śrāddha*, shall attain that same destination.
And he who does not give a *śrāddha* to a worthy neighbor...
If I were to give [this] to one who is unworthy, or to the husband of a *vṛṣalī*,
or to those who eat fish and tortoises, or to those who sleep on the head of their food, or to the people of Sindh— then may I go to their fate tomorrow, and may I not slay Jayadratha.

"May I quickly go to the destination of those who drink liquor, those who violate the bounds of propriety, those who are ungrateful, and those who revile their brothers— if I do not slay Jayadratha. And may I go to the destination of all others who have departed from dharma, whom I have not mentioned here."
May I swiftly attain the destination of those who have been mentioned,
if I do not slay Jayadratha tomorrow when this night has passed.
Furthermore, listen again to this other vow of mine.
If I do not slay Jayadratha before the sun has set— if the sun should go to its setting while this wicked man remains unslain—
then I shall enter the blazing fire right here.
O Lord of the Earth, in the presence of the kings, with the Gāṇḍīva bow in his hand—whether they be Asuras, Suras, or humans; birds or serpents;
those who roam the realm of the ancestors, or the Brahman-sages and celestial seers—[none could withstand him].
Whether it be this world of the moving and the unmoving, or even that which is beyond it— even all these together are not able to protect my enemy,
even if he should enter the lowest depths of the netherworld (rasātala).
Whether it be the celestial city of the gods or the city of Diti,
even that I shall assail at dawn with hundreds of arrows and carry off the head of my enemy.
Having spoken thus, he drew the Gāṇḍīva bow with both his left and right hands;
the sound of that bow, surpassing all other sounds, touched the very heavens. When Arjuna had made his vow, Janārdana blew the Pāñcajanya conch.
There, the enraged Dhanañjaya blew the Devadatta conch;
that Pāñcajanya, its belly completely filled by the breath from Acyuta’s mouth, emitted a thunderous sound.
It made the world— including the netherworld, the sky, and the lords of the quarters— tremble, as if at the end of an eon; then,
the sounds of musical instruments arose from all sides.
When the high-souled one had made his vow, the Pāṇḍavas let out lion-like roars;
the Gāṇḍīva bow seemed to dance with joy, and the arrows remaining in the quivers then seemed to leap forth of their own accord, seeking the fray.
But Bhīmasena, O Bhārata, filled with joy,
looked toward Dhanañjaya and replied in a voice faltering with delight, at the sound of the vow being proclaimed and the blast of Kṛṣṇa’s conch.

This Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, has been slain along with his followers. Now, crushed are those foremost garlands of bonds consisting of grief for your sons and the host of wrath born from them.
"O best of men, this word of great power dispels [all doubts]; it is highly meaningful and desired. Sañjaya said:
Then, with conchs, kettledrums, and small drums, the soldiers,
along with the sūtas and māgadhas, honored the victorious one with hymns of praise;
at that time, the entire formidable army was bewildered by that roar.
That great king of yours became despondent.
Sañjaya said:
Having heard that great roar of the Pāṇḍavas who were longing for their son...
When this was reported there by the spies, Jayadratha rose up,
his heart bewildered by grief and struck violently by sorrow,
as if sinking into a vast and bottomless ocean of lamentation.
Reflecting deeply, the King of the Sindhus went to the assembly of kings;
lamenting in the presence of those lords of men,
he spoke these words, both fearful of Abhimanyu’s father and filled with shame.
"He who was born, it is said, from Pāṇḍu’s wife through the lustful Śakra—that evil-minded one indeed desires to lead me alone to the abode of Yama.
Therefore, may it be well with you; I shall go to my own home, desiring to live."
"Or rather, O bulls among Kṣatriyas, if you are capable of protecting me,
O heroes, then grant me freedom from fear from Pārtha, whom he seeks.
[Grant it] Droṇa, Duryodhana, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the King of Madra, and Bāhlika."

Duḥśāsana and the others were capable of protecting even one struck down by Death; how much more so then by Phalguna alone, who merely desires to slay him? I do not know what has been vowed; I inform you all of this.
"Even all of you, the lords of the earth,
together could not protect me from the great fear I feel upon hearing of the exultation of the Pāṇḍavas;
my limbs seem to fail me, O kings, like those of one about to die."
Surely my death has been vowed by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow;
for thus the Pāṇḍavas cry out in joy even at a time of sorrow. Without him, all four of the other Pāṇḍavas will fall under his power.
Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the asuras, uragas, and rākṣasas are able to alter this; how much less so the lords of men?
Therefore, grant me your permission—may prosperity be yours, O bulls among men!
I shall go into invisibility so that the Pāṇḍavas will not see me;
by adopting this conduct and exerting myself, I shall become one who is led away.

"Duḥśalā surely protects me out of affection for her brother. To him who was thus lamenting, his mind agitated by fear, King Duryodhana spoke because of the great importance of his own purpose: 07,052.012d*0376_02 "Duḥśalā surely protects me out of affection for her brother. 07,052.013a To him who was thus lamenting, his mind agitated by fear, 07,052.013c King Duryodhana spoke because of the great importance of his own purpose.
"O tiger among men, you must not fear; for who indeed, O bull among men, would dare to challenge you in battle as you stand in the midst of these heroic kṣatriyas?
For even among these lords of men, who move with the gait of elephants in rut—"
Even Purandara would tremble before those who have joined the *saṃghāta* array.
I, Vaikartana Karṇa, Citrasena, Vivimśati,
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, and the invincible Vṛṣasena— [are here].
Purumitra, Jaya, Bhoja, Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja,
Satyavrata, the mighty-armed Vikarṇa, Durmukha, Saha,
Duḥśāsana, Subāhu, and Kaliṅga with his weapon raised.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, Droṇa, the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman), and the son of Subala (Śakuni)— these and many other lords of various realms,
accompanied by their armies, shall march against you; let the fever of your mind depart.
The illusory Māyāvī, the powerful and heroic Rākṣasa Alambuṣa,
and these others, surrounded by a vast army, will protect you.
You too are the best of chariot-warriors, a hero in your own right of immeasurable splendor.
O Saindhava, why do you perceive fear from the sons of Pāṇḍu?
Eleven akṣauhiṇīs of my own troops are here for your protection; they are ready and will fight. Do not fear, O Saindhava; let your fear depart.
O King, thus consoled by your son, the ruler of the Sindhus,
together with Duryodhana, approached Droṇa at night.
Having performed a respectful salutation to Droṇa, O lord of the people, he spoke.
Sitting down nearby and bowing, he then asked this;
he inquired about the distinction between Arjuna and himself regarding the range of their aim,
their lightness of hand, and their firmness of shot.
"May the Blessed One tell me the distinction between myself and Phalguna;
O Teacher, I wish to know the difference in our knowledge according to the truth. O Lord, explain this to me exactly as it is."
Droṇa said:
"O dear one, your mastery of the teacher's art is equal to that of Arjuna;
yet, because of his disciplined application and his endurance of hardships, Arjuna is superior to you."
"You must not feel any fear whatsoever of Pārtha in battle;
for I, my dear son, shall protect you from danger—of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, even the immortals have no power over one who is shielded by my arms."
"I shall form that array which Pārtha shall not overcome.
Therefore, fight; do not fear; uphold your own duty.
O lord of men, follow the path of your fathers and grandfathers."
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having offered oblations well into the sacred fires, and having performed many sacrifices, you have no fear of the dread of death;
for such great fortune is difficult to attain even for dull-witted men.
"You shall attain unsurpassed, divine worlds won by the heroism of your arms. Let it be considered that the Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas, the Vṛṣṇis, and other men,
as well as I together with my son, are all impermanent."
In due course, all of us, struck down by powerful Time,
shall go to the other world, accompanied by our respective karmas. And those worlds which ascetics attain by performing austerities— [we too shall reach them].
"Brave Kṣatriyas who rely on the dharma of the warrior attain those [worlds].
Sañjaya said:
"O King, having been thus consoled by the son of Bharadvāja, the ruler of the Sindhus..."
He dispelled the fear of the Pārtha and set his mind upon battle.
Then, O Lord of the People, there was great joy among your troops,
along with the fierce sound of musical instruments mingled with the roar of lion-like shouts.
Saṃjaya said:
When the slaughter of the King of the Sindhus had been vowed by Pārtha,
the mighty-armed Vāsudeva then addressed Dhanañjaya.

Having ascertained the opinion of your brothers, you promised with your own words, "I shall slay the ruler of the Sindhus tomorrow. That was an act of extreme rashness; this burden has been undertaken by you without consulting me.
"How indeed might we not become objects of ridicule for the whole world?
Spies have been dispatched by me into the camp of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son;
having returned quickly, they now report the news to us."
When you had indeed made that vow regarding the slaughter of the King of Sindhu,
and when the slaughter of the King of Sindhu was promised by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
a truly great lion’s roar accompanied by the sound of musical instruments was heard here by them.
Terrified by that sound, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with the Saindhavas stood their ground,
thinking, "This lion’s roar cannot be without cause," O mighty-armed one;
it was a truly immense clamor among the Kauravas.
The roar of elephants, horses, infantry, and chariots was terrifying.
Thinking, "Having heard of Abhimanyu’s slaughter, Dhananjaya will surely set out in the night, afflicted by grief and driven by rage," they remained stationed there.
While they were thus striving, O lotus-eyed one, this true vow of yours, the truthful one, was heard by them regarding the slaughter of the king of the Sindhus. Thereupon,
they all became dejected and terrified, like small deer.
The ministers of Suyodhana and King Jayadratha were seated there.
Then, rising with his ministers, the dejected king, having become deeply despondent, went to his own camp.
They too entered their respective camps in a state of great distress.
The lord of the Sauviras and Sindhus arrived, deeply distressed.
Having consulted regarding all the actions leading to his ultimate welfare at the time for counsel,
he spoke these words to Suyodhana in the assembly of kings:
"Thinking, 'He has slain my son,' this Dhanañjaya will attack me tomorrow;
for he vowed in the midst of the army that he would kill me.
'My son has been killed by him; I shall kill Jayadratha.'"
Thus, various kinds of words were uttered as a vow made by Pārtha;
neither gods, nor *gandharvas*, nor *asuras*, *uragas*,
or *rākṣasas* are able to alter that vow of Savyasācin.

"Protect me in battle; let not Dhanañjaya place his foot upon your heads and seize his prize. Therefore, let this be arranged here. But if you do not provide me protection in the fray, O joy of the Kurus—"
"O King, grant me leave; I shall go back to my home.
Thus addressed, Suyodhana, dejected and with his head hanging down upon hearing that you had pronounced a curse, fell into deep reflection.
Beholding him thus distressed, that king of the Sindhus, out of consideration for him, spoke these words— gentle yet beneficial to himself:
"I do not see among you any archer of such prowess."
Who could withstand Arjuna in the great battle, neutralizing his weapons with his own weapons—
Arjuna who, aided by Vāsudeva, brandishes the Gāṇḍīva bow? Who could stand before Arjuna, even if it were Śatakratu himself?
Even the King of the Gods might fear to fight in front of Arjuna; indeed,
it is heard that even Maheśvara, the Lord of great splendor, was fought by Pārtha on foot on Mount Himavat in the past.
Urged on by the king of the gods, the son of Kuntī, joined with the wise Vāsudeva, slew thousands of Dānavas dwelling in Hiraṇyapura with a single chariot alone.
It is my conviction that he could destroy even the three worlds together with the gods;
just as Sugrīva, having obtained the invincible Rāma, son of Daśaratha, as his ally,
caused Vālin to be slain, so may he do for me here.

"Therefore, O Arjuna, I wish to be permitted by you, or rather, I wish to be protected by the high-souled and heroic Droṇa along with his son, if you so deem it fit. Thus was the preceptor himself earnestly entreated by the king.
The preparations have been made and the chariots are indeed ready;
Karna, Bhūriśravas, the son of Droṇa, the invincible Vṛṣasena, Kṛpa, and the King of Madra— these six are his vanguard.
Droṇa has arranged the army in the "Wagon" formation, with a "Lotus" formation at its center; Jayadratha stands within the pericarp of that lotus at the point of the needle-array,
protected by heroes who are fierce in battle, the King of Sindhu himself.
O Pārtha, these six chariot-warriors are determined to be most difficult to withstand in the use of the bow, in weaponry, in prowess, in vital strength, and likewise in their physical endurance;
without defeating them along with their hosts, Jayadratha cannot be reached.
Reflect upon the prowess of each one of those six individually;
for when these tigers among men are united, they cannot be easily conquered.
Furthermore, I shall consider a policy that is indeed for my own benefit.
Together with ministers who are experts in counsel and with friends, for the sake of accomplishing the task—
Arjuna said:
"You consider those six chariot-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son to be superior in strength."
I perceive that their prowess is not equal to even half of mine. O Madhusūdana, you shall see the weapons of all these men shattered by my own weapon as I strive for the slaying of Jayadratha.
Even if you have the wielder of the thunderbolt as your protector, I shall slay you while you look on;
even while Droṇa looks on and laments along with his followers,
I shall strike down the head of the King of Sindhu to the surface of the earth.
If the Sādhyas, the Rudras, and the Vasus along with the Aśvins;
the Maruts together with Indra, as well as the Viśvedevas and the Asuras;
the Pitṛs along with the Gandharvas, the Suparṇas, the oceans, and the mountains—[should all be on his side].
O Madhusūdana, may the sky, the atmosphere, this earth, the quarters along with their presiding deities,
and all beings— whether domestic or wild, stationary or moving—
become the protectors of the King of the Sindhus.

"Nevertheless, O Kṛṣṇa, you shall see him struck down by my arrows in battle tomorrow; I swear this to you by truth, and I touch my weapon as a witness. And so too shall I slay that great archer who is the protector of that wicked-minded sinner."
"O Keśava, I shall first advance against that very Drona;
for Suyodhana considers this gambling match to be bound up with him.
Therefore, having broken through the vanguard of his army, I shall proceed toward the ruler of the Sindhus."

Tomorrow you shall see those great archers being split apart in battle by me with my sharp-pointed iron arrows, like the peaks of a mountain shattered by thunderbolts; struck down by me in combat as if they were mountain ranges struck by lightning bolts.
Blood will flow from the bodies of men, elephants, and horses—
whether they are falling, have already fallen, or are being pierced by sharp arrows;
for the shafts dispatched from the Gāṇḍīva bow are equal to thought and the wind in speed.
They shall slay men, elephants, and horses by the thousands, even in Videha;
and those men in battle shall behold the terrible weapons that I have acquired from Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, Rudra, and Indra.

"O Keśava, you shall behold all the protectors of the King of the Sindhus being struck down in battle by my Brahmā weapon as their weapons are destroyed; you shall see the heads of those kings severed by the force of my arrows."
Tomorrow in battle, you shall see the earth being strewn by me;
you shall see the vast ground covered and scattered by me. I shall satiate the flesh-eaters and put the enemies to flight.
I shall gladden my friends and I shall strike down the King of Sindhu. Having committed many offenses, being a wicked ally born in a sinful land,
the King of Sindhu, slain by me, will cause his own people to grieve.

"O Kṛṣṇa, at dawn I shall act in such a way that Suyodhana, along with all the Saindhavas— who are eaters of milk and rice, of sinful conduct, and accompanied by their kings— shall be struck down by my arrows on the field of battle and perish."

No other archer in the world shall be considered my equal in battle. O bull among men, there is the divine bow Gāṇḍīva, I myself am the warrior, and you, Hṛṣīkeśa, are the charioteer; what indeed could remain unconquered by me?
"O Blessed One, through your grace, what indeed could be insurmountable for me in battle, O Hṛṣīkeśa? Knowing this, why do you reproach me?
For as there is a mark upon the moon, and as there is water in the ocean,"
"Know this vow of mine to be true, O Janārdana:
just as the ten-necked Rāvaṇa was conquered by Rāma alone, so shall I, through my power, conquer that enemy, the King of the Sindhus."
Do not underestimate my weapons; do not underestimate my firm bow;
do not underestimate the strength of my arms; do not underestimate Dhanañjaya. For, having entered into battle, I shall neither be conquered, but shall rather be victorious.
"By that truth, know Jayadratha to be slain in battle!
Truth is indeed certain in a Brahmin; humility is certain among the virtuous;
prosperity is certain among the capable; and victory is certain in Nārāyaṇa."
"And you, O Mādhava, shall provide for all of that accordingly,
so that while my enemies look on, I shall crush the ruler of the Sindhus.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Arjuna, the son of Vāsava, roaring with joy, himself by his own will gave instructions to the Lord Keśava:
"See to it that my chariot is prepared when the night has turned to dawn."
"O Kṛṣṇa, you must act accordingly, for a great task has been undertaken.
Sañjaya said:
"During that night, afflicted by pain and grief, they sighed like two serpents."
Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya could not obtain sleep at all;
the two heroes, Vāsudeva and Arjuna, did not experience slumber.
Knowing that Nara and Nārāyaṇa were enraged, the gods, together with Indra, [were filled with anxiety].
Distressed, they reflected, "What indeed will this portend?
Fierce, harsh winds blew, foreboding evil for the cattle,
and likewise a halo like a headless torso (kabandha) was seen around the sun.
Dry thunderbolts fell accompanied by crashes and lightning;
the earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled;
and the oceans, the abode of sea-monsters, were agitated, O great king.
The rivers flowing toward the ocean turned their currents upstream;
chariots, horses, men, and elephants were overturned, upside down,
for the delight of the flesh-eaters and for the swelling of Yama’s kingdom.
The mounts discharged excrement and urine and indeed wailed aloud.
Seeing all those dreadful and hair-raising portents,
all the kings became dejected and despaired of their own victory.
O bull of the Bharatas, all those troops of yours were distressed upon hearing the fierce vow of the mighty Savyasācin. Then the long-armed son of Pākaśāsana spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
"Console your sister Subhadrā together with her daughter-in-law.
O Mādhava, free your daughter-in-law from grief along with your sinless sister-in-law.
O Lord, console them with words that are gentle and truthful."
Then, having gone to Arjuna’s house, Vāsudeva, deeply distressed in mind,
consoled his grieving sister, who was afflicted by sorrow for her son, along with her daughter-in-law:
"Do not grieve, O Vārṣṇeyī, on account of the prince and his wife."
O timid one, this end ordained by Time is common to all living beings;
especially for a hero born into a noble family, and particularly for a Kṣatriya.
This death is indeed worthy of your son; do not grieve.
"By good fortune, the heroic great chariot-warrior, whose prowess was equal to his father's,
has attained the destination desired by heroes according to the kṣatriya rite;
having conquered his enemies many times over, he has dispatched them unto death."
He has gone to the inexhaustible worlds of the merit-makers, which yield all desires;
through austerity, celibacy, sacred learning, and wisdom,
your son has attained that very goal which the virtuous desire.
"You are a mother of heroes, a wife of a hero, and one whose father-in-law and kinsmen are heroes.
Do not grieve for your son, O blessed lady; he has attained the supreme goal—he who was devoted to sacred study and who granted the requests of Brahmins."
A cow gives birth to a beast of burden, a mare to a swift runner, a Śūdra woman to a servant, and a Vaiśya woman to a laborer;
but a princess such as you gives birth to a hero.
And that wretched Saindhava, the slayer of children,
shall reap the fruit of his arrogance along with his circle of friends and kinsmen;
for when the night has dawned, O lady of beautiful hips, he who has committed these evil deeds [shall meet his end].
For he shall not escape from the son of Pṛthā, even if he has entered Amarāvatī.
Tomorrow you shall hear that the head of that Saindhava has been taken in battle outside Samantapañcaka; be free from sorrow and do not weep.
Placing the duty of a warrior (kṣatradharma) foremost, the hero has gone to the destination of the virtuous—
a destination which we here, as well as others who live by the sword, shall attain. Broad-chested, mighty-armed, never retreating, and a repeller of adversaries.

"O lady of beautiful hips, your son has gone to heaven; cast off your fever. That heroic great chariot-warrior, endowed with prowess, followed in the footsteps of his father and maternal kin; having slain his enemies by the thousands, that hero was himself slain."
"O Queen, comfort your daughter-in-law; do not grieve excessively, O Kṣatriyā.
Tomorrow, O joyful one, you shall hear very great news of your beloved and become free from sorrow.
That which has been vowed by Pārtha shall be exactly so; it cannot be otherwise."
For whatever your husband intends to do can never be fruitless,
even if it were men, serpents, piśācas, night-stalkers, birds, gods, or asuras.
"They are rushing against the King of Sindhu as he stands in the midst of battle;
he shall not survive even with them at dawn.
Sañjaya said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Keśava, Subhadrā, afflicted by grief for her son and deeply distressed, lamented:
"Alas, my son! How is it that you, having entered the fray, [fell] for me, a foolish woman?"
"O dear one, you who possessed prowess equal to your father have met your end.
My child, how is it that your face— dark as a blue lotus, with beautiful teeth and lovely eyes— is now seen shrouded by the dust of battle?"
Surely they behold you, the hero who never retreated, now fallen—
possessing a beautiful head, neck, arms, and shoulders, with a broad chest and a lean belly,
all your limbs well-formed and lovely, with fine eyes, though now covered with wounds from weapons.
"Indeed, all beings are gazing at you as if at the risen moon. How is it that you, who formerly lay upon a bed covered with costly rugs,
now lie upon the bare ground, cast aside though so accustomed to comfort?"
That mighty-armed hero who was formerly attended by excellent women—
how is he now attended by jackals, fallen in battle?
He who was formerly praised by joyful bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists— [how is he now?]
Today he lies surrounded by terrifying throngs of flesh-eating beasts howling around him;
O Lord, while the Pāṇḍavas remain his protectors, as do the Vṛṣṇi heroes and the heroic Pañcālas, by whom has he been slain like one who is helpless?
O Keśava, since you have been slain even though you had the True Protector as your lord; O sinless son, I, whose sight of you was never sated,
ill-fated as I am, shall clearly go today to the abode of Yama.
"O my son, when shall I again behold your face—broad-eyed, with beautiful hair, sweet-spoken, and fragrant, and free from all wounds?
Come, come, my thirsty child; drink quickly from my full breasts!"
Having ascended her lap, while she was still slow to move and unsatiated in her sight—
fie on the strength of Bhīmasena, fie on the archery of Pārtha,
fie on the prowess of the Vṛṣṇi heroes, and fie on the might of the Pañcālas!
"Fie on the Kekayas, the Cedis, the Matsyas, and the Sṛñjayas,
who do not realize that you, a hero, have been struck down while engaged in battle! Today I see the earth as if it were empty, its splendor destroyed."
Not seeing Abhimanyu, her eyes agitated with grief,
she beheld the grandson of Indra himself, the son of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
the nephew of Vāsudeva, whom the vultures now surrounded.

How shall I behold your nephew, the son of Vāsudeva and wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, deprived of his chariot and struck down by others? Alas, hero! You were seen and then lost; you are like wealth seen in a dream to me.

"Alas! Human life is indeed impermanent, as flickering as a bubble upon the water. This wife of yours, though young, is overwhelmed by mental afflictions; she is of noble birth, virtuous in conduct, and sweet of speech."

Slowly embracing my illustrious daughter-in-law— she who was delicate, large-eyed, with a face like the full moon, her slender limbs like young sprouts, and whose gait was like that of an elephant in rut— [he spoke].
O Abhimanyu, gladden this weak woman with lips like the bimba fruit!
O son, how shall I sustain her— her mind fallen away, aged, and like a cow deprived of her calf— without you?
"Alas, my dear son, you have indeed departed at an untimely hour,
leaving me— so deeply longing for your sight— at the very time when the fruit [of our love] should have been gathered. Truly, the course of destiny is difficult to comprehend even for the wise."
Where you, though having Keśava as your protector, were slain in battle like one who is helpless—
[you who were] among those Brahmins who perform sacrifices, who are charitable by nature, who have disciplined their souls,
who have practiced the vow of celibacy, and who have bathed in sacred fords.

May you attain that destination which belongs to those who are grateful, generous, and devoted to the service of their teachers, and to those who bestow thousands in sacrificial fees; that destination which belongs to brave warriors who fight without retreating.
Having slain your enemies, go to that destination reached by those slain in battle;
to that destination of those who give away a thousand cows and those who perform sacrificial gifts;
and to that auspicious destination of those who bestow desired dwellings.
Go, my son, to that destination attained by those who entrust their treasures to Brahmins worthy of refuge, and by those who have laid down the rod of punishment;
and to that which sages of rigid vows attain through the practice of celibacy.
"Go, my son, to that destination which virtuous wives devoted to a single husband attain;
go to that eternal destination reached by kings through their good conduct,
and purified by the well-guarded merits of those who have fulfilled the four stages of life."
Go, my son, to that destination of those who have compassion for the wretched, who always share their possessions, and who abstain from slander—
those who observe vows, are virtuous in character, and are devoted to the service of their teachers.
Go, my son, to that destination of those whose hospitality is never in vain; go,
my son, to that destination of those who sustain themselves through hardships and calamities, and of those consumed by the fire of grief.

May you attain that destination which belongs to those who always perform service to their father and mother in this world, and to those high-minded men who are devoted to their own wives and approach them only during the proper season.
O son, do not go to that destination of those who consort with the wives of others; rather,
attain that destination which belongs to those who approach all beings with gentleness, who are free from envy,
and who are patient without causing pain to others.

"O son, go to that destination of those who have abstained from honey and meat, who are free from intoxication, hypocrisy, and likewise falsehood, and who have abandoned the practice of harming others;
they are modest, learned in all the scriptures, satisfied with knowledge, and have conquered their senses."
"Go, my dear son, to that destination where the virtuous go.
While Subhadrā was thus lamenting, miserable and emaciated by grief,
the princess of Pañcāla, accompanied by the daughter of Virāṭa, then approached her.
Having wept and lamented at their will, those women, deeply afflicted by sorrow;
and Draupadī, tormented by grief, having likewise wept and lamented,
O King, then fell senseless upon the ground like one driven mad.
But Kṛṣṇa, deeply pained, approached her who was in such great distress; having sprinkled her with water and comforted her, he spoke various beneficial words to her as she wept,
trembling, cast down, and nearly unconscious.
O lotus-eyed one, he spoke these words to his sister:
"Subhadrā, do not grieve for your son; comfort Uttarā, the princess of Pañcāla.
Abhimanyu, that bull among Kṣatriyas, has gone to the celebrated destination."
"O fair-faced one, whatever other men there are in our family,
may they all attain the same destination as the illustrious Abhimanyu;
we shall perform that deed, and so shall our friends."
"Today, your son alone, that great car-warrior, has performed such a feat.
Having thus consoled his sister, as well as Draupadī and Uttarā,
the mighty-armed subduer of foes went to the side of Pārtha.
Then, having given leave to the kings and his kinsmen, O King, the all-powerful Kṛṣṇa entered the inner apartments, while the others returned to their respective abodes. Saṃjaya said:
Then the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, having entered the incomparable palace of Arjuna and touched water, spread out an auspicious bed upon a ground marked with auspicious signs,
using *darbha* grass resembling lapis lazuli.
Then, according to the prescribed rite, he adorned that bed with garlands, parched grain, and auspicious perfumes, surrounding it with his finest weapons.
Then, the humble attendants approached Pārtha, who had already performed the ritual ablutions.
They performed the daily rites and offered the nightly oblation to Tryambaka. Then,
with a joyful heart, Pārtha adorned Mādhava with perfumes and garlands and presented that nightly offering to him.
Smiling, Govinda addressed Phalguna:
"Sleep well, O Pārtha; may it be well with you. I shall depart for the sake of your welfare.
Then, having stationed the gatekeepers and the men guarding the entrance with their weapons ready, he departed.
Accompanied by Daruka, the illustrious one entered his own camp;
he lay down upon a radiant bed, reflecting upon the many tasks at hand—
the Blessed One [considering] for Partha the entire method that dispels grief and suffering.

The lotus-eyed one, the Lord of all lords, having established himself in yoga with a disciplined mind, ordained that which increases splendor and brilliance— the illustrious Viṣṇu, desiring the welfare of all, who brings joy to the victorious.
Not a single person in the camp of the Pāṇḍavas slept that night; O lord of the people, wakefulness seized everyone,
for the high-souled one had made his vow while overcome by grief for his son.
"The sudden slaying of the King of Sindhu by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva—
how indeed shall that mighty-armed son of Vāsava, the slayer of enemy heroes, make his vow fruitful? Thus they reflected.
"Alas, this is a difficult task undertaken by the high-souled Pāṇḍava!
May that king Arjuna, possessed of great heroism, fulfill his vow for the sake of the virtuous; for a great oath has been made by him who is tormented by grief for his son."
The brothers are valiant and possess vast armies;
all this was reported to him by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Let Dhananjaya return once more after having slain the ruler of the Sindhus in battle.
Having conquered the hosts of enemies, let Arjuna fulfill his vow. Having defeated the enemy hosts in battle and maintained his great vow,
if there is any merit whatsoever in us, let him slay the King of Sindhu.
"Having conquered all his enemies, Pārtha will protect us from this great danger"—
expecting this, some stood listening;
and hearing these words, those of noble mind clearly hoped for victory.
"How indeed will this task be accomplished? others asked.
"For without slaying the King of Sindhu, he will enter the fire;
for Dhananjaya, the son of Pṛthā, ought not to make this vow false."
"For the son of Pṛthā, deluded by grief, has committed a great act of rashness. How will the son of Dharma become king once Arjuna is dead?
For in him, the entire victory was concentrated by the Pāṇḍava."
For victory and their very lives depend upon Arjuna.
If we have performed any good deeds, if we have given gifts, or if we have offered oblations—
by the fruit of all that, may Savyasācin conquer his enemies.
O Lord, as they were thus conversing and hoping for victory,
O King, the night passed away with great difficulty.
In the midst of that night, Janārdana awoke.
Remembering Pārtha’s vow, he addressed Dāruka:
"O Dāruka, Arjuna, distressed by the slaughter of his kinsmen, has vowed:
'I shall slay Jayadratha when tomorrow has dawned.'"
But having heard that, Duryodhana will deliberate with his ministers so that Pārtha does not slay Jayadratha in battle;
for all those Akṣauhiṇī divisions will protect Jayadratha.
And Droṇa, together with his son, who has mastered the application of all weapons—
he alone is a hero like the thousand-eyed Indra, the crusher of Daityas and Dānavas—
even he would not venture to slay him in battle while he is protected by Droṇa.
Therefore, tomorrow I shall act in such a way that Arjuna, the son of Kuntī,
will slay Jayadratha before the sun has set.
For neither wives, nor friends, nor kinsmen, nor relatives [count for anything].
There is no one else dearer to me than Arjuna, the son of Kuntī. O Dāruka, I shall not be able to look upon this world for even a moment if it is without Arjuna; yet that shall not come to pass.

I shall destroy the armies of the enemies— along with their horses, chariots, and elephants, together with Karṇa and Suyodhana— for the sake of Arjuna. Tomorrow, let the three worlds behold my prowess in this great battle.
O Dāruka, tomorrow, for the sake of Dhanañjaya who has displayed his prowess in battle, thousands of lords of men and hundreds of princes,
along with their horses, elephants, and chariots, shall flee from the fray, O Dāruka.
Tomorrow you shall behold that royal army crushed by my wheel,
struck down in battle by me in my wrath for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas. Today the gods, along with the asuras and all things moving and unmoving, shall come to know this.
Tomorrow, all the worlds— including the gods, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas— will know that Vāsudeva’s affection for the Pāṇḍavas is unfailing, and that I am a friend of Savyasācin.
"He who hates him hates me; he who follows him follows me"—let this be resolved in your mind, for Arjuna is half of my own body.
Just as you [prepared] this excellent chariot while the night was not yet dawn...

Having prepared [the chariot] according to the scriptures and taking hold of it, O charioteer, you, restrained by your vows, must mount upon the chariot the divine mace Kaumodakī, the spear, the discus, the bow, the arrows,
and all the necessary implements.
Having indeed fashioned a place for the hero Vainateya, who adorns my chariot in battle, upon the seat of my chariot beneath my banner,
he placed a parasol with golden lattices resembling the blazing of the sun.
Having harnessed the excellent horses— Balāhaka, Meghapuṣpa, Sainya, and Sugrīva— which were adorned with divine ornaments fashioned by Viśvakarman,
stand ready and armored, O Dāruka.
Hearing the terrible roar of Pāñcajanya, which is filled with a sound like that of a bull, come to me with speed;
for in a single day, I shall [dispel] my indignation and all my sorrows.
"O Dāruka, I shall remove this distress for my brother, the son of my paternal aunt;
I will strive by every means so that Bībhatsu shall slay Jayadratha in battle while the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra look on."
"O charioteer, against whomever Bibhatsu shall direct his effort for slaughter, I hope that his victory there will be certain. Dāruka said:
Victory alone is certain for him, so how could there be defeat,
O tiger among men, since you have taken up the role of his charioteer?
And I shall do exactly as you instruct me.
"This night has dawned auspiciously for the victory of Vijaya.
Sanjaya said:
But Dhananjaya, the son of Kunti, remained there recollecting that very mantra.
Protecting his own vow, he of inconceivable prowess was bewildered. Then,
in a dream, that high-souled one whose banner bears the foremost of monkeys— tormented by grief and sighing like a serpent vomiting foam— was seen.
Perceiving Arjuna to be unconscious in mind and overwhelmed by grief,
the one of great splendor whose banner bears Garuḍa approached him as he sat in meditation. Yet,
in every situation, Dhanañjaya rose up to greet Kṛṣṇa.
The righteous-souled one never neglected him, always serving him with devotion and love;
rising up, he offered a seat to Govinda, and at that time,
Bibhatsu did not even think of sitting down himself.
Then Kṛṣṇa, possessed of great splendor and knowing Pārtha’s resolve,
spoke these words to the son of Kuntī as he sat while [the other] stood:
"O Pārtha, do not set your mind on despair, for Time is indeed invincible."
Time restrains all beings under the supreme ordinance;
for what reason, then, do you despair? Tell me that, O best of speakers.
A wise man should not grieve; grief is the destroyer of one's purpose.
Whatever task must be done, perform that duty with action;
for the grief of one who fails to act is indeed an enemy, O Dhanañjaya. By grieving, one delights the enemies and causes even one's kinsmen to waste away.
"A man is diminished by that [grief]; therefore, you ought not to grieve. Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, the undefeated Bībhatsu, the wise one, then spoke these meaningful words.
"O Keśava, a great vow was made by me regarding the slaying of Jayadratha:
'Tomorrow I shall kill that evil-souled murderer of my son,' O Acyuta;
it is for the sake of thwarting my vow that the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have acted thus."
The ruler of the Sindhus should be placed at the rear, protected by all the great car-warriors.
O Kṛṣṇa, those eleven Akṣauhiṇīs are very difficult to conquer;
of these, O Mādhava, these ten remain here as the survivors according to the count.
Surrounded by them in battle, as well as by all the great chariot-warriors,
O Kṛṣṇa, how can that evil-souled ruler of the Sindhus be seen? Furthermore,
O Keśava, the fulfillment of the vow will not take place.
"And once my vow has been broken, how could one such as I continue to live?
O Hero, my longing for a means to end this suffering turns within me;
the sun is swiftly departing, and therefore I say this."
Having heard that cause for grief from Pārtha,
Kṛṣṇa, whose banner bears the bird, touched water and stood facing the east;
then the lotus-eyed one of great splendor spoke these words.
For the sake of the welfare of the son of Pāṇḍu, he was chosen for the slaying of the ruler of the Sindhus;
O Pārtha, [he gave you] the supreme, eternal weapon named Pāśupata,
by which the god Maheśvara slew all the Daityas in battle.
If that is known by you today, then tomorrow you shall slay Jayadratha.
Otherwise, seek to know it through your mind by resorting to the bull-bannered Lord;
meditating upon that god with your mind, O Dhanañjaya, remain silent.
"Then, through his grace, you, being devoted, shall attain that great [state].
Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, Dhanañjaya touched water and,
sitting on the ground with one-pointed mind, approached Bhava in thought.
Then, when the auspicious Brāhma-muhūrta had begun,
Arjuna beheld himself in the sky together with Keśava,
surrounded by celestial lights and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Moving with the speed of the wind, Pārtha, together with Keśava, ascended into the sky.
Held by the powerful Keśava by his right arm,
he beheld many wondrous sights as he traveled.
In the northern direction, that righteous-souled one beheld the White Mountain (Śvetaparvata) and the lotus-adorned Nalinī lake in the pleasure-grove of Kubera;
he also gazed upon the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, abounding in much water.
It was endowed with trees that always bore flowers and fruit, possessed crystal stones,
and was crowded with lions and tigers; it teemed with various herds of wild animals, contained holy hermitages, was delightful, and was frequented by charming birds.
And he saw regions of Mount Mandara, resounding with the songs of *kiṃnaras*,
illuminated by various medicinal herbs upon their peaks of gold and silver,
and likewise adorned with blossoming *mandāra* trees.
Adorned with other divine objects fashioned by Viśvakarman,
he reached Mount Kāla, which resembled a mass of smooth collyrium,
as well as the sacred foothills of the Himavat and Mount Maṇimat.
[He saw] Brahmatunga and other rivers, as well as various provinces;
Suśṛṅga, Śataśṛṅga, and the forest of Śaryāti;
the holy site of Aśvaśiras, and the abode of the Atharvans.
And Vṛṣadaṃśa, the lord of mountains, as well as Mahāmandara—
filled with Apsarases and graced by Kinnaras—
Pārtha, accompanied by Keśava, beheld those mountains as he traveled along.

He beheld lands adorned with beautiful waterfalls and embellished with gold ore; he saw the earth, whose body was radiant as moonbeams and garlanded with cities, as well as oceans of wondrous form containing many mines.
Beholding the atmosphere, the heavens, and the earth as he traveled through the station of Viṣṇu,
he was filled with wonder; together with Kṛṣṇa, he passed by like a discharged arrow,
possessing a brilliance equal to that of the planets, the lunar mansions, the moon, the sun, and fire.
Then Pārtha beheld [him] like a blazing mountain;
having reached that mountain,
he saw the high-souled one whose banner is the bull, ever devoted to austerity, stationed upon the mountain peak.
Blazing with his own splendor like a thousand suns, he held a trident; he was matted-haired, fair-complexioned, and clothed in bark and deerskin;
with thousands of eyes, his great-bodied form was adorned with diverse markings.
The god was accompanied by Pārvatī and by radiant hosts of spirits;
he was attended by the resounding echoes of song and instrumental music, joined with rhythmic beats and dancing,
by leaps, clapping, and shouts, and served by holy fragrances.
While he was being praised with divine hymns by sages who discourse upon Brahman—
the protector of all beings, the wielder of the bow, the infallible one—
Vāsudeva, beholding him, touched the earth with his head.
Together with Pārtha, the righteous-souled one praised the eternal Brahman—
the origin of the worlds, the architect of the universe, the unborn, the lord, the imperishable,
the supreme source of the mind, space, wind, and the treasury of lights.
The creator of streams of water and the supreme primordial nature of the earth; the means of accomplishment for gods, dānavas, yakṣas, and humans;
the supreme Brahman of yogins and the manifest treasure-trove of those who know Brahman.

Then Kṛṣṇa paid homage with his speech, mind, intellect, and actions to the creator and destroyer of all that is moving and unmoving— the high-souled one whose wrath is time, and who possesses the rising qualities of Śakra and Sūrya.
Whom the wise perceive as they seek the subtle state of the inner self; whom those who know the *Ṛgveda* sing in their hymns as the Imperishable (*akṣara*);
and whom those who know the *Yajurveda* [behold] as having the color of the sun, beyond all darkness.
Those who know the Sāman hymns sing of him even here;
thus they have concealed him. They both went for refuge to that unborn Bhava, the causal self (kāraṇātman), who is repeatedly that very fire, that very sun, and likewise the Lord.
And Arjuna,
recognizing him as the one who is the beginning of all that has been and is to be, the source of the existence of all beings,
the refuge, the protector, the god, the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, bowed down to that deity again and again.
Arjuna, together with Janārdana, went to the Lord of the worlds.
Then, when the two had arrived, Śarva spoke to them both, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as if laughing.
With a deeply serene mind, Śarva said:
"Welcome to you both, O best of men! Arise, free from fatigue.
And what is desired by your minds, O heroes? Let it be told quickly."
"I shall accomplish for you both whatever purpose has brought you here. Choose what is for your own welfare; I shall grant it all to you.
Then, having heard those words, they rose up with palms joined in reverence.
The two high-minded ones, Vāsudeva and Arjuna, praised Śarva with devotion and a divine hymn,
[addressing] that great-souled and blameless one:
"Homage to Bhava, to Śarva, to Rudra, and to the Giver of Boons!"
Salutations be to the eternal Lord of beasts, to the fierce one with matted hair,
to Mahādeva, to the Terrifying, to Tryambaka, and to Śambhu; salutations to Īśāna, to the slayer of Bhaga, and to the destroyer of Andhaka.
To the eternal teacher of the Kumāras, to the blue-throated one, to the Creator,

to the wielder of the Pināka bow, to the one worthy of oblations, to the Truth, to the All-pervading Lord, always— to the deep-red one, to the smoke-colored one, to the Hunter, to the unconquered one.
To the eternal one with the blue crest, the wielder of the trident, the possessor of divine vision;
to the slayer and protector, the three-eyed hunter whose seed is fire;
to the inconceivable husband of Ambikā, who is praised by all the gods.

To him who has the bull as his emblem, who is tawny-hued, who wears matted locks, and who is a perpetual celibate; to him who performs austerities within the water, who is devoted to the Brahman, and who is unconquered;
to the Self of the universe, the creator of the universe, who stands pervading the entire universe.
Homage, homage to you, who are ever to be served, the source of all beings; to you who are approachable, desirable, worthy of praise, and eternally noble;
to Śarva, the one whose mouth is Brahman, the benefactor, and the auspicious one.

Homage be to the Lord of Speech; homage to the Lord of Creatures. Homage to the Lord of the Universe; homage to the Lord of the Great Ones. Homage to the thousand-headed one, whose wrath extends to a thousand arms.
Homage to the one with a thousand eyes and feet, to the one of innumerable deeds; homage to the golden-hued one and to the one clad in golden armor;
homage to Kadrudra, the all-seeing, and the most formidable slayer.
Homage to Mīḍhuṣṭama, to the one worthy of oblations, to Śraviṣṭha, and to Śruta;
homage to Śipiviṣṭa, to the Mountain, to Budhya, and to Vilmin; homage to Parṇa, to Gehya, to Druhya, and to Prabhṛśa.
Homage to Parṇa, to Śuṣka, to Rajasya, and to Pulastya;
homage to Dundubhya, to Hananya, to Svāyudha, and to Sudhanvan; homage to Stutya, to Pathya, to Kāvya, and to Aśuraratha.
Homage to Somya, to Vātya, to Urvaya, and to Niṣaṅgin; homage to Vaiśanta, to Kūpya, to Nīpa, and to Varūthin.
Homage to Soma, to Rudra, to Tāmra, and to Śivamūrti.
"Homage be to the God of gods, the sustainer of the great elements, who is ever compassionate toward his devotees! O Lord, may our boon be accomplished!
Having thus praised Mahādeva, Vāsudeva, together with Arjuna, [proceeded].
He then propitiated Bhava in order to obtain the weapon;
Bhava bestowed upon Arjuna the understanding required for that weapon which he desired.
Thereupon, Arjuna, with a joyful mind, paid homage to the one whose banner bears the bull.
With eyes wide open in wonder, he beheld that entire treasury of splendors,
and he saw his own nightly, daily offering, which he had prepared for himself, now presented by Vāsudeva in the presence of Tryambaka.
Then, having honored Śarva and Kṛṣṇa in his mind, the Pāṇḍava spoke to Śaṅkara, saying, "I desire a divine weapon. Thereupon,
the Lord, having understood Pārtha’s words regarding the purpose of the boon, [acted].
Smiling, the god addressed Vāsudeva and Arjuna:
"Welcome to you both, O best of men! That which is desired by your minds is known to me. Whatever purpose you have come for, I shall grant it to you."
"O destroyers of enemies, there is a divine lake filled with nectar nearby. There, that divine bow and arrow were deposited by me long ago,
with which all the enemies of the gods were struck down by me in battle."
"Then let the two Kṛṣṇas be brought here with that supreme bow and arrow.
Having said, "So be it," those two heroes, together with Śarva and his attendants,
set out for that divine lake, which was filled with hundreds of celestial wonders.
The two sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, proceeded without agitation to that merit-bestowing place which accomplishes all goals, as taught by the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva). Then,
having reached that lake, which resembled the orb of the sun—
Arjuna and Acyuta beheld a terrible serpent within the water, and they saw another,
a second, excellent serpent with a thousand heads,
emitting vast flames and possessing the brilliance of fire.
Then Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha, having touched water and with palms joined in reverence,
approached those two serpents while paying homage to the bull-bannered Lord;
those two, learned in the Vedas, recited that sacred *Śatarudriya* mantra.
Having gone before Bhava with their whole being and bowing down to the Immeasurable One,
those two great serpents then, by the majesty of Rudra, cast off their serpent forms;
the bow and the arrow became that pair of Śatrughna.
Then, filled with joy, those two high-souled ones took up the bow and the radiant arrow; they brought them forth and presented them to the Great-Souled One.
Thereupon, from the side of the Bull-bannered God, the religious student (Brahmacārī) emerged.
The tawny-eyed, powerful Nīlalohita, the field of asceticism,
took that best of bows and stood there with concentrated mind;
he drew that supreme bow, together with its arrow, according to the prescribed rite.
Observing his bowstring, his grip, and his stance, the Pāṇḍava of inconceivable prowess, having heard the mantra spoken by Bhava, seized that arrow;
and the exceedingly powerful lord released that shaft right into the lake.
And the hero once again placed that bow upon that lake. Then,
knowing that Bhava was pleased, the mindful Arjuna recalled the boon granted by Śaṅkara in the forest and his manifestation before him.
He thought in his mind, "May this be accomplished for me. Knowing that thought of his, Bhava, being pleased, granted him a boon—
the terrible Pāśupata weapon and the fulfillment of his vow.
Then, having again obtained the divine Pāśupata weapon from the Lord,
his hair bristling with joy, the invincible one considered his task accomplished.
Then Arjuna and Hṛṣīkeśa, the subduers of enemies, [repeated their salutations] again and again.
Filled with joy, the two of them bowed their heads to Maheśvara; then,
at that moment, having been granted permission by Bhava, the heroes Arjuna and Keśava returned to their own camp, endowed with supreme delight.
Just as Indra and Viṣṇu, authorized by Bhava, were delighted and desirous of slaying Jambha, so too [were they] for the destruction of the great Asuras. Sañjaya said:
While Kṛṣṇa and Dāruka were thus conversing at that time,
O King, the night passed away; then the king awoke, as the bards,
panegyrists, and those who offer the honey-mixture began their recitations with the sound of hand-clapping.
The bards and chroniclers praised that bull among men;
the dancers danced, and the singers sang songs concerning the praises of the Kuru lineage, sweetly and with melodious voices.
Mṛdaṅgas, jharjharas, bherīs, paṇavas, ānakas, gomukhas,
āḍambaras, conchs, and dundubhis of great sound—
O Bhārata, all these and others as well were likewise present.
Delighted, skilled, and well-trained musicians played;
that great sound, with a resonance like a thundercloud,
touched the heavens and awakened Yudhiṣṭhira, the best of kings, as he slept.
Having awakened comfortably after sleeping upon a most excellent and costly bed,
he rose and went from there to the bath-house for the sake of his necessary duties.
Then, one hundred and eight young men, dressed in white garments and having bathed, [attended him].
The bath-attendants stood nearby with golden jars filled [with water].
Seated comfortably upon an auspicious throne and having put on light garments,
he bathed in waters mixed with sandalwood and consecrated by mantras.
Washed with astringent by powerful and well-trained attendants,
and bathed with fragrant water scented with perfumes,
he donned the turban, which resembled a royal swan and was fastened with ease.
For the purpose of quenching the fire, the mighty-armed one indeed encircled his head with water;
having anointed his body with yellow sandalwood paste,
wearing a garland and unwashed garments, he stood facing the east with palms joined in reverence.
Having brought about one-pointed concentration of his senses and mind, the high-minded son of Kuntī, following the path of the virtuous, muttered his prayers;
then he entered the blazing fire-sanctuary with humility.
Having thus worshipped the kindled fire with purifying oblations sanctified by mantras, he then departed from the house.
Having emerged from the second courtyard, that tiger among men, the king, [proceeded further].
There he saw Brahmins who were knowers of the Vedas, bulls among brahmins— self-controlled, purified by Vedic vows, and bathed in the final purificatory rites (avabhṛtha)—
eight thousand and one hundred followers of Sūrya.

Having caused those twice-born ones to pronounce blessings with unbroken grains and flowers, the mighty-armed Pāṇḍava gave each brāhmaṇa a golden *niṣka* coin, along with honey, clarified butter, and excellent, auspicious fruits.
The son of Pāṇḍu gave a hundred adorned horses, garments, and desired sacrificial fees; likewise, he gave milch cows of the Kapila breed together with bulls,
their horns tipped with gold and their hooves with silver, and having given these, he performed a circumambulation.
Golden svastikas, vardhamānas, and nandyāvartas; garlands, water-pitchers, and a blazing sacrificial fire;
vessels filled with unbroken grains, as well as bracelets and yellow pigment.
Having seen well-adorned and auspicious maidens, curds, clarified butter, honey, water,
auspicious birds, and whatever else was honored,
the son of Kuntī then touched them and proceeded to the outer courtyard.
Then, as that mighty-armed one stood there, his attendants brought a magnificent,
all-auspicious golden throne, adorned with pearls and lapis lazuli,
spread with a most costly coverlet and a canopy.
They brought forth a divine, excellent seat fashioned by Viśvakarman.
As that high-souled one sat upon it, his attendants brought from all sides costly and brilliant ornaments for him.
With all kinds of beautiful flowers and abundant strings of pearls,
the appearance of the high-souled son of Kuntī, adorned with fitting ornaments and attire, O Great King, increased the grief of his enemies.
Fanned by white yak-tail whisks with golden handles that shone like moonbeams,
he gleamed like a rain-cloud amidst flashes of lightning;
he was being praised by bards and honored by panegyrists.
Being sung to by the Gandharvas, the joy of the Kurus sat there;
then, after a moment, there arose a great clamor from the bards,
the sound of chariot wheels, and the clatter of the hooves of horses.
With the roar of elephant bells and the blaring of conchs,
and with the sound of men’s footsteps, the earth seemed to tremble. Then, having reached the inner apartments, he knelt upon the ground.
Having bowed his head in salutation to that Lord of the World who is worthy of worship,
the youthful gatekeeper— wearing earrings, girt with a sword, and clad in armor—
bowed his head once more to the son of Dharma.
He announced to the high-souled one that Keśava had arrived:
"Keśava, with conch, discus, and mace in hand, wearing yellow garments and possessing four arms,
stands at the gate desiring to see you and receive your command."
That tiger among men spoke with a welcome to Mādhava:
"Let him be ushered into my presence; why do you delay?
Let the guest-offering (*arghya*) and a most honored seat be given to him."
Then, having ushered in the descendant of Vṛṣṇi and seated him upon an excellent throne,
Yudhiṣṭhira— having been honored by him in turn— honored him and questioned him.
Sañjaya said:
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, having greeted Janārdana with great joy, spoke to the son of Devakī. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Madhusūdana, has the night passed pleasantly for you?
O Acyuta, are all your faculties clear?
Saṃjaya said:
Vāsudeva also questioned Yudhiṣṭhira regarding that which was appropriate:
"O gentle one, merely from the sight of you, nothing inauspicious has occurred for me.
Thereupon, the Steward (Kṣattṛ) announced that the subjects had arrived.
Permitted by the king, he ushered in those people:
Virāṭa, Bhīmasena, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and Sātyaki;
Dhṛṣṭaketu, the lord of the Cedis, and Drupada, the great car-warrior.
Śikhaṇḍin, the twins, Cekitāna, and the Kekayas;
the Kekayas, Sṛñjayas, Matsyas, and the Pāñcāla kings;
Yuyutsu the Kauravya, and Uttamaujas the Pāñcālya.
Yudhāmanyu, Subāhu, and all the sons of Draupadī—
these and many other kṣatriyas approached that bull among kṣatriyas,
the high-souled one, and they sat down upon their seats.
He showed these and other friends to the son of Pāṇḍu;
and permitted by the son of Pṛthā, they sat down upon their seats. When they were seated upon those most excellent thrones, he paid homage to the king as was fitting.
Seated upon a single throne were the two heroes of great strength,
Kṛṣṇa and Yuyudhāna— those two high-souled ones of great splendor.
Then, while they were listening, Yudhiṣṭhira addressed Madhusūdana.
Addressing the lotus-eyed one, he spoke these sweet words:
"Relying on you alone, as the immortals rely on the thousand-eyed Indra,
we seek victory in battle and eternal happiness."
For you, O Kṛṣṇa, know all those things— the destruction of our kingdom, our expulsion by our enemies, and the various sufferings we have endured.
You are the Lord of all, O lover of your devotees, for us all.
"O Madhusūdana, happiness and even life itself depend entirely upon you.
Therefore, O Vārṣṇeya, act in such a way that my mind may rest in you,
and that Arjuna’s intended vow may be made true."
May your lordship deliver us from this great ocean of suffering and resentment;
O Mādhava, become our raft today for those wishing to reach the further shore. For even one equal to Kārtavīrya could not achieve that in battle.
Just as you protect the Vṛṣṇis in all calamities, O Janārdana, when the charioteer, Kṛṣṇa, exerts himself with effort,
so too, O mighty-armed one, it behooves you to deliver us from this distress.

O bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, become a boat and rescue the Pāṇḍavas who are submerged in the fathomless ocean of the Kurus without a raft! Salutations to you, O eternal destroyer of the world, Lord of the gods of gods!

O Viṣṇu, O Conqueror, O Hara, O Kṛṣṇa, O Vaikuṇṭha, O Supreme Person! Nārada has described you as the ancient one, the best of sages, the boon-granting god who wields the Śārṅga bow; O Mādhava, make that true.
Thus addressed by Dharmarāja in the assembly, the lotus-eyed one, eloquent and possessing a voice like the sound of a water-bearing cloud, replied to Yudhiṣṭhira. Vāsudeva said:
Even among all the worlds, including the gods, there is no wielder of the bow such as Pārtha Dhanañjaya— none who is so heroic,
endowed with divine weapons, valiant, and possessed of great strength.
Skilled in battle, ever-irascible, and the foremost among men in splendor— he who is youthful, with shoulders like a bull, long arms, and great strength;
he who possesses the gait of a lion or a bull and is endowed with glory— he shall slay your enemies.
And I shall act in such a way that Arjuna, the son of Kuntī,
will consume the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son like a blazing fire;
today, [I shall slay] that evil-doer, the base murderer of Subhadrā’s son.
Arjuna shall discharge his arrows toward the path from which there is no return; today,
vultures, hawks, crows, jackals,
and other flesh-eating creatures shall devour his flesh.
Even if all the gods, including Indra, were his protectors,
he would still have reached the capital city of Yama today in this tumultuous fray;
having slain the ruler of the Sindhus, Jishnu will approach you this very day.
"O King, be free from sorrow and fever, and be graced with prosperity.
Sañjaya said:
"While they were thus conversing, Dhanañjaya appeared."
Desiring to see the best of the Bharatas, the king, together with his circle of friends,
[approached]. When Arjuna had entered that auspicious courtyard and stood before him after offering salutations, the bull among the Pāṇḍavas rose up and embraced him with affection.
Having smelled the crown of his head and embraced him with his arm,
and having pronounced the highest blessings, he spoke to him with a smile:
"O Arjuna, it is evident that your great victory in battle is certain."
"Since your form and Janārdana’s appearance are so serene, Jiṣṇu then said to him: 'I have seen a great and supreme marvel; may you be blessed, for it was born from the grace of Keśava.'"
Then Dhanañjaya related that encounter with Tryambaka exactly as it had been seen, for the sake of consoling his friends.
Thereupon, all of them, filled with wonder, touched the earth with their heads.
Having paid homage to the bull-bannered god, they then exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
Then, permitted by the son of Dharma, all those friends, well-armored and eager, set out joyfully for battle.
Having saluted the king, Yuyudhāna, Acyuta, and Arjuna departed joyfully from Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence;
indeed, the two invincible ones, Yuyudhāna and Janārdana, went forth together on a single chariot.

The two heroes went together to the residence of Arjuna. Having arrived there, Hṛṣīkeśa prepared for battle the chariot of that best of car-warriors, which was marked with the emblem of the bull among monkeys.
That excellent chariot, with a roar like a thundercloud and a luster like refined gold, shone like the young sun;
then that tiger among men, being himself ready, stood before the ready [chariot].
When the daily rites were completed, he announced that chariot to the son of Pṛthā;
[he presented] that chariot, with its banner and its flag, to that lion among men.
Then the wearer of the diadem, the best of men in the world, donned his golden armor.
Accompanied by his arrows and bow, he circumambulated his mount;
then, being praised with blessings of victory by those advanced in knowledge and age, who were observant of ritual action and had conquered their senses, he ascended the great chariot.
Having first consecrated that preeminent chariot with victorious battle-mantras,
like the radiant sun at its rising,
that best of chariot-warriors, adorned in gold upon his golden chariot, [ascended].
Pure and radiant, he shone like the sun upon Mount Meru.
Yuyudhāna and Janārdana followed after Pārtha,
just as the two Aśvins followed the god Indra as he went to the sacrifice of Śaryāti.
Then Govinda, the best among those who possess reins, took up the reins,
just as Mātali did for Vāsava when he set out to slay Vṛtra.
Accompanied by those two, Pārtha ascended that preeminent chariot.
Accompanied by Budha and Śukra, like the moon dispelling darkness,
he set forth, seeking the slaughter of the ruler of the Sindhus and slaying hosts of enemies,
together with the lord of the waters and Mitra, as Indra did during the Tārakāmaya war.

Arjuna went forth, bearing a victorious bow and arrows, like the divine Lord Rāghava setting out to slay the lord of Laṅkā. Then, amidst the sounds of musical instruments and auspicious, beautiful hymns of praise, he departed.
As Arjuna departed, the bards and panegyrists praised him;
that sound of the bards and panegyrists, accompanied by blessings for victory and auspicious proclamations,
combined with the resonance of musical instruments, became a source of delight for them.
Then, O King, at that very moment, a pure wind blew, carrying auspicious fragrances;
it gladdened Pārtha while withering his enemies,
and various auspicious omens appeared.

O noble one, many omens appeared portending victory for the Pāṇḍavas, while those for your side were the opposite. Having observed these auspicious signs of victory, Arjuna moved clockwise [around his weapons].
He spoke these words to Yuyudhāna, the wielder of the great bow:
"O bull among the Śinis, since these omens are seen today, my victory in battle appears certain through Yuyudhāna."
Therefore, I shall go there where King Saindhava dwells— he who,
desiring to depart for the realm of Yama, awaits my prowess.
Go, protect the king, for you are indeed my equal in battle.
Just as the slaughter of Saindhava is my supreme duty,
even so is the protection of Dharmarāja a most great task. Therefore, O mighty-armed one, protect the king this very day.
For just as you would be protected by me, so too would you be protected by him;
indeed, I do not see anyone in this world who could defeat you in battle—
not even the Lord of the Immortals himself, who is equal to Vāsudeva in combat.
"O bull among men, O Sātvata, having placed my full reliance upon you or upon the great car-warrior Pradyumna, I would be able to slay the ruler of the Sindhus without any concern;
you must not entertain any doubt regarding me under any circumstances."
"O King, you must provide protection with all your soul;
for wherever the mighty-armed Vāsudeva is stationed, and certainly wherever I am as well, nothing whatsoever can go wrong there."
Thus addressed by Pārtha, Sātyaki, the slayer of enemy heroes, said,
"So be it," and went to where King Yudhiṣṭhira was.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When the next day had dawned, what did they do, filled as they were with pain and grief?
Now that Abhimanyu had been slain there, which of my men fought? For the Kurus knew well the deeds of that Savyasācin.
Tell me, how did my men, having committed that offense, remain fearless?
How did they face that tiger among men as he approached in battle— burning with grief for his son, enraged, and like Death himself at the end of time?
Seeing the king of monkeys as his banner shaking his great bow in battle,
and seeing him distressed for his son, what did my men do?
O Sañjaya, what indeed transpired in the encounter regarding Duryodhana?

A great lamentation was heard by me there, not a sound of joy. Those sounds which were captivating to the mind and brought pleasure to the ear are no longer heard today anywhere in the dwelling of the King of Sindhu.

In the dwelling of Saindhava, there was once a great clamor of various sounds, accompanied by the resonance of conchs and drums from the musical instruments of the bards; yet today, those sounds of my sons praising [him] are no longer heard in my camp.
Where formerly my hearing was constantly filled with the sounds of throngs of bards and genealogists, and of dancers from every quarter,
today I do not hear that uttered sound of the wretched.
O Sañjaya,
dear one, in former times while sitting in the residence of Somadatta, who was possessed of true fortitude, I heard an excellent sound;
today, however, being destitute of merit, I hear it resounding with cries of distress.
I perceive my sons' residence to be devoid of enthusiasm—
Viviṃśati, Durmukha, Citrasena, Vikarṇa,
and my other sons; their voices are no longer heard as they once were.
The Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas who attend upon him as disciples—
the son of Drona, that great archer, the ultimate refuge for my sons—
[they do so] through debates, conversations, offerings, requests, and salutations.

O Sūta, in his house there is no sound today such as there was formerly for him who used to delight day and night with various beloved songs while being attended by many Kurus, Pāṇḍavas, and Sātvatas.
The sound of the singers and dancers who used to attend upon the great archer, the son of Droṇa,
is no longer heard;
nor is that great clamor heard in the evening from the camp of Vinda and Anuvinda.
That great sound of cymbals and singing from the houses of the Kekayas— who are ever joyful—
and the sound of groups of people dancing, which used to be heard today, O dear one, is not heard now.

The sound of those who perform sacrifices, spreading the seven threads [of the ritual] as they attend upon Saumadatti, that treasury of sacred learning— no such sound is heard from them: neither the twang of bowstrings, nor the chanting of the Vedas, nor the clatter of lances, swords, and chariots.
That unceasing sound which used to arise in Droṇa’s house—
the resonance of songs originating from various lands and the blaring of musical instruments— that great sound is no longer heard today.
"O Sūta, ever since Acyuta Janārdana arrived from Upaplavya desiring peace for the sake of compassion toward all beings,
I then spoke softly to the dull-witted Duryodhana."
"O son, make peace with the Pāṇḍavas through the mediation of Vāsudeva;
I consider the time for this to have arrived. Do not overstep [the bounds], O Duryodhana!
Make peace with those brothers and protect the Kṣatriyas."
"If you reject Keśava—
who seeks peace and speaks for your own benefit— then there shall be no victory for you.
He thus refused the scion of the Daśārhas, that bull among all archers.
Though he spoke words that were conciliatory, the mighty-armed one did not follow this improper course—
the counsel of Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and the evil-minded son of Subala—
since he had been rejected by me, the destroyer of my lineage.
Then, following the opinion of both Duḥśāsana and Karṇa,
that evil-minded one, dragged away by Time, abandoned me.
For I did not desire the gambling match, nor did Vidura approve of it.
The King of Sindhu does not desire the gambling match, nor does Bhīṣma desire the gambling match; neither does Vidura, nor Droṇa, nor Bāhlīka,
nor Somadatta, nor Bhīṣma’s grandson (Aśvatthāman).
Śalya, Bhūriśravas, Purumitra, and Jayatsena, as well as Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Droṇa— O Sañjaya, they do not desire this gambling match.
Nor does Jaya, nor the righteous-souled Kṛpa, nor any of my other kinsmen.
If my son were to follow their counsel,
he would live long and free from affliction, together with his kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers.
Furthermore, after me and because of them, he would enjoy this earth.
Gentle, sweet-spoken, and pleasant in address among their kinsmen,
