the noble, esteemed, and wise Pāṇḍavas shall attain happiness;
for a man who is ever devoted to righteousness finds happiness everywhere.
And in the life hereafter, he attains auspicious clarity;
possessing the means and capability, they deserve to enjoy half the earth,
for even their ancestral domain extends as far as the ocean.
The sons of Pṛthā will not overcome you by abandoning righteousness;
even when exhorted, the Pāṇḍavas will remain on the path of dharma.
O dear one, we have kinsmen whose words the Pāṇḍavas will listen to.
Of Śalya, Somadatta, and the high-souled Bhīṣma;
of Droṇa, Vikarṇa, Bāhlika, and Kṛpa;
and of other aged, high-souled Bharatas as well.
"O dear one, those who speak for your sake will carry out their beneficial words.
Whom among them do you think would say anything other than this to you?
Kṛṣṇa would not abandon righteousness, nor would any of them, for they are all your followers."
"I too have spoken these words, consistent with dharma, to those heroes;
for the dharma-souled Pāṇḍavas will not act otherwise.
Thus, O Sūta, I lamented and spoke many times to my son.
I do not think that the fool who has heard [the truth] understands the reversal of time,
wherein Vṛkodara and Arjuna, the Vṛṣṇi hero Sātyaki,
Uttamaujas the Pāñcālya, and the invincible Yudhāmanyu [are present].
The invincible Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the unconquered Śikhaṇḍin,
the Aśmakas, the Kekayas, Kṣatradharmā of the Somaka lineage, the King of Cedi, Cekitāna, and Abhibhū, the son of the King of Kāśī.
The sons of Draupadī, Virāṭa, Drupada the great car-warrior,
the twins who are tigers among men, and Madhusūdana as their counselor—
who in this world, desiring to live, would ever fight against these?
Those subduers of enemies could neutralize even those who were manifesting divine weapons;
however, other than Duryodhana, Karṇa, Śakuni the son of Subala,
and Duḥśāsana as the fourth, I see no fifth person.
"For those whose chariot has Viṣvaksena standing upon it with reins in hand,
and who has the armored Arjuna as their warrior, there is no defeat. Duryodhana will surely not remember these lamentations of mine."
"For you have told me that those two tigers among men, Bhīṣma and Droṇa,
have been slain. Having seen this fulfillment of the fruits of those words spoken by the far-sighted Vidura, I believe my sons are grieving."
Seeing my army overwhelmed by the grandson of Śini and by Arjuna,
and seeing the seats of their chariots empty, I think my sons must be grieving,
just as a great fire fanned by the wind consumes dry undergrowth at the end of winter.
"Could that Dhanañjaya have consumed my army like fire?
Tell us all of that, for you are indeed skilled, O Sañjaya,
in recounting what Pārtha did upon his arrival in the evening after having committed his transgression."

"O dear one, when Abhimanyu was slain, what was the state of your minds? For my men shall never be able to endure the great deeds of that wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow in battle, once they have committed such an offense, O dear one."

"O Sañjaya, what task did Duryodhana have in mind, and what did Karṇa say as a task? And what did Duḥśāsana and the son of Subala say, even when things had come to this state for all my sons gathered together?"
O dear one, that which occurred in battle was due to the extreme misconduct of that dull-witted man— his evil intellect driven by greed, his soul distorted by anger,
a fool longing for the kingdom, whose mind was overwhelmed by passion.
"Whether it was ill-conducted or well-conducted, tell me that, O Sañjaya.
Sañjaya said:
"Indeed, I shall relate everything to you, for I have seen it with my own eyes."

Listen attentively and remain steadfast, for your own misconduct was great. O King, this lamentation of yours is as fruitless as building a dam after the water has already flowed away; do not grieve, O bull of the Bharatas.
Having first shaved his head, he later inquired about the lunar mansion.
"What are you doing, O King? For time is difficult to overcome.
This wondrous decree of Kṛtānta is indeed impossible to transgress.

"Do not grieve, O best of the Bharatas; this is ancient destiny. For if you had previously restrained Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, as well as your sons from the gambling match, this calamity would not have overtaken you."
Furthermore, if at the time when war has arrived you had restrained those who were enraged, then this calamity would not have overtaken you;
and if previously you had said, "Bind Duryodhana, who is beyond control."
If you had urged the Kurus [to peace], this calamity would not have overtaken you; rather,
the Pāṇḍavas, the Pañcālas, all the Vṛṣṇis, and whatever other great men there may be, will perceive this deviation from your intellect.
If you had performed your duties toward your father, established your son on the path of the righteous,
and— without having attained great dharma, desire, wealth, or fame—
had lived according to dharma, this calamity would not have overtaken you.
But you, the wisest in the world, having abandoned the eternal dharma, followed the counsel of Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni. All that lamentation of yours, O King, has been heard by me.
Just as one who is intent on wealth views honey mixed with poison,
Kṛṣṇa did not formerly regard the Pāṇḍava king in that way;
O King, he did not regard Bhīṣma nor Droṇa as he regards you.
But when they realized that you had fallen away from the duty of a king,
from that time on Kṛṣṇa has not held you in such high regard;
and he observes how you remain indifferent even as the sons of Pṛthā are being addressed with harsh words.
The consequence of that has now reached you, who desired the kingdom for your sons;
O sinless one, the ancestral kingdom of your father and grandfather was then lost,
and you obtained the entire earth only after it had been conquered by the Pārthas.
The kingdom and the fame of the Kauravas were acquired by Pāṇḍu,
and thereafter they were increased even further by the Dharma-practicing Pāṇḍavas;
yet that very same deed of theirs has become utterly fruitless now that it has encountered you.
That you, greedy for the prize, have here deprived him of his paternal kingdom, and that you now, O King,
reproach your sons at the time of battle while enumerating their many faults— that is not fitting today.
Furthermore, since you speak so much in disparagement of the Bharatas who are engaged in battle, this is not appropriate for you today;
for kings do not spare their own lives when fighting in war.

Having plunged into the army of the Pārthas, these bulls among Kṣatriyas are fighting. But as for that army which Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna protect, or that which Sātyaki and Vṛkodara protect— who indeed would fight against that host, other than the Kauravas?
Who indeed, being a mortal archer, could withstand in battle those whose warrior is Guḍākeśa, whose counselor is Janārdana, whose protector is Sātyaki, and whose protector is Vṛkodara?
Except for the Kauravas or those who follow in their footsteps,
as long as it is possible to do so, the Kauravas— those heroes devoted to the duty of the kṣatriya— act with devotion toward other lords of men.
"O tiger among men, hear now in truth all about that most perilous battle fought by those tigers among men between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas. Sañjaya said:
When that night had dawned, Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons,
then proceeded to array all his own divisions.
O King, there was the roar of those heroes, who were enraged and impatient for battle.
Various cries were heard from those seeking to slay one another,
as they stretched their bows in battle and rubbed the bowstrings with their hands;
sighing deeply, they cried out, "Where now is that Dhanañjaya?"
Some brandished swords that were unsheathed, well-hilted, sharpened, and well-tempered; others cast forth yellow blades resembling the sky.
And they moved about, practicing with skill the various maneuvers of the sword and the maneuvers of the bow.
Thousands of heroes were seen with their minds set on battle;
others were seen eager for combat, mounted upon elephants and horses. These steeds were adorned with bells, smeared with sandalwood paste, and decorated with gold and diamonds.
Others, lifting up their maces, questioned the Pāṇḍava;
others, intoxicated by the pride of their strength and possessing mighty arms,
crowded the sky with iron clubs that resembled the raised banners of Indra.

Others, adorned with various garlands and ornaments, stood here and there with diverse weapons in hand—heroes intent on battle, wondering, "Where is Arjuna? Where is Govinda? And where is the proud Vṛkodara?"
"Where are those friends of yours who were then calling out to you in battle? Then, blowing his conch shell and himself urging on the horses,
Droṇa moved with great speed, arranging them here and there.
When all those divisions had taken their positions, eager for battle,
O great king, the son of Bharadvāja then spoke to Jayadratha:
"You yourself, the son of Somadatta, and the great car-warrior Karṇa— "
Aśvatthāman, Śalya, Vṛṣasena, and Kṛpa likewise;
a hundred thousand horses, sixty thousand chariots,
and fourteen thousand rutting elephants.
"Twenty-one thousand armored foot-soldiers,
stationed at a distance of three *gavyūtis* from me,
remain there; even the gods, including Indra, are not able to withstand you while you stand in that position."
"How much more so, then, all the Pāṇḍavas? Take heart, O Saindhava!
Thus addressed, Jayadratha, the king of the Sindhus, was comforted and set forth together with the Gāndhāras, surrounded by those great car-warriors.

O Indra among kings, Jayadratha’s horses— well-trained, adorned with golden ornaments, and wearing crests of yak-tail fans— were all mounted by armored riders who stood ready with spears in hand. These steeds moved with great grace.

And those seven thousand and two thousand horses from the Sindhu region were mounted by skilled elephant-riders upon intoxicated elephants of terrifying form, clad in armor and performers of fierce deeds.
With one thousand five hundred [chariots], your son Durmarṣaṇa stands at the very front of all the troops, ready for battle. Following him are your two other sons, Duḥśāsana and Vikarṇa.
For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the King of Sindhu, those two stood at the vanguard; that array,
shaped like a wheel and a cart, was twelve *gavyūtis* long in its rear half and five *gavyūtis* wide, and it was formed by Bhāradvāja.
Stationed here and there by various heroic kings,
and personally arranged by Droṇa with multitudes of chariots, horses, elephants, and infantry,
its rear half was a lotus-shaped array (*padmavyūha*), a womb-array (*garbhavyūha*) exceedingly difficult to penetrate.
A needle-like formation was further arranged, hidden in the center of a lotus;
having thus arrayed this great formation, Droṇa took his position.
At the point of the needle stood the great archer Kṛtavarman.
Immediately after, O noble one, came the king of Kamboja and Jalasandha;
right after them was Duryodhana along with his ministers.
Then followed hundreds of thousands of warriors who never retreat.
All those protectors of the needle were stationed upon the chariot; behind them,
O King, Jayadratha stood within the needle-loop, surrounded by a great force.
O king of kings, Bhāradvāja stood at the front of the chariot;
behind him was Bhoja, who personally protected him.
He was clad in white armor and garments, wore a turban, possessed a broad chest, and had mighty arms.
Drawing his bow, Droṇa stood like the enraged God of Death;
he was the powerful leader and protector of that entire army,
[mounted on] a chariot with banners and red horses, and bearing a standard of a sacrificial altar and a black antelope skin.
Beholding Droṇa’s chariot, the Kurus were filled with joy; a great wonder seized the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas upon seeing the array formed by Droṇa, which resembled a turbulent ocean.
"Beings thought that this array would devour the entire earth, including its mountains, oceans, and forests, crowded with various provinces;
it was filled with many chariots, men, horses, infantry, and elephants."
Beholding the great cart that had been constructed— possessing a terrifying sound, a form of wonderful proportions, and capable of shattering the hearts of enemies— the king rejoiced.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O noble one, when the armies had been arrayed and the war-cries raised,
while the kettledrums were being struck and the mṛdaṅga drums resounded, [the battle began].
Amidst the clamor of the divisions and the sounding of musical instruments,
as the conchs were blown in a hair-raising roar,
the Bharatas, eager for battle, slowly advanced forward.
When the Raudra moment arrived, Savyasācin appeared;
O Bhārata, many thousands of cranes and crows were sporting there in front of Savyasācin.
Multitudes of flesh- and blood-eaters dissolve by the thousands; likewise,
beasts of terrible roar and jackals of inauspicious appearance cry out as we depart toward the south.
O Great King, at the destruction of the world, those portents were indeed such as they are;
they were inauspicious for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, yet auspicious for Pārtha in battle.
Meteors, blazing and accompanied by thunderclaps, fell on all sides.
The entire earth trembled as a terrible fear arose;
harsh winds, accompanied by thunderclaps and raining down gravel,
blew from all sides as the son of Kuntī approached for battle.

Then Śatānīka, the son of Nakula, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata— those two wise men— arrayed the divisions of the Pāṇḍavas. Then, with a thousand chariots and a hundred elephants, they took their positions.
Accompanied by three thousand horses and hundreds upon hundreds of foot soldiers,
your son Durmarṣaṇa stood at the head of the entire army at a distance of just over a thousand bows and spoke.
Today I shall hold back the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, who scorches his foes and is intoxicated with the pride of battle, just as the shore holds back the ocean;
today let them behold the impatient Dhanañjaya in combat.
"O chariot-warriors, you who long for battle, stand firm against me, who am as difficult to withstand as a mass of stone fixed upon a rock;
I shall fight these gathered foes, increasing my fame and honor."
Speaking thus, O great king, that high-souled and highly intelligent one,
surrounded by great archers, O King, stood firm as a great archer himself.
Then, O great king, descendant of Bharata, Arjuna came into view.
Then, like the enraged Antaka, like Vāsava wielding the thunderbolt,
or like the unbearable Death urged on by Time with staff in hand;
like the unshakeable Śūlapāṇi, or like Varuṇa bearing his noose—
Resplendent like the fire at the end of an eon, as if about to consume all creatures once again, Jayo—
the vanquisher who brought an end to the Nivātakavacas— stood firm in truth, impelled by the force of his wrath and indignation, intent on fulfilling his great vow.
Clad in armor, bearing a sword, and wearing a crown of Jāmbūnada gold, he donned bright mail and garments, adorned with beautiful armlets and lovely earrings;
mounted upon his excellent chariot, Nara followed after Nārāyaṇa.

Brandishing the Gāṇḍīva in battle, he shone like the risen sun. Having stationed his chariot ready at the front of the great army, within the range of an arrow’s flight, the powerful Dhanañjaya blew his conch shell.
Then, O noble one, Kṛṣṇa also, remaining unperturbed, together with Pārtha,
blew with great vigor the *pāñcajanya*, the most excellent of conchs.
By the sound of those two conchs, O lord of the people, throughout your army—
Their hair stood on end, they trembled, and their minds were overwhelmed;
just as all living beings startle at the roar of a thunderbolt,
so did your soldiers tremble at the blast of the conch.
The mounts discharged excrement and urine on all sides;
thus the entire army, along with its vehicles, became agitated.
O King, O noble one, the men despaired at the sound of the conch shells.
Some became unconscious, O King, while others were struck with terror.
Then the monkey, together with the spirits dwelling upon his banner, let out a great roar;
with his mouth wide open, he terrified your soldiers.
Then conchs, kettledrums, and clay drums, together with cymbals,
were sounded once again to gladden your army amidst the tumultuous clamor of various musical instruments, shouts, and the slapping of arms.
With lion-roars and the sounding of musical instruments, the great car-warriors were summoned; first came the army of Durmarṣaṇa, followed by Duḥśāsana,
and then that which was arranged in the shape of a wagon, filled with terrible shouts.
In that tumultuous noise, which increased the fear of the timid,
the son of Pākaśāsana (Arjuna), exceedingly delighted, spoke to the descendant of Daśārha (Kṛṣṇa):
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, urge the horses toward where Durmarṣaṇa stands."
"Having broken through this elephant division, I shall enter the enemy host. Thus addressed by Savyasācin, the mighty-armed Keśava urged the horses toward the place where Durmarṣaṇa stood.
A tumultuous and most dreadful battle then broke out between one man and many, causing the destruction of chariots, elephants,
and men. Then, with a shower of arrows, he was like Parjanya pouring down rain.
Pārtha showered his enemies like clouds covering mountains;
and all those chariot-warriors, acting with swift and skillful hands,
then covered both Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya with volleys of arrows.
Then, though being restrained by his enemies in battle, the mighty-armed Pārtha, filled with rage, severed the heads of the chariot-warriors from their bodies with his arrows—
heads adorned with beautiful faces whose eyes were rolling and whose lips were bitten.
The earth was strewn with [heads] adorned with earrings and helmets; likewise,
the ground was covered by those whose brows were knit in indignation and whose lips were bitten in rage.
Like lotus groves destroyed on every side,
the faces of the warriors,
scattered about and variegated with gold, shone as they were drenched in blood.
O King, they appeared like masses of clouds accompanied by lightning;
O King, as their heads fell, a sound arose upon the surface of the earth like that of palm fruits ripened by time falling down.
Then, some headless trunk stood grasping a bow; another stood with a sword drawn and raised aloft in his arm; and yet another, seizing someone by the hair, danced while holding their head.
Those bulls among men, unable to endure the son of Kuntī and greedy for victory in battle, did not even notice their own heads fallen upon the earth;
the ground was covered with the heads of horses and the trunks of elephants.
It was strewn with the arms and heads of heroes;
"This is Pārtha! Where is Pārtha? This is Pārtha!"—thus they cried, O Lord, as they shouted, "Stay, Pārtha! Stay, Pārtha! Where are you going?"

In your armies, among the warriors, everything became as if possessed by Pārtha. Deluded by Time, they struck one another and even themselves; they perceived the entire world as being filled with Pārtha.
Groaning, covered in blood, unconscious, and in intense agony, many heroes lay prostrate, calling out to their friends; they remained with their javelins,
spears, darts, double-edged swords, and battle-axes still in hand.
In that battle,
arms resembling great serpents and like iron clubs— equipped with hand-guards, swords, bows, and lances, along with arrows, armor, ornaments, maces, and armlets— were strewn about.
They writhed, struggled, and coiled themselves up in every direction;
mangled by the supreme arrows, they exerted themselves with fury. Whosoever among the men in battle would provoke Pārtha in return, [he was overcome].
Against each one of them, an arrow of his Antaka sped toward the body,
as he danced along the paths of the chariots and stretched his bow; yet no one there could perceive even the slightest opening in Pārtha’s defense.
As that son of Pāṇḍu exerted himself, swiftly discharging his arrows with such lightness of hand, the enemy warriors were filled with wonder;
[he struck] the elephant and its driver, as well as the horse and its rider.
Phalguna pierced that car-warrior along with his charioteer with his arrows;
that son of Pandu struck down no one who was turning back, who had already retreated, who was fighting, or who stood before him.
Just as the rising sun in the sky destroys great darkness,
so did Arjuna slay the elephant division with his heron-feathered arrows;
your army appeared covered with fallen, mangled elephants.
Just as at the time of universal dissolution the earth is strewn with shattered mountains,
and just as the midday sun is always difficult for living beings to behold,
even so was the enraged Dhanañjaya difficult for his enemies to look upon in battle.
O scorcher of foes, your son’s army was thus shattered in battle, fleeing in agitation and exceedingly afflicted by arrows,
like a mass of clouds being dispersed by a mighty wind.
That army, being driven away, was unable even to look back,
[frightened] by the goads, the tips of bows, the sounds of "hum," the urging of "well done," the strikes of whips and heels, and indeed by fierce words.
Urging their horses on swiftly, your men fled;
both horsemen, chariot-warriors, and foot-soldiers were tormented by Arjuna.
Others likewise urged on their elephants with heels, toes, and goads.
Others, stupefied by his arrows, rushed directly toward him;
your warriors, their enthusiasm destroyed and their minds bewildered at that time.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When that vanguard of the army had been broken and was being slaughtered by Kiritin,
which heroes indeed in that battle advanced against Dhananjaya?
Or rather, having entered the cart-array (śakaṭavyūha), have they become ones whose resolve is now futile?
Taking refuge with Droṇa, they stood behind him as their rampart, free from fear from any quarter.
Saṃjaya said:
When your army had thus been shattered by Arjuna at that time,
When their heroes were slain, their enthusiasm destroyed, and they were intent on flight,
while being repeatedly struck by the son of Pākaśāsana with his finest arrows,
no one there in that battle was able even to look at Arjuna.
Then, O King, seeing his army in such a state, your son Duḥśāsana, filled with intense rage, advanced against Arjuna for battle. He was completely covered in armor variegated with gold.
O great king, Duḥśāsana, a hero of fierce prowess wearing a helmet of Jāmbūnada gold,
covered Savyasācin with a vast army of elephants as if swallowing up this very earth.
The crown prince Piṅgala, who was proud of his strength and pleasing to behold,
[advanced] amidst the clanging of elephant bells, the blaring of conchs,
the sounds of bowstrings being drawn, and the trumpeting of the tuskers.
The earth, the quarters, and the intermediate space were completely enveloped by that sound;
for a moment, it became terrifying and dreadful.
Seeing them falling swiftly, urged on by goads, [he watched].

With a great lion-like roar, Dhananjaya, that lion among men, scattered from all sides with his arrows the enemy's elephant force— elephants with trunks extended, enraged, and resembling winged mountains.
Then, resembling a mass of immovable clouds and crowded with hundreds of banners,
the elephants— distressed by the arrows of Dhanañjaya and fleeing away— appeared like a great ocean tossed up by the wind with its mighty waves.
The diadem-adorned [Arjuna] entered that elephant army like a sea-monster;
like the sun blazing beyond the limits of the horizon at the end of a Yuga,
Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities, was seen in all directions.

By the sound of the horses' hooves and by that clatter of wheel-rims, by the sound of shouting and by the twang of bowstrings, by the noise of various musical instruments and by the roar of the Pāñcajanya conch.
At the roar of Devadatta and the thundering sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
those elephants became sluggish in their speed and lost their senses;
they were pierced by Savyasācin with arrows whose touch was like that of venomous serpents.
Those elephants, struck in battle by sharp arrows impelled from the Gāṇḍīva bow,
were simultaneously overwhelmed as if they had entered a sea of mud.
Pierced in all their limbs by many hundreds of thousands [of arrows],
with many shafts remaining in their feathers and streaming with gushing blood,
they let out a supreme cry while being slaughtered by Kirīṭin.
They fell incessantly upon the earth like mountains whose wings had been clipped; other elephants, struck by arrows in their gums, frontal globes, and temples, shrieked repeatedly like cranes.
And the heads of men mounted on the shoulders of elephants— adorned with diadems and earrings— as they fell upon the surface of the earth, were severed by Kirīṭin with straight-knotted bhalla-arrows.
Like clusters of lotuses, Pārtha made his offering;
men, bound by machines, stripped of armor, afflicted by wounds, and drenched in blood,
hung from the elephants as they wandered in the battle.
Some, pierced by a single well-aimed feathered arrow, fell to the surface of the earth— two or three at a time.
Others were elephants, resembling mountains, who were only mildly provoked.
Struck down upon the earth like mountains shattered by a thunderbolt, they fell; pierced through by iron arrows and vomiting blood from their mouths,
they collapsed with their riders onto the ground like trees atop mountains.
Then Arjuna, intensely enraged and as if burning with his splendor, rained down showers of arrows upon the warriors who would not retreat; he struck their bowstrings,
bows, banners, yokes, and likewise their shafts.
With straight-knotted broad-headed arrows, he crushed the chariot-warriors;
neither aiming, nor drawing, nor releasing, nor even lifting [his bow],
Pārtha was seen dancing with his bow drawn into a continuous circle.
Pierced by iron shafts and vomiting blood from their mouths,
other elephants fell to the surface of the earth in an instant;
innumerable headless trunks (kabandhas) rose up on all sides.
O great king, in that supreme tumult,
severed arms were seen in the battle— still holding bows, finger-guards, swords, and armlets, and adorned with golden ornaments.
With well-equipped chariots, their frames, poles, and shafts shattered; with wheels crushed, axles broken in many ways, and yokes likewise;
and with armor, bows, and arrows scattered here and there.
Strewn with garlands, ornaments, garments, and fallen great banners; with slain elephants and horses, and prostrate kṣatriyas,
the earth there appeared terrible to behold.
O great king, as Duḥśāsana’s army was thus being slaughtered by Kirīṭin, it fled in distress along with its leaders.
When the force had thus retreated, [he approached] the prince, that great car-warrior.
He pierced him with ten arrows and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
How can you depart while still alive? Perform now such an act as befits those wicked words you have spoken, if indeed you so intend!"
Having spoken thus, O King, Pārtha, the crusher of kings,
became violently incensed, O great monarch, and pierced your son.
Thereupon Duḥśāsana, terrified and afflicted by arrows, fled together with his army.
Desiring Droṇa as his protector, he advanced against the cart-array.
Sañjaya said:
Having slain the force of Duḥśāsana, Savyasācin Dhanañjaya—
Desiring to rescue the King of Sindhu, he indeed rushed toward Droṇa’s army. Having approached Droṇa, who stood at the head of the formation,
he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence, with the permission of Kṛṣṇa.
"O Brahmin, look upon me with favor and pronounce blessings for my well-being.
By your grace, I wish to enter that army so difficult to pierce.
You are like a father to me, and indeed equal to Dharmarāja himself."

"O sinless one, just as Aśvatthāman is to be protected by you, O dear one, so too am I always to be protected by you, O best of the twice-born; I tell you this truly, for he is indeed equal to Kṛṣṇa."
"Through your grace, O best of men, I wish to slay the King of the Sindhus in battle; O Lord, protect my vow.
Thus addressed, the Teacher then replied as if smiling:
"O Pārtha, O Lord, it is exactly as you say; such is my view as well.
However, wise men must engage in battle for the sake of their master.
O Bībhatsu, Jayadratha cannot be conquered without first defeating me."
Having said this much, Droṇa covered him— along with his chariot, horses, banner, and charioteer— with showers of sharp arrows while laughing aloud;
then Arjuna, warding off those showers of Droṇa’s arrows with his own shafts, [proceeded].
He tormented Droṇa with great and terrible-looking arrows;
and having paid due respect to Droṇa in battle,
O lord of the people, he pierced him again with nine shafts, adhering to the duty of a warrior.
Having cut his arrows with his own arrows, Droṇa pierced both of them—
Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava— with shafts resembling blazing poison-fire.
Then the Pāṇḍava desired to sever his bow with his arrows.
While the high-souled Phalguna was thus reflecting,
the powerful Drona, remaining unperturbed, swiftly severed his bowstring with arrows;
he then pierced his horses, his standard, and even his charioteer.
Smiling, he covered the heroic Arjuna with arrows.
In the meantime, Pārtha, having readied his great bow,
sought to excel the Teacher, the foremost among all those skilled in weapons.
Seizing them as if they were one, he swiftly released six hundred arrows;
again, he discharged another seven hundred, a thousand more that could not be turned back, and tens of thousands of others, which struck down Droṇa’s army.
By those arrows, well-aimed by the powerful, skillful, and versatile warrior, men,
horses, and elephants were pierced and fell, deprived of life;
and others, fleeing in battle, fell with their weapons shattered and their lives cut short.
Charioteers, along with their horses, afflicted by arrows, fell from their excellent chariots;
and elephants, crushed, cast down, and burnt as if by the thunderbolt, the wind, and fire, fell like mountain peaks, clouds, or celestial mansions.
Thousands of horses, struck down by Arjuna’s arrows,
fell like swans on the slopes of the Himalayas when driven away by the force of water.
The vast multitudes of chariots, horses, elephants, and foot-soldiers were like wondrous torrents of water.
Slain by the arrows of the Pāṇḍava-sun,
which shone like the rays of the sun at the end of a Yuga, those Kuru heroes were scorched in battle by that mass of shafts issuing from the rays of the Pāṇḍava-sun.
That Droṇa-cloud, with the force of his showers of arrows, shrouded [the enemy] just as a cloud covers the rays of the sun; then,
with those exceedingly discharged [shafts] that consume the lives of his foes, he overwhelmed them.
Droṇa struck Dhanañjaya in the chest with an iron shaft (nārāca).
With all his limbs reeling like a mountain during an earthquake,
Bībhatsu regained his composure and pierced Droṇa with feathered arrows.
Droṇa, however, struck Vāsudeva with five arrows,
Arjuna with seventy-three, and his banner with three shafts; for,
O King, the valiant Droṇa sought to distinguish his pupil.

In the twinkling of an eye, he rendered Arjuna invisible with showers of arrows. We beheld the arrows of Bhāradvāja falling in continuous succession; his bow appeared as a wondrous, continuous circle.
O King, those very many arrows released by Droṇa, fletched with heron feathers, rushed toward Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya in battle;
there we beheld a marvel, like the gliding of stones.
Seeing Drona’s prowess, the descendant of Vrishni reflected: "Even though he is but a youth, Partha has not yet crossed over the aged Drona by force;
for he will not overcome him, just as the great ocean cannot overstep its shore."
Having witnessed that battle between Droṇa and the Pāṇḍava at that time,
the highly intelligent Vāsudeva reflected upon the state of affairs. Then Acyuta, observing that Pārtha was deeply agitated, began to reflect.
Having witnessed the prowess of Droṇa as well,
the slayer of Madhu then spoke these words to Dhanañjaya:
"O Pārtha, O Pārtha, O mighty-armed one, let there be no lapse of time for us."
"Let us leave Droṇa; this other task is more important.
Pārtha also said to Kṛṣṇa, "As you wish, O Keśava.
Then, having circumambulated Droṇa, the mighty-armed one departed.
And having turned back, Bībhatsu proceeded while discharging arrows.
Then Droṇa, smiling, said: "O Pāṇḍava, where are you going?
Is it not true that you do not retreat from battle without having conquered the enemy?"
Arjuna said:
"You are my preceptor, not my enemy; I am your disciple, like a son to you. There is no man in the world who could defeat you in battle."
07,066.034 Sañjaya said: Speaking thus, the mighty-armed Bībhatsu, eager for the slaughter of Jayadratha, rushed toward that army with great haste.
The two high-souled Pāñcālya wheel-protectors, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, followed him as he entered your army. Then, O great king, Jaya and Kṛtavarman the Sāttvata [advanced].
Kāmboja and Śrutāyus held back Dhanañjaya;
ten thousand chariots followed them—
the Abhiṣāhas, Śūrasenas, Śibis, and Vasātis.
The Mācellakas, Lalitthas, Kekayas, and Madrakas, as well as the Nārāyaṇas, Gopālas, and the tribes of the Kambojas—
those esteemed as heroes who were previously conquered in battle by Karṇa.
Placing Bhāradvāja at their head, they— having renounced their very selves,
tormented by grief for their son, enraged like Death the Ender,
ready to sacrifice their lives in the tumultuous fray, and clad in armor— advanced against Arjuna, that warrior of diverse skills.
They sought to restrain that tiger among men, a mighty archer of great prowess, as he plunged into the ranks like a leader of an elephant herd;
then there commenced a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.
As the warriors and Arjuna sought one another,
those assembled together resisted that bull among men as he advanced, desiring the slaughter of Jayadratha, just as medical treatments restrain a disease that has arisen.
Saṃjaya said:
Thus hemmed in by them, Pārtha, possessed of great strength and prowess—
the best of chariot-warriors— was swiftly pursued by Droṇa.
Scattering swarms of sharp arrows like the sun its own rays,
he scorched that army as a multitude of diseases afflicts the body.
A horse was pierced, a standard was severed, and an elephant fell along with its rider.
Umbrellas were cast aside, and chariots were deprived of their wheels;
the armies, afflicted by arrows, fled in every direction.
Thus there was a tumultuous battle, in which nothing could be discerned.
O King, as they struck one another in battle with straight-flying arrows,
Arjuna repeatedly caused that army to tremble; for he,
true to his promise, was intent on making his vow come true.
The one with white horses (Arjuna) rushed toward that best of charioteers who had red horses;
then Drona, the preceptor, struck his pupil— the great archer— with twenty-five straight-flying arrows that pierced the vital organs.
Bībhatsu, the best among all wielders of weapons, swiftly rushed toward him,
discharging arrows capable of neutralizing the force of [the opponent’s] shafts; as he was quickly hurling his broad-headed arrows, [Arjuna] countered them with straight-knotted *bhallas* of his own.
The one of immeasurable soul, invoking the Brahmā weapon, pierced him in return.
We beheld that wonderful mastery of Drona in battle,
in that Arjuna, though striving as a youth, could not pierce him back.
Like a great cloud pouring forth thousands of torrents of water,
the Droṇa-cloud rained showers of arrows upon the mountain that was Pārtha.
O noble one, Arjuna neutralized that shower of arrows with the Brahmā weapon alone.
The radiant hero received those arrows, shattering them with his own shafts;
the valiant one, remaining unperturbed, warded off that shower of arrows with his own rain of arrows, yet he did not afflict the Preceptor.
Droṇa, however, struck the one with white horses (Arjuna) with twenty-five swift arrows,
and Vāsudeva on his arms and chest with seventy. But the wise Pārtha, laughing, [assailed] that preceptor who was showering volleys of shafts.
He warded off him who was discharging sharpened arrows in battle;
then those two best of car-warriors, being struck by Droṇa,
turned away from that invincible one who resembled the fire risen at the end of an eon.
Avoiding the sharp arrows released from Droṇa’s bow,
the diadem-adorned son of Kuntī struck down the army of the Bhojas.
Moving between Kṛtavarman and Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja, he [advanced].
He advanced, avoiding Droṇa who resembled Mount Maināka;
then, O best of the Kurus, the Bhoja warrior Duḥsaha, remaining unperturbed, swiftly pierced that tiger among men with ten heron-feathered arrows.
O King, Arjuna pierced him in battle with a sharp feathered shaft,
and again with three other arrows, as if to confound the Sātvata. But Bhoja, laughing, [pierced] Pārtha and Mādhava Vāsudeva.
He struck each one with twenty-five arrows; Arjuna, having severed his bow, pierced him with twenty-one shafts that resembled flames of fire and were like enraged venomous serpents.
Then, O Bhārata, the great car-warrior Kṛtavarman, taking up another bow, quickly pierced him in the chest with five arrows;
and again he pierced Pārtha with five sharpened shafts.
Pārtha struck him between the breasts with nine arrows.
Seeing the son of Kuntī thus engaged against the chariot of Kṛtavarman, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi reflected: "Let there be no lapse of time for us."
Then Kṛṣṇa said to Pārtha, "Do not show mercy toward Kṛtavarman;
setting aside your kinship with the Kurus, crush him and destroy him.
Thereupon Arjuna, having confounded Kṛtavarman with his arrows, [proceeded].

With swift horses, he advanced against the army of the Kambojas. But when Śvetavāhana had entered, the son of Hṛdika, filled with indignation, brandished his bow with arrows fixed and encountered the two Pāñcālya princes.
Kṛtavarman, with arrows from his chariot, intercepted the two Pāñcāla wheel-protectors who were following in Arjuna's wake as they approached;
then the Bhoja warrior pierced them both with shafts made entirely of iron.
With exactly three arrows he pierced Yudhāmanyu, and with four, Uttamaujas;
those two also pierced him with ten arrows each,
and they both cut down his standard and his bow as well.

Then Hārdikya, overwhelmed with rage, took up another bow and, having rendered the two heroes weaponless, covered them with a shower of arrows. Those two, having strung other bows, struck down the Bhoja king.
In that interval, Bībhatsu entered the army of his enemies; however,
those two bulls among men, though striving against the Dhārtarāṣṭra forces, could not find an entrance as they were held back by Kṛtavarman.
Hurrying in battle to crush the enemy ranks, the one with white horses,
the slayer of foes, did not kill Kṛtavarman even though he had come within his reach.
But seeing him approaching in that manner, the heroic King Śrutāyudha—
Highly incensed and brandishing his great bow, he rushed forward;
while the troops were being driven here and there by the son of Pāṇḍu,
the immensely powerful Śrutāyudha advanced, scattering his arrows.
He struck Pārtha with three arrows and Janārdana with seventy;
with an extremely sharp razor-headed shaft, he struck the banner of Pārtha.
Arjuna, however, [struck him] with ninety straight-knotted arrows.
Enraged, he struck him violently, as if striking a great elephant with goads. O King, he could not endure that prowess of the son of Pāṇḍu;
then he struck him with seventy-seven iron arrows.
Having cut his bow and severed his quiver, Arjuna, filled with rage, struck him in the chest with seven straight-knotted arrows. Then that king, overwhelmed by fury, took up another bow.
With nine arrows, he struck Vāsavi in the arms and the chest;
then, O Bhārata, Arjuna, the subduer of enemies, smiling as it were, afflicted Śrutāyudha with many thousands of shafts.
That great car-warrior of immense strength swiftly slew his horses and his charioteer,
and pierced him with seventy iron arrows. Abandoning that chariot whose horses were slain, King Śrutāyudha—
Raising his mace in battle,
the heroic son of Varuṇa, King Śrutāyudha, rushed toward Pārtha;
he whose mother was Parṇāśā, the great river of cool waters.
His mother spoke these words to Varuṇa for the sake of her son:
"May this son of mine be unslayable by his enemies in this world.
Varuṇa, being pleased, replied: "I grant him a boon that is beneficial."
"By means of this divine weapon, this son of yours shall become incapable of being slain;
yet for a human being, there is no such thing as immortality in any way. O best of rivers, everyone who is born must inevitably die."
"He shall always be invincible to his enemies in battles;
by the power of this weapon, let the fever of your mind depart.
Having said this, Varuṇa gave him a mace accompanied by sacred mantras.
Having reached her, Śrutāyudha became invincible in all the worlds;
then the Lord of Waters spoke to him once again:
"She must not be released while fighting; she shall fall upon you alone."
"O Lord, she would indeed slay the one who employs her against [her purpose]," he said;
yet when the time arrived, Śrutāyudha did not act upon those words. Instead, he struck Janārdana with that weapon which slaughters heroes.
The heroic Kṛṣṇa caught her upon his broad shoulder;
she could not shake Śauri, just as the wind cannot move Mount Vindhya.
Then Arjuna, with two razor-headed arrows, [struck] his arms which resembled iron clubs.
The son of Pāṇḍu swiftly pierced that [missile] belonging to the son of the Lord of Waters;
it, blazing like a great meteor, having reached Janārdana,
recoiled against him like a malevolent *kṛtyā* unleashed by one who lacks spiritual mastery.
He struck down the indignant hero Śrutāyudha as he stood firm;
slain, the powerful one fell to the earth, headless and armless,
like a many-branched lord of the forest broken by the wind.
That mace, flashing and blazing like the speed of a thunderbolt,
struck down the hero Śrutāyudha and fell to the earth.
Seeing the mace turned back and Śrutāyudha slain, [he...]
A great cry of "Alas!
Alas! arose there among the troops, O lord of men, upon seeing that Śrutāyudha, the subduer of enemies, had been slain by his own weapon while Keshava was not even fighting.
Then, hurled by Śrutāyudha, that mace struck him down;
just as Varuṇa had foretold in battle, he met his end. Lifeless, he fell upon the earth while all the archers looked on.
As he fell, that beloved son of Parṇāśā shone like a many-branched lord of the forest broken by the wind. Then all the troops and all the army commanders from every side [beheld him].
Seeing Śrutāyudha, the subduer of enemies, slain, they fled;
likewise, the brave Sudakṣiṇa, son of the king of the Kambojas,
rushed toward Phalguna, the slayer of foes, with swift horses.
O Bhārata, Pārtha dispatched seven arrows at him;
having pierced that hero, they entered the surface of the earth.
Thus was he deeply pierced in battle by those sharp arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva.
He pierced Arjuna with ten heron-feathered arrows,
struck Vāsudeva with three, and again hit Pārtha with five; then,
O noble one, Pārtha severed his bow and cut down his standard.
The Pāṇḍava pierced him with two exceedingly sharp *bhallas*;
he, however, having pierced Pārtha with three arrows, then let out a lion’s roar. Then the heroic Sudakṣiṇa [hurled] a spear made entirely of iron.
Enraged, he hurled that terrible, bell-adorned weapon at the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Reaching that great car-warrior like a blazing great meteor,
it pierced him with sparks and fell to the surface of the earth.
Struck deeply by that weapon and overwhelmed by a swoon,
the one of great splendor regained his breath and licked the corners of his mouth;
then Pārtha struck him with fourteen iron arrows feathered with heron plumes.
He of inconceivable prowess pierced Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja— along with his horses, standard, bow,
and charioteer— with other very many arrows, and he shattered the chariot into fragments,
rendering the king's resolve and valor futile.
The Pāṇḍava pierced him in the heart with a broad-edged arrow;
with his vital organs shattered, his limbs collapsing, and his crown and armlets fallen away,
that hero fell headlong like a banner released from its mechanical support.
The glorious king, born on a mountain peak, possessed of beautiful branches and firmly established,
lay there like a *karṇikāra* tree at the end of winter, broken by the wind;
with his two massive arms outstretched, he fell, scattered about.
Bearing upon his head a golden garland that resembled fire,
he lay slain upon the ground— though accustomed to the finest Kāmboja carpets—
adorned with costly ornaments like a mountain with its peaks.
Handsome, with copper-hued eyes, that Sudakṣiṇa,
the son of the king of Kamboja, was struck down by Pārtha;
though his life had departed, the mighty-armed one lay beautiful as he fell upon the earth.
Afflicting all beings, as well as Keśava and Arjuna,
your son’s entire army then fled upon seeing that Śrutāyudha and Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja had been slain.
Saṃjaya said: "O King, when Sudakṣiṇa and the heroic Śrutāyudha had been slain,
your soldiers, filled with rage, rushed impetuously toward Pārtha."
The Abhiṣāhas, Śūrasenas, Śibis,
and Vasātayas then rained showers of arrows upon Dhanañjaya, O King;
the Pāṇḍava crushed six hundred of those noble warriors with his shafts.
Terrified, they fled like small animals from a tiger;
but turning back again, they surrounded Pārtha on all sides as he was slaughtering his enemies in battle and seeking victory over his foes.
As they rushed forward swiftly, Dhanañjaya, with arrows dispatched from the Gāṇḍīva,
caused their heads and arms to fall; the fierce warrior cut off their heads as one plucks lotuses from their stalks.
The ground there was covered without interval by fallen heads;
it was as if shrouded by the shadow of clouds due to the crows, vultures, and hawks in the battle.
While they were being thus destroyed, [the two heroes] were filled with rage and indignation.
Śrutāyus and Acyutāyus fought against Dhanañjaya; those two powerful, rivaling heroes, born of noble lineage and possessed of mighty arms,
discharged showers of arrows at him from both the left and the right.

O great king, those two archers, acting with haste and seeking great glory, were intent on slaying Arjuna for the sake of your son. They [assailed] Arjuna with a thousand straight-knotted feathered arrows.
Enraged, the two of them filled [the chariot] like two clouds filling a pond.
Then Śrutāyus, that best of car-warriors, being provoked to anger, struck Dhanañjaya with a sharp, yellow-tipped *tomara* spear.
Pierced deeply by his powerful enemy, that crusher of foes fell into a profound swoon, causing even Keśava to faint in the battle. At that very moment, however, the great car-warrior Acyutāyu—
With an exceedingly sharp spear, he struck the Pāṇḍava;
for he was like one applying caustic to a wound upon that high-souled Pāṇḍava.
Deeply pierced, Pārtha leaned against his flagpole for support.
Then, O lord of the people, a great lion-roar arose from your entire army, believing Dhananjaya to have been slain;
and Krishna was deeply distressed upon seeing Partha unconscious.
There he comforted Dhanañjaya with these kind words.
Then those two, the best of chariot-warriors, having found their mark, [assailed] Dhanañjaya and Vāsudeva of the Vṛṣṇi clan from all sides with showers of arrows.

With its wheels, its pole, its chariot, its horses, its banner, and its flags, they rendered it invisible in battle; it was like a marvel. But Bībhatsu, O Bhārata, having recovered his breath, slowly [regained his composure].
Just as one who has reached the city of the King of the Dead and returned again,
so did he see his chariot covered by a net of arrows along with Keśava,
and he beheld his two enemies standing before him like two blazing fires.
Then the great car-warrior Pārtha manifested the Śakra weapon.
From it issued forth thousands of straight-knotted arrows. They struck those two great archers, as well as the arrows discharged by them.

Wandering through the sky, they were torn apart by the arrows of Pārtha. Having quickly repelled those shafts with the force of his own arrows, the son of Pāṇḍu proceeded right there, fighting the great car-warriors.

And those two, their arms and heads severed by the showers of Phalguna’s arrows, fell to the earth like two trees blown down by the wind. And there was the death of Śrutāyus and the slaying of Acyutāyus as well.
It was a marvel to the world, like the drying up of the ocean.
Having slain five hundred chariots that followed those two,
Pārtha advanced against the Bharata army, slaying the best of the best.
Seeing Śrutāyus slain and Acyutāyus as well,
O Bhārata, Ayutāyus and Dīrghāyus became enraged;
those two sons of theirs, the best among men, rushed against the son of Kuntī.
Scattering various kinds of arrows, both of them, emaciated by the calamity that had befallen their father,
were sent in a mere moment to the abode of Yama by the supremely enraged Arjuna with his straight-knotted shafts.
Agitating the ranks like an elephant agitating a lotus pond,
the bulls among the Kṣatriyas were unable to restrain the son of Pṛthā;
then the Aṅgas surrounded the Pāṇḍava with a multitude of elephants.
O King, thousands of enraged elephant-riders,
skilled in combat and commanded by Duryodhana, advanced upon elephants resembling mountains;
these included kings from the East and the South, headed by the ruler of Kaliṅga.
As they rushed forward swiftly, he severed their heads and even their formidable arms adorned with ornaments by means of arrows dispatched from the Gāṇḍīva bow.
The earth was strewn with those heads and with arms still bearing their armlets.
The golden-stone-like [bodies] shone as if covered by serpents;
arms severed by arrows and heads struck off were seen falling like birds from trees.
Pierced by thousands of arrows and streaming with blood, the elephants appeared like mountains at the time of dissolution with torrents of liquid red chalk flowing down them;
others, struck down, lay prostrate, slain by the sharp arrows of Bībhatsu.
O King, the Mlecchas mounted upon the backs of elephants— possessing various hideous appearances, wearing diverse garbs, and equipped with a multitude of various weapons—
shone resplendent as their limbs were smeared with blood after being struck by variegated arrows.
Struck by the arrows of Pārtha, the elephants vomited blood;
with their limbs severed by the thousands, along with their riders and followers,
they cried out, fell down, and others wandered aimlessly in all directions.
Greatly terrified and trumpeting loudly, the elephants crushed one another in many ways; those intoxicated beasts, with their weapons tucked within them, were like fierce poison.
They were most terrible, possessing fearsome eyes, and they knew the illusions of the Asuras.
The Yavanas, the Pāradas, and the Śakas, together with the Sunikas— those who are crow-colored, of evil conduct, lustful for women, and fond of quarreling—
the Draviḍas fight there, mounted upon rutting elephants.
The Mlecchas, born from the lineage of cattle, who were like Death itself and skilled in striking— the Dārvas, Abhisāras, Daradas, Puṇḍras, along with the Bāhlikas—
those hosts by the hundreds of thousands could not even be numbered.
They all rained down sharp arrows upon the Pāṇḍava;
those Mlecchas, skilled in various modes of warfare, covered him with their shafts. Dhananjaya, in turn, swiftly released a shower of arrows upon them as well.
Indeed, there was a rain such as that, like a swarm of locusts;
having created a shadow of clouds over the army with his arrows, Dhanañjaya [assailed] those who were shaven-headed,
half-shaven, matted-haired, impure, and had faces covered in matted locks.

By means of his weapons and illusory powers, he struck down all the assembled Mlecchas; pierced by hundreds of arrows, those bands moving in troops fled in fear from the battle, seeking refuge in mountain caves.
With hundreds of arrows, elephants, horses, riders, and Mlecchas were struck down;
upon the ground, vultures, herons, and wolves drank the blood with joy.
The earth was covered with foot soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants, creating a bridge-like surface over which one could pass.

They set in motion a terrible and fierce river, surging with floods of blood, where showers of arrows served as rafts and hair formed the moss and grass; it was filled with helmets for its small fish, like the world at the end of an eon brought forth by Time.
He made the river impassable with elephants and its waters turned crimson by the blood from the bodies of princes, elephant-riders, horsemen, and chariot-warriors;
it was as if, when Indra rains, there is neither high ground nor low ground remaining.
In that way, the entire earth was drenched with blood;
likewise, O lord of the people, the nurse of all beings was flooded with gore—
six thousand excellent heroes and again another thousand superior ones.

That bull among Kṣatriyas dispatched Kṣatriyas to the realm of death with his arrows; pierced by thousands of shafts, the elephants, though properly equipped, lay prostrate upon the earth like mountains struck down by thunderbolts.
Slaying horses, chariots, and elephants, Arjuna moved about like a rutting elephant trampling a forest of reeds,
or like a fire consuming a place abounding in trees, creepers, and shrubs, along with dry fuel, grass, and weeds.
Just as a fire fanned by the wind might consume a forest,
so did the fire that was Dhanañjaya, the son of Pāṇḍu, incensed and impelled by the wind that was Kṛṣṇa, burn the forest of your army with the rays of his arrows.
Making the seats of the chariots empty and covering the earth with men, Dhananjaya, bow in hand, seemed to dance amidst the press of battle,
turning the ground crimson with blood by means of his thunderbolt-like arrows.
Then there flowed a surging river of blood,
like a mountain torrent from the bodies of men, horses, and elephants;
it was strewn with bones for its pebbles, had banners for its trees, and chariots for its pools.
With rocks having severed peaks, with great elephant-trunks as its massive crocodiles,
rich with the mud of flesh, marrow, and bones, crowded with slain horses as its sea-monsters, filled with warriors as its jackals, and teeming with hundreds of headless trunks;
Covered with foam from his *uṣṇīṣa* and teeming with fierce arrows as its fish,
Dhanañjaya, filled with rage, entered the Bharata army, making the ground as terrifying as the playground of Rudra.
As he was thus proceeding, Ambaṣṭha, along with Śrutāyu, sought to restrain him;
O noble one, Arjuna swiftly struck down the horses of that struggling warrior with sharp arrows fletched with heron feathers.
Having severed his bow with other arrows, Pārtha strode forward;
but Ambaṣṭha, his eyes clouded with rage, seized a mace and,
grasping that great weapon, rushed swiftly forward with mace in hand.
He encountered Pārtha and the great chariot-warrior Keśava in battle.
Then, O Bhārata, that hero, laughing and raising his mace,
blocked the chariot and struck Keśava with it.
O Bhārata, seeing Keśava struck by the mace, Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, became violently enraged at Ambaṣṭha;
he then [struck] that best of chariot-warriors, who still held his mace, with gold-feathered arrows.
In that battle, he covered [him] as a cloud covers the risen sun.
Then, with other arrows, Pārtha shattered the mace of that high-souled one; it was like a marvel.
Then, seeing her fallen, he seized another massive mace and struck Arjuna and Vāsudeva again and again. Arjuna, with two razor-headed arrows, [severed] his two upraised arms that still held the mace.
With another feathered shaft, he severed [the demon's] head,
which resembled the banner of Indra; slain, O King, it fell, making the earth resound like the staff of Indra when its binding cords have been released from the mechanical device.
When Ambaṣṭha was thus broken, your army was shattered. Plunged into the array of chariots and surrounded by hundreds of elephants and horses,
he took the lives of the elephant-riders, horsemen, and chariot-warriors with his arrows.
Then Pārtha was seen like the sun obscured by clouds.
Sañjaya said:
Then, when the son of Kuntī had entered with the intent to slay the king of the Sindhus...
Having pierced through Droṇa’s division and the difficult-to-overcome division of the Bhojas, O King, when Sudakṣiṇa— the heir of the Kamboja king—
had been slain and the valiant Śrutāyudha had been killed by Savyasācin;
When the armies had fled and were shattered on all sides,
your son, seeing his own force broken, rushed toward Droṇa;
hurrying along on a single chariot, he approached Droṇa and spoke.
That tiger among men has departed after crushing this great army. In this midst of this terrible slaughter of people, consider with your intellect what must be done next to thwart Arjuna.

"Act in such a way that Jayadratha, that tiger among men, may not be slain; may prosperity be yours, for you are our supreme refuge. For this fire that is Dhananjaya has been fanned by the wind of his wrath."
"The fire consumes my army like a wildfire rising through dry undergrowth.
For once the son of Kuntī has pierced through the host, O scorcher of foes,
the protectors of Jayadratha have fallen into the greatest peril."
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, the resolve of the lords of men was firm:
'As long as he lives, Dhananjaya shall never overcome Drona.
Yet here is that son of Pritha who has bypassed you, O one of great luster, even as you looked on!"
"I consider everyone here to be afflicted today; this strength is no longer mine.
I know you, O highly blessed one, to be devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas;
yet, O Brahmin, I am bewildered as I reflect upon the gravity of our task."
O Brahmin, I conduct my supreme livelihood for you according to my ability,
and I gratify you to the best of my power, yet you do not perceive this. O you of immeasurable prowess, you do not desire us as your constant devotees.
You constantly please the Pāṇḍavas, who are intent on our displeasure;
though you live off us alone, you are devoted to our detriment.
Indeed, I do not recognize you—you are like a razor smeared with honey.
If you had not granted me this boon regarding the subjugation of the Pāṇḍavas— you who are always charming in speech yet exceedingly sharp in heart— [I would have acted otherwise].
I should not have prevented the Lord of the Sindhu from going to his home; rather,
being foolish and hoping for protection from you,
I consoled the Lord of the Sindhu out of delusion and delivered him unto death.
A man might indeed escape even after reaching the jaws of Yama;
but Jayadratha, having fallen under the power of Arjuna, shall not escape in battle.
O rider of chestnut horses, act in such a way that the King of Sindhu may be protected.
"Do not be angry at my distressed lamentations; protect the King of Sindhu!
Drona said:
"I do not find fault with your words; you are equal to Ashvatthaman to me."
I shall tell you the truth; accept it, O lord of the people. Kṛṣṇa is his preeminent charioteer, and his excellent horses are swift.
Having created even a slight opening, Dhanañjaya passes through it with great speed.
"Do you not see the floods of arrows from Kirīṭin falling behind his chariot at a distance of just one krośa, as he moves so swiftly? For,
endowed with my age, I am no longer capable of such rapid movement today."
"And this force has been stationed at the head of the Pārthas' army.
Yudhiṣṭhira must be captured by me while all the archers look on;
thus was my vow made in the midst of the Kṣatriyas, O mighty-armed one."
"Released by Dhanañjaya, he stands before me; therefore, leaving the front of the array, I will not go toward Phalguna. He is a single enemy of equal birth and deeds, yet I am accompanied by allies."

"Go and fight; do not fear, for you are the lord of this world. O King, hero, accomplished and skillful one, having instigated this enmity with the Pāṇḍavas, go yourself quickly, O hero, to where Dhanañjaya has gone."
Duryodhana said:
"O Teacher, how could Dhananjaya— the foremost of all wielders of weapons— be resisted by me, even though he has surpassed you?"
Even Purandara, the wielder of the thunderbolt, might be conquered in battle;
but Arjuna, the conqueror of enemy cities, cannot be defeated in combat—
he by whom both the Bhoja Hardikya and you, who are like a god, have been overcome.
By the power of his missiles, Śrutāyu was conquered and Nibarhita was struck down; Sudakṣiṇa was slain, as was King Śrutāyudha;
and Śrutāyu, Acyutāyu, and hundreds of Mlecchas were killed.

"How shall I fight in battle against that Pāṇḍava, who is invincible and consumes so many enemies? Tell me this, O master of weapons, if you consider it appropriate for me to engage with him in combat today; instruct me."
"I am dependent on you; act as my servant and protect my honor.
Droṇa said:
"O Kauravya, you speak the truth; Dhananjaya is difficult to overcome."
"I, however, shall act in such a way that you will be able to overcome him;
let all the archers in the world behold today this marvel:
the son of Kuntī held fast by you while Vāsudeva looks on."
"O King, I shall now fasten this golden armor upon you,
so that neither arrows nor divine weapons shall prevail against you in battle,
even if the asuras, gods, yakṣas, serpents, and rākṣasas were to attack you."
Even if the three worlds, together with men, were to fight you, there would be no fear for you;
neither Kṛṣṇa, nor the son of Kuntī, nor any other wielder of weapons in battle will be able to pierce your armor with arrows.
"Therefore, putting on your armor, go yourself in haste today to the enraged Arjuna in battle; he shall not withstand you. Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus, Droṇa quickly touched water and,
while reciting a mantra according to the prescribed rite, bound on that most wonderful,
radiant armor for the sake of your son’s victory in that great battle.
Desiring to astonish the world with his knowledge, that best of those who know Brahman,
the mighty-armed one, joined himself with the high-souled teacher.
Drona said:
May Brahmā grant you well-being, and may the twice-born also grant you well-being;
and from those who are the best among the reptiles, may there be well-being for you, O Bhārata. Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Dhundhumāra, and Bhagīratha—
May all the royal sages grant you well-being in every way.
May there be well-being for you from those with one foot and those with many feet;
may there always be well-being for you from those who have no feet in this great battle.
May Svāhā, Svadhā, and Śacī always grant you well-being; may Lakṣmī and Arundhatī likewise bestow auspiciousness upon you, O sinless one. Asita, Devala, Viśvāmitra, and likewise Aṅgiras—
May Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa likewise grant you well-being, O King.
May Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, the Lord of the World, the quarters of space together with their presiding deities,
and the six-faced Kārttikeya, bestow well-being upon you today.
By whom the gods were once defeated in the battle of Tārakāmaya—
that hero was held back and struck down, for he was indeed unslayable by the hosts of deities.
May the blessed Vivasvat grant you well-being in every respect.
May he whose attendants are under his control grant you well-being;
may the four elephants of the quarters, the earth, the terrestrial space, the sky, the planets,
the cardinal directions, and the intermediate directions likewise bestow well-being upon you.
May the Lords of Creatures, the Siddhas who delight in the welfare of the world,
always grant you well-being when praised with this mantra.
O King, he who constantly supports the earth from below—

May that Śeṣa, the best of serpents, grant you well-being. O son of Gāndhārī, in ancient times, when Vṛtra the Daitya displayed his prowess in battle, the foremost of the gods were defeated by him by the thousands, their bodies torn asunder.
Then all the inhabitants of heaven,

including Indra, had their splendor and strength taken away; overwhelmed and robbed of their prowess, the gods, including Indra, fled in haste and sought refuge with Brahmā, terrified of the great asura Vṛtra.
The gods said:
"O best of gods, O foremost of deities, become the refuge for the gods who have been crushed by Vṛtra; protect us from this great fear."
Droṇa said:
Then, to Viṣṇu who stood at his side, and to Śakra and the other foremost gods,
he spoke these truthful words to those best of deities who were despondent.
"The gods, along with Indra and the twice-born, must always be protected by me;
for Tvaṣṭṛ’s energy was exceedingly difficult to withstand, by which Vṛtra was created.
In ancient times, Tvaṣṭṛ performed austerities for ten million years."

"O gods, Vṛtra has been created; having obtained permission from Maheśvara, that powerful enemy will surely slay him only through his grace. The Blessed Lord Hara cannot be seen without going to the abode of Śaṅkara."
"Having seen him, you shall slay the enemy; go quickly to Mandara,
where dwells the source of ascetic powers, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice— the wielder of the Pināka bow, the Lord of all beings, who struck out the eyes of Bhaga."
Having gone together to Mount Mandara along with Brahmā, those gods beheld a mass of splendor possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
He said, "Welcome, O gods; tell me, what shall I do?"
"The sight of me is never in vain; therefore, may you obtain your desires.
When he had spoken thus, all those inhabitants of heaven replied to him:
"Our splendor has been taken away by Vṛtra; become the refuge of the dwellers of heaven."
"O God, behold our forms, shattered by blows;
we have come to you for refuge—be our protector, O Maheśvara.
Maheśvara said:
"It is known to me how this exceedingly powerful being was created by the gods;
born from the vital energy of Tvaṣṭṛ, she is terrible and difficult to restrain for those who have not disciplined their selves.
Nevertheless, I must certainly provide assistance to all the inhabitants of heaven."
"O Śakra, O Lord of the Gods, take this radiant armor born from my own body and fasten it on with this mental mantra for the sake of slaying Vṛtra, the chief of the Asuras and slayer of the gods."
Droṇa said:
Having spoken thus, the giver of boons bestowed that armor and its very mantra upon him. Protected by that armor, he advanced against Vṛtra’s army.
Though various kinds of floods of weapons were hurled at him in that great battle,
the joints of his armor-binding could not be pierced;
protected by that armor, he then [assailed] Vṛtra, the enemy of the gods.
Then, in that battle, the Lord of the Gods himself slew Vṛtra;
Śakra, the leader of the gods, then struck him down fearlessly in the fray. And he gave that armor, which was composed of mantras, to Aṅgiras.
Aṅgiras spoke it to his son Bṛhaspati, who was skilled in mantras;
Bṛhaspati then spoke it to the wise Agniveśya;
Agniveśya gave it to me, and with that I bind this armor for you.
"O best of kings, today for the sake of protecting your body, [I shall do so] with a mantra.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus, the highly effulgent Droṇa then [addressed] your son.
Once again, that bull among teachers spoke these words slowly;
he bound his karma and the teacher addressed these words to your son.
"O King, I bind this armor upon you with the *Brahmasūtra*;
I bind this armor upon you with the *Svasūkta* of Brahmā,
just as it was bound upon Viṣṇu by Hiraṇyagarbha in battle of old."
"Just as the divine armor of Śakra was bound by Brahmā in the Tārakāmaya battle, so do I bind yours. Having bound his armor with the mantra according to the prescribed rite,"
The twice-born one dispatched the king for a great battle. Having been equipped with armor by the high-souled teacher,
O King, the mighty-armed one set out at once for where Dhanañjaya had gone.
With a thousand chariots of the Trigarta strikers,
as well as a thousand elephants in rut endowed with great prowess,
ten thousand horses, and other great car-warriors, [he advanced].
Surrounded [by his forces], the mighty-armed one set out toward Arjuna’s chariot,
amidst the sound of various musical instruments, just like Vairocana,
accompanied by people from various lands.
When your son set forth,
O Bhārata, a great clamor arose among your troops upon seeing the Kaurava host advancing like the unfathomable ocean.
Saṃjaya said:
O great king, when the son of Pṛthā and the descendant of Vṛṣṇi had thus entered [the army],
and Duryodhana, that bull among men, had gone after them from behind;
The Pāṇḍavas, together with the Somakas, rushed toward Droṇa with great speed and a mighty roar; then the battle commenced. That battle became terrible, tumultuous, and hair-raising.
O King, that wonderful sight at the front of the battle arrays of the Pañcālas and the Kurus—
such a thing has never been seen by us before, nor have we ever heard of it. O King, a battle such as that has never been seen before, nor have we ever heard of it.
O lord of the people, when the sun had reached the meridian, such was the battle that took place:
the Pārthas, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, having drawn up their ranks,
struck out and overwhelmed Droṇa’s entire army with showers of arrows.
Placing Droṇa, the foremost of all wielders of weapons, at our head,
we rained down arrows upon the sons of Pṛthā led by the son of Pṛṣata,
like two great clouds driven by contrary winds at the end of winter.
Adorned with chariots, the two beautiful armies shone at their vanguard;
having come together, the two great hosts exerted supreme force,
like the rivers Ganges and Yamunā during the rainy season when their waters are overflowing.
With the winds of various weapons blowing before it, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
with maces for its lightning, that great and most terrible cloud of battle—
stirred by the wind of Bhāradvāja and possessing thousands of torrents of arrows— [rushed forward].
That most terrible one rained down upon the blazing fire of the Pāṇḍava army,
O best of the twice-born, just as a fierce and mighty wind blows at the end of the summer heat, agitating the ocean; he threw the ranks of the Pāṇḍavas into utter turmoil.
With every effort, they rushed toward Droṇa alone,
like powerful torrents of water seeking to breach a great dam;
but Droṇa held them back, as a mountain resists the floods of water.
The Pāṇḍavas, enraged in battle, along with the Pañcālas and the Kekayas—
then other kings as well,
mighty heroes of great strength, turned back from all sides and hemmed in the Pañcālas in the fray.
Then, in that battle, that tiger among men, the son of Pṛṣata, together with the Pāṇḍavas,
repeatedly struck Droṇa, desiring to break through the enemy host;
just as Droṇa poured down showers of arrows upon the son of Pṛṣata.
In that very same way, Dhṛṣṭadyumna rained down showers of arrows; he was a cloud of force with Dhṛṣṭadyumna as the rain-cloud, preceded by the wind of swords, filled with spears,
javelins, and darts, with the bowstring for lightning and the twang of the bow for thunder.
He discharged showers of arrows like a rain of stones in every direction;
striking down the multitudes of excellent chariots and horses, he covered the army.
Whichever group of Pāṇḍava chariots Droṇa assailed with his shafts, [he overwhelmed].
Then, from that point on, the son of Pṛṣata drove Droṇa away with his arrows.
But as Droṇa was thus striving in battle, O Bhārata,
his army split into three parts upon encountering Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Some turned back toward Bhoja, while others went toward Jalasaṃdha;
and still others, being slaughtered by the Pāṇḍavas, fled toward Droṇa himself.
Droṇa, the best of chariot-warriors, then rallied those troops who remained.
And the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna also scattered those [troops] of his;
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, divided into three groups, were slaughtered by the Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas,
like cattle without a herdsman in the forest by many beasts of prey.
"In that tumultuous battle, people thought that Time itself was devouring the warriors who had been confounded by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
just as the kingdom of a wicked king is consumed by famine, disease, and thieves."
In that same way, your army, having fallen into distress, is being routed by the Pāṇḍavas;
while weapons and armor are pierced by the rays of the sun,
the eyes are likewise struck by the dust raised by the troops.
When the armies had been divided into three parts and were being slaughtered by the Pāṇḍavas,
Drona, filled with indignation, then scattered the Pañcālas with his arrows,
crushing those divisions and striking them down with his shafts.
The form of Droṇa became like that of the blazing fire of time;
O lord of the people, that great car-warrior pierced chariots, elephants, horses,
and even foot soldiers in battle, each with a single arrow.

O Bhārata, among the armies of the Pāṇḍavas, there was no one at all who could withstand the sharp arrows discharged from Droṇa’s bow in battle. Scorched by Droṇa’s shafts and roasted by the sun, [the army withered away].
O Bhārata, the army of the son of Pṛṣata wandered here and there;
O bull of the Bharatas, that army, being struck on all sides by the son of Bharadvāja with arrows resembling flames of fire, was consumed.
In the same way, your army, being driven back by the son of Pṛṣata,
became ablaze on all sides like a dry forest consumed by fire,
while the troops were being slaughtered by the arrows of Droṇa and the son of Pṛṣata.
Having risked their lives to the utmost of their power, the soldiers fought on,
O bull of the Bharatas— both yours and those of the enemy;
there was not a single one, O great king, who abandoned the battle out of fear.
But the uterine brothers surrounded Bhīmasena, the son of Kuntī—
namely Vivimśati, Citrasena, and the great chariot-warrior Vikarṇa,
as well as Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti and the heroic Kṣemadhūrti.
Of your three sons, there were exactly three followers:
the radiant King Bāhlīka, a man of noble birth and a great car-warrior, who,
together with his army and ministers, held back the sons of Draupadī.
King Śaibya Govāsana, with more than a thousand warriors,
held back the valiant son of Abhibhū of Kāśī—
Ajātaśatru, the son of Kuntī, who was like a blazing fire.
Śalya, the lord of the Madras and a king himself, chose King [Duryodhana] as his protector.
But the impatient and heroic Duḥśāsana, having stationed his own army,
advanced in anger against Sātyaki, that best of chariot-warriors in battle.
Armed with my own division, clad in armor and mail, I held back Cekitāna along with four hundred great archers; meanwhile,
Śakuni, together with his army, held back the son of Mādrī.
With seven hundred Gāndhāra warriors armed with bows, spears, arrows, and swords,
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti assailed Virāṭa of the Matsyas;
having cast away their lives, those great archers exerted themselves in battle for the sake of their friend.
Bāhlīka, prepared for battle, checked the unvanquished Śikhaṇḍin, the son of Yajñasena,
as he was advancing with great prowess;
and [he also checked] Dhṛṣṭadyumna of the Pañcālas, together with the cruel Prabhadrakas.
The ruler of Avanti, together with the Sauviras, checked the wrathful Ghaṭotkaca— that heroic Rākṣasa who fights with cruel ferocity—
as Alāyudha swiftly rushed toward him in battle while he was advancing in a rage.

The great car-warrior Kuntibhoja, joined by a vast army, checked the wrathful Alambusa, the lord of the Rākṣasas. In this manner, O Bhārata, there were hundreds of such duels between your men and theirs.
O Bhārata, the ruler of the Sindhus was at the rear of the entire army,
protected by car-warriors such as Kṛpa and others who were supreme archers;
he had two very great protectors of his wheels.
O King, the son of Droṇa was on the right and the Sūta’s son on the left;
while those led by the son of Somadatta were his rear-guards,
along with Kṛpa, Vṛṣasena, Śala, and the invincible Śalya.
07,070.051a All those wise and great archers, skilled in battle, 07,070.051c having thus arranged for the protection of the ruler of the Sindhus, then fought on.
07,071.001 Sañjaya said:

"O King, listen as I describe the wonderful battle that took place between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, exactly as it unfolded. Having encountered the son of Bharadvāja, who stood at the head of the military formation..."
Desirous of breaking through Drona’s division,
the sons of Pritha fought in battle while protecting their own array; likewise, Drona’s soldiers also fought the sons of Pritha in battle, seeking great glory.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, highly enraged and desiring the welfare of your son, struck Virāṭa with ten arrows.
And Virāṭa, O great king, stood firm in battle against both of them.
Having exerted their prowess, the two of them, along with their followers, fought back;
a fierce battle ensued between them, with blood for its water,
like that between a lion and two pre-eminent elephants with temples flowing with rut in the forest.
The mighty Yājñaseni struck the impetuous Bāhlīka in battle with sharp,
terrible arrows that pierce the vital organs and the bones; Bāhlīka, in turn, struck the son of Yajñasena with gold-feathered shafts whetted on stone.
Highly enraged, he struck him violently with nine straight-knotted arrows. That battle became terrible, crowded with shafts and spears;
it produced terror in cowards and increased the joy of the brave.
The two brave brothers from Avanti fought against Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
just as both Sālva and Bilvaka fought against Viṣṇu in the Kṛta Yuga. By those two, the sky and the directions were filled there with the arrows they released.
Everything became shrouded in darkness; nothing at all could be discerned.
O King, nothing was recognized, nor did anyone else perceive what was happening.
Śaibya Govāsana, in that battle, [encountered] the son of Kāśya, the great car-warrior.
Accompanied by his army,
the king of Bāhlīka, enraged, fought the great chariot-warriors, the sons of Draupadī,
in battle; he shone like an elephant attacking a rival elephant, or like the mind contending with the five senses.

O best of embodied beings, your son Duḥśāsana fought Satyaki of the Vṛṣṇi clan in battle from all sides with a torrent of arrows, just as the objects of the senses constantly assail the body of those who possess a body.
He struck him with nine sharp, straight-knotted arrows.
Deeply pierced by that powerful and great bowman,
Sātyaki, whose valor is truth, quickly fell into a slight swoon.
Having regained his composure, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi quickly pierced your son, that great car-warrior,
with ten heron-feathered arrows. Both of them, having deeply pierced one another and being mangled by each other's shafts, stood firm.
O King, they both trembled in the encounter like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom. But Alambuṣa, enraged and afflicted by the arrows of Kuntibhoja,
shone with supreme beauty like a *kiṃśuka* tree laden with flowers.
Then the Rākṣasa, having pierced Kuntibhoja with many iron arrows,
let out a terrifying roar at the head of your army.
Thereupon, those two heroes fought one another in the battle.
O Bhārata, all living beings beheld Śakuni and the impetuous Jambha as they were in former times;
and the two sons of Mādrī, enraged in battle, afflicted him with arrows in the fray.
O Great King, that destruction of men, with him as its root, has proceeded forth;
