it was generated by you, greatly increased by Karṇa,
and fanned into flame by your son— this fire of wrath.
O King, Śakuni, who had prepared himself to burn this entire earth,
was turned back by the arrows of the two sons of Pāṇḍu;
he did not know what to do or how to display any prowess in battle.
Seeing him turned away, the two sons of Mādrī, those great car-warriors,
again showered him with arrows, just as two clouds rain upon a great mountain.
Being struck by many straight-knotted arrows, he...
The son of Subala proceeded with swift horses toward Droṇa’s army; likewise,
Ghaṭotkaca rushed impetuously in battle against that heroic Rākṣasa Alāyudha, maintaining a moderate speed.
O great king, the battle between those two was like a wondrous spectacle,
just like that which occurred in ancient times between Rāma and Rāvaṇa in combat.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira [attacked] the king of the Madras in the fray.
Having pierced him with fifty arrows, he struck him again with seven;
then, O King, there commenced between them a most wonderful battle,
like the great battle of old between Śambara and the king of the gods.
Viviṃśati, Citrasena, and your son Vikarṇa,
surrounded by a vast army, fought against Bhīmasena.
Saṃjaya said:
When that hair-raising battle had thus commenced,
the Pāṇḍavas rushed against the Kauravas, who were divided into three groups.
The mighty-armed Bhīmasena held back Jalasaṃdha.
O great king, Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by his army, encountered Kṛtavarman in battle as the latter scattered showers of arrows like the radiant sun; meanwhile,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna rushed against Droṇa in the fray.
Then the battle commenced between all those rushing archers—
the Kurus and the Somakas— who were enraged with one another;
while that destruction was thus occurring, filled with great terror.
While the armies had formed into pairs and were fighting fearlessly,
the mighty Droṇa, together with the powerful son of the Pañcālas,
discharged volleys of arrows; that was like a marvel.
Like lotus groves destroyed on all sides,
Droṇa and the Pāñcālya prince caused the heads of men to fall by the hundreds,
scattered everywhere throughout the ranks of the heroes.
Garments, ornaments, weapons, banners, armor, and implements,
their parts variegated with gold and drenched in blood,
appeared like masses of clouds accompanied by lightning as they lay entangled together.
Your warriors and the sons of Pāṇḍu were wounded in battle; those great car-warriors, drawing bows as long as palm trees, felled elephants, horses,
and men in the fray with feathered shafts.
Swords, shields, bows, heads,
and armor were scattered about in the clash of those high-souled heroes;
countless headless trunks rose up on every side.
O great king, in that most tumultuous carnage,
vultures, herons, cranes, hawks, crows, and jackals were seen; indeed,
O noble one, many flesh-eaters were seen there.
O King, they were devouring flesh and drinking blood; they were tearing out hair and marrow in many ways,
dragging away entire bodies as well as the various limbs of the body.
Then, from here and there, the heads of multitudes of men, horses, and elephants [were seen];
those skilled in weapons, consecrated by the initiatory rites of battle and bearing arrows,
fought fiercely at that time, seeking victory in the fray.
Your warriors moved through the battle in various sword-tracts,
[armed] with double-edged swords, spears, darts, spikes, lances,
and battle-axes; others [fought] with maces, iron clubs, or even with their bare arms when deprived of weapons.
Enraged, the men who had entered the arena of battle struck one another:
chariot-warriors with chariot-warriors, horsemen with horsemen, elephants with choice elephants, and foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers.
Like intoxicated men or like actors on a stage,
others cried out to one another and struck one another in that battle; thus did the conflict proceed without restraint, O lord of the people.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna intermingled his horses with those of Droṇa;
those steeds, swift as the wind, shone brilliantly as they were mixed together in battle—
some the color of pigeons and others crimson red.
O King, the horses shone like clouds accompanied by lightning.
And Dhrṣṭadyumna, beholding Droṇa approaching nearby,
O Bhārata, that hero cast aside his bow and took up a sword and shield.
Desiring to perform a difficult feat, the son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of enemy heroes,
bypassed Droṇa’s chariot with his bow and entered it; he stood upon the middle of the yoke and upon the fastenings of the yoke.
He struck the horses in their haunches, and the troops cheered that feat;
as he moved with his sword, standing upon his red horses,
Drona could find no opening against him, and it was like a marvel.
Just as the flight of a hawk greedy for meat in the forests,
even so was the charge of him who desired to slay Droṇa;
then, with a hundred arrows, he struck down his [Droṇa’s] standard adorned with a hundred moons.
The powerful Droṇa struck Drupada’s son with ten arrows;
with sixty-four arrows he slew his horses, and with two broad-headed shafts (bhalla) he likewise struck down both his standard, his parasol, and his two flank-guards (pārṣṇisārathi).
Then, with haste, he drew back another life-ending arrow to his ear and discharged it, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt hurls the *vajra*,
or as the Lord of Śacī hurls the lightning bolt at Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
With fourteen arrows, Sātyaki cut down that shaft,
and liberated Dhṛṣṭadyumna who had been seized by the preeminent teacher,
O noble one, like a deer seized by a lion by that lion among men.
The bull among the Śinis caused the Pāñcālya to be released from Droṇa.
Seeing Sātyaki as the protector of the Pāñcālya in that great battle,
Droṇa quickly struck him with twenty-six arrows.
Then the grandson of Śini pierced Droṇa, who was as if devouring the Sṛñjayas,
with twenty-six sharp arrows in the center of his chest.
Thereupon, all the Pāñcāla chariot-warriors, greedy for victory, quickly [advanced].
When Droṇa had been set upon by the Sātvatas, they liberated Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Once that arrow had been cut away and Dhṛṣṭadyumna was liberated..."
O Sañjaya,
what did Droṇa— the indignant great archer, the best among all wielders of weapons, a tiger among men, and the grandson of Śini— do in battle against that Yuyudhāna, the foremost hero of the Vṛṣṇis?
Saṃjaya said:
Rushing forward, with his bow as a wide-gaping mouth, he had sharp-edged arrows for teeth and whetted iron shafts for fangs; he was like a serpent whose venom is anger.
With eyes copper-red from fury and indignation, sighing like a great serpent, he [proceeded] with swift,
crimson horses— delighted by the hero among men—
which seemed to leap into the sky and stride everywhere.
Discharging arrows with golden shafts, he rushed toward Yuyudhāna—
a great rain-cloud of falling arrows, with the roar of a chariot for its thunder and the drawing of the bow for its lightning,
flashing with many iron shafts.

Seeing that irresistible cloud-like Droṇa— bearing spears, swords, and thunderbolts, arisen with the impetuosity of wrath, and driven by the wind of his horses— rushing toward him, the hero, conqueror of enemy cities, [prepared himself].
Laughing, the grandson of Śini, who was fierce in battle, said to the charioteer:
"This cruel brahmin, unsteady in his own duty,
is indeed the refuge of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son— he who brings misery and fear."
"Go forth with joyful speed on swift horses to meet the preceptor of the princes, who always considers himself a hero.
Thus addressed, the charioteer then drove Satyaka's chariot forward.
Then Mādhava’s excellent horses, resembling silver in hue and possessing the speed of the wind, swiftly proceeded toward Droṇa. Thereupon,
those two subduers of foes, Droṇa and the descendant of Śini, engaged in combat.
Striking each other with many thousands of arrows,
those two bulls among men made the sky covered by a web of shafts;
both heroes filled the ten directions with their arrows.
Like clouds at the end of the heat, with their showers striking one another,
the sun did not shine then, nor did the wind blow;
the sky was filled with a terrible and continuous darkness, shrouded by a net of arrows.
At that time, it became as if unassailable by other heroes,
for the world was plunged into darkness by the arrows of Droṇa and the descendant of Śini.
Then, between Droṇa and the Sātvata, both of whom were experts in swift weaponry...
No interval could be seen between the showers of arrows from those two lions among men;
from the clashing of the shafts, a sound produced by their impact was heard,
like the roar of thunderbolts hurled by Śakra.
The appearance of the arrows, deeply pierced by iron shafts,
O Bhārata, shone like that of snakes bitten by venomous serpents.
The most terrible twang of their bowstrings was heard.
Like the peaks of mountains being struck incessantly by the thunderbolt,
O King, those two chariots, the horses, and the two charioteers of both sides,
covered with gold-feathered arrows, then appeared most wonderful to behold.
O Lord of the People, there occurred a most terrible shower of stainless, straight-flying iron arrows resembling venomous snakes that have cast off their skins;
likewise, the two umbrellas fell, and the two banners fell as well.
Then, as Droṇa and Satyaki cut each other with sharp arrows,
both had their limbs drenched in blood, both being seekers of victory; with blood flowing from their bodies, they resembled two elephants with rutting secretions streaming from them.
They pierced one another with life-ending arrows;
the sounds of roaring, shouting, and clamor, along with the blasts of conchs and kettledrums,
ceased, O Great King, and no one uttered a word.
The ranks became silent and the warriors desisted from battle;
the people, filled with curiosity, watched the duel between those two.
The chariot-warriors, elephant-drivers, horsemen, and foot-soldiers [all ceased their activity].
Surrounding those two bulls among chariot-warriors with unblinking eyes,
they gazed at them from all sides with wide-open eyes. Likewise, the elephant divisions and the cavalry divisions stood still.
In the same manner, the chariot-divisions stood arrayed in counter-formation,
adorned with banners variegated with pearls and coral, decorated with gems and gold,
and featuring diverse ornaments and golden armor.
With Vaijayantī banners, with woolen blankets for the horses' necks, with stainless and sharpened weapons,
and with golden and silver ornaments upon their heads;
O Bhārata, with the rows of frontal globes and the tusks of the elephants,
the sky appeared like a net of clouds at the end of the summer heat— clouds accompanied by cranes, fireflies, and the lightning-flashes of Airāvata.
Our men and those followers of Yudhiṣṭhira stood watching that battle between Yuyudhāna and the high-souled Droṇa;
the gods, led by Brahmā and Śakra, were situated upon the foremost of their celestial chariots.
The hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, the Vidyādharas and Mahoragas,
Gandharvas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Apsarases,
and birds [fought] with various maneuvers of advancing and retreating, and with wondrous weapons that strike down foes.
They were filled with wonder at those two lions among men; displaying great dexterity of hand with their weapons, those two of mighty strength,
Droṇa and Sātyaki, pierced each other with arrows.

Then, in that battle, the descendant of Daśārha swiftly cut down Droṇa’s arrows with very firm feathered shafts, and also his bow, O one of great splendor. In the mere twinkling of an eye, the son of Bharadvāja took up another bow.
Satyaki quickly strung that bow and cut it asunder;
then Drona, hastening again with bow in hand, stood firm,
but Satyaki repeatedly cut his strung bow with sharpened arrows.
He prepared the path there by which Janārdana proceeded;
thus, one hundred and one bows were severed by that firm archer,
yet no interval was perceived between their aiming and the cutting.
Then, O king of kings, having witnessed that superhuman feat of Yuyudhāna in battle, Droṇa reflected thus in his mind:
"This power of weapons was present in Rāma, in Kārtavīrya, and in Dhanañjaya."
And while that tiger among men, Bhīṣma, was present, as well as this best of the Sātvatas,
Droṇa— foremost of the twice-born— mentally honored that prowess of his,
beholding his lightness of hand to be like that of Vāsava.
The best among those skilled in weapons was gratified, as were the gods together with Indra;
for they beheld the swiftness of the Vṛṣṇi hero, which was like that of Indra himself. Because of his agility, the gods, led by Agni, offered him praise.
The hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
O lord of the people, neither the gods nor the Gandharvas perceived any lightness of hand in Yuyudhāna as he acted with such speed.
The hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas recognized that feat of Droṇa.
Then, O Bhārata, Droṇa, the crusher of Kṣatriyas and the best among those skilled in weapons, took up another bow and fought with his missiles.

Having countered his weapons with his own illusory weapons, Sātyaki struck him with sharpened arrows; that was like a marvel. Seeing his superhuman feat in battle, which was unequaled by others, [the warriors were amazed].
Those who knew yoga honored him with yoga, for he was disciplined;
whatever weapon Droṇa discharged, Sātyaki discharged that very same one. The preceptor, the scorcher of enemies, fought him back without being perturbed.

Thus there arose a tumultuous noise toward the chariot of the invincible one. Then, O great king, the enraged master of the science of archery discharged a divine weapon for the sake of slaying Yuyudhāna.

Seeing that most terrible divine weapon of Agni, which destroys enemies, the great archer then discharged the divine Vāruṇa weapon. A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose upon seeing those two wielders of divine weapons.
Even the beings that move through the sky did not roam in the atmosphere at that time;
for when those Vāruṇa and Āgneya weapons had been aimed by them with arrows,
they could not be neutralized, and then the sun began to decline.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava,
Nakula, and Sahadeva protected Sātyaki,
along with Dhṛṣṭadyumna and others, as well as Virāṭa together with the Kekayas.
The Matsyas and the Śālveya armies quickly approached Droṇa,
while thousands of princes, placing Duḥśāsana at their head,
rushed toward Droṇa who was surrounded by his enemies.
Then, O King, a battle took place between your archers and theirs;
when the world was shrouded in dust and enveloped by a network of arrows,
everything became agitated and nothing could be discerned.
Obscured by the dust raised by the army, the battle proceeded without restraint.
In that interval, Pārtha, having defeated the great car-warriors in combat,
passed through them and stood firm after completing his fight.
Saṃjaya said:
While that battle between Droṇa and the Pāṇḍavas was thus proceeding,
the sun moved across the sky there, with its rays of light.
Covered in dust and their spirits dulled, the soldiers— whether standing firm, fighting, retreating again, breaking,
or victorious— passed that day slowly.
While those armies were thus engaged and greedy for victory, Arjuna and Vāsudeva proceeded toward the ruler of the Sindhus alone; meanwhile,
the son of Kuntī marked out the path for the chariot with his sharpened arrows.
He cleared a path there by which Janārdana proceeded;
wherever the chariot of the high-souled Pāṇḍava advanced,
O lord of the people, right there your armies were torn asunder.
The heroic descendant of Daśārha then displayed his skill in chariot warfare,
demonstrating superior, inferior, and middling circular maneuvers.
Those arrows, marked with his name, yellow in color, and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, [fell upon the enemy].
Bound with sinews, well-jointed, broad, and long-reaching—
arrows made of bamboo and iron, well-proportioned and with various tips—
drank the blood of living beings in battle along with the birds.
Standing upon his chariot, Arjuna shoots arrows at a distance of one *krośa*;
when the chariot has traveled that *krośa*, those arrows slay his enemies.
He does so with well-bred horses that carry him swiftly, possessing the speed of Tārkṣya and the Wind.
Thus did Dhṛṣīkeśa proceed, causing the entire world to marvel;
O lord of the people, the chariot of the Sun does not travel in such a manner,
nor that of Indra, nor of Rudra, nor even of Vaiśravaṇa.

O King, never before had another’s chariot moved in battle as swiftly as Arjuna’s, which followed the speed of his very thought. Having entered the fray in that battle, O King, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes—
O Bhārata, he quickly urged the horses into the midst of the army.
Then, having reached the center of that mass of chariots, those excellent horses,
overcome by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, drew the chariot with great difficulty.
Wounded many times by numerous weapons of those skilled in war, they moved repeatedly in various wonderful circular maneuvers amidst the slain horses,
elephants, and chariots, along with the men.
Having ascended thousands of mountain-like peaks above,
those horses, though possessing the speed of the wind, became slow in their pace due to great exhaustion in that battle, O King.

In the meantime, O King, the two heroic brothers from Avanti, accompanied by their armies, advanced against the son of Pāṇḍu whose mounts were exhausted. They struck Arjuna with sixty-four [arrows] and Janārdana with seventy.
Filled with joy, those two pierced the horses with a hundred arrows.
O great king, Arjuna, enraged in battle and knowing the vital spots, struck them with nine straight-knotted shafts capable of piercing the vitals.
Then those two, enraged, covered Bībhatsu along with Keśava with a shower of arrows and let out lion-like roars.
Śvetavāhana, however, [cut] their two variegated bows with two broad-headed arrows.
In that battle, he swiftly cut down their two banners, which were blazing with gold.
Then, O King, taking up other bows in that encounter,
those two, highly enraged, began to afflict the son of Pāṇḍu with arrows.
But the son of Pāṇḍu, becoming violently incensed at those two,
O Bhārata— that best of weapon-bearers, Dhanañjaya— having gratified them with his arrows,
swiftly severed their bows once again.
Likewise, with other swift arrows, gold-feathered and whetted on stone, he quickly struck the horses along with the foot-soldiers, as well as both rear-guard charioteers;
and with a razor-sharp arrow, he severed the head of the eldest brother from his body.
Slain, he fell upon the earth like a tree uprooted by the wind;
his limbs smeared with blood, he lay as if making the very ground tremble.
Seeing Vinda thus slain, the powerful Anuvinda—
Abandoning his chariot whose horses had been slain, the mighty one seized a mace and rushed forward in battle, remembering the slaughter of his brother;
that great car-warrior, the best among mace-wielders, moved as if dancing with his mace.
But Anuvinda, enraged, struck Madhusūdana on the forehead with a mace; yet, having merely touched him, he could not make him tremble, just as one cannot shake Mount Maināka.
Then Arjuna, with six arrows, [struck] his neck, feet, arms, and head.
He cut him down, and being severed, he fell like a mass of mountains.
Then, O King, seeing those two slain, their followers,
filled with rage, rushed forward scattering arrows by the hundreds.
Having swiftly struck them down with his arrows, O bull of the Bharatas, Arjuna shone like a fire that has consumed a forest at the end of winter.
Having passed through their two armies, Dhananjaya emerged from the difficulty.
He shone like the sun risen after piercing through the clouds.
Seeing him, the Kurus were both terrified and filled with joy once more;
then, O bull of the Bharatas, they showered Pārtha from all sides.
Observing that he was exhausted and knowing the ruler of the Sindhus was still far off,
they surrounded him on all sides with a great lion-roar.
Seeing them highly agitated, that bull among men smiled.
As if hesitating, Arjuna spoke these words slowly to the descendant of Daśārha:
"The horses are afflicted by arrows and exhausted, and the ruler of the Sindhus is still far away. What do you consider to be the most excellent course of action to be done here next?"
"Speak, O Kṛṣṇa, according to the truth, for you are always the wisest of men. With you as their leader, the Pāṇḍavas will conquer their enemies in battle here.
Now, however, understand from me that which is my immediate duty."
"O Mādhava, unyoke the horses and make them comfortable, for they are pierced by arrows.
Thus addressed by Pārtha, Keśava replied to him:
"O Pārtha, that which you have spoken is my own opinion as well."
Arjuna said:
"O Keśava, I shall hold back all the armies;
you, for your part, should perform the next task here according to what is right."
Saṃjaya said:
Having descended from the seat of his chariot, Dhananjaya stood there undaunted,
grasping the Gāṇḍīva bow like an immovable mountain.
Crying out and desiring victory, the Kṣatriyas rushed toward him,
perceiving that Dhanañjaya was on the ground at this vulnerable point;
they surrounded that lone warrior with a vast multitude of chariots.
Drawing their bows and discharging arrows,
they displayed various celestial weapons there in their fury,
covering Pārtha with shafts like clouds shrouding the sun.
The noble car-warriors, O bull among Kṣatriyas, rushed with speed toward that lion among car-warriors, like intoxicated elephants charging at a lion. There,
the great strength of Pārtha’s two arms was beheld.
Then Pārtha, relying on the strength of his mighty arms, was invincible;
for when enraged, he held back vast armies from all sides.
The lordly one, having warded off the weapons of his enemies with his own weapons from every direction, [remained unshaken].
With many arrows, he swiftly covered them all. There in the sky, O lord of the people, a fire with great flames was produced by the friction of those deeply embedded shafts.
In every place, there were great archers sighing and drenched in blood;
horses and elephants were mangled and trumpeting, while the enemies—
those harassers of foes— were enraged heroes seeking victory in the fray.
Amidst those many enraged warriors standing together, a heat as if of a fire was generated.

That ocean of battle, difficult to cross, had arrows for its waves, banners for its whirlpools, and elephants for its crocodiles; it was teeming with foot-soldiers for its fish and resounded with the noise of conchs and drums.

Innumerable and boundless, it was exceedingly turbulent with dust, covered by the tortoise-shells of turbans, garlanded with the foam of banners, an unshakeable ocean of chariots strewn with the rock-like bodies of elephants.
Then Pārtha, having become like a shore, warded off [the arrows] with his feathered shafts.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When Arjuna had reached the earth and Keśava was at the head of the horses..."
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, having encountered this opportunity, why was Pārtha not defeated?
For all the kings were immediately held in check by Pārtha."
As one standing on a chariot [spoke] words unmetrical to one standing on the ground, so did Pārtha, though standing on the earth, alone hold back all those archers standing on their chariots,
just as greed holds back all virtues.
Then, in that battle, the mighty-armed Janārdana, remaining unperturbed, spoke these words to his dear friend Arjuna, the best of men: "O Arjuna,
there is no well here sufficient for the horses in this battle."
Desiring water to drink rather than for bathing,
Arjuna, remaining unperturbed, struck the earth with a weapon while saying, "This is here," and thus created a beautiful lake for the horses to drink from.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned with ruddy geese,
vast in extent, with clear waters and blooming, excellent lotuses; it teemed with shoals of tortoises and fish, was unfathomable, and frequented by sages.
"O Blessed One, in an instant, Pārtha prepared this for the sake of seeing the sage Nārada; thus he then created a beautiful lake of horses,
with arrows for its beams, arrows for its pillars, and an extraordinary canopy of arrows."
Like Tvaṣṭṛ performing a wondrous deed, Pārtha constructed an abode of arrows;
then Govinda, laughing, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
when that house of arrows had been fashioned by Pārtha in that great battle.
Saṃjaya said:
When that water had been produced by the high-souled son of Kuntī,
when the enemy army had been checked, and when the abode of arrows had been created;
The immensely radiant Vāsudeva, quickly descending from his chariot,
released the horses that had been pierced by heron-feathered arrows;
seeing that which had never been seen before, a great lion-roar arose.
The hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, as well as all the soldiers,
were unable to restrain the son of Kuntī as he fought on foot; that bull among men was like a marvel.

As the throngs of chariots with their many elephants and horses rushed forward, Pārtha did not then falter; indeed, his prowess surpassed that of men. Those kings discharged showers of arrows toward the son of Pāṇḍu.
The righteous son of Vāsava, the slayer of enemy heroes, did not waver;
that valiant Pārtha swallowed those incoming nets of arrows, maces, and spears, just as the ocean swallows rivers.
By the great force of his weapons and by the strength of his arms, Pārtha swallowed up those excellent arrows of all the lords of kings. That prowess of both Pārtha and Vāsudeva—
The Kauravas, O great king, honored that most wonderful sight. What more wonderful thing has ever occurred or will ever occur in this world,
than that Pārtha and Govinda liberated the horses in battle?
Those two best of men have instilled great fear in us,
yet they display fierce energy while remaining confident at the head of the battle—
so says Sañjaya.

O Lord, I consider that most wonderful of all: how your army was held back by Pārtha alone in battle, like the ocean surging against its shore. O Bhārata, while the great host was covered by the arrows of Pārtha...
Having reached him as if reaching open space, birds flew about there; yet,
O noble one, not a single man among your troops, though enraged, could advance against him as he stood in battle.
O lord of the people, all your warriors became despondent upon seeing Govinda and Dhananjaya the Pandava there; then,
O Bharata, Hrishikesha smiled as if he were in the midst of women.
Then, O lord of the people, while all your troops looked on, the lotus-eyed one, remaining unperturbed, brought back those horses from within that chamber of arrows created by Arjuna in the battle.
O King, while all the warriors looked on, the lotus-eyed one turned back his horses that had risen from the fray and groomed them with his hands;
he removed their fatigue, exhaustion, trembling, froth, and wounds.
Kṛṣṇa, being skilled in the art of handling horses, removed all [the arrows] from him;
having extracted the shafts with his hands and rubbed those steeds,
he turned them according to rule and gave them water to drink.
When they had obtained water, bathed, eaten their food, and were free from fatigue, he,
being greatly delighted, yoked them once again to that most excellent chariot.
Śauri, the best among all wielders of weapons, [prepared] that preeminent chariot.
Having mounted [the chariot], the one of great splendor, together with Arjuna, departed swiftly;
having harnessed the horses there according to the prescribed ritual,
Govinda moved through the battle, treating the great car-warriors as mere blades of grass.
Seeing the chariot of that foremost of car-warriors yoked with horses that had been watered in battle,
the best of the Kuru forces became despondent once more;
sighing heavily, O King, they were like serpents whose fangs had been broken.
"Fie! Alas, fie! Pārtha and Kṛṣṇa have perished! they cried out individually.
All the troops, thrilled on every side, uttered that hair-raising and wonderful exclamation;
they shouted, "Hurry up! and cried, "This [world] no longer exists!"

While all the kṣatriyas looked on, those two subduers of enemies, clad in armor, disregarded our army as if it were a mere child’s toy, and with a single chariot they moved unimpeded through the midst of us who were crying out and striving.
Having displayed their own prowess before all the kings,

they departed, O King, just as in ancient times Indra and Viṣṇu, desiring the slaughter of Jambha, went forth during the war between the gods and the Asuras, treating the Dānavas as mere blades of grass.
Seeing them both advancing once more, other soldiers then said:
"Hasten, all you Kurus, for the slaughter of Kṛṣṇa and Kirīṭin!
For the descendant of Daśārha has yoked his chariot while all the archers look on."
"He is going toward Jayadratha, having rendered us useless in battle!"—
seeing that great wonder never before seen in combat, O King, some of the rulers of the earth there conversed among themselves.
All the armies and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra have met their end; through the transgression of Duryodhana, the entire warrior class and the whole earth have reached destruction,
yet the king does not perceive this.
"O Bhārata, thus did the Kṣatriyas and others there speak regarding what ought to be done for the King of Sindhu, who has gone to the abode of Yama:
'Let the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose vision is futile and who knows no means, perform that task.'"
Then the Pāṇḍava proceeded even more swiftly toward the ruler of the Sindhus,
while the sun was setting; he went with joyful horses that had drunk their fill of water—
him, the mighty-armed one, the foremost among all wielders of weapons.
The warriors were unable to restrain him, who was like the enraged God of Death.
Then, having put that army to flight, the Pāṇḍava, the scorcher of his enemies,
agitated it for the sake of the ruler of the Sindhus, just as a lion agitates herds of deer.
Penetrating the ranks, the descendant of Daśārha quickly urged on his cranes-colored horses and blew the Pāñcajanya conch;
for he was skilled in the knowledge of bows, elephants, and horses, and possessed great lightness of hand.
May those horses indeed,

swift as thought, victorious, and capable of slaying enemies, conquer even those seeking to flee by their speed— horses that are unfailing, stainless, capable of traveling a *krośa*, and endowed with such excellence of swiftness in battle.
Of those who struck with black whetted darts and were skilled in managing multitudes of chariots— being distinguished by their application and capable of destroying all enemies—
the arrows released by the son of Kuntī from the front fell behind them.
Indeed, those horses, possessing the speed of the wind, carried him even more swiftly than swift;
seeing that terrible chariot with its monkey-banner, which roared like a rain-cloud and had its flag-ends fluttering in the wind, the warriors became despondent.
Then, when the sun was completely shrouded by dust on all sides,
the warriors in battle, afflicted by arrows, were unable to see the two Kṛṣṇas.
Thereupon, the enraged kings surrounded Dhanañjaya.
While many other Kṣatriyas were leading away that bull among men who stood firm, desiring the slaughter of Jayadratha,
Duryodhana rushed toward Pārtha in that great battle as the arrows were being withdrawn.
Saṃjaya said:
O King, seeing Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya having passed through, the very marrow of your men seemed to dissolve out of fear.

But all those high-souled ones, filled with indignation and urged by their inner strength, became steadfast and, possessing a sense of shame, advanced against Dhanañjaya. Those who had gone to the side of the Pāṇḍava in battle were now endowed with wrath and impatience.
Even today they do not turn back, like rivers from the ocean;
but the wicked turned back, like atheists from the Vedas,
and falling into hell, they incurred sin.
Having passed through that array of chariots, those two bulls among men emerged and appeared like the two luminaries released from the mouth of Rāhu;
they were like two fish that had burst through a great net, freed from all distress.
Thus, having torn through that mass of troops, the two dark ones were seen; liberated from the press of weapons within Droṇa’s impenetrable army,
those two high-souled ones appeared like two suns risen at the end of time.
Released from the pressure of missiles and freed from the peril of weapons,
those two great-souled ones appeared as the harassers of their enemies,
like two fish escaped from the touch of fire and from the mouth of a sea-monster.
Like two sea-monsters agitating the ocean, those two agitated the army;
while they were stationed within Droṇa’s division, your men and your sons then formed the conviction that "these two shall not overcome Droṇa."
But seeing those two of great splendor having passed through Droṇa’s army,
O great king, they no longer hoped for the life of the King of Sindhu.
O King, your sons possessed a powerful hope.

"O Lord, those two scorchers of foes have crossed over Drona’s army and the difficult-to-vanquish army of the Bhojas, having rendered fruitless that hope of yours that the two Krishnas would not escape from Drona and the son of Hridika."
Then, seeing that they had passed beyond [the range of the weapons] like two blazing fires,
they lost all hope for the life of the King of Sindhu and predicted his destruction. And those two, who increased the fear of their enemies, spoke to one another without fear.
Regarding the slaying of Jayadratha, Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya spoke these various words:
"That Saindhava has been placed in the midst of six great car-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s side; once he comes within the range of our vision, he shall not escape us."
"Even if Śakra, together with the hosts of gods, were his protector in battle,
we two shall still slay him"—
thus the two Kṛṣṇas spoke to one another at that time, those mighty-armed ones.
Your sons heard that those two tamers of foes were looking toward the king of the Sindhus;
like two thirsty elephants crossing the desert of Marudhanva and proceeding on their way,
they remained just so after drinking water and becoming refreshed.
Having traversed mountains teeming with tigers, lions, and elephants,
those two mighty-armed ones appeared as if they had transcended both death and old age;
for such was the complexion of their faces that people thought so.
Seeing those two liberated from Droṇa—
who was like a venomous serpent or a blazing fire— and from the other kings, who were like radiant suns, your men cried out on all sides.
Those two subduers of enemies, having escaped from Drona’s army which resembled the ocean,
appeared filled with joy, like those who have crossed over the sea. They had emerged from the great flood of weapons protected by Drona and the son of Hridika.
Shining and resembling Indra and Agni in battle,
the two dark warriors, pierced by the arrows of Bhāradvāja’s son and drenched in blood,
gleamed like two mountains covered with blossoming *karṇikāra* flowers.
They have emerged from the lake of Droṇa, which was filled with crocodiles that were javelins and venomous serpents;
they have crossed the waters of the foremost Kṣatriyas,
where iron arrows were the fierce makaras, the twang of bowstrings and the slapping of palms were the thunder, and maces and swords were the lightning.
They were like the sun and the moon released from the clouds of Droṇa’s weapons, as if they had crossed with their own arms the six rivers flowing to the ocean— the Indus being the sixth—
full at the end of the hot season and teeming with great crocodiles.
Having crossed that formidable great river, which was like a towering mass of massive mountains,
those two were carried across in battle just as two travelers safely cross a ford;
thus were the two Kṛṣṇas, the great archers, world-renowned for their glory.
All living beings were struck with wonder at the power of Droṇa’s weapons;
looking toward Jayadratha who stood nearby, desiring to slay him, those two remained like two tigers seeking to seize a ruru deer at a watering hole.
"O Great King, your warriors concluded that Jayadratha was indeed slain, judging by the complexion of their faces;
for the red-eyed, mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava were both prepared for battle."
Beholding the king of the Sindhus, the two of them roared repeatedly with joy—
the descendant of Śūra, with reins in hand, and Pārtha, armed with his bow. The radiance of those two was like that of the sun and the fire.
Joy alone arose in those two as they were released from Droṇa's division,
upon seeing the ruler of the Sindhus nearby like a piece of meat before two hawks;
for they beheld the ruler of the Sindhus as if he were standing right in their presence.
Enraged, they suddenly swooped down swiftly like two hawks upon prey. Seeing that Hṛṣīkeśa and Dhanañjaya had bypassed him,
your son exerted his prowess for the sake of protecting the King of Sindhu.
O Lord, King Duryodhana, having had his armor fastened by Droṇa and being skilled in the training of horses, then advanced into the battle on a single chariot;
having bypassed the two great archers, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha, your son proceeded.
The lord of men advanced ahead toward the lotus-eyed one;
then, as your son passed by Dhananjaya, musical instruments were sounded with great joy throughout all the armies.
There were sounds of lion-roars mingled with the blasts of conchs and drums,
as they beheld Duryodhana standing there in the presence of the two Kṛṣṇas,
and those protectors of the King of Sindhu who resembled blazing fires.
O Lord, seeing your son in that battle, they were filled with joy;
but seeing Duryodhana having passed them by along with his followers, O King, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to Arjuna, appropriate for the occasion.
Vāsudeva said:
"Behold this Suyodhana, O Dhanañjaya, who has overstepped his bounds;
I consider him to have fallen into calamity, for there is no warrior equal to him."
A long-distance shooter, a great archer, skilled in weapons, and fierce in battle;
firm in his mastery of arms and a versatile warrior, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is possessed of great strength.
Brought up in extreme luxury, he is honored by the great chariot-warriors.
O Pārtha, he is always skillful and constantly hates the Pāṇḍavas;
therefore, O sinless one, I consider the time for battle with him to have arrived. Herein lies the gamble for you all, leading either to victory or its opposite.
"O Pārtha, release here the poison of your wrath that has been long accumulated.
This great chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas is the very root of their misfortunes;
he has now come within your reach—behold the fulfillment of your purpose!"
"How indeed could a king seeking his kingdom enter into battle with you?
By good fortune, he has now come within the range of your arrows;
act, O Dhanañjaya, so that he may lose his life."

"Deluded by the intoxication of power, he has not experienced suffering; nor does he know your prowess in battle, O bull among men. For the three worlds, O Pārtha—including gods, asuras, and humans—[depend upon you]."
They are not able to conquer him in battle, much less Suyodhana alone. By good fortune, O Pārtha, he has come near your chariot;
slay him indeed, O mighty-armed one, just as Purandara slew Vṛtra.
O sinless one, for he has constantly exerted himself against your interests;
by deceit, he cheated Dharmarāja at dice.
O giver of honor, many cruel deeds have been committed by him.

"O Pārtha, toward you who are ever sinless, that man of evil mind has always acted wickedly. Having resolved upon a noble course in battle, slay that ignoble, base man who acts according to his own whims, without hesitation."
O Pāṇḍava, keeping in your heart the seizure of the kingdom through deceit, the exile in the forest, and the suffering of Kṛṣṇā, exert your prowess;
by good fortune, he now moves within the range of your arrows.
By good fortune, he strives to thwart your purpose;
by good fortune, he recognizes that you must indeed fight him in battle. And by good fortune, O Pārtha, all the desires you have cherished have become fruitful.
Therefore, O Pārtha, slay in battle Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, the lowest of his lineage,
just as Jambha was slain by Indra of old in the conflict between the gods and the asuras.
Once he is killed by you, let this leaderless army be broken apart.
"Let its final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) be this enmity; cut the root of these evil-minded ones.
Sañjaya said:
"Pārtha replied to him, 'So be it'; this is my duty."
Disregarding everything else, go where Suyodhana is—
he by whom this kingdom has been enjoyed by us for so long a time without a thorn in his side; even now,
displaying my prowess in battle, I shall sever his head in combat.
O Mādhava, would I be able to reach the end of that suffering of the unworthy Kṛṣṇā caused by the violation of her hair?
O Mādhava, would I even [endure] those former sorrows?
"Having slain Duryodhana in battle, I shall somehow be liberated [from my vow]. Speaking thus, the two joyful Kṛṣṇas urged on their excellent white horses in the fray, seeking that lord of men.
O bull of the Bharatas, having approached those two, your son felt no fear even when great danger had arrived, O honorable one;
all the kṣatriyas there praised that of his.
When Arjuna and Hṛṣīkeśa advanced against him without hesitation,
O lord of the people, a great roar then arose from all your troops upon seeing the king in the battle.
While that terrifying clamor of the people was underway,
your son, disregarding [the danger], held back his adversary. But the son of Kuntī was thus checked by your son, the archer.
That scorcher of foes again became filled with fury toward him.
Seeing Duryodhana and Dhanañjaya both thus enraged,
the kings of terrible appearance looked on from all sides.
O noble one, seeing Pārtha and Vāsudeva so enraged,
your son, as if laughing and desiring to fight, challenged them.
Thereupon, both the descendant of Daśārha and Dhanañjaya the Pāṇḍava were filled with joy.
They uttered loud cries of reproach and blew their excellent conchs;
seeing them in such a state of joy, all the Kauravas became hopeless regarding the life of your son.
All those Kurus fell into the deepest grief,
and they considered their son as already offered into the mouth of the fire-god Vaiśvānara.
But seeing Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava thus triumphant, those warriors were filled with joy.
"Killed! The king is killed!"—thus did those afflicted by fear cry out.
Hearing that clamor of the people, Duryodhana said:
"Let your fear depart; I shall send the two Kṛṣṇas to their death."
Having spoken thus to all his soldiers, the lord of men, desiring victory,
addressed Pārtha with impetuosity and spoke these words:
"O Pārtha, whatever weapons you have been trained in— whether divine or human— "
If you were truly begotten by Pāṇḍu, show that quickly to me! Whatever strength and heroism you possess, as well as that of Keśava, exert it quickly upon me; let us behold your manliness.
"They speak of the deeds you have performed behind our backs;
show us here those acts which were endowed with honor toward your master.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, the king pierced him with three arrows that struck his vital organs;
with four high-velocity shafts, he struck the four horses,
and he pierced Vāsudeva in the center of the chest with ten arrows.

Having severed his whip with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he felled it to the ground. Then Pārtha, remaining unperturbed, swiftly pierced him with fourteen stone-sharpened arrows furnished with variegated feathers; they struck his armor and fell away from it.

Seeing that those [previous] arrows had been rendered fruitless, he again dispatched nine and five sharp shafts; yet they too fell away from his armor. Observing those twenty-eight discharged arrows to be ineffective, [he reflected].
Seeing that the arrows he had discharged were rendered fruitless and cut down,
Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes and conqueror of hostile cities, spoke these words to Arjuna:
"I see something never seen before, like the gliding of rocks."
"O Pārtha, do the arrows dispatched by you still accomplish their purpose? O bull among the Bharatas, are the life-force of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
as well as your grip and the strength of your arms, just as they were before?"
"If this final hour of destiny has not yet arrived today for both you and this enemy, then tell it to me as I ask,
O Pārtha; for great is my wonder at seeing these arrows of yours."

O Pārtha, why this mockery today? These arrows of yours—terrible, like thunderbolts and lightning, capable of piercing the bodies of enemies—are falling in vain upon Duryodhana’s chariot in battle; they achieve no purpose.
Arjuna said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, this resolve was instilled in the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra by Droṇa;
this wearing of the armor is the final application of his weapons."
"O Kṛṣṇa, even the three worlds are contained within this armor;
indeed, Droṇa alone knows this, and I have learned it from that most excellent of men.
This armor cannot be pierced by arrows in any way whatsoever."
O Govinda, even by the thunderbolt itself wielded by Maghavan in battle;
O Kṛṣṇa, though you know this, why do you indeed delude me?
Whatever has occurred in the three worlds, and whatever is currently taking place, O Keśava—[tell me that].
Whatever is yet to be, all that is known to you;
indeed, no one knows it as you do, O Madhusūdana.
This Duryodhana, O Kṛṣṇa, has been brought here by Droṇa.
He stands fearlessly in battle, wearing his armor;
yet, O Mādhava, he does not understand what must be done here.
Like a woman, he merely wears this fitted armor.
"Behold, O Janārdana, the strength of my arms and of this bow!
I shall defeat the Kaurava, even though he is protected by his armor. The Lord of the Gods gave this radiant armor to Aṅgiras."
From him Bṛhaspati obtained it, and from him Purandara obtained it;
the Lord of the Gods gave this armor back to me along with its secret manual. Even if this armor of his were divine, or even if it were created by Brahmā himself—
"Today this evil-minded one shall not escape, struck by my arrow.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus, Arjuna consecrated his arrows with mantras and drew them back.
With the Mānava weapon, which is worthy of respect and capable of piercing subtle coverings,
the son of Droṇa likewise cut down those arrows drawn to the middle of the bow with that very weapon, using his own weapon that destroys all other weapons.
Seeing those arrows cut down from afar by the speaker of Brahman,
Śvetavāhana, filled with wonder, informed Keśava:
"O Janārdana, it is not possible for me to employ this weapon twice."
"Indeed, this weapon would surely slay me; behold today my strength!
Then, O King, Duryodhana pierced both Kṛṣṇas in battle with nine straight-knotted arrows resembling venomous serpents.
He rained down even more upon Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava in battle with a great shower of arrows; thereupon, your men rejoiced,
making the sounds of musical instruments and lion-like roars.
Then Pārtha, enraged in battle and licking the corners of his mouth,
could not find any part of his [the opponent's] body that was not protected by armor.
Thereupon, with well-aimed, sharp arrows resembling the God of Death, he struck him.
The valiant Savyasācin rendered the horses lifeless and struck down both the flank-guards and the charioteer;
he severed his variegated bow and his hand-guard,
and proceeded to shatter his chariot into pieces.
And having deprived Duryodhana of his chariot with two sharp arrows,
the son of Kuntī, acting with great effort, pierced him with shafts between the nails and the flesh; agitated by that pain, Duryodhana became intent on flight.
Then Arjuna pierced both of his palms;
seeing that supreme archer fallen into such dire distress and afflicted by Dhananjaya’s arrows, [the other warriors] rushed forward, desiring to rescue him.
With many thousands of prepared chariots, elephants, horses,
and throngs of furious foot soldiers, they surrounded Dhanañjaya.
Then neither Arjuna nor Govinda, nor even their chariot, could be seen.
Enveloped by a great rain of weapons and by throngs of men,
Arjuna then struck down that army with the power of his missiles;
there, hundreds of chariots and elephants fell, their limbs mangled.
Those who were slain and those being slain held back that supreme chariot;
that chariot stood immobilized for the distance of a *krośa* on all sides.
Then the Vṛṣṇi hero quickly spoke these words to Arjuna.
"Stretch your bow excessively, and I shall blow my conch.
Then Arjuna, having powerfully stretched the Gāṇḍīva, struck down his enemies with a great shower of arrows and the sound of his palms.
And Keśava, his eyelashes covered with dust and his face profusely perspiring, blew powerfully and loudly upon the Pāñcajanya conch;
by that wind filled between the lips of Acyuta, [the earth shook].
By the sound issuing forth, amplified within the interior of his conch shell, the entire world— including the asuras in the sky, the guardians of the celestial realms,
and the lords of the universe— becomes agitated, as if everything were bursting apart.
By the sound of that conch and the twang of the bow,
people— both the lifeless and those still possessing life— then fell to the earth. Released by them, the chariot shone like a cloud driven by the wind.
Then the protectors of Jayadratha, along with their followers, became agitated.
Seeing Pārtha suddenly before them, those guards of the ruler of the Sindhus raised various kinds of shouts, making the earth tremble.

The high-souled warriors produced fierce sounds from the whizzing of arrows mingled with the blasts of conchs, as well as the sounds of lion-like roars. Hearing that terrible clamor raised by your men, [the enemy]...
Then Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya blew their conchs;
by that great sound,
O lord of the people, this earth— with its mountains, oceans, islands, and the netherworld— was filled.

O best of the Bharatas, that sound, having pervaded all ten directions, echoed right there within the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas; for your car-warriors there, having seen Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya—
Then those great car-warriors, reaching a state of supreme fury and acting with haste,
beheld the two highly fortunate Kṛṣṇas clad in armor;
they rushed forward in great anger, and it was like a marvel.
Saṃjaya said:
But your men, upon seeing those two best of the Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, and Kurus, hastened forward first with the intent to kill them; likewise, Vijaya [Arjuna] rushed toward his enemies.
With great chariots adorned with gold, covered in tiger skins, and resounding,
they illuminated all directions like blazing fires; and with their bows, O lord of the earth, which were backed with gold and difficult to behold, they shone forth.
Uttering incomparable cries like enraged serpents,
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Karṇa, Vṛṣasena, Jayadratha,
Kṛpa, the King of Madra, and the son of Droṇa— the best among chariot-warriors— [advanced].
Those eight great car-warriors, as if drinking up the sky with their horses,
illuminated the ten directions with their tiger-skin-covered chariots adorned with golden moons.
Clad in armor and highly enraged, they advanced in chariots that resounded like masses of clouds.

They shrouded all the directions with sharp arrows and covered Pārtha as well. Then those swift and variegated Kaulūtaka horses, carrying those great car-warriors, shone brilliantly, illuminating the ten directions.

O King, the foremost warriors of the Kurus, desiring to protect your son, [advanced] with noble, high-sped horses of various breeds— those from the mountains, those from the river regions, and the finest steeds from Sindh.
They quickly rushed from all sides toward Dhanañjaya’s chariot;
those best of men, O King, seizing their great conchs, blew them,
filling the heavens and the earth with its oceans.
In that very manner, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya blew their conchs—
the two most excellent among all beings and the finest of all conchs on earth;
the son of Kuntī blew the Devadatta, and Keśava blew the Pāñcajanya.
The sound of Devadatta, impelled by Dhanañjaya,
pervaded the earth, the atmosphere, and all the directions;
likewise did the Pāñcajanya, impelled by Vāsudeva.
Transcending all sounds, it filled both heaven and earth. While that terrible tumult of noise was thus occurring—
inspiring terror in the timid and increasing the joy of the brave—
O king of kings, while the kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and mṛdaṅgas were being sounded in great variety,
those renowned as great chariot-warriors, who desired the welfare of Duryodhana, [advanced].
Unable to endure that sound, those enraged and supreme archers—
kings from various lands who protected their own armies—
those intolerant heroes and great car-warriors blew their massive conch shells.
O Lord, wishing to repay the deeds of Keśava and Arjuna,
your army was stirred by the sound of conchs;
with its chariots, elephants, and horses agitated, it became as if ill at ease.
Like space itself set in motion, that place, resounding with the blasts of conchs from the heroes,
became intensely agitated as if filled with the roar of thunderclaps.
O King, that immense sound made all the directions reverberate.
He terrified that army like the gathered forces at the end of a Yuga.
Then Duryodhana and those eight kings, all great car-warriors,
surrounded the son of Pāṇḍu for the sake of protecting Jayadratha.
Then the son of Droṇa struck Vāsudeva with seventy-three arrows,
Arjuna with three broad-headed shafts, and his standard and horses with five.
Arjuna, in turn, struck him with six hundred arrows.
When Janārdana was thus pierced, he became exceedingly enraged;
the valiant hero struck Karṇa with twelve arrows and Vṛṣasena with three, and then severed Śalya’s bow, along with the arrow fixed upon it, at the handle.
Taking up another bow, Śalya pierced the Pāṇḍava;
Bhūriśravas with three gold-feathered arrows sharpened on stone,
Karṇa with thirty-two, and Vṛṣasena with five.
Jayadratha pierced him with seventy-three arrows, Kṛpa with ten, and the King of Madra with ten; thus they struck Phalguna in battle. Then the son of Droṇa covered Pārtha with sixty arrows.

He struck Vāsudeva with seventy arrows and Pārtha again with five; then that tiger among men, whose horses were white and whose charioteer was Kṛṣṇa, laughing, pierced them all in return, displaying his lightness of hand.
Having pierced Karṇa with twelve arrows and Vṛṣasena with three shafts,
he cut off Śalya’s bow at the handle in that battle;
then, having pierced the son of Somadatta with three arrows and Śalya with ten shafts.
With eight sharp arrows shaped like flames of fire, he pierced the son of Droṇa;
with twenty-five he struck Gautama, and with a hundred, the ruler of the Sindhus;
then again, he struck the son of Droṇa with seventy shafts.

But Bhūriśravas, filled with rage, cut through the whip of Hari and struck Arjuna with seventy-three arrows. Then, with hundreds of sharp shafts, he who has white horses [Arjuna] assailed those enemies.
Enraged, he swiftly repelled them, just as a great wind disperses the clouds.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"The standards of various forms, blazing with exceeding splendor..."
"Tell me, Saṃjaya, of those belonging to the sons of Pṛthā and to my own people.
Saṃjaya said:
"Hear from me of the standards of various forms belonging to those great-souled ones."
Learn from me their forms, their colors, and their names. O Indra among kings, upon the chariots of those great car-warriors, various banners were seen, blazing like fires.
Golden, with golden crests and adorned with golden garlands,
they were like the golden peaks of the great golden mountain;
the various banners of many colors were exceedingly beautiful.
Those banners were surrounded on all sides by their pennants; covered everywhere by those pennants of various colors and hues, they shone brilliantly.
Then those pennants, stirred by the wind, [fluttered about].
O bull of the Bharatas, playful women appeared dancing in the midst of the arena; and banners with the hue of Indra’s bow,
being shaken by the chariot-warriors, graced those great car-fighters.
We beheld the terrifying banner of Dhanañjaya in battle, featuring a lion’s tail, a fierce face, and the emblem of a monkey;
that preeminent monkey, O King, was adorned with many flags.
The banner of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow terrified that army;
likewise, O Bhārata, we beheld the top of the banner of Droṇa’s son, bearing a lion’s tail and possessing a radiance like that of the rising sun.
The raised standard of the son of Droṇa was made of gold, shaken by the wind, possessing a luster equal to the banner of Śakra, and served as the emblem of the lords of the Kauravas. Furthermore,
the banner of the son of Adhiratha bore a golden elephant-girth.
O great king,
in that battle, Karna’s banner— adorned with flags and golden garlands—
was seen filling the sky as if it were dancing upon the seat of the chariot, stirred by the wind.
The preceptor of the Pāṇḍus and the illustrious Brāhmaṇa Kṛpa Gautama possessed a well-adorned bull;
O King, that great car-warrior shone with that bull.
Just as the chariot of the destroyer of Tripura shines with a bull, so too did Vṛṣasena’s golden peacock, adorned with jewels and gems,
stand at the head of the army as if about to cry out, beautifying it.
By that peacock, the chariot of that high-souled one shone,
O king of kings, just as Skanda’s chariot shines with his resplendent peacock;
and on the tip of the banner of Śalya, the king of Madra, there was what appeared like a flame of fire.
We beheld Sītā, peerless and auspicious, made of gold. O noble one,
seated upon his chariot, that Sītā shone like the furrow (sītā) when it has sprouted with every kind of seed, endowed with splendor.
On the tip of his standard was a silver boar belonging to the King of Sindhu, shining brilliantly like a pale-red sun and adorned with a network of gold;
with that silver banner, Jayadratha shone resplendent.
Just as Pūṣan shone of old in the war between the gods and the asuras, so too does the sacrificial post of the wise Saumadatti, who is devoted to sacrifice,
shine like the sun; and here the moon is also visible.
O King, that golden sacrificial post of Saumadatti shines resplendently,
like the lofty post erected at the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices.
But the great silver elephant of Śala, O Great King, [shines likewise].
The banner was adorned with peacocks having limbs variegated with gold;
that banner, O bull of the Bharatas, graced your army just as the great white elephant graces the army of the king of the gods.

O King, lord of the people, your son shone most brilliantly upon that excellent, variegated chariot, which bore a jeweled elephant-standard covered in gold and resounded with the tinkling of hundreds of small bells.

Then, with his great banner in the battle, that bull among the Kurus [stood out]. These nine supreme banners were raised high upon your army; resembling the suns at the end of a Yuga, they illuminated the host.
The tenth, however, was the great monkey belonging to Arjuna alone;
by him Arjuna blazed forth like the Himalayas with fire. Then the great car-warriors [discharged] variegated, bright, and very large [arrows].

Those scorchers of foes quickly took up their bows for the sake of Arjuna; likewise, O King, Pārtha, the destroyer of enemies and performer of divine deeds, took up the Gāṇḍīva bow because of your evil counsel.
Indeed, because of your transgression, many men have been slain in battle—
those summoned from various directions, accompanied by their troops, chariots, and elephants.
As they roared at one another, there occurred a violent clash among them.
There, the son of Kuntī, with Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer, performed a supreme wonder against Duryodhana and the others, as well as against the bull among the Pāṇḍavas, in that he,
being alone, fearlessly encountered many.
The mighty-armed one shone as he brandished the Gāṇḍīva bow,
desiring to conquer those tigers among men and wishing to slay Jayadratha.
There, O great king, Arjuna [shone] with thousands of released arrows.
The scorcher of enemies rendered your warriors invisible;
then all those great car-warriors, tigers among men, likewise made Pārtha invisible in that battle from every side with floods of arrows.
When Arjuna, that bull among the Kurus, was thus hemmed in by those lions among men,
a great and tumultuous roar arose from his army.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When Arjuna had reached the ruler of the Sindhus, and the Pāñcālas were hemmed in by the son of Bharadvāja, what did they do together with the Kurus, O Saṃjaya? Saṃjaya said:
In the afternoon, O Great King, during that hair-raising battle,
a game of dice took place between the Pāñcālas and the Kurus with Droṇa as the stake.
For the Pāñcālas, their hearts filled with joy, were eager to slay Droṇa.
O noble one, they roared and rained down showers of arrows;
then a most tumultuous and wonderful battle unfolded between the Pāñcālas and the Kurus— a terrible conflict resembling that between the gods and the asuras.
Having reached Droṇa’s chariot, all the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas,
desiring to break through that army, displayed their great weapons;
the car-warriors stood upon their chariots right up to the perimeter of Droṇa’s chariot.
Causing the earth to tremble, they advanced with moderate speed.
Bṛhatkṣatra, the great chariot-warrior of the Kekayas, rushed toward him,
scattering sharpened arrows that resembled the thunderbolt of the great Indra.
But the highly illustrious Kṣemadhūrti quickly rose up against him,
discharging sharp arrows by the hundreds and thousands;
and Dhṛṣṭaketu, the bull among the Cedis, was also impelled by great strength.
He rushed swiftly toward Droṇa, like Mahendra against Śambara.
As he was suddenly attacking like Death with his mouth wide open,
Vīradhanvan, that great archer, advanced against him in haste.
Then the valiant Droṇa checked the heroic Yudhiṣṭhira, O great king, as he stood ready with his army, desiring victory; likewise,
the powerful one opposed Nakula, who was skilled in battle and full of prowess.
O Lord, your son Vikarṇa encountered Sahadeva as he was approaching; likewise, Durmukha, the crusher of enemies,
covered him with many thousands of swift-flying arrows as he advanced.
Vyāghradatta, however, checked Sātyaki, that tiger among men,
shaking him again and again with sharp, well-whetted arrows;
while the sons of Draupadī, those tigers among men, were discharging excellent shafts.
The son of Somadatta held back those enraged and preeminent chariot-warriors;
likewise, the great car-warrior, the son of Rishyashringa, who was of terrible form and fearsome appearance, checked the advancing Bhimasena as he came on in a rage.

Between those two, the man and the Rākṣasa, there occurred in battle a combat such as had formerly taken place between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, O King. Then Yudhiṣṭhira [struck] Droṇa with ninety straight-knotted arrows.

O best of the Bharatas, O descendant of Bharata, he struck him in all his vital parts. Enraged by the illustrious son of Kuntī, O best of the Bharatas, Droṇa struck him back with twenty-five arrows in the center of the chest.
Furthermore, with twenty more arrows,
Droṇa covered the king in battle with his finest shafts, making him invisible along with his horses, charioteer, and standard, even as all the archers looked on.
The righteous son of Pāṇḍu, displaying his lightness of hand, warded off those arrows released by Droṇa with a shower of his own shafts. Thereupon,
Droṇa became violently enraged at Dharmarāja in that battle.
The archer suddenly severed the bow of that high-souled one.
Then, as his bow was cut, the great car-warrior, acting with haste,
filled him from all sides with many thousands of arrows.
With his arrows, Bhāradvāja rendered King Yudhiṣṭhira invisible and visible by turns;
all living beings thought that Yudhiṣṭhira had already been slain in battle,
while some thought that he had indeed been turned away from the fight.
"O Indra among kings,

King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Dharmarāja, having been deprived of his kingdom by that illustrious Brāhmaṇa, fell into the utmost distress after casting aside that bow which had been shattered by the son of Bharadvāja in battle."
He took up another divine bow, capable of bearing great weight and even more powerful. Then, that hero cut down all those thousands of arrows released by Droṇa in the battle; it was like a marvel.
Having cut down those arrows, the king, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
seized in the battle a spear capable of splitting even mountains—
a golden-staffed, most terrible weapon, adorned with eight bells and inspiring fear.
Having hurled it, the powerful one, filled with joy, let out a mighty roar,
O Bhārata, as if terrifying all living beings with that sound,
upon seeing the spear raised by Dharmarāja in the encounter.
"May it be well with Droṇa!"— thus all beings suddenly cried out.
Released by the king's arm, resembling a snake that has cast its slough,
it set the sky ablaze, as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having reached the vicinity of Droṇa, she was like a serpent-maiden with a flaming mouth,
O Bhārata, resembling the Night of Doom,
or like the daughter of the king of serpents.
O lord of the people, seeing that spear suddenly descending, Droṇa,
the best among those skilled in weapons, then manifested the Brahma weapon.
Having reduced that spear of terrible appearance to ashes, that weapon—
He quickly went to the chariot of the illustrious Pāṇḍava. Then, O Bhārata, the highly wise King Yudhiṣṭhira neutralized that raised weapon of Droṇa by means of the Brahmā weapon itself.
And in that battle, he pierced Droṇa with five straight-knotted arrows;
then, with a sharp razor-headed shaft, he cut asunder his great bow.
Casting aside that broken bow, Droṇa, the crusher of kṣatriyas, [acted].
O noble one, he suddenly hurled a mace at the son of Dharma. Seeing that mace rushing toward him with great force, Yudhiṣṭhira,
the scorcher of foes, seized a mace in his turn and, filled with rage, hurled it.
Those two maces, suddenly released and having struck one another,
emitted fire from their friction and fell together upon the surface of the earth.
Then, O sire, Droṇa became violently incensed at Dharmarāja.
With four sharp, whetted, and excellent arrows, he struck the horses;
with one arrow, he severed the bow that resembled the banner of Indra;
with one he cut down the standard, and with three he afflicted the son of Pāṇḍu.

O bull of the Bharatas, having quickly leaped down from his chariot whose horses had been slain, King Yudhiṣṭhira stood with his arms raised and weaponless. Seeing him deprived of his chariot and especially disarmed, [the enemy attacked].
O Lord, Droṇa bewildered his enemies and all the troops,
discharging multitudes of sharp arrows with light hand and firm resolve;
he rushed toward the king like a fierce lion toward a deer.
Seeing him pursued by Droṇa, the slayer of enemies, a sudden cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the Pāṇḍavas:
"The king has been captured! The king has been captured by the son of Bharadvāja, O noble one!"
Thus arose a great clamor from all sides among the Pāṇḍava army.
Then, having quickly mounted the chariot of Sahadeva,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, departed with swift horses.
Saṃjaya said:
O great king, Kṣemadhūrti then pierced Bṛhatkṣatra, the Kekaya prince of firm prowess, in the chest with arrows as he advanced.

But King Bṛhatkṣatra, desiring to break through Droṇa’s army, quickly struck him in battle with ninety straight-knotted arrows. Kṣemadhūrti, however, being greatly enraged, [assailed] the high-souled Kekaya.
With a sharp, yellow-edged broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he severed the bow; then,
with a straight-knotted shaft, he swiftly pierced the heart of that foremost of all archers, whose bow had been cut.

Then, taking up another bow, Bṛhatkṣatra, as if laughing, deprived the great car-warrior Kṣemadhūrti of his horses, charioteer, and standard. Then, with another sharp, yellowed broad-headed arrow, he struck him.

He struck off from the king’s body the head adorned with flaming earrings. That severed head, with its curly hair and its diadem, suddenly falling to the earth, shone like a celestial light descending from the sky.
Having slain him in battle, the great car-warrior Bṛhatkṣatra, filled with joy,
suddenly rushed against your army for the sake of the son of Pṛthā.
Then the valiant [Duryodhana] encountered Dhṛṣṭaketu as he advanced for the sake of Droṇa.
O Bhārata, Vīradhanvan, the great archer, held them back;
having encountered one another, those two swift warriors, with arrows for teeth,
struck each other with many thousands of shafts.
Those two tigers among men fought with one another like two leaders of elephant herds in rut in a great forest,
or like two enraged tigers having entered a mountain cave.
Those two of great prowess fought with the desire to slay one another;
both those tigers among men tormented each other. That battle was tumultuous and a sight to behold, O lord of the people.
A sight of wonder and amazement for the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas; then, O Bhārata, Vīradhanvan, filled with rage, as if laughing, cut Dhṛṣṭaketu’s bow in two with a broad-headed arrow.
Casting aside that broken bow, the great car-warrior, the King of Cedi,
took up a massive iron spear with a golden shaft.
O Bhārata, having drawn back that spear of great power with both his arms, he—
Exerting himself, he suddenly hurled it toward the chariot of Vīradhanvan. Struck violently by that hero-slaying spear,
his heart pierced through, he quickly fell from his chariot to the earth.
When that hero, the great car-warrior of the Trigartas, had been slain, O Lord, your army was broken on all sides by the sons of Pāṇḍu. Then Sahadeva, filled with rage, encountered Durmukha.
Then Durmukha loosed sixty arrows at Sahadeva and let out a great roar, threatening the Pāṇḍava in battle. Thereupon, the son of Madri, filled with rage, struck Durmukha with ten shafts.
O Bhārata,
seeing the mighty Sahadeva impetuous in battle,
Durmukha, as if laughing, pierced his approaching brother with nine arrows.
The mighty warrior, having severed Durmukha’s standard with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla),
struck down his four horses with four sharpened shafts;
then, with another sharp, polished broad-headed arrow, he [struck him].
With a sharp razor-headed arrow, Sahadeva severed from the body of the charioteer the head adorned with blazing earrings, and he also cut down the great bow of the Kaurava in battle,
piercing him with five more shafts.
O King, descendant of Bharata, having abandoned his chariot whose horses had been slain, Durmukha then ascended the chariot of Niramitra with a dejected mind. Thereupon, O Bhārata,
Sahadeva, enraged in that great battle, [assailed] Niramitra.
In the midst of the army, that slayer of enemy heroes struck him with a broad-headed arrow;
Niramitra, the son of the king of Trigarta, fell from the seat of his chariot, O lord of men, causing distress to your host.

Having slain him, the mighty-armed Sahadeva shone resplendent, just as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, did after slaying the exceedingly powerful Khara. A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the Trigartas, O lord of men.
O King, seeing the mighty prince Niramitra slain,
Nakula conquered your large-eyed son Vikarṇa in battle within a moment; that was like a marvel.

Vyāghradatta, however, with straight-knotted arrows, made Sātyaki invisible within the midst of the army— along with his horses, charioteer, and standard. He rendered him, together with his horses, charioteer, and standard, invisible within the midst of the army.
Warding off those arrows with the skill of a practiced hand,
the heroic grandson of Śini struck down Vyāghradatta along with his horses, charioteer, and standard using his shafts.
O Lord, when that prince, the son of the Magadha king, had been slain, [the battle continued].
The Magadhas, exerting themselves from all sides, rushed toward Yuyudhāna,
discharging arrows and lances by the thousands,
as well as *bhiṇḍipālas*, spears, mallets, and clubs.
In battle, those heroes fought against the Sātvata warrior, who was intoxicated with the frenzy of combat;
but that powerful Satyaki,
himself difficult to vanquish in war, O bull among men, defeated them all with ease while even smiling.
Seeing the Magadhas who remained after the slaughter fleeing in every direction, O Lord, your army, afflicted by the arrows of Yuyudhāna, broke apart;
having destroyed your host in battle, that best of the Mādhavas departed.
Brandishing his excellent bow, the highly illustrious one shone resplendently,
O King, just as Śakra shines after slaying the army of the Daityas;
for the host was being broken by the high-souled Sātvata, O King.
Terrified by the long-armed hero, he did not turn back for battle;
then Drona, becoming violently enraged and suddenly rolling his eyes,
himself rushed toward Satyaki, whose deeds are true.
Saṃjaya said:
The highly illustrious son of Somadatta pierced each of the great bowmen, the sons of Draupadī,
with five arrows, and then pierced them again with seven.

O Lord, severely oppressed by that fierce one, they were suddenly bewildered and could not discern anything at all to do in the battle. But Śatānīka, the son of Nakula, [attacked] the bull among men, the son of Somadatta.
Having pierced him with two arrows, the bold scorcher of enemies let out a roar.
Likewise, the others in that battle, exerting themselves, quickly pierced the indignant son of Somadatta in the encounter with three straight-flying shafts each.
O great king, he discharged five arrows at them;
the highly illustrious one struck each of them in the heart with a single shaft.
Then those five brothers were pierced by the arrows of that high-souled one.
Surrounding the hero with their chariots, they pierced him violently with arrows.
But the son of Arjuna, filled with rage, dispatched his horses to the abode of Yama with four sharpened shafts.
The son of Bhīmasena, having severed the bow of the high-souled son of Somadatta,
uttered a powerful roar and pierced him with sharp arrows. The son of Yudhiṣṭhira, having cut down his standard, felled it to the ground.
Nakula’s son [Sahadeva] dragged the horse-driver down from the seat of the chariot;
and Sahadeva’s son, O King, perceiving that he had been turned away by his brothers,
the high-minded one cut off his head with a razor-sharp arrow.
That head, adorned with gold, fell to the earth,
illuminating the battlefield with a radiance like that of the rising sun.
Seeing the head of the high-souled son of Somadatta falling, [the warriors were struck with grief].
Terrified, O King, your men fled in many directions.
But Alambusa, enraged in battle, fought the mighty Bhimasena, just as Rāvaṇa’s son Lakṣmaṇa once did.
Seeing those two, the man and the Rākṣasa, engaged in combat in battle,
all living beings were then filled with wonder and great joy.
Then Bhīma struck the son of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga with nine sharpened arrows.

Laughing, O King, he pierced the intolerant lord of the Rākṣasas. Then that Rākṣasa, having been pierced in battle, let out a terrifying roar and rushed toward Bhīma as well as those who followed in his footsteps.
Having pierced Bhīma with five straight-knotted arrows,
that subduer of enemies swiftly slew thirty chariots following Bhīma;
then, having killed four hundred more, he struck Bhīma with a feathered shaft.
Then, deeply pierced by the rākṣasa, the mighty Bhīma sat down upon the floor of the chariot, overwhelmed by a swoon. Having regained consciousness, the son of the Wind-god was then consumed by rage.
Drawing his formidable bow, the supreme instrument for achieving great feats,
he afflicted Alambuṣa from all sides with sharp arrows.
Pierced by those many shafts, he resembled a mass of black collyrium.
O King, he shone on all sides like a blossoming *kiṃśuka* tree in full bloom.
Being struck in battle by arrows released from Bhīma’s bow,
he remembered the slaughter of his brother by the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
Then, assuming a terrible form, he addressed Bhīmasena:
"Stay now in battle, O Pārtha; behold my prowess today!
O evil-minded one, I am the powerful Baka, the foremost of Rākṣasas."
"That deed by which my brother was slain by you is unknown to me.
Having spoken thus to Bhīma,
he then vanished and overwhelmed him with a massive shower of arrows.
But when the Rākṣasa had become invisible in that battle, O King,
Bhīma filled the sky with straight-jointed arrows.
Being struck by Bhīma, he mounted his chariot in the blink of an eye.
The wretched one went to the earth and suddenly ascended into the sky;
he assumed many various forms, both high and low— now minute,
now vast, and again massive, like a cloud emitting thunderous sounds.
Various kinds of cries were uttered on all sides;
and from the sky, thousands of streams of arrows fell,
along with spears, *kaṇapas*, darts, spikes, *paṭṭiśas*, and *tomaras*.
Centuries, iron clubs, slings, battle-axes,
stones, swords, mallets, spears, and indeed thunderbolts—
this most terrible rain of weapons was discharged by the Rākṣasa.
He struck down the soldiers of Pāṇḍu’s son at the forefront of the battle.
By him, O King, the elephants of the Pāṇḍava forces were crushed in combat,
as were many horses and foot-soldiers once again.
Chased by his arrows, the chariot-warriors fell from their chariots;
having slain them, he then caused a river to flow, abounding in chariots, with blood for its water, whirlpools of chariots, and teeming with elephants as its crocodiles.
He set in motion a river filled with umbrella-swans and mud, crowded with the serpents that were his arms, and teeming with throngs of *rākṣasa* demons;
O King, it carried away the Chedis, Pañcālas, and Sṛñjayas in many directions.
Carrying away the Sṛñjayas, the Pāñcālas, and the Bāhlikas as well, O King,
the Pāṇḍavas beheld him moving thus fearlessly in battle and witnessed his prowess.
A great joy arose among your troops,
accompanied by a fierce and immense clamor of musical instruments that caused the hair to stand on end;
it gladdened the Rākṣasa in battle and bewildered the Pāṇḍavas.
Hearing that terrible roar of your army, the son of Pāṇḍu could not endure it,
just as an elephant cannot bear the sound of a hand-clap.
Then, his eyes copper-red with rage, he appeared like a consuming fire.
O noble one, he himself, like Tvaṣṭṛ, discharged the Tvaṣṭra weapon.
Thereupon, thousands of arrows appeared on all sides,
and by those arrows, a great rout of your army occurred.
That weapon, dispatched by Bhīmasena in the encounter,
destroyed the great illusion of the Rākṣasa and afflicted the Rākṣasa himself.
Being struck in many ways by Bhīmasena, that Rākṣasa—
Abandoning Bhīma in the battle, he rushed toward Droṇa’s army.
When that high-souled lord of the Rākṣasas had been defeated by him, O King,
the Pāṇḍavas made all directions resound with lion-like roars.
Overjoyed, they honored the mighty son of the Wind-god, just as the hosts of Maruts honored Śakra after he had defeated Prahrāda in battle. Saṃjaya said:
O lord of the earth, seeing Droṇa in that great battle raining down showers of arrows out of wrath,
terrifying that army of the sons of Kuntī,
and violently slaughtering the chariot-warriors, the great archer [Arjuna] then beheld him.
