The mighty-armed Ghaṭotkaca advanced for battle,
O great king, having mounted a chariot adorned with gold, equipped with various weapons, and yoked with creatures having the faces of Piśācas.
Clad in a highly effulgent armor of refined gold,
his limbs adorned with ornaments, and roaring like a rain-cloud,
the mighty son of Hiḍimba, filled with great rage, rushed against Droṇa.
Alambusa, clad in armor and mounted upon a chariot covered with a bear-skin, rushed toward him as he approached;
tall and red-lipped, holding his bow, he stood like a celestial wish-fulfilling tree.
He hurled the *śataghnī*, the massive *musala*, stones, and *tomaras*; likewise, he cast many *musaṇṭhīs*, tridents, *paṭṭasas*,
*karpaṇas* with a hundred edges, and various *pinākas*.
Taking up his bow and uttering terrifying roars, he discharged wheels, razor-headed arrows, slings, *kaṭaṃkaṭas*, and various iron shafts, while accompanied by *kaṅkas*, owls, and crows.
Seeing that fierce and cruel one approaching like Death itself arrived,
O King, that Pāṇḍava army fled, agitated by fear;
but Satyaka, that tiger among men, beheld that Rākṣasa in battle.
Resembling an immortal, he drew his great bow and rushed toward that *rākṣasa*, crying out, "Stay! Stay!
He then overwhelmed Alambuṣa, the lord of the *rākṣasas*, with a rain of missiles.
Then, O Bhārata, seeing the Pāṇḍava armies in flight,
Ghaṭotkaca rushed forward in haste;
he hurled maces, spears, lances, and battle-axes.

Beholding one another from afar with fierce swords that were gold-ornamented hilts and possessed a luster like the sky, those two mighty Rākṣasas let out terrifying roars like two rain-bearing clouds.

Then a terrible battle commenced between those two lions among rākṣasas, just like that which occurred of old in the fray between Rāma and Rāvaṇa. They [hurled] spears, *pinākas*, thunderbolts, swords, and battle-axes.
Then, both of them, enraged with one another, discharged their weapons; and as their bows were drawn by the strength of their arms,
O King, they produced a tremendous sound like that of a mechanical engine.
Then the valiant Alambusa, exerting great effort, hurled at Ghaṭotkaca a discus that possessed the brilliance of the fire of Death;
but the son of Bhīmasena, seeing that swiftly moving discus in mid-air, [intercepted it].
He struck it with his mace, and it shattered into a hundred pieces. Then,
by the sparks of fire suddenly emitted from the blow of the discus,
that army was violently overwhelmed as if by falling stinging insects.
Then, his wheel having been repelled, that hero, overwhelmed with rage,
swiftly hurled a spear and a thousand spears,
which were blazing and emitting thousands of garlands of flames.
Resembling meteors at the end of an eon, sharp, with golden shafts and great roars—
seeing those falling, Ghaṭotkaca cut them down with crescent-headed arrows and iron shafts feathered with heron plumes.
Then, his limbs overcome with rage,
that Rākṣasa unleashed a most terrible shower of arrows toward Ghaṭotkaca’s chariot,
as Alambuṣa moved fearlessly about in the battle.
The son of Hiḍimbā advanced swiftly and pierced him with sharp arrows;
a terrifying battle ensued between those two lions among Rākṣasas,
as they employed various illusions like Śakra and Śambara.
Alambusa, becoming violently enraged, struck Ghaṭotkaca;
a battle then took place between those two foremost leaders of the Rākṣasas,
O Lord, just like that which occurred in the past between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
Such a battle took place between those two lions among Rākṣasas. Then Ghaṭotkaca, having pierced Alambuṣa in the middle of the chest with twenty iron arrows, roared repeatedly like a lion.

In the same way, O King, Alambuṣa, having pierced the son of Hiḍimbā— who was fierce in battle— again and again, roared boldly, filling the sky on all sides. Thus did those two immensely powerful lords of the Rākṣasas become violently enraged.
They fought one another without distinction by means of illusions,
both arrogant and creating hundreds of illusions to delude each other;
highly skilled in illusory combat, they engaged in a battle of illusions.
O King, whatever illusion Ghaṭotkaca displayed in battle, Alambuṣa, O monarch, destroyed each one with his own illusion. As he was thus fighting, being an expert in the warfare of illusions—
Seeing Alambusa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, the Pāṇḍavas became enraged.
O King, Bhīmasena and the others, exceedingly furious, rushed at him from all sides with their excellent chariots.
O noble one, having hemmed him in with a multitude of chariots,
they showered him from all sides with arrows, like people pelting an elephant with firebrands.
Having warded off that force of their weapons by means of his own illusory power of arms, he—
Released from that multitude of chariots like an elephant from a forest fire,
he drew his formidable bow, which sounded like Indra’s thunderbolt,
and struck the son of Māruta with twenty-five arrows and the son of Bhīmasena with five.
Having pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with three arrows and Sahadeva with seven,
O noble one, he struck Nakula with seventy-three and each of Drupada’s sons with five; then he let out a terrible roar.
Bhimasena pierced that Rakshasa with nine arrows, Sahadeva with five, Yudhishthira with a hundred,
Nakula with sixty-four, and the sons of Draupadi each with three.
Having pierced the Rākṣasa with fifty arrows in battle,
the mighty Haiḍimba struck him again with seventy and let out a roar;
by that great roar, this earth was made to tremble.
O King, [the earth] was filled with mountains, forests, trees, and bodies of water. That great archer, having been pierced on all sides by those great car-warriors,
pierced each of them in return with five arrows.
O best of the Bharatas, the son of Hiḍimbā, filled with rage, pierced that enraged Rākṣasa in battle with seven arrows. Thus deeply pierced by the powerful one, that mighty lord of the Rākṣasas—
He swiftly discharged arrows with golden feathers, sharpened on stone;
those straight-knotted shafts then entered the Rākṣasa,
like fierce and mighty serpents in a rage entering a mountain.
Then, O King, those Pāṇḍavas and Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Hiḍimbā, being agitated, dispatched sharpened arrows from all sides.
Being struck in battle by the Pāṇḍavas, who appeared victorious, [he was overwhelmed].
Having fallen into the condition of a mortal, he did not know what ought to be done.
Then the son of Bhīmasena, that mighty warrior skilled in battle,
beholding him in such a state, set his mind upon slaying him.
He exerted a great force toward the chariot of the lord of the Rākṣasas; meanwhile,
Ghaṭotkaca, remaining unperturbed and desiring to slay Alambuṣa, released a massive shower of arrows like a blazing fire.
From the fierce chariot of Alambusa and from the chariot of Ghaṭotkaca as well,
arrows emerged toward the quarters like bees from the sky;
O lord of men, a shadow like that of a cloud was created there by those shafts.
Nothing at all could be discerned when darkness was created by those arrows;
then, with a broad-headed shaft released from an ear-to-mouth draw, the mighty Ghaṭotkaca severed the head of Alambusa’s charioteer.
Then, with other swift razor-sharp arrows, Ghaṭotkaca struck him in battle, severing his axle,
pole, and yoke; then Kirmīra, frantic with rage, quickly leaped down from his chariot.

Upon him, he [Duryodhana] indeed rained down a terrible shower of illusory weapons. Ghaṭotkaca, too, quickly leaping from his chariot, destroyed that very weapon of his enemy in battle with an illusory weapon of his own.
Being hard-pressed in battle by the son of Hiḍimbā,
O great king, that Alambuṣa vanished and continued to fight Ghaṭotkaca.
Seeing him thus moving from place to place, having entered into invisibility, Ghaṭotkaca—
The immensely powerful one struck him with his swift-moving mace;
thereupon, afflicted by the blow,
Alambusa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, suddenly leapt into the sky like the king of birds.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, unperturbed and sword in hand,
sprang up with great speed like a rain-cloud about to pour forth its waters;
seeing him rushing toward him, Kirmīra, the best of Rākṣasas, [prepared for battle].
Raising his sword with his right hand and shielding his chest with his armor, Ghaṭotkaca rushed with speed toward the impetuous one, like a lion springing upon a standing lion.
Both Alambusa and Ghaṭotkaca, impelled by their great speed,
then struck each other's thighs directly;
by that mutual impact of those two lions among Rākṣasas, [they were both shaken].
When one mountain struck the other, a great roar arose;
then, having suddenly approached again,
those two foremost of Rākṣasas fell upon each other fiercely, traversing various paths with their swords.
The two swords, having fallen upon their bodies,
shattered and fell like the thunderbolt hurled with force by Maghavan against the slopes of mountains;
then the troops beheld that most terrible battle.
The battle between those two Rākṣasas was like that between two hawks over a piece of meat.
Then those two best of Rākṣasas, with eyes reddened by blood,
appeared like two tigers or like clouds colored by the twilight.
They both performed thousands of circular maneuvers like hawks; with swords in hand, they were like two winged birds. Then, having whirled that sword, the son of Kirmīra [attacked] Pāṇḍu.
Ghaṭotkaca hurled [his sword] to sever his head,
and those two, having met upon the vast earth, both brandished their blazing swords simultaneously; then, with their arms, the two Rākṣasas grappled with one another.
Striking each other with blows to the head and blows to the chest, yet neither being struck down, the two heroes then engaged in combat again and again, mingling their weapons;
they resembled the peaks of a scorched mountain or a mass of crushed collyrium.
Rushing from chariot to chariot, the enraged son of Hiḍimbā seized him;
he tore him from the chariot just as Garuḍa seizes a serpent.
Having lifted him up with his two arms, he whirled him around again and again.
Endowed with strength, agility, and prowess, the enraged son of Bhīmasena crushed him quickly upon the ground like a full water-jar against a stone,
terrifying all the troops in battle.
With all his limbs shattered and his bones and ornaments crushed,
Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa was slain by the heroic Ghaṭotkaca.
Then the army of the Pāṇḍavas, seeing him struck down, [was filled with joy].
Overwhelmed by a surge of joy, she let out a tremendous roar;
then the Rākṣasa fell swiftly to the ground, lifeless,
like a mountain peak struck down by the force of a thunderbolt.
O Great King, by that great falling warrior, ten elephants among your troops were slain because of his immense size; then,
once that night-stalker was killed, the Pārthas became joyful in mind.
They let out lion-like roars and waved their garments about.
And your warriors, seeing the mighty lord of the Rākṣasas,
Alambuṣa of terrifying form, slain like a shattered mountain, [were struck with fear].
O bull of the Bharatas, the armies raised a cry of "Alas!
and the people, filled with curiosity, beheld that Rakshasa fallen upon the earth like a coal dropped by chance.
Having slain that Rākṣasa, the foremost among the powerful, Ghaṭotkaca let out a mighty roar, just as Vāsava did after slaying Bala. He was then honored by his fathers and his kinsmen.
When that difficult deed had been accomplished, Ghaṭotkaca,
having slain that Rākṣasa who resembled Vṛtra,
mounted his own chariot once more and roared, desiring victory.
Having slain his enemy, Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Pāṇḍu, then rejoiced greatly on the field of battle with a joyful heart.
Alambusā was cooked like Alambusā [fruit];
then a great clamor arose,
accompanied by the sound of conchs and various kinds of arrows.
Hearing that, the Kauravas roared in response;
then a sound arose that intensely touched the very earth.
Then, having approached King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma—
Proclaiming his own deed, he fell with joined palms at [his father's] feet.
Smelling him on the head and embracing him, the eldest Pāṇḍava,
his eyes wide with joy, said, "I am pleased," O King.
When Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa had been crushed by Ghaṭotkaca and was dead,
everyone rejoiced once that night-stalker had been slain.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"How did Yuyudhāna oppose Bhāradvāja in battle? O Saṃjaya, tell me this in truth, for my curiosity is great.
Saṃjaya said:
"Listen, O king of great wisdom, to the hair-raising battle between Droṇa and the Pāṇḍavas led by Yuyudhāna, O noble one,
upon seeing his army being slaughtered by Yuyudhāna."
Droṇa himself rushed against Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth. As the great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, was suddenly charging,
Sātyaki struck him with twenty-five small arrows.
Droṇa, too, displaying his prowess in battle, concentrated his mind and swiftly pierced Yuyudhāna with five gold-tufted arrows sharpened on stone. Those arrows,
which feed upon the flesh of enemies, having pierced his very firm armor, [penetrated his body].
O King, they fell upon the earth like hissing serpents.
The long-armed one, enraged like an elephant struck by a goad,
pierced Droṇa with fifty iron arrows resembling fire.
Bharadvāja, pierced in battle by Yuyudhāna,
quickly struck back at the striving Sātyaki with many arrows. Then that great archer of immense strength became even more enraged.

He afflicted the Sātvata with a hundred straight-jointed arrows. Being thus struck in battle by the son of Bharadvāja, O lord of the people, Sātyaki could not perceive what at all remained to be done.
And Yuyudhana, O King, became dejected of countenance upon seeing Bhāradvāja discharging sharp arrows in battle;
beholding him thus, O lord of the people, your sons and the soldiers were likewise struck with dismay.
With hearts full of joy, they roared repeatedly like lions.
Hearing that terrible sound and seeing Mādhava being oppressed,
Yudhiṣṭhira, O King, spoke to all the troops, O Bhārata.
This hero, the best of the Vṛṣṇis, Sātyaki, who performs deeds of truth, is being swallowed by that warrior in battle, like the sun by Rāhu. Rush forth! Go where Sātyaki fights!
And he said this to Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the prince of the Pāñcālas, O lord of men:
"Restrain Droṇa very quickly; let not the twice-born one slay Satyaka.
Charge at Droṇa swiftly; why do you stand still, O son of Pṛṣata?"
Do you not see the terrible danger that has come upon us from Droṇa?
There, the great archer Droṇa is playing with Yuyudhāna in battle,
like a child with a bird tied by a string.

"Let all the chariot-warriors, led by Bhīmasena, proceed right there together with you, remaining vigilant against the chariot of Yuyudhāna. I myself shall follow behind you, accompanied by my troops."
"Rescue Sātyaki today, for he has fallen between the fangs of Death!
Having spoken thus, the Pāṇḍava king then rushed at Droṇa in battle with his entire army for the sake of Yuyudhāna.
There arose a great clamor as they all desired to fight Drona alone— blessings be upon you— from the Pandavas and the Srinjayas on every side.
Those tigers among men, having come together, [assailed] the great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvaja.
They rained down sharp arrows feathered with the plumes of herons and peacocks;
yet Drona, smiling, received those heroes himself,
just as one welcomes arriving guests with water and a seat.
Satiated by the arrows of that bowman, the son of Bharadvāja,
they were like guests who have reached the house of a hospitable host, O King;
and none of them were able even to look at the son of Bharadvāja.
O Lord, as the midday sun with its thousand rays had arrived,
Drona— the best among the wielders of weapons— scorched all those great archers with volleys of arrows, just as the sun scorches with its beams.
O King, being slaughtered in battle, the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas found no protector, like elephants sunk in the mud. And Droṇa’s great arrows were seen gliding across the field.
Scorching on all sides like the rays of the sun,
twenty-five Pāñcālas— renowned as great car-warriors and highly esteemed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna— were slain by Droṇa in that encounter.
Among all the armies of the Pāṇḍus and likewise among the Pañcālas,
as well as among the heroic Pañcālas and the Kekayas,
the men beheld the heroic Droṇa slaughtering the best of the best.
Having slain a hundred Kekayas and put them to flight on all sides,
O great king, Droṇa stood like Death with his mouth wide open,
[attacking] the Pañcālas, Sṛñjayas, Matsyas, Kekayas, and even the Pāṇḍavas.
The mighty-armed Droṇa conquered them by the hundreds and thousands; a great clamor arose from those being slain by Droṇa’s arrows,
like that of forest-dwellers in the wilderness being consumed by fire.
There, O King, the gods along with the Gandharvas and the Pitṛs said:
"These Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, together with their armies, are fleeing;
for Droṇa is thus slaughtering the Somakas in battle."
Not a few advanced at all, nor did others even strike;
while that fierce slaughter of the best of heroes was thus proceeding, Pārtha suddenly heard the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch.
The king of conchs, blown by Vāsudeva, resounded loudly while the heroes were fighting to protect the ruler of the Sindhus,
and as the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra roared toward Vijaya’s chariot.
When the roar of the Gāṇḍīva had vanished on all sides,
King Pāṇḍava, overcome by dejection, reflected:
"Surely it is not well with Pārtha, since the king of conchs is sounding thus."
And as the Kauravas, filled with joy, roar again and again,
Sañjaya said:
"Clearly, today all the great car-warriors of the world are perishing."
O noble one, having heard the terrible roar of the Pāñcajanya conch,
Ajātaśatru, the son of Kuntī, reflecting thus with an agitated inner soul, addressed the Sātvata.
With a voice faltering with tears, fainting again and again,
and looking toward the next course of action, he addressed Śaineya, that bull among the Śinis:
"O Śaineya, that eternal dharma which was observed by the virtuous in ancient times— "
"In this hour of crisis, when the duty of a friend must be performed, that time has now come for him.
And among all the warriors, O bull of the Śini clan, though I reflect upon them,
I do not recognize anyone as a greater friend to him than you, O Sātyaki."
For he who is always well-disposed and he who is ever devoted— such a person,
it is my opinion, should be appointed to a task in times of crisis;
just as Keśava is eternally the ultimate refuge of the Pāṇḍavas.
In the same way, O Vārṣṇeya, you possess prowess equal to that of Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, I shall place this burden upon you; you ought to bear it.
And you ought never to render my purpose in vain.
Therefore, O bull among men, in this time of distress, provide assistance to Arjuna in battle— though he be your brother, friend, and even your elder—
for you are a hero true to his vows and one who grants fearlessness to his friends.
O hero, you are renowned in the world for your deeds as one whose word is true.
For he who, O Śaineya, would give up his body while fighting for the sake of a friend,
and he who would give the earth to the twice-born— these two acts are indeed equal.
We have heard of many kings who have gone to heaven after giving this entire earth to brahmins according to the prescribed rites;
for this earth has been given by many before and will be given again and again.
"Indeed, has there not been someone here who has sacrificed his life in battle for the sake of a friend? O righteous-souled one, I entreat you thus with palms joined in reverence;
O Lord, the fruit of this would be equal to the gift of the earth, or even greater."
"Kṛṣṇa alone is always the one who grants fearlessness to his friends;
he sacrifices his life in battle, and you, O Sātyaki, are his second.
For a valiant hero seeking glory in combat,"
Only a hero should be a companion, and not any other ordinary person;
for in such a violent conflict as this, O Mādhava,
no protector of Vijaya is to be found in battle other than you.
For the son of Pāṇḍu, praising your deeds by the hundreds,
repeatedly recounted them to me, thereby generating great joy within me; he is swift in the use of weapons, a versatile warrior, and likewise possessed of rapid prowess.
Wise, skilled in all weapons, and heroic, he is never bewildered in combat. Broad-shouldered, broad-chested, long-armed, and wielding a great bow,
he is possessed of great strength and great valor— that high-souled one is a great car-warrior.
"He is my disciple and my friend; he is dear to me, and I am dear to him. Yuyudhana is my ally and will crush the Kauravas.
And if Keśava should arm himself for our sake, O Indra among kings," so it was said.
O great king, whether it be Rāma, or Aniruddha, or the great car-warrior Pradyumna, or Gada, or Sāraṇa, or even Sāmba along with the Vṛṣṇis,
they are there for the sake of assistance at the forefront of that supreme battle.

"Nevertheless, O dear one, Dhananjaya said to me in the Dvaitavana forest: 'I shall employ that tiger among men, the descendant of Śini, whose prowess is truth, to provide assistance; for there is no one else equal to him.'"

O Vārṣṇeya, you ought not to let the intention of Dhananjaya— nor that of both he and myself and Bhīma— be rendered fruitless as he truthfully recounts your virtues in the assembly of noble men behind our backs.
And furthermore, while wandering among the sacred fords, I went toward Dvārakā;
there too, O Śaineya, I observed your devotion toward Arjuna. Such friendship as that has not been perceived by me in others.

"O Mādhava, just as you have attended to us while we were in distress, [consider] your noble birth, your devotion, your friendship, your role as our preceptor, your kindness, your prowess, and your high lineage."
"O mighty-armed one, out of compassion for Satya and for what is fitting, O great archer, you ought to perform this deed.
For Suyodhana has gone forth suddenly, clad in armor by Drona."

Those great car-warriors of the Kauravas have already departed; moreover, a very great clamor is being heard directed toward Vijaya. Therefore, O descendant of Śini, O Mādhava, you ought to go there with speed.
"Bhīmasena, we, and our troops, being fully prepared, shall hold back Droṇa if he advances against you. Behold, O descendant of Śini, the armies fleeing in the battle."
And a great roar arose in the battle as the Bharata host was being shattered, O dear one,
like the ocean during the change of the moon by the force of a mighty wind;
the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons was thus scattered by Savyasācin.
With chariots, men, and horses rushing about,
this army, raising a cloud of dust, moves in every direction;
it is surrounded by the Sindhu-Sauvīras, who fight with claws and spears.

Phalguna, the slayer of enemy heroes, cannot slay Jayadratha as long as this army— composed of utterly devoted warriors— is not held in check; for all these men have renounced their very lives for the sake of the King of Sindhu.

Behold this army of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, so difficult to approach— a forest of arrows, spears, and banners, teeming with horses and elephants. Hear the roar of the kettledrums and the abundant sounds of conch shells.
Hear the sounds of lion-roars and likewise the rattling of chariot rims; hear the noise of elephants and of infantry by the thousands, as well as the sound of charging cavalry shaking the very earth.
The Saindhava army is in front, behind Drona’s army;
for because of its great numbers, O tiger among men, it could afflict even the Lord of the Gods. Immersed in such boundless force, one might even lose one's life.

And when he has been slain in battle, how could one such as I continue to live? Alas, I have fallen into a most miserable state of existence. Dark-complexioned, youthful, with curly hair, and handsome is that Pāṇḍava.
O dear one, that light-handed archer and versatile warrior has entered the Bharata host;
at sunrise, O mighty-armed one, the day is already passing away. Therefore, O Vārṣṇeya, I do not know whether he lives or not.
And that great army of the Kurus, resembling the ocean,
was entered all alone by Bībhatsu, O dear one; the mighty-armed one penetrated that host, which was unbearable even for the gods in a great battle.
My mind does not function at all today regarding how to fight;
even the impetuous Droṇa oppresses my army in battle,
O mighty-armed one, as you yourself have witnessed how that twice-born one maneuvers.
O Mādhava, you are wise; you ought to accomplish, with great purpose and efficiency, the tasks that have arisen simultaneously for those gathered here.
Among all my undertakings, this is always considered by me to be the most important task.
"Arjuna must be protected in this battle;
I do not grieve for the descendant of Daśārha, the lord and protector of the world,
for he, my dear, is capable in combat of conquering even the three worlds united together."
"O tiger among men, I tell you this truth:
how much more so can he defeat this utterly weak army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son?
Yet Arjuna himself, O Vārṣṇeya, has been hard-pressed by many in battle."
One should abandon one's life in battle; therefore, I feel despondency. Follow his path, so that those like you may follow it—being urged by one such as me at such a time as this for one such as he.

One such as you should go to one such as him; go to him, Satyaka! Indeed, a friend, exerting the utmost prowess for the sake of a friend's duty, should never be distressed in any way while seeking the path of his friend.
In battle, among the foremost heroes of the Vṛṣṇis, only two are considered Atirathas:
the mighty-armed Pradyumna and you, O renowned Sātvata. You are equal to Nārāyaṇa in weaponry and equal to Saṃkarṣaṇa in strength.
O tiger among men, you are indeed equal to Dhanañjaya in heroism;
surpassing both Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are experts in all forms of warfare,
the virtuous in this world today proclaim you to be a tiger among men.
"He would fight against all the worlds— including gods, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— and he would conquer many enemies;
thus do people in the world speak of your virtues."
In assemblies, they always speak of him as being quite exceptional;
O Mādhava, there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished by Sātyaki. Therefore, O one of great strength, do what I shall tell you.
For there is high regard for both you and Pārtha in the world;
O mighty-armed one, you ought not to act otherwise here. Casting aside your dear life-breaths, range through the battlefield like a hero.
For the Daśārhas, O Śaineya, do not protect their lives in battle.
Avoiding combat, lack of steadfastness, and fleeing from the fray—this is the path of cowards and the wicked; it is not the way followed by the Daśārhas.
"O dear one, Arjuna is your elder and a righteous soul, O bull among the Śinis;
and Vāsudeva is also your elder. Furthermore, he is the elder of the wise Pārtha. Knowing these two reasons, I spoke thus to you."
"Do not disregard my words, for I am indeed the elder of your elder.
This is the opinion of Vāsudeva, as well as of myself and Arjuna.
What I have told you is the truth; go where Dhanañjaya is."
"O you whose prowess is truth, having understood these words of mine,
enter this army of the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
my dear; and having entered, engage with the great car-warriors according to the proper rule."
"O Sātvata, display in battle your own prowess as is fitting.
Saṃjaya said:
[He spoke] words that were full of affection, pleasing to the heart, and sweet of syllable.
Having heard those words of the King of Dharma, which were timely, varied, and spoken with self-assurance, Sātyaki, the bull among the Śinis and best of the Bharatas,
replied to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O Acyuta, I have heard all these words spoken by you;
they are logical, wonderful, and conducive to fame for Phalguna.
At such a time as this, having seen one like me who is esteemed [by you],"
O Indra among kings, you ought to speak to me just as you would to Pārtha. For my sake, my life is not to be protected by any means whatsoever.
Furthermore, commanded by you, what would I not do in the great battle?
"Commanded by you, O lord of men, I could fight the three worlds together with their gods, asuras, and humans; how much more so this very weak force?
Today, however, I shall fight Suyodhana’s army on all sides."

"And I shall be victorious in battle, O King; I tell you this truly. Having encountered Dhananjaya while he is in good health, and once Jayadratha is slain, O King, I shall return again to your presence."
"O lord of men, I must certainly inform you of everything that Vāsudeva and the wise Phalguna have said;
for I have been repeatedly and firmly urged by Arjuna."
In the midst of the entire army, while Vāsudeva listens,
O Mādhava, protect the king today with vigilance,
having resolved upon a noble course in battle, until I slay Jayadratha.
"O mighty-armed one, having entrusted the king to you or to Pradyumna, the great car-warrior, I would go after Jayadratha without further concern.
Thus indeed was that deposit entrusted by Savyasācin.
"O Dhanañjaya, Bhāradvāja considers you a source of fear today;
for you know Droṇa in battle to be impetuous and esteemed as the best,
and you have always heard, O Mādhava, the vow that Droṇa has made."
Bhāradvāja is eager to seize Dharmarāja;
Droṇa is indeed capable of capturing Yudhiṣṭhira in battle.
Thus, having entrusted Dharmarāja, that best of men, to you—
"Today I shall go indeed for the sake of slaying the ruler of the Sindhus.
Therefore, O Mādhava, you must today be vigilant in battle and protect the son of Pāṇḍu;
for if the King of Dharma is protected, my victory is certain."
"O Mādhava, having slain Jayadratha, I shall certainly return,
lest Droṇa forcibly seize Dharmarāja in battle. O Mādhava, once that best of men has been captured by the son of Bharadvāja..."
"If the slaughter of Saindhava does not occur, there will likewise be displeasure for me. This being the case, O best of men, since the Pāṇḍava is a speaker of truth,
our departure back toward the forest will clearly be necessary once again."
This victory of mine will clearly become fruitless if Drona, enraged in battle, should seize Yudhiṣṭhira. Therefore,
O mighty-armed Mādhava, for my sake today—
For the sake of victory and for the sake of fame, protect the king in battle. O Lord,
you have been placed as a trust with me by Savyasācin,
who constantly perceives danger from the son of Bharadvāja.
Moreover, O mighty-armed lord,
he always perceives no other opponent in battle besides the son of Rukmiṇī or even me, when facing the wise son of Bharadvāja.
"O great king, Bhīma is indeed equal to the wind in strength.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, I cannot bring myself to disregard this high regard [for him], nor can I disregard the words of my preceptor, nor can I abandon you."
The preceptor, because of his lightness of hand, though clad in impenetrable armor,
would treat him in battle like a child playing with a bird—
if only the son of Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna), bow in hand, were here like the god whose banner bears the sea-monster.
I would indeed entrust you to him, for he will protect you just as Arjuna does.
Prepare your own protection; who will be your protector when I have departed?
Who can withstand Droṇa in battle until I reach the Pāṇḍava?
"And let there be no fear for you today, O King, arising from Arjuna;
that mighty-armed one never falters when he has taken up a burden.
As for those Sauvīraka warriors, as well as the Saindhavas and Pauravas,"
The northerners, the southerners, and whatever other great chariot-warriors there may be— those who, O King, are celebrated as noble car-warriors headed by Karṇa—
all these together are not worth a sixteenth part of the enraged Arjuna.
O King, the entire earth— with its gods, asuras, and humans, along with the hosts of rākṣasas, kinnaras, and great serpents— is fully mobilized;
yet together with all mobile and immobile beings, it is not a match for the son of Pṛthā in battle.
Knowing this, O Great King, let your fear regarding Dhanañjaya depart;
for where those two heroes, the great archers, the two Kṛṣṇas of true prowess are present,
no failure in action can possibly occur there in any way.
Reflect upon your divine nature, your mastery of weapons, your yoga, and your indignation in battle; reflect also upon your gratitude and your compassion for your brother.
This is even as I depart from here, going toward Arjuna.
O King, reflect upon Droṇa’s mastery of diverse weapons in battle;
for the preceptor, O King, is intensely eager to seize you,
while guarding his own vow and seeking to make it true, O Bhārata.
"Provide for your own protection this very day; who will be your protector when I have departed?
O Pārtha, it is because of confidence in you that I would go toward Phalguna.
For I have no confidence, O Pārtha, as long as I must go to the son of Pāṇḍu."
"O Great King, O Kauravya, I shall not go anywhere without leaving you behind in this great battle; I tell you this truth. I do not see any chariot here that could be your protector."
"O King, O Pandava, regarding him whom you consider capable of being our protector— having deliberated upon this repeatedly with your intellect, O best among the wise,
and having perceived through your intelligence what is the highest good, then, O King, command me."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O mighty-armed Mādhava, it is exactly as you say;
yet, O noble one, my mind finds no peace regarding the one with white horses."
"I shall exert the utmost effort toward my own protection;
go now, with my permission, to where Dhananjaya has gone. [I must decide] between protecting myself in battle or going after Arjuna."

Having deliberated upon these two options with my intellect, I prefer that you go there yourself. Therefore, O tiger among men, mount your vehicle and set out where Dhanañjaya has gone; Bhīma shall follow behind you.
The mighty Bhīma will also provide protection for me,
as will the son of Pṛṣata along with his brothers, and the kings of great strength;
and the sons of Draupadī, my dear, will protect me— of this there is no doubt.
The five Kekaya brothers, the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, Virāṭa, Drupada, the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin,
the powerful Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Kuntibhoja, O noble one.

Nakula, Sahadeva, the Pāñcālas, and the Sṛñjayas—these, O dear one, being fully concentrated, will protect him; of this there is no doubt. Neither Droṇa with his army nor Kṛtavarman can prevail over him in battle.
He will not be able to overcome me, nor will he dare to attack me;
and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the scorcher of foes, will valiantly hold back the enraged Droṇa in battle, just as the shore holds back the ocean.

Wherever the son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of enemy heroes, stands in battle, Droṇa’s powerful army shall not advance there by any means. He has arisen from the sacrificial fire for the destruction of Droṇa.
Armed with armor, arrows, sword, and bow, and adorned with excellent ornaments—
O Lord, this Pāñcāla prince, together with all the archers of the Pāṇḍavas, will surely hold back the enraged Droṇa in battle.
"Go with confidence, O descendant of Śini; do not feel any anxiety on my account.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, enraged in battle, will hold Droṇa at bay.
Saṃjaya said:

Having heard those words of the King of Dharma, that bull among the Śinis feared danger from Pārtha and especially sought to avoid the reproach of the world for having abandoned the lord of the earth. He was particularly intent on protecting himself from public censure.

"Let them not say of me as I approach Phalguna, 'He is afraid. Having thus resolved in many ways, the highly illustrious Sātyaki, who is fierce in battle, spoke to Dharmarāja in words that were somewhat indistinct."
With a voice faltering from grief, his mind overwhelmed by sorrow,
that bull among men spoke these words to Dharmarāja:
"Reflecting upon how things are now," he then addressed Dharmarāja.
"If you consider the protection already accomplished, may it be well with you, O Lord of the People;
I shall follow Bībhatsu and carry out your command.
For there is no one in the three worlds who is a match for the Pāṇḍava."
"O King, he who is indeed most dear to you— I tell you this truly— I shall follow his path at your command, O giver of honor;
for your sake, there is nothing whatsoever that I would not do."
O best of men, just as the word of my preceptor is distinguished to me,
so too are your words even more distinguished to me;
for both your brothers, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, are dear to you.
"Know me, O bull among kings, to be established in the welfare of those two. Having accepted your command upon my head for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, O Lord,
I shall break through this impenetrable army and advance, O best of men."
"I shall enter Droṇa’s army, enraged like a great fish entering the ocean. O King, I will go there where that King Jayadratha is—
where he stands, relying upon his troops, afraid of the Pāṇḍava."
Protected by the best of excellent chariot-warriors, such as the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, Kṛpa,
and others, O lord of the people, I consider that path from here to be three *yojanas* long,
where that son of Pṛthā stands, intent on the slaughter of Jayadratha.

"O King, even if he has gone three yojanas away, I shall follow his track with a firm inner resolve until the slaughter of the Saindhava. For what man indeed would fight without being commanded by his preceptor?"
"O King, commanded by you, what man like me would not fight? O Lord, I recognize that region where I shall go—
where that king of the Sindhus, the slayer of children, resides."
I shall agitate this ocean-like army, which resembles the sea roaring like the ocean itself, crowded with *huḍa*-clubs,
spears, maces, darts, swords, shields, ṛṣṭis, and *tomaras*,
and thronged with the finest missiles and weapons.

This elephant force of a thousand that you behold belongs to the lineage named Añjanaka, where these heroic warriors are stationed along with many Mlecchas who are skilled strikers and eager for battle.
O King, these elephants resemble clouds and are like rain-bearing clouds pouring forth water;
once dispatched by their riders, they would never turn back,
O King, for there is no defeat for them except through death.
"Furthermore, O King, those chariot-warriors whom you see all around are the princes known as the Rukmarathas,
great car-fighters (mahārathas) who are skilled in chariots, weapons, and elephants, O lord of the people."

They have reached the further shore of the science of archery (dhanurveda) and are experts in fist-fighting; likewise, they are specialists in mace-fighting, skilled in wrestling, and proficient in the use of the sword,
as well as in the clash of sword and shield.

O King, those men who are brave and learned vie with one another; they constantly desire to conquer their fellow men in battle. O King, having been defeated by Karṇa, they now follow the lead of Duḥśāsana.

Vāsudeva also praised these noble chariot-warriors; they are constantly desirous of pleasing Karṇa and remain under his command. It was at his very word, O King, that they turned back from the one who rides white horses.
Unwounded and untired, with firm shields and bows,
they have surely stationed themselves for my sake by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son;
O Kaurava, having crushed them in battle, act for your own pleasure.
"O King, after that I shall follow in the footsteps of Savyasācin;
as for these other seven hundred elephants that you behold, covered in armor and mounted by Kirātas."
O King, those well-adorned servants whom the Kirāta king gave up when he was captured by Savyasācin— desiring his own life—
these were formerly your steadfast laborers.
"Behold the reversal of time: today they desire to fight with you alone!
These are their great officers—Kirātas intoxicated by war, experts in the training of elephants, and all of them born from fire."
All these, who were once victorious in battle, have today been conquered by Savyasācin; though they are now prepared for my sake, they remain under the sway of Duryodhana.
Having pierced these Kirātas, who are intoxicated with war, with his arrows, O King—
I shall follow the Pāṇḍava, who is intent on the slaughter of Saindhava.
As for these very great elephants born of Añjana’s lineage— rough yet well-trained, with temples and faces flowing with rut—
O King, these men from the northern mountains, well-adorned with armor made entirely of Jāmbūnada gold,
have attained their mark in battle; they are like Airāvata in combat,
though now occupied by fierce bandits.
It was occupied by fierce and heroic mountain-dwellers,
harsh and preeminent warriors clad in black iron armor;
there were those of bovine origin and those of monkey origin.
There are others of many different origins, as well as those of human origin;
this army of the wicked is proclaimed to be smoke-colored—
the army of Mlecchas, evildoers who dwell in the fastnesses of the Himalayas.
Having obtained this entire circle of elephants,
as well as Kṛpa, the son of Somadatta, Droṇa— the best of chariot-warriors—
and likewise the King of Sindhu and Karṇa, Duryodhana held the Pāṇḍavas in contempt.

Driven by time, he disregards Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the two from Avanti, the ruler of the Sindhus, the son of Droṇa, and the son of Somadatta; impelled by fate, he considers himself to have already achieved his purpose.
And all of them have come within the range of my iron shafts;
they shall not escape, O son of Kuntī, even if they were as swift as thought.
They have always been honored by him who lives off the prowess of his enemies.
"O King, those chariot-warriors who are seen here with golden banners, oppressed by the flood of my arrows, shall meet their destruction;
they are the Kambojas named Durvāraṇas, if you have heard of them."
They are brave, accomplished in learning, and perfected in the science of archery;
for they are closely united and deeply desire one another's welfare.
And these Akṣauhiṇīs of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, O Bhārata, are filled with fierce resolve.
"O Great King, those Kuru heroes stand ready for my sake, protected and vigilant; they have presented themselves before me alone. Yet I shall crush them, just as fire consumes blades of grass."
"Therefore, O King, let the chariot-fitters properly equip my chariot with all the side-arms and all the necessary implements. Indeed,
in this battle, various kinds of weapons must be taken."
"The chariot must be prepared with fivefold excellence, just as instructed by the teachers. For I shall encounter the Kambojas, who are enraged like venomous serpents,
raining down various weapons and fighting with diverse arms."
I shall encounter the Kirātas, who are like poison in their strikes,
who have been constantly cherished by the king, and who desire the welfare of Duryodhana;
and I shall also encounter the Śakas, whose prowess is equal to that of Śakra.

O King, I shall encounter in battle many warriors who are like fire, invincible and blazing as if they were kindled flames; likewise, I shall meet other various combatants who are like Time itself, difficult to approach and intoxicated with the pride of war.
I shall follow the path of Savyasācin, who has gone three *yojanas*,
he who is the best of chariot-warriors and the foremost of archers;
I shall track the course of that Pāṇḍava as he proceeds toward the rising sun.
"When the sun has moved further on, I shall depart without a doubt.
Therefore, let these excellent horses, endowed with auspicious marks, having rested,
watered, and refreshed, be yoked again to my chariot."
The king placed all his quivers, all his equipment, and various weapons upon the chariot. Then,
having unyoked those four excellent horses from every side, the men [departed].
They caused [the horses] to drink a flavorful draught that induced exhilaration. Then, having drunk and emerged from the water, bathed, eaten their fill, and adorned themselves,
they led forth four horses wearing golden garlands, from which all pain had been removed.
Those horses, golden-hued, well-trained, swift-moving,
joyful in spirit, and composed, were harnessed according to rule to the chariot which was equipped with a great banner bearing a lion with a garland of golden manes.
It was enclosed with golden pavilions adorned with jewels and coral,
decorated with banners shining like pale clouds,
and furnished with raised golden-staffed umbrellas and an abundance of weapons and equipment.
He had them harnessed according to the prescribed rites, adorned with golden ornaments.
Dāruka’s younger brother, his dear friend and charioteer,
announced that the chariot was ready, just as Mātali does for Vāsava.
Then, having bathed, become pure, and performed the auspicious rites of *kautuka*,
Sātyaki— the best among the illustrious— caused a thousand *snātaka* brahmins to be given gold *niṣkas*. Embraced by their blessings, he stood there.
Then he, who was worthy of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), having drunk the *kailāvata* honey,
shone there with blood-red eyes, his gaze unsteady from intoxication. And, having touched the *vīra*-bronze vessel, he was filled with great joy.
For his splendor was doubled, blazing like a fire;
that best of chariot-warriors took up his bow and arrow upon his lap,
and having had the rites for success performed by the brahmins, he donned his armor and was fully adorned.
Honored with parched grain, perfumes, garlands, and by young maidens, he saluted the feet of Yudhiṣṭhira with joined palms; then,
having been smelled on the head by him, he ascended the great chariot.
Having heard the extensive blessings issued from the mouth of the King of Dharma,
he was filled with great joy and ascended that most excellent chariot. Then those horses, joyful, well-nourished, and swift as the wind, [proceeded].
The Saindhava horses, displaying their prowess, bore that invincible victor;
O King, just as those bay steeds formerly bore the chariot of Śakra,
even so did Bhīmasena, honored by the King of Dharma.
Having saluted Yudhiṣṭhira, he set out together with Sātyaki. Seeing those two subduers of enemies about to enter your army, all your warriors stood ready for battle, with Droṇa at their head.
Seeing Bhīma proceeding with his armor fastened, the heroic Sātyaki greeted him and then spoke these joy-inspiring words; then,
his limbs overwhelmed with joy, Sātyaki addressed Bhīma.
"O Bhīma, protect the king; for this is your most important duty. I shall break through and enter this army, which is already ripe for destruction by time.
Both for the future and for the present, the protection of the king is the highest good."
"You know my prowess, O subduer of enemies, and I know yours.
Therefore, Bhīma, turn back if you wish to do what is pleasing to me.
Thus addressed, he said to Sātyaki, "Go, for the accomplishment of your purpose."
"O best of men, I shall provide protection for the king.
Thus addressed, Mādhava replied to Bhīmasena:
"Go, go quickly, O Pārtha! Today my victory is certain."
"Since you, who are affectionate and devoted to me, now stand under my command,
and since these auspicious omens, O Bhīma, speak to me as they do;
therefore, when the wicked Saindhava has been slain by the high-souled Pāṇḍava,"
"I shall embrace the righteous king, of this there is no doubt;
you must also exercise vigilance toward the great car-warrior Droṇa.
Having said this much to Bhīma and dismissed him, the high-minded one—
He gazed upon your army like a tiger at a herd of deer. O lord of men, seeing him about to enter the host, your troops became once more bewildered and trembled violently.
Then, O King, at the command of Dharmarāja, that Sātyaki suddenly advanced with your army, desiring to see Arjuna. Saṃjaya said:
When Yuyudhāna had set out against your army with a desire for battle, O great king, Dharmarāja, surrounded by his own division,
advanced behind Yuyudhāna, seeking to reach Droṇa’s chariot.
Then, O King, when Mādhava had set out, the son of the Pāñcāla king, who is difficult to vanquish in battle,
and King Vasudāna cried out these words within the Pāṇḍava army.
"Come, strike, and rush forward quickly,
so that Satyaki, who is fierce in battle, may pass through with ease;
for many great car-warriors will strive to defeat him."
O great king, having heard the words of the commander-in-chief, the sons of Pāṇḍu advanced from all sides against your army on every side, crying out: "Slay!
Strike! Seize! Pierce! Put them to flight! Charge!"
Saying this, they rushed with speed toward your army; desiring to conquer us in turn, we charged against them,
making the sound of our arrows mingle with the blare of our conchs.
Seeing Yuyudhāna’s chariot, your men rushed toward it;
then a great clamor arose around Yuyudhāna’s chariot,
as your vast army trembled before your son.
O great king, it was split into a hundred pieces by the Sātvata. As it was being torn asunder, the grandson of Śini, a great car-warrior,
struck down seven heroic and mighty archers at the front of the army.
Then, O Indra among kings, he sent other lords of various realms—
those heroes— to the abode of Yama with arrows resembling fire;
he pierced one with a hundred and one with a hundred feathered shafts.

The Lord slaughtered those mounted on elephants and the elephants themselves, as well as those mounted on horses and the horses; he struck down the chariot-warriors along with their horses and charioteers like mere animals.
Thus did he perform wondrous deeds, raining down a torrential shower of arrows.
None of your soldiers indeed dared to charge against Sātyaki;
terrified and crushed by that long-armed hero,
those warriors abandoned the battlefield upon seeing his superhuman prowess.
Seeing that single hero as many, they were bewildered by his splendor as he moved fearlessly about, skilled in battle;
O noble one, with chariots whose axles were crushed and whose seats were broken.
O lord of the people, the ground was strewn with crushed and shattered wheels, fallen banners,
axle-trees, pennants, golden helmets,
and arms smeared with sandalwood paste and adorned with armlets.
O best of men, the earth was covered with the thighs of those people, which resembled the trunks of elephants and were like the coils of serpents;
and it was covered with faces resembling the moon, adorned with beautiful earrings.
O Bhārata, the earth shone with the fallen bull-eyed warriors;
and with elephants, mangled in many ways and lying there like mountains,
the ground gleamed intensely as if strewn with actual mountains.
Adorned with yokes made of refined gold, decorated with nets of pearls,
and with variegated breast-plates, the horses shone brightly;
though they had lost their lives upon reaching the earth, they were brushed clean by the long-armed one.
Having slain various kinds of troops, the Sātvata entered your army,
having utterly routed the host;
then he followed by that very same path by which Dhanañjaya had gone.
Sātyaki desired to advance, but he was then held back by Droṇa. However,
O Sire, having encountered the son of Bharadvāja, Yuyudhāna,
filled with rage, did not retreat, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
Having checked the great car-warrior Yuyudhāna in battle,
Droṇa pierced him with five sharp arrows capable of penetrating the vital organs.
But Sātyaki, O King, pierced Droṇa in that battle with seven arrows.

Droṇa struck him, along with his horses and charioteer, with six arrows that were gold-feathered, whetted on stone, and fletched with the plumes of herons and peacocks. The great car-warrior Yuyudhāna could not endure that act by Droṇa.
Then, letting out a lion’s roar, Sātyaki pierced Droṇa with ten arrows,
and again with six and eight others;
Yuyudhāna once more struck Droṇa with ten shafts.
With one arrow he pierced his charioteer, O noble one, with four the four horses, and with another single shaft he struck the standard in battle;
then Droṇa, with swift-flying arrows, [struck him] along with his horses, driver, chariot, and banner.
Hurrying, he covered him with arrows like swarms of locusts; likewise, Yuyudhāna, remaining unperturbed, covered Droṇa with many swift shafts,
whereupon Droṇa spoke.

But Droṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, being exceedingly enraged, covered Sātyaki— who possessed the prowess of Vāsudeva— with sharpened arrows. Having thus once more shrouded him with a vast net of shafts, he...
Droṇa, laughing, spoke these words to the descendant of Śini:
"Your preceptor has abandoned the battle and fled like a coward;
for, leaving me as I was fighting, he turned to his right."
"O Mādhava, as long as I am fighting today, you shall not escape from me alive,
unless you quickly abandon me in battle and flee like a preceptor.
Sātyaki said:

"By the command of Dharmarāja, I am going along the path of Dhanañjaya; may it be well with you, O Brahmin, let there be no delay for me. The path followed by the Teacher is always trodden by his disciples."
"Therefore, I shall proceed quickly in such a way that my preceptor has not already departed.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Śini bypassed the teacher.
Having set out in haste, O King, Droṇa spoke these words to his charioteer:
"Droṇa will exert every effort to restrain me;
therefore, O Sūta, proceed with vigilance in battle and listen to this further word of mine."
This army of the Āvantyas, possessing great splendor, is now being observed;
it is a vast force, impenetrable by even the greatest of heroic enemies. Immediately following this, however, is that mighty host of the Southerners.
Immediately after that, this great force of the Bāhlikas was stationed near the Bāhlikas; and there was also a great force belonging to Karṇa.
For these armies, O charioteer, were divided among one another.
Supporting one another, they will not abandon the field of battle;
having reached this complete position, a truly great force is seen.
Having reached this opening, urge on the horses with joy.
"O charioteer, maintaining a moderate speed, drive me there where the Bāhlikas are seen with various weapons raised,
and many Southerners led by the Sūta's son."
This army that is seen, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
and occupied by foot-soldiers gathered from various lands—
this great battle-array can then be broken suddenly in combat.
"Let us go quickly to that place, crushing our enemies in battle;
for there, being overjoyed, they have no desire to fight against us. Having encountered one who is alone and very weak, they will not fight."
"Having crushed their strength, I shall go while all the archers look on.
Having said this much, avoiding Brahmā,
the charioteer passed by where Karna’s formidable and very great army was stationed.
"Where these great car-warriors from the south, who are exceedingly enraged, are located.
Saṃjaya said:
"Having conquered them in battle, we shall then proceed against Dhanañjaya."
O King, having heard the words of Yuyudhāna, Yuyudhāna’s charioteer proceeded exactly as instructed, avoiding Droṇa in the battle. Enraged, Droṇa pursued him, scattering many arrows.
As the mighty-armed Yuyudhana advanced, never turning back,
he pierced that vast army and that force of the Southerners,
and having struck Karna’s great host with sharp arrows, he pressed on.
Having swiftly broken through Karṇa’s great army,
Sātyaki entered the boundless Bharata host;
for Satyaka then put that army to flight on all sides.
When Yuyudhāna had entered and the soldiers had fled,
and when that Bhārata army was routed and broken, O Bhārata,
the indignant Kṛtavarman surrounded Sātyaki.
Striking him as he charged with six arrows, the valiant Sātyaki quickly slew his four horses with four more. Then, once again, he struck him with sixteen swift, straight-knotted shafts.
Sātyaki pierced Kṛtavarman between the breasts;
being struck by those many sharp-pointed arrows from the Sātvata,
O great king, Kṛtavarman could not endure it.
Fitting an arrow shaped like a calf’s tooth, which resembled a winding serpent,
he drew it back to his ear, O King, and struck Sātyaki in the chest.
That shaft, having pierced through his armor and his body, [entered the earth].

With its feathers and shaft intact, the arrow, drenched in blood, entered the earth. Then, O King, Kṛtavarman, a master of supreme weapons, severed his bow along with the string and arrows using many shafts of his own.

And in that battle, O King, filled with rage, he pierced Sātyaki of true prowess in the center of the chest with ten sharp arrows. Then, his bow having been shattered, that best of the powerful struck him with a spear.
Sātyaki struck Kṛtavarman’s right arm;
then, taking up another very firm bow, the hero Sātyaki swiftly discharged arrows by the hundreds and thousands.
Those arrows, discharged by the Sātvata in battle,
covered Kṛtavarman like noisy locusts covering a tree;
they completely enveloped Kṛtavarman along with his chariot from every side.
Having completely overwhelmed the son of Hṛdika in battle,
Sātyaki then severed the head of his charioteer with a broad-headed arrow;
that slain driver fell from the great chariot of the son of Hṛdika.
Then, their driver having been slain, those horses fled away in great haste.
Thereupon, the Bhoja king, remaining unperturbed, himself reined in the horses and stood with bow and arrows in hand; the troops applauded him.
Having rested for a mere moment, he urged on his excellent horses;
free from fear, he brought great terror to his enemies.
Then Sātyaki approached him, and he in turn rushed toward Bhīma.
O Indra among kings, Yuyudhāna also, having emerged from Droṇa’s army,
proceeded swiftly and with great haste toward the vast host of the Kambojas.
There, he was hemmed in by many heroic great-chariot warriors.
Then, O King, Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth, did not waver.
Having arrayed his army and entrusted the burden to the Bhoja king, Droṇa,
exerting himself in battle with a desire to fight, pursued Yuyudhāna.
As he was thus pursuing Yuyudhāna from behind,
the greatest warriors in the Pāṇḍava army, filled with rage, checked him.
Having encountered the son of Hṛdika, that foremost of chariot-warriors, they surrounded his excellent chariot.
O King, the Pāñcālas, led by Bhīmasena, were deprived of their energy;
though they exerted themselves, they were held back by the heroic Kṛtavarman.
All of them, striving yet somewhat disheartened, were thus restrained.
He checked them on all sides with a torrent of arrows, leaving their mounts exhausted. Though held back by Bhoja in battle, those heroes,
desiring the glory of the Bhoja army and seeking great fame, stood firm like noble men.
Even when prepared for battle, they were unable even to look upon the son of Hṛdika.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Thus was the army of many kinds, thus well-selected and excellent."
O Sañjaya, this army is thus arrayed according to rule, vast in number,
and always honored by us; it is ever eager for battle, mature, of most wondrous appearance, and possessed of firm prowess from the very outset.
Neither too old nor a child, neither emaciated nor too corpulent, with limbs that are light, well-rounded, long, and full of strength, free from disease,
equipped with armor, and provided with many weapons and accoutrements.

He was thoroughly proficient in many sciences concerning the handling of weapons, and skilled in mounting, leaping down, charging, jumping with intervals, striking accurately, advancing, and retreating.

He has been tested many times with elephants, horses, and chariots; he is skilled in combat with shield and sword, as well as in hand-to-hand wrestling. Having been examined according to the proper method, he has been provided with his wages.

In my army, there was no one who was not a member of a social circle, nor one who was not treated with courtesy, nor one who was not related by kinship; indeed, there was no one who had not been summoned or who had not received pay.
It was filled with men of noble birth and virtuous character, contented, well-nourished, and free from arrogance.
O dear one, he had performed services with honor, was illustrious and high-minded, and was protected by many other eminent ministers of preeminent deeds—
men who were like the guardians of the world and the best among men.
It was protected by many kings who desired to do us a favor, who had followed us out of affection along with their armies and followers;
it was like the great ocean filled from all sides by rivers.

Filled with chariots resembling birds though they lacked wings, and crowded with horses and great elephants with temples flowing with ichor— when my army was thus slaughtered, what else could it be but the work of destiny?
It was a formidable ocean with soldiers for its inexhaustible waters and mounts for its surging waves;
it was teeming with missiles, swords, maces, spears, arrows,
and darts as its fish, crowded with banners and ornaments, and filled with jeweled cloths.
Even with their mounts galloping,
they agitated that deep ocean whose bottom was Droṇa, which had Kṛtavarman as its great lake,
Jalasaṃdha as its massive crocodile, and which was stirred by the rising moon of Karṇa, trembling with the force of the wind.
When that bull among the Pāṇḍavas has swiftly broken through the ocean of my army,
and when Yuyudhana has entered with his single chariot, O Sañjaya,
I see no remnant remaining there once Savyasācin has penetrated it.

O Sañjaya, when those two powerful ones, having seen the king of Sindhu within the range of the arrows of the Gāṇḍīva, had bypassed him and were advancing toward the noble car-warrior Sātvata and my army, they appeared fearless.
What did the Kurus do then, impelled by time? How did they conduct themselves in that terrible and singular hour?
For I consider the Kauravas, O dear one, to have been already swallowed by death when they encountered it.
Indeed, their prowess in battle is not seen today as it once was;
for Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava have entered that fray unscathed,
and there is no one here, O Sañjaya, who can restrain them.
Many warriors have been maintained as great chariot-fighters after being thoroughly tested;
some by appropriate wages and others by kind words. My army, my dear son, contains no one who is maintained without cause.
"For one receives food and wages in accordance with one's own deeds.
Yet, O Sañjaya, there was not a single warrior in my army who had been maintained by me on a small stipend,
nor was there any man hired for wages in exchange for base metals, my dear."
For they were honored by me according to my ability with gifts, honors, and seats;
and likewise, O dear one, by my sons, kinsmen, and relatives.
Yet, as soon as they encountered Savyasācin in battle, they were utterly defeated by him.
"O Sañjaya, when they were seized by the descendant of Śini, what else could it have been but destiny? Whether one is protected in battle or those who are the protectors,
there is but one common path for the one being protected along with his guards."
Seeing Arjuna standing at the front of the ruler of the Sindhus in battle,
what did my son, utterly bewildered, do?
And seeing Sātyaki entering the fray in battle like one fearless, what did he do?
What did Duryodhana consider to be the duty appropriate for the moment, seeing those two best of chariot-warriors, who surpass all weapons, having entered the army? Indeed,
what resolve did my men adopt in battle upon seeing them?
Having seen Kṛṣṇa of the Daśārhas stationed for the sake of Arjuna,
and likewise the bull of the Śinis, I believe my sons are grieving,
seeing the army bypassed by the Sātvata and by Arjuna.
Seeing the Kurus fleeing, I believe my sons grieve;
seeing the chariot-warriors scattered and devoid of energy for victory over the enemy,
I believe my sons grieve as they become intent on flight.
Seeing the seats of their chariots made empty by the Sātvata Arjuna,
and seeing the warriors slain, my sons surely grieve;
they see there thousands of heroes deprived of their horses, elephants, and chariots.
I think my sons grieve for those who are running about distracted in battle;
they grieve for the horses deprived of their riders and the men deprived of their chariots by Sātyaki and Pārtha. It is there that my sons grieve.
Seeing the great elephants fleeing, struck by Arjuna’s arrows—
some fallen and others falling— I believe my sons are grieving,
seeing the throngs of horses slain and being driven away in every direction.
In battle, I believe my sons grieve because of the two Sātvatas and Pārtha;
seeing the throngs of foot-soldiers fleeing in every direction,
I believe all my sons have lost hope for victory and are grieving.

Having seen those two heroes in an instant having bypassed Droṇa’s army unvanquished, I believe my sons are grieving. O dear one, I am utterly bewildered upon hearing that Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya have passed through.

The two Acyutas, together with the Sātvata, have entered my army. Now that the preeminent chariot of the Śinīs has entered the host and passed through the Bhoja division, how indeed did the Kauravas fare?

When the Pāṇḍavas had been thus held in check in battle by Droṇa, how did the combat proceed there? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya. For Droṇa is powerful, a hero, skilled in weapons, and firm in his prowess.

How did the Pāñcālas, who were bound by enmity toward Droṇa and desiring victory for Dharmarāja, fight back against that great archer in battle? Likewise, the great car-warrior Bhāradvāja was also engaged in hostilities with them.
"Tell me everything that Arjuna did regarding the slaying of the King of the Sindhus, for you are skilled in narration, O Sañjaya. Sañjaya said:
O bull among the Bharatas, having encountered this calamity born of your own transgression,
you ought not to grieve like an ordinary man, O hero—
especially when you were previously admonished by wise friends such as Vidura and others.
"O King, you did not hear those words: 'Do not destroy the Pāṇḍavas!
Indeed, he who does not listen to the speech of well-wishing friends who desire his welfare, having encountered great calamity, surely grieves just as you do."
O King, in the past you were entreated by the descendant of Daśārha for peace,
yet the highly illustrious Kṛṣṇa did not obtain that desire from you,
because he recognized your lack of virtue and your partiality toward your own sons.
O best of kings, having understood your duplicity regarding dharma, your envy toward the Pāṇḍavas, and your crooked intention directed against them,
[I heard] many piteous lamentations.
The knower of the truth of all the worlds, the teacher of all the worlds,
and the Lord Vāsudeva then waged a great war against the Kurus.
This vast destruction that you have suffered has come about through your own great transgression.

O giver of honor, you ought not thus to find fault with Duryodhana; for no good deed of yours is seen in the beginning, in the middle, or at the end, O Bhārata, since this defeat has its root in you alone.
"O King, these piteous lamentations that you now utter here are not fitting for one as aged as you, like the circling of a dying man. Therefore,
becoming firm today and understanding the final destiny of the world— "
Listen to how that terrible battle, resembling the conflict between the gods and the asuras,
took place. When the grandson of Śini, whose prowess is truth, had entered your army,
the Pārthas, led by Bhīmasena, advanced against your host.
As those [Pāṇḍavas], accompanied by their followers, suddenly approached with wrathful forms,
the great car-warrior Kṛtavarman alone held them back in battle,
just as the shore holds back the surging ocean of waters.
Just as the shore always restrains the surging ocean,
so did the son of Hṛdika hold back the Pāṇḍava army in battle;
there, they marveled at the extraordinary prowess of the son of Hṛdika.
Because the Pārthas together could not overcome him in battle,
Bhīma, the mighty-armed, having pierced Kṛtavarman with three iron arrows,
blew his conch shell, gladdening all the Pāṇḍavas.
Sahadeva pierced him with twenty arrows, Dharmarāja with five, and Nakula also struck the son of Hṛdika with a hundred.
The sons of Draupadī pierced him with seventy-three, and Ghaṭotkaca with seven.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna also struck Kṛtavarman with three arrows;
Virāṭa, Drupada, and the son of Yājñasenī each struck him with five.
And Śikhaṇḍin, having pierced the son of Hṛdika with five swift shafts, [attacked him].
Piercing him again with twenty arrows as if laughing,
O King, Kṛtavarman then struck each of those great car-warriors from all sides with five arrows and pierced Bhīma with seven.

With great effort, he felled both the bow and the standard from the chariot to the ground. Then, the great car-warrior, acting with haste and filled with rage, struck him— whose bow was shattered— in the chest with seventy sharpened arrows.
Deeply pierced by the excellent arrows of Hārdikya, that powerful warrior,
standing in the midst of his chariot, trembled like a mountain during an earthquake.
Seeing Bhīmasena in such a state, those led by Dharmarāja [approached].
Discharging terrible arrows, they afflicted Kṛtavarman;
having thus hemmed him in with a line of chariots, O noble one,
they joyfully pierced him with shafts in that battle for the sake of protecting the son of the Wind-god.
Then, having regained consciousness, the mighty Bhīmasena seized an iron spear with a golden shaft in that battle and swiftly hurled it from his chariot toward the chariot of Kṛtavarman.
Released from Bhīma’s arm, resembling a snake that has cast off its skin,
that most dreadful weapon blazed fiercely toward Kṛtavarman as it suddenly descended with a radiance like the fire at the end of an eon.
Then, with two arrows, the son of Hṛdika cut that gold-adorned spear in two; severed, O King, it fell to the earth,
illuminating the quarters like a great meteor fallen from the sky.
Seeing his spear destroyed, Bhīma became exceedingly enraged. Then, taking up another bow that was powerful and made a great sound,
the furious Bhīmasena held back the son of Hṛdika in battle.
Then, O King, Bhīma of terrible strength, due to your evil counsel, struck him between the breasts with five arrows. But Bhoja,
O noble one, had all his limbs wounded by Bhīmasena.
He shone upon the field of battle like a red *aśoka* tree in full bloom.
Then, as if laughing, the enraged [Duryodhana] struck Bhīmasena with three arrows in the fight and pierced all of them back in return.
The great archer [Droṇa] pierced those striving mahārathas with three arrows each;
they, in turn, pierced him back with seven arrows each.
Then the great car-warrior, enraged at Śikhaṇḍin, struck him with a razor-headed arrow.
O Bhārata, as if laughing in the midst of battle, he severed the bow;
then Śikhaṇḍin, enraged that his bow was cut,
quickly seized a sword and a radiant shield adorned with a hundred moons in the encounter.
Having whirled his great shield adorned with gold,
he hurled that sword toward the chariot of Kṛtavarman—
[and also] that sword of great luster.
Aiming at Kṛtavarman, he quickly dispatched that sword.
That great sword, having severed his bow along with its arrows in the battle,
O King, fell to the earth like a celestial body fallen from the sky.
At that very moment, however, the great car-warriors, acting with haste,
pierced Kṛtavarman deeply with their arrows in the battle.
Then, casting aside that great bow, he took up another bow.
O best of the Bharatas, Hārdikya, the slayer of enemy heroes, pierced the shattered Pāṇḍavas in battle with three straight-flying arrows each,
and he also pierced Śikhaṇḍin with three and five arrows.
Again, with another arrow, he swiftly cut his bow;
having pierced Śikhaṇḍin with three arrows, he severed his bow as well.
But the highly illustrious Śikhaṇḍin, taking up another bow—
With swift arrows having claws like tortoises, he warded off the son of Hṛdika.
Then, O King, the enraged son of Hṛdika rushed with speed toward the great car-warrior Yājñaseni in battle.
O King, displaying his strength in battle as the cause of the high-souled Bhīṣma’s death, that hero was like a tiger attacking an elephant;
those two were like the elephants of the quarters, or like two blazing fires.
Those two subduers of enemies encountered one another with volleys of arrows,
brandishing their excellent bows, fixing their shafts,
and discharging them by the hundreds like two suns emitting their rays.
Scorching each other with sharp arrows, those two great car-warriors,
heroes resembling the end of an eon, shone like two suns.
Kṛtavarman, however, [assailed] the impetuous great car-warrior Yājñaseni.
Having pierced him with seventy-three arrows, he struck him again with seven. Deeply pierced and pained, he sat down on the floor of his chariot,
dropping his bow and arrow as he was overwhelmed by a swoon.
O bull of the Bharatas, seeing him despondent on his chariot,
your warriors honored the son of Hṛdika and waved their garments.
Likewise, perceiving Śikhaṇḍin to be afflicted by the arrows of the son of Hṛdika, they cheered him on.

The charioteer, hurrying, bore the great car-warrior away from the battle. Seeing Śikhaṇḍin collapsed upon the seat of the chariot, the Pārthas quickly surrounded Kṛtavarman with their chariots in the combat.
There, the great car-warrior Kṛtavarman performed a supreme marvel,
in that he alone held back the Pārthas along with their followers in battle.
Having defeated the Pārthas, he then conquered the Cedis, the Pañcālas, and the Sṛñjayas as well.
And the great car-warrior Kṛtavarman [slew] the highly heroic Kekayas;
being slaughtered in battle by the son of Hṛdika, those Pāṇḍavas fled here and there and could find no steadiness in the fight.
Having defeated the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle, led by Bhīmasena,
the son of Hṛdika stood firm in the fray like a smokeless fire.
Those great car-warriors, being put to flight in the encounter by the son of Hṛdika, [fled].
Afflicted by showers of arrows, they turned away;
bowing their heads in shame, they said nothing at all.
Sañjaya said:
Listen with a focused mind, O King, to that which you ask me:
while that army was being routed by the high-souled son of Hṛdika,
it was bowed down with shame, and your men were filled with joy.
That island which had been for the Pāṇḍavas, who sought a foothold in the bottomless deep—
having heard the terrible roar of your men in that great battle,
O King, the grandson of Śini quickly rushed toward Kṛtavarman.
Filled with rage and indignation, he spoke there to his charioteer:
"O Sūta, drive my excellent chariot toward the son of Hṛdika!
Behold, filled with wrath, he is slaughtering the Pāṇḍava army."
"O charioteer, having conquered him, I shall proceed again toward victory.
When these words had been spoken, O high-minded one,
the charioteer approached Kṛtavarman in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, being greatly enraged, covered the descendant of Śini with sharpened arrows;
thereupon Sātyaki became incensed.
Then the descendant of Śini [discharged] a very sharp broad-headed arrow at Kṛtavarman.
In that battle, he dispatched four other arrows;
they slew his horses, and with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla), he cut off his bow. Then, with sharpened arrows, he pierced his rear-guard and his charioteer.

Then, having deprived him of his chariot, Sātyaki, whose valor is truth, afflicted his army with straight-knotted arrows. Thereupon, that host, tormented by the arrows of Śini’s descendant, broke apart.
Making every effort to flee and wandering here and there,
he then departed in haste;
listen, O King, to what that hero of true prowess did among your troops.
O Great King, having crossed that vast ocean of Droṇa’s army and having joyfully defeated Kṛtavarman in battle,
the hero spoke to his charioteer with composure, saying, "Proceed slowly."
Having seen that army of yours, crowded with chariots, horses, and elephants,
and filled with foot soldiers, he spoke again to his charioteer:
"That force which resembles a cloud and is to the left of Droṇa’s division..."
This vast army of elephants, with Rukmaratha at its head—
these many warriors, O charioteer, are difficult to repel in battle;
commanded by Duryodhana, they have renounced their lives for my sake.
"O charioteer, all these princes are great archers and valiant warriors;
indeed, without first conquering them in battle, it is not possible to reach Jayadratha.
Nor, O Sūta, is it possible for me to reach Pārtha by any means whatsoever."
These stand together here, all of them perfected in the sciences;
they are the noble chariot-warriors of the Trigartas, with banners adorned with gold.
These heroes are stationed facing me alone, ready to fight.
"O charioteer, urge the horses forward quickly; take me there at once.
I shall fight with the Trigartas while the son of Bharadvāja looks on.
Then the charioteer, abiding by the will of the Sātvata, proceeded slowly.
Excellent horses, obedient to the charioteer, carried him in a radiant chariot colored like the sun and adorned with banners;
in battle, they were equal to the speed of the wind and possessed the luster of kunda flowers, the moon, and silver.
Resembling the moon or jasmine and auspicious, they were equal to the wind in speed;
then, as that chariot approached drawn by excellent horses the color of conch shells,
the heroes surrounded it on all sides with a division of elephants.
Scattering various sharp arrows that pierced with ease,
the Sātvata also fought the elephant army with whetted shafts,
like a great cloud at the end of the summer heat raining upon mountains.
Struck by arrows whose touch was like the thunderbolt, the elephants fled,
abandoning the battle, driven by the prowess of Śini’s descendant; their tusks shattered, drenched in blood, and their frontal globes split open.
With their ears, mouths, and trunks shattered, deprived of their drivers and banners, with their armor and bells broken and their great standards cut down,
O King, those elephants— deprived of their riders and fallen blankets— fled in all directions.
Uttering various cries with sounds like those of rain-clouds,
they were torn apart by the Sātvata with iron shafts, calf-toothed arrows, broad-headed missiles,
and *añjalika* arrows.
Wounded by razor-edged arrows and crescent-shaped shafts,
they fled in all directions, vomiting blood, urine, and excrement;
some wandered aimlessly, others stumbled, while still others fell down and fainted.
Thus was that elephant division struck down by Yuyudhāna;
with arrows resembling fire and the sun, it fled in every direction.
When that elephant host had fled, the great car-warrior Jalasandha [advanced].
Exerting himself, he guided the elephant toward the chariot drawn by silver horses; that hero, radiant as gold, wearing golden armlets, pure,
adorned with earrings, a crown, and a conch-shell, was smeared with red sandalwood paste.
His limbs were smeared with red sandalwood paste; he wore armlets and earrings,
bore upon his head a blazing garland made of gold,
and across his chest he wore a golden *niṣka* ornament and a radiant necklace.

O great king, brandishing his gold-adorned bow upon the head of the elephant, he shone like a rain-cloud charged with lightning. As that preeminent elephant of the Magadha king was suddenly charging toward him—
Sātyaki held him back, as the shore holds back the surging ocean. Seeing the elephant restrained by the excellent arrows of Śini’s grandson,
O King, the mighty Jalasandha grew enraged in battle.
