O King, he brought the immensely powerful king of elephants down in battle. Then, though being warded off by the flood of arrows from Śini’s grandson, that valiant and great archer became enraged and [struck] with shafts capable of accomplishing any task.
Jalasandha pierced the grandson of Śini in the great chest;
Satyaka, as if laughing, pierced him back with sharpened arrows.
Then, with another yellow, whetted *bhalla*-arrow, he struck him.
As the hero of the Vṛṣṇis was shooting,
[the Māgadha] cut his bow; O Bhārata, the heroic ruler of Magadha, as if laughing at Sātyaki whose bow had been severed, pierced him with five sharpened arrows.

Though pierced by many arrows by Jalasandha, that valiant one of mighty arms did not tremble; that was like a marvel. Indeed, the powerful hero did not give much thought to those shafts due to his lack of agitation.
Taking up another bow, he said, "Stay! Stay!
Having said this much, the descendant of Śini, as if laughing, pierced Jalasandha very deeply in his great chest with sixty arrows.
With a sharp, yellowed razor-headed arrow,
he cut Jalasandha’s great bow at the handle and pierced him with three shafts.
Jalasandha, for his part, cast aside that bow along with the arrow.
O noble one, he swiftly hurled a lance at Sātyaki. In that great battle, it pierced the left arm of Mādhava and entered the earth like a terrible, hissing great serpent.
When his left arm had been pierced, Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth,
struck Jalasaṃdha with thirty sharp arrows.
Then, seizing a sword, the mighty Jalasaṃdha—
Then, brandishing a great bull-hide shield adorned with a hundred moons and that sword, he hurled them at the Sātvata. Having severed the bow of Śini’s grandson, that sword fell to the earth.
Having descended to the earth, it shone like a whirling circle of fire,
like a wheel of flame cast down from the sky;
then the sword, having reached the surface of the ground, blazed forth.
Then, taking up another bow capable of rending all bodies,
Mādhava looked toward Jalasandha and smiled;
that bow resembled the trunk of a *śāla* tree and possessed a sound like Indra’s thunderbolt.

Drawing his bow, the enraged one pierced Jalasandha with an arrow. Then, the best of the Mādhus, as if laughing, severed Jalasandha’s two arms— adorned with ornaments and armlets— using two razor-sharp shafts.
Those two arms, resembling iron clubs, fell from that best of elephants like five-headed serpents fallen from the earth-supporting mountain.
Then [he beheld] his head, with fine tusks, a handsome jaw, beautiful earrings, and a prominent nose.
With his third razor-sharp arrow, Sātyaki severed his head.
That headless trunk, with its arms still outstretched and terrifying to behold,
drenched Jalasandha’s elephant in blood.
O lord of the people, having slain Jalasandha in battle, the Sātvata warrior acted with haste and struck down the Nishāda prince from the shoulder of his elephant;
he then overwhelmed both the headless trunk and the elephant with showers of arrows.
With his limbs drenched in blood, Jalasandha’s elephant bore a magnificent seat that was clinging and hanging down;
afflicted by the arrows of the Sātvata, it continued to crush its own army.
Uttering a terrible cry of distress, the great elephant fled;
O sire, a great wail of "Alas!
Alas! arose among your troops upon seeing Jalasandha slain by that bull among the Vṛṣṇis.
Your warriors, turning their faces away and intent on flight, fled in every direction,
having lost all enthusiasm for conquering the enemy.
In that interval, O King, Drona, the best among wielders of weapons, [advanced].
O Bhārata, having laid down that immense burden upon Kṛtavarman,
for he alone, possessed of great strength, held back the striving Pārthas in battle;
[Duryodhana] then advanced against the great car-warrior Yuyudhāna with swift horses.
Seeing Jalasandha slain, your son, that bull among the Kurus,
joined by his brothers, rushed against Sātyaki;
then a battle ensued between the Kurus and the son of Satyaka.
Seeing the descendant of Śini thus exalted, the bulls among the Kurus,
filled with rage along with Droṇa himself, surrounded Sātyaki.
Then a battle commenced between the Kurus and the Sātvata.
And the battle between Droṇa and [the Sātvata], O King, was terrible, like that between the gods and the Asuras.
Saṃjaya said:
Having witnessed the deeds of the Sātvata hero in battle, the great car-warriors [prepared] to fight.
Unable to endure him, they prepared for battle and rushed toward the descendant of Śini.
O Great King, all those strikers, exerting themselves and discharging showers of arrows, swiftly fought against Yuyudhāna.
Droṇa struck him with seventy-seven sharpened arrows;
Durmarṣaṇa with twelve, Duḥsaha with ten arrows,
and Vikarṇa also with thirty sharpened, heron-feathered shafts.
Durmukha pierced him on the left side and between the breasts with ten arrows, while Duḥśāsana pierced him with eight;
and Citrasena, O sire, pierced the descendant of Śini with two arrows.
And Duryodhana, O King, afflicted Mādhava in battle with a great shower of arrows,
as did other heroic great-chariot warriors;
thus pierced on all sides by your sons, those great-chariot warriors, [he remained steadfast].
Though he was thus being pierced on all sides by those bulls among the Kurus,
the descendant of Śini pierced each of them in turn with straight-flying arrows;
for Sātyaki, whose eyes are like lotuses, was perfectly accomplished in the use of weapons.
He struck Bhāradvāja with three arrows, Duḥsaha with nine,
Vikarṇa with twenty-five, and Citrasena with seven;
[then] Citrasena with ten and Vikarṇa with twenty-five.
He pierced Durmarṣaṇa with twelve arrows, Viviṃśati with four,
Satyavrata with nine, and Vijaya with ten shafts; then,
having struck Duryodhana with three well-feathered arrows of fierce energy.
Then the great car-warrior Sātyaki, brandishing his bow adorned with golden armlets, quickly advanced against your son, the great car-warrior,
the king of all the world and the best among all wielders of weapons.
He struck him deeply with arrows, and then a battle ensued between the two;
then the combat proceeded between the Kuru hero and the Mādhava hero,
as they discharged sharp shafts and fixed their arrows to the bowstrings.
Those two great car-warriors made themselves invisible to one another in the battle.
Pierced by the Kuru king, Sātyaki shone brilliantly;
he flowed with copious blood like sandalwood exuding its natural sap.
Pierced by the floods of arrows from the Sātvata, your son,
with his golden crest-ornament, shone like a lofty sacrificial post.
But Mādhava, O King, in that battle [overwhelmed] the archer king of the Kurus.
With a razor-sharp arrow, as if smiling, he suddenly severed his bow;
then, he overwhelmed that one whose bow was broken with many arrows. And he was pierced by those arrows from that swift-acting enemy.
The king could not tolerate the enemy’s display of victory in battle.
Then, taking up another formidable bow with a golden back,
he swiftly pierced Sātyaki with a hundred arrows.
Pierced deeply by your powerful archer son,
he was overcome by indignation and afflicted your son in return.
Seeing the king thus tormented, your sons, those great chariot-warriors, [rushed forward].
They immediately covered the Sātvata with a rain of arrows.
Being thus covered by many of your sons, who were great car-warriors,
he pierced each one of them with five arrows and then struck them again with seven.
He quickly pierced Duryodhana with eight swift arrows,
and laughing, he cut asunder his bow that struck terror into his enemies;
then, with his shafts, he brought down the jewel-encrusted elephant-standard.
Having slain the four horses with four sharpened arrows,
the highly illustrious one struck down the charioteer with a razor-edged shaft.
In that very interval, [he targeted] the great car-warrior, the king of the Kurus.
Delighted, he covered him with many arrows capable of piercing the vital organs.
Being struck in that battle by the excellent arrows of Śini’s grandson,
O King, your son Duryodhana suddenly fled.
Having leaped onto the chariot of the archer Citrasena, the world broke out into cries of "Alas! Alas! upon seeing the king being swallowed by Sātyaki in battle, like the moon in the sky by Rāhu.
Hearing that great sound, the mighty car-warrior Kṛtavarman suddenly advanced to where the lord Mādhava was stationed,
brandishing his excellent bow and urging on his horses.
Urging his fierce charioteer with haste, "Go! Go!
he rebuked him. O great king, seeing him rushing toward him like Death himself with gaping jaws, Yuyudhāna spoke thus to his driver:
"Kṛtavarman is rushing swiftly toward us with his chariot, discharging arrows. Go out against him on your chariot—he is the foremost of all archers.
O charioteer, proceed quickly with the chariot toward that best of car-warriors."
"I shall slay that Vṛṣṇi hero, the subduer of enemies, in battle. Then,
with his horses galloping and his chariot equipped according to rule,
he approached the Bhoja king, the peerless standard of all archers, in the fray.
Then those two tigers among men, exceedingly enraged and like two blazing fires, encountered each other with great speed like two powerful tigers.
Kṛtavarman, however, struck the descendant of Śini with twenty-six arrows.
With seven sharp, whetted arrows he pierced his charioteer;
with four supreme shafts, he struck the four noble Saindhava horses of the Sātvata hero, which were well-trained.
Having drawn his great bow, which had a golden back and a golden banner,
he— adorned with golden armlets and clad in golden armor— scattered gold-tufted arrows. Then the grandson of Śini [Śatānīka] discharged eighty shafts at Kṛtavarman.
Filled with haste and desiring to see Dhananjaya, he dispatched [the arrow]. Deeply pierced by his powerful enemy, that scorcher of foes,
though difficult to withstand, trembled like a mountain during an earthquake.
O noble one, he who was formerly immovable now trembled;
Satyaki swiftly pierced Kṛtavarman’s four horses with sixty-three arrows and his charioteer with seven sharp shafts.
To him who stood upon the chariot whose horses and charioteer had been slain, that bull among the Śinis,
Satyaki, fixed a gold-feathered shaft and discharged it—
blazing like a highly enraged serpent.
Sātyaka, that bull among men, dispatched an arrow at the son of Hṛdika;
that shaft, resembling the staff of Yama, entered Kṛtavarman after piercing through his radiant armor adorned with gold.
Having pierced through Kṛtavarman’s armor adorned with gold,
that fierce warrior, drenched in blood, fell to the earth;
struck by the arrows of the Sātvata, he was covered in gore upon the battlefield.

Releasing his bow as he reeled, he fell from that excellent chariot; that bull among men, Siṃhadaṃṣṭra of immeasurable prowess, afflicted by Sātyaki’s arrows, collapsed upon his knees onto the floor of the chariot.
Having warded off Kṛtavarman— who was like the thousand-armed one and as unshakeable as the ocean— Sātyaki then advanced;
for indeed, O Bhārata, Pārtha could not prevail over him in battle by any means whatsoever.
Desirous of seeing him, he indeed set out with speed for where Dhanañjaya was;
though obstructed there by the kṣatriyas according to their strength, that most powerful Sātvata fought on, O King, longing to see the son of Pāṇḍu.
Strewn with swords, spears, and bows, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and flowing with fierce blood from hundreds of the best of Kṣatriyas,
the bull of the Śinis passed through the midst of all the watching armies.
Having pierced the army like the slayer of Vṛtra piercing the host of the Asuras, the son of Hṛdika took heart; then, seizing another great bow,
that powerful warrior stood right there in battle, holding back the Pāṇḍavas.
07,093.001 Saṃjaya said:
07,093.001a While the troops were being driven hither and thither by the grandson of Śini,
the son of Bharadvāja covered them with great showers of arrows.
That tumultuous clash between Droṇa and the Sātvata took place while all the troops looked on, like the encounter between Bali and Vāsava;
a most fierce battle commenced that caused the hair to stand on end.
O king of kings, between the descendant of Śini and the son of Bharadvāja— between those two—
Droṇa then pierced the grandson of Śini in the forehead with three variegated arrows made entirely of iron, which resembled venomous serpents.

O great king, with those straight-flying arrows fixed in his forehead, Yuyudhāna shone like a mountain with three peaks. Then [he discharged] other arrows at him, whose sound was like Indra’s thunderbolt.
Bharadvāja, seeking his weak point,
dispatched those arrows in the encounter; but Dāśārha, the supreme knower of weapons, cut down those shafts as they fell from Droṇa’s bow with two well-feathered arrows each.
O lord of the people, observing that lightness of hand of his, Droṇa laughed and suddenly pierced the bull of the Śinis with twenty arrows;
he then struck him again with fifty and a hundred more.
Excelling Yuyudhāna’s own agility with his own lightness,
O King, body-piercing arrows flew from Droṇa’s chariot like enraged great serpents emerging from an anthill.
In the same way, O noble one, hundreds of thousands of blood-drinking arrows released by Yuyudhāna covered Droṇa’s chariot,
owing to the swiftness of both the foremost of the twice-born and the Sātvata.
We could perceive no difference between those two bulls among men as they stood facing each other.
Then Sātyaki, violently enraged, struck Droṇa with nine straight-knotted arrows and his standard with sharpened shafts.
While Bhāradvāja looked on, having struck the charioteer with a hundred arrows,
the great car-warrior Droṇa, beholding the lightness of hand of Yuyudhāna,
pierced Sātyaki with seventy shafts and his horses with three each.
With one arrow he pierced the banner standing upon Mādhava’s chariot;
then, with another feathered shaft, gold-tufted and broad-headed,
he cut through the bow of the high-souled Mādhava in that battle.

Then the great car-warrior Sātyaki, filled with rage, cast aside his bow and seized a massive mace, which he hurled at the son of Bharadvāja. As that iron mace, bound with cloth bands, came rushing down suddenly—
Droṇa warded him off with many arrows of various forms; then Satyaki, whose valor is truth, took up another bow and pierced the heroic son of Bharadvāja with many stone-sharpened shafts.
Having pierced Droṇa in battle, he let out a lion’s roar;
Drona, the best among all wielders of weapons, could not endure that.
Then, seizing an iron spear with a golden shaft, [he hurled it].
With great speed, he hurled it toward the chariot of Mādhava.
But failing to reach the descendant of Śini, that fierce spear, resembling Time itself,
pierced the chariot and entered the earth with a terrible sound.
Then, O King, the grandson of Śini pierced Droṇa with a feathered shaft,
striking his right arm and afflicting him, O bull of the Bharatas;
even so did the Mādhava, O great king, as if afflicting the Brāhmaṇa.

O King, in that battle Droṇa also cut through the great bow of the Mādhava with a crescent-headed arrow and struck down his charioteer with a chariot-spear. Struck by that chariot-spear, the charioteer of the [Mādhava] fell into a swoon.
Having reached the seat of the chariot, he sat there for a moment;
O King, Sātyaki then performed a superhuman feat:
he fought with Droṇa and himself took up the reins.
Then, O lord of the people, the great car-warrior Yuyudhāna, appearing joyful in battle, pierced the Brahmin with a hundred arrows. At him,
O Bhārata, Droṇa dispatched five shafts.
Having pierced through his armor, they drank his blood in the battle. Pierced by those terrible arrows, Sātyaki became exceedingly enraged;
the hero then discharged shafts toward the one with the golden chariot.

Then, having struck down Droṇa’s charioteer to the earth with a single arrow, he put to flight the horses of that high-souled one with his shafts, their driver having been slain. That chariot, fleeing in battle, described thousands of circles.
O King, he acted like a blazing sun against the king;
then, having slain Drona’s charioteer, he struck him down from the chariot,
and the red-horsed steeds, seizing the vehicle, fled in every direction.
"Attack! Seize them! Run toward Droṇa's horses!"—thus did all the princes, together with the kings, cry out. O King, those great car-warriors quickly left Sātyaki behind in the battle.
From where Drona was, they all suddenly rushed forward.
Seeing them all fleeing, afflicted by the arrows of the Satvata hero,
your army once again became broken and utterly disordered.
Having reached the very gate of the array once more, Droṇa took his stand;
yet, afflicted by the arrows of the Vṛṣṇi, he was carried away by those horses that moved like the wind.
Beholding the array shattered by the Pāṇḍavas and the Pañcālas, the valiant hero [remained firm].
He made no effort to protect the array itself against the descendant of Śini; instead,
having held back the Pāṇḍus and Pañcālas, Drona— like a fire consuming everything—
stood there, inflamed by the fire of his wrath like the sun risen at the end of time.
Saṃjaya said:
Having thus defeated Droṇa and those on your side headed by the son of Hṛdika, that hero among men—
Smiling, the hero of the Śinis, the foremost of the Kuru bulls, spoke these words to the charioteer: "O charioteer,
we are here merely as instruments."
"Let us slay here those who have already been scorched by Keśava and Phalguna, and struck down by that bull among men born from the self of the Lord of the Gods."
"Accompanied by Bhīma and the son of Pṛṣata, I shall slay those who have already been struck down by the wearer of the diadem.
Having spoken thus to him, the bull of the Śinis then—
In that great battle, that powerful slayer of foes and foremost of archers, suddenly scattering arrows in all directions,
swooped down like a hawk upon its prey.
As that hero among men advanced, plunging into the army with horses the color of the moon or a conch shell,
they were unable to restrain him from any side.
O Bhārata, all the hosts [beheld] that foremost of men, who resembled a ray of the sun, whose prowess was irresistible, whose spirit was undaunted, and who was difficult to withstand.
Possessing a splendor equal to that of the thousand-eyed Indra,
like the sun in the sky when the clouds have passed,
he was filled with indignation and was an exceedingly wonderful warrior.
The excellent king Sudarśana, armed with a bow and wearing golden armor, forcibly checked Sātyaki as he was charging forward.
Between those two, O Bharata, there occurred a most terrible encounter,
which your warriors and the Somakas alike praised.
Like the hosts of immortals in the battle between Vṛtra and Indra,
Sudarśana pierced the chief of the Sātvatas in combat with hundreds of extremely sharp arrows.
But the bull of the Śinis,
Sātyaki, who was equal to Śakra himself, likewise cut down those very arrows with his own shafts before they had even reached him.
Whatever arrows Sudarśana discharged, Sudarśana, stationed upon his excellent chariot, cut them into two or three pieces with his own supreme shafts.
Then, beholding his arrows thus destroyed by the force of Sātyaki’s shafts, Sudarśana,
possessed of fierce energy, seemed as if he would consume him with rage.
He released arrows variegated with gold;
again, with three sharp, well-feathered shafts, drawn back to his ear and resembling fire, he struck him.
Having pierced through his body armor,
they entered the body of Sātyaki;
likewise did the son of the protector of the earth [pierce] him.
Aiming with other blazing arrows,
he forcefully struck those four horses, which were as bright as silver, with four shafts.
Thus struck by him,
the swift grandson of Śini, whose prowess was equal to that of Indra, [was hit] by the multitude of Sudarśana’s exceedingly sharp arrows.
Having swiftly slain the horses, he let out a roar;
then, having severed the head of his charioteer with a broad-headed arrow resembling a thunderbolt.
The hero of the Śini clan also forcibly severed Sudarśana’s head,
which was adorned with earrings and radiant as the full moon, using a razor-sharp arrow.
O King, he forcibly severed from the body that radiant face,
just as in the past the wielder of the thunderbolt did to the exceedingly powerful Bala in battle.
Having slain that son and grandson of kings in battle, the powerful bull of the Yadus,
that high-souled one, was filled with supreme joy.
O King,
that great-souled one,
resembling the king of the gods, shone with immense joy in that great battle, like Śakra, the lord of the immortals.
Then, having warded off your army with floods of arrows, he went toward Arjuna himself,
emerging on a chariot yoked with excellent horses.
Desiring to cause wonder among the worlds, that hero among men performed that foremost feat which was truly marvelous;
the assembled best of warriors honored it.
He consumed with his arrows those enemies who were within the range of his shafts, just as fire consumes everything in its path.
Sañjaya said:
Having defeated Kṛtavarman and the son of Bharadvāja in battle,
the wise and high-souled Sātyaki, that bull among the Vṛṣṇis,
then also vanquished Duryodhana and the heroic Sudarśana.
Having slain Jalasandha in battle, as well as King Śūrasena, O King,
and many kinds of Mlecchas in the encounter, along with the son of Kāśya,
the Niṣādas, the Taṅkaṇas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Magadhas as well;
The Kekayas and the Śūrasenas, as well as those dwelling in the mountains;
the Kāmbojas and the Yavanas, and also the Vasātis and the Śibis;
the Kosalas and the Magadhas, and the Yātudhānas along with the Satittiras.
Having slain these and others in battle, Sātyaki advanced in the fray toward a terrible river of blood, with hair for its moss and grassy banks, strewn with spears as its crocodiles,
and adorned with umbrellas like its swans.

Having slain Sudarśana in battle, he who carries the brave to the world of heroes spoke these words to his charioteer— [a river] difficult for cowards to cross, ever flowing toward the realm of the valiant,
thick with chariots, horses, and elephants, and garlanded with waves of arrows and spears.
It was filled with sword-fish and mace-crocodiles, resounding with the great noise of heroic weapons;
it was fierce, life-taking, and echoing with the blare of musical instruments and the shouts of men.
It was unpleasant to touch for the warriors and difficult to withstand for those seeking victory.
"O dear one, we have crossed the great ocean of Droṇa’s army,
which was difficult to traverse and filled with man-eaters in the form of Jalasandha’s forces;
it was endowed with heroism, courage, and strength, and frequented by heroes as its merchants."
I consider this remainder of the army to be like a shallow stream, like a tiny river that must be crossed; urge the horses forward without agitation.
I believe Savyasācin is now within reach of my hand.
Having conquered the invincible Droṇa along with his followers in battle,
and having encountered the son of Hṛdika, that foremost of warriors, I consider Dhanañjaya to have already arrived;
for no fear arises within me even upon seeing my armies in their great numbers.

Behold the ground traversed by the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, Kirīṭin, which has been made uneven by the fallen throngs of infantry, horses, chariots, and elephants— like dry grass and weeds consumed by a blazing fire in the summer heat.
That army fled as it was shattered by that high-souled one;
O charioteer, this dust, resembling the red hue of silk, is being raised by the chariots, elephants, and horses running about in all directions.
"I believe the one with white horses and Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer is close at hand;
this is the sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow of immeasurable power that is being heard,
for this roar is heard like the thundering of a rain-cloud."
As the Gāṇḍīva bow of immeasurable power is being drawn wide in battle,
I believe Kirīṭin is close to the ruler of the Sindhus;
such is the sound heard from the troops, resembling the roar of the ocean.
"Since such omens are indeed appearing before me,
Arjuna shall slay the King of Sindhu before the sun has set.
Proceeding with care, go toward the enemy host while gradually calming the horses."
Where these Kāmbojas— armed with excellent shields, clad in armor, performers of cruel deeds, and intoxicated by battle— stand at the head of Suyodhana,
along with the Yavanas, who carry bows and arrows and are skilled strikers.
The Śakas, Kirātas, Daradas, Barbaras, and Tāmraliptakas,
along with many other Mlecchas holding various weapons in their hands—
all of them stand facing me alone, seeking battle.
"Having slain these men, along with their chariots, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers, in battle,
consider this most terrible and difficult-to-cross [ocean] already crossed.
Sūta said:
"O Vārṣṇeya, O you of true prowess, I have no anxiety,
even if the son of Jamadagni were to stand before me in a great rage,
or Droṇa, the best of chariot-warriors, or Kṛpa, or even the Lord of Madra."
Nevertheless, O mighty-armed one, there would be no cause for alarm relying upon you;
for by you, O destroyer of enemies, very many have been conquered in battle,
and never before have I experienced any anxiety whatsoever.
"O hero, having encountered this mere puddle in battle, what more is there to say? O long-lived one, by which path shall I lead you to Dhanañjaya?
With whom are you angry, O Vārṣṇeya, and for whom has death arrived?"
Whose mind today dares to go to Saṃyamanī? But who, upon seeing you in battle— possessed of prowess and resembling Yama, the Ender at the end of time— will flee from the fray?
"O mighty-armed one, whom does King Vaivasvata remember today?
Sūta said:
"Thus he acted in battle, like the Destroyer himself."
Then the grandson of Śini, with a joyful heart, spoke thus to his charioteer. Sātyaki said:
"I shall slay these shaven-headed men, just as Vāsava slays the Dānavas."
"I shall fulfill my vow; carry me toward the Kambojas alone.
Having wrought their destruction today, I shall quickly go to the son of Pāṇḍu. Today the Kauravas, together with Suyodhana, shall behold my prowess."
The king explained the various purposes of that great weapon—
the Makaradhvaja, the Mahāmūṣṭi, and the Kṛṣṇādureṣupātana—
to the son of the hero’s son, who was filled with agitation regarding its release in battle.
O Sūta, when the Muṇḍa division has been slain and all the armies have been repeatedly struck down,
Suyodhana will suffer great anguish today upon hearing the manifold cries of the Kaurava host as it is being shattered in battle.
Today, in this battle, I shall demonstrate the path taught by my preceptor against the high-souled chief of the Pāṇḍavas, he of the white horses;
today, as I fight, my arrows shall be like those of Phalguna.
Seeing those fallen upon the chariots and elephants, the enemies grieve;
today, seeing thousands of the foremost warriors struck down by my arrows,
King Duryodhana will fall into remorse.
Today, as I discharge my excellent arrows with swift hands,
the Kauravas shall behold my bow resembling a whirling circle of fire;
they shall see those whose limbs are covered by my shafts, streaming profusely with blood.
Seeing the slaughter of the soldiers, Suyodhana will be filled with remorse;
seeing the best of elephants in battle, their every limb drenched in blood and mangled by my arrows.
Today, as I slay the best of the best with my wrathful form, that Suyodhana shall think this world to be twice as full of Arjunas. Today, thousands of kings have been slain by me in battle.
Seeing this in the great battle, King Duryodhana will suffer deeply;
today the Kauravas shall recognize my affection, devotion, strength, heroism, and gratitude toward the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.
"Having slain thousands of kings, I shall manifest my prowess among the monarchs.
Sañjaya said:
"Thus addressed, the charioteer then [yoked] those well-trained, noble-drawing steeds."
He vigorously urged on the horses that resembled the moon;
thus impelled by the Vṛṣṇi hero, that well-trained charioteer then drove those excellent steeds, which were as bright as the moon and displaying their full speed.
Driven by their drivers, those Saindhava horses carried Satyaka in battle;
drinking in the sky as it were, those excellent steeds,
possessing the speed of thought and the wind, quickly brought Yuyudhāna to the Yavanas.
Having encountered Satyaki, who never retreats in battle,
many Yavanas of great strength and light-handedness covered him with showers of arrows.
O King, all those shouting warriors discharged their arrows and missiles; however, the impetuous Sātyaki severed them with his straight-knotted shafts, so that those arrows did not reach him.
With gold-tufted, well-sharpened, vulture-feathered, and straight-flying arrows,
the fierce one severed the heads and arms of the Yavanas,
as well as their armor made of śaikya-iron and bronze on all sides.

Having pierced through their bodies, those arrows then entered the surface of the earth. Being slaughtered in battle by the heroic Sātyaki, those Mlecchas fell there upon the ground by the hundreds, deprived of life.
With arrows that were perfectly full-drawn and released, continuous and dense, he pierced five, six, seven, and eight Yavanas;
and with thousands of Kambojas and Shakas, O lord of the people.
Of the Śabaras, Kirātas, and likewise the Barbaras;
with the slain Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Kirātas, and Barbaras,
and with the foot-soldiers, having been killed in battle by the heroic Sātvata.
O King, the battlefields became covered with those who had fallen. Thus, having slain and cut down that Yavana army, Mādhava made the earth impassable, mired in flesh and blood.
There, the descendant of Śini wrought havoc, decimating your army;
the earth was strewn here and there with the heads of Dasyus— heads still wearing helmets yet shorn of hair— resembling birds stripped of their plumage.
With all their limbs drenched in blood,
those headless trunks (kabandhas) covered the entire battlefield, making it appear like the sky shrouded by copper-colored clouds.
With straight-flying, well-jointed arrows whose touch was like the thunderbolt of Indra, [the field was strewn].

Slain along with their horses and chariots, they covered the earth. O great king, the grandson of Śini cut down their weapons and arrows with straight-knotted shafts, as well as the necks of the Yavanas.
Those straight-jointed arrows, impelled by Yuyudhāna,
pierced their bodies and fell upon the surface of the earth;
those heroes, being thus struck down in battle by the Vṛṣṇi hero, [perished].
Struck by weapons, the Kambojas fall upon the earth along with their followers;
O Bhārata, with the severed arms of the Kambojas and the Yavanas,
the ground shines here and there like five-headed serpents.
With but few remaining, broken, their lives in peril and deprived of consciousness,
those armored warriors were defeated in battle by Yuyudhāna, O great king;
they struck their horses with their heels and whips.
Adopting the highest speed, O Bhārata, he fled in all directions out of fear, having routed the Kamboja army— which was difficult to conquer in battle—
as well as that army of the Yavanas and the great force of the Śakas.
Then that tiger among men, Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth,
having joyfully defeated your warriors, urged his charioteer, "Drive on!
Having witnessed that deed of his in battle, which had never been performed by others before, [the enemy was struck with wonder].

The *cāraṇas*, together with the *gandharvas*, paid him great honor. O lord of the people, seeing him proceeding as Arjuna’s rear-guard protector, the *cāraṇas* were filled with joy, and even those on your side honored him.
None of your men could withstand the joy of the Vṛṣṇis.
Sañjaya said:
Having defeated the Yavanas and the Kambojas, Yuyudhāna then [approached] Arjuna.
That best of chariot-warriors, a tiger among men with arrows for his fangs and the luster of variegated armor, passed through the midst of your army,
terrifying your troops like a tiger scenting deer.
Moving along the paths on his chariot, he brandished his bow with great force—
a bow with a golden back, possessing immense speed, and adorned with golden crescent-shaped ornaments.
He was clad in golden armlets and a helmet, and completely covered by golden armor.
That hero, the best of those with golden banners, shone like the peak of Mount Meru; equipped with his bow and wheel in battle, radiant with the brilliance of his splendor,
that sun among men gleamed like the sun risen in autumn.
With the stride and shoulders of a bull, with eyes like a bull, that bull among men shone in the midst of your troops like a bull in the midst of cattle;
he resembled an elephant in rut and moved with the gait of an elephant in rut.
Like tigers seeking to kill an elephant in rut standing in the midst of its herd,
your sons, O King, rushed at Sātyaki in battle and surrounded him in the fray.
Having bypassed Droṇa’s division and the difficult-to-cross division of the Bhojas, having crossed the ocean of Jalasaṃdha and the army of the Kambojas,
he has indeed emerged from that sea of troops, freed from the crocodiles that were the son of Hṛdika.
Your car-warriors, highly enraged, surrounded Sātyaki:
Duryodhana, Citrasena, Duḥśāsana, Vivimśati, Śakuni, Duḥsaha, the youthful Durmarṣaṇa, and Kratha.
And many other heroic warriors, armed with weapons and difficult to approach,
pursued from behind the advancing Sātyaki in their indignation.
Then, O noble one, a great clamor arose from your army.
Seeing all of them charging forward like the ocean at the time of the full moon, its force stirred up by the Maruts, that bull among the Śinis spoke to his charioteer as if laughing, "Drive slowly."
"O charioteer, this army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son,
consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, has been raised up and is swiftly advancing toward me alone,
making all the quarters resound with the roar of its chariots."
"O dear one, shaking the earth, the intermediate space, and even the oceans,
I shall hold back this ocean of an army in the great battle,
just as the shore holds back the mass of water swollen during the full moon."
"Behold my prowess, O charioteer, like that of Indra in a great battle—
terrible with quivers, shield, and sword, and crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots;
it is as if the surging ocean were rushing toward the shore."
For hundreds of thousands of warriors stand having encountered me;
I shall scatter the armies of the enemies with my sharp arrows. Behold the foot-soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants slain in battle.
"By means of arrows resembling fire, I shall take the lives of thousands of the Videhas!"—
as the infinitely powerful Sātyaki was speaking thus,
those soldiers, eager for battle, quickly approached him.
To those heroes who were crying out, "Kill!", "Rush forward!", "Stay!", and "Look, look!", Sātyaki, with sharpened arrows,
slew three hundred horses and four hundred elephants as they spoke thus.
Light-handed and a versatile warrior, the bull of the Śinis laughed as he fought;
that tumultuous clash between him and those archers proceeded like the battle between the gods and the asuras, causing a great destruction of men.
O Great King, a battle resembling that between the gods and the asuras commenced.
O Sire, the army of your son, which resembled a mass of clouds,
was countered by the grandson of Śini with arrows like venomous serpents.
Though being covered by nets of arrows in that battle, that heroic one,
O Great King, undauntedly slew many of your men with arrows whose touch was like fire, discharged from a bow drawn back to his ear.
O Indra among kings, I witnessed a truly great marvel there:
not a single arrow of Sātyaki was in vain, O Lord;
indeed, not one shaft failed its mark, for every one of them pierced his body.
That great ocean of an army— thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, and turbulent with waves of foot soldiers— came to rest upon reaching Śaineya as its shore; with its men,
elephants, and horses in a state of agitation, it churned again and again.
That army, being slaughtered on all sides by him with his arrows—
the chariot-warriors, infantry, elephants, and horsemen struck down by shafts—
wandered here and there like cows afflicted by the cold.
I did not see any foot-soldier, chariot, elephant, rider, or horse there that was not pierced by the arrows of Yuyudhāna. O King, Phalguna did not cause such a slaughter there as he did then.
O King,

O bull of the Bharatas, the grandson of Śini, free from fear and endowed with lightness of hand, displayed his skill as he fought, surpassing even Arjuna in the manner in which Sātyaki caused the destruction of the armies.
Then King Duryodhana pierced the charioteer of the Sātvata with three arrows, and the four horses with four sharp shafts;
having struck Sātyaki with three, he pierced him again with eight.
Duḥśāsana pierced the bull of the Śinis with sixteen arrows;
Śakuni with twenty-five, Citrasena with five,
and Duḥsaha pierced Sātyaki in the chest with fifteen.
Smiling, that tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, though thus struck by those arrows,
pierced every one of them with three shafts each, O great king, having deeply wounded his enemies with his exceedingly sharp missiles.
The descendant of Śini, moving with swift prowess like a hawk in battle,
moved through the fray like a hawk— light and skillful. Having severed the bow of Saubala and cut away his hand-guard, he [proceeded].
The bull among the Śinis pierced Duryodhana with three arrows in the center of the chest,
Citrasena with a hundred, Duḥsaha with ten,
and Duḥśāsana with twenty.
Then, O lord of the people, your brother-in-law took up another bow,
pierced Sātyaki with eight arrows, and struck him again with five;
Duḥśāsana did so with ten, and Duḥsaha with three shafts.
And Durmukha, O King, pierced Sātyaki with twelve arrows;
Duryodhana, O Bhārata, having pierced the Mādhava with seventy-three,
then struck his charioteer with three sharp shafts.
Satyaki again pierced all those brave great car-warriors, who were striving together as one, with five arrows each. Then that best of chariot-warriors [struck] the charioteer of your son.
He struck him swiftly with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), and being slain, he fell to the earth.
O Lord, when that charioteer had been felled, your son’s chariot was carried away from the battlefield by those horses that moved like the wind.
Then, O King, O lord of the people, your sons and the soldiers,
beholding the king’s chariot, fled away by the hundreds. Seeing that army in flight there, O Bhārata, Sātyaki—
Having routed all your troops on every side, O King, Sātyaki advanced toward the chariot of the one with white horses, scattering sharp, stone-sharpened arrows feathered with gold.
O noble one, seeing that mighty-armed hero advancing, your men,
as if he were invisible though clearly seen, performed other actions;
they watched him as he took up his arrows and protected his charioteer.
And your men honored him as he liberated himself.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"As Śaineya was departing after having utterly crushed that great army, Arjuna—"

"O Sañjaya, those sons of mine were devoid of shame; what did they do? And how could they maintain such fortitude in battle while wishing for death, having witnessed the conduct of Śini’s grandson, which was equal to that of Savyasācin?"

"What indeed will those defeated warriors say regarding their kṣatriya duty in the midst of the army? And how did the highly illustrious Sātyaki prevail in battle? And how was it, O Sañjaya, that he overcame my sons while they were still alive?"
Tell me truly how the descendant of Śini advanced in battle;
for this, O dear one, is most wonderful that I hear from you—
the combat of a single man against many enemies who were indeed great chariot-warriors.
"I consider it a misfortune regarding my ill-fated sons that they were slain in battle by the high-souled Sātvata; for my entire army,
O Sañjaya, was not a match for him alone."
Let all the Pāṇḍavas stand aside from the enraged Yuyudhāna;
having utterly defeated Droṇa— the skillful one who is intoxicated with battle— in combat,
he will slay my sons just as a lion slaughters herds of cattle.
That bull among men, Yuyudhāna, who could not be slain even by many brave warriors such as Kṛtavarman striving diligently in battle—
he cannot be conquered in combat, yet he will slay my sons.
"Phalguna did not fight such a battle there as the highly illustrious grandson of Śini fought. Sañjaya said:
O King, because of your own ill-advised counsel and that of Duryodhana,
listen attentively, O Bhārata, to what I shall say to you. Listen, O King, to the account of the battle which brought about the destruction of men, horses, and elephants.
Due to the misconduct of Duryodhana and your own evil counsel,
they turned back once more, having made mutual *saṃśaptaka* vows and resolved upon the highest intent for battle at the command of your son.
Three thousand [warriors], led by Duryodhana—
the Śakas, Kāmbojas, Bāhlīkas, Yavanas, and Pāradas,
as well as the Kuṇindas, Taṅgaṇas, Ambaṣṭhas, Paiśācas, and Samandaras— [followed].
They rushed toward the descendant of Śini like moths into a fire;
and five hundred brave warriors from the mountains, O King, who fight with stones and were mounted on chariots, charged against the descendant of Śini.
Then, with a thousand chariots and a hundred great car-warriors,
with a thousand elephants and two thousand horses,
and with hundreds of thousands of throngs of foot-soldiers bearing various weapons in their hands—
Discharging various showers of arrows, the great car-warriors and innumerable foot-soldiers rushed toward the descendant of Śini,
O Bhārata, as they urged them all on, saying, "Slay him!"
O Great King, Duḥśāsana surrounded Sātyaki;
there we beheld the great and wonderful feat of Śini’s descendant, in that he,
alone, fought with many without any agitation.
He struck down the array of chariots and that force of elephants,
as well as all those horsemen and the Dasyus on every side;
the great army, shattered by his arrows, fled in many directions.
There, with wheels crushed and shattered, with supreme weapons broken,
with axles snapped in many places, with the poles and frames of the chariots destroyed,
and with the yokes mangled and banners cast down;
O noble one, O Bhārata, the earth was strewn with armor and yak-tail fans,
covered there with garlands, ornaments, garments, and chariot-trappings,
like the sky overspread with planets.
And excellent elephants, assuming the form of mountains, fell down,
O Great King, along with the remains of the Mlecchas, resembling heaps of crushed collyrium,
as well as other deer— the Mandas, Bhadras, and Mṛgamandas.

In various places, the earth was strewn with those who resembled mountains as they lay down— some auspicious, some of dull intellect, some like the *mṛgabhadra* deer, some sluggish, some with sluggish pride, and even some like slow-moving wild beasts.
O Bhārata, they were born in the lineage of Añjana and Vāmana;
likewise, they were born in the lineage of Supratīka and the Mahāpadma lineage,
as well as in the lineage of Airāvaṇa and other lineages.
O King, many excellent elephants born of the Kumuda lineage and those originating from the race of Airāvata lie slain,
having been struck down in battle by Sātyaki with iron arrows resembling fire.
O King, there Sātyaki struck down excellent horses from Vanāyu, the mountains, Kamboja, Araṭṭa,
and Bāhlīka, as well as foot soldiers born in various lands and of various castes.
There, the descendant of Śini struck them down by the hundreds and thousands.
As those [troops] were being driven away, Duḥśāsana said to the bandits:
"Turn back, you who are ignorant of dharma! Fight! What is the use of your fleeing?"
And having observed all of them, your son Duḥśāsana urged on those heroic mountaineers who fight with stones:
"They are skilled in stone-battles; Sātyaki does not know this."

"Kill this one who desires battle, for he knows nothing of fighting with stones! Likewise, all the Kurus are unskilled in fighting with stones; charge at him and do not fear—he shall not reach you, O Sātyaki!"
All those mountain kings, with stones in their hands, rushed toward the descendant of Śini like ministers rushing toward a king. Then,
the mountain-dwellers [assailed him] with boulders resembling young elephants.
With weapons raised, they stood longing for death against Yuyudhāna;
likewise, others, desiring the slaughter of the Sātvata,
were urged on by your son and obstructed him from every direction with slings.

Those Mlecchas, thirsting for battle and possessing firm hands, rushed toward the descendant of Śini with stones, just as wise ministers approach a king. As they were thus attacking, desiring a battle with rocks, [the opponent acted].
Satyaki, having readied his bow, discharged thirty arrows;
with iron shafts resembling serpents, that bull among the Śinis shattered that tumultuous shower of stones hurled by the mountaineers.
O noble one, by those blazing fragments of stone, which resembled swarms of fireflies, the armies were mostly slaughtered while crying out "Alas! Alas!
Then, five hundred heroes raised up massive boulders.
O King, with their arms lopped off, they fell upon the surface of the earth;
furthermore, another thousand and likewise hundreds of thousands fell,
unable to reach Sātyaki, with their arms severed along with their palms.
By those very mountains crushed by the *bhallaka* arrow of the Sātvata,
the Mlecchas fell and were slain here and there,
their lives departed; they were being slaughtered in battle by the high-souled Sātvata.
They rained down a most terrible shower of stones upon the Sātvata;
yet he slew many thousands of those heroic stone-fighters who stood there striving against him, and that was like a marvel.
Then, as the Daradas, Khaśas, Taṅgaṇas, Ambaṣṭhas, and Kuṇindas— with iron-clad hands and spears in hand— again rained down a shower of stones from all sides using goatskin bags,
Satyaki warded off each and every one that was hurled at him.
The mighty one, watching him, pierced him in return with iron shafts; O King,
as the mountains were being split apart in the sky by his sharp arrows,
the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry fled at the sound.

Strewn with fragments of stone, both men and birds were unable to remain standing, as if stung by bees; they were drenched in blood, their heads and temples shattered, being the survivors of the slaughter.
O King, elephants with shattered heads and severed tusks, and with trunks flung aside, were rendered maimed by the hundreds;
having slain five hundred warriors in a mere instant, O noble one.
The descendant of Śini moved through the midst of the army like one skilled of hand;
the elephants turned back toward Yuyudhāna’s chariot,
and the sound of stones being shattered by his arrows was heard.
Like the sound of raindrops falling upon lotus petals,
O noble one, a tumultuous noise then arose from your army as it was being afflicted by Mādhava, like the roar of the ocean.
Hearing that tumultuous noise, Droṇa said to his charioteer:
"O Sūta, this great car-warrior of the Sātvatas, enraged in battle,
moves through the fray like Death himself, rending the army in many ways."
"O charioteer, drive the chariot to where this tumultuous noise arises;
surely Yuyudhana has encountered those who fight with stones.
For indeed, all the chariot-warriors are being carried away by their fleeing horses."
Mangled and stripped of their weapons and armor, they fell here and there;
in that tumultuous fray, the charioteers were unable to restrain the horses.
O King, while the wise son of Bharadvāja was speaking thus—
Then the charioteer replied to Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons:
"O long-lived one, the Kaurava army is fleeing in every direction;
O long-lived one, the afflicted army of the Kurus is indeed running away."
Behold the warriors broken in battle, fleeing here and there;
and these heroic Pāñcālas, united with the Pāṇḍavas,
are indeed rushing from all sides, desiring to slay you alone.
"O subduer of enemies, decide here upon what must be done that is appropriate for the occasion—
whether it be staying or departing— for Sātyaki has already gone far.
O noble one, while Bhāradvāja was speaking thus, [the battle continued].
The descendant of Śini was seen destroying various kinds of chariots;
being slaughtered in battle by Yuyudhāna,
your men abandoned Yuyudhāna’s chariot and fled toward Droṇa’s army.
But those charioteers with whom Duḥśāsana had previously turned back now all fled in fear toward Droṇa’s chariot. Saṃjaya said:
Seeing Duḥśāsana’s chariot stationed nearby,
the son of Bharadvāja then spoke these words to Duḥśāsana:
"Duḥśāsana, why have all these charioteers fled?"
"Is all well with the king? Does the ruler of the Sindhus still live?
For you are here as a prince, the brother of the king, and a great chariot-warrior; why then do you flee from battle after having attained the status of heir apparent?"

"O slave-girl, you have been defeated at dice; now act according to my will! Become the bearer of garments for my elder brother, the king. All your husbands no longer exist; today they are equal to sterile sesame seeds."
O Duḥśāsana, having spoken thus previously, why do you now flee? Having yourself created this great enmity with the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas,
how is it that you are terrified upon encountering Satyaki alone in battle?
"Previously, while playing at dice, you did not realize that these dice would become arrows as terrible as venomous serpents,
and that they would bring forth unpleasant words, especially toward the Pāṇḍavas."

For in the past, the suffering of Draupadī was rooted in you. Where now is your pride and your arrogance, and where is that heroic boasting, O hero? Having provoked the sons of Pṛthā, who are like venomous serpents, where will you go?
This Bharata army and King Suyodhana himself are to be pitied,
since you, their harsh brother, are intent on flight.
Surely, O hero, [this army] was being shattered and afflicted by fear by you [in the past].
Relying on the strength of your own arms, you ought indeed to protect the army;
yet today, having abandoned the battle out of fear, you gladden your enemies. O slayer of foes, when you, the leader of the host, have fled, [the army will follow].

"O sinless one, who else would stand in battle when terrified, seeking refuge while you yourself are afraid? For as you fight today against this single Sātvata, your mind is set on fleeing from the fray."
O Kaurava, when you behold the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, Bhīmasena, and the twins in battle, what will you do?
[You shall see] the arrows of Phalguna in combat, possessing a splendor equal to that of the sun and fire.
The arrows of Sātyaki are not equal to those from which you flee in fear;
O hero, go quickly and enter the womb of Gāndhārī,
for I see no peace for you as you run across the earth.
If your mind has already been set upon flight,
then let the earth be surrendered peacefully to the King of Dharma,
before Phalguna’s iron arrows, resembling snakes that have cast their sloughs, are loosed.
They will not enter your body until they have made peace with the Pāṇḍavas;
as long as those high-souled sons of Pṛthā do not cast aside this earth by slaying your hundred brothers in battle, so long must you make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
As long as King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, does not become enraged, and as long as Kṛṣṇa, who delights in battle, remains so, make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
[Do this] while the mighty-armed Bhīma, having plunged into the vast army...
He will not destroy your brothers; therefore, make peace with the Pāṇḍavas. Addressed by me, who am peaceful, preserve what remains, O Suyodhana!
Cease hostilities, O hero, with the sons of Pṛthā, and protect all the rulers of the earth.
Previously, Bhīṣma spoke to your brother Suyodhana, saying:
"The Pāṇḍavas are invincible in battle, O gentle one; make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
But your dull-witted brother Suyodhana did not do that.
"I have heard that Bhīma will drink even your blood; and that word of his shall indeed come to pass, for it is not false. O most foolish one, do you not know the prowess of Bhīma?"
He with whom you have begun this enmity by fleeing from battle— resolute in combat, fight the Pāṇḍavas with diligence! Go quickly by chariot to where Sātyaki stands.
"O Bhārata, deprived of you, this army will surely flee;
therefore, fight Satyaki of true prowess for your own sake in battle.
Thus addressed, your son did not say anything at all.
Treating what he had heard as if unheard, he proceeded toward Sātyaki,
joined by a great army of Mlecchas who do not retreat;
and having encountered Yuyudhāna in battle, he fought him with great effort.
Droṇa, the best of chariot-warriors, likewise rushed furiously against the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas,
employing a moderate speed;
and having entered the army of the Pāñcālas in battle, Droṇa [advanced].

He indeed put the warriors to flight by the hundreds and thousands. Then, O great king, Drona, having proclaimed his name in the battle, wrought a great slaughter among the Pandus, Panchalas, and Matsyas.
Then the radiant Vīraketu, the son of the Pāñcāla king, rushed against Bhāradvāja’s son as he was conquering the armies here and there. Having pierced Droṇa with five straight-jointed arrows, he...
With one arrow he pierced his banner, and with seven he struck his charioteer;
the powerful warrior let out a mighty roar and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
There, O Great King, I witnessed a marvel in that battle.
When Droṇa did not advance against the Pāñcālya in the fierce battle,
O noble one, the Pāñcālas, beholding Droṇa hemmed in in the fray,
surrounded him on all sides, O King, desiring victory for the son of Dharma.
O King, with arrows resembling fire, costly javelins,
and various weapons, they overwhelmed Drona alone from all sides. Having destroyed those multitudes of arrows on every side, O King, Drona—
Like the wind blowing great clouds in the sky,
or as the wind constantly disperses massive clouds in the firmament,
he then [discharged] an exceedingly terrible arrow, resembling the sun and fire.
The slayer of enemy heroes fixed his arrow against the chariot of Vīraketu.
O King, having pierced the Pāñcālya, the joy of his clan, that arrow—
dripping with blood and as if blazing— quickly entered the earth.

Then the prince of the Pañcālas, the joy of his lineage, swiftly fell from his chariot like a great *campaka* tree blown down by the wind from a mountain peak. When that mighty archer and powerful prince had been slain, [the battle continued].
The Pāñcālas quickly surrounded Droṇa on all sides,
O Bhārata— namely Citraketu, Sudhanvan, Citravarman,
and likewise Citraratha— all of them distressed by the calamity that had befallen their brothers.
Desirous of battle, they rushed together against the son of Bharadvāja,
discharging showers of arrows like clouds at the end of the summer heat;
those mighty archers made the son of Bharadvāja invisible in the fray.
Being struck in many ways by those great car-warriors, the princes,
that bull among the twice-born summoned his wrath for their destruction;
then Droṇa released a net consisting of arrows upon them.
O best of kings, being struck by Droṇa’s arrows drawn back to his ear, those princes truly did not know what ought to be done.
Seeing them bewildered in battle, O Bhārata, Droṇa seemed to laugh.
Enraged in battle, he deprived the princes of their horses, charioteers, and chariots;
likewise, with other well-sharpened broad-headed arrows,
that highly illustrious one struck down their heads as if plucking flowers.
They severed the heads [of their enemies] as if they were groves of palm trees;
O King, those highly resplendent ones fell from their chariots onto the earth like the Daityas and Dānavas in the ancient battle between the gods and the asuras.
Having slain them in battle, O King, the powerful son of Bharadvāja brandished his formidable bow with its golden back;
repeatedly whirling that swan-backed, difficult-to-gaze-at weapon, he displayed his skill.
O King, it shone upon him like lightning in the midst of a cloud.
Seeing the Pāñcāla great-chariot warriors, who were like gods, slain,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna became violently enraged and shed tears from his eyes.
Enraged, he turned toward Droṇa’s chariot in the battle.
Then, O King, a sudden cry of "Alas!
Alas! arose upon seeing Drona hemmed in by the arrows of the Pāñcālya prince in that combat.

Being covered in many ways by the high-souled son of Pṛṣata, Droṇa did not waver; instead, smiling, he continued to fight. Then, O great king, the prince of the Pañcālas, overwhelmed with rage, [assailed] Droṇa.

Enraged, he struck him in the chest with ninety straight-knotted arrows. Deeply pierced by the powerful one, the highly illustrious son of Bharadvāja sat down upon the seat of his chariot and fell into a swoon.
Seeing the Tathāgata thus, the valiant Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
full of prowess, quickly cast aside his bow and seized a sword;
that great car-warrior then leaped down from his chariot with great haste.
O noble one, he swiftly ascended the chariot of Bhāradvāja;
with eyes bloodshot with rage, he desired to sever the head from the body. Then the mighty Droṇa, having recovered his composure, took up his bow.
Seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna approaching nearby with the intent to slay him, O King,
he fought the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle with finger-measured arrows, for he was constantly a close-range combatant.
O King, those arrows known as *vaitastika*, which were used by close-range combatants, were well-known to Droṇa; he discharged them at Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Being struck by those many shafts, that one of great strength—

Leaping swiftly from his chariot, his momentum broken yet full of prowess, the hero— firmly resolved upon his purpose— rushed toward his own vehicle. Having ascended his chariot and grasped his great bow, the warrior stood ready.
In that battle, the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna pierced Droṇa;
and Droṇa also, O great king, pierced the son of Pṛṣata with arrows.
That battle between Droṇa and the Pañcāla prince was then truly wonderful.
Like Śakra and Prahlāda, both desiring the three worlds,
they performed various circular maneuvers, including *yamaka* and other formations;
moving about as experts in the paths of combat, they then mangled each other with arrows.
In that battle, Drona and the son of Prishata, bewildering the minds of the warriors,
discharged showers of arrows like clouds pouring rain in the monsoon season; those two great-souled ones covered the sky, the quarters, and the earth with their shafts.
That wondrous battle between those two was honored by the hosts of beings,
O great king— by the kṣatriyas and all the other soldiers present there.
The kṣatriyas said, "O King, this is Vainateya!"

"Droṇa, having encountered Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle, will surely fall under the power of our king; the Pāñcālas cried out thus. Droṇa, however, acting with haste in the fight, [attacked] the charioteer of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
He caused his head to fall off like a ripe fruit from a tree.
Then, O King, the mounts of that high-souled one fled;
as they were fleeing, [he struck] the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas as well.
The valiant Droṇa put them to flight here and there in battle;
having defeated the Pāṇḍus and the Pāñcālas, the powerful son of Bharadvāja,
that subduer of enemies, re-established his own array and stood firm.
"O Lord, the Pāṇḍavas were not even able to overcome him in battle.
Saṃjaya said:
"Then, O King, Duḥśāsana rushed toward the descendant of Śini."
With a great multitude of chariots originating from various lands,
O best of the Bharatas, he discharged many arrows on all sides,
making the ten directions resound with a roar like that of a rain-cloud.
Seeing that Kaurava rushing toward him in battle, the mighty-armed Sātyaki charged forward and covered him with a shower of arrows;
those warriors, led by Duḥśāsana, were thus shrouded by the floods of his shafts.
They fled in fear from the battle while your son looked on, O king; as they were fleeing, O Indra among kings, your son Duḥśāsana stood there free from fear and struck Sātyaki with arrows.
With four arrows he struck his horses, and with three shafts he pierced his charioteer;
having wounded Sātyaki with a hundred arrows in the fray, he let out a roar.
Then, O great king, Mādhava became enraged at him in that battle.
With straight-flying arrows, he rendered that chariot, charioteer, and banner invisible;
scattering thousands of shafts like a rain-bearing cloud,
he pierced Sātyaki with sixty and then with sixteen arrows.
He could not shake him as he stood in battle, like Mount Maināka;
yet that hero completely covered Duḥśāsana with arrows,
just as a spider envelops a mosquito that has come near it with its web.
The conqueror of enemies quickly covered Duḥśāsana with arrows. Seeing Duḥśāsana thus pierced by hundreds of shafts,
the king urged the Trigartas toward the chariot of Yuyudhāna.
Those three thousand Trigarta chariot-warriors, skilled in battle and performers of cruel deeds, went into the presence of Yuyudhāna;
they surrounded him with a great multitude of chariots.
Having made their resolve firm for battle and having sworn their oath among themselves as *saṃśaptakas*,
they exerted themselves in the fight, discharging showers of arrows;
[Arjuna] then struck down five hundred of their foremost warriors at the head of the vanguard.
Slain by the arrows of the foremost of the Śinis, they fell swiftly like great trees broken by the force of a mighty wind;
O lord of the people, with their chariots shattered in many ways and their banners as well.
O great king, the earth there, strewn with fallen horses adorned with golden crests— mangled by the arrows of Śini’s grandson and drenched in streams of blood— shone like blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
Being slaughtered in battle by Yuyudhāna,
your men found no protector, like elephants sunk in the mud.
Then they all turned back toward Droṇa’s chariot.
Like great serpents entering their holes out of fear of the king of birds,
[the enemy fled]. Having slain five hundred warriors with arrows resembling venomous snakes,
and having thus struck down and scattered those thousands of combatants, he [proceeded].
That hero proceeded slowly toward the chariot of Dhanañjaya.
As that best of men was advancing, your son Duḥśāsana quickly pierced him with nine straight-knotted arrows.
But that great archer pierced him in return with five sharp arrows—
gold-feathered, vulture-winged, straight-flying shafts—
smiling, as it were, O Great King, O Bhārata.

Duḥśāsana, having pierced him with three arrows, pierced him again with five. Śaineya, however, having pierced your son with five swift shafts and having severed his bow in battle, proceeded toward Arjuna in amazement.
Then the enraged Duḥśāsana, desiring to kill the Vṛṣṇi hero as he was advancing, hurled a spear made entirely of iron. But then Sātyaki [warded off] that terrible spear of your son.
O King, he cut it into a hundred pieces with sharp, heron-feathered arrows.
Then, O lord of men, your son took up another bow,
pierced Sātyaki with ten shafts, and let out a lion’s roar.
But Sātyaki, enraged in battle, having confounded your son,
struck him between the breasts with three straight-knotted arrows, O illustrious one— arrows resembling flames of fire.
Then, with four sharpened arrows, he struck his horses;
and being enraged, he struck his charioteer as well,
and again pierced him with eight arrows made entirely of iron and tipped with sharp points.
Duḥśāsana, however, pierced Sātyaki with twenty arrows;
he dispatched stone-sharpened shafts, fletched with vulture feathers, at that hero.
O great king, the descendant of Satvata also pierced him between the breasts.
Then, with exactly three arrows of great velocity and straight joints,
that great car-warrior struck his horses;
and, highly enraged, he struck the charioteer with arrows of straight joints.
The master of supreme weapons, with a single broad-headed arrow, cut off his bow; with five, his hand-guard;
and with two broad-headed arrows, his standard and his chariot-spear. With sharp shafts, he likewise struck down both of his flank-drivers.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, with his arrows, he [struck] both the outriders and the charioteer. With his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain,
and his charioteer killed, he was carried away by the Trigarta general on his own chariot.
O Bhārata, having rushed toward him for a mere moment,
the grandson of Śini did not wish to kill Duḥśāsana even though he had reached him in battle;
the mighty-armed one did not slay him, remembering the words of Bhīmasena.
O Bhārata, the slaughter of all your sons in battle was indeed vowed by Bhīmasena in the midst of the assembly hall;
likewise, O Lord, Sātyaki has conquered Duḥśāsana in combat.
He went in haste, O King, to where Dhanañjaya had gone.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Were there no great car-warriors (*mahāratha*) at all in that army of mine?"
Those who neither slew nor even restrained Sātyaki as he advanced—
when you describe to me the deed performed by that Vṛṣṇi hero in battle,
O Sañjaya, even Śakra himself would not venture to perform such a feat.
Having heard of the incredible and inconceivable deeds of that great-souled hero among the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, my mind is distressed;
for alone in battle, he of true prowess performed such a feat.
Possessing strength equal to Śakra in battle, like Mahendra among the Dānavas,
or perhaps that place was empty when Sātyaki departed—
[for] that bull among men alone was indeed crushing those numerous armies.
"Therefore, O Sañjaya, I have no sons as you describe. How did the descendant of Śini, being alone, depart from those high-souled ones while they were fighting? Tell me that, O Sañjaya."
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, the mobilization of your armies— consisting of chariots, elephants, horses,
and infantry— was tumultuous and resembled the end of a Yuga."
"O giver of honor, among the multitudes of your army in its daily arrays,
it is my opinion that there is no assembly in this world equal to it. Regarding this, the gods and the *cāraṇas* gathered together have spoken."
"O lord of the people, such arrays as were formed by Droṇa for the slaughter of Jayadratha have never before existed on the surface of the earth, nor will there ever be any like them again."
"Surely the earth has been uprooted by those who have assembled for the sake of battle"—
thus did the people there speak upon seeing that gathering of men,
which sounded like the roar of oceans lashed by fierce winds.
O best of men, in that battle there were many hundreds and thousands of kings assembled from both your army and that of the Pāṇḍavas, as they rushed at one another with their vast hosts.
At that time, O King, there were millions and billions of your men, and likewise thousands upon thousands of the Pāṇḍavas—
furious heroes of firm deeds in battle.
There arose a very great, tumultuous,
and hair-raising clamor from the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus as they roared at one another; indeed,
there were thousands of war-cries and shouts of "kilakila" there.
O Bhārata, the tumultuous sounds of kettledrums and the whizzing of arrows were heard,
as well as the cries of men striking one another down. Then, O Sire, Bhīmasena and Dhṛṣṭadyumna raised a loud shout.
"Nakula, Sahadeva, and Dharmarāja Pāṇḍava—
come, strike, and charge with might!
For the two heroes, Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava, have entered the enemy host."
"Act quickly so that they may proceed with ease toward the slaying of Jayadratha," he urged the troops.
"In their absence, the Kurus would have achieved their purpose and we would be defeated."
"Wherever those two high-souled conquerors of enemy cities have gone,
you all must join together and swiftly agitate that ocean-like army, just as winds of great velocity churn the sea."
O King, urged on by Bhīmasena and the Pāñcālya,
those warriors of supreme splendor struck down the Kauravas in battle, casting aside their own dear lives and desiring death in combat through weapons.

For the sake of heaven and for the sake of their friends' cause, they did not spare their own lives; likewise, O King, your warriors, seeking great glory and having resolved upon noble conduct in battle, stood ready for combat alone.
While that tumultuous and greatly fearsome battle was raging, Sātyaki, having slain all the troops, proceeded toward Arjuna; there,
the luster of the armor was variegated by the rays of the sun.
They struck down the weapons of the soldiers on all sides in that battle;
obstructed by their own banners and weapons, they illuminated the worlds.
While the Pāṇḍava warriors were thus striving, [the son of Ghaṭotkaca], free from fear, [acted].
O great king, Duryodhana plunged into that vast army. O Bhārata, that tumultuous encounter between them and him was a great event that brought about the destruction of all the troops.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When the armies had retreated in such a manner and he himself was in such a state of distress,
O Sūta, did Duryodhana not turn his back on the battle?"
The encounter of one against many in a great battle—
especially when it involves a king— appears to me to be unequal. He has been raised in extreme luxury, endowed with fortune, and is the lord of the world.
"Having encountered many, did he not turn his back on them?
Sanjaya said:
"O King, descendant of Bharata, the battle of your son was a marvel."
Listen as I relate the wonder of both the one and the many:
by Duryodhana, the Pāṇḍava army was suddenly and utterly churned in battle,
like a lotus pond by a great elephant.
O Kaurava, seeing the army thus arrayed by your son,
the Pāñcālas, led by Bhīmasena, rushed against him.
He [the son] struck Bhīmasena with ten arrows and each of the two sons of Mādrī with three.
With three arrows each he struck the two heroic twins, and with seven he struck Dharmarāja; with six he struck Virāṭa and Drupada, and with a hundred he struck Śikhaṇḍin;
with twenty he struck Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and with seven he struck the son of Dharma.
Having pierced the Kekayas with ten arrows each and the sons of Draupadī with three each,
he mangled hundreds of other warriors, along with their elephants and chariots,
in battle with fierce shafts, like the enraged God of Death destroying all creatures.
Neither joining nor releasing [the arrows], with his bow drawn into a circle,
he was seen slaughtering his enemies through both his skill and the power of his weapons.
As he was slaying those foes, his great gold-backed bow [remained constant].
O noble one, the eldest Pāṇḍava cut that [bow] into three pieces with two broad-headed arrows. The people in the battle saw it moving incessantly in circular motions;
then King Yudhiṣṭhira severed his bow with two broad-headed arrows.
O Kauravya, as your son was striving in the battle,
he pierced him with many well-aimed, sharp arrows;
having quickly struck his armor, they shattered and entered the earth.
Then the Pārthas, filled with joy, surrounded Yudhiṣṭhira,
just as the gods and great seers joyfully surrounded Śakra upon the slaying of Vṛtra.
Then King Duryodhana, firmly grasping his bow, [advanced].
Then, O King, taking up another bow, your powerful son, shouting "Stay! Stay! to the Pāṇḍava king, rushed toward him—that great car-warrior, your son, who was speaking thus.
The Pāñcālas, joyful and eager for victory, advanced against him;
Droṇa received them, desiring to protect the Pāṇḍava in battle,
just as a mountain withstands water-laden clouds driven by a fierce wind.
In that manner, your great army shone forth, scorching [the enemy];
then, suddenly and with great joy, it rushed toward the ocean of your troops,
agitating them on all sides like a sea-monster approaching the ocean.
O King, there occurred in that battle a great conflict, increasing the population,
between the Pāṇḍavas and your men, O mighty-armed one;
then once again a great roar arose from where Dhanañjaya was.

O Lord, O mighty-armed one, in that great battle within the midst of the Bharata army and among your archers, the sound of Mādhava was exceedingly hair-raising compared to all other sounds for Arjuna.
At the gate of the array in that great battle, Droṇa also fought together with his enemies.
Thus, O lord of the earth, this destruction occurred upon the earth when Arjuna, Droṇa, and the great car-warrior of the Sātvatas were all enraged.
O elder brother of Pāṇḍu, a terrible slaughter was then taking place there,
resembling the sport of Rudra and resulting in the destruction of all embodied beings.
Sañjaya said:

In the afternoon, O Great King, a battle took place between Droṇa and the Somakas, with a roar like that of the rain-clouds. Then that hero among men, composed in mind, mounted his chariot drawn by chestnut horses.
Employing moderate speed, he rushed against the Pāṇḍavas in battle;
that mighty archer of great strength, devoted to your pleasure and welfare,
was born from an excellent jar and [flew] with sharp, variegated-feathered arrows.
O King, he struck down the Somakas, the Sṛñjayas, and the Kekayas as well; for,
O Bhārata, as if selecting the very best among the warriors,
the powerful son of Bharadvāja sported in battle, O King.

Bṛhatkṣatra, the great car-warrior of the Kekayas— the eldest of five brothers, a great car-warrior who vied with his kin, the eldest among those five heroic brothers, and fierce in battle— rushed toward him.
Releasing sharp arrows and completely shrouding his preceptor,
he was like a great cloud pouring down rain upon Mount Gandhamādana,
O Great King; at that moment, Droṇa [discharged] gold-feathered shafts whetted on stone.
Enraged, he dispatched seventeen arrows;
but those terrible shafts released from Droṇa’s bow, resembling venomous serpents,
he joyfully severed one by one in battle with ten arrows each.
Seeing that agility of his, the best of the twice-born laughed and dispatched eight straight-knotted arrows;
he sent forth those eight arrows, and again and again, thousands more.
Seeing those arrows swiftly falling, released from Droṇa’s bow,
he warded them off with an equal number of sharp and firm shafts.
Then, O great king, amazement arose among your troops.
O great king, having seen that most difficult feat performed by Bṛhatkṣatra,
the ascetic Droṇa, surpassing the Kekaya prince in battle, then manifested the divine Brāhma weapon.
O King, the unshakable Kaikeya,

the mighty-armed one, warded off that which had been unleashed in battle by means of the very Brahma weapon; O lord of the people, he neutralized that discharged Brahma weapon with the Brahma weapon itself.
Having repelled that weapon of Bhāradvāja in the encounter, O king of kings,
the Kaikeya prince, observing the weapon discharged by Droṇa in the battle,
neutralized that Brahma-weapon with the Brahma-weapon itself.
Then, O Bhārata, when that Brahmāstra had been neutralized, Bṛhatkṣatra pierced the Brāhmaṇa with sixty gold-feathered arrows whetted on stone;
Droṇa, the best of men, struck him in return with a steel shaft (nārāca).
Having pierced his armor, that arrow entered the surface of the earth,
O best of kings, just as a released black cobra enters an anthill;
thus did the shaft pass into the ground after piercing the Kaikeya prince in battle.
O Great King, having been deeply pierced by Droṇa, who was skilled in weapons,
he was overcome with great rage; turning his beautiful eyes toward him,
he struck Droṇa with seventy gold-feathered arrows sharpened on stone.
And with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he struck his charioteer in the arms and chest.
But Drona, O sire, having been pierced in many places by Brihatkshatra,
discharged sharp shafts toward the chariot of the Kekaya prince.
Having thrown the great car-warrior Bṛhatkṣatra into confusion,
Droṇa slew his four horses with four feathered shafts and struck down his charioteer from the seat of the chariot with an arrow.
Having severed both the banner and the umbrella with two [arrows], he cast them down upon the ground;
O Bhārata, he discharged a sharp shaft toward the Kekaya prince.
He loosed arrows in all directions to bewilder the Kekaya king.
O King, Drona pierced him between the breasts with a feathered shaft;
he was the eldest of his five brothers and possessed great strength and prowess.
O great king, being deeply pierced by that arrow in the center of his chest, he quickly [fell].
Then, O bull among the twice-born, that tiger among men, his heart pierced, fell from the chariot; thereafter, with a well-aimed iron shaft,
he struck Bṛhatkṣatra in the chest.
O King, when Bṛhatkṣatra, the great car-warrior of the Kekayas, had been slain,
the son of Śiśupāla, filled with intense rage, spoke these words to his charioteer:
"O charioteer, go to where Droṇa stands clad in armor."
Slaying all the Kekayas and the host of the Pañcālas, [Duryodhana spoke]. Having heard those words of his, the charioteer brought that best of car-warriors to Droṇa by means of swift Kamboja horses.
And Dhṛṣṭaketu, the bull among the Cedis, endowed with exceeding strength,
suddenly rushed toward Droṇa like a moth into a flame. He then pierced Droṇa, along with his horses, chariot, and standard, with sixty arrows.
Again, as if prodding a sleeping tiger with other sharp arrows,
Droṇa severed the bow at its middle with a whetted razor-headed shaft while the powerful king was striving in the encounter.

Then the great chariot-warrior, the son of Śiśupāla, taking up another bow, again pierced Droṇa with well-sharpened and firm arrows. The mighty Droṇa, having slain his horses and his charioteer, [proceeded].
As if laughing, he severed the charioteer’s head from his body,
and then struck him with twenty-five arrows; thus,
in that battle, the King of Cedi was deprived of both his chariot and his bow.
Enraged, he hurled a mace toward the chariot of Bhāradvāja. But the King of Cedi, leaping down from his chariot and seizing a mace with haste,
hurled it back at Bhāradvāja like an angry female serpent.
As that heavy mace, made of solid stone, adorned with gold, and terrifying in its fierce form, came rushing down suddenly,
the son of Bharadvāja struck it down with many thousands of arrows.
Struck down by the son of Bharadvāja, that mace fell to the earth,
wearing crimson garlands and garments like a star falling from the vault of heaven.
Seeing his mace destroyed, the impatient Dhṛṣṭaketu—
He swiftly hurled a lance and a gold-glittering spear. But in that great battle, the mighty Drona, with practiced hand, cut the lance with three arrows and suddenly severed the spear as well.
Having severed the *tomara* with five [arrows], he cut the *śakti* with seven;
those two, severed, fell to the earth like two snakes by Garuḍa.
Then, for the sake of slaying him who desired his death, he [discharged] a sharp arrow at him.
The powerful Bhāradvāja dispatched [an arrow] in battle;
having pierced the armor and the heart of that one of immeasurable energy,
the arrow entered the earth like a swan entering a lotus lake.
O King, having been deeply pierced in the heart by him, that great car-warrior,
the highly illustrious Dhṛṣṭaketu, quickly fell from his chariot;
indeed, O King, he was like a hungry blue jay devouring a moth.
Likewise, the heroic Droṇa seized Dhṛṣṭaketu in that great battle.
When the King of Cedi had been slain,
