his son— who was an expert in supreme weapons— fell under the sway of indignation and entered that paternal division.
Smiling at him as well, Droṇa dispatched him to the abode of Yama with his arrows,
just as a powerful great tiger in the vast forest slays a young deer.
While those Pāṇḍava warriors were thus being decimated, O Bhārata—
The heroic son of Jarāsaṃdha rushed toward Droṇa himself.
O great king, covering Droṇa with sharp arrows,
he quickly rendered him invisible, just as a cloud obscures the sun.
Seeing that agility of his, Droṇa, the crusher of kṣatriyas,
swiftly discharged arrows by the hundreds and thousands,
covering that best of chariot-warriors standing on his chariot in battle.
Then, while all the archers looked on, he slew the son of Jarāsaṃdha;
whosoever hid himself from Droṇa, him Droṇa, who was like the Destroyer,
seized, just as Death seizes all beings when their time has come.
Then Drona, the great archer, having proclaimed his name in the battle,
bewildered the sons of Pandu with many thousands of arrows.
Then there were arrows marked with Drona’s name, gold-feathered and sharpened on stone.
In that battle, they slaughtered men, elephants, and horses on all sides;
being struck down by Droṇa like the great Asuras by Śakra,
the Pāñcālas trembled like cows afflicted by the cold.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, as the armies were being slaughtered by Droṇa, a terrible cry of distress arose among the Pāṇḍavas;
they were scorched by the sun and struck down by his arrows.
Then the Pāñcālas, their minds terrified and bewildered by the shower of arrows from the son of Bharadvāja in that battle, fell into despair; indeed,
the great car-warriors of the Pāñcālas were seized as if by the grip of a thigh-grasper.
O great king, the Cedis, the Sṛñjayas, and likewise the Somakas,
filled with joy, rushed toward the son of Bharadvāja with a desire to fight; and the Cedis, Pañcālas, and Sṛñjayas spoke to one another on the battlefield.
"Kill Droṇa! Kill Droṇa!
they cried, as those tigers among men rushed toward the highly effulgent Droṇa, striving with all their might, desiring to lead him in battle to the abode of Yama.
But as those heroes were striving, the son of Bharadvāja dispatched them to Yama with his stone-tipped arrows, especially the leaders of the Cedis.
O Bhārata, while those foremost of the Cedis were being destroyed, [the battle continued].
Afflicted by the arrows of Droṇa, the Pāñcālas trembled; O noble one, seeing such deeds performed by Droṇa, they cried out toward Bhīmasena at the chariot of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
"Surely this Brāhmaṇa has practiced great and difficult austerities,
for he thus consumes the bulls among Kṣatriyas with his prowess in battle. For war is the duty of a Kṣatriya, while supreme austerity is that of a Brāhmaṇa."
An ascetic who has mastered the sciences can consume even with a mere glance;
the bulls among the Kṣatriyas who entered the Droṇa-weapon, which is like the touch of fire,
were many who perished there, O Bhārata, in that terrible and insurmountable [fire].
"According to his strength, according to his energy, and according to his courage, the one of great splendor,
Drona, bewildering all beings, slaughters our forces.
Having heard those words of theirs, Kṣatradharman stood firm.
With a crescent-shaped arrow, the mighty Kṣatradharman, his mind agitated by rage, severed Droṇa’s bow along with the arrow fixed upon it.
Becoming even more enraged, Droṇa, the crusher of kṣatriyas,
took up another bow that was radiant and exceedingly swift;
fixing upon it a sharp, stainless, firm arrow capable of bearing a great weight, he—
Drawing it back to his ear, the powerful preceptor discharged that excellent arrow;
taking away the life of Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s son,
it struck Kṣatradharman and fell to the surface of the earth.
With his heart pierced, he fell from his vehicle onto the surface of the earth.
Then, when the son of Dhṛṣṭadyumna was slain, the armies trembled;
thereupon the great car-warrior Cekitāna rushed against Droṇa.
Desiring to slay his enemy, he discharged arrows in the battle;
he pierced Droṇa in the center of the chest with ten arrows,
and struck his charioteer with four and his four horses with four more.
The preceptor pierced his right arm with sixteen arrows,
his standard with sixteen arrows, and his charioteer with seven.
Then the preceptor struck him in the arms and chest with three arrows.
Having struck down the standard with seven arrows, he slew the charioteer with three;
when his driver was killed, O noble one, those horses fled, carrying the chariot away from the battle, covered by the arrows of Bhāradvāja.
Seeing Cekitāna’s chariot fleeing with its driver slain,
a great fear then entered the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas. Those heroes— the Cedis, Pāñcālas, and Sṛñjayas— were gathered together on the battlefield.
Causing them to flee in every direction, O noble one, Droṇa shone brilliantly.
With hair as grey as his ears, dark-complexioned, and over eighty years of age, the aged Droṇa moved about in battle like a youth of sixteen.
Then, O great king, as Droṇa moved about fearlessly,
his enemies regarded that slayer of foes as if he were the wielder of the thunderbolt himself.
Thereupon, O great king, the wise Drupada spoke to the monarch.
This greedy man slays the Kṣatriyas like a tiger slaying small deer. The wicked and evil-minded Duryodhana shall attain miserable worlds,
for it was through his greed that these bulls among Kṣatriyas were slaughtered in battle.
"By the hundreds they lie upon the ground like slaughtered bulls,
their limbs drenched in blood and made into food for jackals and wild dogs.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, Drupada, the lord of an akṣauhiṇī, [fell silent].
Placing the Pārthas at his front, he swiftly rushed toward Droṇa in battle.
Saṃjaya said:
While the arrays of the Pāṇḍavas were being churned up here and there...
The Pārthas, along with the Pañcālas and the Somakas, pursued them for a very long distance while that fierce,
hair-raising battle was thus proceeding—
a terrible destruction of the world like the end of a Yuga, O Bhārata.
While Droṇa displayed his prowess in battle, roaring again and again,
and while the Pañcālas were being depleted and the Pāṇḍavas slaughtered,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, saw no refuge whatsoever.
O king of kings, he reflected: "How will this come to pass?
Then, having looked in all directions with a desire to see Savyasācin, Yudhiṣṭhira beheld neither Pārtha nor Mādhava.
Not seeing that tiger among men, who bore the marks of a bull among monkeys,
and not hearing the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow, his senses were distressed;
and he did not see Sātyaki, the foremost chariot-warrior of the Vṛṣṇis.
With his body overwhelmed by anxiety, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
found no peace at that time, not seeing those two bulls among men;
for the highly illustrious King of Dharma was fearful of public reproach.
The mighty-armed one reflected upon the chariot of Śini’s descendant:
"In this battle, I have sent Śaineya Sātyaki— the truthful one who grants fearlessness to his friends— to follow in the footsteps of Phalguna."
For this one person has indeed become two for me today;
both Sātyaki must be known to me as such, and the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya.
Having sent Sātyaki after the tracks of the Pāṇḍava...
I shall send even Kaṃsa as a foot-soldier into battle against the Sātvata;
I will make every effort to search for my brother,
for if I do not seek out Yuyudhāna, the world will censure me.
Having searched for his brother, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
abandons Sātyaki of the Vṛṣṇi clan, whose prowess is truth;
out of fear of public censure, I [abandon] that Vṛkodara, the son of Pṛthā.
I shall dispatch a messenger on the path of the high-souled Mādhava;
for just as my affection is for Arjuna, the slayer of enemies,
so too is it for the Vṛṣṇi hero, the Sātvata who is fierce in battle.
The joy of Śini’s lineage was assigned a task too heavy for him by me;
yet, out of deference to his friend and out of respect, that one of great strength entered the Bharata army like a makara entering the ocean.
For this sound is heard of those heroes who do not retreat,
as they fight one another with the wise Vṛṣṇi hero;
indeed, having deliberated in many ways, I have determined that the time has come for a most powerful [action].
"In that very place, it pleases me to go to the archer Bhīmasena, the son of Pāṇḍu, where those two great chariot-warriors have gone;
for there is nothing on earth that is unbearable for Bhīma."
For he is indeed capable, by relying on the strength of his own arms, of directly confronting all the archers on earth who are prepared for battle;
it is by relying on the strength of the arms of that high-souled one that they all [stand firm].
"We have returned from our forest exile and have not been defeated in battles;
for once Bhīmasena, the Pāṇḍava, has gone from here toward the Sātvata,
both the Sātvata and Phalguna will indeed find themselves well-protected in combat."
Granted, those two— the Sātvata and Phalguna— are not to be grieved for in battle,
as they are protected by Vāsudeva himself and are both experts in weapons;
nevertheless, I must certainly act to destroy my own sorrow.
"Therefore, I shall appoint Bhīma as the pursuer of the Sātvata;
thus, I consider my plan regarding Sātyaki to be fulfilled.
Having thus resolved in his mind, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma—
"O King, lead me toward Bhīma," he said to the charioteer.
Hearing the words of Dharmarāja, the charioteer, who was skilled in horses,
brought the gold-adorned chariot to the presence of Bhīma.
Having approached Bhīmasena and reflecting on what was appropriate for the occasion,
the king fell into a state of dejection, issuing many instructions there;
overcome by that dejection, the monarch summoned Bhīma.
O King, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, spoke these words:
"I do not see the banner of that younger brother of yours, Bhīmasena, who, on a single chariot, conquered the gods along with the gandharvas and the daityas."
Then Bhīmasena spoke thus to the King of Dharma, who had fallen into such a state:
"I have neither seen nor heard of such dejection in you before;
for in the past, you were indeed our refuge when we were torn by suffering."
"Arise, arise, O Indra among kings! Command me; what shall I do for you?
For there is nothing impossible or unattainable for me, O giver of honor. Give your orders, O best of the Kurus, and do not set your mind on grief."
With his face withered and his eyes filled with tears, the king, hissing like a black cobra, spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"Just as the blare of the conch Pāñcajanya is heard..."
Just as the great roar of the Pāñcajanya conch is heard,
blown by the glorious and enraged Vāsudeva,
surely your brother Dhanañjaya lies slain today.
Now that he has been slain, Janārdana will surely fight—
he whose courageous prowess the Pāṇḍavas rely upon,
and whom they approach in times of fear, just as the immortals approach the thousand-eyed Indra.
That hero, desiring to seize the ruler of the Sindhus, followed the Bharata army. O Bhīma, we know his departure, but not his return;
he is dark-complexioned, youthful, Guḍākeśa, handsome, and mighty-armed.
Broad-chested, with great shoulders and the gait of an elephant in rut,
with eyes like those of a cakora bird and copper-hued eyes, he increases the misfortune of his enemies;
for the sake of my pleasure and welfare, he has come here from the world of Śakra.
Serving the elders, steadfast, grateful, and true to his promise,
Dhanañjaya entered that vast army which was raining down wealth;
and once Arjuna, the destroyer of enemies, had entered that formidable host, [the battle commenced].
The heroic Sātvata has been dispatched as Phalguna’s follower;
I know his departure, O Bhīma, but not his return again. This, O subduer of enemies—blessings be upon you—is the cause of my grief.
"O mighty-armed one, for the sake of Arjuna and on account of the Sātvata,
he grows like a fire fed again and again with oblations;
I do not see his banner, and because of that, I am overcome by dejection."
Know him to be that tiger among men, the Sātvata, and a great car-warrior (*mahāratha*).
He followed behind that great car-warrior, your younger brother;
not seeing that mighty-armed one, I am overcome by dejection.
Now that Pārtha has been slain, this leader surely fights on;
he has no ally at all, and for that reason I am overcome by dejection. Therefore, tell me once more about him, the red-eyed one, along with Keśava.
"O Pāṇḍava, having seen that the two Kṛṣṇas are well, as well as Sātyaki of the Sātvatas, you should send me word with a lion’s roar;
for this sound of the blowing Pāñcajanya is being heard."
O Pāṇḍava, since he is being filled with weapons by the enraged Vāsudeva,
the heroic Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, must surely have been slain;
for even when that son of Pṛthā is dead, the one whose banner bears Garuḍa continues to fight.
For there is no other who performs such dear service for him, O Pāṇḍava;
therefore, Kṛṣṇa, skilled in battle, surely fights in the fray—
he whose heroic power the Pāṇḍavas depend upon.
"O scorcher of foes, my mind is not at peace regarding those two;
therefore, O Kaunteya, go there where Dhanañjaya and the highly heroic Sātyaki have gone, if you deem it your duty."
"O knower of dharma, listen to my words: I am your eldest brother.
You should not regard Arjuna in that way; rather, you should know Satyaki as such.
O Pārtha, desiring to do what is pleasing to me, he has gone forth against Savyasācin."
Bhīmasena said:
"That chariot which in former times bore Brahmā, Īśāna, Indra, and Varuṇa— [it has entered] a path difficult to traverse, terrible, and inaccessible to those who have not disciplined their souls."
Having mounted him, the two Kṛṣṇas have gone; there is no fear for them.
Bearing your command upon my head, here I go; do not grieve.
Having met those tigers among men, I shall deliver your message to them.
Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus, the powerful one departed after repeatedly entrusting Yudhiṣṭhira to Dhṛṣṭadyumna and his friends.
Then the mighty Bhīmasena said this to Dhṛṣṭadyumna:
"O mighty-armed one, it is known to you how the great car-warrior Droṇa is employing every possible means to capture the King of Dharma."
"O son of Pṛṣata, I have no business in going away such as the urgent task we have regarding the protection of the king. Having been addressed thus by the son of Pṛthā, I did not dare to reply."
I shall proceed to where that Saindhava stands, desirous of death;
one must abide by the word of Dharmarāja without hesitation.
I shall follow the path of my brother and of the wise Sātvata.
"Therefore, exerting yourself today in battle, protect Yudhiṣṭhira, O Pārtha;
for this is the supreme duty among all tasks in combat.
Thus, O Great King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna spoke to Vṛkodara.
"O mighty-armed son of Pṛthā, go according to your desire without hesitation. O Kaunteya, as long as I am alive, the son of Bharadvāja will by no means slay Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle."
"He will effect the subjugation of Dharmarāja in battle. Then, having entrusted the king to Dhṛṣṭadyumna and having saluted his eldest elder brother, the Pāṇḍava proceeded to where Phalguna was.
O Bhārata, the son of Kuntī was embraced by Dharmarāja;
the slayer of enemies was kissed on the head and embraced by the king,
and likewise kissed on the head and granted auspicious blessings.
Having performed circumambulations for the brahmins, who were honored and satisfied in mind,
and having touched the eight auspicious objects and drunk the *kairātaka* honey-wine,
the hero— possessed of double his wealth— had the corners of his eyes reddened with intoxication.
Having had auspicious rites performed by the brahmins, which indicated the dawning of victory,
and perceiving his own intellect to be the cause of the joy of triumph,
he was swiftly shown the rising of victory by favorable winds.
The mighty-armed Bhīmasena, clad in armor and adorned with beautiful earrings, wearing armlets and a protective breastplate, equipped with arrows— the best among chariot-warriors—
mounted his prepared chariot, which was furnished with all necessary implements.
His armor, made of black iron and adorned with gold, possessed great splendor;
it shone like a rain-cloud clinging to a mountain and flashing with lightning.
He was beautifully arrayed in garments of yellow, red, black, and white.
And with his throat-protector, he shone like a cloud accompanied by Indra’s bow.
When Bhīmasena had set out with the desire to fight against your army,
O lord of the people, the terrible sound of the Pāñcajanya conch arose once more.
Hearing that great and terrible roar, which struck fear into the three worlds,
the mighty-armed son of Dharma spoke again to Bhīma:
"This conch, born of the waters, has been blown forcefully by the foremost hero of the Vṛṣṇis."
The king of conchs makes the earth and the atmosphere resound;
surely a great calamity has befallen Savyasācin,
for the wielder of the discus and mace is now fighting together with all the Kurus.
"Surely today the noble Kuntī beholds a great calamity, as do Draupadī and Subhadrā along with their kinsmen. Therefore,
O Bhīma, go with all haste to where Dhanañjaya is."
"O Pārtha, all the cardinal and intermediate directions seem to be spinning for me out of a desire to see Dhanañjaya, and this is because of the Sātvata.
Thus was he urged by that son of Dharma in the midst of battle.
The mighty-armed Bhīmasena, powerful and clad in armor and mail, [was there];
and again he addressed Bhīmasena, saying, "Go, go!
Then, O King, the powerful Bhīmasena, son of Pāṇḍu—
With his finger-guards of iguana-skin bound on and his bow grasped,
that brother, who acted for the pleasure of his brother, was sent forth by his brother with great force;
Bhīma struck the drum and blew his conch shell repeatedly.
Letting out a lion’s roar and repeatedly drawing his bowstring,
he struck terror into the hearts of the heroes with the sound of his palms;
displaying his formidable self, he suddenly rushed toward his enemies.
Swift, well-trained, and excellent horses, displaying their prowess and endowed with the speed of thought or the wind, carried him as he was joined by Viśoka;
while Pārtha, drawing the bowstring with his hand, broke and snapped [the enemy ranks].
Dragging it hither and thither, he threw the vanguard of the army into utter confusion.
As that mighty-armed hero advanced, the Pāñcālas along with the Somakas [beheld him];
and seeing him approaching in his terrible form, your sons [prepared for battle].
The heroes followed behind him, like the immortals following Maghavan;
O great king, his uterine brothers— Duḥśāsana, Citrasena, Kuṇḍabhedin, and Vivimśati— surrounded him along with their armies.
Durmukha, Duḥsaha, Vikarṇa, and Śala; Vinda and Anuvinda, Sumukha, Dīrghabāhu, and Sudarśana;
Vṛndāraka, Suhasta, Suṣeṇa, and Dīrghalocana.
Abhaya, Raudrakarman, Suvarman, and Durvimocana—
these foremost of chariot-warriors, together with their armies and followers,
being prepared for battle, rushed toward Bhīmasena, O heroes.
Surrounded on all sides by those heroes in battle, that great car-warrior was beheld;
but upon seeing them, the valiant Bhīmasena, son of Kuntī,
rushed forward with speed like a lion toward small deer.
There those heroes displayed great celestial weapons,
warding off Bhīma with their arrows like clouds obscuring the rising sun;
having bypassed them with speed, he rushed toward Droṇa’s division.

And from the front, he overwhelmed the elephant division with showers of arrows. In a very short time, the son of the Wind, having discharged his swift shafts toward all directions, scattered that elephant host.
Terrified like deer in the forest by the roar of a *śarabha*,
all the elephants fled, uttering terrible cries; then,
having bypassed them with speed once more, he rushed toward Droṇa’s division.
The preceptor checked him, as the shore checks the surging ocean;
O King, Drona quickly covered his chariot— along with its horses, driver, and banner— in that battle, and it was like a marvel.
Smiling as it were, he struck him on the forehead with an iron shaft;
there the Pāṇḍava shone like the sun with its rays directed upward.
But the Teacher thought, "This man is Phalguna for me."
"Bhīma will pay his respects," he said to Vṛkodara.
Then, as Bhīma was about to perform the honors according to the conduct due to a superior, he spoke to Bhīmasena:
"Bhīmasena, it is not possible for you to enter the enemy's army."
"O mighty one, if that younger brother of yours, Kṛṣṇa, has entered [the army] with my consent without first defeating me in battle amidst the enemy, then indeed,
O sir, it is not possible for you to enter here."
Then Bhīma, having heard those words of his preceptor, was freed from fear;
yet, filled with rage and breathing heavily with eyes red as copper, he spoke to Droṇa:
"O wretch of a Brahmin, Arjuna shall not enter the field of battle without your permission."
For once he has entered, that invincible one could penetrate even the army of Śakra himself. It was by him, while performing the highest honors, that you were indeed respected.
I am not Arjuna, O Droṇa; I am the compassionate Bhīmasena, your enemy.
"You are our father, our elder, and our kinsman, and we are indeed your sons;
thus we all consider you, standing here bowed before you.
Today, that very thing appears to be reversed as you speak to us.
"If you consider yourself an enemy, then let it be so here;
O Bhīma, I shall perform against you this deed worthy of an enemy. Then Bhīma whirled his mace like Antaka wielding the staff of Time.
O King, he hurled it at Droṇa, who then leapt down from his chariot;
that weapon then crushed Droṇa’s vehicle along with its horses, driver, and standard.
We then beheld that wonderful prowess of the son of Pāṇḍu.
Having deprived Droṇa of his chariot, the mighty Bhīmasena advanced against your troops from all sides;
and by his sheer power, he crushed many warriors like the wind crushing trees.
O King, he of prowess equal to the wind moved through the battle;
then your sons surrounded that best of chariot-warriors once more,
for he had been defeated by that high-souled Pāṇḍava.
Mounting another chariot, Droṇa, the best among strikers,
reached the gate of the military formation (*vyūha*) and stood ready for battle; he exerted himself just like Bhīma, guarding the formation itself.
Then, O great king, the valiant Bhīmasena, filled with rage,
covered the vanguard of chariots with showers of arrows.
Your sons, those great car-warriors, were being slaughtered in that battle.
Desiring victory, they fought against Bhīma of terrible strength in battle. Then Duḥśāsana, enraged and wishing to slay the son of Pāṇḍu, hurled a sharp chariot-spear made entirely of iron.
As that great spear hurled by your son came flying toward him, Bhīma split it in two; it was like a marvel. Then, enraged, he struck Kuṇḍabhedin with other sharpened arrows.

The mighty one slew Suṣeṇa and Dīrghanetra, striking each of the three with three arrows. Then he again slew Vṛndāraka, the hero who increased the fame of the Kurus, among your heroic sons as they fought.
O Great King, the formidable Bhīma killed three of your sons— Abhaya, Raudrakarman, and Durvimocana— with three arrows; thus, your sons were being slain by that more powerful warrior.
They surrounded Bhīma, the best among strikers, on all sides;
casting aside the external fear of death, they hemmed in Vṛkodara.
They rained arrows upon that Pāṇḍava of terrible deeds in the battle.
Like clouds at the end of the heat showering rain upon the mountain,
that slayer of enemies, the heir of Pāṇḍu, received that rain of arrows as a mountain receives a shower of stones, and he did not waver.
Vinda and Anuvinda together, as well as your son Suvarman,
the son of Kuntī sent to the abode of Yama with his arrows, as if laughing.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, [he struck] your heroic son Sudarśana.

He pierced him swiftly in battle; he fell and died. Having struck him down in combat with a lance, he dispatched him to death. In a very short time, he [assailed] that division of chariots with swift arrows.
Having assailed all directions, the son of Pāṇḍu scattered them,
just as the sun drives away the mist; he put the quarters to flight with the roar of his chariot,
like deer at the sound of thunder.
O lord of the people, being slaughtered in battle, all your sons fled together with their chariots, afflicted by the fear of Bhīmasena;
yet the son of Kuntī pursued that great army of your sons.
O King, in that battle he pierced the Kauravas from all sides.
Being slaughtered by Bhīmasena, O Great King,
your men abandoned Bhīma in the fray and fled, urging on their excellent horses.
Having conquered them in battle, the mighty Bhimasena,
that son of Pāṇḍu, let out a lion’s roar and made a sound with his arms;
and having produced a great clapping of hands, the exceedingly powerful Bhīma [triumphed].
Making a terrifying sound, Bhīma, the son of Vāyu,
indeed made a great slapping noise with his palms and went into the presence of Droṇa,
having terrified the chariot-division and slain the best of the best warriors.
Having bypassed even the chariot-warriors, he rushed toward Droṇa’s division.
Sañjaya said:
Having emerged from that array of chariots like the sun from the darkness, [he approached].
Desiring to hold his ground, the preceptor covered him with showers of arrows;
yet [the opponent], as if drinking up those floods of shafts issuing from Drona’s excellent bow,
advanced against his uterine brothers, bewildering the army with his illusory power.
Adopting a supreme onset in battle, those great archers,
urged on by your sons, surrounded him from all sides.
Thus hemmed in, O Bhārata, Bhīma seemed as if laughing.
Roaring like a lion, the powerful one raised his terrible mace against them and hurled it with great force, crushing them,
like the thunderbolt of Indra cast by the concentrated-souled Indra himself.
O Great King, she crushed your soldiers in battle,
filling the earth as it were with her great roar;
blazing with splendor and terrifying, she struck fear into your sons.
Seeing her falling with great speed, enveloped in splendor,
all your men fled, uttering terrible cries;
and they perceived that unbearable sound of hers, O noble one.
Hearing that unbearable lion’s roar of Bhīma in the battle,
the chariot-warriors there then fell from their chariots, O men;
those of your side were being slaughtered by Bhīma with mace in hand.
They fled in battle, terrified like deer scented by a tiger.
Having routed those enemies in the fray, the unassailable son of Kuntī,
like Suparṇa, the king of birds, passed through the army with great speed.
O great king, as that leader of the leaders of chariot-divisions was thus causing such havoc,
the son of Bharadvāja advanced against Bhīmasena.
Droṇa, however, having checked Bhīma in battle with waves of arrows, [remained there].
Suddenly he let out a roar, striking fear into the Pāṇḍavas.
That battle between Droṇa and the high-souled Bhīma, O great king, was exceedingly great and terrible, like the encounter between the gods and the asuras.
But when heroes were being slain in battle by the hundreds and thousands with sharp arrows released from Droṇa’s bow,
the Pāṇḍava then leaped down from his chariot and exerted his full speed.
Closing his eyes, O King, Bhīmasena advanced on foot toward Droṇa;
placing his head upon his shoulder and keeping his hands firmly against his chest,
the powerful warrior summoned the speed of the wind and Garuda.
"Just as a bull receives the rain with ease,
so did Bhīma, that tiger among men, receive the shower of arrows.
Being struck in battle, O noble one, he [approached] the chariot of Droṇa."
Grasping the pole with his hand, the one of great strength hurled it away.
But Drona, O King, having been swiftly struck by Bhima in that encounter,
was seen by your warriors with eyes wide open in amazement.
Quickly abandoning his broken chariot on the ground, Droṇa mounted another chariot and proceeded to the gate of the formation. At that time,
the Preceptor was thus departing with his back turned, his enthusiasm shattered.
Having rushed forward with speed, Bhīma seized the pole of that chariot;
then, intensely enraged, Bhīma hurled even that great car-warrior away. In this manner, eight chariots were cast aside by Bhīma as if in play.
But Droṇa, in the twinkling of an eye, mounted his own chariot once more;
at that moment, O Kauravya, his driver quickly urged on the horses,
and it was like a marvel to Bhīmasena.
Then the mighty Bhīmasena, mounting his own chariot,
rushed with speed against the army of your son.
Crushing the kṣatriyas in battle, he was like a violent wind uprooting trees.
Tearing through the army like the current of the Indus uprooting mountains,
Bhīmasena reached the division of the Bhojas protected by the son of Hṛdika; having crushed it in many ways, O King, he advanced further.
Terrifying the ranks with the sound of his palms, O noble one,
he conquered all the armies like a tiger among bulls. Having bypassed the army of the Bhojas and the host of the Kambojas, he advanced.
Likewise, beholding the numerous other hosts of Mlecchas who were skilled in battle,
and also seeing Sātyaki— that bull among men— engaged in combat,
the son of Kuntī then proceeded with speed toward him on his chariot, prepared for action.
O great king, Bhīmasena, the son of Pāṇḍu, desiring to see Dhanañjaya, passed beyond your warriors in battle;
there he beheld Arjuna, that bull among men, engaged in combat.
Seeing Arjuna there, who had exerted his prowess for the sake of slaying the king of the Sindhus, he then let out great roars,
O Great King, like a thundering cloud at the onset of the rainy season.
O Kauravya, Pārtha and Vāsudeva heard that great roar of him as he bellowed in the encounter with Bhīmasena;
then both Pārtha and Mādhava let out a mighty cry.
O great king, Vāsudeva and Arjuna rushed forward, roaring like two bulls, upon hearing the roar of that powerful warrior,
as they repeatedly shouted in their desire to see Vṛkodara.
O great king, hearing the roar of Bhīmasena and of the archer Phalguna, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was filled with joy;
and the king became free from sorrow upon hearing that great clamor.
The Lord, having expressed his hope for Dhanañjaya’s victory in battle,
[beheld] Bhīmasena roaring thus, fierce in combat;
then the mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, smiled.
Having reflected with his mind, that best of the upholders of dharma spoke what was in his heart:
"O Bhima, you have given your word and acted accordingly upon your elder’s command;
for victory in battle does not belong to those whom you hate, O Pāṇḍava."
"By good fortune, Savyasācin Dhanañjaya lives through this battle;
by good fortune, the hero Satyaki, whose valor is truth, is safe;
and by good fortune, I hear Vasudeva and Dhanañjaya roaring."
By whom Śakra was conquered in battle and the bearer of oblations (Agni) was gratified— he,
the slayer of enemies in combat, Phalguna, lives by good fortune! Relying upon the strength of his arms, we all continue to live.
By good fortune Phalguna lives, the slayer of enemy armies;
by good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives, by whom alone on his chariot the Nivātakavacas— so difficult even for the gods to conquer— were utterly defeated.
By good fortune, that son of Pṛthā lives, who defeated all the Kauravas assembled for the sake of seizing the cattle at the city of Matsya;
he who [slew] fourteen thousand Kālakeyas in the great battle.
By good fortune, that son of Pṛthā lives— he who by the strength of his own arms slew fourteen thousand Kālakeyas, those great archers,
as well as the powerful king of the Gandharvas, all for the sake of Duryodhana.
By good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives, he who by the power of his weapons has been victorious;
by good fortune Phalguna lives— he who wears a diadem and garlands, who is mighty, whose horses are white, and whose charioteer is Kṛṣṇa, and who is ever dear to me.
Will Dhananjaya— who, tormented by grief for his son and desiring to perform a difficult deed,
made a vow while seeking the slaughter of Jayadratha— slay the ruler of the Sindhus in battle?
"Will I indeed meet Arjuna before the sun has set— he who is protected by Vāsudeva and has fulfilled his vow? And is the King of the Sindhus still intent on the welfare of Duryodhana?"
Felled by Phalguna, he will gladden his enemies. Will King Duryodhana, upon seeing the ruler of the Sindhus struck down by Phalguna in battle, establish peace with us?
Having seen his brothers slain by Bhīmasena in battle,
will the dull-witted Duryodhana perhaps seek peace with us?
Having seen many other warriors struck down upon the surface of the earth...
I hope that the dull-witted Duryodhana will feel remorse;
I hope that our enmity with Bhīṣma alone will be pacified;
and I hope that Suyodhana will make peace for the sake of preserving the rest of us.
While he was thus reflecting in many ways, O King,
and was overwhelmed with compassion, a terrible battle took place.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
But who were the heroes that could withstand Bhīmasena of great strength as he roared in that manner, with a sound like the thundering of clouds? Indeed,
O Sañjaya, I do not see anyone in the three worlds who could face him.
Whoever should stand before Bhīmasena in battle when he is enraged—
like Time himself raising his mace in a great conflict—
I do not see anyone, my dear son, who could stand upon the field of war.
Who could stand in battle against him who destroys chariot with chariot, elephant with elephant, horse with horse, and likewise man with man— even Śatakratu himself?
When Bhīmasena was enraged and desiring to slay my sons,
who stood before him, intent on the welfare of Duryodhana?
For the grass and weeds that are my sons are being consumed by the forest fire of Bhīmasena.
Which heroes stood at the front to face him as he was about to consume the battlefield?
For seeing my sons being driven away by Bhīma in battle,
like all creatures by Time itself, who were they that surrounded Bhīma?

I have no such fear of Arjuna, nor of Kṛṣṇa, nor even of the Sātvata; nor do I have the kind of fear I have of Bhīma, who was born from the sacrificial fire. [I fear] the blazing fire of Bhīma, who desires to consume my sons.
"Who were the heroes who rallied around him? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said:
"While the great car-warrior Bhīmasena was thus roaring..."
Amidst that tumultuous roar,
the powerful and wise Karṇa also rushed forward;
drawing his mighty bow to its utmost limit, the impatient hero advanced.
But Karṇa, desiring battle and wishing to display his strength, the powerful one,
blocked Bhīma’s path like a tree against the wind.
And Bhīma, seeing Vaikartana standing before him with such impetuosity, [was filled with agitation].
The hero grew violently enraged; he hurled sharpened stones at him,
but Karṇa received them and sent his own arrows back against him,
while all the warriors then watched with effort.
At the encounter between Karṇa and Bhīma,
the limbs of the chariot-warriors and the horsemen seemed to tremble upon hearing the sound of their palms;
having heard the terrible roar of Bhīmasena on the field of battle.
The bulls among the Kṣatriyas thought that the sky and the earth were joined together;
again, by the terrible roar of the high-souled Pāṇḍava,
the bows of all the warriors in battle fell to the ground.
Upon hearing that roar in battle, the weapons fell from the arms of some of the weak-spirited, while the life-breaths fled from others;
and all, being terrified, discharged excrement and urine.
O Great King, the mounts became despondent;
hearing that terrible clamor, they discharged excrement, urine, and blood,
and then they stood motionless.
Many terrible omens appeared in great numbers;
the sky was completely covered by vultures, herons, and cranes,
O King, during that tumultuous encounter between Bhīma and Karṇa.
Then Karṇa struck Bhīma with twenty arrows and swiftly pierced his charioteer with five swift shafts.
But Bhīmasena, laughing, returned the fire upon Karṇa in that battle.
The mighty and swift-acting Bhīma [struck] with sixty-four arrows;
at him, the great archer Karṇa discharged four arrows. But before they had reached him, Bhīma [cut them down] with straight-knotted shafts.
O King, displaying his lightness of hand, he cut [the bow] into many pieces.
Karna then covered him with numerous showers of arrows. Though being covered in many ways by Karna, the son of Pāṇḍu—
The great car-warrior cut Karna’s bow at the handle and pierced him with many straight-knotted arrows. Then the Suta’s son took up another bow and strung it.
In that battle, the great car-warrior of formidable deeds pierced Bhīma;
then Bhīma, violently enraged and impetuous, drove three straight-knotted arrows deep into the chest of the Sūta’s son.
O bull of the Bharatas, with those arrows lodged in the middle of his chest, Karṇa then shone like a towering three-peaked mountain at midday,
or like the sun endowed with triple radiance.
And blood flowed from him, pierced by those supreme arrows,
like streaks of red chalk flowing from a mountain that oozes its mineral ores.
Afflicted by that severe blow, Karṇa wavered slightly.
Having fixed a formidable arrow to his bow, O noble one, he pierced him;
and then he discharged arrows again by the hundreds and thousands.
He was suddenly covered by Karṇa, that firm archer.
Smiling, the son of Pāṇḍu swiftly severed the bowstring;
with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he dispatched his charioteer to the abode of Yama,
and that great car-warrior deprived the four horses of their lives in the battle.
O lord of the people, having leaped down from his chariot whose horses had been slain, the great car-warrior Karṇa mounted the chariot of Vṛṣasena; meanwhile,
the powerful Bhīmasena, having defeated Karṇa in battle, [remained there].
He let out a tremendous roar, resembling the thundering of a rain-cloud.
Hearing that roar, Yudhiṣṭhira was filled with joy,
O Bhārata, believing that Karṇa had been defeated by Bhīmasena.
Then the Pandava army raised a clamor of conchs on all sides;
Yudhiṣṭhira filled the battlefield with shouts of joy,
and hearing the roar of the enemy host, your men also let out a great cry.
Pārtha cast aside the Gāṇḍīva bow, and Kṛṣṇa likewise silenced his conch;
having drowned out that sound, O Great King, the roar of the bellowing Bhīma was heard throughout all the armies, O Bhārata.
The roar of Bhīmasena was heard, and it was like something miraculous.
Then those two subduers of enemies exerted themselves with their weapons separately;
the son of Rādhā began mildly, while the Pāṇḍava began with firm force.
Then, as Bhīmasena exerted himself in the battle,
that army became so turbid that nothing could be discerned;
and Bhīma, O great king, rushed toward the son of Vaikartana.
Just as the son of Pāvaka [Kārttikeya] did against Tāraka in the great army of the Asuras,
so too did that great battle between Bhīma and Karṇa take place;
Bhīmasena, meanwhile, held him back with a mighty shower of arrows.
O noble one, Bhīma pierced his charioteer and his four horses with arrows,
and he cut down his standard and his banner with straight-knotted *bhalla* shafts;
he also shattered the chariot and its two wheel-protectors.
Karna also, the best of chariot-warriors, shaken by Bhimasena,
O King, rushed at Bhima with sword and shield, being powerful himself;
but Bhima, O noble one, cut off that sword along with the shield.
O Great King, seeing Karna oppressed by Partha with many arrows, Duryodhana addressed Duḥśāsana:
"Behold Karna fallen into distress; quickly provide him with a vehicle."
Thus addressed, King Duḥśala then rushed forward;
the great car-warrior Karṇa mounted the chariot of Duḥśala.
Having approached suddenly, Pārtha pierced those two with ten arrows.
Having pierced Karṇa once more, he took the head of Duḥśala.
O noble one, seeing Duḥśala slain by Bhīmasena,
Karṇa seized that very bow and pierced the Pāṇḍava.
In that battle, the two heroes of great strength fought one another like two powerful wielders of the thunderbolt in the midst of their enemies;
Bhīma pierced their horses and their charioteer again and again.
The mighty Pārtha, laughing, rushed toward Karṇa;
then, as Bhīmasena exerted himself in the encounter,
that army was shattered into fragments, and nothing could be discerned.
Saṃjaya said:
When that army had been thrown into confusion and Arjuna had gone toward the ruler of the Sindhus,
your son, along with the Sātvata, Bhīmasena, and others, advanced against Droṇa.
Hurrying on a single chariot and reflecting upon his many duties,
that chariot of your son,
endowed with the utmost speed and possessing the velocity of thought and wind, swiftly rushed toward Droṇa.
"O King, seen here and then vanished from this spot, the monarch fled away with his chariot. After only a moment, O noble one, your son reached Droṇa;
with eyes bloodshot from fury, your son spoke to him."
With great impetuosity, the joy of the Kurus spoke these words:
"Arjuna, Bhīmasena, and the unconquered Sātyaki—
these great car-warriors, having defeated all the vast armies,"
Having bypassed and slain vast armies,
those subduers of enemies reached the presence of the King of Sindhu;
and there too, all of them, remaining undefeated, exerted themselves.

"If the great car-warrior Pārtha has already bypassed you in battle, O giver of honor, how have you been bypassed by Sātyaki and Bhīma? It is as wonderful in this world as the drying up of the ocean."
"O foremost of Brahmins, the world speaks of your victory extensively— of how you were conquered by the Sātvata Arjuna and likewise by Bhīmasena;
how was Droṇa, who had reached the further shore of the science of archery, defeated in battle?"
"Thus do the warriors speak; this report of yours is indeed incredible. Surely my destruction in battle is certain, since three chariot-warriors have bypassed you, O tiger among men."
Since this matter has come to such a pass, speak what you wish to say. O giver of honor, that which is gone is gone; consider now what remains.
What task of the King of the Sindhus must be done next, as the time for it has arrived?
"Therefore, may your lordship speak quickly; let that be properly arranged.
Drona said:
"O great king, there is much to be considered regarding the task at hand; hear from me what must be done."
For three of the Pāṇḍavas' great chariot-warriors have already passed away;
as much danger as there is from behind, so much is there ahead of them.
Yet I consider that [the path] where Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya are to be far more significant.
That army of the Bharatas has been hemmed in from both the front and the rear.
In this situation, I believe our duty is the protection of the ruler of the Sindhus;
for he, O dear one, is the one among us who must be most carefully guarded against the wrathful Dhanañjaya.
For when the two heroes, Yuyudhāna and Vṛkodara, had gone after the ruler of the Sindhus,
this very game of dice— which was born of Śakuni’s cunning— was reached. Neither victory nor defeat occurred there in the assembly hall.
"O dear one, today we shall see victory and defeat for us as we gamble here.
Those terrible dice which Śakuni cast in the assembly of the Kurus—
regarding them as mere dice, he did not realize they were arrows difficult to withstand."
Those dice are not sharpened and terrible;
they are your own armor, O dear one, where those many Kurus stand surrounding you. Know, O lord of the people, that the army is the gambling table, and the arrows are the dice.
"And the stake, O King, was the ruler of the Sindhus; this was the final decision of the game.
For the great gambling match with the enemies was centered upon the king of the Sindhus. In this matter, victory or even defeat was certainly dependent upon you."

"O Great King, here all of you ought to protect the ruler of the Sindhus in battle at the cost of your own lives, according to the prescribed rites. For us, who are staking everything there, O dear one, victory and defeat are both certain."
Go yourself quickly to that place where those supreme archers stand ready guarding the King of Sindhu, and protect those guards;
as for me, I shall remain right here and dispatch others.
"And I shall destroy the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas.
Then, at the command of his preceptor, Duryodhana set out swiftly,
exerting himself for fierce deeds along with his followers.
The two Pāñcāla protectors of the wheels, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, having approached the army from the outside, proceeded toward Savyasācin;
for they had previously been held back by Kṛtavarman, O great king.
O King, when Arjuna had entered your army with a desire to fight,
the Kuru king saw those two heroes approaching the flank of the host;
having pierced the side of the army, the two heroes entered your forces.

Together with those two, the mighty Duryodhana, the descendant of Bharata, quickly engaged in a supreme battle with his two brothers who were themselves hurrying forward. Both of them, with bows raised, rushed toward him.
Renowned as great chariot-warriors and preeminent among Kṣatriyas in battle,
Yudhāmanyu pierced him with thirty heron-feathered arrows,
his charioteer with twenty, and his four horses with four.
Duryodhana cut down Yudhāmanyu’s standard with a single arrow;
he also severed his quivers and bow from that excellent chariot,
and with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla), he struck his charioteer down from the seat of the car.
Then, with four sharp arrows, he pierced the four horses;
and Yudhāmanyu the Pāñcālya and Uttamaujas likewise,
having broken through the army on its flank, entered toward Phalguna.
The hero struck them with arrows capable of piercing bone;
he struck Yudhāmanyu with seven and Uttamaujas with six.
Those two great car-warriors pierced him in return with well-sharpened shafts.

But the valiant Uttamaujas, with a broad-headed arrow, cut off his bow. Then, seizing another bow of great splendor, the mighty descendant of Kuru, filled with rage, covered the two Pāñcālas with arrows.
But Yudhāmanyu, filled with rage, quickly discharged thirty iron arrows into the space between the breasts of your son;
likewise, Uttamaujas, enraged, [struck him] with arrows adorned with gold.
He pierced his charioteer and sent him to the abode of Yama.
O king of kings, Duryodhana also slew the four horses and both the flank-charioteers of the Pāñcālya Uttamaujas.
But Uttamaujas, his horses slain and his charioteer killed in the battle,
quickly ascended the chariot of his brother Yudhāmanyu; that scorcher of foes swiftly mounted Yudhāmanyu’s chariot.

Having reached his brother’s chariot, he struck Duryodhana’s horses with many arrows; slain by them, they fell to the ground. When those horses had fallen, [Arjuna] cut off [Duryodhana’s] excellent bow with a supreme shaft.
Yudhāmanyu quickly [seized] his bow and quiver in the encounter;
then that great car-warrior, leaping down from his chariot whose horses and driver had been slain,
took up a mace and rushed toward the two Pāñcālya princes.
Seeing that enraged conqueror of enemy cities rushing toward them,
Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas leaped down from the seat of their chariot.
Then, the mace-wielder [Śālva] [attacked] that excellent chariot adorned with gold.
With his mace, he crushed [his opponent] in battle along with his horses, charioteer, and standard.
O lord of men, such was the deed your son performed—
he who is the best among mace-wielders and a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) in all the worlds.
Having slain him, your son— that scorcher of foes— his horses killed and his charioteer slain,
quickly mounted the chariot of the King of Madra.
As for those two mighty princes, the foremost among the Pañcālas—
Mounting another chariot, they both advanced against Dhanañjaya.
Sañjaya said:
"O Great King, while that hair-raising battle was underway..."
When the armies were in turmoil and being afflicted on all sides,
O bull of the Bharatas, the son of Rādhā challenged Bhīma to battle,
just as a rutting elephant in the forest charges at another rutting elephant.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When those two of great strength, Karṇa and Bhīma,
fought together near Arjuna’s chariot, what was that battle like?"
For previously Karṇa was defeated by Bhīmasena in combat;
how then did the great car-warrior Rādheya advance against Bhīma once more?
Or how did Bhīma advance against the son of the Sūta in battle?
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, having surpassed Bhīṣma and Droṇa— those renowned as great chariot-warriors and the most excellent car-fighters on earth—
felt no fear from any other source except for the archer Karṇa.
He never sleeps, constantly worrying about that great car-warrior;
out of fear of that mighty-armed one, he has not slept for many years,
as he perpetually reflects upon the prowess of the high-souled son of Rādhā.
How indeed did Bhīma fight that son of a Sūta in battle—
he who was devoted to Brahman, endowed with heroism, and never retreating from combat?
How did Bhīma fight Karṇa, the foremost of warriors, in the encounter?
How indeed did those two heroes, the son of the Sūta and Vṛkodara, fight when they encountered Arjuna’s chariot?
For previously, brotherhood had been shown, and that son of the Sūta was even compassionate.
How did Bhīma fight while recollecting Kuntī’s words,
or how did Bhīma, remembering the enmity committed in the past, fight with the Sūta’s son,
that hero, in the encounter?
"O Sūta, my son Duryodhana always hopes that Karṇa will defeat the Pāṇḍavas together in battle;
such is the hope for victory in combat held by my dull-witted son."
How did Bhīma fight that Bhīmasena of terrible deeds,
relying upon whom my sons have provoked enmity with those great car-warriors?
O dear one, how indeed did Bhīma fight that son of a Sūta?
Recalling the many various injuries arising from the son of the Sūta, how did Bhīma fight with the son of the Sūta— he who,
being heroic, had conquered the entire earth with a single chariot?
How indeed did Bhīma fight that son of a Sūta in battle—
he who was born together with earrings and armor?
How did Bhīma combat that son of a charioteer in the encounter?
In former times, O father, for the sake of celestial weapons, he worshipped Bhārgava;
through his grace, he obtained the Brahmāstra from that best of the Bhrigus.
[Tell me] how the battle between those two took place and who among them was the victor.
"Tell me that in truth, for you are skilled, O Sañjaya.
Sañjaya said:
"But Bhīmasena, having bypassed the son of Rādhā, the foremost of chariot-warriors—"
He desired to go where the two heroes, Kṛṣ�ṇa and Dhanañjaya, were staying.
As he was departing, O Great King, the son of Rādhā rushed toward him and showered him with heron-feathered arrows, just as a cloud rains upon a mountain.
Then the mighty son of Adhiratha, smiling with a face like a blooming lotus,
challenged Bhīma as he was advancing in battle.
Karṇa said:

"O joy of the Pāṇḍavas, that which was never even imagined in your dreams by those who caused you terror in battle— why do you now show me your back out of a desire to see Pārtha? This is not worthy of a son of Kuntī."
Standing before me, he overwhelmed me with showers of arrows.
Bhīmasena could not tolerate that challenge from Karṇa in battle;
drawing his bow into a half-circle, he fought the son of the Sūta.
With straight-flying arrows of great iron,
he rained down upon him who was armored and prepared for the single combat, the best among all wielders of weapons;
desiring to bring an end to the strife, he sought to strike and struck down Karṇa.
Having slain him and desiring to slay all the others, that mighty scorcher of foes,
the indignant and enraged Pāṇḍava, O noble one, loosed various fierce showers of arrows upon him.
The highly illustrious son of the Sūta, by means of his illusory weapons (*astramāyā*), swallowed up those showers of arrows from him who moved like an elephant in rut; for he,
O great king, was perfectly honored by that science (*vidyā*) according to the prescribed rules.
Like his preceptor, the great archer Karṇa moved about in the battle;
smiling as it were at Bhīmasena who was fighting with such fury, the impatient son of Rādhā rushed toward Vṛkodara.
The son of Kuntī could not endure that smile of Karṇa in the midst of battle,
while the heroes were fighting and looking on from all sides.
Then Bhīmasena struck him, who had approached, between the breasts with calf-toothed arrows.
The powerful and enraged warrior pierced him as one strikes a great elephant with goads; then,
with twenty-one well-aimed, sharp, and well-feathered arrows, he pierced Citravarman, the charioteer of the Suta's son.
The hero Karṇa pierced the horses— covered in nets of Jāmbūnada gold and possessing the speed of the wind— with five arrows each. Then, a net consisting of arrows was cast toward Bhīmasena’s chariot.
O King, within half a blink of an eye,
the Pāṇḍava was seen there along with his chariot, his banner, and his charioteer; at that moment,
O great king, he was completely covered by arrows discharged from Karṇa’s bow.
Karna pierced his firm armor with sixty-four arrows and,
filled with rage, struck him in the side with iron shafts that pierce the vital organs. Then, disregarding those arrows of great velocity released from Karna’s bow, [he remained unshaken].
Without any agitation, Vṛkodara embraced the son of the Sūta;
O great king, though bearing the arrows resembling venomous serpents discharged from Karṇa’s bow, Bhīma felt no pain in the battle.
O Great King, having struck terror [into his opponent], the immensely powerful Bhīmasena of immeasurable prowess severed Karṇa’s bow with thirty-two sharp,
keen-edged broad-headed arrows.
In that battle, the powerful Bhīmasena pierced Karṇa;
with no effort at all, Karṇa covered the mighty-armed Bhīmasena— who was desirous of slaying the ruler of the Sindhus— with his arrows.
The son of Rādhā first fought Bhīma in battle with mildness, but Bhīma likewise fought him with fury, recollecting their former enmity. The impatient Bhīmasena could not endure that insult.
That conqueror of enemies swiftly loosed a shower of arrows upon him. O King, those formidable arrows dispatched by Bhīmasena in the encounter fell on all sides like chirping birds.
O Great King, those gold-feathered arrows released from Bhīmasena’s bow rushed toward the son of Rādhā like wolves toward a small deer;
yet Karṇa, the best of chariot-warriors, remained covered by them on all sides.
O King, he discharged fierce showers of arrows in the battle;
Vṛkodara, with many broad-headed shafts, cut down those arrows— which resembled thunderbolts and graced the field of combat— before they had even reached him.
And once again, O Bhārata, Karṇa Vaikartana covered the great car-warrior Bhīmasena with a shower of arrows in that battle;
he released yet another rain of shafts toward the son of Pāṇḍu.
O Bhārata, while being thus afflicted from all sides by Karṇa in battle, we beheld Bhīma there with his body covered by arrows in that conflict,
like a porcupine bristling with its quills.
In that battle, the hero bore those gold-feathered arrows, whetted on stone and released from Karṇa’s bow, just as the sun bears its own rays;
with all his limbs drenched in blood, Bhīmasena shone resplendent.
Like a *palāśa* tree in the forest with flowers resembling refined gold,
or like an *aśoka* tree in springtime with its abundant clusters of blossoms; such,
O great king, was the conduct of Karṇa in that battle, as Bhīma observed it.
The great archer could not endure this; rolling his eyes in rage,
he struck Karna with twenty-five iron shafts,
like a white mountain covered by venomous snakes with hidden feet.
And just as fierce and excellent serpents enter an anthill,
they swiftly pierced him with seven sharp arrows resembling venomous snakes;
Bhīma, in turn, pierced him again with six and then with eight.

Then, in that great battle, the valiant Bhīmasena— possessing the prowess of an immortal and himself innocent of any offense— desiring to provoke a quarrel, struck the Sūta’s son in his vital parts. Thereupon, the powerful Bhīmasena became enraged at Karṇa.
He swiftly cut his bow as well as all his equipment;
nevertheless, the Pāṇḍava quickly pierced him in the chest in that battle. But the Pāṇḍava, having pierced him again with seven excellent arrows—
O King, with many other arrows resembling venomous serpents,
he swiftly struck the four horses and the charioteer with his shafts.
With iron shafts resembling the rays of the sun, he pierced Karṇa in the chest;
O noble one, they all passed through Karṇa and entered the earth,
just as the rays of the sun, O King, pierce through a cloud.
Once comforted, Karṇa indeed desired to fight again;
Bhīmasena, out of intense anger, pierced him once more with a feathered shaft.
Having suffered great distress, his bow severed and tormented by arrows, [he remained there].
Thus,
O Bhārata, that man who prided himself so much, Karna, casting aside his shame out of fear of Bhīmasena, retreated to another chariot.
He withdrew from the battle to fight, O bull of the Bharatas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Saṃjaya, he in whom my sons' hope for victory was always placed—"
Seeing him turned away from the battle, what did Duryodhana say? And how did the mighty Bhīma, who boasts of his own prowess, fight?
O dear one, what did Karṇa do after that in the encounter?
Saṃjaya said:
O Indra among kings, due to your transgression,
the battle broke out once more upon seeing Bhīmasena in the fray like a blazing fire.
He was himself a disciple of Bhārgava, the Lord of Beings, and a wielder of the bow; he was either equal to him in the mastery of divine weapons and illusions, or rather, Vṛṣa was superior to him.
As a disciple endowed with the qualities of a disciple, he was like Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
O Bhārata, that Karṇa, who was conquered by Bhīmasena, the son of Pāṇḍu,
became his disciple; he was equal to him in the mastery of weapons,
or perhaps even superior, being endowed with all the virtues of a disciple.
Just as Kāla, Antaka, and Yama were conquered by Bhīmasena,
so too was he effortlessly defeated by Bhīma, the son of Kuntī;
yet, mounting another chariot duly prepared, he returned once more.
Karna advanced against the son of Pāṇḍu like an ocean tossed by the wind;
O lord of the people, seeing the enraged son of Adhiratha,
your sons considered Bhīmasena to be already offered as a sacrifice into the mouth of Vaivasvata.
Bhīmasena, provoked to anger by Rādheya in that battle,
made a great sound with his bow and a terrifying sound with his palms,
and advanced toward the chariot of Rādheya.

Once again, O King, lord of the people, there occurred from that point a great and most terrible clash between the son of the Sūta and Bhīma. For those two mighty-armed warriors were enraged, each desiring the death of the other.
They gazed at one another as if burning each other with their eyes;
those two great car-warriors, subduers of enemies, enraged and with eyes red with fury, sighed deeply and,
having encountered one another in battle, hacked at each other.
Like two highly enraged tigers, like two swift-flying hawks,
or like two furious śarabhas, they fought with one another.
Then Bhīma remembered the sufferings at the game of dice and those endured in the forest.
In the city of Virāṭa, that subduer of enemies experienced great suffering,
as did the seizure of kingdoms abounding in jewels by your sons,
and the constant afflictions inflicted by you and your sons.
That you desired to burn the innocent Kuntī along with her sons;
and the suffering inflicted upon Kṛṣṇā in the midst of the assembly by those evil-minded men,
as well as the seizing of her hair by Duḥśāsana.
O Bhārata, harsh words were spoken by Karṇa:
"Seek another husband; you have no husbands left.
All the sons of Pṛthā have fallen into hell, resembling sterile sesame seeds."
O Kauravya, what the Kurus said then in your presence—
your sons who desired to enjoy Kṛṣṇā as a slave-girl—
and also when they saw them departing as exiles, clad in black antelope skins.
Karna spoke harsh words in the assembly in your presence; especially incited by the gambling match at the appointed time, your son behaved with insolence,
treating the sons of Pṛthā as if they were mere blades of grass.
For, established in equanimity, he felt compassion for those who were in distress and whose minds were clouded by fury;
and as the righteous-souled Vṛkodara, the slayer of enemies, reflected from his childhood upon those sufferings, he became weary of life.
Thus remembering those many kinds of terrors, resembling blazing fires,
that tiger among the Bharatas, casting aside all regard for his own life, drew his massive, gold-backed, and unassailable bow and rushed toward Karṇa.
With nets of arrows made of steel, whetted on stone and radiant as the sun, Bhīma shrouded the splendor of the sun as he advanced toward Karṇa’s chariot.
Then, laughing, the son of Adhiratha quickly discharged sharp shafts at him.

The great car-warrior, mighty-armed and possessed of great strength, dispersed Bhīmasena’s nets of arrows with his own feathered shafts; then the son of Adhiratha pierced Bhīma with nine sharpened arrows of great velocity.

Like an elephant being restrained by goads, Vṛkodara, though struck by those feathered shafts, rushed undaunted toward the son of the Sūta. As that bull among the Pāṇḍavas approached with impetuous speed, [he was met]...
Karna advanced to fight him, like one rutting elephant against another.
Then, having blown his conch shell which resounded like a hundred kettledrums,
the army was agitated with joy, like the surging ocean.
Seeing that army raised up, consisting of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry,
Bhīma approached Karṇa and covered him with arrows.
He [then struck] the horses, which were the color of *ṛśya* deer, with his own excellent steeds that were the color of swans.
As Karṇa intermingled with the Pāṇḍava in battle, shrouding him with arrows,
your sons’ army let out a cry of "Alas! upon seeing his deer-colored horses, swift as the wind, mingled with those of a white hue.
Those horses, swift as the wind, mingled together, O great king, shone greatly— some white and some black— like clouds in the sky.
Beholding Karṇa and Vṛkodara both enraged, their eyes copper-red with fury...
The great car-warriors among your men trembled with terror;
the battlefield of those two became as dreadful as the realm of Yama,
O best of the Bharatas, as difficult to behold as the city of the King of the Dead.
Beholding that wondrous spectacle like a grand assembly, the great chariot-warriors could not clearly discern victory for either side as each sought to repel the other;
they watched the clash between those two who were close with mighty weapons.
O King, O Lord of the People, this is due to the evil counsel of you and your son.
For those two slayers of enemies, covering each other with sharp arrows,
made the sky covered with nets of shafts by means of their showers of arrows.
Desiring to slay one another with sharp arrows, those two great car-warriors appeared most beautiful to behold, like two rain-bearing clouds;
those subduers of enemies discharged arrows adorned with gold.
O Lord, they made the sky radiant as if with blazing meteors;
discharged by those two, the arrows fletched with heron and peacock feathers shone like rows of intoxicated cranes in the autumnal sky.
Then, O great king, Bhīma, having pierced Karṇa with three arrows,
struck down his charioteer from the seat of the chariot with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla) and slew his four white horses with sharp arrows.

Having cast aside his banner and umbrella, he shattered the chariot into a hundred pieces; he deprived Karṇa of his chariot while your son looked on. Thus, deprived of his chariot, Karṇa was utterly defeated by Bhīmasena.
Mounting another chariot, he pierced the son of the Maruts once again;
like two proud great elephants goring one another with the tips of their tusks, those two hacked at each other and struck one another down.
Seeing Bhīma, the subduer of enemies, engaged with the Sūtaputra,
Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya considered that too great a burden for Bhīma alone.
There, [the warriors] were struck hard by the arrows released by both the son of Adhiratha and Bhīma.
Having leaped over the distance of an arrow's flight, horses, men, and elephants fell down;
O Great King, by those falling, those already fallen, and many others deprived of life, a great destruction of your sons' troops was wrought.
O bull of the Bharatas, in an instant the earth became covered with the lifeless bodies of men, horses,
and elephants, resembling the sporting ground of Rudra at the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I consider the prowess of Bhīmasena to be most wonderful,
in that he fought Karṇa, who possesses swift valor, in battle."
Karna, who in battle could hold back even the thirty gods when they were fully prepared for war, bearing all their weapons— along with the Yakṣas, Asuras, and men—
how could he [be defeated] by the son of Pāṇḍu, who shines as if with splendor in the fray?
He did not retreat in the encounter, O dear Sañjaya; tell me that.
And how did their battle proceed further—this gamble for life—in which, I believe, victory or defeat was entirely dependent?
"O Sūta, having obtained Karṇa in battle, my son Suyodhana was confident that he could conquer the Pārthas, along with Govinda and the Sātvatas.
But now, having heard that Karṇa has been repeatedly defeated by Bhīma of terrible deeds..."
"O Sañjaya, as Bhīmasena fights in battle, a stupor seems to take possession of me;
I believe the Kauravas are already destroyed by my son's wicked policies,
for Karṇa will not defeat the Pārthas, those great archers."
Whatever battles Karṇa fought with the sons of Pāṇḍu,
in every instance the Pāṇḍavas conquered Karṇa on the field of battle.
O dear one, the Pāṇḍavas are unconquerable even by the gods led by Indra himself.
And my dull-witted son Duryodhana does not realize this,
even though my son has seized the wealth of Pārtha as if it were the wealth of the Lord of Riches;
following the counsel of Karṇa, my son thinks only of his own self-interest.
Like a fool seeking honey who does not perceive the precipice, he—
having seized the kingdom of the high-souled ones through deceit— he whose wisdom is rooted in deceit,
considers himself victorious and treats the Pāṇḍavas with contempt.

Overcome by affection for my son and lacking self-control, I too acted so that those high-souled sons of Pāṇḍu, who were established in righteousness, were treated with deceit. Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pṛthā, is ever desirous of peace and is far-sighted.

Thinking him to be incapable, my sons rejected him; yet that son of mine, though of very dull intellect, disregarding them, spoke [thus] regarding those many sorrows and all kinds of injuries during the gambling match.
Keeping him in his heart, the mighty-armed Bhīma fought the Sūta’s son.
Therefore, Sañjaya, tell me how Karṇa and Bhīma,
those two best of warriors seeking each other’s death, fought in battle.
Saṃjaya said:
"Alas, I shall describe to you that life-and-death game of dice between those two,
while all the armies and even Keśava and Arjuna looked on."
"Listen, O King, to how the battle between Karṇa and Bhīma took place—
between those two who desired to slay each other, like two elephants in a forest.
O King, the son of Vaikartana, enraged, [assailed] the wrathful Bhīma, the subduer of foes."
Having exerted his prowess, he pierced him with thirty arrows—
highly impetuous, with bright points, and adorned with gold.
O best of the Bharatas, the son of Vikartana struck Bhima with those shafts.
As he was shooting, Bhīma cut his bow with three sharpened arrows;
then, with a broad-headed shaft, he felled the charioteer from the seat of the chariot to the ground.
Desiring the death of Bhīmasena, that bull-like son of Vikartana—
He grasped a spear with a shaft variegated with gold and lapis lazuli;
and having seized that great spear, which was like another spear of Time (Kāla),
the mighty son of Rādhā raised it up and fixed it for release.
The son of Rādhā, having released a spear like Purandara hurling the thunderbolt, hurled it at Bhīmasena as if it were the end of his life;
seeing that spear in the sky, possessing a brilliance equal to Śakra’s thunderbolt—
The powerful son of the charioteer let out a truly great roar;
hearing that roar, your sons were then filled with joy.
[They beheld] that [arrow] released from Karna’s arm, possessing the splendor of the sun and fire.
Bhīma cut that spear in mid-air with seven swift arrows. Having severed the spear, which resembled a sloughed-off serpent, Bhīma then seemed,
O noble one, to be seeking the very life-breath of the Sūta’s son.
Enraged, he discharged nine arrows feathered with peacock plumes,
gold-tufted, whetted on stone, and resembling the staff of Yama in battle.
Karna, too, seizing another formidable bow backed with gold, [prepared to strike].
Drawing his bow, the one of great splendor discharged nine arrows;
the son of Pāṇḍu cut those gold-adorned shafts with nine straight-knotted arrows of his own, likewise adorned with gold.
O King, having cut down those nine great arrows released by Vasuṣeṇa,
Bhīma, O great monarch, let out a roar like a lion.
Those two, roaring like two bulls in the presence of a cow in heat, were both exceedingly powerful.
Like two tigers, they roared excessively at one another;
desiring to strike each other down and seeking each other's weak points,
they glared at one another like two great bulls in a cow-pen.
Like two great elephants attacking one another with the tips of their tusks,
they struck each other with arrows released from bows drawn to their full stretch;
O Great King, they scorched one another with showers of shafts.
Glaring at one another with eyes wide open in anger,
laughing at each other and repeatedly reviling one another,
they fought each other while sounding their conchs.
O noble one, Bhīma once again severed his bow at the handle;
with his arrows, he sent those conch-colored horses to the abode of Yama,
and likewise struck down his charioteer from the seat of the chariot.
Then Karṇa, the son of Vikartana, fell into an insurmountable state of anxiety;
being covered by arrows in that battle, his horses slain and his charioteer killed,
he was bewildered by the net of shafts and did not know what ought to be done.
Then, seeing Karṇa fallen into such distress, King Duryodhana, as if trembling with rage, commanded Durjaya:
"Go, Durjaya! Before the Pāṇḍava devours the son of Rādhā."
"Quickly slay Tūbaraka, who is augmenting the strength of Karṇa!
Thus addressed, your son replied, "So be it," and rushed at Bhīmasena— who was already engaged in combat— scattering his arrows.
He struck Bhīma with nine arrows, his horses with eight,
his charioteer with six, his standard with three, and him once more with seven. Bhīmasena, also enraged, [struck] him along with his horses and driver with swift-flying shafts.

Karna, weeping in distress, circumambulated your son, who was difficult to conquer, with his vital organs pierced; he lay on the ground, crushed and writhing like a serpent, though still adorned with ornaments.
Having deprived his extreme enemy of his chariot, he, smiling,
covered him with multitudes of arrows, like a *śataghnī* with spikes.
Even so, Karṇa, though pierced by those shafts, remained a great car-warrior (*atiratha*).
The scorcher of foes did not abandon Bhīma in battle, even though he appeared enraged.
Sañjaya said:
Thus deprived of his chariot and once again defeated by Bhīma, Karṇa—
Mounting another chariot, he instantly pierced the Pāṇḍava;
like two great elephants attacking one another with the tips of their tusks,
they struck each other with arrows released from bows drawn to their full stretch.
Then Karṇa powerfully afflicted Bhīma with a multitude of arrows;
he let out a powerful roar and pierced him again in the chest.
Bhīma, in turn, pierced him back with ten straight-flying arrows.
He pierced him again with twenty straight-knotted arrows;
but Karna, O King, having pierced Bhima in the middle of the chest with nine shafts,
struck his standard with a single sharp arrow.
Then Pārtha pierced him with sixty-three arrows,
like a great elephant struck by goads or a horse by whips.
O Great King, he was thus deeply pierced by the illustrious Pāṇḍava.
Licking the corners of his mouth, the hero, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
swiftly severed the bow of the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
Then, O great king, he [discharged] an arrow capable of rending the entire body.
Like Indra hurling his thunderbolt at Bala, he discharged [the shaft] at Bhīmasena.
Released from the bow of the Sūta’s son, that stone-tipped arrow with its variegated feathers pierced Pārtha in battle and entered the earth, tearing it asunder.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
without hesitation hurled at the Sūta’s son his heavy six-sided mace, made entirely of Śaikya iron, four cubits long, and adorned with golden bands.
With that mace, the enraged Bhārata struck the excellent, well-trained horses of Adhiratha’s son, O Bhārata, just as Indra strikes the Asuras with his thunderbolt. Then,
O bull of the Bharatas, the mighty-armed Bhīma [struck him] with two razor-sharp arrows.
Having severed the standard of the son of Adhiratha, he then struck down the charioteer.
Seeing the charioteer slain and the banner brought low, [he beheld] the excellent horses— possessed of great strength and great speed— struck down by the mace.
Having abandoned his chariot— its horses and driver slain and its banner fallen— Karna stood there, O Bhārata, stretching his bow with a heavy heart. There we beheld the wondrous prowess of Rādheya.
When that best of chariot-warriors, deprived of his chariot, held back the enemy,
King Duryodhana, seeing the son of Adhiratha— the foremost of car-fighters— deprived of his vehicle in the battle,
then addressed Durmukha, O King.
"O Durmukha, this son of Rādhā has been deprived of his chariot by Bhīma;
provide that best of men with a chariot, O great car-warrior!
Having heard Duryodhana’s words, O Bhārata, Durmukha then—
Hurrying forward, he checked Karṇa and Bhīma with his arrows; seeing Durmukha following in the wake of the Sūta’s son in the battle,
the son of Vāyu was filled with joy and licked the corners of his mouth.
Then, O great king, having checked Karṇa with his stone-tipped arrows,
the Pāṇḍava swiftly dispatched his chariot toward Durmukha.
At that moment, O great king, he struck him with nine straight-knotted shafts.
With well-feathered arrows, Bhīma dispatched Durmukha to the abode of Yama. Then, O King,
when Durmukha had been slain, the son of Adhiratha mounted that very chariot and shone resplendent like the blazing sun.
Seeing Durmukha lying there with his vital organs pierced and drenched in blood,
Karṇa’s eyes filled with tears, and for a moment he could not move forward. Passing by him as he lay lifeless, Karṇa performed a circumambulation around him.
Sighing long and hot breaths, the hero did not know what to do.
But in that interval, O King, Bhīmasena discharged fourteen iron arrows feathered with vulture plumes at the son of the Sūta.
O great king, those gold-feathered arrows of immense power, variegated with gold, pierced his armor and illuminated the ten directions; those blood-drinkers then drank the blood of the Sūta’s son.
O lord of men, like enraged serpents impelled by Time,
those arrows shone as they glided across the earth;
gliding over the ground, drenched in blood, they appeared magnificent.
Like great serpents half-entering their holes in a fury, they rushed forward;
then the son of Rādhā, without hesitation, pierced them with fourteen exceedingly fierce iron shafts adorned with gold.
Those terrible feathered arrows, having pierced Bhīmasena’s left arm,
entered the earth like winged birds entering Mount Krauñca. Those iron shafts shone brightly as they penetrated the ground.
As the sun was setting, his radiant rays seemed to fade;
so too Bhīma, pierced in battle by iron arrows that split his vital organs,
bled profusely like a mountain discharging water.
Exerting himself, Bhīma pierced the Sūta’s son with three feathered arrows possessing the speed of Garuḍa, and struck his charioteer with seven.
O great king, Karna was overwhelmed and afflicted by Bhīma’s great strength.
The highly illustrious one fled on swift horses, abandoning the battle;
though he considered himself a man of honor, he retreated from the field of combat.
But Bhīmasena, stretching his bow adorned with gold—
In that battle, he stood as a super-ratha (atiratha), blazing like a sacrificial fire.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I consider destiny alone to be supreme; fie upon useless human effort!"

Wherein the son of Adhiratha, though exerting himself, could not overcome the Pāṇḍava in battle; how then can Karṇa hope to conquer the sons of Pṛthā along with Govinda in combat? Indeed, I do not see any warrior anywhere in the world who is the equal of Karṇa.
"Thus I heard Duryodhana muttering repeatedly:
'Karna is indeed powerful, a hero with a firm bow who has conquered fatigue. So spoke the dull-witted Suta, Duryodhana, in the past."
"Even the gods would not be able to withstand me in battle when I am aided by Vasuṣeṇa; how much less, O King, the sons of Pāṇḍu, who are devoid of strength and deprived of their senses?
Having seen him there defeated like a venomless serpent,"
What did Duryodhana say when Karna had withdrawn from the battle?
"Alas! He has brought only Durmukha, who is unskilled in battles, into the fire like a moth, being utterly deluded."
Who indeed, except for that son of mine, would have entered [the fray],
having cast himself into the terrible fire like a moth into a blazing flame?
Aśvatthāman, the King of Madra, Kṛpa, and Karṇa were united together.
"O Sañjaya, they are surely unable to stand before Bhīma;
for they know his most terrible strength, which is like ten thousand elephants,
as well as the cruel resolve of him who possesses the energy of the Wind-god."

Why will those who know his strength, impetuosity, and heroism provoke in battle one whose deeds are cruel and who resembles Yama, Kāla, and Antaka? Only the mighty-armed Karṇa, relying on the strength of his own arms, [will do so].
Disregarding Bhīmasena, the son of the Sūta fought in battle; he who,
like Purandara against an Asura, had conquered Karṇa in combat— that son of Pāṇḍu cannot be defeated by anyone in war.
Who, desiring to live, would dare to challenge Bhīma, who alone, having crushed Droṇa, entered my army in search of Dhanañjaya? For who indeed,
O Sañjaya, could venture to stand before Bhīma?
Just as a Dānava might turn back after reaching the city of Mahendra when his thunderbolt is raised,
a mortal might perhaps return even after reaching the city of the King of the Dead;
but having encountered Bhīmasena, one would never return.
Like moths entering a fire, those of small intellect entered [Bhīma],
being utterly deluded as they rushed toward the enraged Bhīmasena— those who,
in the assembly hall, had relied upon the slaughter of my sons by Bhīma.
Having heard that curse uttered by the fierce and impetuous one while the Kurus were listening,
and having reflected upon it after seeing Karṇa defeated,
Duḥśāsana, along with his brother, desisted out of fear of Bhīma.
