And that evil-minded one, O Sañjaya, who repeatedly said in the assembly,
"Karna, Duḥśāsana, and I shall defeat the Pāṇḍavas in battle"—
surely he has now seen Karna defeated by Bhīma and deprived of his chariot.
O Sañjaya, having seen Karṇa defeated by Bhīma in battle, and because of his rejection by Kṛṣṇa, he surely suffers greatly; likewise,
having seen his armored brothers slain in combat by Bhīmasena.
"Surely my son suffers greatly due to his own transgression.
For who, desiring life, would go against the Pāṇḍava—
Bhīma, with his terrible weapons, enraged and standing like Time itself?"
A man situated even in the midst of the submarine fire (Vaḍavāmukha) might indeed be released;
but it is my conviction that one who has fallen into the mouth of Bhīma cannot be released.
Neither the Pāṇḍavas, nor the Pañcālas, nor Keśava and Sātyaki [can save him].
"Enraged in battle, they know how to protect their lives.
Alas, O Sūta, the lives of my sons are surely lost!
Sañjaya said:

"O Kauravya, that you grieve now while this destruction of men is underway— of this, there is no doubt, you are the root cause of its ruin. Having yourself created this great enmity, you remained steadfast in the words of your sons."
Though being spoken to thus, you did not accept it, like a mortal rejecting wholesome medicine;
having yourself drunk the *kālakūṭa* poison so difficult to digest, O Great King,
now reap its full fruit, O best of men.
Having now obtained the fruit of that [action], it is just like having drunk poison.
Regarding that well-performed, well-executed, and nobly born deed in the great battle,
why do you revile the warriors as they fight according to their strength?
In this regard, I shall describe to you how the battle unfolded.
Having seen Karṇa defeated by Bhīmasena,
O noble one, those five brothers, great archers, could not endure it.
Durmarṣaṇa, Duḥsaha, Durmada, Durdhara, and Jaya—
clad in variegated armor— rushed headlong against that Pāṇḍava. Surrounding the mighty-armed Vṛkodara on all sides, they assailed him.
Covering the directions with arrows like swarms of locusts,
Bhīmasena, as if smiling, received those youths of divine form who were suddenly approaching him in battle.
Having seen your sons near Bhīmasena, O King,
the son of Rādhā advanced against the mighty Bhīmasena,
discharging gold-feathered arrows sharpened on stone.
But Bhīma rushed swiftly toward him, even as your sons tried to restrain him;
then the Kurus, surrounding Karṇa on all sides,
covered Bhīmasena with straight-jointed arrows.

O King, Bhīmasena then dispatched those bulls among men, along with their horses, to the abode of Yama with twenty-five arrows; O King, Bhīma, wielding his formidable bow, sent your five sons, together with their charioteers, to the realm of death with his shafts.
Deprived of life, they fell from their chariots along with their charioteers,
like great trees bearing variegated flowers broken by the wind. There we beheld the wonderful prowess of Bhīmasena.
Having checked the son of Adhiratha with his arrows and slain your sons,
O Great King, that son of the Suta, though being restrained on all sides by Bhima with sharp shafts, cast his gaze upon Bhimasena.
Then Bhīmasena, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
stretched his great bow and repeatedly glared at Karṇa.
Saṃjaya said:
But seeing his sons fallen, the powerful Karṇa was overcome by great anger and became despondent regarding his own life; at that moment,
the son of Adhiratha regarded himself as one who had committed an offense.
Seeing that his own son had been slain in battle by Bhīma before his very eyes,
he rushed toward Bhīmasena in a fit of rage and agitation; remembering their former enmity, he struck him down in his frenzy.
Having pierced Bhīma with five arrows, the son of Rādhā, as if laughing,
struck him again with seventy gold-feathered shafts whetted on stone. But Vṛkodara, the son of Pṛthā, could not endure that mockery.
Then he pierced the son of Rādhā with a hundred straight-knotted arrows;
and having again struck him with five sharp, swift shafts,
he once more pierced the son of Rādhā in battle with five iron arrows.
O noble one, he cut the bow of the Sūta’s son with a broad-headed arrow. Then, O Bhārata, taking up another bow, the dejected Karṇa covered Bhīmasena on all sides with arrows.
Having slain his horses and struck down his charioteer, Bhīma laughed a great laugh, having returned the favor for what had been done to him. Then that bull among men cut through his bow with arrows.
O Great King, that great-sounding bow with a golden back fell down; then that massive, gold-backed, and unassailable bow also fell. Thereupon, the great car-warrior Karṇa descended from that chariot.
Seizing his mace in the battle, he hurled it at Bhīmasena.
Seeing that mace suddenly descending, Vṛkodara,
O King, warded it off with arrows while the entire army looked on.
Then the powerful Pāṇḍava, hastening and desiring the slaughter of the Sūta’s son, discharged thousands of arrows.
Karna, having warded off those shafts with his own arrows in that great battle, [proceeded].
With his arrows, he caused Bhīmasena’s armor to fall;
then he struck him with twenty-five small shafts.
As all living beings looked on, it was like a marvel.
Then, O great king, the enraged Bhīma, in that battle, dispatched nine straight-knotted arrows at the son of the Sūta, O honorable one. They pierced his armor as well as his right arm.
Like fierce serpents entering an anthill, they fell upon the earth;
covered by the floods of arrows discharged from Bhīmasena’s bow,
Karṇa once again turned his back on Bhīmasena.
But seeing the son of Rādhā standing on foot in the battle,
enraged by Bhīmasena, King Duryodhana said:
"Hasten from all sides with diligence toward the chariot of the son of Rādhā!"
Then, O King, having quickly heard their brother’s words, your sons rushed toward the Pāṇḍava in battle, discharging sharp arrows. Citropacitra, Citrākṣa, and Cārucitra were the names of his bows.
O King, as those warriors of variegated weapons and variegated armor— fighters of diverse skills— suddenly advanced in battle, the great car-warrior Bhīma,
the great chariot-fighter Bhīmasena, quickly rushed toward them as they were charging forward.
In that battle, he struck down those who were prepared, along with their horses, charioteers, and banners;
slain, they fell to the earth like trees uprooted by the wind.
O King, having seen your sons, those great car-warriors, thus slaughtered.
With his face bathed in tears, Karṇa was overcome by dejection;
however, mounting another chariot that had been duly prepared,
the valiant warrior once more advanced against the Pāṇḍava in battle with great haste.
Having pierced each other with gold-feathered arrows whetted on stone,
O Great King, they both shone like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
Then, with thirty-six sharp, keen-edged *bhalla* arrows, they struck one another.
Enraged, the Pāṇḍava shattered the armor of the Sūta’s son;
and the mighty-armed Sūta’s son, O bull of the Bharatas, pierced the son of Kuntī with fifty straight-jointed arrows.
With their limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste and bearing great wounds inflicted by arrows,
they shone, drenched in blood like two suns risen at the end of time.
With their bodies sprinkled with blood, their armor pierced by arrows, they stood there.
Deprived of their armor, they shone like two snakes that have cast off their skins;
blazing with the fiery energy of their wrath, their eyes red with fury,
O Great King, they gleamed like two smokeless fires.
Like two tigers, those tigers among men, those subduers of enemies, mangled one another with their arrow-fangs as they brandished them;
discharging showers of arrows, the two heroes rained down like clouds.
Like two elephants locked in combat, they shone resplendent in the midst of the arena, piercing each other with sharp arrows while possessing the prowess of rutting elephants;
in that battle, they covered one another with nets of shafts.
Making all the quarters resound with their two chariots,
they moved about; O great king, as those two high-souled ones maneuvered their chariots in circular turns and other formations, they shone like Vṛtra and the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Like two elephants, those subduers of enemies appeared beautiful as they pierced each other’s limbs with arrows, like tusks;
they roared, leaped, and sported with one another.
Performing various maneuvers with their chariots, those two best of car-warriors roared like two powerful bulls in the presence of a cow,
or like two valiant lions— those two lions among men of great strength.
Glaring at one another with eyes bloodshot with rage,
those two of great prowess fought like Śakra and Vairocana;
brandishing their bows with arms adorned with ornaments, they struck out.
Bhīma shone in battle like a rain-cloud charged with lightning;
that great cloud of Bhīma, with the roar of his bow for its thunder and his showers of arrows for its rain, advanced,
O Great King, against the mountain of Karṇa.
Then, O Bhārata, with a thousand arrows released from his bow,
the Pāṇḍava overwhelmed Karṇa, just as a cloud covers a mountain with showers of rain;
he quickly shrouded Bhīma as a rain-cloud covers a mountain with water.
There, your sons beheld the prowess of Bhīmasena,
as he covered Karṇa with arrows furnished with beautiful feathers and vulture-winged shafts;
thus he gladdened Pārtha and the illustrious Keśava in battle.
Bhīma fought against Karṇa, while Sātyaki and his two wheel-protectors watched; O great king, your sons beheld the prowess, the strength of arms, and the fortitude of that self-knowing son of Pāṇḍu.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard the sound of Bhīmasena’s bowstring and palms, the son of Rādhā could not endure it,
just as an intoxicated elephant cannot bear the roar of a rival elephant.
Having retreated for a moment from the range of Bhīma's arrows,
the son of Adhiratha saw your sons fallen from their chariots;
he then beheld your sons struck down by Bhīmasena.
Seeing those slain by Bhīmasena, he became dejected and sorrowful;
sighing long and hot breaths, he once more advanced against the Pāṇḍava.
With eyes copper-red from rage, he hissed like a great serpent.
Discharging his arrows, Karṇa shone like the sun with its rays;
O bull of the Bharatas, Vṛkodara was completely covered by the arrows released from Karṇa’s bow, which spread out like the web of rays of the sun.
The variegated arrows, fletched with peacock feathers, released from Karṇa’s bow,
entered Pārtha from all sides like birds entering a tree for shelter;
the arrows discharged from Karṇa’s bow fell together from every direction.

Adorned with golden shafts, they shone like a row of swans in flight. O King, the arrows of Adhiratha’s son were seen issuing forth from his bow, his standard, his chariot-fittings, his umbrella, the tip of his pole, and his yoke.
Filling the sky with arrows of great velocity, which travel through the air and are feathered with bird-plumes,
the son of Adhiratha released variegated shafts adorned with gold.
As he rushed forward like Death himself exerting his power, Vṛkodara [beheld him].
Having cast aside his life, he pierced [him] with nine arrows in a fit of rage;
seeing that unbearable momentum of Karṇa and those great showers of arrows, the heroic Pāṇḍava was not at all distressed.
Then the Pāṇḍava, having dispersed the nets of arrows from the son of Adhiratha,
pierced Karṇa with twenty more sharp shafts;
for just as the Sūta’s son had covered Pārtha with his arrows, so did he now cover him in return.
In that very same manner, the Pāṇḍava covered Karṇa with his arrows in the battle.
O Bhārata, seeing the prowess of Bhīmasena in combat,
your men cheered and the Cāraṇas were filled with joy.
Bhūriśravas, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, the King of Madra Jayadratha, Uttamaujas, Yudhāmanyu, Sātyaki, Keśava, and Arjuna—
O King, these ten preeminent great chariot-warriors (*mahāratha*) among the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas.
"Excellent! Excellent! they cried out with force, letting forth lion-like roars.
While that tumultuous and hair-raising sound was proceeding, O King, Duryodhana spoke to your sons in haste.
"Go to the king, the princes, and especially to Karna— may you be blessed— who seek protection from Vṛkodara,
before Bhīma’s arrows, loosed from his bow, slay the son of Rādhā."
"O great archers, strive for the protection of the Suta's son! Commanded thus by Duryodhana, O noble one, the seven uterine brothers,
filled with fury, rushed toward Bhimasena and surrounded him.
Having approached the son of Kuntī, they enveloped him with showers of arrows,
like clouds during the rainy season covering a mountain with torrents of water.
Those seven enraged great car-warriors then afflicted Bhīmasena.
O King, like the seven planets at the time of the destruction of all creatures,
the son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava, then pressed his well-adorned bow with his left hand and gripped it firmly with his fist, O King.
Recognizing their human equality, the lord, exerting himself, fixed seven arrows resembling the rays of the sun and discharged them at them,
as if casting out the life-breaths from the bodies of your sons.
Then, O great king, remembering their former enmity, Bhīmasena deprived those sons of their lives from within their bodies. O Bhārata, those arrows discharged by Bhīmasena struck the Bhāratas.
Piercing through the sky, those gold-feathered arrows, sharpened on stone, flew upward;
having pierced their hearts, those gold-adorned shafts left the earth behind and departed along with their very lives.
O great king, those seven horses, adorned with gold and having their manes and tips stained with blood, shone like *suparṇas* moving through the sky; O lord of kings,
having drunk the blood of your sons, they emerged.
With their vital organs pierced by arrows, they fell from their chariots onto the earth,
like great trees growing on mountain peaks shattered by an elephant.
Śatruñjaya, Śatrusaha, Citra, Citrāyudha, and Dṛḍha—

Citrasena and Vikarṇa— these seven have been struck down. Vṛkodara, the son of Pāṇḍu, grieves most intensely out of sorrow for all your sons who have been slain, and especially for his dear friend Vikarṇa.
"This vow was given by me: they must be slain in combat.
O Vikarṇa, therefore you have been killed; my vow has been preserved. You went to the battle, O hero, mindful of the duty of a warrior."
O King, you were especially devoted to our welfare; yet,
whether by justice or injustice, this single one of great luster has been slain in battle— for the dharma of war is indeed cruel.
Saṃjaya said:
The son of Gaṅgā, possessed of unfathomable intellect and equal to the preceptor of the gods on earth,
though unconquerable even by the thirty deities, has been made to relinquish his life in battle.
"O best of the Kurus, in the dharma of battle there are no personal ties.
Having slain them while the mighty-armed son of Rādhā looked on,
the joy of the Pāṇḍus let out a terrible lion’s roar.
O Bhārata, that roar of the heroic Dharmarāja seemed to announce his great victory in battle;
it was as if he were proclaiming that combat and likewise the triumph of Bhīma.
Hearing that great roar of the bowman Bhīmasena in the battle, Dharmarāja experienced supreme joy. Then,
O great king, being delighted, he [caused] the loud sounds of musical instruments to resound.
Pārtha received Bhīmasena’s roar from all sides and,
filled with great joy because Vṛkodara had given his signal, advanced in battle against Droṇa, the foremost of those who wield weapons.
"O Great King, seeing that thirty-one of your sons, those great car-warriors,
had been slain, Duryodhana remembered those words of Vidura.
That beneficial advice of Vidura has now come to pass."
Reflecting thus, the king offered no reply to what your evil-minded son, of small intellect, had said at the time of the gambling match when he,
together with Karṇa, brought the Pāñcālī into the assembly hall.
And that harsh speech which Karṇa spoke to Kṛṣṇā in the assembly hall,
O lord of the people, in the presence of the sons of Pāṇḍu and yourself, and in the vicinity of all the Kauravas and the Preceptor—
"O Indra among kings, while you and all the Kauravas were listening, she said:
'The Pāṇḍavas are destroyed, O Kṛṣṇā; they have gone to eternal hell.
Choose another husband! This is the fruit that has now come upon her."

When your sons, having brought Draupadī into the assembly hall, spoke harsh words to the Pāṇḍavas— those fierce archers— inciting their wrath; and when your sons uttered further insults, such as calling them "sterile sesame seeds" and the like.
Those high-souled Pāṇḍavas have been incited by those seeking to provoke them.
O Kaurava, Bhīmasena, discharging that fire of wrath which has remained dormant for thirteen years, will bring about the end of your sons.
O best of the Bharatas, though Vidura lamented much for you and could not find peace, he and his sons have now reaped the fruit of that consequence; enjoy it.

By you, who were aged, steadfast, and a perceiver of the true meaning of affairs, the words of your friends were not heeded; in this matter, destiny was the ultimate resort. Therefore, do not grieve, O tiger among men; this great calamity is yours alone.
"O Indra among kings, I consider you yourself to be the cause of the destruction of my sons; for Vikarṇa has been slain, as well as the heroic Citrasena,
along with your other excellent sons who were great chariot-warriors."
O mighty-armed one, whatever of your sons Bhīma beheld as they came within the range of his vision, he slew them with great haste. Thus,
O bull of the Bharatas, did that fierce battle proceed.
"Indeed, because of you, I beheld my army being consumed by thousands of arrows released by the Pāṇḍava and by Vṛṣa. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sūta, this is a great misfortune, especially for me; I believe, O Sañjaya, that it has now come upon me as I grieve. 'What is gone is gone'—this was the thought established in my mind."
"O Sañjaya, what shall I do now?
Tell me how this destruction of heroes, born of my own misconduct, has come to pass; for I have become despondent, O Sañjaya."
Saṃjaya said:
O great king, Karṇa and Bhīma, displaying their prowess in that great battle,
rained down showers of arrows like two rain-bearing clouds.
Arrows marked with the name Bhīma, gold-feathered and sharpened on stone,
entered Karṇa upon reaching him as if piercing his very life.
In the same way, those released by Karṇa were like venomous serpents.
In that battle, Bhīma was overwhelmed by hundreds and thousands [of arrows];
O great king, as their shafts fell from all sides,
a tumult arose among your troops like that of the ocean.
O subduer of enemies, your army was slaughtered in the midst of the host by Bhīma’s terrible arrows, which were like venomous serpents, discharged from his formidable bow;
O King, [the field was covered] with fallen elephants, horses, and men.
The earth appeared strewn as if with trees blown down by the wind;
being struck in battle by arrows shot from Bhīma’s formidable bow,
your warriors fled and cried out, "What is this?"
Then that army of the Sindhus, Sauvīras, and Kauravas was scattered;
driven away by the arrows of great velocity from both Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava,
they were for the most part afflicted by those shafts, with their horses, men, and mounts slain.

Having abandoned both Karṇa and Bhīma, they fled in every direction. "Surely the dwellers of heaven are deluding us for the sake of Pārtha, since our army is being slaughtered by arrows originating from Karṇa and Bhīma."
Speaking thus, those warriors of yours, oppressed by fear,
abandoned the range of the arrows and stood still, desiring to witness the battle.
Then, in that great conflict, a river of terrible form began to flow.
And it became especially a source of increasing terror for the timid,
arising from the floods of blood of elephants, horses,
and men, and strewn with lifeless humans, elephants, and steeds.

With chariots adorned with trailing poles and banners, decorated with gold, and embellished with elephants, horses, and ornaments— chariots that were overturned, their wheels, axles, and poles shattered.
With equipment of gold, with bows of great value,
and with thousands of gold-feathered arrows and iron shafts released by Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava— like snakes that have cast off their skins— ;
With multitudes of spears and javelins, and swords along with battle-axes;
with maces, clubs, and sharp-edged spears adorned with gold; and with thunderbolts of various forms, as well as pikes and iron bars.
O Bhārata, the earth shone with various *śataghnī* weapons,
with golden armlets, bracelets, earrings, and beautiful gems;
likewise, it was strewn with discarded bangles and finger-rings.
O Māriṣa, O Bhārata, with crest-jewels, turbans, and golden threads; with armor and finger-guards, with necklaces and golden coins;
and with garments, umbrellas, and even scattered yak-tail fans.
With elephants, horses, and men mangled by weapons, along with chariots and ornaments,
and with various objects scattered here and there— fallen and cast away— the earth shone like the sky filled with planets.
Seeing their inconceivable, marvelous, and superhuman deeds, the *cāraṇas* and *siddhas* were filled with wonder;
it was like the progress of fire aided by the wind through dry grass in battle.
The fierce advance of the son of Adhiratha, who had Bhīma as his companion,
became like a forest of reeds when two elephants charge it— his standard and chariot having been struck down, and his horses, men, and elephants slain.
O Bhārata, such was that great army in the encounter;
O lord of men, your army resembled a mass of clouds.
And there was a supreme clash between Karṇa and Bhīma in the battle.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O great king, Karna, having pierced Bhima with three arrows,
struck him again with four sharp-pointed shafts feathered with heron plumes.
He released many diverse showers of arrows. Being struck by the Sūta’s son, O Great King, the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena did not waver, like an immovable mountain being pierced.
O king of kings, in that battle Bhīmasena pierced Karṇa in the ear with a sharp, yellow, feathered arrow equipped with a barb;
O noble one, he struck him most violently in the fray with that shaft cleansed in oil.
O great king, he struck the large golden earring from Karna’s ear onto the ground, like a blazing light falling from the sky,
resembling a wild ruddy goose crying out from the sandy banks of the Ganges.

Then, a pure and supreme ear-ornament, fashioned by the divine architect, fell from the center of his ear; it was set with jewels and rubies, possessed the fierce brilliance of fire, and was made from a single piece of nectar-like lotus-metal.
Then, with another broad-headed arrow, the mighty Bhīma, as if smiling, struck the Sūta’s son violently in the middle of the chest.
O Bhārata, Bhīma then quickly discharged ten iron shafts at him once more.
In that battle, O noble one, he discharged arrows of great velocity, resembling the staff of Yama;
these, being impelled by him, reached the forehead of the Suta’s son and entered it like serpents into an anthill.

With those arrows lodged in his forehead, the Sūta’s son shone as if he were wearing a garland made of blue lotuses, just as he did in former times. Thus deeply pierced by the swift Pāṇḍava, Karṇa was sorely wounded.
Grasping the pole of the chariot, he closed his eyes;
after a moment, having regained consciousness, Karṇa, the scorcher of foes,
with all his limbs drenched in blood, summoned a supreme rage.
Then, enraged in battle and oppressed by the wielder of the firm bow, Karṇa,
possessed of great speed, made a rush toward the slaughter of Bhīmasena. To him,
O King, Karṇa discharged a hundred arrows feathered with vulture plumes.
O Bhārata, impatient, powerful, and enraged, he dispatched [his forces];
then the Pāṇḍava loosed fierce showers of arrows,
disregarding him in battle and paying no heed to his prowess.
Disregarding them, the mighty-armed Bhīma of terrible prowess—
then, O great king, Karna, the scorcher of foes, being enraged, struck the wrathful Pāṇḍava in the chest with sharpened arrows.
Those two tigers among men, like two fanged tigers with arrows for their teeth, having encountered one another, immediately tore at each other;
and in that battle, they showered each other like two clouds.
Terrifying each other with the sounds of their palms,
they covered one another in the fray with various nets of arrows;
enraged in battle, each sought to counter the other's actions.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, having severed the bow of the high-souled son of Rādhā with a razor-headed arrow, pierced Karṇa with a feathered shaft.
Discarding that severed bow, the high-minded son of the Sūta—
He took up another bow, one that could withstand great force and bear a heavy burden;
yet Vṛkodara cut that one down as well within half a blink of an eye.
And he likewise [cut down] the third, the fourth, the fifth, and the sixth.
Vṛkodara [struck] the seventh and the eighth, as well as the ninth and the tenth,
and also the eleventh, the twelfth, and the thirteenth,
as well as the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the sixteenth.
In that manner, Bhīma severed seventeen, and even eighteen bows of Karṇa; thus he cut down many of Karṇa’s bows,
until Karṇa stood with a bow in his hand once more within half a blink of an eye.
And having seen the destruction of the Kuru, Sauvīra, and Saindhava forces,
he beheld the earth covered with fallen armor, banners, and weapons,
as well as crushed and broken chariots and other horses galloping away in haste.
Seeing the best of men deprived of their splendor with hair covered in dust,
and seeing the bodies of elephants, horses, and men everywhere lying lifeless,
the body of the Sūta’s son blazed forth with fury.
Stretching his great bow adorned with gold,
O King, the son of Rādhā glared at Bhīma with a fierce gaze.
Then, discharging arrows in his wrath, the Sūta’s son shone resplendent.
Like the radiant sun at midday in autumn,
O King,
the formidable form of Ādhiratha’s son, with its rays of hundreds of arrows, was like the body of the sun when its beams are fully expanded.
As he took up his swift-flying arrows with both hands, fixed them,
drew them back, and released them, no interval could be seen in the battle;
his weapon, whirled in a circle, was as terrible as a wheel of fire.
O great king, as Karṇa discharged arrows from both his left and right hands,
those well-sharpened shafts with golden feathers, released from Karṇa’s bow,
O great king, shrouded the quarters and the radiance of the sun.
Then, a multitude of gold-tufted,
straight-knotted arrows released from the bow was seen in many ways across the sky;
for the arrows issued forth from the bow of the son of Adhiratha.
O King, arranged in rows, they shone like cranes in the sky;
the son of Adhiratha released arrows that were fletched with vulture feathers, whetted on stone, adorned with gold, possessed of great velocity, and tipped with blazing points.
Shaken by the force of his bow and adorned with gold,
those arrows were incessantly scattered toward the chariot of Pārtha;
embellished with jewels, they shone by the thousands in the sky.
Like swarms of locusts,
the arrows discharged from the bow of Adhiratha’s son fell as he loosed them; yet, though many were released,
they appeared as if they were but a single, long, and towering shaft.
Like a rain-cloud covering a mountain with torrents of water,
the enraged Karṇa covered Bhīma with showers of arrows.
There, O Bhārata, was the strength, heroism, and prowess of Bhīma.
And your sons, together with the Kurus, watched his resolve;
yet Bhīma, disregarding that rising shower of arrows which was like the surging ocean, rushed furiously toward Karṇa.
O lord of the people, Bhīma possessed a great bow with a golden back;
when drawn into a circle, it was like a second bow of Indra,
and from it arrows issued forth as if filling the sky.
With gold-feathered, straight-knotted arrows shot by Bhīma,
a garland formed in the sky shone as if it were made of gold.
Then, those nets of arrows remained suspended in the firmament, arranged in their respective divisions.
Struck by the feathered shafts of Bhīmasena, the weapons shattered; likewise,
by the floods of Karna’s arrow-nets,
both [sides] were struck in that battle by straight-flying arrows whose touch was like sparks of fire.
The sky was completely covered by those various flights of gold-feathered arrows;
at that time, the sun did not shine, nor did the wind blow,
and as the firmament was shrouded in a net of shafts, nothing whatsoever could be discerned.
Covering Bhīma with various kinds of arrows, the Sūtaputra advanced,
disregarding the prowess of that high-souled one. As they both discharged nets of arrows there, O noble sir, [the battle raged].
Becoming like the wind, they were seen locked together with one another;
O best of the Bharatas, from the mutual impact of the arrows of those two lions among men, fire was produced in the sky.
Enraged and desiring his death, Karṇa dispatched at him sharp arrows polished by smiths and adorned with gold;
[Arjuna] shattered each one of those in the sky into three pieces with his own shafts.
Distinguishing himself from the Sūta’s son, Bhīma cried out, "Stay!
And once more, the Pāṇḍava, impatient, powerful, and enraged like a fire wishing to consume all, loosed fierce showers of arrows.
Then, from the striking of their leather arm-guards, there arose a crackling sound for those two;
there was a great slapping of palms and a terrifying lion-like roar,
as well as the rattling of chariot rims and the harsh twang of bowstrings.

O King, the warriors ceased their fighting, desiring to witness the prowess of Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava as they sought each other’s death; the celestial seers, Siddhas, and Gandharvas honored them, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
And likewise, the hosts of Vidyādharas released a rain of flowers.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, impetuous and of firm prowess,
having warded off the weapons with his own weapons, pierced the Sūta’s son with arrows.
The mighty Karṇa, having warded off Bhīmasena’s arrows,
dispatched nine iron shafts resembling venomous serpents in the battle;
then Bhīma cut them down in mid-air with an equal number of feathered arrows.
He [pierced] the iron arrows of the Suta’s son and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Then the mighty-armed hero Bhīma, enraged like the Destroyer at the end of time, released at the son of Adhiratha an arrow that was like a second staff of Yama.
As it was flying toward him, O King, the powerful son of Rādhā, as if laughing, cut down that arrow of the Pāṇḍava with three shafts;
yet the Pāṇḍava again released fierce showers of arrows.
The son of the Sūta, Karna, fearlessly seized all those weapons from the fighting son of Pāṇḍu through his mastery of weaponry;
with straight-knotted arrows, he [seized] his quivers and his bowstring.
Karna Vaikartana cut through the reins, the traces, and the horses;
then, having slain his horses once more, he pierced the charioteer with three arrows.
The charioteer, leaping down, quickly fled toward the chariot of Yuyudhana.
Smiling as it were, the enraged son of Rādhā, blazing like the fire of cosmic destruction, cut down Bhīma’s standard and struck down his banners.
Deprived of his bow, O great king, he seized a chariot-spear.
Enraged, he whirled it and hurled it toward Karna’s chariot.
As that gold-adorned spear, shining like a great meteor, came flying toward him, the son of Adhiratha, exerting himself, cut it apart with ten arrows.

O King, severed by the arrows of Karṇa— who was shooting with wonderful skill for the sake of his friend— that shield fell in ten pieces. Then the son of Kuntī took up another shield adorned with gold.
Seeking either the sword or victory over death itself,
Karna,
as if laughing, suddenly shattered that [sword] of his with many exceedingly fierce arrows, O Bhārata.
Deprived of his shield and chariot, O Great King, he was overwhelmed with rage;
whirling his sword, he hurled it swiftly toward Karna’s chariot.
That well-sharpened blade, having severed the bow and the string of the Suta’s son, [fell].
The sword fell to the earth like a snake fallen from the sky;
then, laughing, the son of Adhiratha took up another bow,
one with a firm string and greater speed, being enraged in battle against the slayer of his enemies.
O great king, Karna exerted himself, desiring to slay the son of Kuntī, discharging thousands of well-sharpened arrows with golden shafts; at that,
the powerful Bhimasena, whose valor is truth, became enraged.
Being struck by the arrows released from Karṇa’s bow, that powerful warrior ascended into the sky, distressing Karṇa’s mind;
and seeing those deeds of his in battle, [the warriors] desired victory.
Resorting to a feigned faint, the son of Rādhā deceived Bhīmasena;
not seeing him, who was hidden in the interior of the chariot with his senses overwhelmed,
he stood upon the surface of the earth, having reached the enemy's standard.
All the Kurus and the Cāraṇas honored him for that,
when he desired to slay Karṇa from his chariot like Tārkṣya slaying a serpent. With his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, he remained steadfast, observing his own duty.
Leaving his own chariot behind, he stood firm for battle alone;
then the son of Rādhā, having struck him down,
rushed toward that Pāṇḍava who stood ready for combat in the fray, filled with fury.
Those two of great strength, meeting upon the vast arena and vying with one another,
roared like two clouds in the sky at the end of the summer heat.
A violent clash ensued between those two enraged lions among men.
As the two of them, like a god and a dānava, could not tolerate one another in battle,
the son of Kuntī, his weapons exhausted and assailed by Karṇa,
bypassed Bhīma and severely afflicted him with arrows.

Then, deprived of his bow, his chariot, and his shield, and having been cast down from his seat, he could not endure it; though previously so fierce, he was now deeply distressed, tormented by Karṇa’s weapons.
He beheld the mountain-like elephants slain by Arjuna, fallen upon the ground.
Deprived of his weapons, he entered the herd of elephants in order to obstruct the path of the chariot; having reached the elephant pen and entered that fortress of chariots,
the Pāṇḍava, desiring to preserve his life, did not attack the son of Rādhā.
Then, desiring to establish order, Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities, raised up an elephant slain by the arrows of Dhanañjaya and stood firm upon it,
like Hanumān atop a mountain endowed with great medicinal herbs.
Karna again pierced that elephant of his with arrows;
he then hurled tens of thousands of chariots, tens of thousands of horses,
and likewise tens of thousands of men against Karna of immeasurable splendor.
The powerful one seized spears, swords, javelins, clubs, maces, hammers,
and mallets from the surface of the earth and hurled them at Karṇa;
he drove those thrown weapons forward with a force like that of a mighty wind.
Then Vṛkodara, having reached the field of battle, swiftly cut [the foe] like a bull possessed by a great planet; free from despondency,
he rushed toward the son of Rādhā like the wind itself incarnate.
Then the Pandava, roaring, hurled elephant limbs at Karna;
wheels, horses, and whatever mounts he saw upon the ground— whatever it was—
the enraged Pandava seized and flung it at Karna.
He cut down every one of those [weapons] as they were hurled, with his own sharp arrows.
Bhīma, too, raising his most terrible fist whose core was like a thunderbolt,
desired to slay the Sūta’s son in an instant, remembering Arjuna.
Though capable and competent, the son of Pāṇḍu did not slay Karṇa,
guarding that vow which had been made by Savyasācin.
Bhīma, thus distressed, [was struck] again and again with sharp arrows.
The son of the charioteer rendered his limbs overwhelmed by a swoon;
yet Karna did not slay him while he was disarmed, remembering the words of Kuntī. Then Karna, rushing forward, seized him by the tip of his bow.
As soon as he was touched by the bow, he hissed like an angry serpent;
snatching that bow away from him, he struck Karṇa on the head.
Struck by Bhīmasena, his eyes became blood-red with rage.

Smiling as it were, the son of Rādhā said to Bhīmasena again and again: "O beardless one! O fool! O glutton! O you who have not mastered weapons! Do not fight, O child, you who are a coward in battle!"

O Pāṇḍava, where there is food of many kinds, as well as edibles and drinks, there you are fit, O evil-minded one; but by no means in battles. Or rather, O Bhīma of very wicked mind, having become a sage, you eat fruits.
"Go to the forest, O son of Kuntī; you are not skilled in battle. You are suited for subsisting on fruits and roots, as well as for feeding guests;
I do not consider you fit for the employment of weapons, O Vṛkodara."
"I know you to be a cook, a servant of the Matsya king.
You are accustomed to subsisting on flowers, roots, and fruits, and to vows and religious observances; O Bhīma, you are suited for the forest, not for being skilled in battle."
"Where is battle, and where is the state of a sage? Go to the forest, Vṛkodara!
You are not suited for war, my dear; find delight instead in dwelling in the woods.
You are merely hurrying the cooks, servants, and slaves about the house."
"O Vṛkodara, you are fit to strike him out of anger for the sake of food," said Sañjaya.
Having seen him thus deprived of his chariot and remembering [the past], Karṇa spoke these words.
O lord of the people, Bhīmasena also repeatedly reminded him of those unpleasant things that had occurred during their childhood,
as well as the harsh deeds they had previously committed.
Bhīmasena said:
"O son of Rādhā, O son of the Sun, you who are superior in strength, listen to my words! In this world, there is no warrior to be found anywhere who is your equal.
If I am to be sought out by you, then what is the use of much talk?"
"Then, if you do not seek me out, I shall depart; release me!
Having thus deprived the Pāṇḍava of his chariot and having loudly reviled him, he, filled with supreme joy, displayed himself before Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava.
Then, while he was crouching there, Vṛṣa struck him again with his bow;
laughing, he then spoke these words to Bhīma:
"One must fight elsewhere; one should not fight with those such as I."
For those who fight with men like me, this and more is possible. Go where those two Kṛṣṇas are; they will protect you in battle.
Or go home, O son of Kuntī; what use have you for war, you child?
O Bhīma, you are indeed considered by me to be the ancient one who truly embodies the meaning of sound; for you are the son of Māruta, the son of the Wind-god, supreme in weapons and missiles,
as well as in the knowledge of the meaning of sacrificial scriptures and in the expositions of Dharma.
“You are always clever, Bhīma, but you are not skilled in battle.
Smiling as he spoke, Vṛṣa touched him on the neck with his hand—
marked with the signs of the umbrella, thunderbolt, and goad— while calling to mind his mother’s words.
Having heard these exceedingly harsh words of Karṇa, Bhīmasena, laughing, spoke these words to Karṇa while everyone was listening:
"O wicked one, you have been defeated by me many times; yet you boast of yourself in vain."
Victory and defeat have been seen by the ancients in the world even for Mahendra; therefore,
O one born of a low family, engage in a wrestling match with me,
just as the mighty and wealthy Kīcaka was slain.
"In that same way, I shall cause you to be slain while all the kings look on.
Having understood Bhīma's intention, Karṇa, the best among the wise,
withdrew from that battle while all the archers looked on.
Bhīma, the best among chariot-warriors, also received a curse from the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) because he previously failed to offer a salutation when he went to steal the lotus;
for this very reason, he has incurred fear of Karṇa.
Then Karna, acting upon his mother's words, released [the weapon] as well. Having thus deprived him of his chariot, O King,
Karna boasted in the presence of that lion of the Vṛṣṇis and the high-souled Pārtha.
But Bhīma, of terrible prowess, desiring to speak to him,
did not act quickly, for he remembered the great strength of Arjuna; instead,
that heroic warrior swiftly shattered his bow.
Then, O Great King, having seen this, the immensely radiant Vāsudeva said,
"O Sañjaya,
O Arjuna, Arjuna! Behold Bhīma being oppressed by Karṇa!"
Thus addressed then by the high-souled Keśava, Pārtha,
his eyes bloodshot with rage, overcome by indignation, looked upon Bhīmasena in that state as if burning him with his gaze.
Seeing Vṛkodara deprived of his chariot by Karṇa and being threatened,
Arjuna became violently enraged, his eyes bloodshot with anger;
then, O King, he whose banner bears the monkey discharged arrows polished on stone.

Urged by Keśava, he discharged it at the Sūta’s son. Then the arrows released from Pārtha’s arms, adorned with gold and originating from the Gāṇḍīva, entered Karṇa like swans entering a Krauñca mountain.
Dhananjaya drove the Suta’s son away from Bhimasena with arrows discharged from the Gandiva that were like snakes with their heads raised;
his bow having been cut by Bhima, he was struck by the arrows of Dhananjaya.
Karna fled swiftly on his great chariot away from Bhima;
Bhima too, that bull among men, mounting the vehicle of Satyaki,
followed his brother Savyasacin, the son of Pandu, in the battle.
Leaping down quickly, the charioteer went to Yuyudhāna’s chariot;
then Dhananjaya, his eyes copper-red with rage, swiftly loosed an iron shaft toward Karṇa like the Destroyer himself sending forth Death.
Like Garuḍa in the sky seeking the best of serpents,
that iron shaft, impelled by the Gāṇḍīva, swiftly flew toward Karṇa;
but the son of Droṇa cut that iron shaft down in mid-air with a feathered arrow.
Desiring to rescue Karṇa from the fear of Dhanañjaya, that great car-warrior [Kṛpa] then, O great king,
the enraged Arjuna pierced the son of Droṇa with sixty-four arrows;
Satyajit, wishing to protect him, rushed against Pārtha.

The mighty warrior pierced that king with a single arrow. O great king, the son of Droṇa cut down the iron shaft (*nārāca*) discharged by Pārtha at Karṇa with his own stone-tipped arrows, and cried out, "Do not go! Stay!"
Afflicted by the arrows of Dhananjaya, the son of Droṇa quickly entered that army, which was crowded with rutting elephants and thick with chariots. Then,
in the battle, there arose the twanging of gold-backed bows.
The mighty son of Kuntī, Dhananjaya, overwhelmed that sound with the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow;
thus he pursued the son of Droṇa from behind as he fled,
terrifying the army with his arrows over what seemed like no very long distance.

Having torn open the bodies of men, elephants, and horses with his iron shafts, Arjuna scattered that army— consisting of men, horses, and elephants— with arrows fletched with the feathers of herons and peacocks,
O best of the Bharatas.
The son of Pākaśāsana (Indra), exerting himself, struck back at Pārtha.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I believe that today I must once again give my own [kingdom] to the Pāṇḍavas."

Indeed, for a man in this world, conflict with one who is stronger can never lead to his welfare; rather, he should live by bowing at the feet of the enemy, even if it means eating the leftovers of his foe, or by doing something else entirely.
While living, the next world is accomplished in every way; likewise, for one who does not live, there is neither happiness nor a supreme goal.
When destruction has occurred in every respect, the fool does not perceive the need for action.
For one consumed by false pride does not perceive what has been done and what remains to be done.
O Saṃjaya, my blazing glory falls day after day;
many of my warriors have been slain—I consider this to be the reversal of Time.
But Dhanañjaya, filled with rage, entered my army—
which was protected by Droṇa and Karṇa and was impenetrable even by the gods—
his prowess being augmented by those two of mighty valor.
Accompanied by Kṛṣṇa and Bhīma, and by the bull of the Śinīs—
since that time, grief has been burning my heart like fire. For I see the protectors of the earth, along with the ruler of the Sindhus, as if already devoured.
Having committed a most grievous offense against the Diademed One (Arjuna), how could the King of Sindhu escape with his life once he has come within the range of his vision?
And by inference, O Sañjaya, I see that the ruler of the Sindhus no longer exists.
Tell me, who am asking you, how that battle took place when the king of the gods, Śakra of great splendor, was enraged; and how he,
having repeatedly agitated and stirred up the vast army, [acted].

"Like a single enraged elephant entering a lotus pond, that hero of the Vṛṣṇis entered alone. Tell me, Saṃjaya, who are so skilled, the battle fought by that hero for the sake of Dhanañjaya exactly as it happened."
Saṃjaya said:
While that Bhīma, the foremost of men, was thus being oppressed by the son of Vikartana as he advanced,
O King, having observed him in the midst of those heroes among men,
the preeminent warrior of the Śini clan pursued him on his chariot, roaring like the wielder of the thunderbolt at the end of the summer heat.
Like the sun blazing at the end of the rainy season,
striking down his enemies with his firm bow,
he caused your son’s army to tremble.
As that hero among men moved through the field of battle on horses with the brilliance of silver,
your warriors were unable to restrain him as he advanced.
All the chariots [followed] the foremost of the Mādhavas, O Bhārata;
he was full of indignation, an undaunted warrior,
bearing a bow and clad in golden armor.
Alambusa, that best of kings, having rushed forward, checked Sātyaki, the foremost of the Mādhavas;
between those two, O Bhārata, there occurred a fierce encounter.
No Tathāgata whatsoever ever existed; rather,
all your warriors and those of the enemy alike gazed upon those two who were radiant in battle.
The excellent king Alambusa forcibly pierced him with ten arrows,
yet he [the opponent] struck those very arrows even before they had reached him.
The bull among the Śinis also cut [them] with arrows;
again, he [cut them] with three sharp, well-feathered arrows, drawn back to the ear and resembling fire.
Having pierced through his body armor,
they entered the body of Sātyaki;
with those arrows, which possessed the power of fire and wind, they struck his frame.
Having pierced them with other blazing arrows,
he forcibly struck those four silver-bright horses with four shafts.
Thus struck by him,
the swift grandson of Śini, who possessed the prowess of the wielder of the discus, was assailed by Alambuṣa’s most vehement arrows.
He struck down the horses with four arrows,
and then, having severed the head of his charioteer with a broad-headed shaft resembling the fire of cosmic destruction.
Having slain that prince and grandson of kings, he severed from his body the radiant face, which shone like the full moon and was adorned with earrings.
O King, that bull among men, the crusher of foes in battle,
then followed after Arjuna himself,
having held back your troops.
Having observed the best of the Vṛṣṇis following close behind,
thus moving amidst the enemies and slaughtering the forces of the Kurus with his arrows;
Then the Saindhava horses, well-trained and excellent, carried him along like the wind repeatedly driving away masses of clouds—
horses as bright as cow’s milk, the *kunda* flower, the moon, or snow.
Excellent horses, covered with nets of gold,
went wherever that lion among men desired; then those sons of his rushed forward together.
And other warriors of yours, O Bhārata, acting swiftly and making your son Duḥśāsana— the foremost of combatants— their leader, O Ājamīḍha, [advanced].
Surrounding him on all sides in that battle,
those leaders of the host struck the descendant of Śini; yet he, the most eminent of the Sātvatas, [fought back against them].
The hero, the slayer of enemies and grandson of Śini, having quickly warded them off with a net of arrows resembling fire, checked them with feathered shafts.
Raising his bow, O descendant of Ajamīḍha, he also slew the horses of Duḥśāsana;
then Arjuna attained great joy in that battle.
And Kṛṣṇa, seeing that hero among men,
Saṃjaya said:
"Beholding him, the mighty-armed one, advancing toward Duḥśāsana’s chariot..."
Hurrying where haste was required,
those great archers of the Trigartas, whose banners were adorned with gold,
surrounded the king of Ānarta who had entered that ocean of an army seeking the welfare of Dhanañjaya.
Then, having hemmed him in on all sides with a multitude of chariots,
those enraged and supreme archers overwhelmed him with showers of arrows;
yet he conquered those princes who were striving in that great battle.

Satyaki, whose prowess is truth, having encountered fifty enemies in the midst of the Bharata host— which was filled with the clatter of palms and bristling with swords, spears, and maces— stood there like one without a raft in the middle of a waterless sea.
Then the Trigartas, acting in concert once more,
surrounded him with a vast and formidable array of chariots,
O bull of the Bharatas, drawing their exceedingly large bows.
There we beheld a marvel, the conduct of Śini’s descendant in battle:
having seen him in the western quarter, we saw him again in the east because of his swiftness;
likewise he extended himself toward the north, the south, the east, and the west.

Like one dancing in the water when weary, he came to dry land; then, O hero, having returned to the midst of the fray, that great car-warrior, intoxicated by battle, moved alone through the arena as if multiplied manyfold.
The hero moved as if dancing, just like a hundred chariots;
seeing that conduct of his, who advanced with the prowess of a lion,
the Trigartas, filled with distress, turned back toward their own people.
Having bypassed that army, that bull among men defeated the Trigartas and the Śūrasenas as they strove in the great battle; then,
alone, that mighty-armed scorcher of enemies [conquered] thousands.
That bull among men slew the armored foot-soldiers;
then other heroes of the Śūrasenas held him back in battle with showers of arrows, like goads restraining an elephant in rut.
Sātyaki held back those striving warriors for a moment;
then he, whose strength and prowess were inconceivable, fought with the Kaliṅgas,
having bypassed that army of the Kaliṅgas which was difficult to overcome.
Then the mighty-armed one approached Dhananjaya, the son of Pṛthā. O great king, though restrained by them, Satyaka held his ground and struck down very many warriors by the hundreds and thousands.
Slain and struck down by the long-armed one, they fell;
then, proceeding without agitation, he beheld Dhanañjaya,
like one exhausted after crossing through water who has reached dry land.
Seeing that tiger among men, Yuyudhāna took heart.
Beholding him approaching, Keśava said to Arjuna:
"O Pārtha, here comes the descendant of Śini, following in your footsteps."
This disciple and friend of yours, whose prowess is truth,
that bull among men, having treated all warriors as mere straw, has been victorious.
Having caused a terrible calamity for the Kaurava warriors, he stands here.
"O Kirīṭin, Sātyaki approaches, dearer to you than your own life!
Having rendered Droṇa, as well as Bhoja Kṛtavarman, useless with his arrows, this Phalguna-like Sātyaki advances."
Seeking out those dear to the King of Dharma and having slain the very best of warriors,
the heroic and skilled-in-weapons Sātyaki approaches Phalguna;
the one of great strength has performed a most difficult feat in the midst of the army.
Seeking a sight of you, O Pārtha, Sātyaki approaches;
having fought many great car-warriors in battle with a single chariot,
this Sātyaki indeed comes toward you, led by the Preceptor.
Relying on the strength of his own arms and having torn through the army,
this Sātyaki, sent by the son of Dharma, approaches;
O Pārtha, he is your dear disciple and equal to you in prowess.
Having shattered the Kaurava army, here comes Satyaka, O son of Kuntī;
there is no warrior equal to him among the Kauravas in any way. Here comes that very Satyaki, whose prowess is truth.
"Released from the Kuru army like a lion from the midst of cattle,
this Sātyaki approaches, having slain vast hosts of troops under the sons of Pṛthā. Here he comes, amidst the lotus-like faces of thousands of kings."
"O Pārtha, having covered the earth [with arrows], Sātyaki is coming quickly;
having defeated Duryodhana along with his brothers in battle and having slain Jalasandha, this Sātyaki is coming quickly."
Having created a river flowing with floods of blood and having made a river of blood with the gore of chariots, elephants, men,
and horses, this Sātyaki approaches, having laid the Kauravas down like blades of grass.
Having heard these words of Keśava, Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, was then not at all joyful; he spoke these words to Keśava:
"O mighty-armed one, it is not pleasing to me that Satyaki approaches me."
"O Keśava, I do not know the news of Dharmarāja; deprived of the Sātvata, I do not know whether he lives or not. For it was by him, O mighty-armed one, that the king was to be protected."
How is it that he has abandoned him and followed in my footsteps, O Kṛṣṇa? The king was surrendered to Droṇa and the ruler of the Sindhus was not struck down;
yet here is Bhūriśravas, who has advanced against the descendant of Śini in battle.
This exceedingly heavy burden has been placed upon me by the Saindhavas:
for I must recognize the king, and Satyaki must be protected;
Jayadratha must be slain, and the sun is already hanging low.
This mighty-armed one is now exhausted and his strength is diminished;
his horses and his charioteer are also weary, O Mādhava.
But Bhūriśravas is not fatigued, O Keśava, and he has allies with him.
"O Mādhava, Bhūriśravas is skilled in weapons; Satyaka must be protected.
Might there not be safety for him now in this encounter? I hope that Satyaki, whose valor is truth, will not cross over the ocean [of battle] here."
Even if he were to encounter Bhūriśravas, the bull among the Śinis, that one of great prowess might falter upon reaching the mere footprint of a cow;
yet, having met with the high-souled Bhūriśravas, the chief of the Kurus, who is skilled in weapons,
Sātyaki would emerge safe and sound.
"O Keśava, I consider this to be a transgression by the King of Dharma,
who, casting aside his fear of the Preceptor, dispatches Sātyaki—
just as a hawk in the sky swoops down upon meat."
Droṇa constantly hopes that the king may remain safe;
for like a hawk seeking prey, this Brahmin always stands ready to seize the son of Dharma— may the king be well.
Saṃjaya said:
O King, beholding that Sātvata warrior, who was intoxicated with battle, rushing toward him,
Bhūriśravas suddenly charged at him in a fit of rage.
The mighty-armed Kaurava said to that bull among the Śinis:
"By good fortune, you have today come within the range of my vision;
thus, today in battle, I shall attain the desire I have long cherished."
"You shall not escape from me alive if you do not abandon the fight. Having slain you today in battle— you who always pride yourself on being a hero—
I shall bring joy to Suyodhana, the King of the Kurus, O descendant of Daśārha."
Today, O heroes, you shall see Keśava and Arjuna together in battle, fallen upon the surface of the earth, consumed by my arrows. Today,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, shall hear that you have been slain by me.
He by whom you were brought here shall immediately be filled with shame;
today Pārtha Dhananjaya shall witness my prowess when you have been struck down upon the earth, lying there drenched in blood.
For today, this long-desired meeting with you has come to pass,
just as in the past during the war between the gods and the asuras, the meeting of Śakra with Bali. Today, O Sātvata, I shall give you a most terrible battle.
Then you shall know in truth my heroism, strength, and prowess;
today, slain by me in battle, you shall go to Saṃyamanī,
just as Rāvaṇi was slain in combat by Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāma.
"Today, O Mādhava, when you have been slain, Kṛṣṇa, Pārtha, and Dharmarāja will undoubtedly abandon the battle, their enthusiasm destroyed. Today, O Mādhava, having paid them back with sharp arrows,"
I shall delight the wives of those who were slain by you in battle; O Mādhava, once you have come within the range of my sight, you shall not escape,
just as a small deer does not escape when it has entered the domain of a lion.
But Yuyudhana, O King, replied to him as if laughing:
"O Kauraveya, no fear exists for me in battle;
I cannot be intimidated by mere words alone."
"He would slay me in battle who would leave me unarmed;
indeed, he who would slay me in combat would destroy me for eternal ages. What is the use of much idle talk? Act instead through deed."
Indeed, your thundering is as fruitless as that of an autumnal cloud.
O hero, hearing this thundering of yours, laughter arises within me. Let the battle for which you have long desired take place today, O Kaurava!
"O dear one, my mind hastens toward you as you desire battle;
O lowest of men, I shall not turn back today without having slain you.
Then those two bulls among men tore at each other with their words.
Desiring to slay one another and filled with supreme rage, they struck each other in the combat. Those two tigers among men, powerful and rivalrous,
met in battle like two furious elephants intoxicated with rut for the sake of a female elephant.
Bhūriśravas and Sātyaki, both subduers of their enemies,
rained down terrible showers of arrows upon one another like two clouds;
both of them showered each other with volleys of shafts.
Bhurishravas and Satyaki were there;
but Saumadatti, O best of the Bharatas, desiring to slay the descendant of Śini, covered him with swift-flying arrows and pierced him with sharpened shafts.
Having pierced Sātyaki with ten arrows, the son of Somadatta then released other sharpened shafts, desiring to slay the bull of the Śini clan;
Satyaka, in turn, pierced the son of Somadatta with ten swift arrows.
O lord of the people, O master, as the son of Somadatta discharged those sharp arrows at him,
Sātyaki, by means of his illusory weapons (*astramāyā*), swallowed them up in the sky before they could reach him.
Those two heroes of noble lineage, who bring glory to the Kurus and the Vṛṣṇis, rained down showers of arrows upon one another from separate positions—
like two tigers with their claws or two great elephants with their tusks.
They hacked at one another with chariot-spears and arrows;
piercing each other’s limbs and shedding blood,
they paralyzed one another, playing a game of dice where their very lives were the stakes.
Thus those two performers of supreme deeds, who bring glory to the Kurus and the Vṛṣṇis, fought with one another like two lordly elephants of a herd;
in no long time, they were both honored by the world of Brahmā.
Desiring to conquer each other for the highest station,
Sātyaki and the son of Somadatta struck one another with showers of arrows;
they rained them down as if in joy while the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked on.
Then, as those two lords of battle showered down that great rain of arrows,
the people there beheld them fighting like two elephant-leaders engaged in combat for the sake of a female elephant.

O King, repeatedly piercing each other with arrows, they fought in that great arena, both frantic with rage like two lions in a forest; knowing each other's vital spots, they roared as they sought to slay one another in their fury.
Then, like two powerful wielders of the thunderbolt, they crushed one another; exerting themselves,
they cut down each other’s banners and chariot-appurtenances with straight-jointed arrows.
Furthermore, as they showered each other with rains of arrows,
both quickly slew one another’s charioteers;
having killed each other’s horses and shattered their bows, they continued the fray.
Deprived of their chariots, they encountered one another for a sword-fight in that great battle.
Grasping large, beautiful, and variegated shields made of bull-hide, and having drawn their swords from their scabbards, the two of them moved about in the combat.
Moving through various paths and circular maneuvers in their respective turns,
those two crushers of enemies, enraged, repeatedly struck one another;
they were armed with swords, clad in variegated armor, and adorned with golden neck-ornaments and armlets.
Displaying the maneuvers known as *bhrānta*, *udbhrānta*, *āviddha*, *āpluta*, *vipluta*, *druta*,
*saṃpāta*, and *samudīrṇa*, those two illustrious subduers of enemies struck one another with their swords.

Both heroes, seeking out each other's vulnerabilities, leaped about with wonderful agility; displaying their training, dexterity, and grace, O King, those two fierce in battle dragged each other about on the field.
O Indra among kings, after drawing each other aside for a mere moment while all the troops looked on, the two heroes again took heart;
they [seized] their two bright shields and their two large quivers with their swords.
Having struck one another down, those two tigers among men engaged in a wrestling match;
both broad-chested, long-armed, and skilled in hand-to-hand combat,
they locked together with their arms like iron clubs.
Between those two, O King, as they fought in battle, there occurred blows with the arms and likewise acts of seizing and grappling,
produced by the power of their training, which caused all the warriors to rejoice.

A terrifying, great roar arose like that of a thunderbolt striking a mountain; they fought with their arms bound as if by yokes, and by the clashing of their heads, like two elephants with the tips of their tusks or two great bulls with their horns.
With dragging of the feet, binding, with javelins, hooks, and seats;
with the constriction of the feet and belly, as well as with whirling on the ground; with forward and backward thrusts, with falling, rising, and leaping.

Those two high-souled bulls among the Kurus and the Sātvatas fought on; O Bhārata, those two of great strength displayed there all the thirty-two modes of combat that exist in warfare as they engaged in battle.
When the Sātvata’s weapons were exhausted as he continued to fight,
Vāsudeva then said to Arjuna:
"Behold him fighting, though deprived of his chariot."
The banner of all archers in battle.
Sañjaya said:
Kṛṣṇa spoke again to Pārtha, who was intent on slaying the King of Sindhu.
"Behold Sātyaki sinking down; protect him, O Pārtha!
He has entered the Bharata army behind you, O son of Pāṇḍu, and has fought against all the highly heroic Bharatas."
The principal sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and those who were the foremost among the great car-warriors have been slain by the Vṛṣṇi hero by the hundreds and thousands;
now that best of warriors, though exhausted, has arrived at the one who gives profuse sacrificial fees.
"O Arjuna, this man who comes desiring battle is not your equal.
Then, O King, the enraged Bhūriśravas, raising his weapon, struck Satyaki— who was fierce in battle— like one intoxicated elephant attacking another.

Then, O best of kings, as the two foremost warriors, Keśava and Arjuna, stood upon their chariots in battle, enraged and watching one another in the fray, there arose a sound like the roar of clouds nearby, O King.
Then the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa addressed Arjuna:
"O sinless one, behold that tiger among the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, who was invincible in battle even against many armies, now fallen under the power of the son of Somadatta."
"O Arjuna, O slayer of enemies, protect your heroic pupil Sātyaki, who has performed most difficult deeds and, now exhausted, has fallen to the ground;
let him not fall under the power of one devoted to sacrifice."
"O tiger among men, O Lord, let that which is for your sake be done quickly.
Then Dhananjaya, with a joyful heart, spoke to Vāsudeva:
"Behold the bull of the Kurus playing with the hero of the Vṛṣṇis!"
"Like a great elephant in the forest [attacking] a leader of a herd of mad lions," Sanjaya said:
"While Dhananjaya, the son of Pandu, was speaking in this manner..."

A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the troops, O bull of the Bharatas, when the mighty-armed one, having lifted him up, struck Sātyaki down upon the earth. When the descendant of Śini had thus been felled, Kṛṣṇa addressed Arjuna.
Like a lion dragging away an elephant, that best of the Kurus, who bestows abundant sacrificial fees, shone resplendent in battle against the foremost of the Sātvatas. Arjuna said:

O mighty-armed Janārdana, these great chariot-warriors are following me alone; they strive to fight me to the best of their ability. And I certainly fight them, who are intent on finding my weaknesses.
I was protecting Sātyaki and [holding] the son of Somadatta under my control; O Kṛṣṇa, Bhūriśravas could not be slain by me in battle while I was occupied elsewhere,
for my mind was not inclined toward him.

"O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, I must certainly protect the hero of the Vṛṣṇis even at the cost of my own life, for he fights on my behalf. Whether it be unrighteousness or righteousness, O Mādhava, let it be as it may."
Saṃjaya said:
"Let not this great car-warrior lose his life, slain by an enemy.
Having spoken thus to Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna quickly [assailed] the enemies with sharp arrows.
Enraged, he covered Dhananjaya with arrows,
and the others likewise covered him; thus that hero fought repeatedly against Satyaki,
while that tiger among men also kept his gaze fixed upon Bhūriśravas.

Then, drawing his sword from its scabbard in the battle, Bhūriśravas seized him by the hair and struck him on the chest with his foot; then, having stepped forward, that strong-armed warrior raised his arm, which held the sword.
Adorned with golden ornaments, that arm of his shone in the midst of the multitude of chariots like the raised banner of Indra;
then he began to sever from his body his head, which was adorned with earrings.
At that very moment, O Bhārata, the Sātvata also, acting with haste, whirled his head around like a potter’s wheel struck by a staff,
together with the hair-clutching arm of Bhūriśravas.
Seized by that most terrifying [weapon], like a serpent by a five-headed one, the entire great army of the Pāṇḍavas raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!
while your warriors, filled with joy, let out lion-like roars.
But the people, fearing the battle, closed their eyes;
likewise Bhūriśravas became fierce toward the Sātvata when his prowess had vanished.
Thus, seeing the Sātvata being dragged away in the combat, [he acted].
Then, O King, Vāsudeva spoke again to Arjuna:
"Behold, O mighty-armed one, that tiger among the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas— your own disciple, who is not inferior to you in archery— fallen under the power of Saumadatti."
O Pārtha, where Bhūriśravas displayed his prowess in battle, it was no true valor, since he bested the Vārṣṇeya Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth,
while he himself was surrounded by many great car-warriors who were valiant and eager for combat.
Having fought intensely and become utterly exhausted, with his weapons and equipment depleted—
thus addressed by Vāsudeva, the mighty-armed Pāṇḍava mentally honored Bhūriśravas on the battlefield.
Dragging the best of the Sātvatas along as if playing in battle,
he who increases the fame of the Kurus further gladdens me;
for he does not slay Satyaki, the foremost of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.
Like a lion dragging a great elephant in the forest,
O King, Pārtha, having thus honored the Kaurava in his mind,
fought with his enemies while that hero gazed at him again and again.
The long-armed Arjuna replied to Vāsudeva:
"O Mādhava, because my gaze is fixed upon the ruler of the Sindhus, I do not see him;
however, for the sake of the Yādavas, I shall perform this difficult task."
"My disciple is fighting on my behalf against my enemies;
O Kṛṣṇa, I shall deliver him, just as one would rescue a lion cub from a forest fire.
Having spoken these words, the Pāṇḍava acted upon the instruction of Vāsudeva.
Then he fixed a sharp razor-headed arrow upon the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Released from Pārtha’s arm, it fell from the sky like a great meteor and severed with its feathered shaft the arm of Yajñaśīla, which still held a sword.
Saṃjaya said:
That arm, still clutching the sword and adorned with beautiful armlets, fell to the ground like the banner of great Indra cast down from its mechanical support after the festival has ended.
The supreme warrior, about to inflict the greatest suffering upon the world of the living,
had his arm struck off by the invisible Kiritin;
it fell with force to the ground like a five-headed serpent.
Seeing himself rendered useless by the son of Pṛthā, that Kaurava,
out of anger, released Sātyaki and censured the Pāṇḍava.
O great king, with his arm gone, he resembled a bird with only one wing.
Just as a king standing upon the earth with a single-wheeled chariot,
he spoke to the Pāṇḍava while all the kṣatriyas looked on:
"Alas, O son of Kuntī, you have committed a cruel deed!"
While I was distracted and not looking, you severed my arm;
while I was preoccupied with the Sātvata, innocent and my mind turned elsewhere.
"What indeed will you say to King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, when he asks:
'What was Bhūriśravas doing in battle when he was slain by me?
This has been taught directly to you by the high-souled Indra himself."
Whether it was a weapon discharged by Rudra, O Pārtha, or by Droṇa, or even by Kṛpa—
surely you are renowned in the world as one who knows his own duty and is superior to all others; how then could you strike one who was not fighting in battle?

The high-minded do not strike one who is heedless, terrified, deprived of his chariot, pleading for mercy, or beset by calamity; yet this [act you have committed] is the conduct of the base, practiced only by wicked men.
"How was this most difficult deed performed by you, O Pārtha?
For they say, O Dhanañjaya, that a noble deed is easy for a noble man to perform,
but a base deed is far more difficult for a noble man to accomplish on this earth."
"O Pārtha, among whatever people a man dwells and wherever he turns his course, he quickly adopts their character; this very thing is seen in you.
For how could it be otherwise, since you are born of a royal lineage, and especially one of the Kauravas?"
Having deviated from the duty of a Kṣatriya, though you are well-behaved and firm in your vows,
your transgression here is slight; therefore, my son,
I do not reproach you for having committed this base act upon encountering that lowest of the Vṛṣṇis.
But this which you have done for the sake of the Vārṣṇeya is indeed very base;
surely this is not consistent with the wisdom of Vāsudeva, nor is it fitting for you.
For who indeed would fight with another while being distracted?

Such a calamity would befall anyone who were not a friend of Kṛṣṇa. O Pārtha, how is it that you have accepted as authoritative these Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, who are outcasts, whose deeds are corrupt, and who are by their very nature contemptible?
Saṃjaya said:
Thus addressed in battle, Pārtha spoke to Bhūriśravas:
"O King, it is evident that being aged, you merely seek to please your own intellect."
"O Lord, all this that you have spoken is meaningless;
you despise your connection with Hṛṣīkeśa and treat me like a fool.
You are a knower of dharma and one who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures regarding battles."

"I would never commit unrighteousness, even though you are bewildered by my knowledge. O King, the Kṣatriyas fight their enemies surrounded by their respective brothers, fathers, sons, as well as kinsmen and relatives."
Then, relying on the strength of their own arms, they were accompanied by companions and friends; for I [fought] against Sātyaki, my disciple and a dear kinsman,
as he fought for my sake, having renounced his life which is so difficult to give up.
O King, seeing my right arm— intoxicated with battle in the fray— being severed and fallen under the power of the enemy, how could I have looked upon it as you dragged it away, rendered powerless?

Indeed, one who has entered the fray must not protect himself alone; O lord of men, he who fights for another's sake is the one who must be protected. While being protected by them, that king must be guarded in the great battle.
If, upon seeing Sātyaki, I had remained silent in battle,
then I would have suffered separation from him and surely reached hell;
but since he was protected by me, he has been recovered by me.
Fame among one's own kin is the fruit of protecting a friend;
and as for your reproaching me, O King, for being associated with another—what person would not desire such association? In this matter, your intellect has fallen into error.
As you shake your armor, mount your chariot yourself,
draw the bowstring, and fight with your enemies—
thus, in this place crowded with chariots and elephants, and teeming with horses and foot soldiers.
In this deep ocean of an army, where the roar of lion-like shouts rises up,
how will battle be possible for you, who are so valiant in combat and accompanied by your own forces, against Sātyaki?
Having encountered many great car-warriors and having defeated them, Satyaki—
exhausted himself and his horses, and with all his weapons spent— was likewise defeated by you, O great car-warrior, in that battle.

You understand this even better; nevertheless, you remain indifferent. Who will tolerate it when they see Sātyaki fallen into such distress, while you desire to strike off his head with a sword in battle?
But you should reproach yourself, you who do not protect yourself;
how, O hero, will you act toward the man who seeks refuge in you? For [this is the duty] of one who has taken up arms in battle, desiring to slay the son of Vṛṣṇi.

That I severed his arm was not condemned by the world; for what righteous man, O dear one, would honor the slaying of Abhimanyu when he had laid down his weapons, was deprived of his armor, and was rendered helpless?
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed and highly illustrious Yūpaketu,
sighing repeatedly after the heroic Dhanañjaya,
abandoned Yuyudhāna in battle and sat down to fast unto death.
Having spread out his arrows with his left hand, he who was endowed with auspicious marks,
desiring to go to the world of Brahmā, then offered his vital breaths into the vital breaths.
Fixing his sight upon the sun and his tranquil mind upon the water, he remained steady.
Meditating upon the Mahopaniṣad, the sage became absorbed in yoga. Then,
amidst the entire army, the people censured Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya, yet they also praised that bull among men.
They censured these two, yet they praised the one who gives profuse sacrificial fees; though thus reviled, the two Kṛṣṇas did not say anything unpleasant,
and the one whose banner is a sacrificial stake did not rejoice when being praised.
O King,
Bhārata, Dhanañjaya, unable to endure those words of yours and their speech in his mind, spoke with a calm disposition as if merely reminding them.
Phalguna, the son of Pāṇḍu, spoke as if with reproach:
"All kings know this great vow of mine:
no one belonging to my own side can be slain by me, provided he comes within the range of my arrows."
O you whose banner is a sacrificial post, having observed this, you ought not to reproach me;
for it is not proper to reproach another without first understanding the dharma,
especially when one has taken up arms in battle with the intent to slay a hero of the Vṛṣṇis.
"That I cut off his arm—was that dharma not censurable? Since I severed his arm, what was there in that act to be blamed?
He had laid down his weapons; he was but a youth, deprived of his chariot and his armor."
"O dear one, what righteous person would not honor the slaughter of Abhimanyu? Why then do you not censure the killing of Abhimanyu,
while remaining under the authority of the base Duryodhana?"
"O son of Somadatta, this is right for one who provides all assistance;
my own people must be protected by me when a threat to life has arisen.
It is my conviction that those heroes who would slay me face-to-face [must be spared]."
And Satyaka was brought under control by the high-souled Kaurava.
Saṃjaya said:
"Thereafter, I [related] this account concerning the preservation of his vow."
Once again, overcome with compassion and reflecting deeply on this and that, Arjuna, afflicted by grief, spoke to that descendant of Kuru:
"Fie upon the duty of the warrior (kṣatradharma), wherein you, O lord of men, [have become a slayer]."
O joy of the Kurus, for one who has reached such a state as this— the protector and giver of refuge— it is no great burden for Death (Kṛtānta), since even you,
O tiger among men, have fallen into this wretched condition.
O best of kings, Suyodhana shall not indeed enjoy the fruit of his own good deeds,
since you, O tiger among the Kurus, have fallen into this wretched state;
he will go instead to the terrible Raurava hell.
O tiger among men, for whose sake this king has reached such a wretched state— who indeed in this world would strike one such as you, O Supreme Person, were it not for our solemn vow?
Thus addressed by Pārtha, he touched the ground with his head and,
with his left hand, sent forth his right [hand].
Having then heard these words of Pārtha, the one of great splendor—
O great king, Yūpaketu sat silent with his face cast down.
Arjuna said:
"The love that I have for Dharmarāja and for Bhīma, the best among speakers—"
"As Nakula and Sahadeva are [dear] to me, so are you, O elder brother of Śala. Permitted by me and by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa,
go to the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds, just as Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, did."
Vāsudeva said:
"Those worlds of mine are stainless and shine eternally,
desired even by the preeminent gods beginning with Brahmā."
"Go quickly to them, O you who constantly perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice; become equal to me, traveling upon the head of Garuḍa.
Sañjaya said:
While Dhanañjaya was speaking thus, overwhelmed with compassion,
all those soldiers stood with their faces cast downward; then,
after resting for a mere moment, Sātyaki became frantic with rage.
Overcome by indignation and repulsed by the son of Somadatta,
Saṃjaya said:
"Then, having been released by the son of Somadatta, the grandson of Śini rose up."

Taking up his sword and desiring to cut off the head of that high-souled one, Sātyaki sought to slay the sinless elder brother of Śala— him who had been heedless and was struck down by the son of Pāṇḍu, the giver of many sacrificial fees.
O noble one, although he was being restrained by Kṛṣṇa and Phalguna,
the sinful Yuyudhāna committed a cruel act against Pārtha, O lord of men, while he was seated in the vow of fasting and his arm had been severed.
With his arm severed, sitting like an elephant with its trunk cut off,
he was being reviled by all the shouting troops; deeply distressed in mind,
he was being restrained by Kṛṣṇa and the high-souled Pārtha.
While Bhīma, the two protectors of the wheels, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa,
Karṇa, Vṛṣasena, and likewise the ruler of the Sindhus were crying out,
he slew that one of firm vows even as the troops were shouting.
To the lord of the Kauravas, who was seated in the vow of fasting unto death on the battlefield with his arm severed by Pārtha,
