Sātyaki struck off the head with a sword;
Satyaka then indeed cut off the head of that chief of the Kurus.
The troops did not applaud Sātyaki for that deed,
because he had slain the best of the Kurus who had already been struck down by Arjuna;
there, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and men regarded him as equal to the Thousand-Eyed One.
Beholding Bhūriśravas slain in battle while he was engaged in the vow of fasting unto death,
the gods, amazed by his deeds, paid him homage;
and his soldiers uttered many words of praise regarding his side.
"It is not the fault of the descendant of Vṛṣṇi; for it was destined to happen thus.
Therefore, you should not harbor resentment, for anger brings suffering to men.
This hero must be slain; there is no need for hesitation in this matter."
For his death in battle has been ordained for him by the Creator himself, O Sātyaki.
Everyone must surely die—whether later or earlier. Do not think that he is already dead; let there be no such thoughtlessness in your minds.
When that great-armed and high-souled Yūpaketu had been slain, the kṣatriyas, overcome with rage, cried out, "Shame on him!
and said, "It must have been joined by another; so it was destined to be."
Some were despondent, while others were filled with grief.
Sātyaki said:
"He must not be killed! He must not be killed!"—thus you spoke to me.
When the son of Subhadrā, though he spoke words of righteousness, was most unrighteous— when that boy, deprived of weapons,
was slain by you in battle, where then had your righteousness gone?
"For I have made this vow regarding a certain reproach;
having heard it, you should censure me with your whole being, but not Arjuna.
Listen to all of this here, and having heard it, O men, pass judgment."
He who, having crushed me in battle, should strike me down alive with his foot in anger— he shall be slain by me as an enemy, even if he should be one who observes the vows of a sage;
for he would be attacking me while I am still struggling with my arms and eyes intact.
"You think he is dead; this is merely a weakness of your intellect. For his counter-attack has been effectively executed by me, O bulls among the Kurus.
Yet, out of affection for me and in order to protect his own vow, Pārtha [Arjuna] acted thus."
His arm, along with the sword, has been taken away; by this very act, I have been deceived.
That which is destined to happen must come to pass, and it is as if fate itself exerts its influence.
Since he was slain in this conflict, what unrighteous act has been committed here?
Moreover, O monkey, this verse was sung of old on earth by Vālmīki:
"Women must never be killed"— this is what you say, O monkey,
which a man of resolve should always maintain at all times.
"That which causes pain to one's enemies must certainly be done; that has been accomplished by me, so do not reproach me like fools. Sañjaya said:
When this had been said, O Great King, all the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas said nothing at all, but honored him in their minds;
for he was purified by mantras at the great sacrifices.
Of that illustrious one, who gave away many thousands,
there was no one there who rejoiced at his slaughter, like that of a sage dwelling in the forest.
For that illustrious Bhūriśravas, who had been purified by mantras,
there was no difference between being in his own great home and being in the forest.
Having seen the face of that hero and granter of boons, with its beautiful dark hair, eyes as red as a pigeon's, a fine nose, and well-formed cheeks—
The head of the sacrificial horse, severed,
lay like the *havirdhāna* shed to the north;
purified by its splendor struck down by the weapon.
Having cast off his excellent body in the great battle,
the giver of boons, worthy of the best, ascended upwards,
pervading both heaven and earth with supreme dharma.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Sañjaya, tell me everything in detail regarding the birth of Śaineya and that of Bhūriśravas.
He was not conquered by Droṇa, the son of Rādheya, Vikarṇa, or Kṛtavarman;
he was not conquered by Droṇa and Bhīṣma, nor by Karṇa and Kṛpa—
nor by anyone who dares to conquer my entire army.
Having crossed the ocean of the army after making a vow before Yudhiṣṭhira, how was that hero,
who was irresistible in battles, seized by Bhūriśravas, a descendant of Kuru, and forcibly thrown to the ground?
Saṃjaya said:
"Listen, O King, to the origin of Śaineya as it occurred in the past, and also that of Bhūriśravas, concerning which you have a doubt, O monarch."
Brahmā’s mind-born son was Atri, possessed of great ascetic power. Atri’s son was Soma, and Soma’s son is recorded as Budha.
O great king, [Budha’s son] was named Yadu, who was learned in all the scriptures.
Budha had an only son, Purūravas, who possessed the splendor of Mahendra. From Purūravas came Āyu, and from Āyu, Nahuṣa is recorded. From Nahuṣa came Yayāti, a royal sage equal to the gods.
To Yayāti and Devayānī was born a son, Yadu, who was the eldest. In the lineage of Yadu was born the one known as Devamīḍha; his son was Yādava, a hero esteemed throughout the three worlds.
The son of Śūra was Vasudeva, the best of men and of great fame;
he was a hero unsurpassed in archery and equal to Kārtavīrya in battle. And in that very lineage, O King, there was a monarch named Śini who possessed such valor.
At that very time, O King, during the *svayaṃvara* of the daughter of the high-souled Devaka, where all the Kṣatriyas had assembled,
he obtained the lady Devakī for Vasudeva.
Having conquered all the kings, Śini placed her upon his chariot.
Seeing Devakī standing on the chariot of Śūra, that bull among men—
seeing Devakī being led away to Vasudeva— [acted].
O King, the highly energetic Somadatta could not tolerate Śini’s son;
a wonderful and marvelous battle took place between them for half a day,
like the wrestling match between the mighty Śakra and Prahlāda.
But Śini forcibly threw Somadatta to the ground;
raising his sword and seizing him by the hair,
he struck him with his foot in the midst of thousands of kings who were looking on from all sides.
Out of compassion, he was released by him with the words, "Live!
O noble one, while in that state, Somadatta,
overcome by indignation, sought to propitiate Mahādeva.
Mahādeva, the Lord and bestower of boons, was pleased with him and invited him to choose a boon; and that king chose this boon:
"O Blessed One, I desire a son who shall slay the son of Śini."
"In the midst of thousands of kings, he might even strike down [an opponent] with his foot in battle.
Having heard those words of Somadatta, O King, he shook his head and said this: "O monarch, it cannot be so."
Having previously propitiated me through asceticism throughout the three worlds,
he obtained from me an excellent boon by which he is invincible to anyone; nevertheless,
this present effort of mine shall not be in vain.
Your son will indeed confound his grandson in battle;
however, he cannot be killed, for he is protected by Kṛṣṇa. Moreover, I am Kṛṣṇa himself; there is no difference between us at all.
Having said, "So be it," the god vanished there;
and that lord of the earth, his mind not overly joyful, returned to the city.
By means of that granting of a boon, he obtained [the power] for which abundant sacrificial fees were given.
And in that battle, the son of Somadatta struck down the son of Śini before the eyes of all the troops, and he even kicked him with his foot. This,
O King, which you asked me, has been related to you.
O bull among men, the Sātvatas cannot be defeated in battle;
for they are many, skilled in various modes of combat, sure of their aim in war,
and unconquered victors over gods, Dānavas, and Gandharvas.
"Engaged in the conquest through their own prowess, these men do not belong to another;
O Lord, nothing equal to the Vṛṣṇis is seen here—
whether past, present, or future— in strength, O bull of the Bharatas."
Devoted to the instruction of their elders, they do not despise their kinsmen;
neither gods, asuras, nor gandharvas, nor yakṣas, uragas,
or rākṣasas can be conquerors of the Vṛṣṇi heroes in battle, much less human beings.
They were non-violent toward the property of Brahmins, the property of their gurus, and even the property of their kinsmen;
they were protectors of these things in times of any calamity.
They were wealthy yet not arrogant, devoted to the Brahmins, and speakers of truth.
They do not despise the capable, and they uplift the distressed; always devoted to the gods, self-controlled, generous, and free from boastfulness—
for these reasons, the wheel of the Vṛṣṇi heroes is never checked.
O King, someone might carry away Mount Meru or cross the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters; but no one can reach the end of the Vṛṣṇi heroes when they have come together.
This hero, born of Śini’s daughter, is that very Sātyaki.
"All this has been told to you, O Lord, regarding that about which you had doubt, O King of the Kurus, best among men; for your own misconduct was great. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When that Kaurava Bhūriśravas had been slain while in that state,
tell me, Sañjaya, how the battle proceeded further.
Sañjaya said:
When Bhūriśravas had departed for the other world, O Bhārata,
the mighty-armed Arjuna urged Vāsudeva:
"O Kṛṣṇa, urge the horses on swiftly toward where King Jayadratha is!"
"O sinless one, you ought to make my vow fruitful as well. O lotus-eyed one, it is heard that the sun, the great-armed one, is hastening toward his setting amidst the three duties."
O tiger among men, this great task has indeed been undertaken by me; and let it be so that this [sun], protected by the great car-warriors of the Kuru army,
does not set, so that my word may become true.
"O Kṛṣṇa, urge on the horses so that I may slay Jayadratha.
Saṃjaya said:
When the slaughter of Jayadratha was at hand, both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas [prepared for battle].

Smiling, they both gazed at one another, like a mature woman and a young bride. Then the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, who was skilled in the management of horses, urged on the silver-colored steeds toward the chariot of Jayadratha.
As he advanced with his unerring arrows,
O great king, the leaders of the army rushed forward in haste as if flying on swift birds;
Duryodhana, Karṇa, Vṛṣasena, and the King of Madra followed behind.
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and the ruler of the Sindhus themselves—
Bībhatsu, having encountered the ruler of the Sindhus standing at the front,
gazed at him with eyes blazing with anger as if consuming him.
Then King Duryodhana quickly spoke to the son of Rādhā:
"Those two bulls among men, Satyaki and Bhīmasena, are performing superhuman deeds; they appear as if they are showing their prowess while remaining on guard."
Seeing Arjuna advancing toward the chariot of Jayadratha,
O King, your son King Suyodhana said to Karṇa:
"O Vaikartana, this is that time for battle!"
O Great-souled One, display your own power so that Jayadratha may not be slain by Arjuna in battle; act in such a way, O Karṇa.
O hero among men, very little of the day remains;
destroy the enemy today with floods of arrows,
O foremost of men, before the end of the day arrives.
"O Karṇa, our victory is indeed certain;
for while the ruler of the Sindhus is being protected until the setting of the sun,
the son of Kuntī, having failed in his vow, shall enter the fire."
O giver of honor, on a world devoid of Arjuna, his brothers along with their followers would not venture to live for even a moment;
and with the Pāṇḍavas destroyed, [the earth] including its mountains, forests, and groves—
"O Karṇa, we shall enjoy this earth with its thorns removed.
O giver of honor, Pārtha has been struck down by fate and is now perverted;
not knowing what ought and ought not to be done, he indeed made that vow in battle."

"Surely, O Karṇa, this vow has been made by the diadem-wearing Pāṇḍava for his own destruction regarding the slaying of Jayadratha. How could Phalguna live, O son of Rādhā, while you, who are difficult to overcome, are still alive?"

While the sun has not yet set, how could Dhanañjaya slay King Jayadratha at the front of the battle— Jayadratha who is protected by the King of Madra and the high-souled Kṛpa, and who is a native of Sindhu?
While he is being protected by the son of Droṇa, by myself, and by Duḥśāsana,
how will Bībhatsu, impelled by Time, reach the King of the Sindhus? Many heroes are fighting and the sun is already hanging low.
"I suspect, O giver of honor, that Pārtha will never reach Jayadratha. Therefore,
O Karṇa, together with me and other heroic great car-warriors— accompanied by the son of Droṇa, the lord of Madra, and Kṛpa— you [must protect him]."
"Exerting the utmost effort, fight against Pārtha in battle!
Thus addressed by your son, O honorable one, the son of Rādhā replied with these words to Duryodhana, the best of the Kurus.

O giver of honor, I remain in this battle now only because I must stand my ground, having been violently agitated in combat by the heroic archer Bhīmasena, who, with his steady aim, has repeatedly overwhelmed me with nets of arrows.
Not a single limb of mine, scorched by the arrows in battle, moves at all;
yet, O King, I shall fight with my utmost power in the fray.
Therefore, Suyodhana, I will strive to the best of my ability.
"How that leader of the Pāṇḍavas might fail to slay the ruler of the Sindhus—
while I am fighting and discharging sharp arrows, the heroic Savyasācī Dhanañjaya shall not reach the ruler of the Sindhus."

"O Kauravya, whatever must be done by one who possesses power and is ever intent on the welfare [of others], that I shall do; for victory rests with destiny. Today, I will exert the utmost effort in battle for the sake of the ruler of the Sindhus."
"O Great King, for the sake of your pleasure, victory rests upon destiny.
Today I shall fight Arjuna, relying on my own manliness;
for your sake, O tiger among men, victory rests upon destiny."
"O best of the Kurus, today let all beings behold the fierce and hair-raising battle between me and Pārtha. Thus spoke Karṇa and the Kaurava to one another on the field of battle."
Arjuna struck down your army with sharpened arrows;
with his sharp-pointed shafts, he severed in battle the arms of the brave, non-retreating warriors— arms resembling iron clubs and like the trunks of elephants.
And with sharp arrows, the mighty-armed one severed heads,
as well as elephant trunks, horse necks, and chariot axles on all sides;
he struck down horse-riders drenched in blood, who still gripped their spears and lances.
Bībhatsu cut each one into two or even three pieces with his razor-sharp arrows. And thousands of excellent horses and elephants fell down,
along with their banners, umbrellas, bows, yak-tail fans, and heads.
Like a fire fanned by the wind burning dry brushwood, Pārtha consumed your army; in a short time, O King, he made the earth drenched in blood.
Having slaughtered the majority of the warriors, that mighty hero left your force devastated.
Protected by Bhīmasena and the Sātvata, the invincible Bībhatsu, whose prowess is truth, approached the ruler of the Sindhus;
O best of the Bharatas, he shone like a blazing sacrificial fire.
Seeing him stationed in that manner, those great archers of yours, esteemed for their prowess and bulls among men, could not endure Phalguna—
namely Duryodhana, Karṇa, Vṛṣasena, and the King of Madra.
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and the ruler of the Sindhus himself,
enraged for the sake of the Sindhu king, surrounded the Diademed One as he danced along the paths of his chariot with the sounds of his bowstring and the slapping of his palms.
All those skilled in battle, experts in warfare, surrounded the son of Pṛthā— who was himself an expert in combat— fearlessly, as if he were Death with his mouth wide open;
placing the ruler of the Sindhus behind them, they sought to slay Arjuna and Acyuta.
Desiring the setting of the sun while the sun was still glowing red,
they drew their bows with arms resembling the coils of serpents and released hundreds of arrows, radiant as sunbeams, toward Phalguna.

Kirīṭin, intoxicated with the passion for battle, having cut each of those arrows— whether already discharged or being shot— as they flew through the air into two, three, or eight pieces, pierced them in turn in the fray.
Meanwhile, he whose banner bore the lion’s tail displayed his own prowess.
O King, the son of Śāradvatī held Arjuna at bay;
having pierced Pārtha with ten arrows and Vāsudeva with seven,
he stood firm in the paths of the chariots, protecting the ruler of the Sindhus.
Then all those great car-warriors, the best of the Kauravas,
surrounded him on all sides with a vast array of chariots,
stretching their bows and discharging their arrows.
By the command of your son, they protected the Saindhava;
there, the strength of the arms of the heroic Pārtha was seen,
as well as the inexhaustibility of his arrows and of the bow Gāṇḍīva.
Having warded off the weapons of the son of Droṇa and the son of Śaradvat with their own weapons,
he struck every one of them with nine arrows each.
Then the son of Droṇa struck him with twenty-five arrows, and Vṛṣasena with seven.
Duryodhana pierced him with twenty arrows, and Karṇa and Śalya each with three;
roaring at him and piercing him again and again,
they surrounded him on all sides while brandishing their bows.
Desiring the setting of the sun, those great car-warriors quickly formed a circular array of chariots, closely surrounding him on all sides;
shouting at him and brandishing their bows, they rushed forward.

They drenched him with terrible arrows, as clouds drench a mountain with water. O King, those heroes, whose arms were like iron clubs, displayed great divine weapons there upon the limbs of Dhanañjaya.
Having warded off those showers of arrows and displaying celestial weapons,
that powerful hero of true prowess, difficult to overcome, having reduced your army to one where most of the warriors were slain, approached the ruler of the Sindhus.
O King, O Bhārata, while Bhīmasena and the Sātvata looked on, Karṇa checked him in that encounter with swift arrows;
Pārtha, for his part, pierced him back with ten shafts on the field of battle.
While the entire army looked on, O noble one, the mighty-armed Sātvata pierced Karṇa, the son of the Sūta,
with three arrows;
Bhīmasena likewise pierced him with three, and Pārtha again with seven.
The great car-warrior Karṇa pierced each of them in return with sixty arrows.
That battle between Karṇa and his many opponents, O King, was truly extraordinary;
we beheld there, O honorable one, the marvelous prowess of the Sūta’s son.
When that single warrior, enraged in battle, held back three charioteers,
the mighty-armed Phalguna struck Vaikartana Karna in all his vital parts with a hundred arrows in that conflict.
With all his limbs drenched in blood, the powerful and heroic son of the Sūta pierced Phalguna with fifty arrows;
seeing that lightness of hand, Arjuna could not endure it in battle.
Then the heroic Dhanañjaya, the son of Pṛthā, acting with haste, cut his bow and pierced him between the breasts with nine arrows;
and for the sake of slaying him in battle, he took up an arrow possessing the brilliance of the sun.
At that moment requiring haste, Dhanañjaya, filled with urgency, hurled [the arrow].
As it came flying with great speed, the son of Droṇa cut that shaft down with a sharp crescent-headed arrow; severed, it fell to the earth.
Then the powerful son of the Sūta, taking up another bow,
covered the Pāṇḍava with many thousands of arrows—
that incomparable rain of weapons arising from Karṇa’s bow.
Like the wind dispersing locusts, Pārtha struck them down with his arrows;
then Arjuna covered [the enemy] with shafts in that battle,
displaying his lightness of hand before all the warriors who looked on.
Narasiṃha, the great chariot-warrior,
rained down sharp arrows;
Karna, the slayer of enemies, likewise covered Phalguna with his shafts.
Desiring to counter each other's deeds with many thousands of arrows,
those two great car-warriors, lions among men, roared like bulls;
they covered the sky with straight-flying volleys of shafts.

Invisible to one another due to the showers of arrows as they struck each other, they continued to provoke one another, saying, "I am Pārtha! Stay! and "I am Karṇa! Stay, O Phalguna!"—thus they tormented each other with the shafts of their words.

Those two heroes fought in battle with wonderful, swift, and skillful maneuvers; they became a sight to behold for the entire assembly of warriors as they were praised in the fray by the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Vātikas.
O great king, those two fought on, each seeking the death of the other.
Then, O King, Duryodhana addressed your warriors:
"Be vigilant and protect the son of Rādhā; do not leave until Arjuna has been slain in battle."
"O son of Rādhā, he will turn back," Vṛṣa said to me.
In the meantime, O King, having witnessed Karna’s prowess,
[Arjuna] struck Karna’s four horses with arrows released from his bow drawn to his ear.
With four excellent arrows, he sent him to the world of death,
and with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla), he struck his charioteer from the seat of the chariot;
he then covered him with arrows while your son looked on.

Being thus covered in battle, his horses slain and his charioteer killed, he was bewildered by the net of arrows and did not know what ought to be done. Seeing him thus deprived of his chariot, [the other] then took him up onto his own chariot.
O great king, Aśvatthāman fought Arjuna once more;
meanwhile, the King of Madra pierced the son of Kuntī with thirty arrows and,
O Bhārata, shrouded Arjuna’s path with a net of shafts.
Śāradvata struck Vāsudeva with twenty arrows and hit Dhanañjaya with twelve stone-tipped shafts;
the King of Sindhu struck him with four, and Vṛṣasena with seven.
O great king, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha each pierced their respective opponents individually;
likewise, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, pierced them in return—
striking the son of Droṇa with sixty-four arrows and the King of Madra with a hundred.
Having pierced the ruler of the Sindhus with ten broad-headed arrows, Vṛṣasena with three shafts,
and the son of Śaradvat with twenty, Pārtha let out a great roar.
They, desiring to thwart the vow of Savyasācin, [advanced].
United together, your men swiftly rushed toward Dhanañjaya. Then Arjuna manifested a weapon with edges on all sides,
terrifying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The Kurus went out to meet that son of Pāṇḍu on costly chariots, raining down showers of arrows;
then, when that tumultuous conflict had arisen—
O Bhārata, even when encountering that most terrible and bewildering [illusion],
that prince, adorned with a diadem and garland, was not deluded as he discharged his arrows.
Desiring the kingdom for the Kurus, the high-souled Savyasācin,
remembering the sufferings endured for twelve years,
[acted] with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva.
He opened up all directions with immeasurable [beings],
and the sky became filled with blazing torches;
many birds fell upon their bodies.
When the wearer of the diadem and garland, filled with rage, slays his enemies with the *ājagava* bow and its tawny string,
that highly illustrious one, adorned with a diadem and garland, wields it with great power.
With his bow,
the conqueror of armies struck down with arrows the foremost heroes of the Kurus, who were mounted upon the backs of the best of horses and the most excellent of elephants.
In that battle, the lords of men wielded heavy maces, iron clubs, swords,
and spears, as well as great weapons of terrifying appearance.
Seizing Pārtha, they suddenly rushed forward;
then he [took up] that great Gāṇḍīva bow, which had a sound like the clouds at the end of an eon and resembled the great bow of Indra.
Laughing loudly, he dragged them with his two arms and advanced swiftly,
burning your men and increasing the realm of Yama;
he [dragged] those exalted ones along with their chariots, horses, and elephant-riders.
And that hero, a great wielder of the bow,
caused the throngs of foot soldiers to increase the realm of Yama in battle, their weapons and lives all destroyed.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard the sound of his bow,
which was as clearly drawn back as that of Antaka himself, [the enemy trembled].

O King, as it was being dragged away by Dhanañjaya, that army of yours became utterly terrible, like a thunderclap or a crash of Indra’s bolt; agitated by terror and bewildered by fear, it was thrown into confusion.
Agitated by the winds at the end of an eon, with its surging waves tossing and its fish and sea-monsters submerged, it became like the water of the ocean;
so did Dhananjaya, the son of Pritha, move through the battle, a sight to behold.

O Great King, we could not perceive the Pāṇḍava as he simultaneously displayed various weapons in all directions— taking them up, fixing them, drawing them back, and releasing them— with such extreme lightness of hand.
Then, O great king, the mighty-armed one, filled with rage, manifested the invincible Aindra weapon, terrifying all the Bharatas. Thereupon,
arrows consecrated with divine mantras appeared.
Then, with hundreds and thousands of blazing fire-tipped arrows released from bows drawn back to the ear— resembling fire and the rays of the sun—
the sky became difficult to behold, as if covered by falling meteors.
Then that darkness of weapons unleashed by the Kauravas—
which was impossible for others even to conceive— Pāṇḍava, as if agitated,
destroyed with valor by means of arrows consecrated with divine weapons.
Just as the sun at the beginning of the day quickly dispels the darkness of night with its rays,
so did the lord [Arjuna] then overwhelm your army with the blazing rays of his arrows,
like the summer sun drying up the waters of a pond.
Then, the rays of arrows discharged by that expert in divine weapons flooded the enemy army, just as the rays of the sun flood the world;
likewise, other arrows of fierce brilliance were released.
They quickly entered the hearts of those heroes like dear kinsmen—
those warriors who, imagining themselves brave, had come against him in battle;
like moths reaching a blazing fire, they went to their destruction.
Thus crushing the lives and the fame of his enemies,
Pārtha moved through the battle like Death personified,
[severing] their crowns, garments, and massive arms adorned with armlets.
With his arrows, he struck off the ears of some adorned with pairs of earrings; he struck down those on elephants along with their lances, horsemen along with their spears,
foot-soldiers with their shields, and chariot-warriors with their bows.
The Pāṇḍava severed the arms of the drivers, still clutching their goads;
there Dhananjaya shone like a blazing fire with its crest of sparks,
his fierce arrows appearing as its radiant flames.

Dhananjaya, who resembled the king of the gods, the best among all wielders of weapons, that bull among men standing upon his chariot, was a sight to behold as he simultaneously displayed great celestial weapons in all directions.
Even though those kings exerted themselves, they were unable to look upon him as he danced along the paths of the chariots, making the sound of his bowstring and palms ring out,
like the sun blazing in the sky at midday.
Wearing his diadem and with arrows gathered in his blazing quiver,
he shone like a great cloud in the rainy season, swollen with water and bearing Indra’s bow.
During that deluge of mighty weapons set in motion by Jishnu, [he stood resplendent].
In that most difficult and terrible [battle], the preeminent warriors sank down amidst bodies with severed faces, trunks with lopped-off arms,
arms from which hands were missing, and hands whose fingers had been cut away.
With elephants whose trunks were severed, whose tusks were cut off, and who were fierce with rut; with horses whose hooves and necks were lopped off, and with chariots hacked to pieces;
and with others whose entrails were torn out, whose feet were severed, and whose joints were cut asunder.

O protector of the earth, we beheld that great battlefield of the sons of Pṛthā, where thousands of beings— some motionless, some quivering, and others shrieking— displayed the graceful dance of death, increasing the terror of the cowardly.
Like the playground of Rudra when he formerly tormented the creatures,
the earth— with its trunks from which the razor-sharp tusks were released— shone in some places as if garlanded with snakes, and in others as if adorned with curved lotuses.
With various turbans and crowns, armlets, bracelets, and earrings; with gold-embroidered garments and the trappings of elephants and horses—
the ground was strewn here and there, covered and crowded with hundreds of diadems.
The earth, variegated and exceedingly radiant, shone like a newlywed bride;
it was a mire of marrow and fat, with waves of flowing blood,
unfathomable with vital organs and bones, and carpeted with hair as its moss and water-grass.
With its banks of heads and arms, crowded with the shattered bones of chests, rich with variegated banners and flags, garlanded by waves of parasols and bows, it was filled with the massive,
lifeless bodies of elephants.
It was strewn with hundreds of chariots as rafts, with throngs of horses for its banks;

it was exceedingly difficult to traverse due to chariot wheels, yokes, poles, axles, and shafts, and it was hard to approach because of spears, swords, javelins, axes, and arrows that served as venomous snakes.
[It was] filled with cranes, herons, and great crocodiles; fierce with jackals and makaras; with vultures as its formidable great sea-monsters; terrifying with the howling of jackals;
and strewn by the thousands with spirits such as dancing pretas and piśācas.

He set flowing a river like the Vaitaraṇī— extremely terrifying, fierce, and dreadful— which carried away hundreds of motionless bodies whose life-breaths had departed, increasing the fear of the timid.
Seeing that prowess of his, which was like that of Death personified,
a fear such as had never before occurred among the Kurus arose on the field of battle.
Then the Pāṇḍava, having seized the weapons of the heroes with his own weapons, [proceeded].
Established in fierce deeds, he proclaimed himself to be fierce;
then, O King, Arjuna passed beyond those excellent chariots,
like the midday sun scorching in the sky.
All living beings were unable even to look upon the son of Pāṇḍu;
we beheld the multitudes of arrows issuing from the Gāṇḍīva bow of that great-souled one in battle, like rows of swans in the sky.
In the sky, they appeared like rows of swans;
having warded off the weapons of the heroes on all sides with his own weapons,
he displayed his fierce nature, established as he was in a terrible deed.
O King, Arjuna, whose charioteer was Sātyaki, passed beyond those excellent chariot-divisions,
as if bewildering them with his iron shafts, desiring the slaughter of Jayadratha;
he discharged arrows in all directions.
Dhananjaya moved swiftly through the battle, a sight to behold;
the swarms of arrows from that high-souled hero appeared like whirlwinds as they hovered in the sky by the hundreds and thousands.
O King, we could not then discern the great archer, the son of Pāṇḍu, as he took up his arrows, fixed them to the string, or released them;
nor could we distinguish all the directions or all the chariot-warriors in that battle.
Having thrown them into confusion, the son of Kuntī rushed toward Jayadratha and pierced him with sixty-four straight-knotted arrows.
Seeing the Pāṇḍava advancing toward the ruler of the Sindhus, the warriors [surrounded him].
Despairing of his life, those heroes turned back from the battle. O Lord, whichever of your warriors rushed toward the Pāṇḍava in that clamor, his arrows fell upon his body, bringing him to his end.
The great car-warrior Arjuna, the best among victors, made your army teem with headless trunks by means of arrows resembling the rays of the sun. Thus,
O Indra among kings, did that fourfold force of yours [fall] at that time.
Having thrown them into confusion, the son of Kuntī rushed toward Jayadratha;
he pierced the son of Droṇa with fifty arrows and Vṛṣasena with three shafts,
while the son of Kuntī, feeling compassion, struck Kṛpa with nine arrows.

Having pierced Śalya with sixteen arrows, Karṇa with thirty-two shafts, and the ruler of the Sindhus with sixty-four, he roared like a lion. Thus pierced by the arrows of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the ruler of the Sindhus likewise [roared].
Greatly incensed, like an elephant tormented by a goad, he could not endure it. He,
whose banner bore the boar, quickly [discharged] straight-flying arrows fletched with vulture feathers,
which resembled venomous serpents and had been polished by smiths.
In that battle, he released sharpened arrows at Savyasācin;
having pierced the Gāṇḍīva bow with three iron shafts, Arjuna with six,
he struck the horses with eight and the standard with a single feathered arrow.

The knower of vital points struck Vāsudeva in all his vital parts with a hundred arrows; then he again covered Pārtha’s banner, Pārtha himself, his diadem, his horses, and his bow, and furthermore, he overwhelmed Arjuna in battle with showers of shafts.
Having warded off those sharp arrows dispatched by the ruler of the Sindhus,
Arjuna simultaneously severed the head of the Saindhava’s charioteer from his body and his well-adorned standard with two shafts.
With his pole shattered, that great boar, struck by arrows and falling apart like a mass of flames, collapsed upon the king of Sindhu. Meanwhile,
Bībhatsu, gazing at the sun, licked the corners of his mouth.
Seeing no opening indeed in him who was surrounded by guards,
his eyes became red with rage, and he appeared like Death with a wide-gaping mouth.
Then Vāsudeva spoke to Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī.
The Blessed One said:
"O bull among the Bharatas, it is not possible for you to slay him without artifice.
I shall provide that means for the obscuring of the sun."
Then, O Pārtha, the King of Sindhu will think that the sun has set here; at that, he will experience both wonder and joy,
due to the recovery of his own life and the fulfillment of his vow.
Seeing him like the sun that has set, the fool, through delusion,
will not be able to protect himself from the arising of joy;
at that very moment, O Dhanañjaya, you must strike.
Saṃjaya said:
"Of that base Jayadratha, who was desirous of seeing the sun"—
having spoken thus to Pārtha, he then quickly withdrew his radiance.

But the powerful Pārtha, perceiving that darkness and seeing it was exceedingly distressing, realized it had indeed been created by Janārdana to destroy the sun; meanwhile, your warriors, upon seeing it, became filled with hearts overflowing with joy.
Raising his head and neck, the Saindhava gazed at the sun.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa spoke to Arjuna, who was filled with grief:
"Behold, O Kaunteya, the king of the Sindhus, the doer of evil."
"O Dhanañjaya, here he stands in the midst of the chariot;
raising his head and neck, he gazes at the orb of the sun.
Sañjaya said:
"Quickly strike off his head from his body with a sharp arrow!
Thus addressed by Keśava, his eyes red with indignation,
he drew forth a sharp shaft that was unbearable even for the immortals.
Thinking that the King of the Sindhus could not be slain as long as the sun had not yet set, Janārdana,
the enemy of the Daityas and Hari, called to mind his discus, the Sudarśana.
Then the Blessed One commanded him, who appeared as soon as he was thought of:
"Envelop him, like the sun that has set, with darkness.
O lord of the people, having been thus addressed by the Blessed One, he became darkness.
Ignorance is like blinding darkness that robs the sun of its radiance.
At that very moment, as the sun was swiftly moving toward its setting,
Janārdana spoke there in haste to the Pāṇḍava.
O Pārtha, this Saindhava stands in the midst of six heroic great chariot-warriors, O mighty-armed one; desiring life, he remains there in fear.
Without first conquering these six chariot-warriors in battle, O bull among men—

"O Arjuna, it is not possible to slay the King of Sindhu through straightforward means; therefore, I shall employ a stratagem here regarding the obscuring of the sun. That sole ruler of Sindhu will clearly perceive that the sun has set."
O Lord, out of joy and desiring to live, that man of evil conduct will not protect himself by any means for the sake of your destruction; therefore,
O best of the Kurus, you must strike him at that vulnerability.
"No further concern need be felt; the sun has set.
To this Bībhatsu replied to Keśava, "So be it.
Then Kṛṣṇa created darkness to serve as a veil for the sun.
Hari, the Lord of Yogins, joined with yoga as a yogi;
when darkness was created by Kṛṣṇa, the sun set,
O lord of men, and your warriors rejoiced at the destruction of Pārtha.
O King, those soldiers in battle, though filled with joy, could not see the sun;
they raised their faces upward, and even King Jayadratha,
while looking at the sun, likewise gazed upon it as the king of the Sindhus looked on.
Kṛṣṇa spoke these words once more to Dhanañjaya:
"Behold the heroic lord of the Sindhus, O best of the Bharatas, who has cast aside his great fear of you while gazing at the sun."
"O mighty-armed one, this is the time for the slaying of this evil-minded one!
Quickly sever his head and make yourself successful! Thus addressed by Keśava, the powerful son of Pāṇḍu—
He struck down your army with arrows resembling the sun and fire;
he pierced Kṛpa with twenty arrows, Karṇa with fifty,
and he struck both Śalya and Duryodhana with six arrows each.

O King, having likewise pierced Vṛṣasena with eight arrows and the ruler of the Sindhus with sixty, the mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu, having deeply wounded other warriors of your side with his shafts, rushed toward Jayadratha.
Seeing him standing nearby like a licking fire,
the protectors of Jayadratha fell into a state of extreme peril.
Then, O great king, all your warriors, desiring victory, [advanced].
In that battle, they drenched the subduer of Pāka with showers of arrows;
being repeatedly covered by nets of shafts,
the mighty-armed son of Kuntī, the unconquered joy of the Kurus, grew enraged.
Then, O King, that tiger among men, the son of Pākaśāsana, desiring to slaughter your army, unleashed a tumultuous net of arrows.
Being struck down by that hero in battle, those warriors of yours, O King, [fell].
Terrified, they abandoned the ruler of the Sindhus; neither did they flee together.
There we beheld the marvelous prowess of Kuntī’s son, such as the highly illustrious one performed—neither has there been, nor will there ever be, another like it.
He struck down elephants and those mounted upon them, as well as horses and those mounted upon them; likewise, Rudra slaughtered the chariot-warriors like sacrificial animals.
O lord of men, I saw no one there in that battle who could withstand him.
Neither elephant, nor horse, nor even man who was not struck by Pārtha’s arrows remained;
with their eyes covered by dust and darkness, the warriors fell into a terrible stupor and could no longer recognize one another.
O Bhārata, with their vital organs pierced by those arrows impelled by Pārtha, the soldiers wandered aimlessly, stumbled, fell, sank down,
and fainted, like living beings at the time of a great and terrifying universal destruction.
While that great, difficult-to-cross, and most terrible battle was raging,
the dust of the earth was laid by the sprinkling of blood and the swiftness of the wind upon the surface of the ground thus drenched with gore.

O King, on the field of battle, the chariot wheels of your warriors sank up to their navels in blood; and thousands of elephants, their riders slain and their limbs mangled, lay there in a state of frenzy.
Crushing their own ranks and uttering cries of distress, they fled away;
O lord of men, horses with fallen riders and foot-soldiers,
struck by the arrows of Dhanañjaya, fled in fear, O King.
With disheveled hair and stripped of armor, bleeding upon the earth,
the men fled in terror, abandoning the front of the battle;
some there on the ground were seized by a paralysis of the thighs.
And others hid themselves in the midst of the slain elephants. Thus, O King, having routed your army, Dhanañjaya struck down the protectors of the Sindhu king with his terrible arrows.
The Pāṇḍava covered Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, Vṛṣasena, and Suyodhana with a fierce net of arrows;
O King, he did not grasp them, nor did he withdraw them, nor did he release them, nor even aim them.
In that battle, Arjuna could not be seen in any way because of his swiftness with weapons;
only the circle of his bow was constantly visible as he drew it,
and arrows were seen issuing forth from all sides.
Having cut the bows of both Karṇa and Vṛṣasena,
he struck down Śalya’s charioteer from the seat of the chariot with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla),
having deeply pierced both his sister’s son and his maternal uncle with his shafts.
Arjuna, the best among victors, [overcame] the son of Droṇa and the son of Śaradvat in battle;
having thus thrown those great car-warriors of yours into confusion,
the Pāṇḍava drew forth a terrible arrow resembling fire.

Resembling Indra’s thunderbolt, consecrated with divine mantras for weapons, capable of bearing every burden, and eternally honored with perfumes and garlands— the great Kuru joy, having duly joined it with the *vajra* weapon, [prepared for battle].
As the mighty-armed Arjuna was quickly fitting an arrow to the Gāṇḍīva bow, O King,
a great roar arose from all living beings in the sky as that flaming-tipped shaft was being joined to it.
And there Janārdana, hurrying, spoke again:
"O Dhanañjaya, cut off the head of the evil-minded Saindhava;
the sun desires to go to its setting, that best of mountains."
Listen now to my words regarding the slaying of Jayadratha:
"O Pārtha, O Pārtha, this head shall indeed fall to the earth by your hand,
once the sun has reached the setting mountain and is hastening toward its decline."
Listen to how that deed regarding the Saindhava occurred.
Vṛddhakṣatra, the father of the Saindhava, was renowned throughout the world;
after a long time, he obtained a son here, the Saindhava.
Then, an invisible voice, resonating like the thunder of clouds, spoke to King Jayadratha, the slayer of enemies:
"This son of yours, among mortals, by virtue of his lineage, character, self-restraint, and other qualities— "
O Lord, he shall be equal to both lineages in his virtues;
he will be the preeminent Kṣatriya in the world, eternally honored by heroes. And when this archer fights against enemies in battle—
"An enraged enemy, unobserved on the ground, will cut off his head.
Having heard this, O subduer of foes, the King of Sindhu reflected for a long time and,
tormented by affection for his son, spoke thus to all his kinsmen:
"Whoever shall cause the head of my son— who is fighting in battle and bearing a great burden— to fall upon the earth,
his own head too shall split into a hundred pieces; of this there is no doubt."

"If indeed there be any merit for me in asceticism or self-restraint," having spoken thus, Vṛddhakṣatra then established Jayadratha upon the kingdom and departed for the forest, applying himself to the practice of austerity.
O you whose banner bears the monkey, that radiant one is performing a fierce and formidable penance outside this Samantapañcaka;
therefore, having severed Jayadratha’s head in the great battle, [bring it here].
O slayer of enemies, O performer of wondrous deeds, with your divine and terrible weapon,
O younger brother of the son of the Wind-god, quickly cause the head of the Lord of Sindhu, adorned with earrings, to fall into the lap of Vṛddhakṣatra, O Bhārata.

If you then cause his head to fall upon the surface of the earth, your own head too will split into a hundred pieces; of this there is no doubt. And so that the king, the lord of the earth, may not know of this.
"Act thus, O best of the Kurus, having taken recourse to this divine weapon;
for by the power of this weapon of Paśupati, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished or performed by you."
O Dhananjaya, son of Vasava, let such a policy be adopted so that this head of Saindhava falls upon Vriddhakshatra with arrows alone, even as it does in all the three worlds.
Having heard these words,
Arjuna, licking the corners of his mouth and filled with haste, took up that weapon and struck off the head of his enemy at the gate of Vṛddhakṣatra’s hermitage.

That single arrow, lying in its quiver— terrible, possessing a touch like Indra’s thunderbolt, consecrated with divine mantras, capable of enduring every burden, and eternally honored with perfumes and garlands—
shone with a brilliance equal to Indra’s thunderbolt.

O descendant of Kuru, the mighty-armed Arjuna, having duly joined that weapon which utterly shatters all things and is always honored with perfumes and garlands, quickly fixed it upon the Gāṇḍīva bow with the Raudra missile.
Intent on slaying the ruler of the Sindhus, Arjuna swiftly discharged [the weapon].
Then Dhananjaya quickly drew that arrow, radiant as the sun,
desiring to sever the head of the high-souled Sindhu king from his body.
But that arrow, released from the Gāṇḍīva bow, swift as a hawk,
severed the head of the Lord of Sindhu and soared into the sky;
it carried away the head of the Saindhava like a bird from the top of a tree.
As it was about to fall upon his head, Kṛṣṇa then said to Arjuna:
"O Pārtha, O Pārtha, ensure that this head does not reach the surface of the earth.
Sañjaya said:
"Do so, O best of the Kurus; I shall tell you the reason for that as well.
Having heard his words, Dhanañjaya, acting with haste through the power of his weapons, once again seized that [weapon] from above with his arrows.
To cause dejection among the ill-disposed and to bring joy to his friends,
Arjuna played for a long time, as if in sport, moving sideways, upwards, downwards, and again upwards, and even casting himself down.
Beholding that great and wonderful army from all sides,
the Pāṇḍava, while still engaging the kings in combat, at that moment rendered them like clusters of *kadamba* flowers with his arrows, thereby bringing their heads down.
The son of Pāṇḍu then fought those six great chariot-warriors;
O Bhārata, we then beheld a most wonderful sight there,
as that head was carried away outside of Samantapañcaka.
Jayadratha’s lotus-face, its stalk severed by Arjuna’s arrows and drenched in the water of blood,
was seen by men as it hung suspended above him.
Like a single lotus released by a *vidyādhara*,
like the king of the gods against the enemies of the gods, he,
adorned with a crown and garlands, scattered his rivals.
Just as the darkness-dispelling sun rises upon the darkness,
so the wise one, having fulfilled his complete vow,
then spoke to Keśava, the son of Pāṇḍu.
How far shall I carry this?
For what purpose must it not be cast down upon the earth? And where is this to be taken? Tell me this.
"I am able to bend my head toward whatever region of the earth Your Majesty names.
At that very moment, however, King Vṛddhakṣatra—
O noble one, your radiant kinsman was performing his twilight devotions when,
as he sat there, he caused the head of the King of Sindhu— still adorned with black hair and earrings— to fall into his lap.

O subduer of enemies, that head with its beautiful earrings fell unnoticed onto the lap of King Vṛddhakṣatra while the wise monarch was engaged in his prayers. Then, for that intelligent Vṛddhakṣatra...
As he rose up suddenly, that head fell to the surface of the earth. Then, O subduer of enemies, as the ground touched the crown of that king’s son, his own head also shattered into a hundred pieces.
O King, that head fell upon the surface of the earth in a hundred pieces;
then all living beings were filled with the utmost wonder,
and Vāsudeva praised the great car-warrior Bībhatsu.
Then, O King, having seen Jayadratha,
the king of the Sindhus, slain by Kiritin,
that darkness was withdrawn by Vāsudeva, O bull of the Bharatas.
O protector of the earth, O best of kings, it was only later that your sons and their followers realized,
"This is an illusion employed by Vāsudeva.
Thus, O King, he was slain by Pārtha of immeasurable splendor.
Having slain eight *akṣauhiṇīs*, your son-in-law, the ruler of the Sindhus, was killed;
and seeing Jayadratha slain, O lord of men,
all the gods were struck with wonder at that deed of Pārtha.
"In every way, since Janārdana is his constant protector in battle, how could he not be victorious?"— thus did all beings believe. For this reason, the Pāṇḍava caused his head to fall.
Outside the Syamantapañcaka, having performed that great feat with arrows alone in due order and having slain Jayadratha,
Pārtha began to withdraw the Pāśupata weapon.
O Bhārata, when that weapon was withdrawn by the son of Kuntī,
a cool and fragrant breeze blew there as if to gladden all; and the dwellers of heaven, witnessing both its discharge and its withdrawal, were filled with wonder.
They were filled with supreme wonder and praised the Pāṇḍava;
having thus fought them with his weapons, the heroic Dhananjaya,
the son of Pāṇḍu, subsequently struck off the head of Jayadratha.
O King, as that head was being severed in battle by arrows resembling venomous serpents, your warriors— Śalya, Karṇa, and Kṛpa— were bewildered by Savyasācin. They beheld his head falling down.
Afterward, his body fell to the ground, causing all the kings to grieve. Having seen the great car-warrior, the king of the Sindhus, slain in battle,
much water fell from the eyes of your sons out of sorrow.
They shed tears from grief and became hopeless of victory.
Then, O King, when Jayadratha had been slain by Pārtha, the mighty-armed Keśava and Arjuna, the scorcher of foes, both blew their conchs.
When that hero, the ruler of the Sindhus, world-renowned, had been slain,
O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha attained incomparable joy;
and Bhīmasena also, as if awakening the son of Pāṇḍu, [roared] in the midst of battle.
With a great lion’s roar, he filled the heaven and earth.
And Bhīma, that lion of the Vṛṣṇis, Yudhāmanyu, O Bhārata,
and the valiant Uttamaujas, each blew their conchs separately.
Hearing that great roar, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
considered the ruler of the Sindhus to have been slain by the high-souled Phalguna.
Then, gladdening his own warriors with the sound of musical instruments, he spoke.
He advanced in battle against the son of Bharadvāja with a desire to fight;
joy arose among the army of the Pāṇḍavas as their hearts were gladdened.
Then, O King, as the sun was setting, the battle commenced.
A hair-raising battle took place between Droṇa and the Somakas.
Desiring to slay the son of Bharadvāja with every effort, those great car-warriors fought on, O King, after the ruler of the Sindhus had been killed.
But the Pāṇḍavas, having achieved victory and slain the ruler of the Sindhus,
then fought against Droṇa from every side, intoxicated by their triumph.
Arjuna, too, [assailed] the warriors on your side who were the best of chariot-fighters in battle.
O great king, having slain the Sindhu king,
he who wore a diadem and garlands scattered his enemies on all sides, just as the King of the Gods scatters the enemies of the gods.
Just as the sun, the destroyer of darkness, rises over the gloom,
so did the hero fulfill his former vow.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, whoever hears this account of good conduct here with devotion quickly overcomes untimely death and attains all prosperity.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When that hero, the ruler of the Sindhus, had been slain by Savyasācin,
tell me, O Sañjaya, what my men did then,
while all my warriors looked on in that great battle.
How was the ruler of the Sindhus slain in battle by Savyasācin?

How did he, though protected by the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, and Karṇa in that great conflict, enter the terrible fire-mouthed mouth of Phalguna? O noble one, [tell me] how the ruler of the Sindhus [perished].
When that great archer had been slain, O Sūta, what did the dull-witted Suyodhana do next, together with his brothers? Saṃjaya said:
O venerable one, seeing Saindhava slain in battle by Pārtha,
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, then fell under the sway of indignation and covered the Pāṇḍava with a great shower of arrows.
And the son of Droṇa, mounting his chariot, rushed against Phalguna, the son of Pṛthā.
Then those two best of chariot-warriors, from their respective chariots, both showered that most excellent of car-fighters from both sides with sharp arrows.
Thus afflicted by those two great showers of arrows, that mighty-armed one,
the best of chariot-warriors, fell into extreme distress. Desiring not to slay his preceptor in battle, nor even the preceptor’s son, he [remained there].
There, Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, acted as their preceptor; warding off the weapons of the son of Droṇa and of Śaradvat’s son with his own weapons,
he discharged arrows of diminished velocity, desiring not to slay them.
Those arrows, impelled by the desire for victory, did not strike them excessively;
yet, due to their great number, those two fell into extreme distress from the shafts.
Then, O King, the son of Śaradvat was afflicted by the arrows of the son of Kuntī.
He sank down upon the seat of the chariot and fell into a swoon. Perceiving that his master was overwhelmed and afflicted by arrows,
and knowing him to be slain, the charioteer carried him away.

When Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, had fallen in battle, O Great King, Aśvatthāman also withdrew from the presence of the Pāṇḍava to another chariot. Seeing the son of Śaradvat unconscious and afflicted by arrows, Pārtha [withdrew as well].
Still upon his chariot, the great archer Kṛpa lamented piteously;
with a face full of tears and dejected, he spoke these words.
Seeing this, the highly wise Kṣattṛ (Vidura) addressed the king.
As soon as this wicked Suyodhana, the bringer of ruin to his lineage, was born,
it was right that he be sent to the other world;
for from him a great danger will arise for the leaders of the Kurus.
Those words of the truth-speaker have now come to pass;
for because of them, I see Kṛpa today lying upon a bed of arrows.
Fie on the conduct of the kṣatriyas! Fie on strength and prowess!
For who like me would seek to harm a Brahmin preceptor?
My preceptor is the son of a seer, the beloved friend of Droṇa;
he lies here upon the seat of his chariot, oppressed by my arrows.
Though I did not wish it, he was severely afflicted by my arrows;
he sank down upon the seat of his chariot, as if crushing my very life-breaths.
For even while I was tormented by his shafts, that one of great splendor remained worthy of being gazed upon.
Overwhelmed by grief for his son and tormented by arrows,
he was struck down by many shafts as he met his end according to the tenfold law; falling now, he causes me further sorrow because of the slaughter of my son.
"O Kṛṣṇa, behold how the wretched one has fallen, collapsed upon his own chariot.
Those bulls among men who, having imparted knowledge to their teachers,
bestow upon them their desired objects in this world, attain the state of divinity."
But those lowest of men who, having received knowledge from their teachers,
destroy that very [knowledge], being of evil conduct, they indeed go to hell.
Therefore, this deed has certainly been done by me today for the sake of hell.
When Kṛpa, while seated in his chariot, struck the preceptor with a shower of arrows,
Kṛpa had previously told me,
"O descendant of Kuru, you must never strike your teacher under any circumstances."
This word of the virtuous and high-souled teacher has not been carried out by you, as you showered arrows upon him in battle. Homage to that most worshipful Gautama, who did not flee!
"Fie on me, O Vārṣṇeya, for I am about to strike him!
While Savyasācin was thus lamenting toward him,
O King, Gautama was then rendered helpless by Kirīṭin.
Just as a fire fueled by wood blazes when fanned by the fuel of anger,
so did the son of Rādhā rush forward upon seeing the ruler of the Sindhus slain;
leaving the face of the Sindhu king, Karṇa advanced against the Sātvata.
As the son of Rādhā was rushing toward Arjuna’s chariot,
the two Pāñcālya princes and Sātyaki suddenly charged forward.
Seeing the son of Rādhā approaching, the great car-warrior Pārtha [prepared himself].
Laughing, he addressed these words to the son of Devakī:
"There goes the son of Adhiratha toward the chariot of Sātyaki;
he surely cannot endure that Bhūriśravas has been slain in battle."
"O Janārdana, urge the horses wherever he goes;
let not that bull among men, Sātyaki, follow the path of Somadatta’s son.
Thus addressed by Savyasācin, the mighty-armed Keśava [did so].
The one of great splendor replied with these words appropriate for the occasion:
"O Pāṇḍava, this mighty-armed bull among the Sātvatas is alone sufficient for Karṇa; how much more so when accompanied by the two sons of Draupadī?"
O Pārtha, a combat with Karṇa is not yet appropriate for you;
for his Vāsavi weapon stands like a great blazing meteor,
O slayer of enemy heroes, being worshipped and guarded for your sake.
I do not consider Karṇa to be an ordinary man; therefore, I have no desire for battle with him.
For Karṇa alone is powerful enough to defeat us by his might;
indeed, we, even with our armies and mounts, are not capable of defeating Karṇa.
This is the great flaw of Karṇa: that he falters at every step due to both negligence and compassion; for this reason, he is considered the most easily overcome.
Therefore, let Karṇa advance against the Sātvata in whatever manner may be.
"I shall know the time of this evil-minded one, O Kauravya,
when he shall strike him down to the earth with sharp arrows;
then, O Pārtha, you shall go to fight that evil-minded man."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Let that encounter between the heroic Karṇa and the descendant of Vṛṣṇi—
which was desired by Karṇa— take place with that man of exceeding splendor."
When Bhūriśravas had been slain and the ruler of the Sindhus (Jayadratha) struck down,
and seeing the son of Somadatta killed, how did that battle proceed?
And as for Sātyaki, who was deprived of his chariot, which chariot did he mount?
"And as for the two Pāñcāla wheel-protectors, tell me that, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said:
"Indeed, I shall describe to you exactly what occurred in that great battle."
Be steadfast and listen to the wicked conduct of yourself while all the armies, as well as Keśava and Arjuna, look on.
For this was already known in the mind of Kṛṣṇa, O Lord.
"Just as the hero Sātyaki was to be defeated by Yūpaketu,
O King, so Janārdana knows both the past and the future;
therefore, having summoned his charioteer Dāruka, he gave him his command."
"O King, let my chariot be yoked at dawn," said the mighty Dāruka,
carrying in his heart the command previously given by Kṛṣṇa during the night;
for neither gods, nor Gandharvas, nor Yakṣas, Uragas, nor Rākṣasas [could have done so].

Are there any among men who could be victors over the two Kṛṣṇas? Or are there any warriors whatsoever present in either of the two armies? The gods, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā), as well as the Siddhas, know that [to be so].
Hear now of their incomparable power and how that battle took place:
seeing Sātyaki deprived of his chariot and Karṇa with his weapon raised,
Mādhava then blew his conch shell with great force upon the bull-hide shield.
Having understood the message and heard the sound of Śaṅkha,
Dāruka brought forward for him a chariot with a banner bearing the emblem of Suparṇa;
at Keshava’s command, he prepared that chariot joined with Dāruka.
The grandson of Śini ascended [the chariot] which resembled the blazing sun, drawn by horses that moved at will— Sainya, Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka—
who were preeminent among steeds, possessed great speed, and were adorned with golden trappings.
Having mounted that chariot, which was like a celestial vehicle (*vimāna*),
he rushed toward the son of Rādhā, scattering many arrows.
At that time, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas were also his wheel-protectors.
Leaving Dhanañjaya’s chariot, they advanced against the son of Rādhā. O great king, the son of Rādhā too, discharging a shower of arrows,
rushed in great fury toward the unshakable Śaineya in battle.
"Neither among the gods, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Asuras, Uragas, or Rākṣasas,
has such a battle been heard of on earth or in heaven. At this,
that army— along with its chariots, horses, men, and elephants— ceased its struggle.
O Great King, having witnessed the deeds of those two whose minds were bewildered by passion,
everyone beheld that superhuman battle between those two best of men, O King, as well as the charioteership of Dāruka.

The gods, gandharvas, and dānavas dwelling in the vault of heaven were filled with wonder at the charioteer standing upon his chariot— descendant of Kaśyapa— as he performed circular maneuvers, returning turns, and movements of going forth and coming back.
They were intensely focused on watching the battle between Karṇa and the descendant of Śini;
for the sake of their allies, those two powerful and rival warriors exerted their prowess in the fray—
Karṇa, who resembled an immortal, and Yuyudhāna Sātyaki.
But Karṇa, of immeasurable prowess and devoted to your welfare, [fought on].
O great king, those two rained showers of arrows upon one another;
Karṇa then overwhelmed the grandson of Śini with volleys of shafts.
Unable to endure the death of both Jalasaṃdha and the Kaurava,
and seeing Jalasaṃdha slain as well as Bhūriśravas,
Karṇa was overwhelmed with grief and hissed like a great serpent.
Enraged in battle, as if burning him with his very eyes, that subduer of foes rushed again and again with great speed at the descendant of Śini;
the mighty-armed one pressed him hard while all the kṣatriyas looked on.
Beholding him thus enraged, Sātyaki pierced him in return;
Satyaka, the bull among the Vṛṣṇis, assailed him with arrows.
Thereupon, O King, the delighter of the Cedis performed a marvel.
And he pierced Karṇa in return with the sharp arrows discharged by him;
then those two heroes, both experts in battle and desiring victory, mangled one another out of rivalry.
Like an elephant against a rival elephant with a great shower of arrows,
those two tigers among men, meeting like two swift-moving tigers,
fought with battles thick with shafts, competing and intoxicated by war.
Those two of incomparable prowess hacked at one another in battle. Then the grandson of Śini, the subduer of foes, pierced Karṇa again and again in all his limbs with arrows made entirely of iron.
With a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he struck down his charioteer from the seat of the chariot;
with sharpened shafts, he slew the four white horses;
and that bull among men, having cut the standard into a hundred pieces with a hundred arrows, [felled it].
He cut down the banner and the parasol, and shattered the chariot into a hundred pieces;
he deprived Karṇa of his chariot while your son looked on.
Then, O King, your men, those bulls among men, became despondent.
Vṛṣasena, the son of Karṇa, Śalya the lord of Madra, Kṛpa, the king of Madra, and Vṛṣasena— these,
along with the son of Droṇa, surrounded the descendant of Śini from all sides in the encounter.

Then everything became so utterly confounded that nothing could be discerned, once the heroic son of the Sūta had been deprived of his chariot by the brave Sātyaki— that hero among men, Satyaka— having thus acted.
Then, O King, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among all the troops. Karna too, O King, overwhelmed and afflicted by the arrows of the Sātvata, ascended the chariot of Duryodhana, sighing heavily.
Honoring the friendship he had maintained with your son since childhood, and fulfilling the promise made by granting him the kingdom, O King,
he [Duryodhana] then addressed your sons while Karṇa stood there deprived of his chariot.
The self-controlled Sātyaki did not slay those heroes headed by Duḥśāsana,
guarding once again the vow previously made by Bhīmasena; he rendered them carless and distressed, but did not deprive them of their lives.
The slaughter of your sons had been promised by Bhīmasena,
and at the second game of dice, the slaughter of Karṇa was vowed by Pārtha. Yet, with Karṇa at their head, they then made no effort toward his death.
Then Karna, together with your sons, made an effort to slay him,
but those foremost of chariot-warriors were unable to kill Satyaki. Satyaka, however, effortlessly scattered your sons with his arrows.
The son of Droṇa, Kṛtavarman, and likewise other great car-warriors—
hundreds of the best among the Kṣatriyas— were defeated by him with his bow alone,
as he desired the next world and the welfare of Dharmarāja.
In prowess, Sātyaki, the crusher of enemies, is equal to the two Kṛṣṇas;
he conquered all your troops as if laughing. Indeed, in this world, there may be either Kṛṣṇa or Pārtha as the wielder of the bow.
"Or the Śaineya, that tiger among men—the fourth is not to be found.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Mounted upon the invincible chariot of Vāsudeva, Sātyaki..."
The youth, equal to Vāsudeva, deprived Karṇa of his chariot while your army looked on; that youth, equal to Vāsudeva and like Pārtha in battle, rendered Karṇa chariotless as your troops gazed.
Proud of the strength of his own arms, did that Satyaki— who is the sole hero among all Kṣatriya warriors— mount another chariot driven by the Sūta's son, Dāruka?
"I wish to hear this, for you are skilled in speaking.
I consider him unbearable; tell me about him, Saṃjaya.
I consider Sātyaki to be unbearable, with the roar of a mass of chariots like a thundering cloud."
"O Sañjaya, tell me further what those two did again.
Sañjaya said:
"Listen, O King, how the high-minded one [Dhṛṣṭadyumna] took another chariot for him."
The younger brother of Dāruka quickly prepared the chariot, which was fashioned according to the rules of construction,
bound with bands of iron and gold, equipped with a pole and a seat, studded with thousands of stars, and adorned with a lion-bannered flag.
O lord of the people, [he was mounted] upon excellent horses, swift as the wind, adorned with golden trappings and harnesses;
they were white like the moon, firm, surpassing all sounds,
and equipped with variegated golden armor.

He prepared a chariot that resounded with the clanging of networks of bells, flashing with spears and javelins like lightning, equipped with all the materials for battle and an abundance of weapons and accoutrements, and which possessed a roar as deep as a thundercloud.
Mounting it, the descendant of Śini charged against your army;
Dāruka also proceeded as he desired toward the presence of Keśava.
O great king, Karna likewise [mounted his chariot] with horses white as conch shells and cow’s milk.
With excellent horses of great speed, clad in variegated golden armor,

[he ascended] that foremost chariot— equipped with golden girths and banners, fitted with mechanical devices and flags, well-managed by a skilled driver, and provided with an abundance of weapons and equipment.
Having mounted it, Karna also rushed against his enemies.
All this that you asked me has been related to you;
furthermore, learn now of the destruction brought about by your own misconduct.
Thirty-one of your sons were struck down by Bhīmasena;
with Durmukha, that ever-victorious warrior,
at their head, hundreds of heroes were slain by the Sātvata and by Arjuna.
"O noble one, having placed Bhīṣma and Bhagadatta at their head,
this destruction occurred, O King, due to your evil counsel.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When those heroes had thus departed, O Sañjaya, what indeed did Bhīma do then, both for them and for me? Tell me that, O Sañjaya;
what indeed did Bhīma, Arjuna, and Sātyaki do there at that time?
Saṃjaya said:
Deprived of his chariot and tormented by the arrow-like words of Karṇa, Bhīmasena,
overcome by indignation, spoke these words to Phalguna.
"O Tūbaraka! O fool! O glutton! he said to me again and again.
"O you unskilled in weapons! Do not fight, O child who is timid in battle!
Thus did Karṇa speak to me while you were looking on, O Dhanañjaya.
"O Bhārata, he who speaks thus to me deserves to be slain; and by him I have been addressed.
O mighty-armed one, this vow was made by me together with you.
O Kaunteya, as it is for me, so it is for you—of this there is no doubt."
"O best of men, remember these words of mine for his destruction;
O Dhanañjaya, act in such a way that this becomes true.
Having heard those words of Bhīma, he of immeasurable prowess—
Having heard the words of Bhīmasena, Arjuna, who possesses the prowess of an immortal, then approached Karna slightly in the encounter and said:
"Karna, Karna! You of vain vision, son of a Sūta, you who praise yourself!"
"O you of unrighteous mind, listen now to what I shall say to you:
for heroes in battle, there are two outcomes—victory and defeat.
And these two, O son of Rādhā, are even uncertain for Vāsava himself when he fights."
"O shameless one, you abandon the battle and flee again and again!
Behold the majesty of Bhīma and his noble birth, O Karṇa;
he has not uttered a harsh word toward you, even though you are intent on flight."
Furthermore, O son of a charioteer, having encountered that heroic Pāṇḍava by mere chance, you deprived him of his chariot and slew him;
O Rādheya, you have acted in a manner worthy of your lineage.
O best of men, you do not understand what has been proposed at this moment.
I think you treat the Kṣatriya order like a jackal;
let there be battle for you as your ancestral duty, while another task suited to your lineage remains.
"O son of Rādhā, I too say this to you at the forefront of battle:
perform all your duties in the midst of all weapon-bearers. Even for Vāsava himself, absolute success in combat is not found."
Desiring death, you were deprived of your chariot by Yuyudhāna and released;
knowing "you are to be slain by me," he conquered you and released you alive.
By chance, you have now deprived Bhīmasena of his chariot.
That victory of Bhīmasena was obtained by you through mere chance; however,
O son of Rādhā, it was unrighteous that you spoke thus to Bhīma,
who, knowing the laws of war, was fighting without fleeing.
That you spoke so harshly after having somehow deprived him of his chariot—
this is a very great unrighteousness and an ignoble act.
Having conquered a woman, they do not boast excessively, nor do they utter foul speech.

The virtuous, heroic, and bull-like men among men do not revile anyone; but you, O son of a Sūta, with your vulgar intellect, speak such various things out of fickleness— much that is incoherent, unworthy of being heard, and unexamined.

Since you spoke such unpleasant words to Bhima regarding that hero who fulfills his duty to the best of his ability in battle, who fights with prowess, and who is devoted to the vows of the noble— this speech of yours is not true.
While all the troops, as well as Keśava and I myself, were looking on,
you were deprived of your chariot many times in battle by Bhīmasena;
yet the son of Pāṇḍu did not say anything harsh to you.
"Because Vṛkodara was made to hear so much harshness by you,
and because my son Saubhadra was slain by you behind his back,
therefore receive now the immediate fruit of this arrogance."
"O evil-minded one, you have broken his bow for your own destruction.
Therefore, O fool, you and your servants, troops, and mounts are to be slain by me. Perform all your final duties; a great danger has come upon you."
"Indeed, I shall slay Vṛṣasena before your very eyes in battle;
and whatever other kings, through delusion of intellect, shall come against me,
and whoever else shall approach me as their slayer in the fray."

"I shall slay them all; I swear this by my weapon in truth. And you, O fool of unrefined intellect and excessive pride, I shall slay you, the shaven-headed one, and you, Karṇa, who are so arrogant in battle."
Seeing him struck down by Arjuna, the foolish Duryodhana will suffer great remorse; for when the slaughter of Karṇa’s son was vowed,
a great and tumultuous roar then arose from the chariot-warriors.
While that tumultuous battle, fraught with great terror, was still raging,
the thousand-rayed sun, its beams dimmed, went down to the western mountain.
Then all those best of kings performed their evening devotions.
They appeared with supreme luster, like fires incarnate. As the sun was turning red, Dhanañjaya,
hurrying along with the two protectors of his wheels and the bull of the Śinis, [advanced].
O sinless one, Yudhāmanyu, accompanied by Bhīma who stood upon his chariot,
advanced for battle against the heroic followers of Jayadratha.
Then, O King, Hṛṣīkeśa [beheld] him stationed at the head of the battle.
Embracing Bībhatsu, who had fulfilled his vow, he said this:
"By good fortune, O Jiṣṇu, you have accomplished your great vow;
and by good fortune, the wicked Vṛddhakṣatra has been slain along with his son."

O Bhārata, even the army of the gods would falter in battle upon encountering the force of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons, O Jiṣṇu; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. Reflecting upon it, I do not see any man anywhere in the worlds who could withstand him.
"O tiger among men, were it not for you, who could have fought this army?
For the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, many lords of the earth— possessing great power, some equal to you and others even superior— have assembled together."
Having encountered you, enraged in battle, those armored warriors could not withstand you;
for no one would have been able to display such prowess in combat as this valor and strength of yours, which is equal to that of Rudra, Śakra, and Antaka.
O scorcher of enemies, just as you have acted today alone,
so too, when the evil-minded Karṇa has been slain along with his followers,
I shall further honor you, who have conquered your foes and destroyed your enemies.
Arjuna replied to him: "O Mādhava, by your grace, this vow of mine—which would have been difficult even for the gods to fulfill—has been successfully completed.
Victory is no wonder for those who have you as their protector, O Mādhava."
"By your grace, Yudhiṣṭhira shall regain the entire earth.
O Vārṣṇeya, this burden is yours alone; O Lord, victory is yours alone.
We are your dependents and your servants, O Madhusūdana."
Thus addressed, Kṛṣṇa, smiling and driving the horses slowly,
showed Pārtha the great and cruel battlefield.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Seeking victory in battle and great, celebrated fame,
these heroic kings lie prostrate upon the earth, slain by your arrows;
their weapons and ornaments scattered, and their horses, chariots, and elephants destroyed.

With their armor shattered and torn, they fell into a state of supreme distress; though some were still alive and others had lost their lives, all those lords of men appeared endowed with a supreme radiance, such that even the lifeless ones seemed as if they were still living.
Behold the earth completely covered with their gold-feathered arrows and various sharp weapons, as well as with mounts and armaments,
along with armor, shields, necklaces, and heads adorned with earrings.
O Bhārata, the earth shines with turbans, crowns, garlands, crest-jewels, and garments; with necklaces, armlets, and radiant golden coins (niṣkas); and with various other wonderful ornaments.
With trailing undercarriages, quivers, banners, and standards; with equipment, chariot bases, and curved pole-shafts;
and with variegated wheels and axles shattered in many ways on the battlefield.
With yokes, traces, quivers, bows, and arrows;
with elephant-blankets, rugs, iron clubs, and goads;
and with spears, slings, quivers, pikes, and battle-axes.
With spears and javelins,
with lances and staffs, with *śataghnīs* and *bhuśuṇḍīs*,
with swords and axes, as well as with maces, clubs, and *kuṇapas*.
And with whips fashioned of gold, O bull of the Bharatas,
and with bells, various ornaments for the lordly elephants,
as well as garlands, diverse decorations, and costly garments.
Strewn with those who had been cast down, the earth shone like the autumnal sky filled with planets.
For the sake of the earth, lords of the earth were slain upon the earth;
embracing the earth with their limbs, they lay as if asleep with a beloved mistress.
And these elephants, resembling Airāvata and appearing like mountain peaks,
were shedding copious blood from the wounds of weapons as if they were mountains with cavernous openings from which streams of red chalk-water were flowing.
O hero, behold those struck down by your arrows groaning upon the earth;
behold the fallen horses adorned with golden trappings,
and the chariots resembling cities of the Gandharvas, now bereft of their masters.

O Lord, O Pārtha, behold the horses on the ground— once as magnificent as celestial chariots— now with their banners and pennants severed, their axles broken, their charioteers slain, their poles and yokes cut away, and their seats shattered.
O hero, behold the foot-soldiers slain by the hundreds and thousands—
bowmen and shield-bearers lying there drenched in blood,
their hair covered in dust as they embrace the earth with all their limbs.
Behold, O mighty-armed one, the warriors whose bodies are pierced by your arrows; behold the field crowded with fallen elephants, chariots, and horses,
and filled with a mire rich in blood, fat, and flesh.
O best of men, behold this surface of the earth, a feast for night-stalkers, dogs, wolves, and piśācas; O Lord,
this great calamity has befallen you.
On the field of battle, he performed deeds that increased his glory,
even while Śatakratu, the best of gods,
was slaying the Daityas and Dānavas in a great conflict.
While still pointing out that terrain of the enemy to the diadem-wearing Arjuna, Janārdana, the slayer of foes, quickly approached the Pāṇḍava Ajātaśatru.
He announced that Jayadratha had been slain, amidst chowries, fans, and variegated banners; with horses, chariots, and elephants;
and with various elephant housings and the trappings of horses scattered about.
Behold the earth strewn with various maces and costly chariot-fenders, covered as if with variegated cloths; and see others fallen from their well-equipped elephants along with the beasts themselves.
Behold others, like lions driven by thunderbolts falling from mountain peaks,
pierced through and lying upon the earth together with their horses; and behold the throngs of foot soldiers and riders submerged in floods of blood.
Saṃjaya said:
Thus showing the battlefield to the Diademed One (Arjuna), Kṛṣṇa,
together with his own people, joyfully blew the Pāñcajanya conch.
Pointing out that very region of the enemy, Janārdana, the slayer of foes wearing a diadem,
approached the Pāṇḍava Ajātaśatru directly.
He announced that Jayadratha had been slain;
then Sātyaki and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava,
as well as both Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, the two sons of the Pañcāla king, advanced toward the son of Pṛthā.
Having warded off the son of Droṇa with their arrows, as well as Karṇa along with the kings,
those chariot-warriors proceeded to where King Yudhiṣṭhira was.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, approaching King Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, he, with a heart full of joy, announced that the ruler of the Sindhus had been slain by Pārtha:
"By good fortune you prosper, O Indra among kings; you have slain your enemy, O best of men!"

"By good fortune, your younger brother has indeed fulfilled his vow. Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, O Bhārata, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the conqueror of enemy cities, was filled with joy; he then leaped down from his chariot.
