Then, his eyes overflowing with tears of joy,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, descended from his chariot and embraced the two Kṛṣṇas— Keśava and Arjuna— with a heart full of exultation, O King.
Having wiped his bright face, which possessed a luster like that of a white lotus,
he spoke to Vāsudeva and Dhananjaya the Pāṇḍava:
"By good fortune, I behold you two great car-warriors in battle, having successfully fulfilled your burden."
"By good fortune, the wicked Saindhava, that lowest of men, has been slain! O Kṛṣṇa, by good fortune, great joy has been bestowed upon me;
by good fortune, the hosts of enemies have indeed been submerged in an ocean of grief."
Nothing whatsoever in the three worlds is difficult for them to achieve,
O Madhusūdana, for whom you, the teacher of all the world, are their protector. Through your grace, O Govinda, we shall conquer our enemies.

Just as in the past, O Pākaśāsana, through your grace you achieved victory over the Dānavas— whether it be the conquest of the earth or even the conquest of the three worlds— victory is indeed certain for those, O Vārṣṇeya, with whom you are pleased, O Mādhava.
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, by your grace I shall obtain the supreme kingdom;
for them there shall be no sin nor defeat in battle—
those for whom you, O Mādhava, the Lord of the lords of the thirty gods, are well-pleased."
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, by your grace, the illustrious Śakra, lord of the hosts of gods,
attained victory over the three worlds at the forefront of battle. And by your grace alone, O Lord of the Thirty-three, the gods [attained their sovereignty]."
O Kṛṣṇa, O slayer of enemies, by means of the prowess arising from your grace, they have attained immortality and enjoy imperishable worlds; likewise,
Śakra attained the lordship of the gods after slaying thousands of Daityas through that same valor.
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Hero, by your grace this world of moving and unmoving beings remains established in its own course and engages in prayers and oblations.
Previously, all this was a single ocean, consisting of darkness."

"O Supreme among Men, through your grace the world has attained illumination. Those who have taken refuge in Hṛṣīkeśa— the creator of all worlds, the Supreme Self, the Infallible— are never deluded at any time."
Those who have taken refuge in the ancient, supreme god, the eternal God of gods, the teacher of the deities, are never deluded at any time—
[in Him] the god who is without beginning or end, the creator of the world, and the imperishable.

O Hṛṣīkeśa, those who are devoted to you cross over all difficulties. To him who takes refuge in that supreme, ancient Person, who is the highest of the ancient ones— to him, the supreme prosperity is ordained.
The protector of all worlds, that which is the eternal Brahman; the origin of the worlds, the architect of the universe, the imperishable syllable, the imperishable;
the supreme source of the mind, space, wind, and the treasury of lights.
He who has mastered the four Vedas and he who is celebrated in the Vedas— by taking refuge in that Great-Souled One, one attains unsurpassed prosperity;
[he is] the creator of all castes and the supreme source of the world.

I take refuge in you, the unborn, the causal self, the beloved of the Pāṇḍavas— the supreme Brahman of all yogas, the radiant treasury of those who know Brahman, the creator and the withdrawer of all that is moving and unmoving.
O Supreme Lord, Lord of the highest lords, Lord of animals, Lord of men,
Lord of the lords of all lords— salutations to you, O Puruṣottama!
O Lord of the lords of lords, Sovereign, Master Mādhava, may you prosper!
O source and dissolution of all, O soul of all, O wide-eyed one! He who is the friend of Dhanañjaya and he who is devoted to the welfare of Dhanañjaya—
he prospers in happiness by taking refuge in that protector of Dhanañjaya.

With his senses, mind, and self thrilled with joy, the high-minded king was unable to speak for a moment due to that vigor; then, filled with delight, his eyes overflowing with tears of joy, he remained silent for a while.
Extremely delighted, he spoke these words with a faltering voice:
"O lotus-eyed one, having heard this pleasant news from you,
I do not reach the end of my joy, like one wishing to cross the ocean."
"O Kṛṣṇa, this deed performed by the wise Pārtha while protected by you, O Govinda— by slaying the wicked Jayadratha— is truly most wonderful. Yet,
it is not at all surprising for those of whom you are the refuge."
You have always remained with your whole soul devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial;
and it was by relying upon you that we raised our weapons,
just as the gods did against Śakra in the battle for the destruction of the Asuras.
"O Janārdana, this deed is impossible even for the gods;
yet Phalguna has accomplished it through the power of your intellect, strength, and heroism.
O Kṛṣṇa, from my childhood I have heard of your deeds."
As soon as we were favored by you out of affection and love— with many great, divine, and superhuman [powers]—
at that very moment I knew that the enemies were slain and the earth had been won.
O sinless one, the ancient seer Mārkaṇḍeya, who knows your deeds,
as well as the sage Asita Devala and Nārada of great asceticism, have in the past proclaimed your majesty and your power.
My grandfather Vyāsa has told you that you are the supreme ordinance;
you are splendor, you are the Supreme Brahman, you are truth, and you are great austerity.
You are the highest good, you are foremost glory, and likewise the cause of the universe.
All this world, both stationary and moving, was created by you;
when the dissolution has arrived, it indeed enters back into you—
the god who is without beginning or end, the Lord of the universe, the Prajāpati.
Those who know the Vedas declare the Creator to be unborn and unmanifest; they call him the self of all beings, the Great Self, infinite, and facing in every direction.
Even the gods do not know that primordial secret Lord of the Universe.
To Nārāyaṇa, the supreme deity, the Supreme Self, the Lord;
to Hari Viṣṇu, the source of knowledge, the ultimate refuge for those seeking liberation;
to the supreme, ancient Puruṣa, who is higher than even the ancient ones.
The number of such qualities and deeds of yours, both in heaven and here on earth—
pertaining to the past, present, and future— is not found to be calculable here.
We must be protected in every way by you, along with Śakra and the other inhabitants of the celestial realms.
"By those who have not made you their friend, you who are endowed with every virtue"—
when the King of Dharma had thus addressed the highly illustrious Hari,
Janārdana replied with these fitting words:
By your fierce asceticism and supreme righteousness,
and indeed by your goodness and straightforwardness, the wicked Jayadratha has been slain. And this tiger among men [Arjuna], O Lord, has been strengthened by your constant meditation upon him.
Having slain thousands of warriors, Jishnu struck down Jayadratha. In skill, in the strength of his arms, and likewise in composure,
in speed, and in hitting the mark with unerring precision, there is no one equal to Partha anywhere.
Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, this Arjuna, your brother among the Pāṇḍavas,
having caused the destruction of the army in battle, took the head of the King of Sindhu. Then, O lord of the people, the son of Dharma embraced Jiṣṇu.
Wiping his face, the Lord comforted him:
"O Phalguna, you have performed a most great deed,
one that is unbearable and impossible even for the gods led by Indra."
"By good fortune, O slayer of foes, you have cast off your burden and destroyed your enemies. By good fortune, this vow has been made true by the killing of Jayadratha.
Having spoken thus to Guḍākeśa, the highly illustrious Dharmarāja [concluded].

The king touched him on the back with his hand, which was fragrant with merit. When Keśava and the Pāṇḍava had both been addressed thus, those two great-souled ones, filled with joy, then spoke to the king, the lord of the earth.
O Bhārata, the wicked King Jayadratha has been consumed by the fire of your wrath;
and even the vast, swelling army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons is being slaughtered in battle—
it is already slain and shall utterly perish.
O slayer of enemies, these Kauravas have indeed been struck down by your wrath;
for having provoked you, the hero whose very glance kills, the evil-minded Suyodhana, along with his friends and kinsmen, shall lose his life in battle.

Struck down by your wrath, Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus, who was formerly difficult even for the gods to conquer, now lies upon a bed of arrows. For victory in battle is indeed hard to attain for them, O slayer of enemies.
O Pāṇḍava, those with whom you are angry have indeed fallen under the power of death;
O giver of honor, the kingdom, life-breaths, beloved sons, and various pleasures of those with whom you are angry perish before long.
"I consider the Kauravas, along with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen, to have been destroyed.
The Blessed Lord said:
"It is even so, O mighty-armed one; the Kauravas have been destroyed in battle."
While you, O Yudhiṣṭhira, who are ever devoted to the duties of kings, were thus enraged,
the mighty-armed Bhīma and the great car-warrior Sātyaki, both wounded and mangled by arrows, saluted their eldest elder.
Those two great archers remained there, surrounded by the Pāñcālas.
Seeing those two heroes standing before them with palms joined in reverence,
the son of Kuntī, Bhīma, and Sātyaki all rejoiced.
"By good fortune, I behold you two heroes released from the ocean of the army,
from that unassailable crocodile of Droṇa and the abode of the makaras that is the son of Hṛdika.
And by good fortune, all the kings on earth have been defeated in battle."
"By good fortune, I see you both victorious in battle;
by good fortune, Droṇa has been defeated in the fray, as has the mighty Hārdikya;
and by good fortune, Karṇa has been brought to defeat in combat by the Vikarṇis."
O bulls among men, Śalya has been turned away by you both;
by good fortune, I see that you two, the best of chariot-warriors and experts in combat, have returned safely from the battle.
"By good fortune, I behold my two heroic sons, who carry out my every word and are restrained by their reverence for me; they have crossed the ocean of the army, O sinless ones,
those heroes who glory in battle and never flee from combat."
"By good fortune, I behold you both, who are as dear to me as my own life.
Having spoken thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, embraced Yuyudhāna and Vṛkodara—
those two tigers among men— and shed tears out of joy.
Then, O lord of the people, the entire army of the Pāṇḍavas was filled with joy upon seeing their victory, and they set their minds on battle. Sañjaya said:
O King, when Saindhava had been slain, your son Suyodhana,
his face drenched with tears, dejected and devoid of energy for conquering the enemy,
became dispirited and sighed hotly like a serpent whose fangs have been broken.
Your son, who had brought harm to the whole world,
fell into extreme agony upon seeing that great and terrible slaughter of his own army wrought in battle by Jiṣṇu, Bhīmasena, and the Sātvata.
Pale, emaciated, and dejected, with eyes overflowing with tears, he thought:
"There is no warrior on earth equal to Arjuna;
neither Droṇa, nor Rādheya, nor Aśvatthāman, nor Kṛpa."
"O noble one, they were not capable of standing before him when he was enraged;
for having conquered all my great car-warriors in battle, Pārtha slew the ruler of the Sindhus in the fray, and no one could restrain him."
In every respect, this great army of the Kauravas is already as good as destroyed;
for there exists no protector for it, not even Purandara himself in person,
relying upon whom they have exerted their weapons in battle.
That Karṇa has been defeated in battle, and Jayadratha has indeed been slain—
he who used to speak harsh words to the Pāṇḍavas in the midst of the assembly,
and by whom the slaughter of Savyasācin in combat was vowed.
That Karna has been defeated in battle, and the ruler of the Sindhus has been struck down— he upon whose prowess I relied when I treated Acyuta, who was entreating me for peace,
as if he were a blade of grass; that Karna has been conquered in war.
O King, bull of the Bharata race, with his mind thus despondent, your son— the wrongdoer toward all the world— approached to see Droṇa;
he then related that entire great slaughter of the Kurus.
And as the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were being defeated and sinking,
Duryodhana said:
"O Teacher, behold the slaughter that has been wrought upon the consecrated kings!"
Having placed my grandfather Bhīṣma, the hero, at the forefront,
this greedy Śikhaṇḍin, having slain him, now draws the vanguard of the army forward, accompanied by all the Pāñcālas with his heart’s desire fulfilled.
Moreover, another invincible disciple of yours, Savyasācin,
having slain seven akṣauhiṇīs, killed King Jayadratha—
[the king] of those well-wishing friends who desired our victory.
How shall I attain freedom from my debt to those who have gone to the abode of Yama— those lords of the earth who, for my sake,
desired the earth and now lie upon the earth, having abandoned their sovereignty over it?
Having brought about such destruction of my friends, I am a base man;
I do not dare to purify myself even with a thousand horse-sacrifices,
for I am greedy, sinful, and likewise a transgressor of dharma.
Striving and desiring victory, they have reached the abode of Vaivasvata.
How was it that the earth did not open a chasm for me— in this assembly of kings— to receive one of such fallen conduct who bears malice toward his friends?
Thus, I was unable to save my grandfather Bhīṣma, his limbs drenched in blood, as he lay slain in battle in the midst of kings. Therefore, I am a base man, a betrayer of friends, and unrighteous.

What will that invincible conqueror of the next world say when he encounters Jalasandha, that great archer, seeing him slain by Sātyaki— that hero and great car-warrior who exerted himself for my sake and gave up his life?

Having seen Kāmboja slain, as well as Alambuṣa and many other friends, what purpose is there for me to live today? Those heroes who strove for my sake, never turning their backs in battle, have been killed.
O scorcher of foes, having today discharged my debt to them to the best of my ability by defeating my enemies,
I shall gratify them with water along the Yamunā.
"O best among all wielders of weapons, I promise you truly;
I swear by my sacrifices and charitable works, by my valor, and even by my sons—
that having slain all those Pāñcālas along with the Pāṇḍavas in battle,"
I shall obtain peace through them, or else I shall go to the same world as they in battle. For now my allies do not seek to protect me, being unprepared;
indeed, O mighty-armed one, they consider the Pāṇḍavas superior, and no longer regard us in that way.
For death itself was ordained by him who is true to his promise in battle;
yet you show indifference toward Dhananjaya because of your affection for him as a good disciple.
Therefore, all those who desired our victory have been slain.
I see only Karṇa now as one who desires our victory;
for when a dull-witted man, failing to recognize a friend as he truly is,
employs him for the sake of a friend's purpose, that very purpose fails.

Such was the deed performed by those who called themselves my friends— deeds done through delusion, greed, and wicked conduct in various ways. Jayadratha has been slain, as has the heroic son of Somadatta.
The Abhiṣāhas, Śūrasenas, Śibis, and Vasātis—
such as I am, I shall go today to where those bulls among men lie slain,
having fought for my sake against the Diademed One in battle.
"Indeed, I have no purpose for life without those bulls among men;
may your honor, the preceptor of the sons of Pāṇḍu, grant us your permission.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O dear one, when the King of the Sindhus had been slain in battle by Savyasācin,
and likewise when Bhūriśravas was killed— what then was the state of your minds? And how did Droṇa respond when thus addressed by Duryodhana in the assembly of the Kurus?"
"O Saṃjaya, tell me what he said after that.
Saṃjaya said:
O Bhārata, there was a great clamor among your troops."
Seeing Saindhava slain as well as Bhūriśravas,
they all disregarded everything that had been counseled by your son;
indeed, they all held your son’s counsel in contempt.
"By which mantra hundreds of bulls among the Kṣatriyas have been slain.
Hearing these words of your son, Droṇa was dejected;
after reflecting for a moment as if in deep thought, he spoke while being greatly afflicted.
“Duryodhana, why do you thus cut me with word-arrows,
while I am constantly speaking of Savyasācin as one who is eternally invincible in battle?
By this alone, O Kaurava, it is sufficient to know Arjuna’s nature in combat.”
When Śikhaṇḍin, protected by Kirīṭin, slew Bhīṣma—
who was unslayable by gods and men— having seen him struck down in battle, it was then that I realized this army of the Bharatas would no longer exist.

That hero whom we considered the bravest of all men in the three worlds— now that he has been slain, what remains for us to rely upon? Those very men with whom our father Śakuni used to gamble in the assembly of the Kurus...
"Those are not dice; they are sharpened arrows that scorch the enemy.
You mistake those shining, whetted shafts for dice. O dear one, these very arrows, impelled by victory, are slaying us."
Those very things which Vidura was then proclaiming that you did not understand,
and those auspicious words spoken for the sake of your welfare by the high-souled and steadfast Vidura as he lamented— you did not listen to them.
This terrible and great slaughter has now come to pass;
it is because of the contempt for those words spoken on your behalf, O Duryodhana,
by one who disregarded the beneficial advice of friends acting out of sincere concern.
The fool who acts according to his own whims will soon be an object of pity.
O kings, one should not desire sin here for the sake of the next world,
especially since you brought Kṛṣṇā into the assembly while we were looking on.
O son of Gāndhārī, you have now reaped the fruit of that unrighteousness— of having seized one born into a noble family who was undeserving of such treatment and who practiced all virtues;
otherwise, you would have suffered even greater suffering for your sin in the next world.
And when you, having defeated those Pāṇḍavas by foul means at dice,
then exiled them to the forest clad in the skins of the ruru deer;
and even though they always practiced dharma as if toward your own sons—

Who indeed in this world, other than I— a man who merely calls himself a brahmin, yet is endowed with the rites from conception (*garbhādhāna*) onwards as well as the initiation (*upanayana*), but has not performed [the required] duties— would dare to act treacherously?
He who does not study that [Veda] would be a mere Brahmin-in-name. This wrath of the Pāṇḍavas was brought forth by you, Śakuni,
with the consent of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the assembly of the Kurus.
Joined with Duḥśāsana and nurtured by Karṇa,
you have repeatedly disregarded the words of the Steward (Vidura);
for that has established the roots of the tree of our anger toward those great-souled ones.
O King of great strength, enjoy its flowers and fruits! How was he slain in your midst— relying upon the King of Sindhu— he who, having defeated all of you, had surrounded Arjuna?
"How is it, O Kauravya, that while you, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Aśvatthāman are still alive, the ruler of the Sindhus has met his death?
For all those kings attend upon your fierce splendor."

How was he slain in your midst while seeking to protect the King of Sindhu? For that lord of the earth placed his special hope for protection from Arjuna upon me alone, as well as upon you, O Duryodhana.
Therefore, since I have found no protection from Phalguna,
I see no means whatsoever for saving my own life;
I feel as if I am sinking into the sin of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
"I see that I shall not slay the Pāñcālas along with that Śikhaṇḍin; why then do you cut me down with word-arrows while I am thus distressed,
O Bhārata, having become incapable of protecting the King of the Sindhus?"
Seeing the golden banner of Bhīṣma, who was true to his word and whose deeds were untiring, fallen in battle— how can you hope for victory? For there,
in the midst of the great chariot-warriors, the ruler of the Sindhus was slain.
Bhūriśravas has been slain; what do you consider remains there?
O King, if even the invincible Kṛpa still lives—he who did not follow the path of the King of Sindhu—I honor him.
And, O Kauravya, you saw Bhīṣma slain while your younger brother Duḥśāsana was performing a most difficult feat—
he who was considered as good as unslayable in battle even by the gods led by Vāsava.
"O King, I reflect upon this: 'You possess no wealth.
O Bhārata, O noble one, these armies of the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas are now charging against me together today."
"Without slaying all the Pāñcālas, I shall not remove my armor;
I will perform this deed in battle for your benefit, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. O King, you must tell my son Aśvatthāman in the midst of the fray:"

The Somakas must not be released by you who would protect your own life; furthermore, fulfill that word with which you were instructed by your father. Be firm in compassion, self-restraint, truth, and uprightness.
"Skilled in virtue, wealth, and pleasure, yet without oppressing either virtue or wealth,
you should perform your duties with virtue as your primary concern," he said again and again.
"The Brahmins should be satisfied by both sight and mind, and they should be served according to one's ability."

"One must not do anything displeasing to them, for they are like the flames of fire. But here I am, O slayer of foes, entering the armies for a great battle, O King, having been pierced by the arrow of your words."
"And you, Duryodhana, maintain your forces if you are able;
for even at night the Kurus and Sṛñjayas will fight with fury.
Having spoken thus, Droṇa then advanced against the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas.
Stealing away the splendor of the Kṣatriyas like the sun among the stars,
the powerful destroyer of the Kṣatriyas sighed long and hot.
Sañjaya said:
Then King Duryodhana, thus urged by Droṇa,
fell under the sway of indignation and set his mind solely upon battle.
And then your son Duryodhana spoke to Karṇa.
Behold how the diadem-adorned Pāṇḍava, with Kṛṣṇa as his ally,
has broken through the array formed by the Preceptor— a formation difficult even for the gods to pierce—
despite your efforts and those of the high-souled Droṇa.
While the foremost of warriors looked on, the ruler of the Sindhus was struck down.
Behold, O son of Rādhā, the kings who are the preeminent on earth in battle,
slain by Pārtha alone like other beasts by a lion.
"O destroyer of enemies, while I was striving in battle,
my army has been reduced to a mere remnant by the son of Śakra.
For how could Phalguna [have overcome] Droṇa in combat, who was unwilling [to yield]?"

Arjuna, having fulfilled his vow by slaying the ruler of the Sindhus, has broken even that array so difficult to pierce, despite all efforts made against him in battle. Behold, O son of Rādhā, the many lords of the earth struck down upon the ground.

O hero, how could the Pāṇḍava have slain in battle those who possessed prowess equal to that of Mahendra, even though they were unwilling? For Phalguna was always dear to the high-souled teacher, Droṇa.
Then, O crusher of foes, Drona granted him passage;
having given the Sindhu king safety from battle, Drona, the scorcher of enemies, gave way to the wearer of the diadem. Behold my lack of merit!
If you had indeed granted permission for him to go home earlier,
there would not have been this destruction of men in battle against the King of Sindhu;
Jayadratha, seeking his own life, would have gone back to his home.
"Having obtained safety from Droṇa in battle, that ignoble man has been held back by me;
I shall protect the ruler of the Sindhus in combat, so Phalguna shall not reach him.
The ruler of the Sindhus, who was obstructed by the brahmin for the destruction of my army, [is now protected by me]."
Although I, unfortunate as I am, exerted myself in the battle, all my troops have been slain and King Jayadratha has been killed. Behold, O Karṇa, the best of warriors by the hundreds and thousands!

By arrows marked with the name of Pārtha, they have all been sent to the abode of Yama. How was it that, while we many looked on, the King of the Sindhus and thousands of warriors perished in battle by means of a single chariot?
"Today my brothers, Citrasena and the others, have been destroyed in battle upon encountering Bhīmasena, while we evil-minded ones looked on.
Karṇa said:
"Do not reproach the preceptor; that twice-born man is fighting to the best of his ability, according to his strength and according to his resolve, having renounced his own life.
If Śvetavāhana has entered [the city] by bypassing him..."
In this matter, there shall not be even the slightest fault on the part of the Teacher in any way whatsoever. Accomplished, skillful, young, brave, trained in weapons, and swift in prowess,
he shall mount a chariot marked with the sign of a monkey and equipped with divine weapons.
And having seized the horse, he who was clad in impenetrable armor,
the heroic one, taking up the divine and undecaying *gāṇḍīva* bow,
showered sharp arrows, proud of the strength of his arms.
When Arjuna advanced against Droṇa, it was indeed appropriate for him; for the teacher was old, O King, and thus incapable of swift movement, being unable,
O lord of men, to exert himself with his arms.
"Because the one with white horses and the dark charioteer has already bypassed him,
I see no fault in Droṇa for this reason;
I consider the Pāṇḍavas invincible in battle even by Droṇa, who is skilled in weapons."
For indeed, Śvetavāhana has entered here having bypassed him;
I do not believe that what is seen by fate can ever be otherwise anywhere. Therefore, O Suyodhana, as we fight with all our might—
The ruler of the Sindhus has been slain, O King; in this matter, destiny is considered supreme.
Even though you exerted the greatest effort alongside us on the field of battle, destiny has indeed struck down our human prowess and acted against us afterwards.

"O Great King, for those who constantly strive through both guile and valor, success is not achieved; in this matter, destiny is considered supreme. Having frustrated our efforts, destiny proceeds to accomplish its own purpose."
"Surely the destruction of people must proceed along this path; therefore, while we exert ourselves, fate acts against us from behind. Whatever action a man afflicted by fate performs anywhere,"
Whatever has been done and done by him is thwarted by fate;
yet that which ought to be done by a man who is resolute must be performed without hesitation, for success is established in fate.
O Bhārata, the sons of Pṛthā were defeated by deceit and by the administration of poison;
they were burned in the house of lac and defeated at dice. Relying on the principles of statecraft, they were even sent away to the forest.
Whatever you have accomplished with great effort has been struck down by fate;
fight, exerting yourself and making death your only point of retreat. As you strive and they strive, fate will follow its own course for both you and them.
O hero, O upholder of the Kurus, no intentional good deed is ever seen to be performed by them, nor is any evil deed of yours committed through a lack of intelligence;
for destiny is the ultimate authority over everything, whether it be well-done or otherwise.
For destiny, whose work is never other, remains awake even while men sleep;
joined with it, a man is directed toward what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. Your armies are many, and likewise your warriors are many.
The battle did not proceed in such a manner against the sons of Pāṇḍu;
by those few, you many strikers have been brought to destruction. I suspect that this is the work of destiny, by which human effort has been rendered futile.
Saṃjaya said:
O lord of men, while they were thus conversing at length on various matters,
the armies of the Pāṇḍavas came into view in the battle.
Then, O King, due to your evil counsel, a battle commenced between your men and the enemies, in which chariots and elephants became entangled with one another. Saṃjaya said:
O lord of men, that army of yours, with its surging flood of elephants and horses,
having rushed against the Pandava host, fought them on all sides;
the Panchalas and the Kurus likewise fought one another.
Initiated for the great realm of Yama and for the world beyond,
those heroes, having encountered other heroes in battle with arrows, *tomaras*,
and spears, quickly pierced one another and sent them to the abode of Yama.
A great and terrible battle, flowing with blood, broke out between chariot-warriors and chariot-warriors as they struck one another down;
and the elephants, O Great King, having encountered one another, [did the same].
Furious and intoxicated with rut, they tore [their enemies] apart with their horns.
In that tumultuous battle, horsemen seeking great glory pierced other horsemen with spears, javelins, and axes.
And foot soldiers by the hundreds, O mighty-armed one, with weapons in hand,
struck one another, O King, being ever-vigilant in their prowess;
[they proclaimed] the lineages, the names, and the families, O noble sir.
For from what we have heard, we know that the warriors of the Pañcālas and the Kurus,
roaming about in battle like those devoid of fear, dispatched one another to the other world with arrows, spears, and axes.

O King, with thousands of arrows released by them, the ten directions did not shine as before, even though the sun had already set. While the Pāṇḍava warriors were thus fighting, he remained fearless.
O great king, Duryodhana,
deeply afflicted by the slaughter of the ruler of the Sindhus,
plunged into that army; reflecting that he must die, he entered the enemy host.
Making the earth tremble, as it were, with the roar of his chariot,
your son advanced against the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
O Bhārata, that encounter between him and them was tumultuous.
It became a great cause of destruction for all the armies.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When the armies had been thus slaughtered and he himself was in such a state of distress,"
"O Sūta, I trust that Duryodhana did not turn his back in battle?
A great encounter took place between one man and many;
indeed, it appears to me especially perilous for the king."
Having been raised in extreme luxury, he was the lord of the world and worthy of protection;
having encountered many foes alone, did he not turn his back on them?
Drona, Karna, Kripa, and Kritavarman the Satvata—[did he face them all?]
"How did those who desired the kingship not protect the king in battle?
For by all possible means, the lord of the earth must be protected in battles;
this is the supreme policy in war, as seen therein by the great seers."
"When my son had indeed entered the great army of the enemies," Sañjaya said,
"what did my best chariot-warriors do, O Sañjaya?"
O King, descendant of Bharata, hear from me as I describe the wonderful and marvelous battle of your son— how he, though alone, fought against many,
while being held back by Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa.
He entered the Pāṇḍava army like a makara entering the ocean,
scattering thousands of arrows here and there at that time,
and pierced both the Pañcālas and the Pāṇḍavas with sharpened shafts.
Just as the sun, having risen, destroys the darkness with its rays, so shall your son of great strength destroy that army. [He is like] the sun at midday, scorching with its beams.
Likewise, O Bhārata, the Pāṇḍavas were unable even to look at your son as he scorched them in the midst of battle with waves of arrows;
they were intent on flight and lacked the will to conquer their enemy.
The Pāñcālas fled in all directions as they were being slaughtered by your high-souled son, the archer, with his gold-feathered arrows of bright points;
being tormented by those shafts, the Pāṇḍu soldiers quickly fell down.
And seeing him in that supreme battle, with his mouth wide open like the life-taking Antaka arrived, the warriors fled out of fear;
for your men had never before performed such a deed in combat.
O lord of the people, just as your son, the king, acted,
so was that Pāṇḍava army crushed in battle by your son,
like a lotus pond with full-blown lotuses trampled on all sides by a mighty elephant.

The army of the Pāṇḍavas became like a lotus pond whose luster has been destroyed by the wind and the sun when its water has run dry, through the fiery energy of your son. O Bhārata, seeing the Pāṇḍu army thus slaughtered by your son, [the warriors were overcome].
Led by Bhīmasena, the Pāñcālas rushed forward;
he [Kṛtavarman] struck Bhīmasena with ten arrows, each of the two sons of Mādrī with three,
Virāṭa and Drupada with six, and Śikhaṇḍin with a hundred.
He pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna with seventy arrows and the son of Dharma with seven; he struck the Kekayas and the Cedis with many sharpened shafts,
and having pierced the Sātvata with five, he struck each of the sons of Draupadī with three.

Having pierced Ghaṭotkaca in battle, he roared like a lion; then, enraged like the Destroyer at the end of an eon, he mangled hundreds of other warriors, along with their elephants, horses, and chariots,
in that fray with his fierce arrows.
O lord of men, that Pāṇḍava army, being slaughtered in battle by your son with his stone-tipped arrows, fled from him,
the Kuru king, who was like the scorching sun in that great conflict.
O King, the soldiers of the son of Pāṇḍu were unable even to look at him.
Then, O best of kings, King Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with wrath,
rushed toward the lord of the Kurus, your son, desiring victory.
Then those two Kuru princes, subduers of their enemies, Duryodhana and Yudhiṣṭhira, both exerting their prowess for the sake of their own interests, encountered each other in battle.
Thereupon, the enraged Duryodhana [struck him] with straight-jointed arrows.
He quickly pierced him with ten arrows and cut down his standard with one shaft;
O King, he then struck Indrasena on the forehead with three arrows—
the beloved charioteer of the high-souled Pāṇḍava king.
Furthermore, that great car-warrior cut off his bow with another arrow;
then, with four arrows, he pierced his four horses.
Thereupon Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with rage, [seized] his bow as if in the blink of an eye.

Seizing another [bow] with speed, he warded off the Kaurava. As he was slaying those enemies, O noble one, the eldest Pāṇḍava cut that great gold-backed bow into three pieces with two broad-headed arrows.
And he pierced him with ten well-aimed, sharp arrows;
having pierced his vital organs, they all shattered and entered the earth.
Then the delighted warriors surrounded Yudhiṣṭhira.
Just as the gods surrounded Purandara for the slaying of Vṛtra,
and as the gods [surrounded] Śatakratu while he was fighting with Vṛtra,
so then, O noble one, did King Yudhiṣṭhira [surround] your son.
In that battle, he discharged an arrow that was exceedingly difficult to ward off;
Yudhiṣṭhira, having cried out to the king, "Alas, you are slain!", released that most fierce and irresistible arrow, which shone like the rays of the sun.
Pierced by that arrow released up to his ear, the Kaurava was deeply struck;
with his consciousness utterly clouded, he sank down upon the seat of his excellent chariot.
Then, O Indra among kings, a great roar arose from the Pāñcāla troops on all sides as they rejoiced, crying out, "The king is slain! And there,
O noble one, the fierce sound of the whizzing arrows was heard.
Then Droṇa suddenly appeared there in the battle,
and Duryodhana, filled with joy and firmly grasping his bow,
rushed toward the Pāṇḍava king, crying out, "Stay! Stay!"
As that heroic great car-warrior, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, was speaking thus,
the Pāñcālas, eager for the king, swiftly advanced against him;
Droṇa, however, received them, desiring to protect the best of the Kurus.
Like the sun dispelling clouds driven by fierce winds,
O King, there then arose a great battle that increased the carnage,
between your men and the enemy who had assembled with a desire to fight.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the self-controlled teacher, having spoken properly to my son Duryodhana who transgresses his instructions, then entered among the Pāṇḍavas in anger—
Having entered and moving about in battle, that hero stood firm; how did the Pāṇḍavas surround Droṇa, the great archer? Who protected the right wheel of the high-souled preceptor?
And who protected him from behind as he was slaying his enemies in battle?
Which heroic warriors followed at the back of that hero? And which chariot-warriors stood before him as his adversaries?
I think that an excessive, unseasonable cold must have touched them; I think they trembled like cattle in the winter,
when those invincible great archers entered the Pañcālas.

Dancing along the paths of his chariot, that best among all wielders of weapons— the bull among car-warriors of the Pāñcālas— burning away all the armies like an enraged comet, how did he meet his death?
Saṃjaya said:
In the evening, having slain the ruler of the Sindhus and having met with the king, Pārtha and the great archer Sātyaki both rushed toward Droṇa.
Likewise, Yudhiṣṭhira and the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena quickly,
each with their own separate army, rushed toward Droṇa alone. In the same way, the wise Nakula and the invincible Sahadeva [did the same].
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śatānīka, Virāṭa along with the Kekayas,
the Matsyas, and the armies of the Śālveyas, advanced against Droṇa himself in battle;
and likewise King Drupada, protected by the Pāñcālas.
O King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s father advanced against Droṇa himself;
the sons of Draupadī, those great archers, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, along with their armies,
advanced against the highly effulgent Droṇa alone.
Six thousand Prabhadrakas and Pāñcāla strikers advanced against Droṇa alone, placing Śikhaṇḍin at their head;
likewise did the other tigers among men, the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas.
United, they turned back toward Droṇa alone, that bull among the twice-born.
When those heroes had advanced for battle, O bull of the Bharatas,
a terrible night fell, increasing the fear of the timid.
O King, that night was inauspicious and fierce for the warriors, leading them toward their end;
it brought about the destruction of the lives of elephants, horses, and men. During that terrible night, jackals howled on all sides.
With mouths full of flaming morsels, they announced a terrible danger;
and owls were also seen, foreboding immense peril—
especially a most dreadful one for the army of the Kauravas.
Then, O king of kings, a great clamor arose among the armies,
produced by the loud sound of kettledrums and the resonance of clay drums,
as well as by the trumpeting of elephants and the neighing of horses.
And from the falling sounds of hooves, a tumult arose on all sides;
then, O great king, there occurred a most terrible battle between Droṇa and the Sṛñjayas from every direction during the twilight.
When the world was shrouded in darkness, nothing at all could be discerned,
due to the dust raised on all sides by the army;
the blood of men, horses, and elephants mingled together.
Enveloped by a state of distress, we could not see even the dust of the earth;
it was like a bamboo forest burning on a mountain at night,
amidst the resounding blasts of mṛdaṅgas, ānakas, jharjharas, and paṭahas.
With the sounds of *phetkāras*, neighing, and various noises, everything appeared utterly chaotic;
there was a terrible *caṭacaṭā* sound from falling weapons.
O King, shrouded in darkness, neither one's own side nor the enemy could be distinguished.
At the onset of night, O king of kings, all that became like a scene of madness; the dust of the earth was then laid to rest by the blood,
and darkness descended upon the golden armor and ornaments.
Then that Bharata army, adorned with jewels and gold,
appeared like the sky filled with stars during the night, O bull of the Bharatas;
it resounded with the cries of jackals and crows, and was crowded with spears and banners.
Resounding with dreadful cries and filled with the sounds of shrieks and shouts,
a great, tumultuous, and hair-raising noise then arose,
pervading all directions like the roar of Mahendra’s thunderbolt.
At midnight, O great king, that Bharata army was seen,
illuminated by armlets, earrings, golden neck-ornaments, and weapons.
There, elephants and chariots were adorned with gold.
At night, they appeared like clouds accompanied by lightning;
spears, javelins, maces, arrows, clubs, darts,
and battle-axes were seen falling down, shining like blazing fires.
With Duryodhana as its precursor wind, chariots and elephants as its clouds,
the sound of musical instruments as its thunder, and bows as its lightning amidst its banners;
with Droṇa and the Pāṇḍavas as its rain-clouds, and swords, spears, and maces as its thunderbolts— [the battle-cloud].

Desiring to fight, they entered that most terrifying army— an army with arrows for its torrential rain, with the wind of its missiles, intensely crowded with heat and cold, dreadful, astonishing, fierce, life-destroying, and without a raft to cross.
At that terrible onset of night, resounding with a great clamor—
inspiring terror in the timid and increasing the joy of the brave—
that most dreadful and fierce nocturnal battle was then proceeding.
The Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas, united and enraged, rushed against Droṇa.
O King, whosoever among them advanced against that great-souled one, he turned them all back; some he sent to the abode of Yama.
Those thousands of elephants and tens of thousands of chariots, along with millions and hundreds of millions of foot soldiers and horses,
were all pierced by Droṇa alone with his iron arrows at the onset of night.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When that invincible one of immeasurable prowess had entered among the Sṛñjayas—
unable to endure it and filled with fury— what indeed was your resolve at that time?
Having thus spoken to my son Duryodhana, who transgresses the scriptures,
what did Pārtha do next— that immeasurable soul—
after the heroic Saindhava and Bhūriśravas had been slain?
When that invincible one of great splendor had entered among the Pāñcālas,
what did that unassailable scorcher of enemies think? And what did Duryodhana consider to be the duty appropriate for the occasion?
And who followed that hero, the bestower of boons and foremost of the twice-born?
Which heroes marched behind that valiant one as he fought?
And who fought in front of him as he struck down his enemies in battle?
"O Lord, I think all the Pāṇḍavas, afflicted by the arrows of Bhāradvāja,
must be trembling like emaciated cows in the winter.
Having entered among the Pañcālas, that great archer, the crusher of enemies— "
How indeed did that tiger among men meet his death,
when all the armies had gathered together at night and the great car-warriors were assembled?
When various things were being thrown into confusion,
who among them at that time remained wise? You speak of those who were slain, those who were entangled, and those who were utterly defeated.
When my chariot-warriors were deprived of their chariots in the battles,
and while they were being overwhelmed by the Pāṇḍavas with their spirits broken,
what light was there for them in that blinding darkness, and what was their state of mind then?
You always speak of the Pāṇḍavas as being joyful and exultant,
while my own men are joyless, dejected, and terrified. How was it then that those sons of Pṛthā did not flee from there?
"How did it become light at night among the Kurus, O Sañjaya?
Sañjaya said:
"O King, while that most terrible night-battle was then taking place..."
At night, the Pāṇḍavas, together with their soldiers, rushed against Droṇa.
Then Droṇa, with his swift-flying arrows, dispatched all the Kekayas and the sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna to the realm of death.
O King, O Bhārata, those great car-warriors who stood before him, he dispatched them all to the other world while that heroic great car-warrior,
the son of Bharadvāja, was then crushing them.
O King, the powerful Śibi, filled with rage, turned back against him. Beholding that great car-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas rushing toward him,
Droṇa pierced him with ten arrows made entirely of iron.
Śibi pierced him in return with thirty sharpened arrows,
and smiling, he struck down his charioteer with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla).
Droṇa, having slain the horses and the charioteer of that high-souled one...
Then he struck off his head, along with its helmet, from his body.
Thereupon, Duryodhana quickly commanded another charioteer for him;
with the horses taken up by him, he once more charged at the enemies.

And the son of the Kaliṅga king, enraged by the previous slaughter of his father, rushed toward Bhīmasena in battle with the army of the Kaliṅgas. Having pierced Bhīma with five arrows, he struck him again with seven.

With three feathered shafts he struck Viśoka, and with one he struck the standard. Then the enraged Vṛkodara, himself filled with rage, rushed from his chariot to that heroic warrior of the Kaliṅgas and struck him with his fist.
When he was struck by the fist of the powerful Pāṇḍava in battle,
all his bones suddenly fell apart one by one. When he had been slain in that manner by him, a great lion-roar arose.
"Excellent! Excellent!"—thus did the Pāñcālas cry out to the Pāṇḍava, O Great King.
But Karṇa and his brothers, those great chariot-warriors, could not tolerate this;
they struck Bhīmasena with iron arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then Bhīma, abandoning the chariot of Śatru, went to the chariot of Dhruva; he crushed Dhruva, who was incessantly discharging arrows, with his fist,
and Bhīma returned to his own chariot.
Rising up again with speed, he struck down his younger brother as if effortlessly tossing a glass gem with a single fist;
struck suddenly, he was crushed to powder and turned into nothing but blood.
Likewise, there was Cūrṇa, and likewise Drumas, the brother of Karṇa;
he too, having been slain by the mighty son of Pāṇḍu, fell down. Having struck him down, O great king, the exceedingly powerful Bhīmasena—
Having reached Jayarāta’s chariot, he roared repeatedly like a lion. Then, having seized Jayarāta with his left hand while roaring, the mighty-armed one likewise grasped his charioteer, O King.
With his palm, he destroyed him who stood right before Karṇa.
Seizing those two heroes by their feet while Karṇa looked on, Bhīma whirled them around on the ground and slew them; they were deprived of life.
Karna, however, hurled a golden spear at the son of Pandu; then the joy of Pandu, laughing, seized that very spear and,
being difficult to overcome, hurled it back at Karna in the battle.
The bird Śakuni cut it down in mid-air with his oil-drinking arrow. Having performed this great feat in battle, he of wondrous prowess mounted his own chariot once more and rushed against your army.
O lord of the people, as that mighty-armed one approached— terrible and like the enraged God of Death intent on slaughter— your sons restrained him.
Then, O King, your sons rushed toward Bhīma’s chariot.
Covering Vṛkodara with a great shower of arrows,
Bhīma then, as if laughing in the midst of battle,
dispatched both the charioteer and the horses of Durmada to the abode of Yama with his shafts.
Then Durmada leaped onto the chariot of Duṣkarṇa;
those two brothers, the scorchers of their enemies, mounted upon a single chariot,
charged at Bhīma from the midst of the front of the battle.
Just as the two sons of the Lord of Waters [the Aśvins] struck Tāraka, the best of the Daityas,
so then your two sons, Durmada and Duṣkarṇa,
mounting a single chariot, pierced Bhīma with their arrows.
Then, while Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, Duryodhana,
Kṛpa, Somadatta, and Bāhlīka looked on, as well as the heroic Durmada and Duṣkarṇa, the Pāṇḍava [struck] that chariot.
The mighty-armed subduer of foes ascended while all the archers looked on;
with a kick of his foot, he caused the enemy to sink into the earth.
Then your two powerful and heroic sons, Duṣkarṇa and Durmada—
Striking him with his fist, the enraged Bhīma crushed him with his foot.
Then, as the army raised a cry of "Alas!", the kings, seeing Bhīma, said:
"This is Rudra in a terrible form, seeking to devour the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, all the kings fled; deprived of their senses, they urged on their mounts, and no two of them fled together. Then, at the onset of night, the army was utterly shattered.
Greatly honored by the bulls among kings, the mighty Vṛkodara, possessed of great strength and eyes like blossoming lotuses,
paid homage to King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then the twins, Drupada, Virāṭa, and the Kekayas,
as well as Yudhiṣṭhira, attained supreme joy;
and they honored Vṛkodara most highly.
Just as the gods [approached] Hara after Andhaka had been struck down,
so then your sons— resembling the son of Varuṇa and filled with wrath— together with their high-souled preceptor, [advanced].
Desiring to fight, they surrounded Vṛkodara from all sides with chariots, infantry, and elephants;
then the twins, the sons of Drupada, along with their troops, [did the same].
Yudhiṣṭhira, Drupada, Virāṭa, and the Sātvatas, along with Ghaṭotkaca, Jaya, Vijaya, Drumasena, Vṛka,
and the Saṃjayas, held back your sons.
Then, at the onset of night— a time of great terror, exceedingly dreadful, and terrifying as if shrouded by thick masses of darkness— it became a feast for many wolves, dogs, and vultures.
The wonderful battle between those great-souled ones, O best of kings.
Sañjaya said:
After his son had sat down in a fast unto death and was slain by Sātyaki, then—
Somadatta, becoming violently enraged, spoke these words to Sātyaki:
"O Sātvata, having utterly abandoned that duty of the Kṣatriyas which was observed of old by the high-souled gods, how is it that you are now devoted to the way of the robbers?"
How could a wise man devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya strike in battle one who has turned his back, one who is dejected, one who has laid down his weapons, or one who begs for mercy? Indeed,
it is said that among the Vṛṣṇis, there were only two renowned great chariot-warriors (mahārathas) in that regard.
O mighty-armed Pradyumna, and you yourself, O Sātvata,
how could you commit such a cruel and despicable act against one who was seated in the vow of fasting unto death and whose arm had been severed by Pārtha?
"Reap now, in this encounter, the fruit of that evil deed! Today, O fool, I shall strike down your head with a feathered shaft through my prowess.
I swear it by my two sons of the Sātvatas, and by my cherished merit."

O disgrace to the Vṛṣṇis, if I had not slain you— who pride yourself on being a hero— along with your sons and younger brothers, while you remained unprotected by Pārtha Jiṣṇu during this past night, I would have fallen into a terrible hell.
Having spoken thus, the exceedingly enraged and mighty Somadatta blew his conch shell with a piercing sound and let out a lion’s roar.
Then [the son of Somadatta], whose eyes were like lotus petals, whose teeth were like those of a lion, and who was possessed of great strength—
Then the Sātvata, violently incensed, spoke to Somadatta:
"O Kauraveya, no fear whatsoever exists in me, even as I fight with you and the others; there is not the slightest anxiety in my heart."
"O Kaurava, even if you fight me while protected by your entire army, still there shall be no distress for me on your account, O descendant of Kuru,
because of your words which are the very essence of battle and yet despised by the virtuous."
Established as you are in the duty of a kṣatriya, you cannot frighten me;
O lord of men, if you have a desire to fight with me today,
strike mercilessly with sharpened arrows, and I shall strike back at you.
The heroic Bhūriśravas, your son and a great chariot-warrior, has been slain;
and likewise, O King, Śala has fallen, emaciated by the calamity that befell his brother.
Today, I shall also slay you, along with your sons, cattle, and kinsmen.

Stand now alert in battle, for you are especially a Kuru. In King Yudhiṣṭhira, all these qualities— generosity, self-control, purity, non-violence, modesty, fortitude, and forbearance— are eternally and inseparably present.
"O you who have the drum as your banner, you were already struck down by his splendor in the past;
together with Karṇa and the son of Subala, you shall meet your destruction in battle.
I swear this by the feet of Kṛṣṇa and by my own meritorious deeds."
"If I, provoked to anger in battle, do not slay you, O wicked one, along with your son—
if you flee, abandoning [the fight]— then you shall be released.
Having thus addressed one another, their eyes were bloodshot with rage.
Then, as those two best of men were about to engage in a shower of arrows,
Duryodhana, having surrounded Somadatta with a thousand elephants and ten thousand chariots, took his stand.
And Śakuni, the best among all wielders of weapons, highly incensed,
surrounded by his sons, grandsons, and brothers who possess the prowess of Indra—
your mighty-armed young nephew, whose frame is as firm as a thunderbolt— [advanced].
More than a hundred thousand horses protected that wise one on all sides as he guarded the great archer Somadatta;
and being himself protected by those powerful warriors, he covered Satyaki with his shafts.
Seeing him being covered by those straight-jointed arrows,
the mighty-armed Dhṛṣṭadyumna, of true prowess, being a Sātvata, advanced in anger leading a great army to protect him.
O King, the roar of the masses of troops as they struck one another was like the sound of oceans tossed by fierce winds. Then Somadatta pierced the Sātvata with nine arrows.
Sātyaki struck that bull among the Kurus with ten arrows.
Deeply pierced in battle by that powerful man of firm bow,
he sank down onto the floor of his chariot and lost consciousness.
Observing him thus deprived of his senses, the charioteer, filled with haste,
carried away the hero, the great car-warrior Somadatta, from the battlefield;
seeing him unconscious and afflicted by the arrows of Yuyudhāna.
Then Droṇa rushed forward with the intent to slay the Yadu hero. Beholding him approaching, those led by Yudhiṣṭhira surrounded the high-souled one, desiring to protect the leader of the Yadus.
Then the battle commenced between Droṇa and the Pāṇḍavas,
like that of Bali against the gods in ancient times out of a desire to conquer the three worlds.
Then, with a net of arrows, he covered the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
The highly energetic Bhāradvāja pierced Yudhiṣṭhira,
struck Sātyaki with ten arrows, the son of Pṛṣata with twenty shafts,
Bhīmasena with nine, and likewise Nakula with five.
The mighty-armed one [Droṇa] struck Sahadeva with eight arrows, Śikhaṇḍin with a hundred, the sons of Draupadī each with five arrows,
Virāṭa the Matsya with eight, and Drupada with ten arrows.
Having pierced Yudhāmanyu with three arrows, Uttamaujas with six in the combat,
and having struck other soldiers as well, he rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
Being slaughtered by Droṇa, those soldiers of the son of Pāṇḍu...
O King, they fled in fear toward the ten directions, crying out piteously; seeing that army being driven back by Droṇa, Phalguna,
the son of Pṛthā, feeling a slight surge of agitation, quickly advanced against his preceptor.
O King, seeing Bībhatsu charging toward him in battle, Droṇa turned back that army of Yudhiṣṭhira; then once more,
a battle took place between the son of Bharadvāja and the Pāṇḍavas.
O King, Drona, surrounded on all sides by your sons,
scattered the Pandava armies like fire consuming a heap of cotton.
He was like the blazing sun, possessing a splendor equal to a flaming fire.
O King, having seen Droṇa incessantly and excessively— his bow drawn into a circle like the scorching sun, with arrows for rays—
heating the enemy and burning through the army, no one could restrain him.
Whichever man stood before Droṇa, his arrow cut off that very man's head and sent it to the earth. Thus was that Pāṇḍava army being slaughtered by the high-souled one.
Seeing his army utterly broken by Droṇa in the night, O Bhārata, Jīṣṇu fled again in fear while Savyasācin looked on;
he then spoke to Govinda: "Proceed toward Droṇa’s chariot."
Then the descendant of Daśārha urged on the horses, which possessed a luster like silver, cow’s milk, the kunda flower, and the moon, toward Droṇa’s chariot;
and Bhīmasena, seeing Phalguna proceeding toward Droṇa, [did likewise].
He said this to his own charioteer: "Carry me toward Droṇa’s army.
Having heard his words, O best of the Bharatas, Viśoka drove the horses behind Jiṣṇu, who was true to his promise.
Seeing those two brothers exerting themselves and rushing toward Drona’s army, O great king,
the Pañcālas, Sṛñjayas, Matsyas, Cedis, Kārūṣas, Kośalas,
and the great car-warriors of the Kekayas followed after them.
Then, O King, there occurred a terrible battle that made the hair stand on end.
Bībhatsu took your army’s right flank and Vṛkodara the northern;
with those two great multitudes of chariots, they seized your forces.
O King, seeing those two tigers among men, Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the mighty Sātyaki rushed forward;
their roar was like that of oceans lashed by fierce winds.
O King, as the floods of troops were then striking one another,
the son of Droṇa, enraged upon seeing Sātyaki in battle after the slaughter of the son of Somadatta,
rushed in fury toward the Sātvata at the head of the fray.
Beholding that chariot of Śaineya rushing toward him,
the son of Bhīmasena, filled with great rage, checked his adversary with a massive,
terrible iron shield covered with bear-skin.
Mounting a great chariot that was thirty *nālikās* in length,
equipped with deployed mechanical defenses, and sounding like a mass of great clouds,
he yoked it with steeds resembling elephants— neither horses nor indeed elephants.

It was adorned with a fluttering eight-spoked wheel and a crowing banner with its beak raised high, appearing like a king of vultures; it bore blood-drenched flags and was decorated with garlands of entrails.
Mounted upon a vast chariot equipped with eight wheels,
he was surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī of Rākṣasas of terrible form, who carried pikes and mallets and held rocks and trees in their hands.
Seeing him with his great bow raised— resembling Death himself with staff in hand at the time of the world's end— the kings were struck with distress.
Then they beheld him, who resembled a mountain peak, of terrifying form, and inspiring fear.
With a mouth fierce with fangs, spike-like ears, and a large jaw;
with hair standing erect, deformed eyes, a blazing face, and a sunken belly;
with a throat like a great cloud and hair covered by a crown.

Seeing Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Rākṣasas, with his great bow raised— terrifying to all beings like Death with its gaping maw, blazing as he approached, and causing agitation among his enemies— [the monkeys were struck with fear].
Afflicted by fear, your son’s army was thrown into great agitation,
like the Ganges with its upward-tossing waves when stirred by a whirlwind;
terrified by the lion-roar uttered by Ghaṭotkaca.
The elephants discharged urine and the men were greatly distressed; then, a rain of stones fell there from all sides upon the earth,
released by the Rākṣasas who had gained even greater strength during the time of twilight.
Iron wheels, *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles, spears, *tomaras*, spikes,
*śataghnīs*, and *paṭṭiśas* fell incessantly.
Seeing that fierce and most terrible battle, the lords of men—
Your sons and Karṇa, being distressed, fled in all directions; there, only the proud son of Droṇa, who boasted of his skill in weapons, did not waver,
and he destroyed with his arrows the illusion created by Ghaṭotkaca.
When Māyā had been slain,
the indignant Ghaṭotkaca discharged terrible arrows; those arrows entered Aśvatthāman like serpents, frantic with rage, entering an anthill with great speed.
Those arrows, smeared with blood, having pierced the son of Śaradvat,
entered the earth swiftly— gold-feathered and sharpened on stone.
But Aśvatthāman, enraged, light-handed, and full of prowess, [pierced him in return].
He pierced the enraged Ghaṭotkaca with ten arrows.
Then the furious Ghaṭotkaca swiftly hurled a discus.
Ghaṭotkaca, however, was deeply pierced in his vital organs by the son of Droṇa.
Greatly distressed, Bhaimaseni seized a wheel with a hundred thousand spokes,
its edge sharp as a razor, radiant like the rising sun, and adorned with jewels and diamonds;
he hurled it at Ashvatthaman with the intent to kill him.
Moving with great speed, it was struck and scattered by the arrows of Droṇa’s son;
like the resolve of an unfortunate man, it fell fruitlessly to the earth.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, seeing the discus quickly brought down, [acted].
He covered the son of Droṇa with arrows, just as Rāhu obscures the sun;
then the illustrious son of Ghaṭotkaca, resembling a mass of crushed collyrium,
checked the advancing son of Droṇa as a king of mountains resists a hurricane.
Afflicted by the arrows of Bhīmasena’s grandson, Añjanaparvan,
he shone like Mount Meru struck by torrents of rain from a cloud.
But Aśvatthāman remained unperturbed, possessing the prowess of Rudra, Upendra, and Indra.
With one arrow he cut down the banner of Añjanaparvan;
with two he struck the charioteer, and with three the triple-bamboo pole of his chariot.
With one arrow he severed his bow, and with four he slew the four horses.

From the hand of the carless warrior, he [Bhīma] severed with a very sharp arrow the sword that was raised, which was studded with golden spots. O King, the mace of the son of Hiḍimba’s son, adorned with golden armlets, was quickly [seized] by [Bhīma].
Whirled about and struck by the arrows of Droṇa’s son, that [club] too fell down.
Then, leaping into the sky and roaring like a dark cloud at the end of time,
Añjanaparvan rained down a shower of trees from the firmament.
Then the son of Droṇa pierced Māyādhara, the son of Ghaṭotkaca, in the sky with arrows, just as the sun pierces a cloud with its rays. Descending once more, he stood upon his gold-adorned chariot.
Like the exceedingly lofty and majestic Mount Añjana, a bearer of the earth,
the son of Droṇa struck that son of Bhīma’s son, who was clad in iron armor,
just as Maheśvara struck Andhaka with Mount Añjana.
Then, seeing his mighty son slain by Aśvatthāman,
he approached the son of Droṇa with his armlets trembling in rage;
undaunted, he addressed these words to the hero, the son of Śaradvat’s daughter.
Scorching the Pāṇḍava army like a fierce fire consuming a forest, [Dhṛṣṭadyumna said:
"Stay! Stay! O son of Droṇa, you shall not escape from me alive.
Today I shall slay you, just as the son of Agni slew the Krauñca bird."
Aśvatthāman said:
"Go, child, and fight with the others, O you of godlike prowess!
For it is not right, O son of Hiḍimbā, that a father should be oppressed by his own son."
"Indeed, O son of Hiḍimbā, I have no anger toward you;
however, a person possessed by rage might even kill himself.
Saṃjaya said:
Hearing this, the son of Bhīṣmaka, his eyes copper-red with rage and overwhelmed by grief for his son, addressed the distressed Aśvatthāman:
"O son of Droṇa, am I a coward like an ordinary man in battle?"
That you try to frighten me with these words is an untrue speech;
for I was indeed born from Bhīma into the great Kuru lineage,
the son of the Pāṇḍavas who never retreat in battles.
"I am the sovereign lord of the Rākṣasas, equal to the Ten-necked one in strength. Stay! Stay! O son of Droṇa, you shall not escape from me alive.
Today, on the field of battle, I shall destroy your desire for war."
Having spoken thus, the exceedingly powerful Rākṣasa, his eyes copper-red with rage,
rushed furiously at the son of Droṇa like a lion toward a lordly elephant;
Ghaṭotkaca then showered him with arrows as thick as chariot axles.
Like a rain-cloud with its torrents, [Arjuna] showered a rain of arrows upon the son of Droṇa, the bull among chariot-warriors;
but the son of Droṇa shattered that rain of arrows with his own shafts before it could reach him.
Then, in the sky, there occurred as if another battle of arrows.
Then, with sparks produced by the clashing of weapons,
the sky at the onset of night shone as if variegated by fireflies.
Having observed that the illusion had been destroyed by the son of Droṇa, who was proud in battle—
Then Ghaṭotkaca, having become invisible once more, created an illusion:
he became a massive mountain, exceedingly high with peaks thick with trees, from which spears, lances, swords, and clubs flowed like torrents of water.
Seeing that mountain, which resembled a mass of collyrium,
as it was being struck by many falling volleys of weapons, the son of Droṇa was not shaken. Then, as if smiling, the son of Droṇa invoked the Vajra weapon.
By that weapon, the lord of mountains was hurled and quickly perished.
Then, becoming a dark cloud in the sky adorned with Indra’s bow,
he, most fierce, covered the son of Droṇa in battle with showers of stones.
Then, aiming the Vāyavya weapon, that best of those skilled in weapons,
the son of Droṇa, dispersed the rising dark cloud. Covering all directions with his multitudes of arrows, the son of Droṇa [prevailed].
The best of bipeds slew a hundred thousand chariots;
then, seeing Ghaṭotkaca returning on his chariot with his bow drawn,
surrounded by many Rākṣasas yet remaining unperturbed, [he attacked].

Together with the followers of Hiḍimba’s son, who resembled lions and tigers, possessed the prowess of elephants in rut, and were mounted upon elephants, chariots, and even the backs of horses— with their mouths, heads, and necks wide open— [the army advanced].
[He was surrounded] by the descendants of Pulastya and the Yātudhānas, who were of dark nature and possessed fierce prowess;
they were heroes bearing various weapons, adorned with diverse armor, endowed with great strength, making terrifying sounds, and having eyes rolling in their agitation.
Then, seeing your son despondent as he was surrounded in battle by Rākṣasas who were frantic for combat, the son of Droṇa said to him:
"Stay, Duryodhana! You must not give way to agitation today."
Together with these heroic brothers and these kings who possess the prowess of Indra, I shall slay your enemies; you shall have no defeat. I promise this truly to you; comfort your army.
Duryodhana said:
"I do not consider this surprising— that you possess such a great mind,
O son of Gautama's daughter, and that you have such supreme devotion toward us."
Saṃjaya said:
Having thus addressed Aśvatthāman, he then spoke to the son of Subala,
who was surrounded by a hundred thousand chariots that graced the battlefield.
"Go forth against Dhanañjaya with sixty thousand elephants!
Karna, Vṛṣasena, Kṛpa, and likewise Nīla,
as well as the northerners, Kṛtavarman, Purumitra, and Śrutārpaṇa [should follow]."
Duḥśāsana, Nikumbha, Kuṇḍabhedin, Urukrama, Purañjaya, Dṛḍharatha, Patākī, Hemapaṅkaja,
Śalya, Aruṇa, Indrasena, Saṃjaya, Vijaya, and Jaya.
Kamalākṣa, Puru, Krāthī, Jayavarmā, and Sudarśana—
these six tens of thousands of foot soldiers shall follow you.
O maternal uncle, slay Bhīma, both the twins, and Dharmarāja as well.
"O uncle, my hope for victory rests in you, just as the lord of the gods' hope rested in the Asuras.
Slay the sons of Kuntī, who have been torn apart by the arrows of Droṇa’s son and whose bodies are severely wounded, just as the son of Agni slew the Asuras."
Thus addressed by your son, O King, the son of Subala departed swiftly,
desiring to please your sons and wishing to consume the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, in that battle, a combat commenced between the son of Droṇa and the Rākṣasa.
At night, like the tumultuous battle between Śakra and Prahrāda,
Ghaṭotkaca, filled with rage, struck the son of Gautamī in the chest with ten firm arrows resembling poison and fire.
Struck deeply by those arrows discharged by the son of Bhīma,
he trembled while standing in the midst of his chariot like a tree shaken by the wind.
Furthermore, with an añjalika shaft, he [struck] his [opponent's] great radiance.
Ghaṭotkaca swiftly cut the bow held in the hand of Droṇa’s son.
Thereupon, Droṇa’s son took up another great bow capable of bearing a heavy strain and rained down sharp arrows like a cloud pouring down torrents of water.
Then, O Bhārata, Śāradvatīputra dispatched gold-feathered, foe-slaying arrows toward those sky-rangers. Afflicted by those shafts, that host of broad-chested Rākṣasas—
Like lions [attacking] a frantic herd of elephants,
the Lord, having scattered the hosts of Rākṣasas along with their horses, charioteers, and chariots by means of his arrows,
consumed them like the divine Fire at the end of an eon.
Having consumed an akṣauhiṇī with his arrows, he shone intensely upon the Nairṛtas, just as the divine Maheśvara shone in heaven after burning Tripura in former times,
or like the fierce Vasu after burning all beings at the end of a yuga.
The son of Droṇa, the best among victors, shone as he overcame your enemies.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, enraged, urged on that great army of Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds, saying, "Slay the son of Droṇa!"
Then, having received that command from Ghaṭotkaca, the Rākṣasas—
whose mouths were wide with blazing fangs, who were terrible in form and fearsome,
with gaping maws, long tongues, and eyes intensely red with rage— [set forth].
Making the earth resound with a great lion’s roar,
they rushed toward the son of Droṇa to slay him, armed with various weapons and missiles—
spears, *śataghnīs*, iron clubs, thunderbolts, pikes, and axes.
Swords, maces, javelins, clubs, battle-axes,
spears, lances, *kaṇapas*, sharp *kampanas*,
*hulas*, *bhuśuṇḍis*, stone balls, and iron pillars likewise.

Then, with eyes copper-red with rage, Rākṣasas of terrible prowess hurled hundreds and thousands of most fearsome mallets, capable of rending enemies in battle, at the head of the son of Droṇa. They became entangled upon his head.
Then, beholding that immense shower of weapons falling upon the head of Droṇa’s son, those warriors were struck with terror;
yet Droṇa’s son remained unperturbed by that formidable downpour that had arisen.
He destroyed them with arrows whetted on stone that were like thunderbolts;
then, with other gold-feathered shafts consecrated by divine mantras, the high-minded son of Droṇa swiftly struck down the Rākṣasas.

Afflicted by those arrows, that host of broad-chested Rākṣasas appeared like a frantic herd of elephants thrown into confusion by lions. Those Rākṣasas, violently enraged, were struck by the son of Droṇa.
Enraged and desiring to slay the son of Droṇa, those mighty warriors rushed forward.
There, O Bhārata, the son of Droṇa displayed this wonderful prowess, which is impossible for any other among all living beings to perform.
In the very instant that the son of Droṇa, an expert in great weapons, consumed the army of Rākṣasīs with blazing arrows while the lord of the Rākṣasas looked on,
the son of Droṇa shone resplendent in battle as he scorched the host of demons.
Like the fire of universal destruction at the end of a Yuga,
he consumed the armies with arrows resembling venomous serpents—
amidst those thousands of kings on the side of the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata.
No one was able to even look at the son of Droṇa in battle,
except for the heroic Ghaṭotkaca, the immensely powerful lord of the Rākṣasas.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, his eyes became red with rage.
Striking palm against palm and biting his lip,
he spoke in anger to his charioteer, "Carry me toward the son of Droṇa.
He then proceeded with that chariot of terrible form, adorned with a victorious banner.
Once again, that slayer of enemies engaged in a single combat with the son of Droṇa.
Uttering a great roar like a lion, he of terrible prowess,
the Rākṣasa, then became enraged and hurled [his weapon] at the son of Droṇa.
Having set aside his bow upon the chariot, the son of Droṇa leaped up and seized that most terrible thunderbolt fashioned by Rudra, which possessed eight wheels;
he hurled it at him and then leaped down from his own chariot.
Having reduced the chariot, along with its horses, driver, and standard, to ashes, that weapon of great splendor,
as terrible as a thunderbolt, pierced the earth and entered it.
Upon seeing that feat of the son of Droṇa, all living beings offered him worship.
O King, having leaped down and approached the chariot of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Bhīmasena then seized that terrible,
great bow fashioned by Śaṅkara, which was as formidable as Indra’s rainbow.
He released sharp arrows once more into the great chest of the son of Droṇa;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, remaining unperturbed, also released arrows resembling venomous serpents—
gold-feathered shafts— into the breast of Droṇa’s son.
Then the son of Droṇa released thousands of iron arrows at them both;
they too, with shafts resembling tongues of fire, struck down his missiles.
A most fierce battle took place between those two lions among men.
O bull of the Bharatas, that which caused joy to the warriors and to the son of Droṇa was witnessed;
then Bhīma advanced toward that place with a thousand chariots, three hundred elephants, and six thousand horses.
Then the son of Droṇa, whose soul is righteous and who performs deeds without effort, fought against the Rākṣasa, the son of Bhīma, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna along with his followers. There,
the son of Droṇa displayed a most wonderful prowess.
O Bhārata, it was impossible for anyone else among all living beings to achieve this;
in the mere twinkling of an eye, he destroyed an Akṣauhiṇī of Rākṣasas, along with their horses, charioteers, chariots, and elephants, using his sharp arrows.
While Bhīmasena, the son of Hiḍimbā, the son of Pṛṣata, the twins,
the son of Dharma, Vijaya, and Acyuta looked on,
they were struck deeply with straight-flying iron arrows.
The elephants fell to the ground like two-peaked mountains;
with their severed trunks twitching here and there,
the earth, strewn with them, shone as if covered with slithering serpents.
The earth shone with scattered golden staffs and royal umbrellas,
like the sky at the end of an eon filled with planets and the risen sun and moon;
it was a land where raised banners were the frogs and the drums were the sprawling tortoises.
It was graced by rows of parasols like swans and garlands of foam-like whisks; it was filled with herons and vultures as its great crocodiles, crowded with many weapons as its fish,
abounding in fallen elephants as its massive boulders, and teeming with slain horses as its sea-monsters.
With great embankments formed by the chariots cast about, with banners as its beautiful trees,
with arrows for its fish, most terrible with spears and pikes for its fierce water-snakes, with marrow and flesh for its great mud, and with headless trunks for its drifting rafts.

The son of Droṇa set flowing a river with a great current of blood, mottled with hair for its moss, bringing terror to the timid, and arising from the destruction of the bodies of lordly elephants, horses, and warriors.
Resounding with the cries of warriors and filled with waves of blood,
he advanced toward that most terrifying great ocean of Yama’s abode;
having slain the Rākṣasas with his arrows, the son of Droṇa assailed the son of Hiḍimbā.

Once again, filled with extreme rage, the mighty and powerful son of Droṇa pierced the sons of Pṛthā, along with Vṛkodara and the son of Pṛṣata, with volleys of iron shafts; then that lordly warrior slew Drupada’s son, named Suratha.
Furthermore, in battle, he struck down Śrutajaya, the younger brother of Suratha,
as well as Balānīka, Jayānīka, and Jayāśva; then,
roaring like a lion, the son of Droṇa struck again with a sharp arrow.
O Indra among kings, the son of Droṇa dispatched Śrutāhvaya to the abode of Yama;
and with three other sharp, well-feathered arrows, he sent the powerful Śatruñjaya, who wore a garland of gold,
to the world of Śakra.
He slew Pṛṣadhra and the proud Candradeva,
and in battle he struck down ten of Kuntibhoja’s sons with ten arrows.
Aśvatthāman, highly incensed, fixed a fierce, straight-flying shaft.
Drawing his excellent bow back to his ear,
he swiftly released a terrible, supreme arrow resembling the staff of Yama, aiming it at Ghaṭotkaca.
That great shaft pierced the heart of that Rākṣasa.
O lord of the earth, that arrow, along with its feathers, quickly entered the ground.
Knowing him to be slain and fallen, O king of kings, the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna removed him from the presence of Droṇa’s son to another chariot.
O King, having thus defeated Yudhiṣṭhira’s army in battle when their chariots were turned away from him, the heroic son of Droṇa let out a roar,
O Bhārata, being honored by all beings and by your sons.
Then the earth became covered on all sides with night-stalkers who had met their end, lying slain and fallen, their bodies pierced and mangled by hundreds of arrows.
Inaccessible and extremely fierce as if with mountain peaks,
it was [filled] by hosts of Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Piśācas,
as well as Nāgas, Suparṇas, Pitṛs, and birds.
The hosts of Rākṣasas and the hosts of Bhūtas, as well as the Apsarases and the gods, honored the son of Droṇa.
Sañjaya said:
Having seen the sons of Drupada as well as the sons of Kuntibhoja,
and thousands of Rākṣasas slain by the son of Droṇa,
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, [were filled with grief].
And Yuyudhāna, prepared for battle, set his mind solely upon the fight. But Somadatta, enraged at seeing Sātyaki in the fray,
covered him on all sides with a great shower of arrows.
Then there occurred a battle that greatly increased fear, a terrible conflict between your men and the enemy, both desiring victory.
Seeing him approaching, [they struck him] with gold-feathered arrows sharpened on stone.
With ten arrows, Bhīma pierced the Kaurava for the sake of the Sātvata;
Somadatta, in turn, struck that hero with a hundred.
But the Sātvata, filled with rage, [assailed] him who was overwhelmed by the afflictions caused by his sons.
He pierced Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa— who was advanced in years and enriched with all virtues— with ten sharp arrows that fell like thunderbolts;
then, having struck him with a spear, he pierced him again with seven more.
Then, for the sake of Sātyaki, Bhīmasena hurled a new, firm,
and terrible iron club at the head of Somadatta;
and Sātyaki released an excellent arrow that resembled fire.
Enraged in battle, he struck Somadatta on the chest with a sharp, well-feathered shaft; then, simultaneously, two terrible weapons— a mace and an arrow—
fell upon Somadatta’s body, and that great car-warrior collapsed.
When his son was thus bewildered, Bāhlīka rushed forward,
discharging showers of arrows like a rain-cloud pouring down its season's downpour.
Then Bhīma, for the sake of the Sātvata, struck Bāhlīka with nine arrows.
Afflicting the high-souled one, he pierced him at the head of the battle; then the mighty-armed son of Pratipa, filled with rage, drove a spear into Bhīma’s chest,
just as Purandara hurls his thunderbolt.
