Struck by that [mace], Bhīma trembled and fainted; but regaining his senses, the powerful one hurled a mace at him. That mace, dispatched by the Pāṇḍava, took Bāhlīka’s head.
Slain, he fell upon the earth like the king of mountains struck by a thunderbolt.
When that hero Bāhlīka, a bull among men, had been killed,
ten of your sons, equal to the son of Daśāratha, assailed Bhīma.
Nāgadatta, Dṛḍharatha, Vīrabāhu, Ayobhuja,
Dṛḍha, Suhasta, Virajas, Pramāthin, and Ugrayāyin—
seeing them, Bhīma grew enraged and seized his weapons for accomplishing great tasks.
Aiming at each one individually, he struck them in their vital organs;
pierced and deprived of their strength,
they fell from their chariots like trees on mountain peaks shattered by a fierce wind.
Having struck down those sons of yours with ten iron arrows, Bhīma overwhelmed Karṇa’s beloved son, Vṛṣasena. Then there was the famous brother of Karṇa named Vṛṣaratha.

He struck Bhīma with iron arrows, but the mighty one (Bhīma) in turn slew him as well. Then, O Bhārata, having destroyed seven chariots belonging to your brothers-in-law with his iron shafts, the hero Bhīma crushed Śatacandra.
Unable to endure the slaughter of the great car-warrior Śatacandra,
five heroic brothers of Śakuni— all great car-warriors— namely Gajakṣa, Śarabha, Vibhu, Subhaga, and Bhānudatta, rushed forward.
Rushing forward, they struck Bhīmasena with sharp arrows;
being pierced by those iron shafts like a bull by the force of a rainstorm,
that exceedingly powerful warrior slew five chariot-warriors with five arrows.
Seeing those heroes slain, the best of kings trembled;
then Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with rage, began to destroy your army while the son of Kuṇi and your sons looked on, O sinless one.
In battle, Yudhiṣṭhira dispatched the Ambaṣṭhas, the Mālavas, the heroic Trigartas, and the Śibis— these hosts— to the realm of death;
as well as the Abhīṣāhas, the Śūrasenas, the Bāhlīkas, and the Vasātikas.
Having carved up the earth, the king made it a mire of blood;
with his arrows in battle, Yudhiṣṭhira dispatched the hosts of Yaudheyas, Araṭṭas, Rājanyas, and Madrakas— those heroes— to the realm of death.
"Kill! Seize! Grasp! Pierce!
Cut them down!"—such was the tumultuous clamor directed toward Yudhiṣṭhira’s chariot.
Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira putting the armies to flight, Droṇa [rushed at him].
Urged on by your son, he covered [Droṇa] with arrows;
but Droṇa, extremely enraged, pierced the king with the Vāyavya weapon,
and he destroyed that divine weapon of his with his own weapon.
When that weapon had been neutralized against Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Bharadvāja,
filled with supreme rage and desiring to slay the joy of the Pāṇḍus, hurled the Vāruṇa, Yāmya, Āgneya, Tvāṣṭra, and Sāvitra weapons.
The mighty-armed son of Dharma, remaining undaunted, struck down with his own weapons those missiles already discharged and those being discharged by the pot-born Agastya;
yet the one born from a jar remained intent on fulfilling his vow.

Desirous of slaying the son of Dharma and devoted to the welfare of your sons, O Bhārata, that lord of the Kurus, who moves with the gait of an elephant or a lion, manifested the Aindra and Prājāpatya weapons.
Broad-chested and with large red eyes,
he of undiminished splendor manifested the Māhendra weapon and destroyed their other weapons.
When his weapons were being frustrated, Droṇa, filled with rage and desiring the slaughter of Yudhiṣṭhira, invoked the Brahma weapon. Then,
enveloped by that terrible darkness, I could discern nothing at all.
And all living beings, O lord of the earth, were struck with supreme terror upon seeing the Brahmā weapon raised; but Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
O king of kings, warded off that weapon with the Brahmā weapon itself.
Then those leaders of the army praised those two bulls among men,
Droṇa and Pārtha, both great archers and experts in every form of warfare.
Thereafter, having released the son of Kuntī, Droṇa [advanced] against Drupada’s host.
O Bhārata, with his eyes copper-red with rage, he scattered [the enemy] with the Vāyavya weapon;
with his eyes agitated by fury, he dispersed them using the Vāyavya weapon.
Being slaughtered by Droṇa, those Pāñcālas fled in fear.
While Bhīmasena and the high-souled Pārtha looked on,
the diadem-wearing Arjuna and Bhīma then suddenly turned back,
surrounding your army with two great arrays of chariots.

Bībhatsu [Arjuna] from the right flank and Vṛkodara [Bhīma] from the left rained down two great showers of arrows upon the son of Bharadvāja. At that time, the Sṛñjayas and the Pāñcālas of great prowess likewise [assailed him].
O Great King, the Matsyas, together with the Sātvatas, pursued them.
Then that Bharata army, being slaughtered by the Diademed One (Kiritin),
was once again shattered by both darkness and sleep.
Though they were being restrained by Droṇa and by your son himself,
O great king, those warriors could not then be held back.
Saṃjaya said:
Seeing that great army of the Pāṇḍavas surging forward and considering it to be irresistible, Duryodhana spoke to Karṇa:
"O you who are devoted to your friends, this is the moment that has arrived for your friends."
"O Karna of great strength, protect all our warriors in battle against the Panchalas,
Matsyas, Kaikeyas, and the Pandava maharathas,
who surround us on all sides, enraged like hissing serpents."
"These Pāṇḍavas, appearing victorious, are shouting with great joy,
as are the many throngs of Pāñcāla chariot-warriors who are like Śakra himself.
Karṇa said:
"Even if Purandara himself were to arrive here to protect Pārtha, I would swiftly defeat him as well and then slay the son of Pāṇḍu.
I promise this truly to you; take heart, O Bhārata."
"I shall slay the sons of Pāṇḍu and the assembled Pañcālas;
I promise you victory, just as the son of Agni promised it to Vāsava. O King, I live only because I must do what is pleasing to you."
Of all the sons of Pṛthā, Phalguna is the strongest;
against him I shall release the unerring spear fashioned by Śakra.
O giver of honor, when that great archer is slain, his brothers—
They will become subject to your will, or they will go back to the forest; while I live, O Kauravya, do not give way to despair at all. I shall conquer all the Pāṇḍavas together in battle.
"Having shattered the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, and even the assembled Vṛṣṇis with floods of arrows, I shall give the earth to you. Saṃjaya said:
To Karṇa, who was speaking thus, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, spoke these words to the mighty-armed son of the Sūta, as if smiling:
"Excellent, excellent, O Karṇa! The bull among the Kurus now has a protector."
"O son of Rādhā, if things could be accomplished merely by words with you as their protector, then,
O Karṇa, you would have boasted many times in the presence of the Kuru prince;
yet not even the slightest prowess or strength is seen in you."
"O son of a Sūta, you have encountered the sons of Pāṇḍu many times in battle;
everywhere you were defeated by the Pāṇḍavas. O Karṇa, it was even so when the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was being carried away by the Gandharvas."
Then the armies fought, yet you alone fled;
and even when all the Kauravas were assembled in the city of Virāṭa,
they were defeated in battle by Pārtha, as were you, Karṇa, along with your younger brothers.
"You are not even capable of facing a single Phalguna on the field of battle;
how then do you dare hope to conquer all the Pāṇḍavas along with Kṛṣṇa?
O Karṇa, son of a Sūta, fight without speaking so much, for you are merely boasting."

"He who exerts his prowess without having spoken [his resolve]—that indeed is the vow of a virtuous man. But you, O son of a Sūta, having merely roared like a waterless autumn cloud, are seen to be fruitless, O Karṇa; and the king does not realize this."
O son of Rādhā, you roar only so long as you do not see Pārtha;
for once you have seen Pārtha, your roaring will become impossible. You roar only because you have not yet encountered those arrows of Phalguna.

For one pierced by the arrows of Pārtha, roaring becomes difficult to achieve. Kṣatriyas are heroes by their arms; the twice-born are heroes by their words; Phalguna is a hero by his bow; Karṇa is a hero by his desires.
"Who could strike down Pārtha, by whom even Rudra was gratified? Thus was Karṇa, the best among strikers, then addressed with harsh words by Śāradvata; he then spoke these words to Kṛpa.
Heroes always roar like clouds in the rainy season,
and they swiftly yield fruit, just as seeds sown in the proper season. I see no fault in heroes at the forefront of battle.
For those who boast in battle while bearing their respective burdens,
whatever burden a man resolves in his mind to carry, destiny surely provides assistance therein.
"Accompanied by my resolve and bearing this burden in my mind,
O Brahmin, if I roar, what is lost to you in that?
True heroes do not roar in vain, like water-laden clouds."
"Having recognized my own capability, the wise then roar. Today, being prepared in battle, I am able to conquer by force both Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava together; therefore, O Gautama, I roar."
"Behold, O Brahmin, the fruit of this my roaring, along with my followers:
having slain the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle, together with Kṛṣṇā, the Sātvatas,
and all thorns removed, I shall give the earth to Duryodhana."
Kṛpa said:
"O son of a Sūta, what is the use of our much prattling? Attain your own fruit; my words of counsel, spoken from the heart, are not to be accepted by you, O son of a Sūta."
When you indeed insult the two Kṛṣṇas and the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja, victory there is certain for them, O Karṇa, since they are experts in battle among gods,
Gandharvas, Yakṣas, humans, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Even when clad in armor for battle, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava are invincible.
He is devoted to Brahman, truthful in speech, self-controlled, a worshiper of his elders and the gods,
eternally delighting in dharma, and especially skilled in the use of weapons.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, is steadfast and grateful;
his brothers are powerful, have trained in all weapons, are devoted to serving their elders, wise, constant in righteousness, and illustrious.
And his kinsmen, endowed with Indra-like prowess, deeply devoted, and skilled strikers— Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, Daurmukhi, Janamejaya,
Candrasena, Bhadrasena, Kīrtidharman, Dhruva, and Dhara.
Vasucandra, Dāmacandra, Siṃhacandra, Suvedhana,
and likewise the sons of Drupada, including Drupada himself who is skilled in great weapons— for their sake the King of Matsya has prepared himself along with his followers.
Śatānīka, Sudaśana, Śrutānīka, Śrutadhvaja, Balānīka, Jayānīka, Jayāśva, Rathavāhana,
Jayānīka, and Jayapriya.
Vijaya, Labdhalakṣa,
Candrodaya, Kāmaratha, and the auspicious brothers of Virāṭa; the twins,
the sons of Draupadī, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca.
For those for whose sake they fight, there is no destruction.
Indeed, let the entire world— including gods, asuras,
and humans, along with hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, as well as spirits, serpents, and elephants— be at their disposal.
Bhīma and Phalguna could, by the power of their weapons, leave nothing remaining;
and Yudhiṣṭhira might consume the earth with his terrible gaze.
Yet Śauri, whose strength is immeasurable, has donned his armor for their sake.
"O Karṇa, how can you venture to conquer those enemies in battle?
O son of a Sūta, this is indeed a great lack of judgment on your part,
that you venture to fight with Śauri in combat."
Saṃjaya said:
Thus addressed, O bull of the Bharatas, the son of Rādhā,
Karna, smiling then spoke to his preceptor Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat.
"O Brahmin, the words you have spoken concerning the Pāṇḍavas are true.
These and many other virtues indeed reside in the sons of Pāṇḍu;
the sons of Pṛthā are invincible in battle even by the gods led by Vāsava."
"Even though [the enemies] are accompanied by Daityas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas,
I shall nevertheless defeat the sons of Pṛthā with the spear given by Vāsava.
O twice-born one, this spear granted to me by Śakra is indeed unfailing."
"With this [weapon] I shall slay Savyasācin in battle.
Once the Pāṇḍava is slain, Kṛṣṇa and his uterine brothers will by no means be able to enjoy the earth without Arjuna."

And on this earth devoid of Arjuna, they would undoubtedly perish. When all of them have perished, O Gautama, this earth together with its oceans will come under the power of the Kuru prince without any effort.
"In this world, all objectives are accomplished through well-guided conduct; there is no doubt about this.
Knowing this truth, O Gautama, I roar.
But you are old, a brahmin, and moreover, incapable in combat."
"Out of delusion, you disregard me, though I have shown affection toward the sons of Pṛthā.
O twice-born one, if you speak such unpleasant words to me here again, then, O evil-minded one, I shall raise my sword and cut out your tongue."
And as for your desire to praise the Pāṇḍavas in battle, O brahmin,
while terrifying all the Kaurava troops, O evil-minded one—
listen here to my words as I speak them correctly, O twice-born one.
Duryodhana, Droṇa, Śakuni, Durmukha, Jaya,
Duḥśāsana, Vṛṣasena, you yourself, the King of Madra,
Somadatta, Bhūri, as well as the son of Droṇa and Vivimśati— [all these are here].
Where all these men, clad in armor and skilled in battle, might stand—
who, even an enemy with strength equal to Śakra, could conquer them in combat? For they are heroes, masters of weapons, powerful, and seekers of heaven.

"Knowing the dharma and skilled in battle, they could slay even the gods in combat. Clad in armor and desiring victory for the Kuru prince, these men will stand in the fray seeking the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas."
I consider victory to be dependent on destiny, even for those who are exceedingly strong,
since the mighty-armed Bhīṣma lies here covered by hundreds of arrows;
as do Vikarṇa, Citrasena, Bāhlīka, and Jayadratha.
Bhūriśravas, Jaya, Jalasaṃdha, Sudakṣiṇa,
Śala— the best among chariot-warriors— and the heroic Bhagadatta;
these and other kings are difficult to conquer even by the gods.

"O lowest of men, the heroic and more powerful Pāṇḍavas have been slain in battle; what else do you consider it to be but the working of destiny? And as for those enemies of Duryodhana whom you constantly praise, O twice-born one,"
Even among them, hundreds and thousands of heroes have been slain;
all the armies, including both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, are wasting away. I do not perceive the power of the Pāṇḍavas here in any way whatsoever.
"O lowest of the twice-born, those whom you always consider to be powerful—
I shall strive to the best of my ability to fight them in battle for the sake of Duryodhana’s welfare; victory rests with destiny."
Saṃjaya said:
Having seen his maternal uncle thus insulted by the Sūta’s son,
the son of Droṇa raised his sword and rushed forward with great speed.
Then, extremely enraged like a lion toward an elephant in rut,
he spoke these words in the presence of the Kuru king as he looked on.
Aśvatthāman said:
O lowest of men, O evil-minded one, because of your hatred for Śūra, you revile your maternal uncle as he truthfully praises the virtues of Arjuna,
boasting of your own prowess before all the archers of the world.
Seized today by an excess of pride, you took no one into account in battle;
where now is your prowess and where are your weapons, since the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, having defeated you in combat, slew Jayadratha while you were looking on?
O lowest of Sūtas, you vainly desire with your mere fancies to conquer him who, in the past, personally fought against Mahādeva in battle—
that foremost of all wielders of weapons, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa.
O charioteer, even the gods and asuras together with Indra are not able to conquer Arjuna—
the world’s sole hero and the unconquered— in battle;
how much less can you, O evil-minded one, along with these lords of the earth?
"O Karna, you of evil intellect, look! Stay now, O lowest of men!
Today, O you of wicked mind, I shall sever your head from your body.
Sanjaya said:
As he was springing forward with speed, O great king, King Duryodhana himself and Kṛpa, the best of men, restrained him. Karṇa said:
"This man is a hero who boasts of his prowess in battle, yet he is evil-minded and the lowest of the twice-born. Let him encounter my valor; release him, O best of the Kurus!
Aśvatthāman said:
"O son of a Sūta, you of evil intellect, this [pride] of yours is forgiven by us;
however, Phalguna shall destroy this overflowing arrogance of yours.
Duryodhana said:

"Aśvatthāman, be gracious; you ought to forgive me, O giver of honor. Indeed, anger should not be harbored against the son of the Sūta in any way—whether toward you, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Droṇa, the King of Madra, or the son of Subala."
"A great task depends upon you; be gracious, O best of the twice-born!
For here all these Pāṇḍavas are approaching from every side, O Brahmin, summoned by the son of Rādhā and desiring to fight."
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O great king, the high-minded son of Droṇa, though filled with rage and resentment, was pacified by the king and became composed.
Then the high-minded teacher Kṛpa spoke these words,
O king of kings, his gentleness having quickly returned due to his mild nature.
Thereupon, O King, those Pāṇḍavas and the illustrious Pañcālas—
Hearing the words of Duryodhana, the mighty Aśvatthāman, O King, bestower of honor, became appeased toward the Sūta’s son; and they all arrived there together, threatening him again and again.
Karna also, the best of chariot-warriors, raising his bow, the heroic and radiant one,
surrounded by the foremost of the Kauravas like Śakra by the hosts of gods,
took his stand relying upon the strength of his own arms.
Then, O great king, the battle commenced between Karṇa and the Pāṇḍavas,
who were filled with fury and made the air resound with lion-like roars.
Then those Pāṇḍavas, O king, and the illustrious Pañcālas—
Seeing the mighty-armed Karṇa, they then raised a loud shout:
"Here is Karṇa! Where is Karṇa? Stay, Karṇa, in this great battle!
Fight together with us, O evil-minded one, O lowest of men!"
But others, seeing the son of Rādhā, spoke with eyes reddened by anger:
"Let this arrogant son of a Sūta, this small-minded man, be slain!
There is no purpose in him remaining alive for all these tigers among kings."

This man of evil deeds, the eternal enemy of the sons of Pṛthā, stands here abiding by the counsel of Duryodhana; he is indeed the root of all calamities. "Kill him! they cried, as the Kṣatriyas rushed forward.
Covering [him] with a great rain of arrows, those great car-warriors,
urged on by the son of Pāṇḍu, rushed forward for the sake of slaying the Sūta’s son.
Seeing all those great car-warriors thus rushing toward him, [he...]
Seeing that ocean of troops, which resembled a city and was surging upward, the son of the Suta neither trembled nor fell into fear; for he,
undefeated in battles, desired to please your sons.
O bull of the Bharata race, that powerful and mighty warrior, acting with great speed, held back that army on all sides with a flood of arrows;
then the kings, in turn, warded him off with a rain of shafts.
Wielding their bows by the hundreds and thousands,
they fought against the son of Rādhā, just as hosts of Daityas once fought against Śakra;
yet Karṇa [withstood] that shower of arrows discharged by the kings.
O Lord, he scattered them on all sides with a great shower of arrows;
that battle between those who sought to strike and counter-strike was like the battle of Śakra against the Dānavas in the war between the gods and the asuras.
There we beheld the wonderful lightness of hand of the Sūta’s son,
in that his enemies, though striving in battle, could not reach him in the fray;
for that great car-warrior, having warded off those showers of arrows from the kings, [proceeded].
Upon the yokes, poles, umbrellas, banners, and horses,
the son of Rādhā discharged sharp arrows engraved with his own name.
Thereupon, those kings, afflicted by Karṇa, became utterly bewildered.

They wandered here and there like cows afflicted by the cold; we beheld there, in various places, throngs of horses, elephants, and chariot-warriors struck down by Karṇa as they were being slaughtered.
O King, with fallen heads and arms strewn everywhere,
the entire earth was covered by those heroes who never retreated—
by those already slain, those being killed, and those groaning on all sides.
The battlefield became fierce, resembling the city of Vaivasvata.
Then King Duryodhana, having witnessed the prowess of Karṇa,
approached Aśvatthāman and spoke these words.
"There Karna fights in battle, clad in armor against all the kings;
behold this fleeing army, afflicted by Karna's arrows,
like the demonic host shattered by Karttikeya."
Having seen this army defeated in battle by the wise Karṇa,
here comes Bībhatsu with the intent to slay the Sūta’s son;
so that the great car-warrior Sūta’s son may be seen by all who look on.

"The son of Pāṇḍu would not slay him in battle; therefore, let such a policy be ordained. Then the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and the great car-warrior Hārdikya advanced against Pārtha, desiring to rescue the Sūta’s son.
O king of kings, Bibhatsu too, surrounded by the Pāñcālas,
saw the son of Kuntī approaching like Vṛtra against the divine host;
then Karṇa advanced against him, like the majestic Śakra.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Sūta, seeing Phalguna enraged and resembling Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time,
what did Karṇa Vaikartana do in response?
For that great car-warrior was always in competition with Pārtha,
and he constantly hoped to defeat Bībhatsu in a most terrible battle;
yet he [now] encountered that perpetual and extreme enemy who had suddenly arrived.
"O Sūta, what did Karṇa Vaikartana do in response?
Saṃjaya said:
Seeing the Pāṇḍava approaching like an elephant facing a rival elephant..."
Karna, remaining utterly undaunted, rose up against Dhananjaya;
but the radiant Pandava, the scorcher of his enemies, checked that son of Vikartana as he was rushing forward with speed by means of straight-flying arrows.
O noble one, Karna covered him with a net of arrows;
and, highly incensed, he pierced him with three straight-flying shafts.
Having severed the bowstring of the Gāṇḍīva, he struck Acyuta.
The mighty Pārtha could not endure that agility of his;
quickly stringing his bow Gāṇḍīva with a new, firm cord,
he took up for him arrows whetted on stone, with bright points and straight-flying.
The scorcher of enemies dispatched thirty arrows at the Sūta’s son; then, the powerful and valiant one,
as if laughing, furiously pierced him in the tip of his left arm with a single iron shaft.

When he was pierced, the bow fell from his hand by the force of the blow. Taking up that bow again within half a blink of an eye, the one of great strength covered Phalguna with floods of arrows like a master archer.
O Bhārata, Dhananjaya, as if smiling, dispersed with a shower of his own arrows that rain of shafts released by the Sūta’s son;
O King, having encountered one another, they both assailed each other with a downpour of arrows.
Seeking to counter each other's deeds, those two great archers covered one another with arrows;
that battle between Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava in the fray was a marvel,
like that of two wild elephants enraged over a female elephant.
Then Pārtha, the great archer, seeing Karna’s prowess,
acted with haste and severed his bow at the handle;
he also sent the four horses to the abode of Yama with broad-headed arrows.

Then the scorcher of enemies severed the charioteer’s head from his body. Thereupon, Pārtha, the joy of the Pāṇḍus, pierced him— whose bow was broken, whose horses were slain, and whose charioteer was killed— with four arrows.
But leaping quickly from that chariot whose horses had been slain, that bull among men,
afflicted by arrows, swiftly mounted the chariot of Kṛpa;
impelled by the floods of Arjuna’s arrows, he was covered like a porcupine.

Desirous of saving his life, he climbed onto the chariot of Kṛpa. O bull of the Bharatas, seeing the son of Rādhā defeated and driven away by the arrows of Dhanañjaya, your warriors fled in the ten directions.
O King, seeing them fleeing, King Duryodhana then turned them back and spoke these words:
"Enough of your flight, O heroes! Stay, O bulls among the Kṣatriyas!"
"I myself shall go into battle for the sake of slaying the son of Pṛthā;
I will kill the Pārthas along with the Pañcālas and the Somakas. Today, as I fight against the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow,"

The sons of Pṛthā shall behold my prowess, like that of Time itself at the end of an eon. Today, warriors in battle shall see my nets of arrows released by the thousands, appearing like swarms of locusts.
Today, as I discharge a rain of arrows from my bow,
the soldiers in battle shall behold me like a cloud at the end of the summer heat.
Today, O Pārtha, I shall conquer you in combat with my straight-jointed shafts.

"Stand firm in battle, O heroes; cast away your fear of Phalguna. For, having encountered my prowess, Phalguna shall not prevail, just as the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, cannot overstep its shore."
Having spoken thus, the invincible king, his eyes bloodshot with rage, set out toward Phalguna surrounded by a vast army. Then,
seeing that mighty-armed one advancing, the son of Śaradvat—
Approaching Aśvatthāman, he spoke these words:
"This mighty-armed king, impatient and overwhelmed with rage,
desiring to fight Phalguna, has adopted the course of a moth [flying into a flame]."
"O tiger among men, restrain the Kaurava while we are looking on, before he, having encountered Pārtha, abandons his life-breaths;
do so before he comes within the range of Phalguna’s arrows."
O hero, quickly restrain that Kuru king before he is reduced to ashes by the terrible arrows of Pārtha, which resemble snakes that have cast their sloughs;
let him be turned back from the battle while this is still possible.

O giver of honor, while we stand here, I see this as improper: that the king himself, without any support, goes out to battle against Pārtha. I consider the life of the Kaurava to be difficult to preserve when facing Kirīṭin.
While he was fighting with Pārtha like an elephant against a tiger,
the son of Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons, being thus addressed by his maternal uncle,
quickly spoke these words to Duryodhana:
"O son of Gandhārī, as long as I live, you ought not to go to war,
disregarding me, O Kauravya, who am ever desirous of your welfare.
You should have no anxiety regarding the victory of Pārtha."
"I shall hold back the son of Pṛthā; stay here, Suyodhana!
Duryodhana said:
"The Teacher indeed protects the sons of Pāṇḍu as if they were his own sons."
"O best of the twice-born, you too always show indifference toward them.
Is it because of my own misfortune that your prowess in battle has failed, or is it for the sake of pleasing Dharmarāja or Draupadī? We do not know that."
"Fie on me, a greedy man, because of whom all my kinsmen— deserving of happiness and unconquered— have encountered supreme suffering!
For who indeed is the foremost among wielders of weapons, equal to Maheśvara in battle?"
"Only one who is not the son of Gautamī could fail to destroy his enemies even when capable;
O Aśvatthāman, be gracious and annihilate these my adversaries. Even the gods, O sinless one, are not able to stand within the range of your weapons."
"O son of Droṇa, slay the Pañcālas and the Somakas along with their followers!
Protected by you, we shall slay the remainder.
For these Somakas and the illustrious Pañcālas, O Brahmin, [are formidable]."
"O mighty-armed one, O best of men, restrain those [Kekayas] who are roaming through my armies with fury like a forest fire;
for if they are protected by Kiritin, they will soon leave nothing remaining."
"O subduer of enemies, go quickly with all haste to Aśvatthāman!
Whether first or last, O noble one, this task is yours;
for you, O mighty-armed one, were born for the sake of the slaughter of the Pāñcālas."
"O Acyuta, you shall indeed make the entire world devoid of Pañcālas;
thus did the Siddhas speak these words, and it shall come to pass accordingly.
Therefore, O tiger among men, slay the Pañcālas along with their followers."
"Even the gods, together with Indra, are not able to stand within the range of your weapons; how much less the sons of Pṛthā along with the Pañcālas? These words of mine are true:
the Pāṇḍavas, together with the Somakas, are no match for you in battle."
"O hero, I tell you this truly: you must fight by force. Go, go, O mighty-armed one! Let there be no delay for us, for this army is fleeing, tormented by the arrows of Pārtha."
"For you are indeed capable, O mighty-armed one, by means of your own divine splendor,
to subdue the sons of Pāṇḍu and the Pañcālas, O giver of honor.
Saṃjaya said:

Thus addressed by Duryodhana, the son of Droṇa, who is fierce in battle, made an effort to slay the enemy just as Indra makes an effort to slay the Daityas. O mighty-armed Kaurava, he replied: "It is exactly as you say."
"O mighty-armed one, these words are true for your son:
the Pāṇḍavas have always been dear to me as well as to my father."
In that same way, O bull of the Kurus, we two are dear to them;
yet, O father, we shall fight in battle to the best of our ability, having cast away our lives like those who are fearless.
I, Karṇa, Śalya, Kṛpa, and the son of Hṛdika—[all these shall do so].
"O best of kings, in the twinkling of an eye we could destroy the Pāṇḍava army;
and they too, O bull of the Kurus, could destroy the Kaurava army in half a twinkling,
O mighty-armed one, were it not for our being in battle."

"O Bhārata, when those who wish to fight the Pāṇḍavas with all their might encounter us who likewise desire to fight them, their energy, upon meeting our energy, is pacified. The army of the Pāṇḍavas cannot be conquered by force alone."
While the sons of Pāṇḍu are alive, I tell you this as the truth:
those sons of Pāṇḍu are capable and would fight for their own sake;
why, O Bhārata, would they not slay your armies?

For you, O King, are most greedy and skilled in deceit, O Kaurava; being proud and suspicious of everyone, you therefore suspect us as well. I consider you, O King, to be contemptible, evil-minded, and a sinful man.
"O wretched one, you who are possessed by evil, you suspect even others among us. But I, having exerted every effort for your sake and renounced my own life,
am now going to battle for your cause, O joy of the Kurus."

"I shall fight with the enemies and I shall conquer the most excellent among them. O subduer of foes, for the sake of your pleasure, I will fight in battle against the Pāñcālas, the Somakas, the Kekayas, and the sons of Pāṇḍu."
Today, scorched by my arrows, the Pāñcālas and the Somakas shall flee in all directions like cattle tormented by a lion. Today, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, shall witness my prowess.
He will regard the world, along with the Somakas, as being made of Aśvatthāman;
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
will fall into despondency upon seeing the Pāñcālas, together with the Somakas, slaughtered in battle.

"O Bhārata, those who shall challenge me in battle, I will slay them; for once they have come within the reach of my arms, O hero, they shall not escape. Having spoken thus to your son Duryodhana, the mighty-armed one—

That best of living beings, desiring to do what was pleasing to your sons, turned back toward the battle, putting all the archers to flight. Then the son of Gautamī spoke to the Pāñcālas and the Kaikeyas.
"O great car-warriors, all of you strike here upon my body;
stand firm and fight, displaying your lightness of hand with weapons.
Thus addressed, they all let fall a rain of missiles.
O great king, like clouds pouring rain toward the son of Droṇa,
they showered him; having warded off those arrows, the son of Droṇa struck down ten heroes in the presence of the sons of Pāṇḍu and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O lord.
Being slaughtered in battle, those Pāñcālas and Sṛñjayas likewise abandoned the son of Droṇa in the fray and fled in the ten directions.
Seeing those heroic Pāñcālas along with the Somakas fleeing, [he pursued them].
O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna rushed against the son of Droṇa in battle;
he was surrounded by a hundred brave warriors on chariots that were decorated with gold, roared like water-laden clouds, and never retreated.
Dṛṣṭadyumna, the great car-warrior and son of the king of the Pañcālas,
seeing the warriors struck down, spoke these words to the son of Droṇa:
"O evil-minded son of the preceptor, what is the use of these others being slain by you?"
"Come together with me if you are a hero in combat;
I shall slay you—stand now before me!
Then the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna [addressed] that son of the preceptor.

O bull of the Bharatas, he struck them with sharp arrows that pierce the vital organs. Those swift-flying arrows, gold-tufted with bright points and capable of rending the entire body, entered the son of Droṇa as they were formed into a continuous line.
Like unrestrained bees seeking honey at a flowering tree,
[the arrows struck him]. Deeply pierced and violently enraged, like a serpent trodden upon by a foot,
the proud son of Droṇa, unperturbed and with arrow in hand, spoke.
"O Dhṛṣṭadyumna, stand firm and wait for a moment,
while I dispatch you to the abode of Yama with my sharpened arrows.
Having thus addressed the son of Pṛṣata, the son of Droṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, [proceeded].

With a light hand, he covered him on all sides with a flood of arrows. Being thus shrouded in battle by the son of Droṇa, that warrior difficult to vanquish in combat then threatened the son of Droṇa with these words: "O son of the Pāñcālas!"
O brahmin, you do not know my vow, nor indeed my origin:
"Having slain Droṇa, you must surely be killed by me, O evil-minded one.
Therefore, I do not kill you today in battle while Droṇa still lives.
"O evil-minded one, when this night has arrived and before dawn breaks,
I shall slay your father today; thereafter, I will lead even you to the world of death in battle— this is the firm resolve in my mind."
Whatever hatred you have for the Pārthas and whatever devotion you have for the Kauravas, show that now by standing firm; you shall not escape from me alive.
For a twice-born man who, having abandoned the status of a Brāhmaṇa, delights in the dharma of a Kṣatriya—
"You, O lowest of men, deserve to be slain by all the world!"—
having been addressed with these harsh words by the son of Pṛṣata, that best of the twice-born summoned a fierce anger and cried out, "Stay! Stay!"
As if burning him with his very eyes, he gazed at the son of Pṛṣata;
then, hissing like a serpent, he covered him with arrows.
O best of kings, while being thus shrouded in battle by the son of Droṇa, [he...]
Surrounded by all the Pāñcāla armies, that best of car-warriors,
the mighty-armed one, remained unshaken, relying upon his own fortitude;
and he indeed loosed various kinds of arrows at Aśvatthāman.
Those two, intent on the gamble of life in that battle, turned back toward one another once more;
full of indignation, they warded each other off with floods of arrows,
those great archers discharging showers of shafts in every direction.
Beholding that battle between the son of Droṇa and the son of Pṛṣata— terrible in form and fearsome— the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Vātikas offered their praise.
Filling the sky and the intermediate directions with floods of arrows, those two [continued their combat].
Having created a great darkness with their arrows, they fought while remaining invisible;
dancing as it were on the battlefield with their bows drawn into circles,
they were intent on slaying one another and each desired victory over the other.
Those two mighty-armed ones fought with wonderful, swift, and skillful prowess,
being honored in the battle by thousands of leading warriors;
seeing them engaged in combat, they appeared like two wild elephants in a forest.
A tumultuous joy arose in both armies;
there were lion-like roars, O noble one, and they blew their conchs. Musical instruments were sounded by the hundreds and by the thousands.
In that tumultuous battle, which increased the fear of cowards,
that combat remained equal for a mere moment.
Then, O great king, the son of Droṇa [assailed] the high-souled son of Pṛṣata.
Having struck down the banner, the bow, the umbrella, both flank-guards, the charioteer,
and the four horses in battle, he rushed forward,
piercing all those Pāñcālas with straight-jointed arrows.

He of immeasurable soul put them to flight by the hundreds and by the thousands. Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the Pāṇḍava army trembled upon seeing the great feat of the son of Droṇa, which was like that of Vāsava himself in battle.
Having slain a hundred with a hundred [arrows], that great car-warrior of the Pañcālas,
and having struck down three great car-warriors with three sharpened shafts,
the son of Droṇa did so while Drupada’s son and Phalguna looked on.
He destroyed the majority of the Pāñcālas who stood arrayed against him.
Being slaughtered in battle along with the Sṛñjayas, those Pāñcālas fled,
abandoning the son of Droṇa, their chariots and banners scattered.
Having conquered his enemies in battle, that great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa,
let out a tremendous roar like a rain-cloud at the end of the summer heat. Having slain many heroes, Aśvatthāman shone resplendent.
Having conquered thousands of enemy hosts in battle, he was being honored by the Kauravas on the field of war, like the purifying fire at the end of an eon after it has reduced all beings to ashes.
The powerful son of Droṇa shone resplendent,
like the lord of the gods after slaying the hosts of his enemies.
Saṃjaya said:
Then Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava,
O great king, surrounded the son of Droṇa on all sides.
Then King Duryodhana was hemmed in by the son of Bharadvāja.
He advanced against the Pāṇḍavas in battle, and then a conflict ensued,
O great king, terrible in form and increasing the fear of the timid.
[It involved] the Ambaṣṭhas, Mālavas, Vaṅgas, Śibis, and also the Traigartakas.
Enraged, Yudhiṣṭhira dispatched the hosts to the realm of death; having cut down the Abhīṣāhas, Śūrasenas, and kṣatriyas intoxicated with battle,
Bhīma made the earth a mire of blood.
With sharp arrows, Kirīṭin dispatched the Yaudheya, Āraṭṭa, and Rājanya kings, as well as the Madraka tribes, to the realm of death in battle;
they were severely oppressed by his straight-flying iron shafts.
The elephants fell to the earth like two-peaked mountains;
with their severed trunks rolling here and there,
the ground, strewn with them, shone as if covered with slithering serpents.

The earth shone with scattered royal umbrellas variegated with gold, like the sky at the end of an eon strewn with the sun, the moon, and other planets. "Strike! Strike back! Do not fear! Pierce! Cut them down! [these were the cries].
Thus there arose a tumultuous clamor around the chariot of the one with red horses;
but Drona, exceedingly enraged in that encounter, scattered them with the Vayavya weapon,
as an irresistible wind disperses the clouds.
Being slaughtered by Droṇa, those Pāñcālas fled in fear while Bhīmasena and the high-souled Pārtha looked on. Thereupon, both Kirīṭin and Bhīma suddenly turned back.
Having surrounded your army with a great multitude of chariots,
Bībhatsu took the right flank and Vṛkodara the left;
together they showered the son of Bharadvāja with two great volleys of arrows.
Then, O great king, the Sṛñjayas, the Pāñcālas, and the Matsyas, along with the Somakas— all those great car-warriors— followed those two;
likewise did the noble car-warriors and strikers on your son’s side.
Accompanied by a vast army, they advanced toward Droṇa’s chariot.
Then that Bharata host, being slaughtered by the Diademed One (Arjuna),
was once again shattered by both darkness and sleep.
O Great King, though they were being restrained by Droṇa and by your son himself,
those warriors could not then be held back;
that great army was being torn asunder by the arrows of the son of Pāṇḍu.
When the world was enveloped in darkness, she fled in every direction.
Abandoning their mounts by the hundreds, some kings there,
O great king, fled in all directions, overcome by fear.
Saṃjaya said:
Beholding Somadatta brandishing his great bow,
Sātyaki said to his charioteer, "Carry me toward Somadatta."
"O charioteer, I shall not return from the battle without having slain the enemy, that lowest of the Kauravas, the Bāhlika; this word of mine is the truth.
Then the driver urged on those swift Sindhu horses.
Horses the color of conch shells, surpassing all sounds in battle and possessing the speed of thought or the wind, bore Yuyudhāna,
O King, just as the bay horses once bore Indra when he was intent on slaying the Daityas in ancient times.
Beholding that Sātvata rushing impetuously toward him in battle,
the mighty-armed Somadatta, remaining unperturbed, advanced against him,
discharging showers of arrows like a rain-bearing cloud.
He covered the descendant of Śini, just as a cloud covers the sun; yet,
O bull of the Bharatas, Sātyaki remained unperturbed in battle and covered that bull among the Kurus from all sides with floods of arrows.
Somadatta, however, pierced Mādhava in the chest with sixty arrows;
and Sātyaki also, O King, pierced him with sharp shafts.
Sātyaki struck back at Somadatta with whetted arrows.

Wounded by each other’s arrows, those two bulls among men shone like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom during the flowering season, their every limb drenched in blood as they brought glory to the Kurus and the Vṛṣṇis.
Glaring at one another as if burning each other with their eyes,
those two crushers of enemies moved along the circular paths of their chariots;
for they were of terrible form, like two rain-bearing clouds.
With their limbs pierced by arrows and mangled on all sides,
O Indra among kings, they appeared like two porcupines wounded by shafts;
covered with gold-feathered arrows, the two of them shone brightly.
O King, covered by those arrows like two great trees enveloped by fireflies in the rainy season,
those two great car-warriors, with all their limbs set ablaze by the shafts,
appeared in battle like two enraged elephants amidst flaming torches.
Then, O great king, in that battle, the great car-warrior Somadatta cut through the large bow of Mādhava with a crescent-shaped arrow. He then struck him with twenty-five shafts.
Hurrying at a time when speed was required, Satyaki then took up another more powerful bow and quickly pierced Somadatta with ten arrows;
he then swiftly struck him again with five shafts.

Then, O King, with another broad-headed arrow, Sātyaki— as if laughing— severed the golden standard of Bāhlīka in battle. But Somadatta, remaining unperturbed upon seeing his banner fallen, [continued the fight].
He struck Śaineya with twenty-five arrows;
the Sātvata, enraged in battle, also cut the bow of the archer Somadatta in that encounter with a sharp razor-headed shaft.

Then, O King, with a hundred straight-knotted arrows feathered with gold, he pierced him in many places, like an elephant with broken tusks. Thereupon, the great car-warrior Somadatta took up another bow.
The mighty warrior covered Sātyaki with a shower of arrows;
then, highly incensed, Sātyaki pierced Somadatta in battle,
while Somadatta in turn afflicted Sātyaki with a net of shafts.
For the sake of the Sātvata, Bhīma slew the son of Bāhlika with ten arrows;
meanwhile, Somadatta, remaining unperturbed, struck the descendant of Śini with shafts.
Then, for the sake of the Sātvata, the son of Bhīmasena took up a new, firm [bow].
He hurled a terrible iron club at Somadatta’s chest.
As that fearsome-looking club came rushing toward him with great speed,
the Kaurava, as if laughing, split it in two in the midst of the battle.
Severed in two, that great iron club fell like a massive mountain peak split by a thunderbolt. Then,
O King, Sātyaki [struck] Somadatta in the encounter.
With a broad-headed arrow he severed the bow, and with five more he cut off the hand-guard;
then, O Bhārata, with four swift arrows he sent his four excellent horses to the presence of the King of the Dead.
Then that tiger among chariot-warriors, the bull of the Śinis, laughing, severed the head of the charioteer from his body with a straight-knotted broad-headed arrow (bhalla).
Thereafter, he [discharged] a most terrible arrow, blazing like fire.
O King, the Sātvata released a gold-feathered arrow, sharpened on stone;
O Bhārata, that excellent and terrible shaft, released by the powerful grandson of Śini, fell swiftly upon his chest, O Lord.
Deeply pierced by that powerful Sātvata, the mighty-armed mahāratha Somadatta fell down and died. Seeing Somadatta slain there, the great chariot-warriors—
And the Pāṇḍavas, O great king, together with the Madras and the Prabhadrakas,
rushed toward Yuyudhāna with a great shower of arrows. Seeing Yuyudhāna being covered by those arrows, Yudhiṣṭhira—

Accompanied by a vast army, he rushed against Droṇa’s division. Then Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with rage, put to flight the great force of your warriors with his arrows, even as the son of Bharadvāja looked on.
Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira putting the armies to flight, Droṇa,
his eyes bloodshot with rage, rushed toward him with speed;
then he pierced Pārtha with seven exceedingly sharp arrows.
Yudhiṣṭhira, also enraged, pierced him in return with five arrows. Deeply pierced, the mighty-armed one licked the corners of his mouth and cut down Yudhiṣṭhira’s banner as well as his bow.
With his bow severed, that best of kings, acting with haste at a time requiring speed,
swiftly took up another firm bow in the battle.
Then the monarch pierced Droṇa with a thousand arrows.
With its horses, charioteer, banner, and chariot, that [army] became like a marvel.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, Drona, distressed for a moment and tormented by the impact of the arrows, sat down on the seat of his chariot.
Then, regaining consciousness after a moment, that best of the twice-born was possessed by great anger and discharged the Vāyavya weapon. Thereupon,
the heroic Pārtha, remaining unperturbed, drew his bow.
O Bhārata, he neutralized that weapon with his own weapon in battle;
and the Pāṇḍava cut through the long bow of the Brāhmaṇa. Then Droṇa, the crusher of Kṣatriyas, took up another bow.
The bull among the Kurus cut that too with sharp, broad-headed arrows.
Then Vāsudeva spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, O mighty-armed one, listen to what I shall say to you."
"Cease from battle with Droṇa, O best of the Bharatas;
for Droṇa always desires to seize you in combat.
I do not consider a battle between him and you to be appropriate."
"That which was created for his destruction will slay him tomorrow.
Avoiding your preceptor, go where King Suyodhana is;
for a king should fight with a king, as battle with one who is not a king is not desired."
Go there, O son of Kuntī, surrounded by elephants, horses, and chariots, with as many followers as you require;
for Dhananjaya and Bhīma,
that tiger among car-warriors, are fighting with the Kauravas.
Having heard the words of Vāsudeva, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
reflected for a moment upon that terrible battle and then,
the slayer of enemies, proceeded swiftly to where Bhīma was stationed.
Striking down your warriors like Death with his mouth wide open,
he made the surface of the earth resound with the great roar of his chariot,
just as a rain-cloud at the end of the summer heat makes the ten directions thunder.
As Bhīma was slaying his enemies, the Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira took up his rear guard with a vast array of chariots, like a forest fire that has broken out;
thus did the king of kings, Yudhiṣṭhira, approach the presence of Bhīma.
When [Arjuna] had desisted from slaying the Kauravas, being urged by the words of Viṣṇu,
Droṇa also began to strike down the Pāṇḍus and Pāñcālas at the onset of night,
making your troops resound with the slapping of his palms, O honorable one.
Saṃjaya said:
While that battle was thus proceeding— terrible in form and inspiring fear,
and while the world was shrouded in darkness and dust, O lord of the earth—
Standing in the fray, the warriors could not see one another;
that great battle proceeded by means of inference and the calling out of names. It was a supreme slaughter of men, elephants, and horses, causing the hair to stand on end.
O best of kings, the heroic Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, along with Bhīma, the son of Pṛṣata, and Sātyaki, agitated one another’s armies. Those great car-warriors struck down the troops on all sides.
Enveloped on all sides by darkness and dust, they fled in every direction. As those warriors, their minds terrified, ran away in all directions, O great king, they were slaughtered in the battle.
Thousands of great car-warriors slaughtered one another in battle,
bewildered by the darkness as if in blindness, due to the counsel of your son.
Then, O Bhārata, all the troops and the protectors of the army [were likewise struck down].
They became bewildered in that battle when it was enveloped in darkness.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Of those [Kauravas] who were being overwhelmed by the Pāṇḍavas and whose vigor had been destroyed..."
Immersed in blinding darkness, what was your state of mind then? And how did light appear for them, or again for my own troops,
when the world was thus enveloped in gloom, O Sañjaya?
Saṃjaya said:
Then all the troops who remained after the slaughter,
having assigned protectors for the army, once again formed a battle array.
Droṇa was in the front and Śalya in the rear;
likewise, the son of Droṇa and the son of Subala were on the flanks,
while you yourself, O King, [were] at the head of all the forces.
O King, Duryodhana approached while concealing himself in the night; he spoke with words of conciliation to all the hosts of infantrymen.
"Having cast aside all your supreme weapons,
take up blazing lamps in your hands. Thus were they urged by that best of kings.
Then, filled with joy, the hosts of celestial sages, gandharvas, and divine seers, as well as the vidyādharas and throngs of apsarases, took up the lamps.
The nāgas, along with yakṣas, uragas, and kinnaras,
standing in the heavens, joyfully took up the lamps as they descended from the deities of the quarters.
Lamps filled with fragrant oil were seen,
especially those offered by Nārada and Parvata,
as they exhorted [the kings] for the sake of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas.
That army, arrayed once more with its banners,
shone in the night with the brilliance of fire,
adorned with costly ornaments and celestial jewels.
With blazing weapons falling upon them,
there were five lamps on each chariot, and three lamps on each elephant.
A great lamp was placed beside each horse by those Pāṇḍavas and Kauraveyas;
in an instant, all the lamps were prepared.
And they quickly set the army ablaze;
indeed, all the troops were being assailed by foot soldiers holding fire and oil in their hands.
They were seen being illuminated in the night,
just as clouds in the sky are made visible when lit by lightning; so it was when the army was thus illuminated.
O Indra among kings, Droṇa, resembling fire and scorching everything on all sides, shone resplendent in his golden armor like the sun, garlanded with rays, having reached the meridian.
In the ornaments made of Jāmbūnada gold, in the pure golden neck-ornaments, in the excellent shields,
and in the weapons that were as bright as fire;
Thereupon, counter-reflections appeared there: maces made of śaikya-iron, bright clubs,
and spears whirling upon the chariots.
O descendant of Ajamīḍha, those blazing parasols, accompanied by yak-tail fans, repeatedly produce counter-reflections with their rays.
Likewise, O King, blazing great meteors and swaying golden garlands shone there as they were being brandished by those striving in battle.
Then that army shone with the luster of weapons, was illuminated by the light of lamps,
and was made radiant by the brilliance of ornaments.
O King, it became intensely radiant:
the weapons, yellowed and smeared with blood,
were brandished by heroes against those who would harm their bodies.
They produced a blazing radiance there,
like lightning in the sky at the end of the summer heat,
as they were shaken by the force of the impact.
As they struck one another and fell with great speed,
the faces of those men then shone like great lotuses tossed by the wind.
Just as light would vanish even from the sun when a great forest is set ablaze,
so too did your blazing army perish.
O Bhārata, beholding that blazing army of ours in that great danger and terrible form,
the Pārthas likewise acted with haste.
Then, among all the troops, they urged on the multitudes of foot-soldiers and set up lamps;
for every elephant, seven lamps were prepared.
In each chariot there were ten lamps:
two on the backs of the horses, others on the sides,
others on the banners, and others at the rear.
In all the armies, others were on the flanks;
behind, in front, and on all sides,
as well as in the midst, others stood with blazing fires in their hands.
Men moved about in both armies;
in all the troops,
the throngs of foot soldiers were intermingled with multitudes of elephants, chariots, and horses.
Likewise, others in the midst [of the army], with blazing fires in their hands,
illuminated the army of the son of Pāṇḍu;
they set that banner-bearing host ablaze.
Likewise, the army protected by the son of Pāṇḍu was set ablaze by him;
thus that powerful force was consumed by that blazing power.
Scorched as if by fire by the sun-like planet, which was radiant and emitting light,
the splendors of those two [the sun and the planet] filled the earth and the intermediate space.
Surpassing all directions,
those aged ones shone intensely with that light; both their army and yours became brilliantly illuminated.
O King, by that light which ascends to heaven,
the hosts of gods,
as well as the multitudes of gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and siddhas, were awakened.
All the Apsarases gathered there,
and the place was crowded with gods, Gandharvas,
Yakṣas, lords of Asuras, and throngs of Apsarases.
With the fallen heroes ascending to heaven,
the battlefield became like a celestial realm,
illuminated by the lamps of chariots, horses, and elephants.
With its warriors enraged, its horses slain or fleeing, and its great army arrayed with chariots, cavalry, and elephants,
it became like the battle-array of the gods and asuras.
That [battle] had a fierce wind agitated by the mass of their powers, clouds in the form of great chariots, the roar of chariots and horses,
a rain of showers of weapons, and torrents of blood.
That night, as the battle between the gods and men proceeded,
that high-souled preeminent brahmin, resembling a great fire, scorched the Pāṇḍavas.
Like the sun situated in the midst of its rays at the end of the rainy season, so did it appear, O lord of men.
Sañjaya said:
When the world was thus illuminated, yet shrouded by dust and darkness,
the heroes then gathered together, each desiring to slay the other.
Having come together in battle, O King, they bore weapons, spears, and swords.
They looked at one another, having committed offenses against each other,
amidst thousands of lamps blazing on all sides—
lamps set with jewels, possessing golden handles, and sprinkled with scented oil.
O Bhārata, with the exceedingly brilliant splendors of the gods, Gandharvas, lamps, and other lights, the earth then shone like the sky with its planets;
the battlefield gleamed with hundreds of blazing meteors.
As if the earth itself were burning at the destruction of the worlds,
all the quarters blazed on every side with those lamps;
they appeared like trees covered by fireflies during the gloom of the rainy season.
Then those heroes engaged separately with other heroes; elephants encountered elephants, horses met with horses,
and chariots, filled with joy, clashed with the best of chariot-warriors.
At that terrible onset of night, by the command of your son,
a great clash of the fourfold army took place;
then, O Great King, Arjuna [assailed] the host of the Kauravas.
Endowed with haste, he scattered them, destroying all the kings.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When he had entered my son's army in a state of fury..."
When that invincible one, who could not be withstood, had entered, what was in your minds then? What did the troops think as the scorcher of enemies advanced?
And what did Duryodhana consider to be the duty appropriate for the occasion?
And who advanced against that hero, the subduer of enemies, in battle? And who protected Droṇa when the one with white horses had entered?
Who guarded his right wheel, and who was on Droṇa’s left?
Who were the heroes who followed behind that hero as he fought? Who went before him as he struck down his enemies in battle,
when those unvanquished great archers entered among the Pāñcālas?
Dancing, as it were, along the tracks of his chariot, that tiger among men,
the valiant Drona, consumed the throngs of Pāñcāla chariots with his arrows;
how did he, who was like the enraged fire itself, meet his death?
For you describe the enemies as indeed undistracted and invincible,
joyful and exultant in battle; but you do not describe my own men thus, O Sañjaya, but rather speak of them as slain, dejected, and scattered.
[Seeing] my own chariot-warriors deprived of their chariots in the battles,
Sañjaya said:
"Having understood the intention of Droṇa, who was desirous of fighting during that night..."
O great king, Duryodhana addressed his obedient brothers—
Vikarṇa, Citrasena, the mighty-armed Kaurava,
Durdharṣa, Dīrghabāhu, and those who followed in their footsteps.
"O all you who are vigilant and valiant, protect Droṇa from behind!
Let the son of Hṛdika guard the right wheel and Śalya likewise the left;
and let those heroes among the Trigartas who remain after the slaughter, those great car-warriors, do the same."
Your son urged all of them forward to his front:
"The preceptor is indeed well-prepared, and the Pāṇḍavas are exceedingly vigilant;
protect him with great care as he slaughters the enemies in battle."
For Droṇa is powerful in battle, swift-handed, and heroic;
he could conquer even the thirty gods in combat, let alone the sons of Pṛthā along with the Somakas.
Therefore, all of you great car-warriors must join together and exert yourselves with the utmost diligence.
"O kings, protect Droṇa from Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the great car-warrior of the Pañcālas!
Among the Pāṇḍava armies, I see no warrior,
O monarchs, who could defeat Droṇa in battle except for Dhṛṣṭadyumna."
I believe that the protection of Bhāradvāja must be undertaken with one's whole soul;
for if he is protected, he will slay the Somakas and the Sṛñjayas along with their kings.
And when all the Sṛñjayas have been slain at the front of the army—
The son of Droṇa will undoubtedly destroy Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle;
likewise, the great car-warrior Karṇa will conquer Arjuna in combat;
and I too, clad in armor, shall defeat Bhīmasena in the fray.
The warriors have forcibly struck down the remaining Pāṇḍavas, whose energy has been diminished. Clearly, this victory of mine will endure for a long time;
therefore, O great car-warriors, protect Droṇa alone in battle.
Having spoken thus, O best of the Bharatas, your son Duryodhana then commanded his army in that dreadful darkness. Thereupon,
O bull of the Bharatas, that battle commenced in the night.
In both armies, which were desirous of a terrible victory,
Arjuna oppressed the Kaurava host and the Kauravas likewise oppressed Arjuna,
afflicting one another with the discharge of various weapons.
The son of Droṇa covered the king of the Pañcālas, and the son of Bharadvāja covered the Sṛñjayas with straight-knotted arrows in that battle,
O noble one, among the armies of the Pāṇḍavas, the Pañcālas, and the Kauravas.
A terrible clamor arose as they struck one another;
such a battle, so full of great terror, had never before been seen by us, nor by our ancestors, during that night.
Saṃjaya said:
O lord of the people, while that fierce night-battle was thus proceeding for the destruction of men, men,
and elephants, O king.

King Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to his own warriors, O lord of men; Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, addressed the Pāṇḍavas, the Pañcālas, and the Somakas in that battle which brought about the destruction of all beings.
"Run! Go toward Droṇa himself with the intent to slay him! At these words of the king, O monarch, the Pāñcālas and the Somakas likewise rushed toward Droṇa, uttering terrible roars.
Roaring back at them, we advanced in anger against them in battle, according to our strength, our energy, and our courage.
Then Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
O great king, Dhrṣṭadyumna rushed toward Droṇa himself, seeking to slay him like one rutting elephant charging another; meanwhile,
the descendant of Śini scattered showers of arrows all around.
O King, the Kuru Bhūri advanced at the head of the battle; then Karṇa Vaikartana, O King, held back the Pāṇḍava Sahadeva, that great car-warrior who was advancing with the intent of reaching Droṇa.
Then Duryodhana himself advanced in battle against Bhīmasena, who was approaching like Death with his jaws wide open; likewise,
he advanced against Nakula, the best of warriors and skilled in every form of combat.
O King, Śakuni Saubala quickly warded off Śikhaṇḍin,
the best of chariot-warriors, as he advanced on his chariot;
and Kṛpa Śāradvata, O King, warded him off in the encounter.

Then, O Great King, Duḥśāsana, exerting himself to the utmost, checked the advancing Prativindhya, who was drawn by horses resembling peacocks. Next, he opposed the son of Bhīmasena as he approached, a master of a hundred illusions.
Aśvatthāman, honoring his father’s pride, held him back;
meanwhile, Vṛṣasena restrained the great car-warrior Drupada in battle, along with his army and followers, as he sought to reach Droṇa.
O Bhārata, the King of Madra, highly incensed, checked Virāṭa as he rushed forward for the sake of Droṇa’s slaughter; likewise,
he opposed Śatānīka, the son of Nakula, who was advancing impetuously in battle.
Citrasena quickly obstructed Arjuna, the best of warriors and a great car-warrior who was fleeing, with his arrows, desiring to slay Droṇa; and Alambuṣa,
O great king, the lord of the Rākṣasas, held him back.
Likewise, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the prince of the Pañcālas, with a joyful countenance, checked the great archer Droṇa as he was slaughtering the enemies in battle; and likewise,
the other great car-warriors of the sons of Pāṇḍu who had arrived.
O King, your chariot-warriors resisted them with might;
elephant-riders, swiftly encountering other elephants in that great battle,
were seen fighting by the hundreds and thousands.
At midnight, O King, horses rushing at one another with great speed appeared like winged mountains; horsemen,
with spears, javelins, and swords in hand, clashed together with other horsemen.
O Great King, they encountered one another, each shouting separately; many men gathered there against one another in groups,
with maces, clubs, and various weapons.

But Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, being enraged, checked Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, as the shore holds back the surging ocean. Yudhiṣṭhira, however, pierced the son of Hṛdika with five swift arrows.

He pierced him again with twenty arrows and cried out, "Stay! Stay! But Kṛtavarman, O Sire, being greatly enraged, cut the bow of Dharmaputra’s son with a broad-headed shaft and pierced him with seven more.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, taking up another bow,
struck Hārdikya in the arms and chest with ten arrows.
But Mādhava, O noble one, was pierced in battle by the son of Dharma.
He trembled with rage and struck him with seven arrows;
but Pārtha, having cut his bow and severed his hand-guard,
O King, dispatched five sharp arrows whetted on stone.
Having pierced his armor, which was highly precious and adorned with gold,
those fierce arrows entered the earth like serpents entering an anthill.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, he took up another bow.

He pierced the Pāṇḍava with sixty arrows and his charioteer with nine. Then, O best of the Bharatas, that Pāṇḍava of immeasurable soul, setting aside his great bow upon the chariot, hurled at him a spear resembling a serpent.
That great, gold-adorned [spear], hurled by the Pāṇḍava,
pierced his right arm and entered the surface of the earth.
At that very moment, however, Pārtha took up his bow once again.
He covered the son of Hṛdika with straight-jointed arrows.
Then, in that battle, the heroic and preeminent chariot-warrior of the Vṛṣṇis deprived Yudhiṣṭhira of his horses, driver,
and chariot within half a blink of an eye.
Then the eldest Pāṇḍava took up a sword and shield;
Mādhava shattered those in battle with his sharp arrows. Then, seizing an unassailable lance with a golden shaft, he—
In that battle, Yudhiṣṭhira swiftly dispatched [the mace] toward the son of Hṛdika.
As it came rushing suddenly, released from the arm of Dharmarāja,
the son of Hṛdika, with practiced hand, cut it in two as if smiling.
Then, in the battle, he covered the son of Dharma with a hundred arrows;
and, filled with rage, he tore through his armor with sharp shafts.
That armor of the high-souled one was shattered by the arrows of Hārdikya.
O King, it was shattered in battle like a cluster of stars falling from the sky.
With his bow broken, his chariot lost, his armor shattered, and tormented by arrows,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, quickly withdrew from the field of battle.
But the mighty Kṛtavarman, having defeated Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
once again protected the wheel of Droṇa.
Saṃjaya said:
But Bhūri, O King, repelled Śaineya, the best of chariot-warriors, as he was charging, like an elephant from a watering-trough. Then the enraged Sātyaki struck him with five sharpened arrows.
He quickly pierced him in the heart, and his blood flowed forth.
In that same manner, the Kuru warrior pierced Śaineya, who was fierce in battle,
in the middle of the chest with ten sharp arrows during the combat.
O Great King, those two mangled each other severely with arrows,
their eyes bloodshot with rage as they drew their bows in fury.
O Great King, there occurred between them a most terrible shower of weapons.
As those two, resembling Yama and Antaka, stood enraged and discharging arrows,
O King, they remained in battle having covered each other with shafts;
for a moment, that combat appeared to be perfectly equal.

Then, O great king, the descendant of Śini, as if laughing, became enraged and cut the bow of the high-souled Kaurava in that battle. Then, he struck him, whose bow was broken, with nine sharpened arrows.
He quickly pierced him in the heart and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Being deeply pierced by his powerful enemy, that scorcher of foes took up another bow and struck back at the Sātvata warrior.
Having pierced the Sātvata with exactly three arrows, O lord of the people,
he cut his bow with an exceedingly sharp broad-headed shaft as if laughing.
With his bow broken, O great king, Sātyaki was overwhelmed with rage.
He hurled a spear of great velocity at his broad chest;
with his body pierced by that spear, he fell from his excellent chariot like the red-bodied planet Mars falling by chance from the sky with its rays aflame.
But seeing that hero slain, the great car-warrior Aśvatthāman rushed with speed toward the descendant of Śini in the encounter,
O lord of men, addressing the Śaineya, "Stay! Stay!"
Like a cloud raining upon Mount Meru, he showered him with a torrent of arrows.
As that enraged warrior rushed toward the chariot of Śini’s grandson,
O King, the great car-warrior Ghaṭotkaca let out a roar and spoke.
"Stay! Stay! O son of Droṇa, you shall not escape from me alive!
Today I shall slay you, just as Skanda slew Mahiṣa;
today on this field of battle, I shall strip away your desire for war."
Having spoken thus, the Rākṣasa, slayer of enemy heroes, his eyes copper-red with rage,
rushed furiously at the son of Droṇa like a lion toward a lordly elephant.
Ghaṭotkaca then showered him with arrows as thick as the axles of chariots.
Like a rain-cloud with its torrents, [Arjuna] assailed the son of Droṇa, that bull among chariot-warriors;
but the son of Droṇa, smiling in the midst of battle, swiftly struck down that approaching shower of arrows with his own shafts resembling venomous serpents.
Then, with hundreds of sharp, swift arrows capable of piercing the vital organs,
he covered Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Rākṣasas and subduer of enemies.
Covered by those arrows from him at the forefront of the battle, that Rākṣasa—
O Great King, he appeared like a porcupine with its quills bristling;
then the powerful son of Bhīmasena, overcome with rage,
mangled the son of Droṇa with fierce arrows that sounded like thunderbolts.
With razor-sharp arrows, crescent-headed shafts, iron bolts, and feathered barbed arrows; with boar-eared arrows, hollow-nosed shafts, and sharp, earless arrows—
they rained down that incomparable shower of weapons, sounding like the crash of a thunderbolt.
As it fell upon him, the enraged son of Droṇa, his senses undisturbed,
dispersed that most difficult-to-withstand weapon with terrible arrows consecrated by divine mantras—
just as the wind scatters great clouds, he of great splendor.

Then, O great king, a battle of arrows took place in the sky as if it were another conflict— terrible in form and increasing the joy of the warriors. Then, sparks produced by the friction of the massed weapons appeared on all sides.
At the onset of night, the sky shone as if covered with fireflies; Drona’s son, having completely shrouded all directions with his multitudes of arrows,
overwhelmed the Rākṣasa for the sake of your sons.
Then, in the midst of the deep night, a battle commenced between the son of Droṇa and the Rākṣasa in that conflict, like the encounter between Śakra and Prahrāda.
Then, in the fray, Ghaṭotkaca struck the son of Droṇa with ten arrows.
Enraged, he struck him on the chest with arrows resembling the fire of time. Pierced by those long shafts from the Rākṣasa,
the mighty son of Droṇa wavered in battle like a tree shaken by the wind.
Overcome by delusion, he leaned against his flagpole;
then, O lord of people, your entire army raised a cry of "Alas!
and all your men, O ruler of the earth, thought him to be slain.
But seeing Aśvatthāman in such a state on the battlefield, the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas let out lion-like roars. Then, having regained consciousness, the mighty Aśvatthāman—
Pressing his bow with his left hand,
that crusher of enemies drew it back to his ear and released an excellent arrow—
terrible and like the staff of Yama— swiftly aiming it at Ghaṭotkaca.

O lord of the earth, that fierce and well-feathered supreme arrow, having pierced the heart of that Rākṣasa, entered the earth. O great king, being thus deeply pierced, he sat down upon the floor of his chariot.
Seeing the son of Hiḍimbā bewildered by the son of Droṇa, who was proud of his prowess in battle, the charioteer of the mighty lord of the Rākṣasas,
being greatly agitated, quickly led him away from the field of battle in the presence of the son of Droṇa.
Having thus pierced Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Rākṣasas, in battle,
the mighty son of Droṇa let out a tremendous roar.
O Bhārata, he was honored by your sons and by all the warriors.
With his form he blazed like the sun at midday;
but as Bhīmasena was fighting against the chariot of the son of Bharadvāja,
King Duryodhana himself pierced him back with sharp arrows.
O Sire, Bhīmasena pierced him with nine arrows,
and Duryodhana likewise struck back with twenty shafts;
covered by those arrows, the two of them became invisible upon the field of battle.
Like the moon and the sun in the sky shrouded by a mass of clouds,
King Duryodhana then pierced Bhīma with feathered arrows,
O best of the Bharatas, and cried out, "Stay! Stay!"
Having severed his bow and standard with nine arrows, Bhīma pierced that best of the Kauravas with ninety straight-knotted shafts.
Then, O Sire, Duryodhana became enraged at Bhīmasena.
Taking up another, even greater bow,
O King, that best of the Bharatas discharged his arrows while all the archers looked on.
Having struck down those arrows discharged from Duryodhana’s bow, Bhīma struck the Kaurava with twenty-five small shafts.
But Duryodhana, O Sire, became enraged at Bhīmasena.
Having severed the bow with a razor-sharp arrow, he pierced [him] back with ten shafts.
Then the mighty Bhīmasena, taking up another bow,
quickly struck the king with seven sharpened arrows.
With great swiftness of hand, he quickly cut that bow of his as well; and in the same way,
O Great King, he severed Bhīma’s second, third, fourth, and fifth bows, each time as soon as it was taken up.
O great king, your son, appearing victorious and intoxicated with pride,
then, as his bows were being severed again and again,
hurled a beautiful spear made entirely of iron into the battle.
Indeed, like the sister of Death, blazing like the crest of a comet,
parting the sky as it were, and possessing a radiance equal to fire—
that spear was cut into three pieces by the Kaurava before it had even reached him.
While all the world and the high-souled Bhīma looked on,
O great king, Bhīma then whirled a heavy,
immensely radiant mace and hurled it with speed toward Duryodhana’s chariot.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, that heavy mace suddenly crushed the horses and the charioteer of your son in the encounter.
But your son, O king of kings, [leapt] from his gold-adorned chariot.
Suddenly leaping onto the chariot of the high-souled Nandaka,
Bhīma then, believing your son— the great car-warrior— to have been slain,
let out a mighty lion-roar as if to threaten the Kauravas.
Your soldiers also believed the king had been slain;
then they all cried out "Alas! Alas! from every side. Hearing that roar of all those terrified warriors, [the enemy]—
O King, having heard the roar of the high-souled Bhīmasena and believing Suyodhana to have been slain, King Yudhiṣṭhira then rushed with speed to where Vṛkodara, the son of Pṛthā, was.
O lord of the people, the Pāñcālas, Kekayas, Matsyas,
and Sṛñjayas advanced with all their might against Droṇa alone, desiring to fight.
Then a truly great battle took place there between Droṇa and his enemies.
Immersed in terrible darkness and slaughtering one another,
Sañjaya said:
"O Lord of the People, then Sahadeva approached, seeking to reach Droṇa."
O Bhārata, Karṇa Vaikartana held Sahadeva at bay in battle; but Sahadeva, having pierced the son of Rādhā with nine swift arrows,
struck him again with ten sharp, straight-knotted shafts.
Karna pierced him in return with a hundred straight-knotted arrows,
and with great lightness of hand, he swiftly cut his strung bow asunder.
Thereupon, the powerful son of Madri took up another bow.
He pierced Karṇa with twenty arrows, and that was like a marvel.
Having slain his horses with straight-knotted shafts,
Karṇa then swiftly sent his charioteer to the abode of Yama with a broad-headed arrow.
Deprived of his chariot, Sahadeva took up a sword and a shield;
however, Karna, as if laughing, shattered those as well with his arrows.
Then [Sahadeva took up] a heavy, most terrible, great mace adorned with gold.
He dispatched it in battle toward the chariot of Vaikartana.
As that [missile], hurled by Sahadeva, was suddenly rushing toward him,
Karṇa checked it with his arrows and brought it down to the ground.
Seeing his mace destroyed, Sahadeva, filled with haste, hurled a spear at Karṇa; but Karṇa cut that down as well with his arrows.
Then, leaping quickly from his excellent chariot in great agitation, he [Karṇa]—
O great king, seeing Karṇa stationed there, Sahadeva then seized a chariot wheel and hurled it toward the son of Adhiratha.
As it came rushing suddenly like the uplifted wheel of Time, it fell upon him.
The son of the charioteer cut [them] down with many thousands of arrows. When that [chariot] had been rendered useless by that high-souled one,
he [cut] the shafts, the traces, and various kinds of yokes.
He hurled elephant limbs, horses, and many dead men toward Karṇa; Karṇa scattered them with his arrows. Then the son of Mādravatī, realizing himself to be disarmed, [fled].
Being held back by arrows, Sahadeva abandoned the battle;
O bull of the Bharatas, having pursued him for a moment,
the son of Rādhā spoke these words with a laugh to Sahadeva, O lord of people.
"Do not fight in battle, O hero, with superior chariot-warriors;
fight with those who are your equals, son of Mādrī—heed my words and do not hesitate.
Then, prodding him with the tip of his bow, he spoke these words once more.
"Here is Arjuna, striving in battle against the Kurus;
go there, O son of Mādrī, or go home if you so prefer.
Having spoken thus to him, Karṇa, the best among chariot-warriors, departed by means of his chariot.
He advanced toward the armies of the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas as if laughing;
yet that slayer of foes did not kill the son of Mādrī when he was within his grasp in battle,
O King, because that great car-warrior of true promise remembered the words of Kuntī.
Then, O King, Sahadeva, dejected and tormented by arrows,
burned by the dart-like words of Karṇa, lost all desire for life;
he then ascended the chariot of the high-souled Pāñcālya.
In that battle, the great car-warrior [Kṛtavarman], acting with haste against Janamejaya,
covered the archer Virāṭa— who was swiftly approaching with his army for the sake of Droṇa— with a flood of arrows.
The King of Madra shrouded that bowman with a torrent of shafts.
A battle took place between those two firm-bowed warriors in that encounter,
O King, just like the one that occurred in ancient times between Jambha and Vāsava.
O great king, the King of Madra [assailed] Virāṭa, the commander of the army.
He quickly struck him with a hundred sharp, straight-knotted arrows;
the king pierced him in return with nine sharpened shafts,
and again with seventy-three, and yet again with a hundred.
The lord of the Madras, having slain his four chariot-horses in battle,
struck down his charioteer and standard from the seat of the chariot.
Then, quickly leaping down from that chariot whose horses were slain, the great car-warrior—
He stood there, stretching his bow and discharging sharp arrows.
Then Śatānīka, seeing his brother whose mounts had been slain,
swiftly rushed toward him on his chariot while all the world looked on.
Then, in that great battle, the King of Madra pierced Śatānīka as he was approaching with many arrows and dispatched him to the abode of Yama.
When that hero had been slain, Virāṭa, the best of chariot-warriors, [advanced].
He quickly ascended that very chariot adorned with garlands of banners. Then, dilating his eyes in rage and doubling his prowess,
he swiftly covered the chariot of the King of Madra with feathered shafts.

Then the lord of the Madras, enraged, struck Virāṭa, the commander of the army, firmly in the chest with a hundred straight-knotted arrows. Severely pierced, O great king, he sat down on the floor of his chariot.
O bull of the Bharatas, a sharp despondency overcame Virāṭa;
his charioteer then bore him away from the battle, for he was mangled by arrows.
Thereupon, O Bhārata, that great army fled in the night.
Being struck by hundreds of arrows by Śalya, who graces the battlefield,
