they saw that army in flight; O king of kings, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya then proceeded to the place where Śalya was stationed.
But Alambusa, O King, the lord of the Rākṣasas, advanced against them,
mounting an excellent chariot equipped with eight wheels and yoked to horse-faced Piśācas of terrifying appearance.
It had red banners wet with blood, was adorned with crimson garlands,
was made of terrible black iron, and was covered with a great bear-skin; it was driven by a fierce,
multi-colored winged beast that cried out with wide-open eyes.
O King, shining with his upraised beak like the king of vultures as his banner, that Rākṣasa, resembling a heap of crushed collyrium,
blocked the advancing Arjuna, just as the king of mountains obstructs the wind.
O King, as he showered hundreds of volleys of arrows upon Arjuna’s head,
an exceedingly fierce battle took place between the man and the *rākṣasa* in that fray—
a battle that brought joy to vultures, crows, cranes, owls, *kaṅka* birds, and jackals.
O bull of the Bharatas, they produced delight among all who beheld them;
grasping those two bows of great speed and terrible sound, they covered one another, lacerating each other with mighty arrows.
There, for a very long time, the battle remained as if equal.
Then Pārtha, the great archer, brandishing his divine bow,
filled the quarters with arrows and made them resound with the twanging of his bowstring.

Arjuna struck him with a hundred feathered arrows and cut down his lofty standard with nine sharp shafts; he likewise struck the charioteer with three arrows and the triple-bamboo pole with three more.
With one arrow he severed the bow, and with four arrows he struck down the four horses;
with another shaft, he cut his upraised sword in two as he stood deprived of his chariot.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, he pierced him with four sharpened arrows.

Pārtha struck the lord of the Rākṣasas, and being pierced, he fled in fear. Having defeated him, O King, Arjuna quickly approached the vicinity of Droṇa, scattering multitudes of arrows upon men, elephants, and horses.
O great king, being slaughtered by the illustrious Pāṇḍava,
the soldiers fell upon the earth like trees uprooted by the wind,
as they were being destroyed by the high-souled Phalguna.
O lord of the people, the entire army of your sons fled in all directions.
Sañjaya said:
Śatānīka was swiftly consuming your host with his arrows.
O Bhārata, Citrasena, your son, held back the son of Nakula; the son of Nakula, however, deeply pierced Citrasena with a steel-tipped arrow (nārāca),
and he in turn struck him back with ten sharpened shafts.
O great king, Citrasena again struck Śatānīka in the center of the chest with nine sharpened arrows in that battle. Nākuli, for his part, [pierced] his armor with straight-knotted shafts.
He caused it to fall from his body, and that was like a marvel. O King, your son, now divested of his armor, shone intensely,
O Indra among kings, like a serpent that has cast off its skin at the proper time.
Then, O great king, with sharp arrows, the son of Nakula cut down the standard and the bow of his opponent as he strove in the battle.
With his bow shattered and his armor stripped away in that encounter, that great car-warrior—

O great king, he took up another bow capable of rending enemies. Then, in that battle, the enraged Citrasena, a great chariot-warrior among the Bharatas, swiftly pierced the son of Nakula with nine arrows.
Then, O Sire, Śatānīka, that best of men, filled with rage, slew Citrasena’s four horses and his charioteer.
Thereupon, the great car-warrior Citrasena leaped down from that chariot.
The mighty warrior struck Nākulin with twenty-five arrows. As he was performing that deed in battle, the son of Nakula cut his gem-adorned bow with a crescent-headed shaft.
With his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
he quickly ascended the chariot of the high-souled Hārdikya. Meanwhile, Drupada, that great car-warrior, together with his army, sought to reach Droṇa.
Then Vṛṣasena quickly advanced, scattering hundreds of arrows;
but Yajñasena, O sinless one, pierced that great car-warrior, the son of Karṇa, in the arms and chest with sixty shafts in that battle.
But Vṛṣasena, filled with rage, struck Yajñasena, who stood upon his chariot,
between the breasts with many sharp arrows.
In that battle, both of them had their limbs pierced by arrows and were covered with thorns of shafts.
O great king,
with their armor pierced by gold-feathered arrows with straight points,
and drenched in streams of blood, the two shone in that great battle like two porcupines bristling with quills.
Resplendent like refined gold, wonderful as two *kalpa* trees,
and like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom, they shone upon the field of battle.
Then, O King, Vṛṣasena struck Drupada with nine arrows.

Having pierced him, he struck him again with seventy arrows and then with three more. Struck by Vṛṣasena’s arrows, the lord of the earth retreated. Then, discharging thousands of arrows, he shone forth.
O great king, like a raining cloud, the son of Karṇa [showered arrows].
Then Drupada, filled with rage, cut Vṛṣasena’s bow in two with a sharp, yellow broad-headed shaft.
Taking up another bow, new, firm, and bound with gold, he drew from his quiver a stainless, yellow, sharp,
and sturdy broad-headed arrow; having fixed it to the bow, he gazed intently at Drupada.
Drawing it back to his ear, he released it, terrifying all the Somakas;
having pierced his heart, it entered the depths of the earth. Struck by Vṛṣasena’s arrow, the king fell into a state of fainting.
Remembering the duty of a charioteer, the driver drove him away;
when that great car-warrior of the Pañcālas had been broken, O king of kings,
Drupada’s army then had its armor shattered by arrows.
O King, as the night grew terrifying, they fled in battle;
with those blazing lamps abandoned on all sides,
O King, the earth shone like a cloudless sky filled with planets.
With their fallen armlets, O great king, the earth shone like a rain-cloud with flashes of lightning during the monsoon season. Then,
terrified of Karṇa’s son, the Somakas fled in all directions.
Just as the Dānavas were terrified by the fear of Indra during the Tārakāmaya war,
so too the Somakas, being afflicted by him in battle and fleeing,
shone forth, O Great King, illuminated by their lamps.
Having conquered them in battle, O Bhārata, the son of Karṇa shone like the sun when it has reached midday;
among those thousands of kings, both yours and the enemy's.
The powerful Vṛṣasena stood alone, blazing with splendor;
having defeated the heroic great chariot-warriors of the Somakas in battle,
he proceeded swiftly to where King Yudhiṣṭhira was.
Then, as Prativindhya, enraged and consuming his enemies in battle,
advanced, your son Duḥśāsana, a great car-warrior, went out against him;
O King, the encounter between those two was truly wondrous to behold.
O great king,
when Prativindhya was performing difficult feats in battle,
the great car-warriors in your army honored him, like the planets Mercury and Venus in a cloudless sky.
Duḥśāsana pierced him in the forehead with three arrows.
Deeply pierced by your powerful archer son,
that mighty-armed one shone like a mountain with its peaks.
But in that battle, the great car-warrior Prativindhya, having pierced Duḥśāsana with nine arrows, struck him again with seven. Therein, O Bhārata, your son performed a difficult feat.
With fierce arrows, he struck down Prativindhya’s horses;
with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla), he felled his charioteer and brought down his banner;
and, O King, he shattered the chariot of that archer into a hundred pieces.

O Lord, filled with rage, he cut the banners, quivers, reins, and yokes into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his straight-jointed arrows. Deprived of his chariot, that righteous-souled one stood firm, bow in hand.
He fought your son, scattering many hundreds of arrows;
with a razor-sharp shaft, he cut off his bow like one of practiced hand. Then, he struck him with ten broad-headed arrows once his bow had been severed.
Seeing him there deprived of his chariot, his brothers, who were great car-warriors,
rushed forward with speed along with a vast army.
Then he leaped onto the radiant vehicle of Sutasoma.
O great king, seizing his bow, he pierced your son;
then all your men, surrounding your son and accompanied by a vast army, advanced against him in battle.
Then, O Bhārata, at that terrible hour of midnight, a battle commenced between your men and theirs, increasing the population of Yama’s kingdom. Sañjaya said:
As Nakula was impetuously slaughtering your army in battle, the son of Subala, filled with rage, rushed against him and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Those two heroes, having long been enemies, were each desirous of slaying the other.
They struck each other with arrows released from bows drawn to their full stretch.
Just as the son of Subala quickly discharged showers of arrows,
even so did Nakula, O King, displaying his skill in battle.
Then those two heroes in battle, bristling with arrows,
O great king, shone like two *śālmali* trees covered in thorns;
and they gazed at each other askance, O king, with wide-open eyes.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, as if burning each other to ashes,
your enraged brother-in-law pierced the son of Mādrī in the heart with a single sharp, barbed arrow, as if laughing.
But Nakula, deeply pierced by your brother-in-law, the archer,
sat down upon the seat of his chariot, and a faintness came over him.
Seeing his enemy, that proud and ultimate adversary, fallen into such a state, he was overcome.
O King, the bird let out a cry like a rain-cloud at the end of the summer heat. Then,
having regained consciousness, Nakula, the son of Pāṇḍu,
rushed again toward the son of Subala like Death with his mouth wide open.
Enraged, O bull of the Bharatas, he pierced Śakuni with sixty arrows,
and again with another hundred iron shafts in the middle of his chest.
Then he severed his bow, along with the arrow fixed to it, at the handle.
Quickly cutting down the standard,
Nakula, the son of Pāṇḍu, felled it from the chariot to the ground; and with a single sharp, yellow, whetted arrow, he pierced through both thighs.
Then, with his winged falcon brought down by the hunter,
he was deeply pierced, O Great King, and sat down upon the floor of the chariot,
clinging to the flagpole like a lover to his beloved.
O sinless one, seeing your brother-in-law fallen unconscious,
the charioteer quickly bore him away from the front of the army by means of the chariot. Then the Pārthas and those who were their followers raised a great cry.
Having conquered his enemies in battle, Nakula, the scorcher of foes, spoke angrily to his charioteer: "Carry me toward Drona's army.
Hearing those words of the wise son of Madri, [the charioteer obeyed].
O King, he advanced in battle toward where Droṇa was fighting. But against Śikhaṇḍin, who was seeking to reach Droṇa in the encounter, O Lord of the People,
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, exerted himself and rushed forward with great speed.
As the subduer of enemies, Gautama, was swiftly approaching Drona,
Śikhaṇḍin, as if laughing, pierced him with nine broad-headed arrows. O great king, having been thus struck, the Preceptor pierced him in return with five swift shafts.
Then, acting for your pleasure, he pierced him back with twenty arrows.
O lord of the people, a great battle ensued between those two, terrible in form,
like the battle between Śambara and the king of the gods in the war between the Devas and Asuras.
Those two great chariot-warriors, heroes intoxicated with the pride of battle, covered the sky with a net of arrows like two clouds at the end of the summer heat; that sky,
already terrible by nature, became even more terrifying.
And that night, O best of the Bharatas, for the warriors who were intent on battle,
was like the Night of Doom— terrible in form and inspiring fear.
But Śikhaṇḍin, O great king, [cut down] the great bow of Gautama.
Then, with a crescent-shaped arrow, he severed that [bow] together with its string and shaft.
O King, Kṛpa, enraged by him, hurled a terrible spear—
gold-handled, with an unblunted tip, and polished by a smith.

As it was falling toward him, Śikhaṇḍin cut it apart with many arrows; blazing and emitting great radiance, it fell to the earth, illuminating it. Then Gautama, the best of chariot-warriors, took up another bow.
O great king, he covered Śikhaṇḍin with sharp arrows;
being thus shrouded in battle by the illustrious Gautama,
Śikhaṇḍin, the best of chariot-warriors, sank down upon the seat of his chariot.
O Bhārata, seeing him sinking in battle, Kṛpa Śāradvata struck him with many arrows as if wishing to kill him;
he beheld that great car-warrior, the son of Yajñasena, turned away from the fight.
The Pāñcālas and the Somakas surrounded him on all sides,
and likewise your sons, together with a vast army, surrounded that best of the twice-born; then the battle commenced once more.
O King, as the chariots rushed at one another in battle,
there arose a tumultuous noise like that of roaring clouds; likewise, O lord of the people, there was the sound of charging cavalry and elephants.
O King, the battlefield shone with mutual cruelty on all sides; O Great King, the earth trembled at the sound of the rushing foot-soldiers, like a woman terrified by fear.

O King, having encountered one another, many chariots rushed forward with even greater speed and seized their opponents, just as crows seize locusts. Likewise, great elephants in rut seized other elephants that were already maddened with rut.
O Bhārata, on that very spot they exerted themselves to hold their ground; having encountered one another—
horsemen meeting horsemen and foot-soldiers meeting foot-soldiers—
they closed in upon each other in battle and, being enraged, did not retreat.
As the soldiers ran, rushed forward, and even turned back again, a most tumultuous noise arose from the troops there in the night;
and lamps were blazing upon the chariots, elephants, and horses.
O great king, they appeared like massive meteors fallen from the sky;
O best of the Bharatas, that night, illuminated by those lamps,
became like day at the head of the battlefield, O King.
Just as the darkness pervading the world perishes when the sun appears,
so too was the terrible darkness destroyed by the blazing lamps that adorned [the place],
reaching as far as heaven, earth, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate points.
Pervaded by dust and darkness, yet again illuminated by splendor, all the radiance of the weapons, the armor, and the jewels of the great-souled ones vanished,
eclipsed by the light of those lamps.
While that tumultuous battle was raging at the onset of night,
O Bhārata, no one could distinguish himself, thinking "I am this person.
In that conflict, O best of the Bharatas, a father slew his own son.
Out of delusion, a son struck his father, as did a friend his friend; likewise, a kinsman struck a kinsman, and a maternal cousin struck his uncle.
Thus, both their own kin and those of others slaughtered one another.
The battle that took place at night was limitless, terrible, and inspiring of fear.
Sañjaya said:
While that most tumultuous and terrifying battle was proceeding...
O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna advanced against Droṇa himself;
polishing his excellent bow and repeatedly drawing the string,
he approached Droṇa’s chariot adorned with gold.

O great king, as Dhṛṣṭadyumna advanced with the desire to bring about Droṇa’s end, the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas surrounded him. Seeing that Droṇa, the best of teachers, was thus surrounded, [the warriors stood firm].
Your sons, exerting themselves on all sides, protected Droṇa in the battle. Then, at the onset of night,
those two oceans of armies clashed like two terrifying seas, tossed by the wind and agitated with living creatures.
Then, O great king, the prince of the Pañcālas quickly pierced Droṇa in the heart with five arrows and let out a lion’s roar.
Having struck him with twenty-five arrows in that battle, O Bhārata, Droṇa—
With another broad-headed arrow, he cut through his opponent’s bow of great luster.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, pierced by Droṇa, O bull of the Bharatas,
quickly cast aside his bow and bit his lip.
Then, O great king, the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna, filled with rage,
took up another excellent bow, desiring to bring about Droṇa’s end. Drawing that variegated bow back to his ear, the slayer of enemy heroes—
Then he discharged a terrible arrow, the end-maker of Droṇa. Released by that powerful one in the great battle, that fierce shaft illuminated the army like the risen sun.
Seeing that terrible arrow, the gods, gandharvas, and humans spoke these words: "O King, may it be well with Droṇa in battle!
But that shaft, before reaching the preceptor’s chariot—
O King, Karṇa, with great dexterity, cut that arrow into twelve pieces. O noble one, O King, severed into many fragments by the son of the Sūta,
that shaft, mangled by Karṇa’s arrows, fell swiftly to the ground.
Having cut down that arrow in battle with straight-jointed shafts,
Karṇa pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the fray with ten arrows;
Drona’s son pierced him with five, and Drona himself with seven.
Śalya pierced the Pāñcālya prince with nine arrows, Duḥśāsana likewise with three, Duryodhana with twenty,
and Śakuni with five; all those great car-warriors struck him swiftly.
Pierced by those seven heroes in battle for the sake of protecting Droṇa,
O King, he unperturbedly pierced them all back with three arrows each;
he struck Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, and your own son.
Having pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna with their bows in that battle,
those two best of chariot-warriors quickly struck him back with five arrows each.
But Drumasena, O King, being enraged, pierced him with a feathered shaft.
With three other arrows he quickly struck him, saying, "Stay! Stay!
But he (the opponent) pierced him in return with three sharp, straight-flying shafts—gold-feathered, whetted on stone, and capable of ending life in battle.

Then, with another broad-headed arrow, the valiant hero struck off Drumasena’s head— adorned with earrings blazing with gold— from his body. That head fell to the ground in battle, its lips bitten together.
Seeing Dyumatsena slain like a ripe palm fruit blown down by a great wind, the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
O King, rushed toward Karṇa with many sharp arrows.
Having pierced those heroes again with well-sharpened arrows,
the hero [Arjuna] cut the bow of the son of Rādhā— who fought with such skill— with broad-headed shafts (bhalla). Karna, however, could not endure that severing of his bow.
Like a fierce lion tearing at a tail,
he took up another bow, his eyes red with rage and panting,
and rained down a shower of arrows upon the mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
But seeing Karṇa enraged, those six heroic bulls among chariot-warriors quickly surrounded the son of the Pāñcālya king with the intent to kill him—
him who was placed at the forefront of those six preeminent warriors of your side.
"We considered Dhṛṣṭadyumna to have already entered the jaws of Death.
At that very moment, however, Sātyaki of the Daśārha clan, scattering his arrows,
came to the rescue of the valiant Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
As that great archer Sātyaki, who is fierce in battle, was approaching,
the son of Rādhā pierced him with ten straight-flying arrows.
O great king, Sātyaki in turn pierced him with ten shafts.
While all the heroes were looking on, he cried out, "Do not go! Stay!
Then there occurred a terrible encounter between the mighty Sātyaki and the high-souled Karṇa, like that between Bali and Vāsava.
Terrifying the Kṣatriyas with the sound of his palms, that bull among Kṣatriyas,
the mighty Sātyaki, made the earth tremble as if with the roar of his bow, and pierced Karṇa, whose eyes were like lotuses.
O great king, the Sūta’s son fought against Sātyaki;
Karṇa pierced the descendant of Śini with hundreds of arrows, including *vipāṭhas*, *karṇis*, *nārācas*, *vatsadantas*, and *kṣuras*.
Likewise, Yuyudhāna, the preeminent car-warrior of the Vṛṣṇis, showered Karna with arrows; that battle became equal [in intensity].
And your men, O great king, as well as the armored son of Karna, [rushed forward].
They quickly pierced Sātyaki from all sides with sharpened arrows. O Lord,
having warded off their weapons and those of Karṇa with his own weapons,
the enraged Sātyaki pierced Vṛṣasena between the breasts.
Pierced by that arrow, O lord of the people, the heroic Vṛṣasena collapsed unconscious upon his chariot, casting aside his bow.
Then Karṇa, the great car-warrior, believing Vṛṣasena to have been slain, [was overcome with grief].
Tormented by grief for his son, he afflicted Sātyaki in return. But Yuyudhāna, that great car-warrior, being thus oppressed by Karṇa, quickly pierced Karṇa with many arrows again and again.
Having pierced Karṇa with ten arrows and Vṛṣasena with seven, the Sātvata hero cut off the hands and the bows of those two. They,
having strung other bows that struck fear into their enemies, [continued the fight].
They both pierced Yuyudhāna from all sides with sharpened arrows.
While that battle, which caused the destruction of the best of heroes,
was raging, O King, the great roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow was heard exceedingly loud.
O King, having heard the rattling of the chariot and the twang of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
the Sūta’s son spoke these words to Duryodhana:
"Having slain all the Śibis and the foremost among those bulls among men,"
The great sound of the *gāṇḍīva* bow, as Pārtha wielded that supreme weapon, struck terror into the mighty archers of the Paurava clan;
he remained fixed right there.
"The roar of a chariot is heard, like the thundering of Vāsava;
clearly, the Pāṇḍava is performing an action suited to himself.
O King, this army of the Bharatas is being torn asunder in many ways."
The scattered divisions never stand firm;
like a mass of clouds driven apart by the wind,
they are shattered upon encountering Savyasācin, like a broken boat in the ocean.
O King, the great roar of hundreds of leading warriors fleeing as they are pierced by arrows discharged from the Gāṇḍīva is heard,
O tiger among kings, like thunder in the sky at midnight.
Hear the various kinds of sounds—both cries of "Alas! and abundant lion-roars—coming from Arjuna’s chariot. Here stands Satyaki, the lowest of the Sātvatas, positioned in our midst.
If our objective can be achieved here, we shall conquer all our enemies. This son of the King of the Pañcālas has encountered Droṇa,
O King, and is surrounded on all sides by warriors who are the best among men.
"O Great King, if we slay both Sātyaki and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
our victory will undoubtedly be certain.
Let us surround these two heroic great-chariot warriors, just as we did the son of Subhadrā."
"O great king, let us strive to slay the Vṛṣṇi and the Pārṣata!
O Bhārata, Savyasācin advances against Droṇa’s army,
having perceived that Sātyaki is engaged with many of the foremost Kuru warriors."
Let many of the most excellent and preeminent chariot-warriors go there, before Pārtha realizes that Sātyaki is surrounded by many. Therefore, O heroes, hasten greatly to discharge your arrows.
"O Great King, act with well-applied wisdom so that this Mādhava may swiftly depart for the next world. Having understood Karṇa’s opinion, your son spoke to the son of Subala.
O King, just as Indra spoke to the illustrious Viṣṇu in battle,
surrounded by ten thousand elephants that never retreat and surrounded by ten thousand chariots, [he said: "Go against Dhanañjaya!"
Duḥśāsana, Durviṣaha, Subāhu, and Duṣpradharṣaṇa—
these, surrounded by many foot soldiers, will follow you.
O mighty-armed uncle, slay the two Kṛṣṇas and Dharmarāja as well.

O Bhārata, my hope for victory rests in you, just as it rests in Devendra among the gods— [in you] who are like Nakula, Sahadeva, and Bhīmasena. O maternal uncle, slay the sons of Kuntī, just as the son of Pāvaka [Svāhā’s husband] slew the Asuras.
Thus addressed by your son, O Lord, the son of Subala departed for the sons of Pṛthā,
accompanied by a vast army as well as your sons,
desiring to consume the descendants of Pāṇḍu for the sake of pleasing your sons.
Then,
O King, when the son of Subala had advanced against the army of the Pāṇḍavas, a battle commenced between your men and the enemies;
for the Sūtaputra, joined by a great force, [attacked] the Sātvata.
He rushed forward swiftly in battle, scattering many hundreds of arrows;
likewise, all the Pāṇḍavas surrounded Sātyaki.
Then the son of Bharadvāja proceeded toward the chariot of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Then, O Bhārata, there occurred a great battle at night between Droṇa and the heroic Dhṛṣṭadyumna, as well as the high-souled Pāñcālas. Sañjaya said:
Then they all rushed forward in haste, intoxicated by the frenzy of battle, unable to endure him and enraged as they advanced toward the chariot of Yuyudhāna.
O King, they came with well-equipped chariots adorned with gold and silver.
With horsemen and elephants, they surrounded the Sātvata;
then, having hemmed him in on all sides, those great car-warriors let out lion-roars, threatening Satyaki.
Those highly powerful warriors, hastening and desiring the death of the Mādhava, rained sharp arrows upon Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth.
Seeing them falling swiftly, the descendant of Śini, the slayer of enemy heroes, [acted].
Receiving [the challenge], the mighty-armed one released many arrows;
there, the heroic and great archer Sātyaki, who is difficult to vanquish in battle,
cut off heads with fierce, straight-knotted shafts.
With razor-sharp arrows, that Mādhava struck down the elephant-trunks, the horse-necks, and even the arms still grasping weapons of your men;
and with fallen yak-tail fans and white umbrellas, O Bhārata, the field was strewn.
O Lord, the earth became filled with them like the sky with stars;
and as they fought in battle against Yuyudhāna, O Bhārata,
there arose a tumultuous roar like the wailing of the departed spirits.
The earth was filled with that great sound,
and the night became intensely fierce and terrifying. Seeing the army being torn asunder, struck by the arrows of Yuyudhāna, [he saw it] being shattered.
O King, having heard that great and hair-raising roar at midnight,
your son, the best among chariot-warriors, spoke repeatedly to his charioteer, saying, "Drive the horses to where this sound comes from."
Urged on by him, the charioteer then drove those excellent horses toward the chariot of Yuyudhāna. Thereupon, Duryodhana, enraged, firm with his bow, and having conquered all fatigue, [advanced].
Swift-handed and a versatile warrior, he rushed toward Yuyudhāna. Then, with twelve arrows released from a fully drawn bow— meat and blood-eaters— the descendant of Madhu pierced Duryodhana.
Duryodhana, having already been afflicted by him with arrows in that manner,
pierced the descendant of Śini in return with ten shafts, filled with indignation.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, a tumultuous battle ensued.
A terrible conflict took place between all the Pāñcālas and the Bhāratas. Then, O Bhārata,
the grandson of Śini, enraged in battle, pierced your son, that great car-warrior,
in the chest with eighty arrows.
Then, in that battle, he sent his horses to the abode of Yama with his arrows;
and with a feathered shaft, he swiftly struck down the charioteer from the chariot.
O lord of the people, your son remained standing on that chariot whose horses had been slain.
He loosed sharpened arrows toward the chariot of Śini’s grandson;
but Śini’s grandson, with great dexterity, O King, cut down those fifty arrows dispatched by your son in that battle.

Then, O noble one, with another broad-headed arrow, Rabhasa impetuously severed the great bow of your son at the handle in that battle. Thus deprived of his chariot and his bow, the lord and master of all the worlds remained there.
He quickly ascended the radiant chariot of Kṛtavarman. When Duryodhana had turned back, O lord of the people, the grandson of Śini put your army to flight with his arrows in the middle of the night.
O King, Śakuni, surrounding Arjuna on all sides with many thousands of chariots, thousands of elephants,
and likewise thousands of horses, raised a tumultuous uproar everywhere.
Scattering great celestial weapons toward Arjuna,
those Kṣatriyas, impelled by Time, fought against Arjuna.
Arjuna [encountered] those thousands of chariots, elephants, and horses.
Exerting himself and causing great destruction, he warded him off;
then, in that battle, the heroic Śakuni, son of Subala,
pierced Arjuna with sharpened arrows as if laughing.
Then, in that battle, the son of Subala, his eyes copper-red with rage, being himself furious, pierced Arjuna, the slayer of enemies, violently with twenty arrows;
and once again, he obstructed that great car-warrior with a hundred more.
O Bhārata, Arjuna, however, pierced him with twenty arrows in that battle;
then he pierced the other great archers with three arrows each.
O King, having warded them off with multitudes of shafts in the fray, Dhanañjaya prevailed.
He slaughtered your warriors like the wielder of the thunderbolt slaying the asuras;
with thousands of severed arms and bodies strewn across the earth, O great king,
the ground there shone as if covered with flowers.
With heads adorned with diadems, beautiful noses, and lovely earrings; with lips bitten in rage and eyes likewise bulging out;
wearing golden neck-ornaments and crest-jewels—those who had been so dear to the kṣatriyas.
The earth shone as if strewn with fallen lotuses;
having performed that fierce deed, Bībhatsu of formidable prowess pierced Śakuni again with five straight-knotted arrows.
He struck Ulūka with three great iron arrows; pierced by him, Ulūka, his prowess doubled by rage,
pierced Arjuna in return with many thousands of shafts.
Having pierced him thus, Ulūka struck Vāsudeva and let out a great roar, filling the surface of the earth. Arjuna, however, moving swiftly, severed Śakuni’s bow.
And he led the four horses toward the abode of Yama. Then, O bull of the Bharatas, O lord of people, the son of Subala leaped down from his chariot and quickly mounted the chariot of Ulūka.
Those two great chariot-warriors, father and son, mounted upon a single chariot,
showered Pārtha with arrows like two risen clouds drenching a mountain.
Having pierced them both, O great king, the son of Pāṇḍu struck them with sharpened shafts.
Routing your army, he scattered it in hundreds with his arrows;
O King, lord of the people, your forces were dispersed on all sides like clouds torn asunder by the wind.
O best of the Bharatas, that army, being thus slaughtered in the night,
fled in all directions, looking about, afflicted by fear;
others, abandoning their mounts in the battle, urged them on [to flee].
In that dreadful darkness, they ran about in confusion.
Having defeated your warriors in battle, O bull of the Bharatas,
Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya, filled with joy, blew their conchs.
O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, having pierced Droṇa with three arrows,
quickly severed the string of his bow with a sharp shaft.
Then Droṇa, the crusher of kṣatriyas, placed that bow back into its quiver.
The hero took up another bow, more powerful and stronger. Then, O King, Drona, having pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna with seven swift arrows,
struck his charioteer with five shafts in that battle.
Having quickly warded him off with arrows, the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna then scattered the Kaurava army by the hundreds and thousands.
While that force was being slaughtered, O Sire, of your son...
A terrible river, with waves of surging blood,
began to flow between the two armies, carrying away men, horses, and elephants,
O King, like the Vaitaraṇī leading toward the city of Yama’s realm.
Having routed that army, the powerful and radiant Dhṛṣṭadyumna shone exceedingly, like Śakra among the hosts of gods. Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin blew their great conch shells.
The twins, Yuyudhāna, and Vṛkodara the Pāṇḍava—
at this very time, O Sire, the great car-warrior, the son of the Sūta,
wrought a terrible slaughter among the Pāṇḍava troops.
Having defeated thousands of chariots belonging to your men,
the great car-warriors among the Pāṇḍavas, appearing radiant with victory, let out lion-like roars while your son and Karṇa looked on, both intoxicated with pride.
Likewise, O lord of the people, [it was so] for the heroic Droṇa and for the son of Droṇa.
Sañjaya said:
Having seen his own army fleeing while being slaughtered by those high-souled ones, [Duryodhana spoke].
O lord of the people, possessed by great wrath, your son approached Karna and Drona— the best among victors— and, overcome by indignation,
that master of speech uttered these words.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, Duryodhana urged on Droṇa and Karṇa; they both quickly fell under the sway of indignation. "The battle here has been set in motion by you two in your wrath."
Having seen the ruler of the Sindhus slain in battle by Savyasācin,
and seeing my army being slaughtered by the force of the Pāṇḍavas, you two—
though capable of victory over them— looked on as if you were powerless.
"O givers of honor, if I am to be abandoned by you, then I should not have been told at that time:
'We two shall defeat the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle. Had I heard those words from you then, with your full consent,"
He has created enmity with the Pāṇḍavas that will lead to the destruction of warriors.
O bulls among men, if I am not to be abandoned by you two,
let these two of great prowess fight with their own corresponding valor.

"I had indeed initiated this vast war by relying on a great army against you two along with the Pāṇḍavas, yet all of that has been rendered useless. Those two heroes have been goaded by your son with the whip of his words."
Like two serpents that have been struck, the two of them engaged in battle;
then those two best of chariot-warriors, the foremost archers in all the world,
rushed against the Pārthas led by Śaineya in the fray.
In that same manner, the sons of Pṛthā, united and surrounded by their own army,
advanced against those two heroes who were roaring again and again.
Then Droṇa, the great archer, [struck] the bull of the Śinis with ten arrows.
The best among all wielders of weapons, enraged, swiftly pierced him;
Karna struck with ten arrows, your son with seven,
Vṛṣasena with ten, and the son of Subala also with seven.
O Kaurava, these [warriors] surrounded the descendant of Śini in the tumultuous battle;
meanwhile, Droṇa dispatched the Pāñcālas who had arrived there to the abode of Yama.
At that very moment, however, the great car-warrior, the son of the Sūta, [advanced].
O King, Karṇa, the great archer, having set his mind upon a most formidable battle, quickly advanced toward the chariot of Dhṛṣṭadyumna;
and he beheld Droṇa in the fray, slaughtering the Pāṇḍava host.
The Somakas quickly pierced him from all sides with showers of arrows.
Then, O lord of the people, Drona took away the lives of the Kshatriyas,
just as the sun, O King, destroys the darkness with its rays, O Bharata.
O lord of the people, as the Pāñcālas were being slaughtered by Droṇa,
a tumultuous sound was heard from them as they cried out to one another—
some for their sons, some for their fathers, and others for their brothers and maternal uncles.
Abandoning their sister's sons, their friends, as well as their kinsmen and relatives, they depart in haste, desiring to live;
yet others, deluded by ignorance, go directly toward him.
The warriors of the Pāṇḍavas in battle likewise went to the other world;
thus, O King, that Pāṇḍava army, being slaughtered by those high-souled ones,
fled in the night, casting away thousands of torches.
While Bhīmasena, Vijaya, Acyuta, the twins, the son of Dharma, and the son of Pṛṣata were looking on,
the world was shrouded in darkness and nothing could be discerned.
By the light of the Kauravas, the enemies were seen fleeing;
and as that army was retreating, O King, the two great car-warriors Droṇa and Karṇa struck at its rear, scattering many arrows.
When the Pāñcālas had been broken and were being routed on all sides,
Janārdana, with a heavy heart, addressed Phalguna:
"These two great archers, Droṇa and Karṇa, [are facing] the son of Pṛṣata and Sātyaki."
Together, they struck the Pāñcālas violently with their arrows.
By the rain of shafts from these two, our great car-warriors were shattered;
O son of Kuntī, though being restrained, the army could not stand its ground.
Seeing her fleeing, Keśava and Arjuna said:
"Do not flee in terror; cast away your fear, O Pāṇḍavas!
Here we both stand against all these armies, properly arrayed and with weapons raised."
Let us strive to restrain both Droṇa and the Sūta’s son;
for these two are powerful, heroic, skilled in weapons, and boastful of victory. If neglected, they, being enraged, will destroy our army this very night.
While the two of them were thus conversing, the one of terrible deeds and great strength,
this fierce Bhīma, returned once more with his army and advanced. Seeing Vṛkodara approaching in that manner, Janārdana [spoke] there.
O King, as if gladdening the Pāṇḍava, he spoke once more:
"Here is Bhīma, who delights in battle, surrounded by the Somakas and the Pāṇḍavas;
filled with rage, he approaches with speed against the mighty Droṇa and Karṇa."

"Fight together with him against the great car-warriors of the Pañcālas, O son of Pāṇḍu, for the sake of encouraging all the troops. Then those two tigers among men, both Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava, [prepared for battle].
Having encountered Droṇa and Karṇa, they stood firm at the forefront of the battle.
Then that great army of Yudhiṣṭhira turned back once more;
thereafter, both Droṇa and Karṇa crushed the enemies in combat.
O King, that tumultuous and great battle broke out at night, like the clash of two oceans swollen by the rising of the moon. Then,
your army cast away the lamps from their hands.
At the close of the day, he fought with the Pāṇḍavas like one possessed by madness,
while the world was shrouded in an exceedingly dreadful cloud of dust and darkness;
seeking victory, they fought by means of their names and lineages alone.
For their names were being heard, O great king,
as they were called out by the kings striking one another in battle, as if at a svayaṃvara;
yet suddenly it became silent, and once again a great roar arose.
O best of the Kurus, wherever those lamps were seen among the angry warriors— whether they were fighting, victorious, or even being defeated—
there those heroes fell like moths into the flame.
Thus, as they fought, the deep night became profound for the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas alike, O king of kings. Sañjaya said:
Then Karna, the slayer of enemy heroes, seeing the son of Prishata in battle,
struck him in the chest with ten arrows that pierce the vital organs.
O Sire, Dhrishtadyumna also quickly pierced him in return.
Delighted, he cried out, "Stay! Stay! while striking with five arrows.
Then those two great car-warriors, having covered each other with shafts in that battle, pierced one another again with arrows released from bows drawn to their full stretch.
Then, in that encounter, Karṇa pierced the charioteer and the four horses of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the chief of the Pāñcālas, with his arrows;
he also cut through his excellent bow with sharp shafts.
And with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he felled his charioteer from the seat of the chariot.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
the valiant one quickly leaped down from the chariot, seizing a mace.
Though pierced by Karṇa with straight-jointed arrows,
he approached Karṇa and slew his four horses;
then the son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of enemy heroes, turned back again with great speed.
Having quickly mounted Dhanañjaya’s chariot, that best of chariot-warriors,
though restrained by the son of Dharma, desired to go toward Karṇa;
but Karṇa, possessed of great splendor, [uttered a roar] mingled with a lion’s cry.
He drew his great bow and blew loudly into his conch shell.
Seeing the son of Pṛṣata victorious in battle, those great car-warriors—
the Pañcālas together with the Somakas— were overcome by indignation.

Taking up weapons of every kind for the sake of slaying the son of Śūrasena, they set out toward Karṇa, making death their only point of return. Seizing a terrible iron club, he crushed Karṇa’s horses.
Pierced by him with many arrows resembling venomous serpents,
Yudhiṣṭhira’s army then retreated on foot;
and, O noble one, he ascended the chariot of Sahadeva.
The charioteer also yoked other horses to Karṇa’s chariot— Saindhava steeds, white as conch shells, possessing great speed, and well-trained in drawing the vehicle.
Having found his mark, the son of Rādhā [assailed] the great car-warriors of the Pañcālas.
Exerting himself, he oppressed them with his arrows like a cloud striking mountains;
thus afflicted by Karṇa, that great army of the Pāñcālas fled in extreme terror,
like a doe harassed by a lion.
Men were seen falling swiftly here and there from horses, from elephants, and from chariots onto the surface of the earth;
and at that very time, the son of the Sūta, a great car-warrior, [appeared].
O Bhārata, Karna wrought a terrible slaughter among the Pāṇḍava troops in that great battle;
as a warrior was charging, Karna severed his arms and even his head adorned with earrings with his razor-sharp arrows.
O lord of the people, O honorable one, he cut off the thighs of another who was mounted on an elephant, as well as those of others mounted on the backs of horses or standing on the ground;
and many great car-warriors, as they fled, did not even realize what had happened.
With their own limbs and mounts mangled in the battle,
those Pāñcālas along with the Sṛñjayas, being slaughtered in the fray,
even mistook the mere rustling of grass for the son of the Sūta.
Even their own warriors, fleeing in battle and deprived of their senses, mistook one another for Karṇa; thus, terrified, they fled. O Bhārata, those broken divisions were running away in retreat.
Karna rushed forward swiftly, scattering arrows from behind them;
looking at one another, utterly bewildered and deprived of their senses,
they were unable to stand their ground as they were driven away by that great-souled hero.

O King, struck by Karṇa with his supreme arrows and by Droṇa as well, the Pāñcālas fled in all directions, looking about in terror. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, beholding his own army in flight, [was overcome with grief].
Having resolved to retreat, he spoke these words to Phalguna:
"Behold Karṇa, the great archer, standing with bow in hand at this terrible hour of night, scorching like the sun."

O Pārtha, this incessant sound of your kinsmen crying out like those who are helpless is heard as they are struck down by Karṇa’s arrows; it is heard from him as he is both fitting and releasing his swift shafts.
"I see Jayavikrānta; he will certainly destroy us. O Dhanañjaya, whatever you perceive as the next necessary action for the time being, perform that which is directed toward the slaying of Karṇa."

Thus addressed, the mighty-armed Pārtha then spoke to Kṛṣṇa; King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, was terrified by the extreme prowess of Rādheya. "Since things have come to this pass, what should be done at this time regarding the army of Karṇa? he asked again and again.
"May your lordship decide quickly, for the army is fleeing; O Madhusūdana, there is no standing firm for those who are being driven by Droṇa’s arrows, broken,
and terrified by Karṇa."
And I see Karṇa roaming about fearlessly,
scattering sharp arrows at the noble chariot-warriors as they flee;
I cannot endure this conduct of his at the forefront of the battle.
"O tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, it is as evident as a snake feeling the touch of a foot.
Therefore, may you go quickly to where the great chariot-warrior Karṇa is;
I shall slay him, and not he me, O Madhusūdana."
Vāsudeva said:
"O son of Kuntī, I behold Karṇa, that tiger among men of superhuman prowess, moving about in battle like the king of the gods."
"O Dhanañjaya, tiger among men, there is no one else in battle who can advance against him except for you or the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca; yet,
O sinless one, I do not yet consider the time for you to go to be right."
O mighty-armed one, [he awaits] his encounter with the Sūta’s son in battle;
for that Vāsavi weapon of his stands blazing like a great meteor.
Indeed, O mighty-armed one, it assumes a fierce form for your sake.
For this spear is being guarded by the Sūta’s son in battle;
let the mighty Ghaṭotkaca, therefore, advance against the son of Rādhā.
For he was born of Bhīma, the mighty one, and possesses the prowess of a god;
in him are divine, Rākṣasa, and Āsura weapons.
Ghaṭotkaca is constantly devoted to you and desires your welfare.
"He will conquer Karṇa in battle; of this I have no doubt.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Pārtha, the mighty-armed lotus-eyed one—
Then that Rākṣasa summoned himself, and he appeared before them,
O lord of the people, clad in armor, bearing arrows, a sword, and a bow.
Having then saluted Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya, he stood there.
Then, being delighted, he said to him, "I am here; instruct me.
Thereupon, the descendant of Daśārha, as if smiling, addressed the son of Hiḍimbā—who resembled a cloud, with a blazing face and glowing earrings—saying:
"O Ghaṭotkaca, my son, understand that which I shall tell you:
this is the time for your prowess to be displayed, and not for anyone else.
You must be like a raft for your kinsmen who are sinking."
"You possess various weapons and Rākṣasa illusions;
behold, O son of Hiḍimbā, how Karṇa is driving the army of the Pāṇḍavas at the front of the battle,
like cattle being driven by a herdsman."
This Karṇa, a great archer, wise and of firm prowess,
slays the bulls among the Kṣatriyas within the ranks of the Pāṇḍavas;
these men of strong bows scatter vast showers of arrows.
Oppressed by the flame-like arrows of the Suta’s son at midnight, they are unable to stand their ground; tormented by that shower of shafts,
these Pāñcālas flee like deer out of fear of a lion.
"O you of terrible prowess, there exists no other restrainer of this son of a Sūta, who has thus grown powerful in battle, except for you. Therefore,
O mighty-armed one, perform here that deed which is appropriate for yourself."

It is for the sake of the splendor and the power of weapons of their maternal uncles and their fathers that men desire sons, O son of Hiḍimbā. How might he deliver us from suffering? Therefore, you must deliver your kinsmen.
"O Ghaṭotkaca, fathers desire sons for their own sake,
thinking that those who are beneficial will rescue them from this world in the world beyond.
For your weapon-power is terrible, O Bhīma, and your illusions are difficult to overcome."
O son of Bhīma, O scorcher of foes, as you constantly fight in battle,
become the further shore for the Pāṇḍavas who have been broken by Karṇa with his sharp arrows and are sinking among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
For at night, the Rākṣasas become even more possessed of immeasurable prowess;
they are powerful, exceedingly difficult to withstand, heroic, and move with great valor.
Slay Karṇa, that great archer, in battle during the dead of night by means of your illusory power.
"The sons of Pṛthā, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, will slay Droṇa.
Having heard these words of Keśava, O Kauravya, Bībhatsu also addressed the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, the tamer of foes.
"O Ghaṭotkaca, you, the long-armed Sātyaki,
and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava— these three, in my judgment, are the foremost among all the troops.
Therefore, may you go forth and engage Karna in a single combat by night."
The great car-warrior Sātyaki shall be your protector from the rear; O hero, supported by the Sātvata, slay the heroic Karṇa in battle,
just as Indra in former times slew Tāraka with Skanda as his companion.
Ghaṭotkaca said:
"O mighty-armed lord, it is exactly as you say to me;
commanded by you, I shall go with the desire to slay Karṇa."
"I am indeed a match for Karṇa and a match for Droṇa,
O best of men, as well as for other high-souled Kṣatriyas skilled in weapons;
today, in the night, I shall give battle to that son of a Sūta."
As long as the earth shall endure, people will speak of him;
and here I shall not spare the brave, nor the timid, nor those with palms joined in supplication—
I shall slay them all, abiding by the duty of a Rākṣasa.
Saṃjaya said:
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed son of Hiḍimbā, the slayer of enemy heroes,
rushed toward Karṇa in that tumultuous fray, terrifying your army.

As he charged forward, enraged like a serpent with a flaming mouth, the son of the Sūta, that supreme archer, received him while discharging his own arrows. A battle then took place between those two, Karṇa and the Rākṣasa, in the night.
"O tiger among kings, they roared like Śakra and Prahlāda.
Saṃjaya said:
"While that battle between Karṇa and the Rākṣasa was thus proceeding,"
O King, seeing Ghaṭotkaca proceeding with great haste toward the chariot of the Sūta’s son, desiring to slay Karṇa in battle,
your son spoke these words to Duḥśāsana:

"Having seen this prowess of Karṇa in battle, this Rākṣasa quickly advances toward Karṇa; therefore, restrain that great car-warrior. Surrounded by a vast army, go to where that one of great strength is."
Karna Vaikartana desires to fight with the Rakshasa in battle.
O giver of honor, protect Karna in the fray with diligence, surrounded by your army;
let not the terrible Rakshasa destroy Karna through negligence.
In the meantime, O King, the powerful son of Jaṭāsura,
the best among strikers, approached Duryodhana and said:
"O Duryodhana, your enemies are renowned and intoxicated with the pride of battle."
"Commanded by you, I wish to slay the Pāṇḍavas along with their followers.
In former times, my father Jaṭāsura, the leader of the Rākṣasas,
was struck down by those base sons of Pṛthā after he had employed a rite intended to destroy the Rākṣasas."
"O Lord, commanded by you, I wish to go and pay my respects to him;
O Indra among kings, you ought to grant me permission to do so with the flesh of enemies today— [to offer it] to all the sons of Kuntī, headed by Vāsudeva."
"Having slain them, I shall devour my sons along with my followers.
Then the king, being greatly pleased, said to him again and again:
"Together with Droṇa, Karṇa, and the others, I am sufficient for the slaughter of my enemies."
But you, commanded by me, go and slay Ghaṭotkaca in battle—
that Rākṣasa of cruel deeds, born of a Rākṣasa and a human,
who is ever devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas and is a destroyer of elephants, horses, and chariots.
"Send him through the air in battle to the abode of Yama!
Having said "So be it," the massive-bodied one summoned Ghaṭotkaca;
thus commanded by your son, the mighty one replied, "So be it."
Jaṭāsuri covered the son of Bhīmasena with various weapons; and the son of Hiḍimbā alone crushed Alambala, Karṇa, and the invincible Kuru army, just as a great wind scatters the clouds.
Then, seeing that the chariot was composed of illusion, Alambala swiftly struck Ghaṭotkaca with multiform volleys of arrows;
and having pierced the son of Bhīmasena with many shafts, Alambala—
With volleys of arrows, he put the army of the Pāṇḍavas to flight. O Sire, the Pāṇḍu forces, being routed by him in the dead of night, were scattered like clouds driven by the wind.

O King, thus pierced by the arrows of Ghaṭotkaca, the Kuru army fled in the dead of night, casting away thousands of torches. Then Alambala, enraged in that great battle, [attacked] the son of Bhīmasena.

He struck him with sharpened arrows like goads used against a great elephant. Ghaṭotkaca cut that chariot, its driver, and all its weapons into pieces as small as sesame seeds, and let out a most dreadful roar.
Then, with volleys of arrows, he showered Karna, the other Kurus by the thousands,
and Alambala, just as a cloud rains upon Mount Meru.
Thereupon, the army of the Kurus was thrown into great agitation, tormented by the Rakshasa.
O great king,
Jaṭāsuri, deprived of his chariot and with his charioteer slain,
furiously crushed Ghaṭotkaca in battle with a firm fist as they repeatedly struck one another from above.
Struck by that fist, Ghaṭotkaca trembled like a mountain with its clusters of trees and shrubs during an earthquake; then,
[he was struck] by that arm which resembled an iron club and was the slayer of hosts of enemies.
The son of Bhīmasena struck Jaṭāsuri violently with his fist; then,
having overwhelmed him, the enraged son of Hiḍimbā swiftly seized him and crushed him against the surface of the earth with his two arms that resembled the banners of Indra.
Having freed himself from Ghaṭotkaca, Jaṭāsuri rose up again and rushed toward Ghaṭotkaca with great speed; Alambala,
too, having thrown and lifted up the Rākṣasa, [attacked him].
In the heat of battle, he crushed Ghaṭotkaca onto the surface of the earth with fury;
then Ghaṭotkaca, raising his right arm,
struck him in the chest.
A tumultuous and hair-raising battle took place between those two roaring giants, Ghaṭotkaca and Alaṃbala,
as they, both masters of illusion, vied with one another through their magical powers.
Those two of great heroism fought like Indra and Virocana;
becoming fire and the ocean, they became again Garuḍa and Takṣaka, then great clouds and mighty winds, and finally the thunderbolt and the great mountain.
Again they became an elephant and a tiger, again the moon and the sun;
thus, creating hundreds of illusions and desiring to slay one another, Alambala and Ghaṭotkaca fought in a most wonderful manner.
With iron clubs, maces, spears, mallets, and sharp-edged spears,
as well as with pestles and mountain peaks, those two struck one another;
furthermore, the foot-soldier and the chariot-warrior fought with horses and elephants.
Then the son of Bhīmasena, filled with rage, forcefully raised Alambala;
those two foremost of Rākṣasas, masters of great illusion, fought in battle.
Then, O King, Ghaṭotkaca, desiring to slay Alambala—
Highly incensed, he sprang up and swooped down like a hawk;
seizing the massive-bodied lord of the Rākṣasas, Alambala,
he lifted him up and struck him down upon the ground, as Viṣṇu did to Maya in battle.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, seizing a sword of wondrous appearance— a scimitar— threw it down upon the ground; it fell terrified, emitting a roar again and again.
He seized him by the hair and severed from his body that terrible head of fearsome appearance;
even as he was quivering in battle and uttering a terrifying roar.
O great king, he of immeasurable prowess cut off the head of his enemy—
tawny-eyed, with distorted teeth and a flaming tongue—
and that rakshasa, seizing it by the hair, held it smeared with blood.
Ghaṭotkaca quickly advanced toward Duryodhana’s chariot;
seizing that head, which was blood-stained and covered in hair,
Ghaṭotkaca departed in haste.
Having bypassed the warriors Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, that exceedingly powerful one approached;
and having drawn near to Suyodhana, the Kuru warrior and subduer of enemies, that mighty-armed Rākṣasa smiled.
Having cast his head— its face disfigured and its hair disheveled— onto the chariot,
he let out a terrifying roar like a cloud in the rainy season.
Then, O King, he spoke these words to Duryodhana:

"This kinsman of yours has been slain; you have witnessed his prowess. You shall see again this end of Karṇa, and likewise your own. Having seized Karṇa’s head and looked upon it once more, Suyodhana—
He who desires the triad of his own duty, wealth,
and pleasure should not approach a king, a Brahmin, or a woman with empty hands.
Remain well-pleased for now until I have slain Karṇa.
Having spoken thus, O lord of men, he then advanced toward Karṇa,
scattering hundreds of sharp arrows and releasing them upon Karṇa’s head.
Thereupon, a battle ensued, terrible in form and fearsome.
"O Great King, it was a source of amazement in that battle between the man and the Rākṣasa.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"In that encounter where Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca [fought]..."
How did that battle unfold when they clashed at midnight? What was the nature of the combat with that terrible *rākṣasa*,
by whom Karna, the son of Vaikartana, was defeated in battle?
What is his chariot like, and what are all his illusory powers and weapons?
What is the size of his horses, and likewise his chariot-banner and bow?
What is his armor like, and what is his neck-guard like?
"You have been questioned; explain this, for you are skilled, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said:
"He has blood-red eyes, a massive body, copper-colored lips, and a sunken belly."
With hair standing on end, a golden beard, spike-like ears, and a massive jaw;
with a mouth gaped open as far as his ears, sharp fangs, and a terrifying countenance;
with an exceedingly long, copper-colored tongue and lips, drooping eyebrows, and a thick nose.
Blue-bodied, with a red neck, mountain-like in stature, and terrifying;
large-bodied, long-armed, large-headed, and possessed of great strength; with disheveled hair, a rough touch, and prominent, protruding calves.
With thick hips and a deep-set navel, he was large with loose-fitting garments;
likewise, the great illusionist wore armlets and bracelets,
bearing a golden breast-plate upon his chest like a mountain bearing a garland of fire.
On his head shone a bright, golden crown, variegated and adorned with many beautiful parts, resembling an ornamental archway; likewise,
he wore earrings with the brilliance of the rising sun and a splendid garland made of gold.
Wearing a vast bronze armor of great luster,
O King— which resembled a cluster of stars and possessed a radiance equal to the full moon—
he also wore a great necklace made of refined gold.
By that [chariot], he indeed shone like a rain-cloud with lightning;
it resounded with the tinkling of hundreds of small bells and was adorned with red flags and banners.
Its body was covered with bear-skins, and that great chariot measured a *nalva* in size.
It was equipped with all kinds of excellent weapons, adorned with garlands of banners,
fitted with eight wheels, and possessed a roar as deep as a thundercloud. There, [there were] beings resembling elephants, red-eyed and terrifying.
Horses endowed with the speed of desire and color, powerful and tireless, drew the fierce Rākṣasa; carrying him, those strong steeds,
with their massive manes, neighed again and again.
Excellent horses of great speed, with faces of various forms and bellowing loudly,
were yoked to his chariot and carried that lord of the Rākṣasas.
His charioteer was the Rākṣasa Virūpākṣa, whose face and earrings were ablaze.
Terrible in form, massive-bodied, formidable, and with a distorted face,
he seized the horses in battle with rays resembling the beams of the sun;
accompanied by him, he stood like the sun with Aruṇa.
Like a great mountain enveloped by a massive cloud, a vast,
sky-reaching banner was raised upon his chariot;
perched upon it was an exceedingly terrifying, flesh-eating vulture with a crimson head.
Brandishing his bow, which possessed a firm string and emitted a roar like the thunderbolt of Indra,
he clearly displayed that weapon twelve cubits long and one span in thickness;
with arrows as large as chariot axles, he covered all the directions.
On that night which carried away heroes, he rushed against Karṇa;
as he stood firm upon his chariot brandishing his bow,
the roar of his bow was heard like the crash of a thunderbolt.
O Bhārata, your entire army, being terrified by him,
trembled like the great waves of the ocean.
Beholding that Virūpākṣa, the terrifying one, as he was charging toward them—
Smiling as it were, the son of Rādhā quickly checked him;
then Karṇa advanced toward him, shooting at the one who was shooting from close range,
like an elephant against an elephant, or a bull of the herd against a bull.
O lord of the people, O King, that encounter between Karṇa and the Rākṣasa was tumultuous, like that between Indra and Śambara. Grasping their bows of great speed and terrifying sound, those two—
Hewing at one another with great arrows, they covered each other; then, with straight-knotted shafts released from bows drawn to their full stretch,
they warded off one another, piercing through their bronze armor.
Like two tigers with their claws or two great elephants with their tusks,
they mangled one another with chariot-spears and arrows; indeed, while severing each other’s limbs, they were simultaneously fitting new shafts to their bows.
Scorched by volleys of arrows, they were unable even to look at one another; burning with arrow-meteors, they became difficult to behold.
With all their limbs mangled and drenched in streams of blood, the two of them...
They shone like two mountains of red chalk with water flowing down them;
their limbs pierced by the tips of arrows and rending one another,
those two of great splendor did not waver from each other despite their exertions.

That night-battle, O King, continued for a long time as if it were equal, while Karṇa and the Rākṣasa gambled with their very lives in the fray. As he fixed his sharp arrows and discharged them without ceasing, [the battle raged on].
At that time, O King, when Karṇa surpassed Ghaṭotkaca, both our own troops and the enemy became terrified by the roar of his bow;
then that best of weapon-knowers manifested a divine weapon.
Seeing the celestial weapon discharged by Karṇa, Ghaṭotkaca,
the Rākṣasa and joy of the Pāṇḍavas, manifested a great illusion;
he was accompanied by [beings] bearing spears and mallets, with mountains and trees in their hands.
Surrounded by a vast army of Rākṣasas of terrifying form,
they saw him with his great bow raised; seeing him approaching like the Destroyer of Beings bearing the fierce Staff of Time, those kings were struck with terror.
Terrified by the lion’s roar emitted by Ghaṭotkaca,
the elephants discharged urine and the men were greatly distressed. Then, a massive and most fierce rain of stones fell from all sides.
At midnight, they were assailed by the forces of the Rākṣasas with increased might;
iron wheels, *bhuśuṇḍī*s, spears,
and javelins fell incessantly, as did spikes, *śataghnī*s, and *paṭṭiśa*s.
Seeing that fierce and exceedingly terrible battle, the lords of men,
your sons, and your warriors were distressed and fled in all directions;
yet there, Karna alone— the proud one who boasted of the power of his weapons— was not shaken.
And with his arrows, he destroyed the illusion created by Ghaṭotkaca. When that illusion was dispelled, Ghaṭotkaca, out of indignation,
discharged terrible arrows which entered the Sūtaputra.
Then, smeared with blood, those arrows, having pierced Karṇa in that great battle,
entered the earth like enraged serpents.
But the son of the Sūta, enraged, light-handed, and full of prowess—
Passing over Ghaṭotkaca, he pierced him with ten arrows. Severely pained by the Sūtaputra’s arrows in his vital organs, Ghaṭotkaca seized a divine, thousand-spoked discus.
Enraged and desiring to slay him, the son of Bhīmasena hurled at the son of Adhiratha a sword with a razor-sharp edge, radiant as the rising sun and adorned with precious jewels;
but it was cast away with extreme velocity, intercepted by Karṇa’s arrows.
Like the resolve of an unfortunate man, that [discus] fell fruitlessly to the earth.
But Ghaṭotkaca, enraged upon seeing the discus struck down,
covered Karna with arrows, just as Rahu covers the sun.
But the son of the Sūta, unperturbed and possessing the prowess of Rudra, Upendra, and Indra,
quickly covered Ghaṭotkaca’s chariot with feathered arrows.
Then, by the enraged Ghaṭotkaca, that mace adorned with golden armlets—
Struck by Karna’s arrows, that [elephant] too fell down after being cast off and whirled around.
Then, leaping into the sky and roaring like a dark cloud,
the massive-bodied creature rained down a shower of trees from the firmament.
Then Karṇa pierced the illusory son of Bhīmasena in the sky with arrows,
just as the sun pierces a cloud with its rays.
Having slain all his horses and shattered his chariot into a hundred pieces, [he struck him].
Karna rained down arrows like Parjanya pouring forth rain;
there was not even a space of two fingers' breadth on his body that remained unpierced.
In a mere moment, he appeared like a porcupine with its quills bristling.
Neither his horses, nor his chariot, nor his banner, nor Ghaṭotkaca himself could we see in that battle, for they were completely shrouded by floods of arrows. But he,
neutralizing Karna's divine weapon with his own weapon, [destroyed it].
With illusory combat, the master of illusion fought the Suta’s son;
he then engaged Karṇa through both illusion and dexterity,
moving through the net of arrows in the sky while remaining invisible.

O best of the Kurus, O Bhārata, the son of Bhīmasena, a master of great illusion, employed a mighty *māyā* through his own magic, as if to delude them. Making his faces deformed and his countenance hideous, he assumed various misshapen forms.
By means of his illusory power (māyā), he swallowed the divine weapons of the Sūta’s son;
then once more, that massive-bodied one was seen to have been cut into a hundred pieces in battle,
fallen from the sky, lifeless and devoid of energy.
Thinking him slain, those bulls among the Kurus let out a great roar;
yet he was seen again in all directions with new bodies,
once more possessing a massive form, a hundred heads, and a hundred bellies.
The mighty-armed one appeared like Mount Maināka;
then that Rākṣasa, becoming the size of a thumb,
whirled about horizontally and upwards like a wave tossed up by the ocean.
Having split the earth, he submerged again into the waters;
then he was seen there having emerged once more in another place.
Having descended, he stood once again upon his gold-adorned chariot.
Having enveloped the earth, the sky, and the very quarters with his illusory power,
clad in armor, and approaching Karna’s chariot with his earrings swaying upon his face,
he spoke these words without agitation to the Suta’s son, O lord of the people.
"O son of a Sūta, you shall not leave while I am alive;
today on the field of battle, I shall destroy your desire for war.
Having spoken thus, the Rākṣasa of cruel prowess, his eyes copper-red with rage, stood there.
He leapt into the sky and let out a loud laugh;
then, like a lion attacking a lordly elephant, he struck Karna. Ghaṭotkaca rained down arrows as large as chariot axles upon him.
Like a rain-cloud with its showers, he [Arjuna] assailed Karna, the bull among chariot-warriors;
and Karna, for his part, shattered that shower of arrows once it had reached him.
And having seen that illusion thwarted by Karna, O bull of the Bharatas...
Then Ghaṭotkaca, having become invisible once more, created an illusion:
he became a vast and lofty mountain, thick with trees upon its peaks, from which spears, javelins, swords, and maces flowed like torrents of water.
Seeing that mountain, which resembled a mass of collyrium and bore fierce weapons like waterfalls, Karṇa was not shaken; rather,
as if smiling, he then invoked a divine weapon.

Then that lord of mountains, struck by the weapon, was indeed shattered and vanished. Thereupon, becoming a dark cloud in the sky adorned with a rainbow, he most fiercely covered the Suta’s son with showers of stones.

Then, aiming the Vāyavya weapon, Karṇa Vaikartana, the bull among those skilled in weapons, dispersed that Kālamegha cloud. Covering all directions with his multitudes of arrows, Karṇa shrouded them on every side.
O great king, he struck down the weapon discharged by Ghaṭotkaca.
Then, laughing in the midst of battle, the mighty son of Bhīmasena manifested a great illusion against the great car-warrior Karṇa.
Seeing Ghaṭotkaca returning once more on his chariot— the best of chariot-warriors—
unperturbed and surrounded by many Rākṣasas who resembled lions and tigers and possessed the prowess of elephants in rut, [he was filled with rage].
Surrounded by those mounted on elephants, those on chariots, and likewise those on the backs of horses—
terrible beings bearing various weapons and adorned with diverse armor—
the cruel Ghaṭotkaca was like Vāsava surrounded by the Maruts.
Seeing him, the great archer Karṇa engaged the Rākṣasa in combat.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, having pierced Karṇa with five swift arrows,
let out a terrifying roar, frightening all the kings.
Then Ghaṭotkaca swiftly cut down the great bow held in Karna's hand, along with its many arrows and the añjalika weapon. Thereupon,
Karna took up another large, firm bow capable of bearing a great strain.
Karna forcibly drew back his bow, which was raised high like Indra’s rainbow;
then, O great king, Karna dispatched gold-feathered, foe-slaying arrows toward the sky-dwelling Rākṣasas.
Afflicted by those arrows, that host of broad-chested Rākṣasas was as agitated as a herd of wild elephants harassed by a lion;
having slain the Rākṣasas, Karṇa once again began to strike the son of Hiḍimbā.
But having witnessed that great feat of the high-souled son of Rādhā,
Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhīmasena, blazed up with rage.
The lordly one, having scattered the Rākṣasas along with their horses, charioteers, and elephants by means of his arrows, [proceeded].
The Lord Fire consumed them like all beings at the end of an eon;
then, O great king, Karṇa scattered the Rākṣasas with his arrows,
making their faces deformed and gaping open.
With his arrows, he cut down the various weapons of the son of Rādhā and covered him with shafts as clouds shroud a mountain with torrents of rain; then,
taking on the form of a city of the Gandharvas, he vanished once more.
Having destroyed the army of the Rākṣasas, the son of the Sūta shone like the god Maheśvara in heaven after burning Tripura in the past,
O noble one, amidst those thousands of kings on the side of the Pāṇḍavas.
"O King, no one at all is able even to look upon him,
O monarch, except for Ghaṭotkaca, the mighty lord of the Rākṣasas,
who is endowed with terrible heroism and strength, like the enraged son of Vivasvat."
As he grew enraged, O King, fire was produced from his two eyes like flaming drops of oil from two great meteors; then,
clapping one palm against the other, he bit his lip.
Mounting again a chariot created by his illusory power (*māyā*),
which was yoked with asses having the faces of *piśācas* and resembling elephants,
he, filled with rage, said to his charioteer: "Do not carry me toward the son of the Sūta."

O lord of the people, that best of chariot-warriors proceeded once again toward a single combat with the Sūta’s son on his terrible-looking chariot. Enraged, the Rākṣasa again hurled [his weapon] at the Sūta’s son.
It was an eight-wheeled, most terrible thunderbolt fashioned by Rudra,
two *yojanas* in height and one *yojana* in length and breadth;
it was made of iron and bristling with spikes like a *kadamba* tree with its filaments.
Having set aside his bow on the chariot, Karṇa leaped down and seized her;

he then hurled her back toward that very chariot, and she, possessed of great splendor, leaped down from it. Having reduced the vehicle—along with its horses, driver, and standard—to ashes, she departed.

Having pierced the earth, it entered the ground; there the gods were filled with wonder. All living beings immediately paid homage to Karṇa, because he had leaped up and seized the great thunderbolt created by the gods.
Having done this in battle, Karṇa ascended his chariot once more. Then the son of the Sūta, that scorcher of foes, released iron shafts—
an act impossible for any other among all living beings, O giver of honor.
What Karṇa had done then in that battle of terrifying aspect—
being struck by iron arrows like a mountain by torrents—
he vanished once more, appearing like a city of the Gandharvas.

Thus, that great master of illusion, the slayer of enemies, destroyed those divine weapons through his illusory power and agility. As those weapons were being struck down by the rākṣasa’s illusion, [the gods were filled with wonder].
Then Karna, remaining unperturbed, fought back against that Rakshasa.
Thereupon, O great king, the mighty son of Bhimasena, filled with rage,
multiplied himself into many forms, terrifying the lords of men.
Then, from all directions, lions, tigers, and hyenas rushed forward,
along with fire-tongued serpents and birds with iron beaks.
Being overwhelmed by those sharp arrows released from Karna’s bow, [he was assailed].
Resembling a city, a mountain, or a forest, he vanished right there.
And there were *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, *yātudhānas*, *śalāvṛkas*,
many *śālāvṛkas*, and wolves with deformed faces.
Desiring to devour Karṇa, they rushed at him from all sides;
then they terrified him with fierce cries and with many raised, terrible weapons drenched in blood.
Karna pierced each one of them with many swift arrows;
having repelled that Rākṣasa illusion with a divine weapon,
he struck his horses with straight-jointed shafts.
Broken, their limbs mangled and backs pierced by arrows, they fell to the earth while that Rākṣasa looked on. Then the son of Hiḍimbā, his magic power shattered, [addressed] Karṇa Vaikartana.
"Having said, 'I shall ordain your death,' he vanished.
Sañjaya said:
"While that battle between Karṇa and the Rākṣasa was thus proceeding..."
The heroic Alāyudha, lord of the Rākṣasas,
advanced with a vast army and approached Suyodhana,
surrounded by thousands of hideous Rākṣasas.
Remembering their former enmity, those heroes assuming various forms slew his kinsman, the valiant crane who devours Brahmins,
as well as the highly energetic Kirmīra and likewise his friend Hiḍimba.
Remembering that long-standing enmity from former times,
and recognizing that this was a night-battle, he desired to slay Bhīma in combat;
like an elephant in rut or a serpent filled with rage.
Eager for battle, he spoke these words to Duryodhana:
"It is known to you, O Great King, how my kinsmen— the Rākṣasas Hiḍimba, Baka, and Kirmīra— were slain by Bhīma."
O King, in the past, he committed the violation of the maiden Hiḍimbā,
having indeed insulted other Rākṣasas as well as us.
O King, I shall [slay] him along with his host, together with his horses, chariots, and elephants.
I have come here myself to slay the son of Hiḍimbā along with his ministers. Today, having killed all the sons of Kuntī led by Vāsudeva, I shall devour them together with all my followers.
"Restrain the entire army; we ourselves shall fight the Pāṇḍavas.
"Therefore, O King, I too, along with my followers, will engage the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
Having heard those words of his, Duryodhana was then filled with joy.
Having honored him, he, surrounded by his brothers, spoke these words:
"Placing you at our head along with your followers, we shall fight the enemies; for my soldiers, their minds set on the end of this enmity, will not stand idly by."
Having said "So be it" to the king, that bull among Rākṣasas rushed swiftly toward Bhīma, accompanied by his man-eating followers,
with a radiant body upon a chariot possessing the splendor of the sun.
O Indra among kings, it was exactly like that of Ghaṭotkaca;
its roar was incomparable, it was adorned with many arches,
its body was covered with bear skins, and that great chariot was a nalva in size.
His horses were swift, with bodies like elephants and harsh voices; a hundred of them, massive in form and feeding on flesh and blood, were yoked to his chariot.
The roar of that chariot was like the thundering of a great cloud.
His bow, too, was exceedingly great, with a firm string and of superior strength;
his arrows were as large as axles, gold-feathered, and sharpened on stone. That hero, too, possessed mighty arms, just like Ghaṭotkaca himself.
His banner, guarded by jackals and vultures,
was like a blazing sun;
and it too was equal in appearance to that of Ghaṭotkaca.
Most glorious, with his face brilliantly illuminated,
wearing blazing armlets and a flaming crown and garland,
he had bound on a flower wreath, a turban, and a fastened sword.
Bearing a mace, a *bhuśuṇḍī*, a club,
and a plow, armed with a bow and possessing a stature like that of an elephant, he [advanced] in that chariot which was as radiant as fire.
Scattering that army of the Pāṇḍavas,
he shone in battle as he moved about,
like a cloud garlanded with lightning in the sky.
And all those preeminent lords of men, O King—
possessing great strength, clad in armor and wielding shields—
fought there filled with joy.
From all sides, the heroic warriors of the Pāṇḍavas [advanced].
Sañjaya said:
Beholding him, the doer of terrible deeds, who had arrived for battle—
All those Kurus experienced great joy,
and likewise your sons, headed by Duryodhana,
felt as if they had found a boat when they were without one, desiring to cross the ocean.
Then the kings, considering themselves as if born again,
honored Alāyudha, the lord of the Rākṣasas, with words of welcome.
While that superhuman and terrifying battle was thus proceeding, [they did so].
During that night, when the encounter between Karṇa and the Rākṣasa was fierce to behold,
neither the son of Droṇa, nor Kṛpa, nor Droṇa, nor Śalya, nor Mādhava were there;
Karṇa alone, a bull among warriors, stood as the combatant in that battle.
The Pāñcālas, along with their kings, looked on with smiles; likewise, O King, your own men— Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others— reeling here and there, cried out, "This is no more!"
Seeing that deed of the son of Hiḍimbā on the field of battle, O great king, your entire army became bewildered, filled with cries of "Alas!", agitated, and senseless, despairing for Karṇa’s life.
But Duryodhana, beholding Karṇa fallen into extreme distress,
then summoned Alāyudha, the lord of the Rākṣasas, and spoke these words:
"This Karṇa, the son of Vikartana, has encountered the son of Hiḍimbā."
He performs a most great deed that is effective in battle;
behold these heroic kings slain by the son of Bhīmasena,
struck down by various weapons like trees by an elephant.
"This portion of the battle in the midst of the kings has been assigned by me to you;
O hero, acting with prowess and with your own consent, destroy him.
Before this wicked Ghaṭotkaca [slays] Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana..."
"Relying on the power of illusion, the crusher of enemies shall bring about his emaciation.
Thus addressed by the king, that rakshasa of fierce prowess,
the mighty-armed one, said "So be it" and rushed toward Ghatotkacha.
Then, O Lord, having released Karna, the son of Bhīmasena also crushed the approaching adversary with his arrows;
a battle then took place between those two enraged lords of the Rākṣasas.
Like two intoxicated elephants in the forest contending for the sake of a female,
Karna— the best of chariot-warriors— having been released by the Rākṣasa,
rushed toward Bhīmasena in a chariot radiant as the sun.
Disregarding him as he approached, and seeing Ghaṭotkaca seized by Alāyudha in battle— like a bull by a lion—
Bhīma, the best among strikers, [advanced] in a chariot with the splendor of the sun.
Scattering showers of arrows, he advanced toward the chariot of Alāyudha. O Lord, beholding him approaching,
Alāyudha then abandoned Ghaṭotkaca and challenged Bhīmasena.
O Lord, Bhīma, the destroyer of Rākṣasas, suddenly approaching him,
overwhelmed that lord of the Rākṣasas along with his host with showers of arrows;
