and likewise, O King, Alāyudha [assailed him] with straight-flying shafts polished on stone.
The subduer of enemies showered the son of Kuntī again and again;
likewise, all those fierce Rākṣasas, bearing various weapons and desiring victory for your sons, rushed toward Bhīmasena.
Being struck by those powerful ones, the immensely strong Bhīmasena pierced all of them with five sharp arrows each. Being slaughtered by Bhīma, those rākṣasas born of donkey lineage—
They let out tumultuous cries and fled in the ten directions;
seeing them being terrified by Bhīma, the mighty Rākṣasa rushed forward with speed and covered him with arrows.
In that battle, Bhīmasena struck him with sharp-pointed arrows;
but Alāyudha, in the fray, cut down some of those shafts discharged by Bhīma and seized others with haste.
Seeing that lord of the *rākṣasas*, Bhīma of terrible prowess then hurled with great force his mace, which resembled the fall of a thunderbolt; as that mace,
wreathed in flames, came rushing toward him with speed, [he met it].
He struck him with a mace, and that mace rebounded toward Bhīma.
Then the son of Kuntī covered the lord of the Rākṣasas with a shower of arrows,
but the Rākṣasa rendered even those futile with his own sharp shafts.
And all those rākṣasas, the soldiers of fearsome form,
at the command of the lord of rākṣasas, slaughtered the chariots and elephants;
likewise the Pāñcālas, the Sṛñjayas, the horses, and the finest of tuskers.
Severely tormented by the rākṣasas, they found no peace there.
But seeing that most terrible event unfolding in the great battle,
that best of men spoke these words to Dhanañjaya:
"Behold Bhīma, O mighty-armed one, fallen under the power of the lord of the Rākṣasas! Follow his path, O Pāṇḍava; do not hesitate.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, Yudhāmanyu, and Uttamaujas—"
"Let the great car-warriors, the sons of Draupadī, together with Nakula, Sahadeva, and the heroic Yuyudhāna, go against Karṇa;
and let them slay the other Rākṣasas at your command, O Pāṇḍava."
"O mighty-armed one, O tiger among men, you too must hold back this army led by Droṇa, for a great danger has arrived. When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, the great car-warriors proceeded as directed.
They went toward Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, and the other Rākṣasas in battle.
Then, with arrows resembling venomous serpents released from a bow drawn to its full extent,
the powerful lord of the Rākṣasas cut through Bhīma’s bow.

O Bhārata, with sharp arrows, that mighty warrior slew his horses and his charioteer in the battle while Bhīmasena looked on. With his horses killed and his charioteer slain, he descended from the seat of the chariot.
Roaring aloud, he hurled at him a heavy and terrible mace.
Then, as that great mace with its fearsome sound came hurtling toward him,
the formidable Rākṣasa struck it down with his own mace and let out a roar.
Seeing that terrifying and fearsome deed of the lord of the Rākṣasas,
Bhīmasena, with a joyful heart, quickly seized his mace.
A tumultuous battle then ensued between those two, the man and the Rākṣasa.
Making the earth tremble violently with the thunderous crashes of their falling maces,
those two, having once more released their maces and closed in upon one another,
struck each other with fists that resounded like thunderbolts.
Taking whatever was at hand— chariot wheels, yokes, axles, frames, and equipment—
the two indignant warriors struck each other down as they encountered one another,
streaming with blood.
Like two great elephants in rut, they dragged each other back and forth again and again.
Dhṛṣīkeśa, who is devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, beheld this;
for the sake of protecting Bhīmasena, he urged the son of Hiḍimbā forward.
Saṃjaya said:
Having seen Bhīma nearby in battle seized by the Rākṣasa,
Vāsudeva then spoke these words to Ghaṭotkaca.
"Behold, O mighty-armed one, Bhīma seized from close range by the Rākṣasa,
while all the troops and you yourself, O one of great splendor, look on! Therefore,
setting aside Karṇa, [subdue] Alāyudha, the lord of the Rākṣasas."

"O mighty-armed one, slay him quickly; afterwards you shall kill Karṇa. Hearing these words of the Vārṣṇeya, the valiant Ghaṭotkaca released Karṇa and fought with the lord of the Rākṣasas, the brother of Baka.
O Bhārata, a tumultuous and fierce battle took place at night between those two Rākṣasas, Alāyudha and the son of Hiḍimbā. Indeed,
[Alāyudha fought] against the warriors of Alāyudha, those Rākṣasas of terrifying appearance.
As those heroes rushed forward with speed, bows firmly grasped,
the great car-warrior Yuyudhana, highly enraged and having taken up his own weapons,
along with Nakula and Sahadeva, cut them down with sharpened arrows.
And in that battle, O King, Kirīṭin Bībhatsu scattered all those bulls among Kṣatriyas on every side as he discharged his arrows;
and Karṇa, too, O King, put the monarchs to flight in the encounter.
Seeing those great car-warriors of the Pāñcālas, headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin,
being slaughtered, Bhīma of terrible prowess rushed swiftly toward Karṇa, scattering his arrows in the battle.
Then they too, having slain the Rākṣasas, arrived where the Sūta’s son was—
Nakula, Sahadeva, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki. They, along with the Pāñcālas, engaged Karṇa in battle, while [others] engaged Droṇa.
But Alāyudha, filled with rage, struck Ghaṭotkaca, the subduer of enemies,
on the head with a massive iron club.
By that blow, the mighty son of Bhīmasena—
Slightly overcome by faintness, the valiant one steadied himself;
then, in that battle, he hurled at him a mace adorned with gold, decorated with a hundred bells, and resembling a blazing fire.
Released with great force by that one of terrible deeds, it crushed his horses, his charioteer, and his loud-sounding chariot. With its horses,
wheels, and axle broken, and its banner and pole shattered, [the chariot lay in ruins].
He quickly leapt from the chariot, resorting to a Rākṣasa illusion;
having employed that illusion, he rained down much blood,
and the sky became filled with dark clouds and flashing with lightning.
Then, in that great battle, there was the falling of thunderbolts accompanied by lightning and peals of thunder, along with a massive crackling sound;
for the Rākṣasa beheld that illusion created by the other Rākṣasa.
Leaping upward, the son of Hiḍimbā destroyed that illusion with his own power of illusion.
Seeing his illusion thus struck down, that master of illusions, by means of his very power of illusion,
unleashed a most tumultuous shower of stones upon Ghaṭotkaca.
The valiant one [Arjuna], with a shower of arrows, dispersed that terrible rain of stones in all directions; it was like a marvel. Then they rained down upon each other with various kinds of weapons.
With iron clubs, spears, maces, pestles, and hammers;
with *pinākas*, swords, javelins, darts, and *kampanas*;
with sharp iron arrows, crescent-headed shafts, arrows, discuses, and battle-axes.
With iron balls, slings, and even *gośīrṣa* mortars,
and having uprooted various large-branched trees from the earth—
such as *śamī*, *pīlu*, *karīra*, and *śamyāka*— O Bhārata.
With *iṅguda*, *badarī*, and flowering *kovidāra* trees,
as well as *palāśa*, *arimeda*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and *pippala* trees,
they struck one another in that great battle.
With various mountain peaks covered in diverse minerals,
there arose a great sound from them, like that of thunderbolts being shattered. O King, that battle between the son of Bhīma and Alāyudha was terrible.
O King, just as in ancient times between Hari and Indra, or between Vālin and Sugrīva,
those two fought with various terrible weapons and arrows; then,
seizing sharp swords, they struck one another.
Those two of great body and great strength, having rushed at one another, seized each other by the hair with their arms;
with their limbs mangled, O lord of men, they both shed profuse sweat.
Blood flowed from those two massive-bodied ones as if they were two mountains being drenched by rain.
Then, rushing forward with speed and whirling the Rākṣasa around,
the son of Hiḍimbā threw him down by force and severed his great head.
Having carried off his head, which was adorned with two earrings,
that one of great strength then let out a most tumultuous roar.
Seeing that his kinsman, the great-bodied subduer of foes, had been slain, [he rejoiced].
The Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas let out lion-like roars; then,
once that *rākṣasa* had been struck down, the sons of Pāṇḍu sounded thousands of kettledrums and tens of thousands of conchs.
That night became exceedingly conducive to their victory;
shining brightly, it gleamed on all sides, garlanded with lamps.
Then the mighty son of Bhīmasena [severed] the head of Alāyudha.
In the presence of Duryodhana, he cast down the lifeless body;
then King Duryodhana, O Bhārata, seeing Alāyudha slain, became extremely agitated along with his army.
"For indeed, having himself come forward and remembering his supreme enmity, he promised Bhīmasena in battle, 'I shall slay him. Therefore,
the king thought that he must certainly be slain by him."
He considered the life of his brothers to be long-lived;
seeing him indeed slain by the son of Bhīmasena,
he regarded Bhīmasena’s vow as already fulfilled.
Saṃjaya said:
Having slain the Rākṣasa Alāyudha, Ghaṭotkaca, with a joyful heart,
stood at the head of the army and uttered various roars.
O great king, hearing that tumultuous sound which made the elephants tremble,
a most terrible fear seized your men.
But as for the mighty son of Bhīmasena, he remained fixed upon Alāyudha.
Seeing them, the mighty-armed Karṇa rushed toward the Pāñcālas;
with ten firm, straight-knotted arrows released from a fully drawn bow, he pierced both Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin.

Then, with supreme iron shafts and arrows, he caused Yudhāmanyu, Uttamaujas, and the noble car-warrior Sātyaki to tremble. As all of them were practicing their aim there, [he struck] from both the left and the right.
O lord of men, only circles of bows were visible;
the thunderous roar of their bowstrings and palms, along with the sound of chariot wheels,
became as tumultuous as the rumbling of clouds at the end of the summer heat during the night.
The twang of his bowstring was indeed like the roar of thunder; his bow was like lightning, with the tips of his banner-poles as its crests;
and he possessed a tumultuous downpour of showers consisting of volleys of arrows.
O King, he became a cloud of battle;
like a mountain, he was unshakable,
possessing a strength equal to a mountain, and he withstood that great downpour.
O lord of men,
Vaikartana, the crusher of enemy hosts,
utterly destroyed them in battle with incomparable arrows resembling the falling of thunderbolts.
With sharp arrows adorned with variegated golden feathers,
the high-souled son of Vaikartana, devoted to the welfare of his sons, struck down his enemies in battle.
Some had their banners cut down and shattered;
some had their bodies pierced and tormented by arrows;
some were deprived of their charioteers, and others were left without their horses.
Quickly struck by Vaikartana,
they found no refuge in the battle and then fled toward Yudhiṣṭhira’s army.
Seeing them broken and turned back,
Ghaṭotkaca was filled with extreme rage;
mounting that chariot variegated with gold and jewels, he—
Having approached Karna Vaikartana, he roared like a lion atop a supreme chariot and pierced him with arrows resembling thunderbolts.
They [struck] with barbed arrows, iron shafts, and stone-tipped arrows, with hollow reeds and those with calf-teeth tips,
with boar-ear-shaped arrows, and those with horned points.
They roared as they rained down razor-sharp arrows, and the atmosphere, covered by those streams of shafts moving crosswise in the battle, shone brilliantly.
With their golden-feathered arrows blazing with light,
like garlands of various flowers,
those two of incomparable power were indeed equal.
They struck each other with supreme weapons; indeed,
no one perceived any distinction between those two foremost of heroes in that battle.
That battle between the son of Ravi and the son of Bhīma was exceedingly wonderful and exceedingly beautiful;
it was tumultuous and terrible with the falling of weapons.
O King, when Ghaṭotkaca could not gain the upper hand over Karṇa— like the fierce heat of the sun and Rāhu in the sky—
the best of those skilled in weapons then manifested a terrible weapon.
Having first slain Karna’s horses with that weapon, the Rākṣasa,
the son of Hiḍimbā, quickly vanished along with Karna’s charioteer.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Since that Rākṣasa, who fought with deceitful stratagems, has thus disappeared, tell me, Sañjaya, what my men did then. Sañjaya said:
Perceiving that Rākṣasa to have vanished,
all the Kurus cried out together:
"How is it that this Rākṣasa is not here, he who fights with deceit?"
He would have slain Karṇa in battle while remaining invisible; then Karṇa, a warrior skilled in swift and wonderful weapons,
covered all directions with nets of arrows.
Indeed, no living being there was harmed,
for the atmosphere had become shrouded in darkness by his arrows; he could neither be seen taking them up nor fixing them to the string.
The son of the Suta was not seen as he touched his quivers with the tips of his fingers, for by his swiftness he covered the entire sky with arrows.
Then we beheld a terrible, fearsome, and cruel illusion created by the Rākṣasa in the sky, shining like blood-red clouds.
Then, O lord of the Kauravas, from that lightning there appeared fierce flashes like blazing crests of fire, as well as flaming meteors.
Another most terrible sound arose,
like thousands of kettledrums resounding together;
then arrows with golden shafts fell.
Javelins, spears, maces, and weapons; battle-axes and swords cleansed with oil;
and *paṭṭiśas* and *tomaras* with flaming tips.
There were radiant iron-bound clubs,
variegated maces, sharp-edged spears,
and heavy bludgeons bound with golden bands.
And *śataghnī* weapons appeared on all sides; great boulders fell here and there by the thousands, along with thunderbolts and lightning.
And wheels with hundreds of razors appeared,
blazing with the radiance of fire;
and those [missiles] consisting of spears, stones, and axes appeared.
Karna was unable to strike down the vast, blazing rain of falling spears, vajras, thunderbolts, and mallets with his own showers of arrows.
Of horses falling, struck by arrows;
of elephants falling, struck by thunderbolts; and of great chariot-warriors struck down by rocks.
A great roar arose from those falling—
those slain by hundreds of various illusions and by the most terrifying blows of diverse weapons.
Struck on all sides by Ghaṭotkaca,
that army of Duryodhana appeared distressed,
whirling and reeling about.
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", they were rolling about, shrinking back, and appearing dejected;
yet those heroes among men, due to their noble nature, remained steadfast.
At that time, they did not turn their backs as that most terrible and fearsome shower of great weapons, consisting of fierce Rākṣasīs, fell upon them.
Seeing the floods of troops being struck down,
a great fear entered your sons; and jackals with tongues blazing like fire appeared.
Hearing hundreds of terrifying roars and seeing the shouting hosts of rākṣasas,
the warriors of the king were struck with panic.
With blazing tongues, sharp faces, and fierce fangs, those terrifying beings with bodies resembling mountains moved through the sky,
their hands clutching spears.
They released a torrent like a path of rain from the clouds;
struck by them with arrows, spears, and tridents, and with fierce maces and flaming iron clubs, [the enemies fell].
They fell, crushed by thunderbolts, *pinākas*, strokes of lightning, discuses, and *śataghnīs*;
likewise, *huḍas*, *bhuśuṇḍis*, stone balls, and *śataghnīs* [fell].
Pillars bound with bands of black iron rained down upon your son’s army; thus,
a terrible dejection manifested itself.
With entrails spilling out and heads shattered,
the heroes lie there with their limbs broken; horses are pierced and elephants are crushed.
Their chariots were completely crushed by the rocks,
as those Yātudhānas of terrible form continued to rain down such a great shower of weapons upon the earth.
Illusions were created there by Ghaṭotkaca;
they did not release him even as he begged or showed fear during that terrible slaughter of the Kuru heroes.
When the time had come and the Kṣatriyas were no more,
those Kauravas, utterly broken, suddenly fled while crying out in lamentation.
"Run away, O Kurus! This is no longer possible;
the gods, led by Indra, are slaying us for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
Thus spoke they as those Bhāratas were sinking.
No island whatsoever existed there while that tumultuous slaughter was taking place,
as the Kuru army was broken and fleeing.
In the lack of visibility during the division of the ranks,
neither the Kurus nor the others could be distinguished;
there was a chaotic and terrible flight beyond all bounds.
Looking toward all directions, O King, we saw them as empty; there I beheld Karna alone, plunging his chest into that shower of weapons.
Then, displaying his divine power against the Rākṣasa, he covered the sky with arrows;
modest and performing a difficult, noble deed.
The son of the Sūta was not at all bewildered in the battle;
then, O King, all the Saindhavas and Bāhlikas, being terrified, gazed intently at Karṇa.
Honoring his lack of confusion in battle and beholding the victory of the Rākṣasa,
they released at him a wheel-equipped *śataghnī* discharged by him.
He struck all four horses simultaneously; lifeless, with their teeth, eyes, and tongues protruding, they fell to the earth upon their knees.
Then, having descended from his chariot whose horses had been slain, he was dejected as the Kurus fled; meanwhile,
the divine weapon was being neutralized by his illusory power (*māyā*).
Reflecting on what was appropriate for the occasion, he did not become bewildered.
Then all the Kurus, seeing Karṇa and that terrible illusion, spoke.
"O Karṇa, slay the Rākṣasa today quickly with all your might!
These Kurus, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are perishing. What will Bhīma and Pārtha do for us?"
Slay this scorching Rakshasa in the dead of night!
He who might escape from our terrible battle should then fight for us against the sons of Pritha in combat.
Therefore, slay this Rākṣasa of terrible form with the spear given by Vāsava;
let not all the Kauravas, who are like Indra himself, perish.
At the onset of night, O Karṇa, the warriors perished;
being slaughtered by the Rākṣasa at midnight,
O King, he beheld his army being destroyed.
And hearing that great roar of the Kauravas,
Karṇa set his mind upon discharging the Śakti,
even as he was being struck by the Rākṣasa in the night.
O King, seeing your army fleeing and hearing the great roar of the Kurus,
the high-souled one set his mind upon discharging the Śakti.
Enraged like a lion and possessed of great indignation, he could not endure that counter-attack in battle;
[he took up] the supreme, invincible *vaijayantī* spear.
Desiring to effect his slaughter,
O King, he took up that [spear] which had been kept for many years and consecrated for the slaying of Phalguna in battle.
That supreme spear which Śakra indeed gave to the son of the Sūta, having exchanged it for his two earrings—
having taken that supreme spear in exchange for the two earrings.
O King, having received from Purandara that armor,
he took up that blazing spear, which was licking [with its flames] and bound with nooses like the Night of Death.
Vaikartana hurled that supreme weapon, which destroys the bodies of enemies, at the Rākṣasa— it was the sister of Death, blazing like a meteor.
O King, seeing that blazing [spear] held in Sauti’s arm, the terrified Rākṣasa fled,
making himself as large as the Vindhya mountain.
O lord of men, seeing the spear held within Karna’s arms,
the beings in the intermediate space roared; and tumultuous winds blew, O King.
Accompanied by a thunderous crash, the firebrand fell to the earth;
blazing, it reduced that illusion to ashes and pierced the Rākṣasa’s heart deeply.
Blazing, she ascended into the night sky,
entering the spaces between the stars;
having fought with various and diverse multitudes of weapons.
Uttering various divine, human, and demonic roars and terrifying cries,
the hero was made to relinquish his beloved life by the spear of Śakra.
And he performed this other wonderful and marvelous deed for the destruction of his enemies:
at that time, his vital organs were pierced by a spear.
O King, shining like a cloud or a mountain,
that lord of the Rākṣasas then fell from the sky to the earth with his life departed and his body shattered.
With his head hanging down, his limbs stiffened, and his tongue lolling,
Ghaṭotkaca assumed a massive form;
he of terrible deeds took on that fearsome appearance.
Having made himself terrible, the son of Bhīmasena fell;
even though slain, he thus crushed a portion of your army,
terrifying the Kauravas.
That Rākṣasa, whose life-force had departed, quickly increased his body to a vast size while still falling,
thereby doing what was pleasing to the Pāṇḍavas.
He swiftly slew your akṣauhiṇī;
then the mingled sounds of lion-roars,
kettledrums, conchs, drums, and cymbals resounded.
Seeing the illusion burnt away and the Rākṣasa slain,
the Kauravas rejoiced and shouted for joy;
then Karṇa was honored by the Kurus.
Just as Śakra, accompanied by the Maruts at the slaying of Vṛtra,
ascended [his chariot] and joyfully entered his own army, so too did he enter after mounting your son who stood upon his chariot.
When that Rākṣasa of great illusion and great splendor, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, had been slain,
what did the sons of Pāṇḍu, filled with indignation, do in that great battle?

O Saṃjaya, what did those who were severely crushed in battle do? And what did those strikers— the Sṛñjayas together with the Pañcālas— who had drawn up their ranks and rushed against Droṇa, do in that great conflict?
After the slaughter of Saumadatti, Drona— intent upon the death of the ruler of the Sindhus—
having cast away his life out of indignation,
plunged into the army like a yawning tiger with its mouth wide open, resembling Death itself.
How did the Kurus and Sṛñjayas advance against Droṇa, who is invincible?
And those led by Duryodhana, who protect the Teacher— O dear one, what did the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa do in that battle?

O Sañjaya, tell me how Savyasācin and Vṛkodara, seeking to slay Bhāradvāja, fared against my men in battle— those two who, through the slaughter of the Sindhu king and the slaughter of Ghaṭotkaca, [have brought such grief].
"Filled with indignation and enraged, how did they fight in battle?
Saṃjaya said:
"Having seen the son of Hiḍimbā slain, like a mountain shattered to pieces,"
All the Pāṇḍavas were dejected in spirit, their eyes clouded with tears;
but Vāsudeva, overwhelmed by great joy,
let out a roar like a lion, as if causing distress, O Bhārata.
Knowing that Ghaṭotkaca had been slain, the powerful Vāsudeva uttered a great roar and embraced Phalguna. Having let out a great roar and having restrained his reins, he [spoke].
Overcome with joy, he danced like a tree shaken by the wind. Then,
having whirled about once more and repeatedly slapped his arms,
Acyuta, standing upon the seat of the chariot, let out a roar at Bhīma.
Perceiving that Vāsudeva of great strength was delighted in mind,
O King, Arjuna spoke to him as if his own heart were not so joyful;
for Dhanañjaya, having observed that exultation of Keśava’s, [felt otherwise].
Arjuna also said, "O King,
O Madhusūdana, this excessive joy of yours today is misplaced,
for a supreme occasion for grief has arrived with the slaying of the son of Hiḍimbā."
Seeing Ghaṭotkaca slain, the armies turned their faces away;
we too were deeply distressed by the fall of the son of Hiḍimbā.
For this cause, O Janārdana, cannot be a minor one.
Therefore, O best among the truthful, being asked today, tell me the truth;
if this is not a secret of yours, you ought to speak it, O subduer of enemies— for when a calamity has actually occurred, men do not rejoice.
Even when there is cause for joy, the wise do not become excessive;
tell me now, O Madhusūdana, what is this aberration of their fortitude?
It is like the agitation of the ocean or the shifting of Mount Meru.
"O Janārdana, I consider this deed of yours to be such lightness [of hand].
Vāsudeva said:
"O Dhanañjaya, listen to me regarding this great joy that has come upon you."
O Dhananjaya of great splendor, know that as soon as Ghatotkaca has wasted this supreme weapon— which instantly brings about extreme clarity of mind— Karna is already as good as slain in battle.

Furthermore, what man is there in this world who could stand before Karṇa with a spear in his hand, as if before Kārttikeya in battle? By good fortune his armor has been removed; by good fortune his earrings have been taken away.
By good fortune, his unfailing spear has been rendered useless upon Ghaṭotkaca; for if he were still clad in his armor and adorned with his earrings,
that powerful Karṇa alone could have conquered even the three worlds together with the gods.
Neither Vāsava, nor Kubera, nor Varuṇa the lord of the waters,
nor Yama would dare to withstand Karṇa in battle;
for you have drawn the Gāṇḍīva, or I have the Sudarśana discus.
The two of them were not able to defeat that bull among men in battle while he was thus equipped; however,
for the sake of your benefit, Śakra used his illusory power to strip this conqueror of enemy cities of his earrings and his armor.
Because Karṇa cut off his armor and gave those two stainless earrings to Śakra, he is indeed known as Vaikartana;
like a furious venomous serpent paralyzed by the power of a mantra.
"O mighty-armed one, even as today Karṇa appears to me like a fire whose flames have been extinguished,
ever since that spear was given to Karṇa by the high-souled Vāsava, it has now been hurled at Ghaṭotkaca."
Having bartered for her with his two earrings and his divine armor,
Vṛṣa considered you as already slain in battle once he had obtained her.
Even though things have come to this pass, he cannot be killed by anyone else.
"O tiger among men, O sinless one, I swear by you, by truth, and by my own self:
because he is devoted to the Brahmins, truthful, ascetic, firm in his vows,
and compassionate even toward his enemies, Karna is known as 'Vṛṣa' (the Bull)."
A hero skilled in battle, mighty-armed, with his bow perpetually raised,
he crushes the leaders of chariot-tigers at the head of the fray, just as a lion in the forest tramples the herds of rutting elephants, leaving them devoid of pride.
Like the sun at midday, O tiger among men, he could not be gazed upon by your high-souled and preeminent warriors;
he was like the autumnal sun with its thousand rays of a web of arrows.
Just as a rain-cloud at the end of the summer heat pours down showers of water,
so did Karṇa, that cloud of celestial weapons, pour forth a rain like the god Parjanya;
even as the gods discharged a shower of arrows upon him from every side.
He cannot be conquered by you while his flesh and blood are flowing;
moreover, O Pāṇḍava, he is now deprived of his armor and his two earrings.
He is the one who, showering volleys of arrows, could even obstruct the sun.
Formerly, he was endowed with ascetic power, possessed of divine form and great majesty;
today, having attained human state, he has been liberated by the gift of Śakra.
Indeed, there must be a singular means for his destruction.

For, being vigilant, you might strike him at his weak point when he is careless, or when he has fallen into distress, like one sunk in the hub of a chariot wheel; but first, you must deliberate upon his true nature.

For even the sole hero Indra, the slayer of Bala, wielding his thunderbolt, could not slay in battle one who is invincible and has raised his weapons; such is the high-souled Jarāsaṃdha, the king of the Cedis.
And the mighty Niṣāda Ekalavya—
all of them were indeed slain one by one by me alone, through various means, for the sake of your welfare.
Furthermore, other lords of the Rākṣasas were slain— namely Hiḍimba, Kirmīra, Baka, and others—
as well as Alāyudha, the crusher of enemy armies.
And Ghaṭotkaca, of fierce deeds and great speed—
Arjuna said:
"O Janārdana, for what purpose and by what means were you employed for our benefit?"
Jarāsaṃdha and other lords of the earth have been slain.
Vāsudeva said:
"Jarāsaṃdha, the king of Cedi, and the mighty Naiṣādin—"
If they had not been slain previously, they would now be formidable;
Suyodhana would certainly have chosen those best of chariot-warriors,
and they, being constantly offended by us, would have sought refuge with the Kauravas.
For those high-souled heroes, skilled in weapons and firm in combat,
could protect the entire army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons like immortals— namely,
the son of the Sūta, Jarāsaṃdha, the king of Cedi, and the son of the Niṣāda.
Relying upon Suyodhana, they would have scorched this entire earth;
hear from me, O Dhanañjaya, those by whom they were slain through strategic means,
for without such means, they could not be conquered in battle even by the gods.
For each one of them individually could fight the entire host of gods in battle, O Pārtha, even when protected by the world-protectors;
for Jarāsaṃdha, provoked and insulted by the son of Rohiṇī, was filled with rage.
For the sake of slaying us, he hurled a mace with a blood-red face;
appearing like a parting line across the sky, blazing with the brilliance of fire,
it was seen as it fell like the thunderbolt released by Śakra.
Upon seeing that mace coming toward him, the son of Rohiṇī discharged the Sthūṇākarṇa weapon for the purpose of repelling it; struck by the force of that weapon,
the mace fell to the earth.
Tearing asunder the goddess Earth and making the mountains tremble,
there was a terrible Rākṣasī named Jarā, swift in her prowess,
who joined together that newborn subduer of foes, Jarāsaṃdha.
For he was born from two mothers with separate bodies; because he was joined together by her, he is therefore known as Jarāsaṃdha.
But she, O Pārtha, having been struck down along with her sons and kinsmen, has gone to the earth.
O Dhananjaya, while you were looking on, Jarasandha was deprived of his mace by that Rakshasi weapon, Sthunakarna, and was slain by Bhimasena in the great battle.
"For if the powerful Jarāsaṃdha were present with mace in hand,
O best of men, even the gods led by Indra would not have been able to slay him in battle. Indeed,
it was for your benefit that the Niṣāda was deprived of his thumb."
Having acted as the preceptor Droṇa through a stratagem, he of true prowess— Naiṣādin,
firm in his valor and wearing finger-guards—
shone like another Rāma while shooting alone as a forest-dweller.
O Pārtha, neither the gods, nor the Dānavas, nor even the Rākṣasas and Uragas together have ever been able to defeat Ekalavya in battle when his thumb is included;
how much less could a mere mortal hope even to look upon him?
Dṛḍhamuṣṭi was skilled and ever ready, discharging his weapons day and night;
yet for your benefit, he was slain by me at the head of the battle.
And the valiant King of Cedi was also killed before your very eyes.
And he too is impossible for all the gods and asuras to conquer in battle—
Yama, Indra, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the hosts of Maruts—
for he was born four-armed, wearing a garland of Jāmbūnada gold.

Invincible by all beings, he might even conquer the dwellers of heaven; for his sake, and for that of other enemies of the gods, I have been born as your companion, O tiger among men, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Hiḍimba, Baka, and Kirmīra were struck down by Bhīmasena;
likewise, Rāvaṇa’s equals in strength and destroyers of the Brahman-sacrifice were slain. Furthermore, the illusory Alāyudha was killed by the son of Hiḍimbā.
And the son of Hiḍimbā was slain by Karṇa through a stratagem with the *śakti* weapon;
for had Karṇa not struck him down with the *śakti* in that great battle,
Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhīmasena, would have been slain by me.
Previously, I did not slay him out of a desire for your welfare;
for this Rākṣasa was a hater of Brahmins and a hater of sacrifices, a destroyer of dharma and evil-souled— therefore, he has been struck down.
O sinless one, Śakradattā was also deceived by me through a stratagem.
For those who are destroyers of dharma must be slain by me, O Pāṇḍava;
indeed, this is my eternal vow for the sake of establishing dharma.
"Brahman, truth, self-restraint, purity, dharma, modesty, prosperity, fortitude, and forgiveness—
I swear to you by the truth that I always delight wherever these qualities are found. You must not feel despondent regarding Karṇa Vaikartana."
"I shall teach you the means by which you will overcome him;
furthermore, Vṛkodara will slay Suyodhana in battle. O Pāṇḍava, I shall also tell you the means for his destruction."
This tumultuous noise is increasing toward the enemy host,
and your troops are fleeing in the ten directions;
for the Kauravas, having found their mark, are scattering your army.
"And this Droṇa, the best among strikers, is consuming your army.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When the spear was rendered futile against the son of the Sūta, that foremost of heroes,"
Why did he abandon all others and not release that [weapon] at Pārtha? For if he had been slain, all the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas would have been slain;
why did he not secure victory in battle by slaying that peerless hero?
"Once challenged, I shall not turn back"—this was his great vow.
Therefore, Phalguna must be personally challenged by the son of the Sūta;
then, having brought Phalguna to a single combat with the [bow] given by Śakra...
"Why did the bull [Duryodhana] not slay them? Tell me that, Saṃjaya. Surely my son was both bereft of intelligence and lacking in allies;
how indeed could he have conquered his enemies when his stratagems were frustrated by his foes?"
For that supreme power of his, which was the ultimate foundation of his victory— that power has been frustrated by Vāsudeva against Ghaṭotkaca,
just as a bilva fruit held in the hand might be snatched away by a stronger man from a cripple.
Thus, that unfailing power became futile against Ghaṭotkaca,
just as when a boar and a dog fight, the gain belongs to the hunter upon the disappearance of both.
O learned one, I think that in battle the gain for Vāsudeva would be the same whether Karṇa kills Ghaṭotkaca or Ghaṭotkaca kills Karṇa.
For if Ghaṭotkaca should slay Karṇa—
That would be a supreme gain for the Pāṇḍavas,
even if Vaikartana were to slay him; for in that case, the task would be accomplished by the destruction of his power.
Thus, having deliberated upon this with his wisdom,
the wise Vāsudeva, that lion among men, caused Ghaṭotkaca to fight with the Sūta’s son in battle.
Doing what was pleasing and beneficial to the Pāṇḍavas,
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, having learned of this intention of Karṇa, the slayer of Madhu..."
Then Janārdana, possessed of great intelligence, O King, assigned the highly powerful Ghaṭotkaca to a duel with the lord of the Rākṣasas,
in order to frustrate the infallible weapon resulting from your evil counsel.
O best of the Kurus, at that very moment we would have accomplished our purpose,
had Kṛṣṇa not protected that son of Pṛthā from the great car-warrior Karṇa; for then,
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he would have fallen to the earth in battle along with his horses, banner, and chariot.
Without Janārdana, the Lord and Master of all yogas, Pārtha could not prevail; yet,
O King, being protected by Kṛṣṇa and guarded by those various and manifold means, Pārtha conquers his enemies when facing them.
But Kṛṣṇa protected the Pāṇḍava with special care from Amoghā;
for had that spear been hurled, it would have slain the son of Kuntī like a thunderbolt striking a tree.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
My son is hostile, a bad counselor, and one who fancies himself wise;
for him this means of slaughter regarding victory has been bypassed.
Or perhaps it is Karṇa, of great intelligence, the best among all wielders of weapons.
"O Sūta, how did he not release that unfailing weapon at Dhanañjaya?
O Gāvalgaṇi, how was it that even this escaped you?
O one of great intelligence, why was this matter not made known by you?"
Saṃjaya said:
"Night after night, this very deliberation constantly occurs between Duryodhana, Śakuni, myself, and Duḥśāsana."
"Tomorrow, O Karṇa, leaving aside all your troops, slay Dhanañjaya.
Then we shall enjoy the Pāṇḍus and the Pañcālas like servants. Or else, once Pārtha has been slain, [we shall enjoy] whichever one among the Pāṇḍus remains."
The descendant of Vṛṣṇi stands firm in battle; therefore, let Kṛṣṇa be struck down. For Kṛṣṇa is the root of the Pāṇḍavas, while Pārtha has risen like the trunk;
the other sons of Pṛthā are like the branches, and the Pañcālas are known as the leaves.
The Pāṇḍavas have Kṛṣṇa as their refuge, Kṛṣṇa as their strength, and Kṛṣṇa as their lord;
indeed, Kṛṣṇa is their ultimate resort, just as the moon is for the luminaries.
Therefore, O son of a Sūta, casting aside the leaves, the branches, and the trunk, [seek refuge in him].
"O Kṛṣṇa, cut down the root of the Pāṇḍavas everywhere and at all times!
For if Karṇa were to slay the descendant of Daśārha, the joy of the Yādavas,
O King, the entire earth would undoubtedly come under your control."

O King, O lord of men, that resolve which was formed regarding Kṛṣṇa will perish at the time of battle for those who are deluded by the splendor of Viṣṇu. For if he were slain, he would lie upon the earth; yet [he is invincible].
O lord of men, surely the entire earth— with its mountains, oceans, and forests— would come under your control, for you are the high-souled delight of the Yadu clan and the Pāṇḍavas.
But that resolve, though thus formed while the Lord of the Thirty-three was awake—
that immeasurable Hṛṣīkeśa— was lost at the time of battle;
for Keśava always protects Arjuna, the son of Kuntī.
For he did not wish to place him in front of the Sūta’s son in battle;
instead, Acyuta stationed other noble chariot-warriors before him,
thinking, "O Lord, how may I render that unfailing spear futile?"
O King, how could that high-minded Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, not protect himself when he thus protects Pārtha from Karṇa? Yet,
upon reflection, we behold the wielder of the discus, the subduer of enemies.

"There is no one in the three worlds who could defeat Janārdana. Then the mighty-armed Sātyaki, whose valor is truth, that tiger among chariot-warriors, questioned Kṛṣṇa concerning the great car-warrior Karṇa.
"And this weapon, O one of immeasurable prowess, was placed upon Karna's ear by Śakti;
for what reason was it not released by the Sūta’s son against Phalguna?
Vāsudeva said:
Duḥśāsana, Karṇa, Śakuni, and the ruler of the Sindhus,
led by Duryodhana, were constantly deliberating:
"O Karṇa, Karṇa, great archer of immeasurable prowess in battle!"
"O best among victors, this power of yours must not be released against anyone else,
except for the great car-warrior Pārtha, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī;
for he is the most illustrious among them, like Vāsava among the gods."
When he has been slain, all the Pāṇḍavas together with the Sṛñjayas will become dispirited, like gods deprived of their sacrificial fires; indeed,
they will certainly be destroyed by Karṇa, except for the high-souled Pārtha.
"So be it," O bull of the Śinis, Karna promised;
yet the slaughter of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow was always in Karna's heart.
However, O best of warriors, it was I who deluded the son of Rādhā.
Since he did not discharge that *śakti* at the Pāṇḍava who has white horses, O best of warriors,
I have neither sleep nor joy in my mind as Phalguna fights, knowing that it is his death.
O bull among the Śinis, seeing that [weapon] rendered futile by Ghaṭotkaca,
I see Dhananjaya today as one released from the very jaws of death;
neither my father, nor my mother, nor you, my brothers, [could have saved him].

One’s life-breaths are not to be protected as much as Bībhatsu is in battle. O Sātvata, were there anything else more difficult to obtain than sovereignty over the three worlds, I would not desire it without Pārtha Dhanañjaya.
Therefore, today a very great joy has arisen in me from Yuyudhāna,
upon seeing Dhananjaya, the son of Pṛthā, like one who has returned from the dead.
And for this reason, the Rākṣasa was dispatched by me into battle against Karṇa.
"For indeed, no one else is capable of overpowering Karṇa in battle at night.
Sātyaki said:
"His victory is certain and his long life shall endure forever."
"O tiger among men, he for whose welfare you have always remained present.
Sañjaya said:
Thus did the son of Devakī then speak to Sātyaki.
Dedicated to the welfare of Dhanañjaya and constantly devoted to his pleasure,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Of Karṇa, Duryodhana, and the others, as well as Śakuni, the son of Subala..."
O dear one, a great loss has been sustained, especially by you,
in that you allowed that spear— which always slays a single foe in battle,
and which is irresistible and unbearable even for the gods led by Indra— to be taken away.
"Why was it not released by Karṇa earlier when the battle had commenced—
neither against the son of Devakī nor against Phalguna, O Sañjaya?
Sañjaya said:
O lord of the people, O best of the Kuru lineage, as we all returned from the battle, this counsel arose among us during the night:
"At the mere break of dawn, when tomorrow has come, [what should be done] for Keśava or Arjuna?"
"O Karṇa, O Karṇa!"— this was the power that had to be constantly invoked.
Then, at the time of dawn, O King, the divine powers caused that resolve of Karṇa,
as well as that of the other warriors, to vanish once again.
I consider fate alone to be supreme, since Karṇa, though possessing it in his hand,
did not slay Pārtha or Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, in battle;
for that spear remained in his hand like the raised Night of Doom.

O Lord, because his intellect was struck down by fate, Karṇa did not release that [weapon] at Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, who was deluded by divine illusion; nor did he release the Vāsavi weapon for the sake of slaying Pārtha, who is equal to Śakra.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"You have been struck down by destiny alone, as well as by the intelligence of Keśava;
for the daughter of Vāsava has departed after slaying Ghaṭotkaca, who was like a blade of grass."
Karna, my sons, and all the other kings have gone to the abode of Vaivasvata because of this ill-conducted [war].
Tell me once more, however, how the battle proceeded.
When the son of Hiḍimbā had been slain, how did those strikers of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas— who,
having drawn up their battle arrays, rushed against Droṇa—
along with the Sṛñjayas and the Pañcālas, conduct the battle?
After the slaughter of Saumadatti and the Saindhava, Drona—
exerting himself out of indignation and casting away his life—
plunged into the army like a yawning tiger or like Death with gaping jaws.
How did the Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas advance against Droṇa as he was discharging his weapons?
And those who protected the Teacher, led by Duryodhana— O dear one, what did the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa do in that battle?
"O Sañjaya, tell me how my men fared in battle against Bhāradvāja, whom Savyasācin and Vṛkodara both sought to slay;
for these two were intent on the slaughter of the King of Sindhu, while those others were intent on the slaughter of Ghaṭotkaca."
"Being indignant and greatly enraged, how did they fight in battle during the night?
Sañjaya said:
"O King, when the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca had been slain by Karṇa in the night,"

While your men, eager for battle, were shouting with joy and charging forward with speed, and while the enemy force was being slaughtered and the night had grown deep, the king fell into a state of extreme despondency.
And the mighty-armed scorcher of foes spoke to Bhīmasena:
"O mighty-armed one, hold back the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son;
for by the assault of Haiḍimba, a great delusion has come over me."
Having thus instructed Bhīma,
the king mounted his own chariot with his face bathed in tears, sighing again and again;
seeing the prowess of Karṇa, he fell into a state of terrible despondency.
Seeing him thus distressed, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words:
"Do not grieve, O son of Kuntī; this is not fitting for you, O best of the Bharatas, such dejection as one finds in an ordinary man."
"Arise, O King, fight! Bear the heavy burden, O Lord. If you fall into despondency, there will be doubt regarding victory.
Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, [arose].
Wiping his eyes with both hands, he spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa:
"O mighty-armed one, you know the supreme goal of all dharmas;
for him who does not recognize the fruit of his own actions, there is the consequence of killing a Brahmin."
For while we were dwelling in the forest, O Janārdana, assistance was rendered to us by that high-souled son of Hiḍimbā, even though he was but a child;
for he learned that the Pāṇḍava of white steeds had gone away for the sake of obtaining celestial weapons.
Having arrived with his companion, protection was provided by that great-souled one;
yet today he has been slain by Karṇa while those evil-minded ones looked on.
O Mādhava, how indeed shall I find liberation from this sinful deed?
"O Kṛṣṇa, that great archer approached me in the Kāmyaka forest;
he dwelt with us until Dhananjaya returned.
During the journey to Gandhamādana, we were delivered from difficult passes by him."
And the exhausted princess of Pañcāla was carried on the back of that high-souled one;
for during the conquest of the quarters, O Kṛṣṇa, at the command of Sahadeva,
the descendant of Pulastya was indeed made to pay tribute by force after he had gone to Laṅkā.
O Lord Janārdana, from the very commencement of these battles,
that high-souled one has performed difficult deeds for my sake;
and there is a natural affection of mine toward Sahadeva.
That very same joy is doubled for me in Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Rākṣasas. That mighty-armed one is devoted to me; I am dear to him and he is dear to me.
It is because of this, O Vārṣṇeya, that I, tormented by grief, fall into despondency.
"Behold the armies being routed by the Kauravas, O Vārṣṇeya! Behold Droṇa and Karṇa, those two great car-warriors, prepared for battle.
Behold the Pāṇḍava host being crushed by these two in the dead of night."
O Mādhava, disregarding the strength of Bhīmasena’s arms and the skill in diverse weapons of Pārtha, the Kauravas displayed their prowess, like two rutting elephants in a vast forest of reeds.
"Here are Droṇa, Karṇa, and King Suyodhana;
having slain the Rākṣasa in battle, they are roaring with joy in the fray. How is this possible while we are still alive, and while you yourself, O Janārdana, are present?"
The son of Hiḍimbā met his death in combat with the Sūta’s son;
having rendered all of us useless while Savyasācin looked on,
O Kṛṣṇa, that mighty Rākṣasa, the son of Bhīmasena, has been slain.
When Abhimanyu was slain by the evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
O Kṛṣṇa, the great car-warrior Savyasācin was not present there in that battle;
and we were all held in check by the wicked-souled ruler of the Sindhus.
Droṇa, along with his son, became the instrument for that deed;
the method for Karna’s slaughter was taught by the preceptor himself,
and as Karna was struggling with his sword, he cut that sword in two.
As he was in a state of distress, Kṛtavarman, acting with cruelty, suddenly slew his horses as well as both his flank-drivers; likewise,
the other great archers struck down the son of Subhadrā while he was fighting.
"O Kṛṣṇa, best of the Yādavas, the ruler of the Sindhus was slain by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva for a trivial reason; that is not at all pleasing to me,
even if it were right for the Pāṇḍavas to act thus in the slaying of an enemy."
"It is my conviction that Droṇa and Karṇa must first be slain in battle;
for these two, O bull among men, are the very root of our sorrows. Having found them in the fray, Suyodhana has become confident."

"Where Drona and the Suta's son with his followers might be slain, there the mighty-armed one slew the ruler of the Sindhus, who dwelt afar. Yet, the subduing of the Suta's son must certainly be accomplished by me."
"Then, O hero, I myself shall go with the intent to slay Karṇa,
while the mighty-armed Bhīmasena has encountered Droṇa’s division.
Having spoken thus, Yudhiṣṭhira departed quickly, hastening forward.
Having drawn his great bow and blown his terrifying conch shell,
he then [advanced] with a thousand chariots, three hundred elephants,
five thousand horses, and three thousand Prabhadrakas.
Surrounded [by his forces], Śikhaṇḍin quickly followed behind the king. Then, the armored warriors beat their kettledrums and blew their conchs;
indeed, the armored ones produced the sounds of conchs as well as the whizzing of arrows.
Then the mighty-armed Vāsudeva said to Dhanañjaya: "Yudhiṣṭhira, preceded by the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas,
is advancing here in haste, overcome with wrath."
"It is not right to remain indifferent toward one who seeks to slay the son of the Sūta. Having spoken thus, Hṛṣīkeśa quickly urged on the horses;
and Janārdana followed after the king who had already traveled a great distance.
Seeing him rushing forward suddenly with the intent to slay the Sūta’s son,
his resolve stricken by grief and as if burning with fire,
Vyāsa approached and spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
"By good fortune, Phalguna lives after encountering Karṇa in battle;
for he preserved his spear, desiring the slaughter of Savyasācin. And by good fortune, O bull of the Bharatas, Jishnu did not enter into a single combat with him."
Competing with one another, these two shall discharge celestial weapons in every way.
When their weapons are being destroyed and he is afflicted,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of the Sūta will surely release the Vāsavi śakti in battle.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, a terrible calamity would have befallen you;
by good fortune, O giver of honor, that Rākṣasa has been slain in battle by the Sūta’s son,
for he was struck down by Time, making the Vāsavi weapon the mere instrument.
"O dear one, it was for your sake alone that the Rākṣasa was slain in battle.
Do not be angry, O best of the Bharatas, and do not set your mind on grief;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this is the inevitable end for all living beings here."
Accompanied by all your brothers and the high-souled kings,
O King, O Bhārata, do battle against the Kauravas in combat;
on the fifth day, the earth shall indeed be yours.
O tiger among men, O Pāṇḍava, always contemplate only dharma— compassion, austerity, charity, forbearance, and truth—
with supreme joy; for where there is dharma, there is victory.
Having spoken thus to the Pāṇḍava, Vyāsa vanished right there.
Sañjaya said:
Thus addressed by Vyāsa, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, [acted accordingly].
O bull among the Bharatas, that hero withdrew from the slaying of Karṇa himself;
but when Ghaṭotkaca had been killed by the Sūta’s son during that night,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, fell under the sway of grief and indignation.
Seeing your vast army being held back by Bhīma, he said this to Dhṛṣṭadyumna: "Restrain the pot-born one!
For you were born from the sacrificial fire for the very purpose of Droṇa’s destruction."
"Armed with arrows, clad in armor, bearing a sword and a bow, you who scorch your enemies, charge joyfully into battle; let there be no fear in you whatsoever.
Janamejaya, Śikhaṇḍin, Daurmukhi, and Yaśodhana [are here]."
Let them, filled with joy, rush from all sides toward the pot-born Droṇa—
Nakula and Sahadeva, the sons of Draupadī, the Prabhadrakas,
and Drupada and Virāṭa, accompanied by their sons and brothers.
"Let Sātyaki, the Kekayas, and Dhanañjaya the Pāṇḍava rush forward with speed, desiring the slaughter of the son of Bharadvāja;
likewise, let all the chariot-warriors and whatever elephants and horses there are do the same."
"Let the foot-soldiers also bring the great car-warrior Droṇa into the fray. Thus commanded by the high-souled Pāṇḍava,
they all rushed with speed toward the Pot-born one, desiring to fight.
As those Pāṇḍavas were suddenly approaching with all their exertion,
Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons, received them in battle.
Then King Duryodhana [advanced] against the Pāṇḍavas with all his exertion.
Highly incensed and desiring to preserve Drona’s life, he rushed forward;
then a battle commenced between the Pandavas and the Kurus, whose mounts and soldiers were exhausted, as they roared at one another.
"Blinded by sleep and exhausted by the battle, O great king,
those great car-warriors were unable to perform any action in the fray.
This night of three watches was of terrible form and fearsome."

That night, which was like a thousand watches, became incomparable and life-taking; for those who were being slain and especially for those who were wounded, day and night seemed to be joined together, as they were particularly blinded by sleep.

For all the kṣatriyas, both yours and those of the enemy, were devoid of energy and dejected in heart; their weapons were spent and their arrows exhausted. Yet they continued to endure in that state, being especially possessed of a sense of shame.
Observing their own duty, they did not abandon their respective divisions;
others, blinded by sleep, lay down having cast aside their weapons—
some upon elephants, some upon chariots, and others upon horses, O Bhārata.
Blinded by sleep, the lords of men perceived no movement at all;
those warriors in battle dispatched one another to the abode of Yama,
while others, losing their senses, mistook their enemies for friends as they drifted in slumber.
In that great battle, blinded by sleep, they discharged various cries and slew even their own kin as well as the enemy; O Great King, many of our men [did likewise] against the foes.
Thinking, "We must fight," they stood with eyes heavy with sleep; others, crushed in the battle and blinded by slumber, struck one another— those heroes, O King, in that terrible darkness.
In that battle, many men, utterly deluded by sleep, did not perceive themselves being struck by their enemies;
having observed such behavior among them, that bull among men—
Bībhatsu spoke these words aloud, making the quarters resound:
"You all, along with your mounts, are exhausted and blinded by sleep;
the army is shrouded in darkness and thick dust."
"If you so desire, O soldiers, cease for a moment; close your eyes right here upon this field of battle. Then, once you have woken and rested, when the moon has risen again—"
"O Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, you shall achieve your respective goals for the sake of heaven through one another.
Having heard those words of the righteous man, who knows all dharma,
those armies approved and spoke thus to one another.
"O King, they cried out, 'Karna! Karna! and 'Duryodhana!';
'Cease, O Pandavas, for the army has withdrawn!'—thus did Phalguna cry out here and there."
"Cease, O Bhārata, the army of the Pāṇḍavas and yours!
At these words of that high-souled one, the gods, the ṛṣis,
and all the noble soldiers rejoiced and paid him homage.
O Bhārata, having heard those gentle words, all the troops,
O King, exhausted from their toil, slept for a moment, O bull of the Bharatas.
Having thus obtained rest, O Bhārata, that army of yours [remained there].
Having attained happiness, she honored the heroic Arjuna:
"In you are the Vedas as well as the weapons; in you are intelligence and prowess. O mighty-armed one, in you is righteousness, O sinless one, and compassion toward all beings."
"O Pārtha, we desire that which you have sought; may that protection be yours. O hero, may you swiftly attain those objects dear to your heart.
Thus did those great chariot-warriors praise that tiger among men.
Overcome by sleep, O lord of the people, they remained silent;
some lay on the backs of horses, others in the seats of chariots, some upon the shoulders of elephants, and others on the bare ground.
Other men lay sleeping here and there, each with their weapons— some with maces, some with swords, some with battle-axes, and others with spears and armor.
Those elephants, with their trunks like the coils of serpents and covered in the dust of the earth, [lay prostrate].
Blinded by sleep, the elephants made the earth cool with the breath from their nostrils; they lay there upon the ground,
sighing like shattered mountains filled with hissing great serpents.
The horses, with their golden harnesses and yokes resting upon their manes, made the earth level and uneven as they tore it up with the tips of their hooves;
O king of kings, they slept there, all still harnessed to their vehicles.
Thus, O bull of the Bharatas, the horses, the elephants, and the warriors,
having desisted from the battle, fell asleep, overcome by great exhaustion. That army, thus broken by sleep, became speechless and lay fast asleep.
Like a wondrous painting skillfully composed by artists upon a canvas,
those youthful Kṣatriyas, adorned with earrings,
had their limbs wounded by one another’s arrows.
Exhausted by the battle,
the heroes slept upon the frontal globes of the elephants, clinging to them like lovers to the breasts of passionate women.
Then, like the breasts of amorous women exhausted by lovemaking at night,
the eastern quarter was adorned by the moon— the lord of the night-lotuses, pale as the cheeks of a passionate woman, and the delight of the eyes.
Emerging from the quarters like a thousand-eyed Indra,
radiant and tawny with rays for its filaments,
it shatters the herds of elephants that are the darkness.
May the lion of the Eastern Mountain arise,
possessing a luster equal to the body of Śiva’s noble bull,
and a radiance like that of the fully drawn bow of Smara.
Charming and beautiful with the smiles of a new bride,
the friend of the lily ponds has spread abroad; indeed,
the moon delights the earth.
Then, after a moment, the Lord, the master who bears the mark of the moon, appeared in the east and displayed the dawn, swallowing the radiance of the luminaries.
Following that dawn, he revealed [the sun] with a luster equal to refined gold.
The great moon slowly released its vast web of rays;
dispelling the darkness with their brilliance, those lunar beams gradually pervaded all the quarters, as well as the sky and the earth.

Then, in a mere moment, the world became as if filled with light; the darkness, which was neither visible nor luminous, quickly vanished when the night-maker (the moon) appeared, illuminating the world as if it were day.
O King, the night-rangers then neither moved about nor remained still;
yet that army, being awakened by the rays of the moon, O King,
woke up like a vast forest of lotuses in the water.
Just as the ocean becomes agitated when stirred by the rising of the moon,
so too did that ocean of an army become stirred by the rising of the moon.
Then, O lord of the people, the battle commenced once again.
"For those who desire the destruction of the world in this world and seek the supreme world [hereafter]," Sañjaya said:
"Then Duryodhana, having approached Droṇa, spoke as follows."
Overcome by indignation, generating both joy and fiery energy, he thought:
"Enemies who have rested in battle, though exhausted and dejected in mind, must not be spared— especially those who have achieved their objective."
We endured that, however, out of a desire to do what was pleasing to you;
yet now these Pāṇḍavas have become even more powerful and have completely exhausted themselves.
We, on the other hand, have entirely declined in both energy and strength.
Protected by you, they flourish again and again;
all the divine weapons, including the Brahmāstra and others,
abide especially within you alone.
"Neither the sons of Pāṇḍu, nor we, nor any other archers in the world are equal to you when you are fighting; I tell you this as the truth,
O best of the twice-born, regarding these worlds including the gods, asuras, and gandharvas."
"You are a master of all weapons and could undoubtedly slay them with divine missiles;
yet you tolerate these men who are especially afraid of you—
either out of respect for your status as my pupil, or because of my own misfortune."
Thus encouraged and provoked by your son, O King, Droṇa, filled with wrath,
spoke these words to Duryodhana:
"Though I am advanced in years, I shall strive with all my might in this battle, O Duryodhana."

Henceforth, I, greedy for victory, must perform a base task: this entire people, who are unskilled in weapons, must be slain by me, who am skilled in weapons. And whatever you deem to be right, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [that shall be done].
"O Kauravya, by your word I shall indeed do that, and not otherwise.
Having displayed my prowess in battle and slain all the Pāñcālas, O King, I shall cast off my armor; I swear this by truth, touching my weapon."
And as for what you think of Kaunteya Arjuna when he is weary in battle— listen, O mighty-armed Kaurava, to his valor in truth:
neither the gods, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Yakṣas, nor the Rākṣasas [can withstand him].
They do not dare to withstand Savyasācin when he is enraged in battle—
he by whom the illustrious Lord of the Gods was encountered at Khāṇḍava and even the pouring rain was warded off with arrows by that high-souled one.
The Yakṣas, Nāgas, as well as the Daityas and others who were arrogant in their strength,
were slain by that lord of men— this too is known to you. Furthermore,
Citrasena and the other Gandharvas were defeated during the expedition to Ghoṣa.
And while you were being carried away by them, you were liberated by Dṛḍhadhanvan;
likewise, even the Nivātakavacas, those enemies of the gods who were incapable of being slain in battle by the deities,
were utterly defeated by that hero.
That tiger among men conquered thousands of Dānavas dwelling in Hiraṇyapura; how could he be overcome by mere mortals?
Indeed, you have witnessed all this with your own eyes, as has this power of yours.
"O lord of the people, while we were still striving, everything was destroyed by the son of Pāṇḍu.
As Arjuna was thus praising him,
O King, your son, filled with rage, then spoke these words again to Droṇa.
"I, Duḥśāsana, Karṇa, and my maternal uncle Śakuni—we shall slay Arjuna in battle today by dividing the Bharata host.
Stay here, O mighty-armed one; you have always been my dear disciple."
Having heard those words of his, Bhāradvāja, as if smiling,
complied with the king and said, "May it be well with you!
For who indeed [can withstand] the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, blazing as if with fiery energy?"
Some Kṣatriya might exhaust that bull among Kṣatriyas, who is himself inexhaustible;
yet neither the Lord of Wealth, nor Indra, nor Yama, nor the Lord of the Waters, nor the Asuras,
Uragas, and Rākṣasas could defeat him while he is armed with his weapons.
But these fools speak those very words that you have uttered, O Bhārata:
"For who, having encountered Arjuna in battle, could return home in safety?
Yet you, because of your excessive suspicion toward everyone, are cruel and fixed in your resolve for evil.
"You desire to say this and that here to those who are devoted to your welfare for the sake of their own good.
You too should go to the son of Kuntī without delay for your own sake;
for you, born of noble lineage, are indeed a kṣatriya and wish to fight."
"Why will you have all these innocent kings slain? You are the root of this enmity; therefore, attack Arjuna!
This wise maternal uncle of yours is devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya."

"Let Gāndhārī, who plays at dice with great skill, go forth against Arjuna in battle. This crooked gambler, skilled in dice, a rogue and a deceiver, a player who understands deceit— this man shall conquer the Pāṇḍavas in combat."
07.160.032a You spoke at great length with Karna, full of joy,
07.160.032c repeatedly in that empty forest out of delusion while Dhṛtarāṣṭra was listening.
07.160.033a And I, O dear one, and Karna, and my brother Duḥśāsana—
"We three, united, shall slay the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle"—this was heard from you as you boasted in assembly after assembly. Fulfill that vow; be true to your word along with them.
"This Pāṇḍava enemy stands before you, invincible.
Observe the duty of a Kṣatriya; your death would be more praiseworthy than victory. You have given gifts, enjoyed pleasures, studied the Vedas, and attained the sovereignty you desired."
"You have accomplished your purpose and are free from debt; do not fear, fight the Pāṇḍava!
Having said this in the battle, Droṇa turned back toward where the enemies were;
then, having divided his army in two, the combat commenced.
Saṃjaya said:
O lord of the people, when only a third of the night remained, the battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, who were all filled with joy, proceeded.
Then Aruṇa, the forerunner of the sun, rose up, stealing away the moonlight and turning the sky copper-red as it were; he illuminated the heavens,
as if delighting the entire world.
In the eastern direction, the solar disc shines like a golden wheel, reddened by the dawn-red glow of the thousand-rayed sun;
from there [came] chariots, horses, and human vehicles.
Having abandoned [the battle], all the warriors of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas,
facing the sun and chanting prayers,
stood with palms joined in reverence as the twilight approached.
Then, when the army had been divided into two, Droṇa, preceded by Duryodhana, rushed against the Somakas, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Pañcālas. Seeing the Kurus split in two, Mādhava spoke to Arjuna.
"I shall place these Kurus to my left, O Savyasācin. Having thus given his permission to Mādhava with the words "Do so," Dhanañjaya turned toward the great archers Droṇa and Karṇa from the left.
Having understood Kṛṣṇa’s intention, the conqueror of enemy cities saw Bhīmasena at the head of the battle and approached him. Bhīma said:
"O Arjuna, Arjuna, O Bībhatsu, listen to my words according to the truth:
the time has now arrived for that purpose for which a Kṣatriya woman gives birth.
If, when this time has come, you do not attain what is beneficial..."
Though your form may seem improbable, you shall act with compassion;
through your valor, discharge your debt to truth, prosperity, dharma, and fame. O best of warriors, Savyasācin, pierce this host and subdue these men.
Saṃjaya said:
Urged by Bhīma and Keśava,
that ambidextrous archer bypassed Karṇa and Droṇa and surrounded [the king] from all sides.
As he advanced toward the head of the battle, scorching those bulls among the Kṣatriyas,
the bulls among the Kṣatriyas exerted themselves with great prowess,
yet they were unable to restrain him as he surged forward like a growing fire.
Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, the son of Subala,
rained down showers of arrows upon Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī. He,
the best among those skilled in supreme weapons, [warded off] the missiles of them all.
O Indra among kings, disregarding him, he covered him with showers of arrows;
having warded off those weapons with his own weapons, the light-handed Dhananjaya pierced them all with ten sharp arrows each.
A rain of dust was stirred up, and likewise a rain of arrows;
a terrible darkness and a great noise then arose. When things had come to such a pass, neither heaven, nor earth, nor the directions could be discerned.
07.161.016c Everything became as if blind, obscured by the dust raised by the army.
07.161.017a Neither they nor we, O King, could recognize one another;
07.161.017b we and they recognized each other only by means of sound alone.
For by that very designation, O King, the monarchs fought one another;
having encountered each other, chariot-warriors were deprived of their chariots and grappled with their hair, armor, and arms.
Then the chariot-warriors, their horses slain and their drivers killed, stood motionless;
though afflicted by fear, they appeared as if still alive,
clinging to their slaughtered elephants as if to mountains.
They were seen devoid of life, along with their riders;
then, having advanced from the battle toward the northern direction,
Droṇa stood in the fray like a smokeless fire.
O lord of the people, seeing him withdrawn to a secluded spot at the head of the battle, the armies of the Pāṇḍavas trembled;
he was resplendent, endowed with glory, and as if blazing with fiery energy.
O noble one, upon seeing Droṇa— who was summoning the enemy host like an elephant in rut— his enemies trembled, wavered, and grew faint;
they did not dare hope to conquer him, just as the Dānavas could not hope to conquer Vāsava.
Some were despondent, some were high-minded and enraged;
some were filled with wonder, and some were indignant. Other lords of men rubbed their palms together with their hands.
Shaking off their other hands, some, filled with rage, wrung their own arms; others, fainting with fury, bit their lips with their teeth;
some brandished their weapons, while others crushed their limbs.
Others of great prowess, having renounced their lives, rushed toward Droṇa;
but the Pāñcālas in particular, tormented by Droṇa’s arrows and suffering intense pain, O king of kings, remained steadfastly engaged in battle.
O great king, upon seeing Droṇa, the Pāṇḍavas trembled;
then the warriors of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas beheld Droṇa blazing with floods of arrows.
Then all the Sṛñjayas and the Pāṇḍavas, desiring to slay Droṇa, advanced against him alone;
then Virāṭa and Drupada also proceeded toward Droṇa in the battle.
As he was thus engaged in battle, exceedingly difficult to conquer in combat,
O lord of the people, three grandsons of Drupada and the great bowmen of the Cedis then advanced against Drona himself in the fight.
With three sharpened arrows, Droṇa took the lives of those three grandsons of Drupada; slain, they fell to the earth. Then, in battle, Droṇa defeated the Cedis, the Kekayas, and the Sṛñjayas.
The great car-warrior Bhāradvāja then defeated all the Matsyas. Thereupon, O great king, Drupada and Virāṭa, out of wrath, showered a rain of arrows upon Droṇa in that battle.
Having struck down that shower of arrows, Droṇa, the crusher of kṣatriyas,
covered both Virāṭa and Drupada with his shafts;
being thus shrouded by Droṇa at the forefront of the battle, the two of them became enraged.
Filled with supreme rage, the two pierced Droṇa with their arrows.
Then, O great king, Droṇa, overcome by anger and impatience,
severed the bows of both with two exceedingly sharp broad-headed shafts.
Then Virāṭa, enraged in battle, hurled ten lances and ten arrows at Droṇa, desiring his death;
and Drupada [threw] a terrible iron spear adorned with gold.
Enraged, he hurled that weapon, which resembled the lord of serpents, toward Droṇa’s chariot.
Then, having severed those ten *tomara*s with well-sharpened broad-headed arrows (*bhallas*),
Droṇa cut down the spear adorned with gold and lapis lazuli with his shafts.
Afflicted by those two aged women who were frantic with rage, the elderly Drona,
the crusher of enemies, then dispatched Drupada and Virata to the abode of Vaivasvata with two well-sharpened broad-headed arrows.
When Virāṭa, Drupada, and likewise the Kekayas had been slain,
and similarly the Cedis, the Matsyas, and the Pañcālas,
and when the three heroes— the grandsons of Drupada— had also been killed.

Seeing that deed of Droṇa, he was filled with anger and grief toward the three grandsons of the Pāñcāla king— those performers of wondrous deeds— as he desired to carry out a difficult task for the slaughter of father and sons.
In the midst of the chariot-warriors, the high-minded Dhṛṣṭadyumna uttered this curse:
"May he from whom Droṇa escapes today, or he who turns his back on Droṇa, be deprived of the merit of his sacrifices and charitable works, as well as of his kṣatriya status and his brahminhood."
Having thus given them his promise in the midst of all those archers,
the Pāñcālya prince, the slayer of enemy heroes, advanced toward Droṇa with his army;
the Pāñcālas struck at Droṇa from one side, while the Pāṇḍavas did so from the other.
Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala,
as well as their principal uterine brothers, protected Droṇa in the battle;
while Droṇa was thus being guarded in the encounter by those high-souled warriors, [the Pandavas attacked].
O sire, although the Pāñcālas exerted themselves, they were unable even to look at him;
thereupon Bhīmasena became enraged with Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O noble one,
and that bull among men lacerated him with fierce words.

Born in the lineage of Drupada and the most skilled among all those who know weapons, what Kshatriya, considering himself a warrior, would look on while an enemy stands before him? Having suffered the slaughter of his father and sons, what man would let such a moment pass by?
Especially after having sworn an oath in the assembly of kings,
this Droṇa— like a kindled Vaiśvānara fire by his own brilliance, with his bow and arrows as fuel— consumes the warrior class with his splendor.
"Before long he will utterly destroy the army of the Pāṇḍavas;
stay here and behold my feat! I myself am going toward Droṇa.
Having said this, Vṛkodara entered Drona’s division in a rage.
Causing your army to flee with arrows released from firm bows drawn to their full stretch,
Bhīma then raised his mace like the Staff of Death itself,
O King, and hurled it at Droṇa, amidst the horses and foot-soldiers on the chariot.
O King, he then crushed Drona’s chariot along with its horses, driver, and banner;
by his might, he crushed many of his own warriors like trees struck by the wind.
Then Drona, the best among strikers, mounted another chariot.
Having taken his position at the gateway of the array, he stood ready for battle;
meanwhile, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the prince of the Pañcālas, having penetrated the vast army,
encountered Droṇa in the fray, and a great, tumultuous conflict ensued.
"O King, never before have we seen or heard of such a battle as this,
wherein at sunrise there arose a great,
tumultuous carnage; O noble one, multitudes of chariots were seen locked in close combat."
The bodies of embodied beings lay slain and scattered;
some, while fleeing elsewhere, were beset on the road by others;
some were struck from behind as they turned their faces away, and others were beaten from the sides.
Thus that closely joined battle became exceedingly fierce;
then, in an instant, the sun reached the hour of twilight.
Sañjaya said:
O Great King, clad in armor just as they were at the front of the battle,
they stood before the thousand-rayed sun as it reached the twilight hour. But when the thousand-rayed sun had risen, possessing the brilliance of molten gold—
When the worlds were illuminated, the battle commenced once more. Those duels which had been joined there before sunrise, O Bhārata, engaged again once the sun had risen.
Chariots encountered horses, horses encountered elephants, and foot-soldiers also encountered elephants; horses met with horses, and foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers, O bull among men;
likewise, men [met] with chariots, and chariots with elephants.
In that battle, warriors both joined together and separated from one another fell down;
having performed their deeds during the night, they were exhausted by the heat of the sun,
and many became unconscious, their limbs overcome by hunger and thirst.

O King, O bull of the Bharata race, a sound arose that touched the very heavens—the blare of conchs, kettledrums, and clay drums; the trumpeting of roaring elephants; and the twanging of bows being drawn and stretched wide.

There was a great and tumultuous uproar from the fleeing foot soldiers, from weapons being hurled down, from the neighing of horses, from the rattling of returning chariots, and from those crying out and roaring.
A tumultuous sound, swelling with a great roar, ascended to the heavens;
the agonized cries of those writhing as they were being mangled by various weapons were heard upon the earth, and at that time there was a great and piteous spectacle.
Among the foot soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants— some falling and others already fallen— as all those divisions became repeatedly entangled, they struck one another:
their own men killed their own, the enemies killed their own, their own killed the enemies, and the enemies killed the enemies.
And swords hurled by the arms of heroes were seen falling upon the warriors and the elephants, like [clothes] being washed in laundry vats;
such was the sound of the swords raised and struck down by the arms of the heroes.
That very sound was like the noise of garments being washed;
meanwhile, with half-sheathed swords, scimitars, javelins, and battle-axes,
there occurred a great, close-quarter combat that was intensely fierce and entangled.
Arising from the bodies of elephants and horses, flowing with the corpses of men, filled with weapons for its fish, and having flesh and blood for its mud;
resounding with the cries of the distressed, and frothing with banners and garments.
The heroes caused a river to flow toward the world beyond;
afflicted by arrows and spears, exhausted, bewildered by the night, and their minds clouded,
the elephants and horses stood still with all their limbs paralyzed.
The heroes lay with their parched faces and heads adorned with beautiful earrings;
the ground was strewn here and there with various implements of war,
and crowded with throngs of carnivorous creatures feeding upon the dead and even those who were half-dead.

There was no path for chariots anywhere on that battlefield; as the wheels sank in, the horses, relying on their own strength, somehow continued to pull the chariots, though they were exhausted, trembling, and afflicted by arrows.
O Bhārata, horses endowed with noble lineage, strength, and vigor, resembling elephants, wandered here and there carrying chariots. That army was overwhelmed,
utterly bewildered, terrified, and distressed, O Bhārata.

At that time, all [the warriors] possessed strength, with the exception of both Droṇa and Arjuna; those two alone were the refuge and the protection for the distressed. Having encountered them, others indeed went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
The entire great army of the Kauravas became agitated,
and as they were locked in combat with the Pāñcālas, nothing could be discerned at all. It was like the sporting ground of Death, increasing the fear of the timid.
When a great destruction of royal lineages had arisen upon the earth,
there was neither Karṇa there, nor Droṇa, nor Arjuna, nor Yudhiṣṭhira;
neither Bhīmasena, nor the twins, nor the Pāñcālya, nor Sātyaki.
Nor did he see Duḥśāsana, nor the son of Droṇa, nor Duryodhana and Saubala;
nor Kṛpa, nor the king of Madra, nor even Kṛtavarman.
He saw neither others, nor himself, nor the earth, nor the quarters of the sky.
"O King, we see the troops locked in combat, shrouded by dust; when that terrible, tumultuous cloud of dust had arisen,
they then thought that a second night had arrived."
Neither the Kauravas, nor the Pāñcālas, nor the Pāṇḍavas could be distinguished;
neither the directions, nor the sky, nor the earth, nor the level ground, nor the uneven terrain could be seen.
They appeared like autumnal clouds flashing with lightning.
Desiring victory, the men then struck down in battle others— whether enemies or even their own kin— who had come within the reach of their hands;
for the dust was stirred up and there was a profusion of blood.
