The dust of the earth was stilled by the swiftness of the wind;
there, the elephants, horses, warriors, chariot-fighters, and foot-soldiers,
drenched in blood, shone like groves of *pārijāta* trees.
Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, Droṇa, and Duḥśāsana—
those four chariot-warriors— engaged with the four Pāṇḍavas;
Duryodhana, along with his brother, engaged with the two sons of Yama.
Rādheya [fought] with Vṛkodara, and Arjuna with the son of Bharadvāja;
all beheld from every side that terrible and great marvel,
the superhuman encounter of those fierce bulls among chariot-warriors.
Along various chariot-paths crowded with diverse chariots,
the car-warriors beheld the wonderful battle of those who fight with marvelous skill;
they strove with valor, each desiring to conquer the other.
Like clouds at the end of the summer heat, they showered volleys of arrows;
those bulls among men, mounted upon chariots as radiant as the sun,
shone like autumnal clouds that have appeared.
O great king, those warriors, filled with rage and impatience—
those rival archers of mighty bows who had exerted themselves—
then encountered one another like rutting bull elephants.
Surely there was no destruction of the body when that time arrived,
since all those great chariot-warriors did not perish simultaneously;
[the field was strewn] with severed arms, feet, and heads adorned with beautiful earrings.
With bows, arrows, spears, swords, axes, and *paṭṭiśas*;
with *nālīkas*, razors, *nārācas*, claws, *śaktis*, and *tomaras*;
and with various other kinds of polished, supreme weapons.
With various and multiform body armor,
with diverse broken chariots, and with slain elephants and horses;
with chariots resembling empty cities, their warriors killed and their banners fallen.
[The field was covered] with non-human horses being dragged here and there in terror,
with those who had repeatedly moved like the wind, with slain heroes still adorned,
and with fans, armor, and fallen banners.
With parasols, ornaments, garments, and most fragrant garlands;
with necklaces, diadems, crowns, turbans, and clusters of tiny bells;
and with breast-jewels, golden coins, and crest-gems.

The battlefield there became like the sky filled with hosts of stars. Then there occurred a clash between Duryodhana and Nakula— between the wrathful and the resentful, and between the resentful and the wrathful.
Then the son of Mādrī,
joyfully scattering hundreds of arrows, placed your son to his left; a great roar arose there as he was thus bypassed in battle by his highly indignant kinsman.
Enraged, O great king, your son King Duryodhana swiftly countered him in battle by moving to his right. Then,
as your son sought to retaliate by keeping him to his right—
The spirited Nakula, skilled in diverse maneuvers, warded him off;
having repelled him from all sides and afflicted him with a net of arrows,
Nakula turned him away, and the troops honored that feat.
"Stay! Stay! Nakula said to your son, calling to mind all the sufferings caused by your evil counsel.
Saṃjaya said:

Then Duḥśāsana, enraged, rushed toward Sahadeva with the fierce speed of a chariot, as if making the earth tremble. As he was charging forward, the crusher of enemies [Sahadeva] swiftly struck him with a broad-headed arrow.
The son of Mādrī cut off the charioteer’s head, along with its helmet;
because of his swiftness, neither Duḥśāsana nor any soldier perceived that the charioteer had been decapitated by Sahadeva.

But when the horses, being unrestrained, galloped off at their own pleasure, Duḥśāsana then realized that the charioteer had lost his presence of mind. Being himself an expert in horses, he took control of the steeds on the battlefield.
The best of chariot-warriors fought with skillful, swift, and wonderful maneuvers;
both his own side and the enemy alike marveled at that feat in battle,
as he moved about the field fearlessly even after his charioteer had been slain.
Sahadeva, however, covered those horses with sharp arrows;
being tormented by those shafts, they quickly fled hither and thither.
Because his reins were still held fast, he was forced to cast aside his bow.
While performing his work with the bow, he released his reins;
through those openings, the son of Mādrī covered him with arrows. Desiring to protect your son, Karṇa then rushed into that interval.
Then Vṛkodara, with three well-aimed broad-headed arrows drawn back to his ear,
struck Karṇa in the arms and chest and let out a roar;
Karṇa turned back toward him like a coiled serpent.
He warded off Bhīma by scattering sharpened arrows;
Karna, for his part, pierced him with sharp shafts that strike the vital organs.
Then a tumultuous battle took place between Bhīma and the son of Rādhā.
Long ago, in the war between the gods and the asuras, like Vṛtra and Vāsava,
those two— both enraged like bulls with rolling eyes—
rushed at one another with great impetuosity in their fury.

As those two, both intoxicated by battle, were locked in close combat there, a mace-duel ensued because their arrows could not penetrate one another. Then Bhīmasena struck the pole of Karṇa’s chariot with his mace.
O King, he quickly shattered it, and that was like a marvel.
Then the heroic son of Rādhā, seizing Bhīma’s mace, hurled it at his chariot; but with his own mace, he shattered that mace.
Then Bhīma again hurled a heavy mace at the son of Adhiratha;
Karna pierced it with ten well-feathered, well-aimed arrows,
and with others he struck Bhīma, while the mace returned once more toward him.
Like a female serpent struck by a mantra, she was assailed by the arrows discharged from his ear; by the impact of that blow, Bhīma’s massive standard fell,
and his charioteer, struck by the mace, lost consciousness.
Overwhelmed with rage, O Bhārata, he discharged eight arrows at Karna’s standard, his bow, and his quiver; with those sharp,
yellow shafts, the mighty Bhīmasena—
O Bhārata, the slayer of enemy heroes cut it down as if laughing;
Karna, however, seizing another unassailable bow with a golden back,
then once more struck his horses with arrows from his chariot.

He swiftly slew those who had the appearance of ṛṣis, as well as both the outriders and the charioteer. With his chariot destroyed, Bhīma, the subduer of foes, leaped onto Nakula’s chariot like a lion leaping upon a mountain peak.
Likewise, O king of kings, the two great car-warriors Droṇa and Arjuna— the teacher and the pupil— both skilled in weapons, fought a wondrous battle in combat,
through their swiftness in aiming, their application of yoga, and the maneuvering of their chariots.
Bewildering both the eyes and the minds of men,
all our warriors as well as those of the enemy ceased their efforts,
beholding that battle between the preceptor and his pupil, the likes of which had never been seen before.
As they careered through diverse chariot-paths in the midst of the army,
those two heroes sought to keep each other to their left;
the warriors beheld that prowess of theirs with great amazement.
Between those two, Droṇa and the Pāṇḍava, there occurred a great battle,
O Great King, like that between two hawks in the sky for the sake of prey.
Whatever Droṇa did, it was with the desire to conquer the son of Kuntī.
The Pāṇḍava quickly parried each of those [attacks] while laughing;
a great fury arose between them both as they faced one another.
The battle between those two, both of whom were experts in divine weapons, began gently at first.
When Droṇa was unable to gain any advantage over the Pāṇḍava, he,
who was highly skilled in the ways of weapons, then manifested his divine missiles:
the Aindra, the Pāśupata, the Tvāṣṭra, the Vāyavya, and the Vāruṇa.
Dhanañjaya struck down every single shaft released from Droṇa’s bow. When the Pāṇḍava duly destroyed his weapons with his own weapons,
Droṇa then overwhelmed Pārtha with supreme divine weapons.

Whatever weapon he employed against Pārtha out of a desire for victory, Arjuna performed that very same act to neutralize each of those weapons. Even as his divine weapons were being struck down according to the prescribed rites, [Arjuna continued his assault].
Droṇa honored Arjuna with his mind alone for his Arjuna-like prowess; and he considered himself superior even to all others on earth, O Bhārata,
because of that disciple who surpassed everyone skilled in weapons from every side.
Though being restrained by Pārtha in the midst of those great-souled ones,
he, striving with affection and smiling, countered Arjuna.
Then, in the sky, thousands of gods and Gandharvas [gathered].
The ṛṣis and hosts of siddhas stood there, desiring to behold [the sight];
that sky, crowded with apsaras and teeming with yakṣas and rākṣasas,
became magnificent once more, like a sky filled with clouds.
There, invisible voices moved back and forth repeatedly,
extolling Droṇa and the high-souled Pārtha as the weapons were being discharged,
setting the ten directions ablaze.
Then the Siddhas and the assembled Rishis there said:
"This is neither a human battle, nor one of Asuras, nor of Rakshasas; it is neither celestial, nor Gandharvan; this supreme conflict is certainly Brahmanic."
This is a wonderful marvel, never seen nor heard by us before:
the Preceptor Drona surpasses the Pandava, and the Pandava likewise surpasses Drona; it is impossible for anyone to perceive any difference between these two by means of any weapon whatsoever.

If Rudra were to divide himself in two and fight himself with himself, only then could a comparison be made; otherwise, no such thing exists. Knowledge resides solely in the teacher, while knowledge and yoga reside in the Pāṇḍava.
In Droṇa, excellence is seen; in the Teacher, both lightness and excellence;
and in Arjuna, these are clearly visible, but not in any other archer. In the Teacher, the target is fixed in one place; in the Pāṇḍava, the target is pierced [in its entirety].
Speed is concentrated in the Teacher; piercing power is concentrated in the son of Pāṇḍu.
Skill is concentrated in the Teacher; hitting the mark is concentrated in the son of Pāṇḍu. Heroism is concentrated in the Teacher; strength and heroism are both concentrated in the son of Pāṇḍu.

"Those two great archers cannot be defeated by enemies in battle, O Great King; yet, if they so desired, these two bulls among men could destroy the entire world together with the gods. Thus they spoke upon seeing those two foremost of men.
When the Pāṇḍava surpassed Droṇa, O Great King, all beings— both hidden and manifest— gathered in throngs. Then the high-minded Droṇa manifested the Brahma-weapon.

O King, that weapon, having been aimed in the great battle, was of terrible form; it scorched Pārtha in the fray as well as the invisible beings. Then the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and trees, trembled.
For a moment, the rivers indeed flowed backward against their currents;
a fierce wind blew, and even the oceans were agitated.
Then, a great terror arose among the armies of both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
When that weapon was raised by the high-souled one against all living beings, Pārtha, remaining unperturbed,
countered that weapon with the very Brahmāstra, O king of kings, and thereby extinguished it all.
When the further shore of neither of those two [armies] nor of either one could be discerned,
that battle was thrown into total confusion by a chaotic melee; then,
O lord of the people, nothing at all could be distinguished once again.
When the tumultuous battle between Droṇa and the Pāṇḍavas had commenced,
Droṇa left Pārtha in the fray and pursued the Pañcālas;
Arjuna, too, leaving Droṇa in battle, put the Kurus to flight.
Then, O King, in that great battle, a tumultuous mass of arrows released by those two became like a shadow, causing fear to the entire world;
the sky was completely covered by nets of arrows, as if by masses of clouds.
Not a single being moving through the air could pass at that time.
Sañjaya said:
While that destruction of men, horses, and elephants was thus proceeding, [the battle continued].

O Great King, Duḥśāsana fought against Dhṛṣṭadyumna. Afflicted by the arrows of Duḥśāsana, he— mounted upon his golden chariot— out of indignation toward your son, covered his [Duḥśāsana’s] horses with a shower of shafts.

In an instant, O great king, that chariot of his— along with its banner and charioteer— was no longer visible, being completely covered by the arrows of the son of Pṛṣata. But Duḥśāsana, O Indra among kings, [attacked] the high-souled Pāñcālya.
Afflicted by the net of arrows, he was unable to stand before him. But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, having turned Duḥśāsana away with his shafts, O king of kings, saw that your son was broken.
Scattering thousands of arrows, he rushed toward Droṇa in battle;
at that moment, Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, intervened,
and three of his uterine brothers surrounded him.
The two sons of Yama, those bulls among men, followed behind him as he advanced toward Droṇa like a blazing fire;
then all seven of those great car-warriors engaged in combat.

O King, indignant yet possessed of great courage, and placing death before them, those pure-souled men of pure conduct— having set heaven as their goal and desiring to conquer one another— engaged in a noble battle.
The wise lords of men, born of noble lineage and performing pure deeds,
fought a righteous war, beholding the supreme goal. Therein was nothing unrighteous, nor was there any combat without weapons.
There is no *karṇin* here, no *nālīka*, no *lipta*, nor a *vastaka*; there is no *sūcī*, no *kapiśa* here, nor any bone of a cow or an elephant;
there is no *cūlī*, no *balīśa* there, nor Yama, nor even the fire.
The arrows were not stuck together, nor were they putrid, nor did they fly crookedly; all held their weapons straight and pure,
desiring both the higher worlds and fame through fair combat.
Then there occurred a tumultuous battle, free from all faults,
between those four warriors of yours and those three Pāṇḍavas.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O King, having bypassed those bulls among chariot-warriors of yours, [advanced].
Seeing them held back by the two Yamas, Śīghrāstra rushed toward Droṇa;
but those four heroes, having been repelled by those two lions among men,
closed in upon them like four winds striking against two mountains.
The two preeminent car-warriors, the twins, together with their two chariots,
were engaged in combat; then Dhṛṣṭadyumna advanced against Droṇa,
having seen the Pāñcālya prince, who was intoxicated with battle, proceeding toward Droṇa.
In that interval, he rushed toward those who were engaged with the twins.
Then, O King, your son Duryodhana, O great monarch, encountered the Sātvata warrior, scattering arrows that feed on blood.
Sātyaki turned back toward him even more swiftly.
Having encountered one another in close proximity, those two tigers among men, the Kuru and the Mādhava, met fearlessly while smiling.
Reflecting with delight upon all the deeds they had performed in their childhood,
looking at one another and laughing again and again,
King Duryodhana then addressed Sātyaki.
Constantly censuring his own conduct, he said to his dear friend:
"Fie on anger! Fie on greed, O friend! Fie on delusion! Fie on impatience!
Fie on the conduct of the Kṣatriyas! Fie on innate physical strength!"
"O bull among the Śinis, since you seek to deceive me and I you,
you are indeed dearer to me than my own life, and I am always so to you. I remember all those deeds that we performed together in our childhood."
"All those [weapons] have now been exhausted by us on the field of battle.
What else remains, O Sātvata, other than fighting you today with anger and greed?
To him who spoke thus, O King, Sātyaki replied:
Laughing, that master of supreme weapons raised his sharp, barbed arrows and said:
"O Prince, this is neither an assembly hall nor the residence of a teacher,
where we once used to play together when we were gathered here, O King."
Duryodhana said:
"O bull of the Śini clan, where has that childhood play of ours gone?
And where is this battle now? For time is indeed difficult to overcome."
"What task indeed remains for us to accomplish with wealth or through the desire for wealth,
since we have all assembled here to fight out of greed for wealth?
Sañjaya said:
To the king who was speaking thus, Mādhava said:
"The warrior class is always of such conduct that it slays even its elders here on earth.
O King, if I am dear to you, then kill me; do not delay."
"O bull of the Bharatas, through your deed I shall go to the worlds of the righteous.
Whatever power and strength you possess, display them quickly to me;
I do not wish to witness this great calamity of my friends."
Having thus clearly addressed and replied, O lord of the people, Sātyaki advanced swiftly, unperturbed and regardless of all else. Seeing him approaching, your son received him.
O King, your son then covered the descendant of Śini with arrows;
thereupon a terrible battle commenced between those two lions of the Kuru and Mādhava lineages, like that between an enraged elephant and a lion.
Then, with ten sharpened arrows released from a fully drawn bow, Duryodhana pierced the Sātvata warrior who was fierce in battle;
Satyaki, in turn, pierced him back with ten arrows in the same manner.
Then Duryodhana, enraged, struck Mādhava with nine arrows in that battle,
and again with fifty, thirty, and ten;
then, O King, your son, laughing, struck Sātyaki.
With thirty sharp arrows released from a bow drawn back to his ear, he pierced him;
then, with a razor-edged shaft, he split his bow—along with the arrow fixed upon it—into two. Thereupon, that light-handed warrior took up another firm bow.
Sātyaki also discharged a flight of arrows at your son;
as that flight of arrows came rushing suddenly with intent to kill,
O King, he cut it into many pieces, whereupon the people raised a great shout.
And with seventy-three gold-feathered arrows, whetted on stone and drawn back to his ear before being released, he impetuously afflicted Sātyaki.
As he was fitting those arrows to the bow, [Duryodhana struck] both the arrows and the strung bow.
Sātyaki swiftly cut [his weapons] and showered him with arrows. Deeply pierced and pained, O Great King, Duryodhana, afflicted by the arrows of the Daśārha, retreated to another chariot.
Having regained his composure, your son again advanced against Sātyaki,
discharging nets of arrows toward Yuyudhāna’s chariot;
likewise, Sātyaki directed his shafts toward Duryodhana’s chariot.
O King, he discharged [arrows] continuously, and that tumultuous conflict ensued.
There, as arrows were being hurled and falling on all sides,
a great roar arose like that of a fire in a vast forest thicket.
The surface of the earth was covered by thousands of arrows from those two,
and the sky became impassable due to their shafts.
There, beholding Mādhava, the best of chariot-warriors, to be the superior one, [the opponent]—
Karna quickly rushed forward, desiring to rescue your son;
but the mighty Bhimasena could not tolerate this,
and he swiftly charged at Karna, discharging many arrows.
Karna, as if laughing, struck back at his sharp arrows,
severed his bow and shafts, and struck the charioteer with his own arrows.
Then Bhimasena, the son of Pandu, filled with rage, took up his mace.
In the battle, he crushed the enemy's banner, bow, and charioteer;
that one of great strength also shattered the wheel of Karṇa’s chariot.
With his wheel broken, he stood upon the chariot as immovable as the king of mountains.
The horses bore that single-wheeled chariot of his for a very long time,
just as the pure Seven Sages bear the single-wheeled chariot of the Sun; meanwhile,
Karna, unable to endure it, fought against Bhīmasena.
With various nets of arrows and diverse weapons in that battle,
Bhīmasena, filled with rage, fought the Sūta’s son. While the tumultuous conflict was raging, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, spoke.
Those tigers among men of the Pañcālas and those bulls among men of the Matsyas—
who are our very life-breaths, who are our heads, and who are our mighty warriors—
those bulls among men are now entangled with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"Why do you all stand here like fools, devoid of sense? Go there where these chariot-warriors of mine are fighting!
Placing the duty of the Kṣatriya before you, let all of you be free from anxiety."
Whether victorious or being slain, you shall go to a desirable destination;
having conquered, you shall perform many sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees,
or, being slain by the gods, you shall attain abundant worlds.
Urged on by the king, those heroic great chariot-warriors, intending to fight,
divided their army into four divisions and swiftly advanced toward Droṇa.
The Pāñcālas, however, from one side, struck Droṇa with many arrows.
Led by Bhīmasena, they surrounded him from one side;
however, three of the sons of Pāṇḍu— those great car-warriors who were straightforward in their conduct—
namely the twins and Bhīmasena, cried out to Dhanañjaya.
"Attack quickly, Arjuna! Drive away the Kurus from Drona!
Then the Panchalas will slay him once his protectors have been struck down. Thereupon, Partha suddenly rushed toward the Kauravas.
On the fifth day, O Bhārata, Droṇa swiftly unleashed those heroes against the Pāñcālas themselves, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna; thereafter,
Droṇa wrought a great slaughter among the Pāñcālas.
Just as Śakra, enraged in battle, formerly brought about the destruction of the Dānavas, so too,
O great king, while the enemies were being slain in combat by Droṇa’s weapon,
those courageous great car-warriors did not tremble before Droṇa in the fray.

O great king, being slaughtered, the Pāñcālas and Sṛñjayas likewise rushed toward Droṇa alone in battle, seeking to confound that great car-warrior. As those Pāñcālas were being destroyed on all sides, [they pressed forward].

A terrifying clamor arose from those being slain by arrows and spears; as the high-souled one slaughtered the Pāñcālas in battle and Droṇa’s weapons were being unleashed, fear entered the hearts of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having seen the vast destruction of the multitudes of horses and men in battle, O Great King,
and having witnessed the immense slaughter of men, elephants, horses,
and foot soldiers, the sons of Pāṇḍu then lost all hope for victory.
I hope that Droṇa, the knower of supreme weapons, will not consume us all,
like a blazing fire at the end of winter burning through dry undergrowth;
for no one is capable of even looking upon him in battle.
Knowing the dharma, Arjuna would never fight against him;
yet, seeing the sons of Kuntī terrified and afflicted by Droṇa’s arrows,
the wise Keśava, intent on their welfare, spoke to Arjuna.
This best of archers, with his bow in hand, cannot be conquered in battle by any means, even by the gods led by Indra; however,
if he were to lay down his weapons in combat, he could be slain by men.
"O slayers of Vṛtra, you who are the leaders of hosts of chariot-warriors,
cast aside dharma, O Pāṇḍava, and apply yourself to the means of victory in battle,
so that he whose vehicle is gold may not slay all of you in combat."
"If Aśvatthāman were killed, he would not fight; this is my thought.
Let some man report to him that he has been slain in battle.
O King, Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, did not approve of this.
But all the others approved, though Yudhiṣṭhira did so with great reluctance.
Then, O King, the mighty-armed Bhīma slew a great elephant in his own army with his mace, thinking it to be Aśvatthāman.
The terrible crushing of Indravarman of Mālava;
then Bhīmasena, approaching Droṇa in the battle with shame,
cried out loudly, "Aśvatthāman has been killed!"
"For the elephant known by the name Aśvatthāman has indeed been slain"—
having kept this in mind, Bhīma then spoke those false words.
Upon hearing those most unpleasant words of Bhīmasena, Droṇa...
With his limbs sinking as if into water upon a sandbank, he felt dejected in his mind; yet,
though he suspected that report concerning his son’s prowess to be false,
and having heard it said that he was slain, he did not waver from his fortitude.
Having regained consciousness, Droṇa recovered his composure in an instant;
reflecting upon his son, who was invincible to his enemies,
he rushed toward the son of Pṛṣata, desiring to slay him as his own death.
He covered him with a thousand sharp, heron-feathered arrows;
then twenty thousand bull-like men of the Pañcālas surrounded him as he moved thus in battle, showering him from all sides with shafts.

O lord of the people, we could not see the great car-warrior Droṇa, who was shrouded by those arrows, like the sun obscured by clouds during the rainy season; then that great car-warrior [Arjuna], having shaken off those multitudes of arrows belonging to the Pāñcālas...
Then Drona, the scorcher of foes, being incensed, invoked the supreme Brahma weapon for the slaughter of those heroic Panchalas. Thereupon, Drona shone resplendent as he struck down all the Somakas.
In that great battle, he also struck off the heads of the Pāñcālas,
as well as their arms, which were shaped like iron clubs and adorned with golden ornaments.
Thus being slaughtered in the fray by the son of Bharadvāja, those kings—
On the earth they were scattered like trees blown down by the wind;
O Bhārata, with the falling elephants and the throngs of horses,
the earth became impassable, mired in flesh and blood.
Having slain twenty thousand throngs of Pāñcāla chariot-warriors,
Droṇa stood in the battle like a smokeless, blazing fire;
and likewise, the powerful son of Bharadvāja was once again filled with wrath.
With a broad-headed arrow, he severed the head of Vasudāna from his body;
furthermore, having slain five hundred Matsyas and six thousand Sṛñjayas,
and having killed ten thousand elephants, he then slew ten thousand horses.
Seeing Droṇa standing there for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas,
the Ṛṣis, led by Agni Havyavāha, arrived swiftly—
Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bhāradvāja, and Gautama.
Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Atri, desiring to lead them to the world of Brahmā,
along with the Sikatās, Pṛśnis, Gargas, Bālakhilyas, Marīcipas,
Bhṛgus, Aṅgirases, and other subtle great ṛṣis.

They all said to Droṇa, who graces the battlefield: "This battle has been fought unrighteously; it is now the time for your death. Lay down your weapons in this conflict, O Droṇa, and come to us as we stand here."
You ought not to perform such a cruel deed again;
for this is especially unbecoming of you, a Brahmin who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and is devoted to truth and righteousness.
O Amogheṣu, lay down your weapons and stand upon the eternal path;
your time to dwell here in the world of men is now complete. By you, with the Brahmā-weapon, those on earth who were ignorant of weapons have been consumed.
"O Brahmin, this deed you have done is not good; it is such as this. O Droṇa, lay down your weapons in battle quickly; do not delay.
O twice-born one, do not commit such an even more wicked act again."
Having heard these words of theirs as well as those of Bhīmasena,
and having looked toward Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the battle, he became despondent. Burning with grief and deeply distressed, he [addressed] Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
Approaching Yudhiṣṭhira, Droṇa spoke these words:
"O Indra among kings, tell me the truth: does my son live?
Tell me whether he is unhurt or slain. Thus he questioned his own son.

For Droṇa’s intellect was firm; he would never, under any circumstances, speak a falsehood even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds. Therefore, he questioned him specifically, and no one else.
For since his childhood, that son of Pāṇḍu had placed his hopes of truth in him; thus,
knowing that Droṇa intended to rid the earth of the Pāṇḍavas by means of battle, Govinda, the Lord of the Earth, spoke in distress to Dharmarāja.
"If Droṇa fights for even half a day while possessed by wrath, I tell you truly, your army will meet its destruction. Therefore, may you save us from Droṇa; truth is superior to falsehood."
One who speaks a falsehood for the sake of saving a life is not touched by untruths; likewise,
there is no sin in lying regarding women, at weddings, for the sake of cattle, for the sake of wealth, or to protect a Brahmin.
While the two were thus conversing, O great king, Bhīmasena spoke these words upon hearing that means for the slaying of the high-souled Indravarman,
the Mālava, as he was plunging into your army.
"The elephant renowned as Aśvatthāman, who was like the elephant of Śakra,
has been slain in battle after displaying great prowess; therefore, O Brahmin, I said to Droṇa,
'Aśvatthāman is killed, O Brāhmaṇa, desist from the battle.'"
"Surely this bull among men did not believe my words;
therefore, O King, honoring the words of Govinda who desires your victory,
report to Droṇa that the son of Śaradvat has been slain."
"O King, this bull among the twice-born would never fight if addressed by you;
for you, O lord of men, are renowned in this world of men as one who speaks the truth.
Having heard those words of his, [Duryodhana] was urged by the speech of Kṛṣṇa.
And because he had been so influenced, O Great King, Yudhiṣṭhira began to speak; though submerged in the fear of untruth and intent on victory,
O King, he spoke indistinctly, saying, "The elephant is slain."
"Previously, his chariot was four finger-breadths above the earth;
but when he had spoken thus, his horses touched the ground.
Having heard those words from Yudhiṣṭhira, the great car-warrior Droṇa—
Tormented by the calamity of his son's death, he became hopeless for his own life; considering himself as one who had committed an offense against the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
and reflecting upon the words of the ṛṣi after hearing that his son was slain.

Seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O King, subduer of foes, he became bewildered and extremely agitated; he was unable to fight as he had before. Beholding him thus deeply distressed, his mind overwhelmed by grief—
Dhrishtadyumna, the son of the Panchala king, rushed forward—
he who had been obtained from the kindled sacrificial fire by Drupada, the lord of men, after he had performed a great sacrifice for the sake of Drona’s destruction.
Taking up his victorious bow, which was formidable and thundered like a rain-cloud,
with its firm string, undecaying, and divine, he fixed upon that bow an arrow resembling a venomous serpent— an arrow resembling a venomous serpent.
Desiring to slay Droṇa, the Pāñcālya prince [discharged] that arrow which was like a great-flaming fire;
its form within the circle of the bowstring was like that of the shining sun surrounded by a halo at the end of the rainy season.
Seeing that bow, which was grasped by the son of Pṛṣata and seemed as if it were blazing,
the soldiers thought that the time of universal destruction had arrived.
Then the powerful son of Bharadvāja [aimed] that arrow which had been fixed by him.
Seeing that the end of his body's time had arrived, he reflected upon it;
then, O king of kings, the teacher exerted himself to restrain him,
yet the divine weapons did not manifest for that high-souled one.
Four days and one night passed for him as he practiced his shooting;
day and night went by for him as he was training with arrows. And within one-third of that day, his feathered shafts were exhausted.
Having encountered the exhaustion of his arrows and being afflicted by grief for his son,
and seeing the failure of his various divine weapons,
he desired to cast away his arms, urged on by the words of the Brahmin.
Driven by his own splendor, he fought in a superhuman manner;
then, taking up another divine bow belonging to the lineage of Aṅgiras,
and arrows resembling the staff of Brahmā, he battled with Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Then, with a great shower of arrows, he overwhelmed him;
and filled with rage and impatience, he struck down Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Thereupon, O King, the son of Pṛṣata, having drawn his great bow—
Desiring to slay the son of Bharadvāja, he released a sharpened arrow;
Droṇa, however, cut that arrow of his into a hundred pieces with his own shafts,
and with sharp arrows, he struck down both his standard and his bow, as well as his charioteer.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, laughing, took up another bow and pierced him in return with a sharp arrow between the breasts. Deeply pierced,
that great archer became as if bewildered in the battle.
With a sharp-edged bhalla-arrow, he severed his great bow;
and having cut through all of his arrows, his deformed weapons, and his other bows, O lord of the people, that invincible warrior [seized] a mace and a sword as well.

Then, filled with rage, that scorcher of foes pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna— with his appearance likewise enraged— with nine sharpened arrows capable of ending life. That great car-warrior [Kṛtavarman] then struck the horses of Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s chariot with the horses of his own chariot.
The immeasurable-souled one, invoking the Brahma-weapon,
caused them to intermingle; those swift steeds, possessing the speed of the wind—
some the color of pigeons and others crimson, O bull of the Bharatas— shone brilliantly as they were thus mixed together.
O Great King, like thundering clouds accompanied by lightning at the onset of the rainy season, those [chariots] shone as they were mingled together at the front of the battle;
likewise, there were the bindings of the poles, the bindings of the wheels, and the bindings of the chariots.
That twice-born one of immeasurable soul destroyed the weapons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
With his bow broken, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
the hero, having fallen into extreme distress, seized a mace.
As it was being hurled at him with sharp arrows, the great car-warrior Droṇa, enraged and of true prowess, struck it down with his own shafts.
Seeing that [mace] destroyed by Droṇa’s arrows, that tiger among men [Dhṛṣṭadyumna]...
He took up a stainless sword and a radiant shield marked with a hundred moons.
Without doubt, when things had come to such a pass, the Pāñcālya prince considered that the time had arrived for the slaughter of that high-souled preeminent teacher.
Then, standing in the seat of his own chariot upon the shaft of that chariot,
the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna, desiring to perform a difficult feat, advanced with sword raised and a radiant shield marked with a hundred moons.
He desired to pierce the chest of Bhāradvāja in the encounter;
he stood indeed amidst the yokes and upon the yoke-fastenings,
and upon the hindquarters of the chestnut horses— the troops honored him for that.
As he stood upon the rows of yokes and even mounted his chestnut horses, Droṇa could find no opening; it was like a marvel. He moved with such speed, like a hawk greedy for meat.
In that same way, there was a fierce onslaught as he sought Drona in battle;
then that powerful and enraged warrior, Drona, struck down all his pigeon-colored horses one by one with a chariot-spear.
Slain, those horses of Dhṛṣṭadyumna fell to the earth;
O lord of the people, the chestnut steeds were released from their entanglement with the chariot.
Seeing those horses slain by that foremost of the twice-born, the son of Pṛṣata [acted].
The great car-warrior Yājñaseni, the best among combatants, could not endure this;
deprived of his chariot, that foremost of swordsmen seized a sword and,
O King, rushed toward Droṇa like Vainateya toward a serpent.
O King, as he sought to slay the son of Bharadvāja, his form shone like the supreme form of Viṣṇu at the slaughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
he moved through various paths and twenty-one different modes.
Moving about in battle, O Kauravya, the son of Pṛṣata displayed [his prowess], wielding his sword and shield as he whirled,
leaped up, whirled around, brandished, sprang forward, rushed, retreated,
and turned back.
The son of Pṛṣata displayed his mastery of the *saṃpāta* and *samudīrṇa* maneuvers;
through his training, he moved through the battle, demonstrating his skill against the Bhārata, the Kauśika, and the Sātvata, desiring to bring about Droṇa’s end.
As he moved along those various paths, armed with sword and shield,
the warriors and the assembled deities were filled with wonder in the battle.
Then, with a thousand arrows, he struck down the [chariot] adorned with a hundred moons.
In that close-quarters combat, that twice-born one [Droṇa] seized the sword and shield of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Those arrows of Droṇa’s, known as *vaitastika*, were capable of striking from close range; they did not belong to anyone else. They were used specifically for hand-to-hand combat.
[The arrows] of Śāradvata, Pārtha, the son of Droṇa, and Vaikartana—
save for Śāradvata, Pārtha, the son of Droṇa, and likewise Vaikartana,
[and save for] Pradyumna, Yuyudhāna, and Abhimanyu— those were your arrows.

Then the preceptor, wishing to slay his pupil who was as dear to him as a son, fixed upon his bow a firm arrow that was most sharpened. But the bull among the Śinis cut it apart with ten sharp shafts.
While he was observing those various maneuvers with sword and shield,
and while your son and the high-souled Karṇa were looking on,
[Arjuna] rescued Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who had been seized by that preeminent teacher.
O Bhārata, those two great-souled ones, Viṣvaksena and Dhanañjaya, beheld Satyaki of true prowess as he moved along the chariot-paths between Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa.
Exclaiming "Excellent! Excellent!", they both honored the descendant of Vṛṣṇi as Acyuta struck down the divine weapons of all his foes in battle;
then Viṣvaksena and Dhanañjaya rushed toward the army.
Then Dhanañjaya said to Kṛṣṇa: "Behold, O Keśava,
how Satyaki, whose prowess is truth, delights me all the more as he sports in the midst of the foremost and most excellent teachers, O Madhūdvaha."

Because of his training, Satyaki— unassuming yet moving through battle, playing with great chariot-warriors and increasing the fame of the Vṛṣṇis— conducts himself in the fray alongside the two sons of Mādrī, Bhīma, and King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Seeing the Sātvata hero invincible in battle, these Siddhas and soldiers were filled with wonder; they cheered him, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!
And all the warriors on both sides honored him for his deeds.
Saṃjaya said:
Having witnessed that feat of the Sātvata, Duryodhana and the others quickly and furiously warded off the grandson of Śini from every side.
O venerable one, Kṛpa and Karṇa, along with your sons,
quickly approached the descendant of Śini in battle and struck him with sharpened arrows;
then King Yudhiṣṭhira and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī [also advanced].
The powerful Bhīmasena surrounded the Sātvata hero,
while Karṇa, the great car-warrior Gautama, and Duryodhana and his followers surrounded the descendant of Śini with a shower of arrows.
O King, Śini’s grandson, while fighting those great car-warriors, suddenly checked that terrible shower of arrows that had arisen;
for he warded off the divine weapons discharged by those high-souled men.
In that great battle, he warded him off according to the rules with divine weapons;
seeing this, Acyuta was greatly delighted and honored him, saying, "Excellent!
Excellent!", and all the warriors likewise honored him for this deed.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, Dhanañjaya Jishnu proceeded toward the chariot of Bhāradvāja to attack your army, while Vāsudeva remained there;
a terrible roar then arose from your men who were desirous of victory.
As they rushed toward Pārtha like Daityas against Vāsava,
O Great King, he made the earth a mire of blood; Pārtha lopped off the heads of horses, men, and elephants.
In that assembly of kings, O Bhārata, a cruel battle broke out,
like that of the enraged Rudra slaughtering animals,
as hands, heads, and bows were severed.
In that field of battle, heaps of discarded umbrellas and yak-tail fans were seen here and there;
likewise, there were chariots with broken wheels and great standards cast down.
The earth became strewn with slain heroic horsemen;
and those warriors, O best of the Kurus, mangled by the falling of arrows,
were seen performing various contortions in that great battle.
While that terrible battle, resembling the conflict between the gods and the asuras, was thus proceeding,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, spoke there to the kṣatriyas:
"O great car-warriors, exert yourselves and charge against the pot-born one!"
This hero, the son of Pṛṣata, having encountered the son of Bharadvāja,
strives to the best of his power for the destruction of Bhāradvāja. Indeed,
such portents as we see here in this great battle [foretell his success].
"Today, the son of Pṛṣata, filled with wrath, will strike down Droṇa in battle.
Therefore, all of you, acting in concert, must protect the Pot-born one.
Thus commanded by Yudhiṣṭhira, the great car-warriors of the Sṛñjayas [advanced]."
Rushing forward with intent, they sought to slay the son of Bharadvāja.
As they all charged toward him, the great car-warrior Bhāradvāja rushed at them with speed, having resolved that he must die.
When he who was true to his promise had set out, the earth trembled;
winds blew with thunderous crashes, terrifying the army,
and a great meteor fell as if it had issued from the sun.
O Sire, the weapons of Bhāradvāja blazed as if with heat, as if foretelling a great danger;
the chariots rattled excessively, and the horses shed tears.
The great car-warrior Bhāradvāja seemed as if his vital energy were drained;
his right eye throbbed and his right arm trembled.
Seeing the son of Pṛṣata before him in battle, he became despondent.
Regarding the sages who discourse on Brahman and their journey to heaven,
he then began to cast off his life-breaths through a noble battle.
Thereupon, he was surrounded on all four sides by the troops of Drupada.
Scorching the hosts of Kṣatriyas, Droṇa moved about in the battle;
having slain twenty thousand Kṣatriyas,
that crusher of foes killed ten tens of thousands with his sharp-pointed, keen arrows.

He stood resolutely in battle like a smokeless fire, having established himself in his Brahmanic self for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas. Then the self-controlled Bhīma deprived the Pāñcālya prince of his chariot and destroyed all his weapons.
Hurrying toward the high-souled one who was not despondent,
the crusher of enemies placed the Pāñcālya prince upon his own chariot and,
looking at Droṇa as he was discharging arrows from close range, spoke to him.

"No man other than you here dares to fight the preceptor; hasten, for his slaughter is the very task upon which the burden has been placed. Thus addressed, the mighty-armed one [prepared] a new [bow] capable of bearing every strain.
Rushing forward, he quickly seized his firm and excellent weapon; then,
enraged and discharging arrows in battle, he sought to hold back the irresistible Droṇa and overwhelmed the preceptor with a rain of shafts.
Those two preeminent warriors, enraged and gracing the field of battle, warded each other off;
they discharged Brahma-weapons and various celestial missiles many times over.
O great king, he [Abhimanyu] covered Droṇa with those great weapons in the fray.
Having neutralized all the weapons of the son of Bharadvāja, the son of Pṛṣata, the infallible one,
scattered the Vasātis, the Śibis, the Bāhlīkas, and the Kauravas as well,
who were seeking to protect Droṇa in battle.

Then, O King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna shone like the sun with its rays, covering all directions on every side with a net of arrows. Droṇa, having cut his bow and pierced him with stone-tipped shafts, [struck him].
He struck him again in his vital parts, and he experienced supreme agony.
Then Bhīma, his wrath firm, having approached Droṇa’s chariot,
spoke these words to Droṇa very softly, O king of kings.

If indeed those wretched Brahmins, though untrained in their own duties and dissatisfied with their own occupations, did not fight, the Kshatriya order would not have met its destruction. For they know non-violence toward all beings to be the highest dharma.
And for him, the Brahmin is the root; and you are the foremost among those who know the Veda.
Having slain the Śvapākas, the Mleccha hordes, and various others, those deluded by ignorance maintain their sons and wives just as you do.
O Brahmin, out of ignorance, like a fool, and through the desire for sons, wives, and wealth,
you have slain many kings for the sake of a single son— just as one ignorant of dharma might act— and now you are slaughtering those lords of men for the sake of that one son.
Standing in improper conduct, how can you not feel shame before those established in their own duties?
O one devoid of right conduct, shameless, a mere Brahmin in name, lowest of men!
Stay now, O evil-minded one; you shall not escape from me alive.
"He for whose sake you took up arms and depending upon whom you live—
he now lies fallen, his back reported to you by Dharmarāja; you ought not to doubt those words."
Having been addressed thus by Bhīma, Droṇa then cast aside that bow;
that twice-born one of righteous soul, intending to renounce his body and desiring to abandon all his weapons, spoke as follows.
O King, the valiant Karna and Duryodhana, acting with haste, cried out, "Karna!
Karna, great archer! Kripa! Duryodhana!
"Exert yourselves in battle!"—this is what I say to you again and again.
"I have exerted every effort in battle, yet you always say to me, 'May it be well with you against the Pāṇḍavas. I shall now cast aside my weapons.
Indeed, I am casting away my very life-breaths; I am departing for heaven this very moment."
Thus, O Great King, he cried out there at the son of Droṇa;
having cast aside his weapon in battle and settled himself upon the seat of his chariot,
he, absorbed in yoga, granted fearlessness to all beings.
Perceiving that vulnerability of his, Dhṛṣṭadyumna rose up;
then, having laid aside that formidable bow with its arrow upon the chariot,
he leaped down from the vehicle armed with a sword and suddenly rushed toward Droṇa.
Then, when the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna had fled from Droṇa,
all beings— both humans and others— uttered cries of "Alas!
upon seeing Droṇa in such a state, fallen under Dhṛṣṭadyumna's power.
They raised a great cry of "Alas! and exclaimed, "Oh, shame!
Droṇa, too, having cast aside his weapons, established himself in supreme equanimity;
having spoken thus and entered into yoga, the one of great asceticism became a mass of light.

With his mind, he went to the ancient Puruṣa Viṣṇu, the Supreme. Raising his face slightly and bracing his chest forward, with eyes closed, established in *sattva*, and having fixed his concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the heart;
Having meditated upon the Lord of the gods of gods, the imperishable and supreme Master, he who is the single-syllabled Brahman "Om," who has become light and possesses great ascetic power,
we then behold the Teacher who is free from all veils.
The Teacher, together with the virtuous, ascended to heaven, which is difficult to reach;
O King, having cast off his body from that most excellent chariot, the light of that high-souled one went forth, having burst through the crown of his head, to the supreme abode.
When he had thus departed, it was our thought that there were two suns;
for the sky, filled with lights, seemed as if it were a single expanse,
and the moon of Bhāradvāja became equal in splendor to the sun.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, that light vanished;
there arose a tumultuous roar from the delighted inhabitants of heaven when Droṇa had gone to the world of Brahmā and Dhṛṣṭadyumna had been rendered unconscious.
We alone— those five of human birth— then beheld that high-souled one, united in yoga, proceeding toward the supreme goal: myself,
Dhanañjaya Pārtha, and the twice-born Kṛpa Śāradvata.
Vāsudeva of the Vṛṣṇi clan and Dharmarāja the Pāṇḍava, O great king, as well as all the others, did not perceive the majesty of the wise son of Bharadvāja as he departed, liberated through yoga.

The human beings did not perceive him as he was departing for the great, divine Brahma-world— that supreme secret of the gods, the highest destination— since they were unaware that he was traveling together with the bulls among sages.

Adopting a yogic posture, the son of Pṛṣata drew his sword and, overcome by rage and indignation, struck down the preceptor— the subduer of enemies— who was drenched in blood after being pierced by hundreds of arrows and had laid aside his weapons, for the sake of reaching the world of Brahmā.
Bearing sword and shield, the son of Pṛṣata rushed forward with great speed;
then, as he charged swiftly with the intent to slay the Preceptor,
all the Pāṇḍavas cried out, and Phalguna leaped down from his chariot.
"He must not be killed! He must not be killed! they cried out from all sides as Phalguna pursued him while the Pāṇḍavas were shouting;
then, transformed, he seized that being who had become Brahman, the source of all beings.
Rebuked by all living beings, the son of Pṛṣata seized the head of that lifeless embodied one;
while the man uttered not a word, he severed the head from the body with a sword.
Filled with great joy when the son of Bharadvāja had been struck down,
he let out a lion’s roar in the battle, brandishing his sword;
he was dark-complexioned, with grey hair reaching his ears, and fifty-eight years of age.
On your account, he moved about in battle like one sixteen years old;
and the mighty-armed Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, said:
"Having driven the chariot there, do not cause Droṇa to be slain."
"Bring the teacher alive; do not kill him, O son of Drupada!
"He must not be killed! He must not be killed! thus cried out your soldiers, and Arjuna, filled with compassion, rushed toward him.
While Arjuna was crying out and all the kings were likewise lamenting,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna slew Droṇa, that bull among men, upon the seat of his chariot;
drenched in blood, that tamer of foes fell from the chariot to the earth.
Like the sun with its crimson rays, he became difficult to behold;
thus did the soldiers see him slain in battle. But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O King, [beheld] that great head of Bhāradvāja.
That great archer hurled it right before your warriors.
But upon seeing the head of Bhāradvāja’s son, O King,
and seeing the preceptor Drona— the Brahmin and teacher— fallen from his chariot, your men...
With their resolve set on flight, they fled in every direction;
but Droṇa, ascending to the heavens, entered the path of the stars.
O King, I alone witnessed that death of Droṇa.
Through the grace of the seer Kṛṣṇa, the son of Satyavatī,
those four became human beings,
like a blazing crest of fire or a flaming meteor.
We beheld the sky as if it were fixed, the majesty of that Great-Souled One;
we beheld that one of great splendor proceeding, having fixed the sky, like a smokeless, blazing meteor moving along.

When Droṇa was slain, the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas, with great speed, rushed at the Kurus who were now devoid of enthusiasm; then the army broke apart. Those [Kurus], consisting mostly of horses, were slaughtered in battle by sharp arrows.
When Droṇa was slain, your men became like those whose life-breath had departed;
having suffered defeat and facing great fear regarding the hereafter,
deprived of both [worlds], they found no steadfastness within themselves.

O King, O Bhārata, while the bodies of the army lay fallen there in a tumultuous mass of tens of thousands of headless trunks, the kings, though searching for the body of the son of Bharadvāja, could not find it at that time.
Twenty-one thousand Uruṇḍas rose up,
O bull of the Bharatas, being cut down by sharp-edged spears, swords,
and lances, while they were tormented by the heat of the weapons amidst a great cry of "Alas!"
Some carried away slain warriors, while others even carried those who were still alive; with the majority of their leaders killed, they became consumed by thoughts of flight,
O Great King, and those warriors then lost all enthusiasm.
O Lord of the People, the chariot-warriors, those mounted on horses and elephants, and the foot-soldiers—
slain and for the most part killed, they lay like the dead, their luster destroyed;
the best of your charioteers were as if covered with ashes.
Having been defeated after engaging in an unrighteous battle,
the Pāṇḍavas, having secured victory and great fame for the hereafter,
raised the sounds of whizzing arrows and let out abundant lion-roars.
Then, O King, Bhīmasena and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
embraced one another and danced amidst the army.
And then Bhīma spoke to the son of Pṛṣata, the scorcher of his enemies:
"O son of Pṛṣata, when the wicked Sūtaputra and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been slain in battle, I shall embrace you again as a victor.
Having said this much, Bhīma was filled with great joy.
With the sound of his arms, the Pāṇḍava made the earth tremble.
Terrified by that sound, your men fled from the battle;
the Pāṇḍavas, however, filled with joy, let out lion-like roars.
Seeing those sons and Sumukha, the son of Pṛṣata, they fled,
abandoning the duty of a warrior and intent on escape. But the Pāṇḍavas, O lord of the people, were indeed joyful upon obtaining victory.
And because they were invincible in battle, they obtained happiness through him. Then, O King, when Droṇa was slain, the Kurus, afflicted by weapons,
their foremost heroes killed and utterly shattered, became deeply devoted to grief.
O lord of the people, seeing their enemies exulting again and again,
they became terrified and dejected, their eyes filled with tears;
deprived of their senses, their enthusiasm destroyed, and their vital energy struck down by despair.
With loud cries of distress, they surrounded your son—
women in their menses, trembling, and gazing toward the ten directions with tearful throats, like the Daityas of old when Hiraṇyākṣa was slain.
Surrounded by them like small animals terrified [by predators], your son, the king, being unable to hold his ground, retreated,
O Bhārata; those warriors of yours were exhausted by hunger and thirst.
Scorched by the sun, they became deeply despondent;
it was like the falling of the sun, the drying up of the ocean,
the overturning of Mount Meru, or the defeat of Indra.
O King, seeing that unbearable fall of Bhāradvāja’s son,
the Kauravas fled in fear, appearing utterly terrified;
Śakuni, the king of the Gāndhāras, fled along with those even more terrified than himself.

Seeing that Rukmaratha had been slain, he fled together with his chariots; the son of the Sūta, having surrounded the great army— the swift host equipped with protective fenders and banners as it was fleeing— retreated out of fear.
Placing at the head of his army a host thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, Śalya, the lord of the Madras, retreated in fear as he looked back upon the field,
which was largely filled with elephants whose heroes had been slain and with many foot soldiers.
Surrounded by the remaining forces of the Bhojas, along with the Kaliṅgas, Aṭṭas, and Bāhlikas, the son of Śaradvat departed, crying out, "Alas!
Alas! And Kṛtavarman, O King, surrounded by them, set forth on very swift horses.
Accompanied by a host of foot soldiers, Ulūka fled from there, O King, terrified and afflicted by fear upon seeing Droṇa struck down—
he who was handsome, young, and distinguished for his valor.
Duhshasana, greatly agitated, fled away surrounded by elephants;
Vrishasena, seeing Drona struck down, quickly departed, taking ten thousand chariots and three thousand elephants.
O great king, the great car-warrior Duryodhana set out for that place, accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots, and surrounded by foot soldiers;
he took with him the remnants of the *saṃśaptaka* force that had been spared by Kiritin.
O King, seeing Droṇa struck down, Suśarman fled;
and the men, mounting elephants, chariots, and even the horses of their enemies,
fled in every direction from the battle upon seeing the one with the golden chariot slain.
Some Kauravas rushed forward in haste, urging on their fathers, others their brothers and maternal uncles; some urged on their sons and their friends,
while others likewise urged on their troops and their nephews.
Relatives and others likewise fled in the ten directions;
then King Duryodhana spoke to Aśvatthāman:
"With disheveled hair and overwhelmed, two do not flee together in one place."
"‘This is not possible!’— thinking thus, O Lord, your men, their enthusiasm destroyed and their vigor shattered, cast off their armor and fled;
other soldiers, O bull of the Bharatas, cried out to one another."
"Stay! Stay! they cried, yet they themselves could not remain there;
having unyoked the draft-oxen from the chariot, the warriors, whose driver had been slain, mounted their well-adorned horses and urged them forward swiftly on foot.
While the army was thus fleeing, terrified and deprived of its vigor,
and while that fearsome host raised cries of "Alas!",
the son of Droṇa advanced against the enemies like a crocodile moving against the current.
A truly great battle took place between him and the hosts led by Śikhaṇḍin—
the Prabhadrakas, the Pāñcālas, the Cedis, and the Kekayas.
Having slaughtered the various divisions of the Pāṇḍava army, he who was difficult to vanquish in combat [remained].
Having somehow escaped from that peril, he who possessed the prowess of an elephant in rut beheld the army fleeing, intent on flight; then,
approaching Duryodhana, the son of Droṇa spoke these words.
"O Bhārata, why does this army flee as if terrified? O Indra among kings, why do you not halt it as it flees from the battle?
And you too, O lord of men, are not in your usual state as before."
"Karṇa and these other kings do not stand their ground;
even in other battles, the army never fled in such a manner. Is all well with your troops, O mighty-armed Bhārata?"
"O King, upon the death of which lion among chariot-warriors has this army of yours reached such a state? Tell me that, O Kaurava. Having heard those words spoken by the son of Droṇa, Duryodhana—
The bull among kings was unable to utter that terrible and unpleasant news;
your son has sunk into an ocean of grief like a shattered boat— a man in bottomless water seeking a raft where there is no raft.
Seeing the son of Droṇa stationed upon his chariot, his vision obscured by tears,
the king then spoke these words with shame to the son of Śaradvat:
"Tell me everything here— blessings be upon you— how this army has been routed."
Then, O King, Śāradvata, falling into distress again and again,
reported to the son of Droṇa how Droṇa had been struck down.
Kṛpa said:
Placing Droṇa, the foremost chariot-warrior on earth, at our head,
we engaged in battle with the Pāñcālas alone.
Then, as the battle commenced, the Kurus and Somakas became intermingled.

Roaring at one another, they struck down each other’s bodies with weapons. While the battle was thus proceeding and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were being decimated in the fray, your father, filled with rage, invoked a celestial weapon.
Then Droṇa, that bull among men, manifesting the Brahma-weapon,
slew his enemies by the hundreds and thousands with broad-headed arrows;
your father, filled with great rage, stood facing his foes.
There, the powerful [Droṇa] struck them down with his might, like a wind felling trees;
the Pāṇḍavas, Kekayas, Matsyas, and especially the Pañcālas,
having encountered Droṇa’s chariot in battle, perished, impelled by Time.

Droṇa dispatched to death a thousand lions among chariot-warriors and two thousand elephants, all consumed by the Brahmā-weapon. He was grey-haired to his ears, dark-complexioned, and fifty-eight years of age.
The aged Droṇa moved about in battle like one sixteen years of age;
while the armies were being distressed and the kings were being slain,
the Pāñcālas, overcome by indignation, turned their faces away from the fight.
When some of them were broken and turned away, the conqueror of enemies,
manifesting divine weapons, became like the risen sun.
Having reached the midst of the Pāṇḍavas, that powerful one, whose rays were his arrows, shone forth.
Your father became difficult to behold, like the sun situated at the meridian;
scorched by Droṇa as if by the blazing sun,
they were burnt in their vigor, devoid of energy, and lost their presence of mind.
Seeing them afflicted by Drona’s arrows, Madhusudana,
desiring victory for the sons of Pandu, spoke these words:
"This foremost of weapon-bearers can never be conquered by his enemies."
"Even against the slayer of Vṛtra himself in battle, you are leaders of hosts of chariot-warriors. Therefore, O Pāṇḍavas, casting aside righteousness, protect your victory;
for upon those striving for victory, prosperity and righteousness both attend."
"So that he whose chariot is adorned with gold may not slay you all in battle—my thought is this: if Aśvatthāman were killed, he would no longer fight.
Let some man falsely tell him that he has been slain in combat."
Kuntī’s son Dhanañjaya did not approve of these words;
however, all the others approved, while Yudhiṣṭhira did so with great difficulty.
Bhīmasena, however, spoke to your father with shame.
"Aśvatthāman has been slain"— this news your father learned. Suspecting it to be false, he, who was so fond of his son, questioned Dharmarāja whether you had been killed or not in battle.
Immersed in that fear of untruth yet intent on victory, Yudhiṣṭhira said this to Aśvatthāman:
"The elephant of Indravarman of Mālava, who was as massive as a mountain, has been slain by Bhīma."
Approaching Droṇa, he then spoke these words aloud:
"He for whose sake you wield your weapons, and looking upon whom you live—
your beloved son Aśvatthāman has been struck down."
Slain, he lay upon the ground like a lion cub in the forest;
though fully aware of the faults of falsehood, that king, being struck down, spoke indistinctly to the best of the twice-born, saying, "An elephant has been killed."
Having heard that great and unpleasant news there, the preceptor became despondent;
crying out for you as you were being slain and tormented by your name,
he restrained his divine weapons and did not fight as he had before.
Seeing him extremely agitated, his mind stricken with grief,
the son of the Pāñcāla king, a man of cruel deeds, rushed toward him.
Seeing that death was ordained for him, he who was skilled in discerning the true nature of the world—
Then, having cast aside his divine weapons in battle, he sat down to fast unto death.
Thereupon, seizing his hair with his left hand,
the son of Pṛṣata cut off his head while the heroes were crying out.

"He must not be killed! He must not be killed! they cried out from all sides. And likewise, Arjuna, leaping down from his chariot, rushed toward him, raising his arms in haste and speaking again and again.

"Bring the teacher alive; do not kill him," said the knower of dharma. Nevertheless, O bull among men, although he was being restrained by the Kauravas and by Arjuna, your father was indeed slain by that cruel man.
Then all the soldiers fled, afflicted by fear;
and we too were devoid of energy, O sinless one, now that your father had been slain.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard that his father had met his death in battle, the son of Droṇa summoned a fierce rage, like a serpent struck by a foot. Then,
O noble one, the enraged son of Droṇa blazed up intensely in the fray.
Just as the carrier of oblations blazes up upon reaching a great quantity of fuel,
so too did Lohitākṣa then become like a hissing serpent, crushing palm with palm and grinding tooth against tooth.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, having heard that his aged father, a Brahmin, had been slain unrighteously by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, what did Aśvatthāman say?"
O Sūta Sañjaya, tell me what that hero said at that time— he who was accomplished in learning, like a blazing fire in his splendor, and who,
as the best among all wielders of weapons, knew the divine missiles.
O Sañjaya, that most righteous man, in whom the human, Varuṇa, Āgneya, Brāhma, Aindra, and Nārāyaṇa weapons— along with their power— were eternally established,
has been slain by Dhṛṣṭadyumna through unrighteous means.
Having heard that the preceptor had been slain, what did Aśvatthāman say—
he by whom, having obtained the science of archery from the high-souled Rāma,
the divine weapons were taught to his son who was desirous of a teacher?
For in this world, men desire nothing else whatsoever as much as a single son who is superior to themselves in virtue;
yet for great-souled teachers, there are indeed secret teachings.
They may give these [skills] to a son or to a devoted disciple;
having acquired all that craft in its entirety and with distinction, O Sañjaya,
the heroic son of Śāradvatī is second only to Droṇa in battle.
With Rāma’s approval, he was equal to Puraṃdara in battle, equal to Kārtavīrya in heroism, equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect,
equal to a mountain in fortitude, and like fire in brilliance— such was the youth.
In depth he is like the ocean, and in wrath he is like the venom of a serpent. That foremost of chariot-warriors in the world, firm with his bow and having conquered fatigue,
moves swiftly in the clamor like the wind, like the enraged God of Death himself.
By whomsoever [this bow] was discharged in battle, the earth was pressed down;
sounding like the roar of thunderclouds, she trembles, overwhelmed by fear. Yet that hero of true prowess does not waver in battle.
Having bathed in the Vedas and bathed in his vows, he was a master of the science of archery; as unshakeable as the great ocean, he was like Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
That most righteous man was [slain] by Dhṛṣṭadyumna through unrighteous means in battle.
Having heard that the preceptor had been slain, what did Aśvatthāman say—
he who was created by that high-souled one as the death of Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
just as the Pāñcālya, the son of Yajñasena, became the death of Droṇa?
Having heard that the preceptor had been slain by that cruel, wicked, and fierce man of very limited vision, what did Aśvatthāman say? Saṃjaya said:
O bull among men, hearing that his father had been slain by a wicked deed through deception,
the son of Droṇa was filled with tears and rage.
O king of kings, as he was thus enraged, a divine form became visible upon him.
Like the Destroyer wishing to seize all beings at the turn of time,
he then wiped his eyes, which were filled with tears again and again,
and sighing in anger, spoke these words to Duryodhana:
Just as my father was struck down by base men who had laid aside their weapons,
so too has that sin been committed by one who bears the banner of righteousness; I have heard of this ignoble and cruel act of the son of Dharma.

Whatever false words were spoken out of greed by that evil-minded and cruel man for the sake of the kingdom— that too is known to me. Furthermore, in battles once they have commenced, victory and defeat are both certain.

"O King, these two things would be equal: therein, death is praised. That death which occurs for one fighting in battle while acting according to the law does not lead to suffering; for such has been observed by that twice-born man."
Without a doubt, my father has gone to the world of heroes;
that tiger among men, having met his end in such a manner, is not to be mourned. Yet, though he was ever devoted to righteousness, he suffered the seizing of his hair.
While all the troops were looking on, that [act] cuts into my very vitals—
that while I was still alive, my father was seized by the hair!
How will other fathers of sons ever again desire to have sons?
Out of desire, anger, contempt, pride, or even through childishness,
as well as out of disregard, people perform unrighteous acts;
so too has this great unrighteous deed been committed here by the son of Pṛṣata.
"Surely that cruel and evil-minded one has treated me with contempt;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna shall witness the most dreadful consequence of his actions,
for that Pāṇḍava is both a speaker of falsehood and a supreme ignoble man."
For he who then deceitfully caused the preceptor to lay down his weapon—
today the earth shall drink his blood, that of Dharmarāja.
O sinless Kauravya, I swear this by truth and by my merit from sacrifices and charitable works.
"I shall by no means live without having slain all the Pāñcālas.
I will strive by every possible means for the slaughter of the Pāñcālas,
and I shall slay the evil-doer Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle."

O Kaurava, by whatever means— whether mild or harsh— I have achieved peace by bringing about the slaughter of the Pāñcālas. O tiger among men, it is for this very purpose that human beings desire a son.
It has been obtained both in this world and the next for protection from great fear;
yet my father has reached such a state as if he were friendless,
even while I, his son and disciple, who am like a mountain, am still alive.
"Fie on my divine weapons! Fie on my arms! Fie on my prowess!
Since Drona, having obtained me as his son, has subjected me to being seized by the hair, O best of the Bharatas, I shall act in such a way that [this shall not happen again]."
"Even when my father has gone to the other world, I shall go there free from debt to him.
Yet, a noble man should never speak praise of himself;
however, unable to endure the slaughter of my father, I shall today here proclaim my own prowess."

Today let the Pāṇḍavas, together with Janārdana, behold my prowess as I crush all the armies, bringing about what is like the end of an eon. For neither the gods, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Asuras, nor the Rākṣasas [can withstand it].
"O bull among men, today you are capable of defeating me as I stand upon my chariot in battle. There is no one else in this world besides Arjuna who is a greater master of weapons than I;
for I am like the sun amidst its blazing rays."
The wielder of divine weapons, having entered the army,
shall today, in this great battle, employ the sons of Kṛśāśva whom I have dispatched;
displaying their own prowess, they will crush the Pāṇḍavas.
"O King, today all the quarters will be seen here by my men as if crowded with torrents of rain; they will be covered, O Great King, by my sharp feathered arrows,
and likewise the intermediate directions by my shafts."
Scattering nets of arrows in all directions with a terrifying roar,
I shall strike down my enemies like a great wind felling trees;
neither Bībhatsu nor Janārdana knows that weapon.
Neither Bhīmasena, nor the twins, nor King Yudhiṣṭhira;
neither that evil-minded son of Pṛṣata, nor Śikhaṇḍin, nor Sātyaki— none of them can do this for me, O Kauravya, including the complete withdrawal of the army.
In former times, after bowing down according to the prescribed rites, my father offered an oblation to Nārāyaṇa while he was present in the form of Brahmā; then,
having personally accepted it, the Blessed One granted him a boon.
Then my father chose the supreme weapon, Nārāyaṇa.
Thereupon, O King, the Blessed One, the best of gods, said to him:
"There shall be no other man anywhere who is your equal in battle."
"O Brahmin, take up this unsurpassed Nārāyaṇa weapon.
But, O Brāhmaṇa, this must never be employed rashly under any circumstances;
for this weapon does not turn back from anyone other than the slaying of the enemy."
"O Lord, it is not possible to know who might not be slain; for one might even kill someone who should not be killed. Therefore, one should not employ this [mantra].
[For] in battle, there is slaughter, flight, and the casting away of weapons."
"O scorcher of foes, these are the methods for neutralizing a great weapon: seeking refuge from one's enemies and fleeing for protection.
For he who oppresses those who should not be slain in battle will himself be oppressed in every way."
My father took that [weapon], and that lord said to me:
"You shall rain down divine showers of weapons many times over;
by means of this weapon, you shall blaze with splendor in battle."
Having spoken thus, that Lord, the Master, ascended to heaven.
This weapon was obtained from Nārāyaṇa by my kinsman;
through his grace, I have obtained this supreme and great weapon.
By means of that [weapon], I shall put to flight the Pāṇḍavas, the Pāñcālas, the Matsyas,
and the Kekayas in battle, just as the Lord of Śacī [Indra] routed the Asuras.
In whatever manner I desire, so shall my arrows become.
O Bhārata, even if my enemies were to display their prowess,
I would wish that my arrows fall upon them even when they are at a distance;
standing on the battlefield, I shall rain down showers of stones as I desire.
With iron-beaked birds, I shall put the great chariot-warriors to flight;
and I shall undoubtedly hurl various battle-axes. Thus, O scorcher of enemies, by means of that great Nārāyaṇa weapon—
I shall utterly destroy my enemies, having rendered the Pāṇḍavas insignificant. This wretched man, a hater of friends, Brahmins, and his preceptor,
who is most despicable and the lowest of the Pañcālas— today he shall not escape from me alive.
Having spoken thus, O noble one, the son of Droṇa then blew his conch shell,
filling the entire earth with its mountains, forests,
and groves. Hearing the sound of that conch, O noble one, your troops—
Casting aside their fear, those great car-warriors turned back toward the battle itself.
Hearing those words of Droṇa’s son, the army rallied;
then all those best of men blew their great conch shells.
Delighted, they struck thousands of kettledrums and ḍiṇḍima drums;
likewise, the earth resounded, oppressed by the hooves and wheel-rims.
That tumultuous noise made the sky, the heavens, and the earth echo.
Hearing that sound, which resembled the roar of thunderclouds, the Pāṇḍavas—
those best of chariot-warriors— gathered together and took counsel among themselves.
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, the son of Droṇa then touched water for purification.
Then he manifested that divine Nārāyaṇa weapon.
Sañjaya said:
When that Nārāyaṇa weapon had thus been manifested, then—
A wind blew, scattering raindrops, and thunder rolled even though there were no clouds;
the earth trembled and the great ocean was agitated.
Furthermore, the rivers flowing toward the sea began to run upstream.
O Bhārata, the peaks of the mountains there were shattered;
the wild beasts moved counter-clockwise around the sons of Pāṇḍu;
they were enveloped in darkness, and the sun became obscured.
Flesh-eating spirits descended upon them with great joy;
O lord of the people, the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas were terrified. Seeing that great and intense chaos, what conversation arose among them?

Then all the kings were distressed and lost their composure, O lord of the people, upon seeing that terrible and fearsome weapon of the son of Droṇa; those who moved through the sky fell there, deprived of their spirits.
The two worlds and the sky itself were entirely enveloped in flames.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When the armies had been turned back in battle by the son of Droṇa..."
Severely tormented by grief and unable to endure the slaughter of his father,
what counsel was given to the Pāṇḍavas when they saw the Kurus advancing and Dhṛṣṭadyumna engaged in defense? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said:
Having first seen the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fleeing,
and hearing once more that tumultuous noise, Yudhiṣṭhira addressed Arjuna.
O Dhanañjaya, when the preceptor Droṇa had been slain in battle by Dhṛṣṭadyumna—
just as the great Asura Vṛtra was slain by the wielder of the thunderbolt—
their spirits were dejected, and they no longer hoped for victory in the fight.
Setting their minds on self-preservation, the Kurus fled like [scattered] herds;
some kings fled swiftly with wandering chariots whose outriders and drivers had been slain, their banners, standards, and umbrellas fallen, and their poles shattered.
Some, having mounted with broken seats and agitated horses, were distraught;
others, terrified, themselves urged on the horses with their feet; and some, overcome by fear, fled in chariots whose yokes, wheels, and axles were shattered.

Some, having abandoned their shattered chariots, fled on foot; others, mounted on the backs of horses, were dragged along with their seats half-fallen from them. Pierced by iron shafts upon the necks of elephants, they were dislodged from their seats.
Some were carried away in the ten directions by elephants fleeing in pain from arrows;
others, deprived of their weapons and armor, fell from their mounts to the earth; some were crushed by the rims of wheels, and others were trampled by horses and elephants.
Crying out, "O father! O son! others fled in fear;
their vigor struck down by dejection, they could not even recognize one another.
Having placed upon [the chariots] sons, fathers, friends, and brothers who were severely wounded, they fled.
Others, having cast off their armor, drenched themselves with water;
and hundreds of thousands of other warriors were intent on flight. Yet, when they saw that army of your son once again standing firm, [they rallied].
Then, O Great King, Dharmaputra spoke to Dhanañjaya:
"Having reached such a state after Droṇa was slain, the army quickly fled;
thus indeed was it swiftly broken when Droṇa was struck down in battle."
"Finding no place to stand, wounded and oppressed by arrows, by whom has he been turned back? If you know, tell me.
There is the sound of neighing horses and the trumpeting of elephants."
And here the great sound of chariot rims is heard mingled with other noises;
these exceedingly intense sounds have arisen in the ocean of the Kurus,
and rising up again and again, they truly cause my men to tremble.
"This tumultuous sound that is heard, making one's hair stand on end—
my mind tells me it could shatter even the three worlds along with Indra.
I believe this is the terrible roar of the wielder of the thunderbolt."
Now that Droṇa has been slain for the sake of the Kauravas, Indra clearly approaches;
our hair stands on end as the chariots and elephants are agitated,
having heard that most terrifying roar there from Dhananjaya’s preceptor.
"Who is this great car-warrior who, having rallied the broken Kauravas,
turns them back for battle like the Lord of the Gods himself?
Arjuna said:
Raising themselves for fierce deeds and relying on fortitude,
the Kauravas blow their conchs, taking refuge in his prowess—
O King, regarding whom you have this doubt, now that the preceptor has been slain with his weapons laid aside.
Having stationed the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, [Duryodhana] asked, "Who is this that roars?"—
[pointing to] that modest, mighty-armed one who moves like an elephant in rut,
equal to Indra and Viṣṇu in prowess, and standing like the Destroyer himself in his wrath.
I shall describe him who is equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence, possessed of statesmanship, a great chariot-warrior, of fierce deeds, and the granter of fearlessness to the Kurus;
upon whose birth Droṇa gave away the wealth of a thousand cows.
This son of Droṇa roars like a rain-cloud at the end of the summer heat;
this Aśvatthāman bellows at the most worthy of Brahmins.
By that hero, as soon as he was born, [the world] was made to tremble, just as by Ucchaiḥśravas.
The earth trembled and all three worlds shook at the sound of his neighing. Having heard that, a hidden being then gave him a name;
thus, this hero now roars, O Pāṇḍava, and is called Aśvatthāman.

He who today, like one without a protector, was attacked and slain by the son of Pṛṣata through such a cruel deed— his protector stands ready. Therein lies the Pāñcālya who seized my preceptor by the hair.
Therefore, the son of Droṇa, knowing his own prowess, would never forgive that;
for it is my opinion that he alone might destroy us all. You have treated your preceptor falsely for the sake of the kingdom.
