By that knower of dharma who was truly virtuous, a very great unrighteousness has indeed been committed.
This infamy shall endure for a long time throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile,
just as it did when Rāma slew Vālin, so too now that Droṇa has been struck down.

"This son of Pāṇḍu, my disciple, is endowed with all virtuous qualities; he will not speak what is false. Having thus placed his trust in you, he then entered into a cloak of truth and spoke an untruth.
"O King, the preceptor was told by you, 'The elephant is slain.
Thereupon, casting aside his weapon, devoid of self-interest and deprived of consciousness, he became overwhelmed, O Lord, just as you have seen him."
Overcome by grief and turning away from his purpose, that teacher, who was devoted to his son, has been slain by his disciple after having abandoned eternal dharma;
for you have caused your teacher to be killed unrighteously once he had laid down his weapons.
"Protect the son of Pṛṣata now, if you are able, along with your ministers,
while he is being devoured by the preceptor’s son, who is enraged because his kinsmen have been slain.
None of us shall be able to save the son of Pṛṣata today."

"He who shows excessive kindness toward all beings will today, upon hearing that his father has been seized by the hair, consume us in battle. For even as I cry out loudly, longing for my preceptor— "
For a teacher has been slain by a disciple who has cast aside his own duty;
when our age has mostly passed and only a very small portion remains,
this great unrighteousness which has now been committed is a perversion of that [remaining time].

Like a father, he was always full of affection; indeed, according to dharma, he was like a father. Yet, O lord of the people, for the sake of a brief reign, that preceptor was slain by Dhṛtarāṣṭra for the sake of Bhīṣma and Droṇa.
The entire earth was bestowed upon him, along with his sons who were devoted to that end. Having obtained such a livelihood and being constantly honored by others,
my father always favored me above all his other sons.
Though he had laid down his weapons and was not being struck down, he was slain in battle by your word;
for even Śatakratu could not have killed him while he was fighting.
This is an act of treachery against that aged preceptor, who has always been your benefactor.
Indeed, for the sake of the kingdom, we—narrow-minded and ignoble—have committed [this act].
Alas! A great sin, a most terrible deed, has been done, in that this virtuous Droṇa was slain out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty.

The son of Vāsava would renounce sons, brothers, fathers, wives, and even life itself out of love for me; indeed, my preceptor knows this of me. Yet, though he was being struck down by me, desiring the kingdom, I overlooked him.
Therefore, O King, O Lord, I have reached this hell with my head hanging downwards.
Having caused the death today for the sake of a kingdom— of an aged Brāhmaṇa, a teacher who had laid down his weapons like a sage— it is better that I die than live.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard the words of Arjuna, O Great King, those great car-warriors there said nothing to Dhanañjaya, whether it was unpleasant or even pleasant.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, filled with rage, spoke to Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, as if smiling:
"Like a sage dwelling in the forest, you speak words consistent with dharma."
O Pārtha, like a Brāhmaṇa of firm vows who has laid down the rod of punishment,
a Kṣatriya who protects from injury, lives by means of protecting from injury, and is patient toward all three types of virtuous men,
quickly attains the earth, righteousness, fame, and prosperity.
O upholder of the lineage, you who are endowed with all the qualities of a Kṣatriya do not shine today as you speak these words like one lacking wisdom,
O Bhārata, while such a sinful and terrible deed is being committed.
Without establishing yourself in your own duty, why do you speak these words?
Your prowess, O son of Kuntī, is like that of Śakra, the lord of Śacī;
yet you do not overstep the dharma, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore.
Who indeed would not honor you today, who, casting aside resentment for thirteen years,
now desires only righteousness?
I myself shall hold back all the Kauravas with my mace.

If, without you, I were not to give the earth to the wise son of Dharma when the fifth day arrives, I would no longer be a Kṣatriya. By good fortune, dear father, your mind today follows its own duty.
"O Acyuta, it is by good fortune that your mind is ever fixed upon compassion. Yet, though you were engaged in righteousness, your kingdom was seized through unrighteousness,
and Draupadī was insulted and dragged into the assembly hall by your enemies."

How is it, O Bhārata, that while those elders— righteous and great— remain, Draupadī suffers such affliction like a courtesan? Indeed, what kind of bilva fruit must have been in the mouths of those high-souled men?
Or were they indeed deaf, or perhaps mute, O Dhanañjaya,
or blind, those who then lived without speaking words of benefit? For in that case, there would be righteousness, and no ignoble act here at all.
And Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others have also acted appropriately;
for together with their sons and disciples, they have equipped themselves to fight in battle. Yet we have been exiled to the forest, clothed in bark and deerskins.
For thirteen years,
we— who delight in truth and righteousness— endured many wrongs from our enemies, though they did not deserve such treatment; yet we have forgiven them even as they remain set upon a path of error.
"O sinless one, these occasions for indignation were endured by you;
being devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya, all this was carried out by you. Together with you, he has begun to cast off that unrighteousness."
"I shall slay those base usurpers of the kingdom along with their followers.
Previously, you said, 'We have come for battle,' and we strove to the best of our ability; yet today, you despise us."
"You do not wish to know your own duty; your speech is merely false.
O crusher of enemies, you cut our vital organs with your words as we are already tormented by fear, like pouring caustic acid into a wound."
"My heart is rent asunder, tormented by you with the arrow of your words. Being a righteous man, you do not perceive this great unrighteousness:
that you do not praise yourself and us, who are worthy of praise."
Even while Vāsudeva stands here, you praise the son of Droṇa;
you praise him who does not deserve even a sixteenth part of you.
It is not proper for one to speak of one's own own virtues oneself.
"O Pārtha, ten thousand nāgas are said to be the strength in my arms;
I could strike down even the assembled gods led by Indra,
along with the hosts of rākṣasas, asuras, uragas, and humans, O Pārtha, with my arrows."
In my wrath, I could split the earth and scatter the mountains;
brandishing my heavy, formidable mace adorned with golden garlands,
I could shatter the trees that resemble mountains, just as the wind does.
Knowing your brother to be such as this, O bull among men,
you ought not to fear the son of Droṇa, O you of immeasurable prowess. Or rather, stay here, O Bībhatsu, together with all these bulls among men.
"Armed with my mace, I alone shall conquer him in this great battle.
Then the son of the Pāñcāla king spoke to Pārtha,
who was roaring like a furious Hari at Hiraṇyakaśipu.
"O Bībhatsu, the duties of the Brahmins are known to the wise:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, giving gifts, as well as receiving gifts and sacrifices;
and the sixth is called study—in which of these are they established?"
"Since Drona was slain by me, why do you reproach me, O Partha?
Having fallen away from his own duty and resorted to the duty of a Kshatriya,
that performer of base deeds slew us with a superhuman weapon."

Likewise, O Pārtha, if one should slay with illusion itself that deceitful practitioner of illusion— who is otherwise irresistible and merely a Brahmin in name— who is not acting rightly, what is there improper in that?
If, when he has been thus struck down by me, the son of Droṇa should [act] out of rage...
He utters a terrifying roar; what is lost to me therein? Nor do I consider it surprising that the son of Droṇa, unable to protect them, will slay the Kauravas with his pure thundering.
And as for what you, being righteous, say of me— that I am a slayer of my preceptor—
it was for that purpose that I was born from the fire as the son of the Pāñcālya king; I am one for whom,
while fighting in battle, there is no distinction between what should be done and what should not be done.
O Dhanañjaya, how could you call him a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya—
he who, overcome by anger, would slay those ignorant of weapons with the Brahmā-weapons?
O best of men, why should he not be slain by every possible means?
Because he is my father’s slayer, how could he not be put to death by me? This wicked man of evil intellect has slaughtered his own kinsmen in battle;
how can there be no sin for me in killing one who calls himself a Brahmin?
"O Arjuna, knowing that he was declared by those who know the dharma to be an unrighteous man, like poison to them— a man who knows the truth of dharma and worldly purpose— why do you reproach him?
That cruel man was struck down by me while on his very chariot."

"O Bībhatsu, that [deed] is worthy of celebration; why do you not rejoice? O Pārtha, having performed this battle—terrible as fire, the sun, or poison, and praiseworthy for the severing of Droṇa’s head—why do you not praise it?"
"He who slew my kinsmen in battle— none other than mine own—
though I have severed his head, I am still not free from my fever.
And it cuts at my very vitals that his head has not been taken by me."
Just as the head of Jayadratha was cast into the territory of the Niṣādas, so too, O Arjuna, the non-slaughter of enemies remains an unrighteousness for a Kṣatriya;
for this is the duty of a Kṣatriya: he should either slay or be slain.

O Pāṇḍava, that enemy was slain by me in battle according to dharma, just as you slew the heroic Bhagadatta, the friend of your father. Having slain the grandfather in combat, you consider yourself to be acting righteously.
Now that my enemy has been slain by me, why do you not acknowledge this merit, O sinful one?
O Pārtha, you do not hold me in high regard, even though I am bowed down before you due to our kinship— like an elephant seated upon a staircase constructed from its own body.
"O Arjuna, I forgive you for all this transgression of speech,
not for any other reason, but solely for the sake of Draupadī and the sons of Draupadī;
for my enmity with the Teacher is well known as one inherited through the lineage of our family."
Thus this world knows it, O sons of Pāṇḍu, and not you:
that the eldest son of Pāṇḍu is not untruthful, nor am I unrighteous, O Arjuna;
for they do not call one a Kṣatriya who does not strike on the field of battle.
"Whether it be his father or even his teacher, if they seek to kill their son or disciple,
he should slay them without hesitation, whether by deceitful or straightforward means.
Thus was it said of old by Brahmā regarding the killing of enemies by Kṣatriyas.
Therefore, that so-called Brahmin, who was my enemy, has been slain by his disciple. A Kṣatriya son who would slay either his father or his teacher—
that Kṣatriya indeed is called a true Kṣatriya, for he slays what is undesirable.
"The wicked one, who betrayed his disciples, has been slain; fight, for victory is yours.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"By that high-souled one, the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches were studied according to the prescribed rules."

While Drona— the son of a great seer, in whom the science of archery was visibly established and who was the very embodiment of modesty— was being reviled at that time by that base-souled, cruel, mean, and treacherous slayer of his preceptor;
Through whose grace the bulls among men perform superhuman deeds in battle, which are difficult even for the gods to accomplish—
while that Droṇa was being reviled by those of evil deeds in his very presence, [how could you remain silent?]
"They do not show indignation there; fie on the Kṣatriya spirit, fie on one who is indignant!
What did all the sons of Pṛthā and all the kings on earth who are wielders of the bow say upon hearing this regarding the King of Pañcāla? Tell me that, Saṃjaya."
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard those words of the son of Drupada, who is of cruel deeds,
all the kings indeed became silent, O lord of the people.
But Arjuna, having seen the son of Pṛṣata looking askance with a sidelong glance, sighed deeply with tears and cried out, "Fie! Fie! Fie!
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, the twins, Kṛṣṇa, and the others did likewise.
O King, they were deeply ashamed, and Sātyaki spoke these words:
"There is no man here who would quickly slay this wicked man, this lowest of men, as he speaks such evil things."
All these Pāṇḍavas reproach you out of a desire to know [the truth],
just as Brahmins censure a dog-cooker for that evil deed. Having committed this great sin, which is censured by all virtuous men—
How are you not ashamed to speak thus, having entered this splendid assembly?
And why does your tongue not split into a hundred pieces, and why does your head not shatter, O base man, as you revile your guru and do not fall through your unrighteousness?
"You are indeed censurable by all the Pārthas and the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis,
since, having committed such a foul deed, you boast in the assembly of people;
having performed such an improper act, you further insult your elder."

"You deserve to be killed; there is no purpose in you living for even a moment. What noble man other than you, the lowest of men, would resolve upon such a thing—to seize by the hair and slay his virtuous and righteous preceptor?"
Seventy-seven of your kinsmen—both those on your side and those on the enemy's—have been struck down; they have been deprived of their fame because of you, a disgrace to your lineage.
Furthermore, he spoke these words to Pārtha, that bull among men, regarding Bhīṣma.
Thus was his end ordained by that high-souled one himself;
even for him, your own uterine brother shall be the slayer, the most wicked of evildoers.
No other on earth exists who is a greater sinner than the sons of the Pāñcāla king.
And he whom your father created as the slayer of Bhīṣma was indeed Śikhaṇḍin, who was protected by him; yet he became the death of that high-souled one.
The Pāñcālas have strayed from dharma; they are base, betrayers of friends and elders.
Having encountered you, my own uterine brother, who has been censured by all virtuous men—
if you speak such words again in my presence,
I shall strike off your head with my mace, which is like a thunderbolt.
Upon seeing you, a slayer of a Brahmin, people look toward the sun;
for the sin of killing a Brahmin is yours as a means for your own atonement,
O Pāñcālaka of wicked conduct, in the very presence of my preceptor.
You do not feel shame at all for repeatedly insulting even the preceptor of your preceptor!
Stay, stay! Endure this single blow of my mace;
and I too shall endure many blows of your mace.
Thus addressed in harsh words by the Sātvata, the son of Pṛṣata, enraged and filled with fury, spoke to Sātyaki as if laughing:
"It is heard, it is heard! And it is forgiven, O Mādhava!"

O ignoble one, you ought not to revile a virtuous and noble man. Forbearance is praised in the world, yet a wicked person does not deserve forbearance; for the evil-minded one thinks, "This man has been conquered."

You, who are of base conduct, lowly in spirit, and fixed in evil resolve— you who wish to speak [thus], you may indeed be spoken of from the tips of your hair to the tips of your nails. O wicked one, death would be better for you than such a way of life.
To hear the root of what must be said, base men will speak;
failing to see faults in themselves, they cast blame upon others for their own defects.
He who was Bhūriśravas, when his arm had been severed, sat down in a vow of fasting by you.
"Was there anything more sinful than that?
While Droṇa was being drawn up by me in battle with divine weapons, he was slain after he had laid down his arms; what cruelty or evil deed was there in that?"
O Sātyaki, how could he who would strike one not fighting in battle, or likewise a sage who has gone to his death-fast, with his arms severed by enemies, be considered a man?
When that heroic one, having slain you, strides upon the earth, [he will be truly formidable].
Why did you not slay him then, having become the best of men? But when he was previously defeated by Pārtha, who acted ignobly,
then that heroic and powerful son of Somadatta was killed.
"Wherever Droṇa puts the army of the Pāṇḍavas to flight,
scattering thousands of arrows, there I go.
Having yourself performed such an act as this, like a Cāṇḍāla,"

If you wish to speak, why do you address me with such harsh words? O lowest of the Vṛṣṇi clan, you are the one who commits cruel deeds, not I. You are the abode of sinful actions; do not speak to me again.
"Be silent; you ought not to speak further to me.
For that which you wish to say to me is indeed a reversal of right and wrong.
If, out of folly, you shall speak such harsh words to me again,"
"I shall send you, with my arrows, to the abode of Vaivasvata in battle.
O fool, it is not possible by righteousness alone;
hear now what kind of conduct even they practiced through unrighteousness."
O Sātyaki, the Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira was previously deceived by unrighteousness,
and Draupadī was likewise afflicted through unrighteousness;
all the Pāṇḍavas were exiled to the forest together with Kṛṣṇā.
O fool, you have likewise seized all his property through unrighteousness;
and the King of Madra, having been deprived by unrighteousness, has been slain here by his enemies; and in the same way, the foolish son of Subhadrā was struck down through unrighteousness.
For this reason as well, Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus, was slain unrighteously;
indeed, Bhūriśravas was also slain by you, who know the dharma, in an unrighteous manner.
Thus have the enemies and the Pāṇḍavas acted toward one another in battle.

O Sātvata, even by heroic warriors who protect [the earth] and know the dharma, the supreme dharma is difficult to discern, and likewise, adharma is very hard to understand. Fight with the Kauravas; do not go to the abode of the ancestors.
Having been made to hear such words— both cruel and harsh—
the illustrious Sātyaki became as if trembling.
Upon hearing that, Sātyaki, his eyes copper-red with rage, took up his mace.
Sighing like a serpent and fixing his bow upon the chariot, he then rushed toward the prince of the Pañcālas and, in a state of fury, said this:
"I will not speak harsh words to you; rather, I shall slay you, for you deserve death."
As that immensely powerful and intolerant warrior rushed forward in a fury against the princess of Pañcāla— resembling Death itself at the end of an eon—
the mighty Bhīmasena was urged on by Vāsudeva.

Leaping quickly from his chariot, the mighty Pāṇḍava restrained with his arms the enraged Sātyaki as he was rushing forward; seizing the powerful warrior who was leaping away, he held him back by force.
Standing firm and planting his feet, that bull among the Śinis,
the best of the strong, was seized by Bhīma at the sixth step with great force; nevertheless, the powerful one freed himself from Bhīma and rose up.
Having released Bhīma, Mādhava departed with the speed of the wind;
then Bhīma, quickly assuming a moderate pace,
held back Sātyaki out of pride as he was on his tenth step.
O lord of the people, having descended from his chariot as he was being carried away by the stronger man,
Sahadeva spoke with gentle words:
"O tiger among men, we have no other friend."
O Mādhava, there is no friend superior to the Andhakas, Vṛṣṇis, and Pāñcālas; likewise, for the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, for you in particular, and for Kṛṣṇa, no other friend exists than we.
O Vārṣṇeya, as the Pāñcālas search throughout the land as far as the ocean's edge,
there is no other supreme ally like the Pāṇḍavas and the Vṛṣṇis;
and you, sir, consider such a friend to be exactly as you are.
"As you are to us, so are we to you.
Thus, that knower of all dharmas, mindful of the duty of friendship, restrained his anger toward the Pāñcāla prince; "Be appeased, O bull among the Śinis!"
"Forgive the son of Pṛṣata; let the son of Pṛṣata forgive you.
We too shall be the ones to seek forgiveness; what else could there be but peace?
O noble one, while the grandson of Śini is being pacified by Sahadeva,"
The son of the Pāñcāla king, laughing, said this:
"Release, release the grandson of Śini, O Bhīma, who is intoxicated with the pride of battle!
Let him attack me, as the wind assails a mountain."
"O son of Kuntī, until I subdue his fury with my sharp arrows— his desire for battle and his hope for life in this conflict—
what indeed can I do regarding this task that has been undertaken?"
"A very great [host] of the sons of Pāṇḍu [is here], for these Kauravas are advancing.
Or rather, Phalguna will hold them all back in battle;
I too shall strike down his head with my arrows."
"He thinks of me as Bhūriśravas with my arm severed in battle;
let him go, for either I shall kill him or he will kill me.
Hearing these words of the Pāñcāla prince, Sātyaki hissed like a serpent.
Stuck between Bhīma’s arms, the powerful one throbbed incessantly;
those two, mighty and endowed with great strength, roared like two bulls.
O noble one, Vāsudeva and Dharmarāja then acted with haste.
Then, with great effort, those two heroes restrained them;
having checked them, those two supreme archers, their eyes bloodshot with rage,
those bulls among Kṣatriyas, desiring to fight the enemies in battle, advanced against them.
Saṃjaya said:
Then the son of Droṇa wrought a slaughter of his enemies,
like the Destroyer unleashed by Time at the end of an eon against all living beings.
The battlefield was like a forest where the banners were its trees, the weapons its peaks, the slain elephants its great boulders;
it was strewn with horses and *kiṃpuruṣas*, covered by bow-vines,
resounded with the cries of spear-bearing *kravyāda* spirits, and teemed with hosts of *bhūtas* and *yakṣas*.
Having slain his enemies with broad-headed arrows, he piled up a mountain of bodies; then,
roaring with great force, that bull among men once again made his vow heard by your son.
Because Kuntī’s son Yudhiṣṭhira, while assuming the cloak of dharma, said to the preceptor as he was fighting, "Lay down your weapon," therefore,
even as he looks on, I shall put his army to flight.
Having put them to flight, I shall truly slay the wicked Pāñcālya;
I will kill all of them if they fight me in battle. I promise you this in truth: turn back the army!
Having heard that, your son rallied his army;
casting aside his great fear with a mighty lion-roar,
he joyfully caused kettledrums, hand-drums, and war-drums to be sounded.
They sounded thousands of *āḍambara*, *mṛdaṅga*, *jharjharī*, and *ānaka* drums, as well as *maḍḍuka*, *paṇava*, *vīṇā*, and *ḍiṇḍima* lutes;
and all those great archers blew their loud-sounding conchs.
Then the earth, struck by hooves and wheel-rims, resounded;
that tumultuous noise made both the sky and the earth reverberate.
Then, having heard that terrible sound which had arisen among the Kurus—
The Pāṇḍavas, together with the Somakas, were filled with wonder.
Having seen the Kurus, O King, uttering terrible roars,
they rushed forward with speed, making death their only point of return.
Then, O King, the encounter between the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies became once again fierce,
like that of two full oceans;
for the Kauravas, rallied by the son of Droṇa, stood firm.
The Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas were uplifted by the slaughter of Droṇa;
as they rejoiced greatly, perceiving victory within themselves,
a mighty surge of fury arose among those enraged warriors upon the field of battle.
O Indra among kings, just as a mountain cannot be obstructed by a mountain, nor the ocean by the ocean, so did the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas stand firm.
Then, thousands of conchs and tens of thousands of kettledrums [resounded].
The soldiers of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies played [their instruments] with great joy;
O noble one, the entire earth trembled and all the quarters resounded,
and even the creatures born in the water were thrown into agitation.
And all those warriors, eager for battle, were likewise filled with joy; while that fierce and terrifying clamor was thus prevailing,
O Bhārata, as the multitudes of chariots from both your side and theirs rushed forward.
Then, from that army being churned, there arose a sound like that of the ocean being agitated— a great roar, comparable to a marvel.
Thereupon, the son of Droṇa manifested the Nārāyaṇa weapon.
Aiming at the army of the Pāṇḍavas and the Pañcālas,
thousands of arrows with blazing tips then appeared in the sky,
like serpents with flaming mouths intent on devouring the Pāṇḍavas.

In that great battle, they enveloped the quarters, the sky, and the army; O King, in an instant, the sky was filled with those most terrifying birds of various forms, just as the rays of the sun pervade the world.
Likewise, O protector of the earth, other iron balls appeared, shining like luminaries in a cloudless sky; and in the four directions there were various *śataghnīs* that emitted fire.
Discuses with razor-sharp edges, like the orbs of the sun,
and nooses of various forms, as well as iron arrows and *añjalika* shafts,
were seen falling by the hundreds and thousands.

O King, O bull of the Bharatas, just as the world becomes overwhelmed at the terrible end of a yuga, so too did the vault of the sky then become filled with objects having the forms of weapons, appearing as if it were composed of light.
Seeing the sky [filled with weapons], the Pāṇḍus, Pañcālas, and Sṛñjayas were agitated.
O lord of men, in whatever manner the great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas fought,
in that very manner did that weapon increase.
Being thus slaughtered by that weapon of Nārāyaṇa,
the elephants fell there, struck down by the multitude of weapons,
like mountains being split asunder by thunderbolts in ancient times.
O lord of the people, the earth became strewn with severed elephant trunks, limbs,
and other arrows as well as spears blazing with gold;
it was turned into a mire of flesh and blood.
O Bhārata, as the drivers fell from their elephants—
mangled, shattered, and having cast aside their bows and armor—
the battlefield became filled like the city of the King of the Dead.
With discarded goads and costly javelins, with the ornaments of elephants, neck-chains, and their armor; with girth-straps,
fire-vessels, and mechanical engines adorned with banners.
O Great King, the ground was strewn with spears and straight-knotted arrows,
with the broken chariots of car-warriors,
with shattered yokes and poles, and with crushed wheels, broken yokes, and axles.
With discarded quivers and very costly bows,
with carriage-poles, banners, and yoking-thongs, O lord of the people, and with reins, goads, and small bells, O honorable one.
With radiant armor, as well as yak-tail fans,
with parasols resembling the moon that ward off rain and heat,
with finger-guards, bracelets, and shining golden neck-ornaments.
O Bhārata, with ear-ornaments, diadems, and costly crowns; with variegated garments, ornaments, and earrings;
and likewise with the severed heads and arms of the high-souled warriors that were cast away.
The earth shone here and there,
covered exactly as it was by variegated breastplates, by radiant networks of bells,
and by slain horses whose tongues were lolling out and which were drenched in blood.
And those warriors devoted to riding horses, scorched by the fiery energy of the weapons, fled in terror, deprived of various limbs and body parts;
O dear one, they cried out repeatedly, "Father! Father! and "Alas! Alas! My son!"
Surely those great car-warriors, the sons of Pāṇḍu, have met their end;
as have Vāsudeva of the Vṛṣṇi clan, along with the Somakas and Sṛñjayas.
For while those heroes were still alive in battle, the soldiers could not have fallen.
"By no means should they suddenly fall into this state!"—
thus spoke the warriors as they were being slaughtered in battle by the enraged son of Droṇa, who was like Time itself at the end of an eon.
Being thus struck by that weapon of Nārāyaṇa,
they were scorched as if by fire and oppressed from all sides in battle,
just as a fire might consume dry undergrowth at the end of the cold season.
O Lord, that weapon thus consumed the army of the Pāṇḍavas;
as the troops were being destroyed by the swelling weapon, O King,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, fell into a state of supreme terror.
Seeing that army fleeing and deprived of its senses,
and observing Pārtha’s state of neutrality, the son of Dharma spoke these words:
"Dhṛṣṭadyumna, flee together with the Pañcāla army!"
"O Sātyaki, you too go home, surrounded by the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas. The righteous-souled Vāsudeva will also do what is appropriate for himself;
he is capable of instructing the world, how much more so himself."
"You must not engage in battle; I tell you all this regarding the entire army.
For I, together with my uterine brothers, shall enter the consumer of oblations [the fire], having crossed the ocean of Bhīṣma and Droṇa—a battle difficult for the timid to traverse."
I shall dwell in the puddle of Droṇa’s cow-hoof print, along with my followers, even though it is devoid of water.
May this desire of Bībhatsu toward me be quickly fulfilled;
for the preceptor of virtuous conduct has been struck down by me in battle.
By him that foolish son of Subhadrā, unskilled in warfare,
was slain by many powerful and cruel men instead of being protected; and by him,
when asked a question, no answer was given as Draupadī entered the assembly hall.
Neglected by him along with his son, she was reduced to the state of a slave;
yet a great effort was made in battle to protect the Saindhava,
so that his vow might be preserved for the sake of thwarting Arjuna.
At the gate of the array, he by whom we, desiring victory, were held back,
has warded off that great army so that it entered according to its strength;
and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, wishing to slay Phalguna, [remained] while the horses were exhausted.
Likewise, equipped with armor for the sake of protecting the ruler of the Sindhus—
that knower of the Brahmā-missile by whom the Pañcālas, headed by Satyajit,
were struck down root and branch despite their efforts to submerge him— [he has been slain].
And he made the utmost effort to seize me,
so that all this was known by you, all you warriors;
for it was by him that we were unjustly exiled from our kingdom.

O great chariot-warriors, although we tried to dissuade him, he desired to follow them; and when they had returned from their forest exile and the appointed time had passed, he constantly demonstrated his affection before your very eyes.
"He who showed us the highest friendship,
though he has been slain for his sake, I shall go to death along with my kinsmen.
While the son of Kuntī was speaking thus, the descendant of Daśārha then acted with haste.
Restraining his army with his two arms, he spoke these words:
"Quickly lay down your weapons and dismount from your mounts;
this is the method ordained here as a countermeasure by the Great-souled One."
"Descend all of you from your elephants, horses, and chariots onto the ground;
for it is thus that this weapon will not slay you when you are unarmed upon the earth. But if you remain armed and continue to fight, it will certainly slay even these."

For in whatever manner the warriors fight against the power of their weapons, in that same manner these Kauravas become even more powerful. By Rāma, the entire earth was rendered devoid of the multitude of Kṣatriyas.
By this terrible weapon, the kṣatriya order was formerly annihilated;
that which is the splendor of Nārāyaṇa, the crusher of the power of other weapons— that weapon was fashioned of old by the powerful Viṣṇu.
When the great Asura Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa was struck down,
O best of kings, at the end of the Dvāpara age, Viṣṇu indeed discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon that had been previously created by him for the purpose of felling that great Daitya.
Formerly, the high-souled Rāma,
having performed austerities and propitiated Viṣṇu, the god of gods and lord of the three worlds,
obtained from him this [weapon] which wards off all other weapons; it has now been acquired by Droṇa.
For this great weapon cannot be warded off by anyone;
this is the method for warding off the Nārāyaṇa weapon, O King.
And those who, having descended from their vehicles, lay down their weapons—
This weapon will not slay those men in battle who, being free from wives, join their palms in reverence and bow down to you, O Hero; however,
it shall strike down any who would even mentally seek to fight against it here.
"He shall slay them all, even those who have gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
O Bhārata, having heard those words of Vāsudeva,
they all desired with their minds and through their efforts to discharge their weapons.
Then, O King, perceiving that they were about to discharge those weapons, Bhīmasena, the son of Pāṇḍu, spoke these words to inspire them:
"By no means whatsoever should weapons be released here by anyone."
I shall ward off the weapon of Droṇa’s son with my swift arrows;
or else, with this heavy mace of golden form,
I will move through the battle like Time itself, shattering the weapon of the son of Droṇa.
"For there is no man here who is equal to me in prowess,
just as no other light is found equal to the sun.
Behold my two firm arms, which resemble the trunks of the king of serpents."
The two of you are capable of toppling even Mount Śaiśira;
indeed, I alone among men here possess strength equal to ten thousand elephants,
just as Śakra is renowned as the peerless adversary among the gods in heaven.
Today behold my prowess in battle with these arms and broad shoulders, as I ward off the blazing, flaming weapon of the son of Droṇa,
should no opponent be found for the Nārāyaṇa-astra.
"Today I shall fight him while the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas look on! O Arjuna, Arjuna, Bībhatsu, you must not lay down the Gāṇḍīva!
Arjuna said:

Like a stain upon the moon, it will bring about your own defilement. O Bhīma, my Nārāyaṇa weapon is directed toward cows and Brāhmaṇas; against these, the Gāṇḍīva must be laid aside, for this is the highest vow.
Having spoken thus, Bhīma, the subduer of enemies, then advanced against the son of Droṇa on a chariot with the roar of a cloud and the splendor of the sun,
making the entire earth tremble and terrifying your army.
Having sounded his conch loudly and made a great noise with his arms, the Pāṇḍava—
upon hearing that sound of the conch and the sound of his arms— your men surrounded him on all sides like a walled enclosure and overwhelmed him with showers of arrows.
Terrified, they trembled and discharged excrement and urine.
With lightness of hand and swift prowess,
Kuntī’s son reached him in the mere twinkling of an eye and covered him with a net of arrows.
Then the son of Droṇa, laughing and addressing him with indifference,
covered him in battle with those consecrated arrows whose tips were ablaze,
like serpents with flaming mouths vomiting fire.
O King, the form of Bhīmasena in that battle became like a mountain covered with fireflies at the close of day, as Pārtha was strewn with golden sparks.
As that weapon of Droṇa’s son was being countered by him,
O great king, it increased in power like a fire fanned by the wind.
Beholding that weapon of terrible prowess thus growing in strength, [he acted].

A great fear entered the vast army of the Pāṇḍus, with the exception of Bhīma. Then, casting all their weapons upon the surface of the earth, they all descended from their chariots, elephants, and horses.
When they had cast aside their weapons and fallen from their mounts, he,
wheeling above them, wherever he beheld warriors who had seized their arms and mounted upon great vehicles, [he struck them down].
Wherever he advanced while taking his steps upon the field of battle, there those [weapons] were seen released in great multitudes. Then,
in the midst of the fray, he beheld Bhīma, the subduer of enemies, with mace in hand.
As the chariot of Droṇa’s son approached undaunted, that vast and terrible power of his weapon fell upon Bhīma’s head;
and all beings cried out "Alas! Alas!", especially the Pāṇḍavas.
Then they beheld Bhīmasena enveloped in splendor.
Sañjaya said:
Seeing Bhīmasena overwhelmed by the weapon, Dhanañjaya—
To counteract that radiance, he enveloped it with the Vāruṇa weapon;
no one perceived him, as he was concealed by the Vāruṇa missile,
due both to Arjuna’s swiftness and the shrouding of his splendor.
Accompanied by his horses, charioteer, and chariot, Bhīma, enveloped by the weapon of Droṇa’s son,
was as difficult to behold as a fire placed within another fire, wreathed in flames;
O King, like the celestial bodies at the end of the night as they head toward the mountain of setting.
In that manner, arrows fell upon Bhīmasena’s chariot;
yet that Vāruṇa weapon, consecrated and originating from Nārāyaṇa,
blazed up once more, enveloping Bhīma on the field of battle.
O noble one, Bhīma, his chariot, his horses,
and his charioteer were all enveloped by the son of Droṇa and entered into the fire,
just as at the end of time the fire consumes the entire world with all its moving and unmoving beings.
The fire would enter the mouth of the All-pervading Lord, and likewise the terrible weapon enveloped it;
just as fire might enter the sun,
or the sun the fire, so that once that splendor had entered, nothing at all could be discerned.
That weapon retreated again and again from Bhīma’s *huṃkāra*, yet it returned to him again and again; at his *huṃkāra*, he released it once more.
Then the gods, along with the *gandharvas*, were utterly amazed upon seeing Bhīma.
Seeing that weapon thus scattered toward Bhīmaratha, and seeing the son of Droṇa prevailing in battle without any rival,
all the Pandava troops became senseless and laid down their weapons.

Then Arjuna and Vāsudeva, those two heroes of great splendor, acting with haste, leaped down from their chariot and rushed toward Bhīma and those great car-warriors who, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, had turned their backs in retreat.

Then, having plunged into that energy of Droṇa’s son, which was born from the power of his weapons, those two exceedingly strong warriors entered it by means of their *māyā*. Consequently, the fire produced by the weapon did not burn them, for they had laid down their weapons.
Due to the employment of the Vāruṇa weapon and because of the prowess of the two Kṛṣṇas,
Nara and Nārāyaṇa then forcibly dragged Bhīma and all his weapons away for the sake of neutralizing the Nārāyaṇa weapon.
Having deprived Bhīma of his weapons, Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya then forcibly struck Bhīmasena down again in battle;
even as he was being dragged away, that great car-warrior, the son of Kuntī, continued to roar aloud.
And that terrible weapon of the son of Droṇa, so difficult to conquer, continued to increase in power.
Vāsudeva said to him: "What is this, O son of Pāṇḍu?
Why, O Kaunteya, do you not desist from battle even though you are being restrained?"
"If these delights of the Kauravas were to be conquered in battle,
we too would fight here, as would these bulls among men;
yet all those on your side have indeed descended from their chariots."
"Therefore, O son of Kuntī, descend quickly from the chariot.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa then threw him down from the chariot onto the ground—
he who was sighing like a serpent, his eyes bloodshot with rage.
When he had been drawn away from the chariot and made to lay down his weapons upon the ground,
then that Nārāyaṇa weapon, the scorcher of enemies, was pacified. When that unbearable splendor had been thus neutralized by the prescribed ritual, [the battle ceased].
All the cardinal and intermediate directions became stainless;
auspicious winds blew, and the beasts and birds grew calm.
O lord of men, the mounts and the warriors were filled with joy.
And when that terrible radiance had been dispelled, O Bhārata,
the wise Bhīma shone forth like the risen sun at the end of the night; there,
the remaining force of the Pāṇḍavas stood firm.
When that army had stood firm, boldly desiring to slay your son,
and when the weapon had thus been neutralized,
O great king, Duryodhana then spoke to the son of Droṇa.
"Aśvatthāman, quickly employ this weapon once more!
For the Pāñcālas have rallied again, seeking victory.
Thus addressed by your son, O noble one, Aśvatthāman—
Sighing deeply and most dejectedly, he said this to the king:
"O King, this weapon does not return; it cannot be employed a second time.
If one attempts to bring it back, there is no doubt that it will slay the user."
And Vāsudeva has employed this counter-weapon;
for he alone among men knows this weapon, and there is none else to be found. He knows both the higher and the lower of all worlds; there is nothing that he does not know.
"O lord of men, this weapon has been neutralized by Kṛṣṇa’s counsel;
otherwise, the death of the enemy in battle would have been ordained,
or his defeat, for death is better than victory."
"For these enemies have been conquered; by laying down their weapons, they are as good as dead.
Duryodhana said:
"O son of the preceptor, if this weapon is not used twice..."
"O best among those skilled in weapons, let the slayers of their preceptors be slain by others with various missiles;
for just as the divine weapons abide in Tryambaka, so do they abide in you. Indeed, were you to desire it, even Purandara himself could not escape you when you are enraged."
"O you of great prowess, skilled in battle, slay these enemies!
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When that weapon had been neutralized and Droṇa had been slain through deceit..."
Thus addressed by Duryodhana, what did the son of Droṇa do next,
having seen the sons of Pṛthā stationed for battle in the fray,
discharging the Nārāyaṇa weapon as they moved at the head of the army?
Saṃjaya said:
Knowing of his father’s death, he whose banner bears the lion’s tail,
casting aside fear, rushed in anger toward the son of Pṛṣata.
Having rushed forward, that bull among men pierced the bull among men with twenty small arrows and, with great speed, struck him again with five;
then, O King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna [assailed] him who was like a blazing fire.
Seeing him, who resembled the fire of time or Yama, extremely enraged as he drew his bow with the strength of his own arms and swiftly releasing arrows,
the son of Pṛṣata rushed toward him in battle.
Then the son of Droṇa, his eyes copper-red with rage as if wishing to consume them with his splendor,
covered Dhṛṣṭadyumna on all sides with a flood of arrows;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, however, being greatly agitated, [struck back] with a straight-knotted shaft.
Enraged, he [Dhrishtadyumna] exerted himself with force and pierced the son of Pṛṣata;
then the son of Droṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, having cut his bow with a thick shaft,
roared and struck Dhrishtadyumna with seventy-three sharpened arrows.
Casting aside that broken bow, the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna took up another bow and struck Aśvatthāman;
enraged, the latter, who was a master of supreme weapons, cut that one down as well.
And that scorcher of foes covered Dhṛṣṭadyumna with arrows as well. Then the son of Pṛṣata, filled with supreme rage, swiftly hurled a gold-adorned spear that blazed like a thunderbolt.
O King, as it was falling suddenly upon him like a female serpent in battle,
he cut it into seven pieces with arrows of supreme sharpness.
Then, seeing that [weapon] severed by the son of Droṇa, the son of Pṛṣata...
Taking up another bow that was even more powerful in battle,
he then pierced the son of Droṇa with two very sharp arrows in the fray;
thereafter, he struck his bow there with two very sharp broad-headed shafts.
The son of Droṇa, as if laughing, cut down [the bow] of Drupada’s son;
then that one of great splendor again covered him with other arrows,
quickly shrouding him along with his horses, charioteer, and chariot in the battle.
Enraged, he put to flight all of his followers who stood at his side with blazing weapons, using straight-jointed arrows; then,
he discharged the Brahmā weapon with the intent to slay Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
The son of Droṇa hurled it [at Sātyaki], but Sātyaki cut it in two. Then Sātyaki, taking up eight sharpened arrows, struck Aśvatthāman— the prince who had been afflicted by shafts.
Striking again with eighty various kinds of shafts, the impatient one pierced his charioteer with three and his four horses with four;
having spoken thus, he quickly covered Sātyaki with sharp arrows.
Then the powerful son of Droṇa, enraged and with eyes copper-red from fury,
was struck by the furious Sātyaki with a straight-knotted arrow while the entire army looked on.

Then, O great king, the son of Droṇa, his soul overwhelmed with rage and skilled in great weapons, covered Sātyaki with arrows and swiftly cut his bow asunder. Thereafter, he [hurled] a most terrible spear, made of iron with a golden shaft.
Satyaki swiftly hurled it, desiring to slay the son of Droṇa.
As it came rushing suddenly like a thunderbolt released by Śakra,
the son of Droṇa cut it down with seven swift arrows even before it had reached him.

Seeing her severely mangled by the arrows of the son of Droṇa, Satyaki, the best of the Sātvatas, took up another bow capable of bearing a great burden and even more powerful; drawing that mighty bow, he— [The remainder of the verse continues: ...struck him with a volley of arrows. His horses were slain, his charioteer was killed, and his standard was struck down; deprived of his chariot, he quickly ascended the chariot of Kṛtavarman. Then, O King, the son of Droṇa, having vanquished Satyaki in battle, ascended his own chariot and pursued the Pāñcālas. He slaughtered them with his sharp arrows, like a lion slaughtering small deer. Having routed those armies, the son of Droṇa shone resplendent, like the sun at the end of the age. Then, O King, the Pāñcālas and the Somakas, seeing the son of Droṇa prevailing, surrounded him on all sides with a great shower of arrows. Enveloped by that great cloud of arrows, the son of Droṇa became invisible, like the sun covered by clouds. But he, too, released a great net of arrows, and that mass of shafts shrouded all the directions. Then, O King, a tumultuous sound arose from the clashing of weapons, as they struck one another in that great battle. There, the son of Droṇa pierced Dhr̥ṣṭadyumna with twelve arrows, Virāṭa with nine, Drupada with seven, and the two Pāñcāla princes, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, with three arrows each. Having pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with sixty-four arrows and Bhīmasena with seventy, he deprived Nakula and Sahadeva of their chariots with three arrows each. Then, O King, the son of Droṇa, having overwhelmed all the Pāñcālas and Somakas in battle, stood alone like a blazing fire without smoke. Thus did the son of Droṇa prevail over the Pāñcālas in that encounter, while the Pāñcālas and the Somakas, though striving, could not withstand the son of Droṇa in battle. Then, O King, the son of Droṇa, having vanquished the Pāñcālas and Somakas in combat, ascended his own chariot and pursued the army of the Pāṇḍavas. He slaughtered them with his sharp arrows, like a lion slaughtering small deer. Having routed those armies, the son of Droṇa shone resplendent, like the sun at the end of the age. Then, O King, the Pāñcālas and the Somakas, seeing the son of Droṇa prevailing, surrounded him on all sides with a great shower of arrows. Enveloped by that great cloud of arrows, the son of Droṇa became invisible, like the sun covered by clouds. But he, too, released a great net of arrows, and that mass of shafts shrouded all the directions. Then, O King, a tumultuous sound arose from the clashing of weapons, as they struck one another in that great battle. There, the son of Droṇa pierced Dhr̥ṣṭadyumna with twelve arrows, Virāṭa with nine, Drupada with seven, and the two Pāñcāla princes, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, with three arrows each. Having pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with sixty-four arrows and Bhīmasena with seventy, he deprived Nakula and Sahadeva of their chariots with three arrows each. Then, O King, the son of Droṇa, having overwhelmed all the Pāñcālas and Somakas in battle, stood alone like a blazing fire without smoke. Thus did the son of Droṇa prevail over the Pāñcālas in that encounter, while the Pāñcālas and the Somakas, though striving, could not withstand the son of Droṇa in battle. Then, O King, the son of Droṇa, having vanquished the Pāñcālas and Somakas in combat, ascended his own chariot and pursued the army of the Pāṇḍavas. He slaughtered them with his sharp arrows, like a lion slaughtering small deer. Having routed those armies, the
With many arrows, he quickly struck Aśvatthāman;
then the son of Droṇa, highly incensed and overwhelmed with rage, covered Mādhava Satyaki in that battle with a net of shafts.
O lord of the people, before those nets of arrows could reach him in the sky, the great car-warrior Yuyudhāna cut them down.
Then, with gold-feathered shafts whetted on stone and released from a fully drawn bow, he struck.
Enraged, he pierced the son of Droṇa very deeply with arrows. Thus severely wounded, the son of Droṇa, who was exceedingly intolerant,
became furious in battle and seemed to consume the descendant of Śini with his eyes.
The one of immeasurable soul covered him from all sides with showers of arrows,
like a rain-cloud at the end of the summer heat drenching a mountain with torrents of water;
then, O King, he pierced the son of Droṇa with sixty-three feathered shafts.
With twenty gold-feathered arrows sharpened on stone, he pierced his charioteer;
then, with four sharp shafts, he struck the four horses.
Piercing them again and again, the son of Droṇa let out a roar, as if making the very earth tremble.
He was taking away the lives of all the world, as if in a great battle; but the mighty son of Pṛṣata, O King, skilled in weapons and well-trained,
rushed toward the son of Droṇa alone, making death his only point of retreat.

Then the Pāñcālya, the best of chariot-warriors and one of immeasurable soul, released a rain of arrows upon the head of Droṇa’s son. Enraged in that battle, the son of Droṇa covered him with feathered shafts.
Remembering the slaughter of his father, he pierced him with ten arrows; then,
having severed the Pāñcāla king’s standard and bow with two well-drawn razor-headed shafts, the son of Droṇa struck him with others.
In that great battle, the son of Droṇa deprived him of his horses, charioteer, and chariot;
and filled with rage, he covered all of his followers with arrows.
Then, O lord of the people, the army of the Pañcālas fled away.
Seeing them in a state of confusion and distress, mangled by a shower of arrows,
and seeing the warriors turned away from battle and Dhṛṣṭadyumna afflicted,
the grandson of Śini quickly urged his chariot toward the chariot of Droṇa’s son in the fray.
With eight sharpened shafts he struck Aśvatthāman; then,
having struck the indignant warrior again with twenty arrows of various forms,
he pierced his charioteer and his four horses with four more.
With great dexterity, he severed the bow and the standard of his opponent as they stood ready for battle; he then destroyed the gold-adorned chariot along with its horses,
and deeply pierced him in the heart in that combat with thirty arrows.
Thus afflicted, O King, the mighty Aśvatthāman,
surrounded by nets of arrows, did not know what ought to be done.
When his preceptor’s son was in such a state, your son, the great car-warrior—
Together with Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the others, he covered the Sātvata hero with arrows; Duryodhana struck him with twenty, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, with three,
Kṛtavarman with ten, and Karṇa with fifty shafts.
Duḥśāsana pierced Sātyaki with a hundred arrows, and Vṛṣasena with seven; they quickly struck him from all sides with sharpened shafts.
Then, O King, Sātyaki [assailed] all those great car-warriors.
In an instant, O King, he rendered them chariotless and turned them away from the fight.
But Aśvatthāman, O bull of the Bharatas, having regained consciousness,
was afflicted with grief and sighed again and again as he reflected.
Then the son of Droṇa, that scorcher of foes, mounting another chariot,
checked Sātyaki while scattering many hundreds of arrows.
Beholding the son of Bharadvāja’s son rushing toward him in battle, [Sātyaki]—

The great car-warrior once again deprived him of his chariot and turned him away from the fight. Then, O King, seeing the prowess of Sātyaki, those Pāṇḍavas sounded their conchs loudly and uttered lion-like roars.
Having thus deprived him of his chariot, Sātyaki, whose valor is truth,
slew three thousand great car-warriors of Vṛṣasena and killed ten thousand elephants along with those of Kṛpa.
And Śakuni slew fifty thousand horses.
Then, O great king, the valiant son of Droṇa, having mounted his chariot,
advanced in a rage against Sātyaki, desiring to slay him.

Seeing him returned once more, Śaineya, the tamer of foes, pierced him repeatedly with sharp and most cruel arrows. Deeply pierced by those shafts of various descriptions, that great archer became filled with indignation.
Yuyudhāna, laughing, spoke these words to the son of Droṇa:
"I know your partiality for the grandson of Śini, you who have slain your own teacher; yet you shall not protect him, nor even yourself, once you are seized by me."
O descendant of Śini, I swear by myself, by truth, and likewise by my ascetic merit (tapas),
that I shall not attain peace until I have slain all the Pāñcālas—
whatever strength belongs to the sons of Pāṇḍu and whatever strength belongs to the Vṛṣṇis.
"Let everything here be prepared; I shall slay the Somakas.
Having spoken thus, the son of Droṇa discharged that best of arrows, well-jointed and radiant as the rays of the sun, at the Sātvata, just as Hari hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra.

That arrow, discharged by him, pierced through his armor and entered the earth, having split it like a hissing serpent entering its hole. With his armor shattered, that hero was like an elephant tormented by a goad.
Casting aside his bow and arrow, with copious blood flowing from his many wounds, sinking and drenched in gore, he sat down upon the floor of his chariot; then,
quickly removed by his charioteer to another chariot away from the son of Droṇa.
Then, with another well-feathered arrow of curved joints,
that scorcher of foes struck Dhṛṣṭadyumna between the eyebrows.
Having already been deeply pierced before, he was now further tormented.

The Pāñcālya sat down in battle and leaned against his flagpole. O King, five heroic chariot-warriors from the side of the Pāṇḍavas rushed with speed toward him, who was being tormented like an intoxicated elephant by a lion.
Kiritin, Bhimasena, Vriddhakshatra the Paurava,
the crown prince of the Chedis, and Sudarshana the Malava—
all of them raised a cry of "Alas! while grasping their bows.
The heroes surrounded the heroic son of Droṇa on all sides;
exerting themselves at a distance of twenty paces, they simultaneously struck the indignant son of the preceptor from every side with five arrows each.
With twenty-five arrows— five of which were as terrifying as venomous serpents— the son of Droṇa simultaneously cut down those [twenty] shafts. Then,
with seven sharp arrows, the son of Droṇa struck Paurava.
With three arrows he struck Mālava, with one Pārtha, and with six Vṛkodara;
then, O King, all those great car-warriors pierced the son of Droṇa simultaneously and individually with gold-feathered shafts whetted on stone.
The crown prince, however, pierced the son of Droṇa with twenty feathered shafts;
then the son of Droṇa afflicted all of them simultaneously,
while Pārtha struck him again with eight, and likewise all the others with three each.
Then the son of Droṇa struck Arjuna with six arrows, Vāsudeva with ten,
Bhīma with five, and the crown prince with four.
Having cut down both the bow and the standard with two arrows,
he pierced both the Mālava and the Paurava with two each,
and struck Bhīmasena’s charioteer with six arrows.
Having again pierced Pārtha with a shower of arrows,
the son of Droṇa let out a terrible lion’s roar as he discharged those well-sharpened, yellow-edged shafts.
The earth, the atmosphere, the sky, the intermediate directions, and the cardinal points were all covered by the terrible arrows of the son of Droṇa, both behind and before him.
To Sudarśana, who was seated upon his own chariot,
he of fierce splendor gave arms that shone like the banner of Indra, and a head possessed of prowess equal to that of Indra.
With three arrows he simultaneously cut [him down],
having struck Paurava with a chariot-spear and shattered his chariot into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his shafts.
Having severed his arms, which were smeared with excellent sandalwood paste,
he cut off the head from the body with a broad-headed arrow—
the youth who was the color of a garland of blue lotuses.
Laughing, he swiftly pierced the beloved Cedi prince with arrows like blazing fire and delivered him, along with his horses and charioteer, unto death.
Seeing Mālava, Paurava, and the crown prince of Cedi slain right before his eyes by the son of Droṇa,
the mighty-armed Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena gave way to supreme rage.
Then, with hundreds of sharp arrows resembling enraged venomous serpents,
that scorcher of foes covered the son of Droṇa in battle. Thereupon, the highly energetic son of Droṇa destroyed that shower of arrows.
The indignant one pierced Bhīmasena with sharpened arrows.
Then the mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful Bhīma, having severed the bow of the son of Droṇa in battle with a razor-headed shaft, pierced the son of Droṇa with a feathered arrow.

Casting aside that severed bow, the high-minded son of Droṇa took up another formidable bow and pierced him with feathered shafts. Those two, the son of Droṇa and Bhīma, were both of great strength and displayed their prowess in the encounter.
Like two rain-bearing clouds, they rained down a shower of arrows;
arrows marked with the name Bhīma, gold-feathered and whetted on stone,
completely covered the son of Droṇa, just as masses of clouds shroud the sun.
In that very same way, Bhīma was quickly overwhelmed by hundreds of thousands of straight-jointed arrows released by the son of Droṇa;
he was being shrouded in battle by the son of Droṇa, who was pre-eminent in combat.
O great king, he did not waver; it was like a marvel.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma dispatched ten sharp iron arrows, adorned with gold and resembling the staff of Yama.

O venerable one, having reached the region of the collarbone of Droṇa’s son, they quickly pierced through and entered it like snakes into an anthill. Thus deeply pierced by the high-souled Pāṇḍava, the son of Droṇa was severely wounded.
Leaning against the flagpole, he closed his eyes.
After a moment, O lord of men, the son of Droṇa regained consciousness and,
drenched in blood, fell into a state of supreme rage upon the battlefield.
Struck firmly by that high-souled Pāṇḍava,
the mighty-armed one exerted his force toward Bhīmasena’s chariot;
then [he loosed] arrows of fierce brilliance drawn back to the ear.
O Bhārata, he dispatched a hundred snakes resembling venomous serpents;
yet Bhīma, who delights in battle, disregarded their prowess,
and the Pāṇḍava swiftly loosed fierce showers of arrows.
Then, O great king, the son of Droṇa, having severed his bow with his arrows,
angrily struck the Pāṇḍava in the chest with sharpened shafts. Thereupon, the highly indignant Bhīmasena took up another bow.
In that battle, he pierced the son of Droṇa with five sharpened arrows;
like two clouds at the end of the summer heat, those two, raining down floods of shafts,
covered one another in combat, their eyes copper-red with mutual rage.
Then, terrifying one another with terrible sounds of their palms, they fought on, highly enraged and seeking to counter each other's blows. Then, having drawn his massive bow adorned with gold, he—
The son of Droṇa gazed upon Bhīma from close at hand as he discharged arrows,
like the sun with blazing rays situated in the midday sky during autumn,
as he was taking up and fixing his swift-flying shafts.

O Great King, as the son of Droṇa discharged his arrows at that time, the people could perceive no interval between his drawing back and his releasing; his weapon appeared like a whirling circle of fire.
Then, arrows released from his bow by the hundreds and thousands appeared in the sky like swarms of locusts.
Those gold-adorned shafts, loosed from the bow of Droṇa’s son, [fell upon the enemy].
Terrible [arrows] were incessantly showered upon Bhīmaratha;
there we beheld the wonderful prowess, strength, heroism, majesty, and resolve of Bhīmasena, O Bhārata.
Bhima of terrible prowess, desiring the slaughter of Drona’s son, regarded that shower of arrows rising up from all sides like a most dreadful downpour of water at the end of the summer heat.
Like a cloud in the rainy season, he released showers of arrows;
that great and terrible bow of Bhīma, with its golden back,
shone in battle as it was drawn like a second bow of Indra.
From that [bow], arrows appeared by the hundreds and thousands,
covering the son of Droṇa, who graces the battlefield, in that encounter.
O noble one, as the two of them were thus discharging nets of arrows...
O King, even the wind was unable to pass through the space between them;
likewise, O great king, the son of Droṇa discharged arrows adorned with gold,
cleansed with oil, and with bright points, out of a desire for slaughter.
In the sky, he severed each of those [arrows] into three pieces with his shafts;
distinguishing himself from the son of Droṇa, he cried out, "Stay! Stay!
And once again, the Pāṇḍava unleashed terrible and fierce showers of arrows.
The powerful one, enraged and desiring the slaughter of Droṇa’s son, released [the weapon]. Then, having quickly warded off that shower of arrows by means of the illusion of his own weapons,
the son of Droṇa, who was skilled in great weapons, cut Bhīma’s bow asunder.
Enraged in battle, he pierced him with a great many arrows;
his bow being severed, the powerful warrior whirled a most dreadful chariot-spear with force and hurled it toward the chariot of Droṇa’s son.
As it was falling suddenly like a great meteor,
the son of Droṇa, displaying his lightness of hand, cut it apart in battle with sharp arrows.
In that interval, Bhīma firmly grasped his bow.
Smiling, Vṛkodara pierced the son of Droṇa with sharp arrows.
Then, O great king, the son of Droṇa tore the forehead of Bhīmasena’s charioteer with a straight-knotted shaft.
O King, deeply pierced by the powerful son of Droṇa, that charioteer fell into a state of confusion and let go of the horses' reins. Then,
while the charioteer was thus bewildered, the horses fled away with great speed.
O king of kings, while all the archers looked on, Bhīmasena [was carried away];
seeing him drawn away from the field of battle by his fleeing horses,
the heroic son of Droṇa, a lord of warriors, slew them in combat.
The undefeated one, filled with joy, blew his great conch shell.
Then all the Pāñcālas and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava [responded].
But then all the Pāñcālas, afflicted by the arrows of Droṇa’s son, [fled].
Terrified, they abandoned Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s chariot and fled in all directions.
As they were thus broken, the son of Droṇa pursued them from behind, scattering arrows after them,
and rushed with great speed against the Pāṇḍava host like Time itself.
Being slaughtered in battle by the son of Droṇa, those kṣatriyas,
O King, perceived the son of Droṇa in every direction out of fear.
Saṃjaya said:
Seeing those heroes fleeing, the unconquered Bībhatsu,
accompanied by the Matsyas and the Somakas, pursued them.
Then, seeing that army broken, Kuntī’s son Dhanañjaya [advanced].
The one of immeasurable soul restrained him, desiring the slaughter of Droṇa’s son.
Then those soldiers, O King, did not remain there at all,
even though they were being steadied with effort by Govinda and Arjuna.
But Bībhatsu alone, having made an alliance with the Somakas,
the Matsyas, and others, turned back against the Kauravas.
Then, quickly bypassing him whose banner bore the lion’s tail, [he advanced].
Savyasācin spoke to the great archer Aśvatthāman:
"Whatever power you possess, whatever heroism, whatever knowledge, and whatever manliness;
whatever affection you have for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and whatever hatred you bear toward us."
"Show me that supreme splendor which you possess further;
that very son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of Droṇa, shall shatter your pride—
he who resembles the fire of cosmic destruction and is the end-maker of his enemies in battle."
"Encounter the Pāñcālya and me as well, along with Keśava;
today in battle I shall destroy the pride of you who are so arrogant.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Sañjaya, the son of the preceptor is worthy of honor and is also powerful;
he feels affection for Dhanañjaya, and he is dear to the son of Vāsava as well. Never before has such harsh speech been uttered by Bībhatsu.
07.172.008c Then why did that son of Kuntī speak so harshly to his friend?
07.172.009 Sañjaya said:
07.172.009a When the crown prince had been slain, as well as Vṛddhakṣatra of the Paurava line, [he spoke thus].

When Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Sātyaki, and Bhīma— though accomplished in the science of archery and skilled in the Mālava weapon— had been defeated, and when Yudhiṣṭhira’s very vitals were struck by those words;
When internal dissension had arisen and he recollected his suffering, O Lord,
an unprecedented wrath born of grief arose within Bibhatsu;
therefore, he spoke words that were unworthy, vulgar, and unpleasant to the son of Droṇa.
Like a coward toward a venerable son of a preceptor,
he spoke thus harshly. O King, having been addressed with such cruel words by Pārtha in a voice that struck at all his vital parts, that greatest of great archers breathed heavily in rage.
The son of Droṇa was enraged at Pārtha, and especially at Kṛṣṇa.
Standing firm on his chariot, that heroic warrior, having sipped water for purification,
took up the Agneya weapon, which is exceedingly difficult even for the gods to withstand.

Aiming at hosts of enemies, both visible and invisible, that delighter of his preceptor, the slayer of hostile heroes, consecrated with mantras a blazing arrow like a smokeless fire; then, pervaded by wrath on all sides, he discharged it.
Then a tumultuous shower of arrows arose in the sky; enveloped by the flames of fire, it fell directly upon Pārtha. Meteors fell from the heavens, and the quarters of the sky did not shine.
And suddenly a fierce darkness descended upon that army;
Rākṣasas and Piśācas gathered together and shrieked aloud;
cold winds blew, and the sun did not shine at all.
The Dānavas also shrieked terribly in all directions;
raining down blood, the clouds thundered in the sky. Birds, beasts, cows, and even the sages of firm vows [were likewise distressed].
Though they were supremely self-restrained, they found no peace;
for the three worlds were tormented, with all its great elements in turmoil and the sun eclipsed, like a patient seized by a fever.
Scorched by the heat of Śara’s splendor, the serpents dwelling in the earth hissed and sprang up, seeking to cast off that terrible heat;
and the water-dwelling creatures, O Bhārata, were likewise consumed by the flames.
Indeed, peace was not found as the reservoirs of water were being scorched;
showers of arrows, swift as Garuḍa and the wind, fell upon the quarters, the sky, the intermediate directions, and the earth in great variety.
By those arrows of the son of Droṇa, discharged with the speed of a thunderbolt,
the enemies were consumed and fell like trees burnt by fire.
"Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna have been slain today by the illusory power of the son of Droṇa."
"O sinless one, such was the opinion of all the snake-charmers at that time;
scorched by the fire, the great serpents fell upon the earth on every side."
Uttering terrifying cries with sounds like the rumbling of clouds,
other great elephants fled there, being scorched;
likewise, others trembled in that dreadful forest, enveloped by the forest fire.
O noble one, the hosts of horses and the throngs of chariots appeared like the tops of trees consumed by a forest fire;
and thousands of multitudes of chariots fell here and there, O lord.
O Bhārata, the blessed Agni consumed that army in battle,
like the Saṃvartaka fire consuming all beings at the end of a Yuga.
Having seen the Pāṇḍava host being consumed in that great conflict, [he acted].

O King, your men, filled with joy, let out lion-like roars. Then, O Bhārata, thousands of musical instruments of various kinds were quickly struck by your joyful warriors, who appeared radiant in their victory.
Then, O Bhārata, while the Pandava army raised a cry of "Alas!
Alas!", multitudes of chariots and millions of horses were being consumed by fire;
likewise, vast throngs of horses and no small number of foot-soldiers perished.
For the sake of increasing the strength of the preceptor’s son, the army became a single mass of flame,
with banners covered in garments and ornaments that raised up like blazing fires.
And as men ran about like fires embodied,
not a single one among the Pandava forces could be seen who was not being consumed by them.
And seeing the son of Drona thus exalted, Partha, the scorcher of foes, [advanced].
Having consecrated the Gāṇḍīva bow,
its string, and his arrows with mantras, that one of great strength swiftly discharged the divine Brahmā weapon, which is peerless among all created things.

O King, the entire Akṣauhiṇī army and Savyasācin the Pāṇḍava could not be seen in that great battle when the world was shrouded in darkness. O King, neither had we ever seen nor heard of anything like it before.
O great king,
Arjuna then invoked the Brahma weapon,
which had been ordained by the Lotus-born One to counteract all other weapons, against that weapon which the indignant son of Droṇa had discharged.
Then, as if in a mere moment, that darkness subsided;
a cool breeze blew and the quarters of the sky became clear.
There we beheld a marvel: the entire akṣauhiṇī army had been slain.
Their forms having become invisible and consumed by the illusion of the weapon,
the two heroes, the great archers Keśava and Arjuna,
were then seen together, like two suns dispelling the darkness in the sky.

Then both the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow and Keśava, remaining unhurt, shone forth on that chariot— which was equipped with banners, standards, and horses, and possessed excellent mechanical fittings and weapons— as it emerged, striking terror into your troops.
Then, in an instant, a tumultuous roar of joy arose among the delighted Pāṇḍavas, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and kettledrums;
for all their own soldiers, seeing the Pāṇḍavas filled with joy, likewise rejoiced.
But the Kauravas, led by Duryodhana, were deeply distressed when they saw the son of Droṇa—
that great archer, the peerless Pārtha in battle—
his mind intent on combat and invincible even by the gods.
Seeing him covering all directions on every side with nets of arrows released from the *gāṇḍīva*, resembling venomous serpents,
and appearing as difficult to behold as the sun while consuming his enemies in battle;
"Both armies thought that Keśava and Arjuna had been slain; but seeing them return with speed and unharmed, they were released and,
filled with joy, both blew their excellent conchs."
Seeing the Pārthas so delighted, your men became distressed;
and seeing the two high-souled ones liberated, the son of Droṇa was deeply pained and reflected for a moment, "What is this? O venerable one.
Having reflected thus, O king of kings, he became absorbed in meditation and grief;
sighing long and hot breaths, he then became despondent.
Thereupon, the son of Droṇa, laying aside his bow, leaped down from his chariot with great speed.
"Shame, shame! All this is false!"—having said this, he fled from the battle.
Then he beheld Vyāsa, who resembled a cloud charged with rain, who was stainless, and who was the very abode of Sarasvatī.
Seeing him standing before him, O scion of the Kuru lineage, the son of Droṇa saluted him with great humility and, his voice choked with emotion, spoke these words:
"O sir! Is this an illusion or a mere chance occurrence? We do not know what this might be."
I ask you, my father, about this doubt; please explain it to me:
how has this weapon been rendered futile, and what transgression have I committed?
Is this a reversal of the natural order, or is it the destruction of the worlds?
Since these two Kṛṣṇas still live, time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Neither Asuras, nor gods, nor Gandharvas; neither Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas;
neither serpents, Yakṣas, nor birds; nor humans in any way whatsoever [can prevail].
They are unable to alter this weapon discharged by me;
having struck down this entire Akṣauhiṇī army, this blazing,
all-destroying, and most terrible weapon released by me shall prevail.
"Why did you not slay these two, Keśava and Arjuna, who possess the nature of mortals?
Tell me this, O Blessed One,
as it truly happened, for I wish to hear all of this in its true essence, O Great Sage."
Saṃjaya said:
Then Vyāsa arrived, having seen that the weapon had been invoked. Having honored him upon his arrival, the son of Droṇa questioned him regarding his doubt.
"By what means were Keśava and Arjuna released, since they were not consumed by that great weapon? Tell me that in truth.
Vyāsa said:
This great matter about which you ask me out of wonder—I shall explain it all to you; listen with a concentrated mind. He who is named Nārāyaṇa was the progenitor even of the ancients.
The primordial god, the Lord of the world, the self-existent master and creator of the universe;
the first of all the world, without beginning or end, the infallible one—
whose true nature the Vedas and the sages indeed expound.

Therefore, the Lord of the World cannot be conquered by any beings even with the mind. Hence, O tiger among men, do not grieve for Arjuna here, who is enveloped in the darkness of ignorance and desires to conquer him.
That power of his is Pārtha; therefore, abandon this grief.
For he is the Lord of All, the Origin of the Worlds, the Supreme Self, the Unseen One (Adhokṣaja);
from a single portion of his thousandfold measure, this [Arjuna] was born.

O best of beings, for the sake of the welfare of the gods and the worlds, the all-creating son of Dharma was born to accomplish a specific purpose. Having taken his stand upon Mount Maināka, he applied himself to intense austerity.
With arms raised high, the one of great splendor, resembling a blazing sun,
the lotus-eyed one withered his own body for sixty thousand years and as many hundreds more, subsisting only on air.
Then, having performed another great penance twice as vast as the previous one,
he filled the space between heaven and earth with his splendor.
By that asceticism, my dear, he became one with Brahman.
Then he beheld the Lord of All, the source of the entire world, the Sovereign who is exceedingly difficult even for all the gods to perceive;
subtler than the subtlest and greater than the greatest.
Meditating deeply, he sang praises to Mahādeva, the most exalted;
to Rudra, the Lord, the Bull, the all-knowing, the unborn, the supreme;
to Hara, Śambhu, the one with matted hair.
Whether he is moving or standing still, he dwells in the hearts of all beings—
the one who is difficult to restrain, difficult to behold, possessed of fierce wrath,
the Great-Souled One, the destroyer of all, the wise one.
Holding a celestial bow and two quivers,
clad in golden armor, he was of infinite prowess—
difficult to restrain, exceedingly hard to overcome, difficult to behold, and unassailable.
[He beheld] that high-souled one, who transcends all pride, who is wise regarding all beings, the god of gods, the supreme atom, the one worthy of praise,
as he was taking up two divine quivers in the battle.
The wielder of the Pināka bow and the thunderbolt, with his blazing trident, holding an axe and a mace, bearing a long sword,
fair-browed, with a mass of matted hair and the moon upon his crest.
Wearing a tiger skin, holding a club and a staff in his hand,
adorned with beautiful armlets and a serpent as a sacred thread, he was graced by all the hosts of spirits and multitudes of beings.
A single mass, a treasury of ascetic powers,
highly praised by those who have transcended age with eloquent words—
[he who is] water, heaven, space, earth, the moon, and the sun.
Likewise, the wind, the fire, the world,
and those of divided conduct are not able to behold him who was born from the Unborn,
the slayer of the enemies of Brahman, the source of immortality.
Those who are untruthful, nihilists, and of evil conduct— whenever they behold those brahmins of virtuous behavior,
their sins are exhausted and they become free from sorrow in their minds.
Devoted to that through austerity, he beheld by means of his devotion the adorable Dharma, which is indeed Viśvarūpa,
the god Nārāyaṇa of such power.
Upon seeing him— the supreme treasury of lights encircled by his rosary— the god of gods rejoiced with a heart full of joy through speech, mind, intellect, and body.
Then Nārāyaṇa, having beheld the Lord who is the source of the universe,
paid homage to the Master who grants boons, who was accompanied by Pārvatī of broad and beautiful limbs,
and who was sporting as a Great Soul surrounded by hosts of elemental beings.
Having saluted the unborn Īśāna, the undisturbed, the causal self, the infallible Rudra— the slayer of Andhaka—
he immediately knelt upon the earth with both knees and placed his joined palms to his head.
The devoted Padmākṣa praised that Virūpākṣa:
"O most excellent creator of beings, from you were born the ancient gods who are now the protectors of the world."
O God, those ancient ones who, having entered this earth, protected your primordial creation— the gods,
asuras, nāgas, rākṣasas, and piśācas— [are present].
We likewise know that all humans, Suparṇas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and all the various hosts of beings are born from you.
The rites dedicated to Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Agni; those of Mitra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Soma—all these actions are for you. Form, light, sound, ether, and wind;
Touch, taste, water, smell, and earth; desire, Brahmā, the Veda, and the Brahmins—
all this, both the stationary and the moving, has originated from you.
Just as drops of water go from the waters to a state of separation,
and again reach unity with them upon their dissolution,
so too does the wise man understand both this origin and this [dissolution].
Having abandoned [the world], one attains union (sāyujya) with the beings there;
in the divine cycle, there are two mental birds,
the downward-branching *pippala* tree, and seven guardians.
The other ten who sustain the city were indeed created by you; you are superior to them,
for they are the speech, its meanings, the deities, and the world-protectors.
