Those others who formerly sustained the worlds have indeed passed away; they were born from you, and you are superior even to them.
The past, the present, and that which is yet to be, as well as the invincible—
all the worlds here have originated from you; indeed,
all existents have proceeded forth from you.
Devote yourself to me, who am devoted to you;
do not harm me with what is harmful. You are my very self, for my being is non-different from yours.
The wise man thus goes to the pure Brahman. I have praised you, O best of gods, seeking your honor and discerning you as the preeminent bull among the divine.
"Grant me those boons that are most difficult to obtain and desired by me; being thus praised, do not disregard me.
To him, the blue-throated wielder of the Pināka bow, whose nature is inconceivable, granted the boons.
Praised by the sages, he offered it to the Arhat, the chief of gods.
Nīlakaṇṭha said:
"By my grace, among humans and in the wombs of gods and gandharvas..."
O Nārāyaṇa, you shall become one whose self possesses immeasurable power;
neither gods, asuras, nor great serpents, nor piśācas, gandharvas, humans, nor rākṣasas shall be able to overcome you.
Neither the Suparṇas nor the Nāgas, nor any born of other wombs,
nor even any god whatsoever shall defeat you in battles—
not by weapon, nor by thunderbolt, nor by fire, nor by wind.
Neither with something wet nor dry, neither with a moving creature nor a stationary object,
neither with the hand nor the foot, nor with wood nor a clod of earth— by my grace, no one shall cause you any injury whatsoever.
"Even if, having gone to battle, you should become superior to me.
Vyāsa said:
"Know that these boons were obtained by Śauri in the past."
This very god moves about, deluding the world by means of his illusory power (*māyā*). Know that the great sage named Nara was born through his ascetic fervor (*tapas*) alone;
know him always, O Arjuna, to be equal to this god.
These two sages, who were the most highly exalted among the gods of old,
are born age after age for the purpose of maintaining the course of the world and for the destruction of the Dānavas.

O wise one of great intelligence, for the sake of establishing the Dharma, you have been born as a fierce and powerful being, possessing splendor and wrath, through the entirety of your past actions and even through your great asceticism.
You, being as wise as a god, having understood that this world is composed of *bhava*,
have drawn yourself away through self-restraints out of a desire for what is dear to him; you have fashioned for yourself a new and auspicious form, the body of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*).
O giver of honor, you have worshipped him with prayers, burnt offerings, and oblations;
thus honored by you, that ancient deity was well-pleased and granted you abundant boons that resided in your heart, O wise one.
The birth, deeds, austerities, and yogic attainments of those two as well as yours are abundant.
By them the Lord was worshipped in the *liṅga*, and by you in an image, age after age.
Whoever worships the *liṅga* with a fasted night-meal (*nakta*) on the fourteenth or eighth lunar day—
As long as he lives, he should remain a bearer of vows and wander through all lands;
he is this very Viṣṇu and Rudra, the auspicious one born from Viṣṇu,
for their single body has been made twofold through yoga for the sake of [divine] purpose.

All the gods consist of Viṣṇu; all the hosts consist of Viṣṇu. Indeed, the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, are pervaded by Viṣṇu. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the embodied forms of that deity.
O mighty-armed one, whatever else belongs to the Infinite,
the God of gods, whose nature is inconceivable, who is invincible, and who is born of Viṣṇu— he who,
knowing Bhava to be the form of all, worships the Lord in the *liṅga*.
In that [state], indeed, reside the eternal applications of the self and the applications of the scriptures;
for thus the gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis, performing sacrifices,
pray for the highest station and the eternal state in the world.
This very Keśava is a devotee of Rudra, for he is born from Rudra;
indeed, Kṛṣṇa alone is to be worshipped with sacrifices, for he is the eternal one. That supreme state of Viṣṇu is constantly meditated upon by the yogins.
Whenever there is a decline of righteousness in the world,
and an uprising of unrighteousness, then he manifests himself;
[as] the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, and Hari.
Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu is to be accomplished as the self-born son of Kaśyapa;
Rāma, Rāma, and Rāma, and Vāsudeva the Yādava—
when the age has declined, Hari shall become the Brahmin Kalkī once again.
By means of his single self, that entire universe— both the stationary and the moving— was created by Viṣṇu, the infinite Great Soul;
he performs ascetic penance out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The world proceeds by means of that which has austerity as its primary principle;
for this reason, Hari constantly practices austerity and seeks boons from this preeminent and most excellent of gods.
Having gone to Badarī together with Viṣṇu, he performed austerities at Viśālā; this has been told to you by me. He who, knowing the origin of all beings, worships the Lord in the Liṅga—
The Bull-bannered Lord bestows upon him exceeding affection.
Sañjaya said:
Having heard those words of his, the great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa—
He paid homage to Rudra and held Keśava in high esteem; with his hair standing on end and his mind subdued, having offered salutations to the great seer,
he turned toward his army and ordered a withdrawal.
Then, O lord of the people, the withdrawal of the Pāṇḍavas and the dejected Kauravas took place after Droṇa had been struck down in battle;
for having fought for five days, Droṇa had destroyed their vast army.
"O King, that Brahmin who had mastered the Vedas went to the world of Brahmā.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, when that great car-warrior Droṇa had been slain there,"
"What did my men and the Pāṇḍavas do after that?
Sañjaya said:
"When that great car-warrior Droṇa had been slain by the son of Pṛṣata,"
When the Kauravas had been broken, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī,
beheld a most great marvel that brought him victory—
the stainless sage Vedavyāsa, who resembled a cloud charged with rain.
O bull of the Bharatas, he questioned Vyāsa, who had arrived by chance:
"As I am slaying my enemies in battle with floods of stainless arrows,
I perceive a man of fiery radiance proceeding ahead of me."
"O Great Sage, in whichever direction I go raising this flaming trident, my enemies in that direction are shattered to pieces;
yet it does not touch the ground with its feet, nor does it ever let go of the trident."
From his spear, by his splendor, thousands of spears issued forth;
because they were shattered by him, people think all those enemies were broken by me. His armies were consumed by him, and I merely burn them from behind.
"O Blessed One, tell me that: who indeed is that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the great wielder of the trident, O Kṛṣṇa, who is equal to the sun in splendor? Vyāsa said:

O Pārtha, you have seen Śaṅkara—the first among the Prajāpatis, the radiant, all-pervading Person; the world, the god of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; the Lord and Master of all worlds; the Sovereign and giver of boons.
Go for refuge to that god, the origin of all, the lord of the world—
Mahādeva, the Great-Souled One, the Sovereign, the matted-haired Śiva;
the three-eyed, mighty-armed Rudra, who wears a topknot and is clothed in bark garments.
To Hara, the God of gods, Sthāṇu, the bestower of boons, the Lord of the world;
the foremost in the universe, the unconquered, the Lord of the world, the Supreme Sovereign; the source of the world, the seed of the world, the Victorious One, the goal of the world.

The soul of the universe, the creator of the universe, whose form is the universe, the illustrious one; the lord of the universe, the source of the universe, the architect of the universe, the sovereign; Śambhu, the self-existent, the lord of beings, the origin of the past, the future, and the present.
Yoga, the Lord of Yoga, the All, the Lord of the lords of all worlds;
the most excellent, the best in the universe, the preeminent, the Supreme Being; the creator of the three worlds, the one refuge of the three worlds.
The Lord of the World, who is exceedingly difficult to conquer, who has transcended birth, death, and old age;
whose nature is knowledge, who is attainable through knowledge, who is both the knower and the object of knowledge, and who is most difficult to perceive;
the pure-souled one, the excellent, the formidable, the self-controlled, whose seed is the universe.
To that eternal Lord of the Earth, the master of all lords of speech,
the giver of boons bestowed through his grace to his devotees—
to him belong those divine attendants of the All-pervading One, possessing various forms.
Some were dwarfish, some had matted hair, and others were shaven-headed; some had short necks and large bellies, while others possessed massive bodies, great energy, and enormous ears.
O Pārtha, they had deformed faces, misshapen feet, and strange attire.
Being worshipped in such a manner by these [beings], that Great God Maheśvara— that Śiva, O dear one, full of splendor— proceeds before you through his grace,
in that terrible battle which causes the hair to stand on end, O Pārtha.
O Pārtha, who could even in thought dare to attack that army then, protected as it was by Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa— those great archers and strikers—
except for the gods or Maheśvara himself, the great archer of manifold forms?
When he stands at the front, no one dares to remain;
indeed, there is no being equal to him found in the three worlds. For even by his scent alone in battle, his enemies—when he is enraged—[are overcome].
Deprived of consciousness and for the most part slain, they tremble and fall;
even the gods in heaven stand paying homage to him,
as do other men in the world and those who have conquered the celestial realm.
Those who, with single-minded devotion, always worship Śiva, Rudra, the Lord of Umā, the boon-bestowing God and Sovereign of All—
having attained victory in battles, they protect this earth.
Having attained happiness in this world, they go to the supreme goal. O son of Kuntī, always pay homage to that peaceful one—
to Rudra, the blue-throated, the youngest, and the most resplendent.
To Kapardin, to Karāla, to Haryakṣa, and to the Giver of Boons; to the One belonging to Yama, to the One with Unmanifest Hair, to the One of Excellent Conduct, and to Śaṃkara;
to Kāmya, to Harinetra, to Sthāṇu, and to Puruṣa.
To the golden-haired one, to the shaven-headed, to the emaciated, and to the one who helps across;
to the sun-maker, to the excellent ford, to the god of gods, and to the impetuous one; to the multiformed Śarva, to the beloved, and to him whose garment is dear.

Homage to the one with the turban, the fair-faced, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful; homage to the Lord of the Tree, the Commander of the Army, the Central One, homage! Homage to Giriśa, the Tranquil One, the Lord clothed in bark.
Salutations to the golden-armed one, to the fierce lord of the quarters; salutations to the lord of the quarters, of the elephants of the quarters, and of space and time;
and salutations to the lord of Parjanya and to the lord of all beings.
Salutations to the Lord of Trees and likewise to the Lord of Waters;
to the one whose body is enveloped by trees, to the Commander of the Army, and to the Middle One;
to the God who holds a sacrificial ladle in his hand, to the Archer, and to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
To the one of many forms, the Lord of the universe, who is clothed in bark;
to the one with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes,
a thousand arms, and a thousand feet.

Having taken refuge in the Lord of the World, the granter of boons, the husband of Umā, the three-eyed Virūpākṣa, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice— one who possesses a thousand arms and whose deeds are beyond counting— O son of Kuntī, [I bow] with salutations.
To the Lord of creatures, the undisturbed; to the imperishable Lord of beings;
to the one with matted hair, whose whirlpools are virile, whose navel is virile, whose banner is virile;
to him who possesses virile pride, the lord of the virile, whose horns are virile, and who is the bull among the virile.
Maheśvara, who has the bull as his emblem, who is as noble as a bull, who is the bull himself, whose eyes are like those of a bull, whose weapons are the bull, whose arrows are the bull,
who has become the bull; he of the great belly and great body, clothed in a leopard skin.
[He saw] the Lord of the World, the giver of boons, shaven-headed, devoted to Brahman, and dear to Brāhmaṇas;
the Lord who holds a trident in his hand, the giver of boons, bearing a sword and a shield,
the wielder of the Pināka bow and the broken axe, the Sovereign and Master of the worlds.

I take refuge in that god who wears garments of bark, who is worthy of refuge, who carries a quiver and holds an axe in his hand, and who is the illuminator of all dharmas; salutations to that Lord of the Gods whose friend is indeed Vaiśravaṇa.
Homage ever to the well-attired one, to the one of excellent vows and great wealth;
to the god of fierce weapons, to Bhava of excellent vows;
to the god with the *sruva*-ladle in hand, to the one with a happy bow, to the wielder of the bow.
Homage to Dhanvantari, to the bow, to the preceptor of archers, and to the wielder of the bow; homage to the god of fierce weapons and to the best of deities;
let there be homage to the one of many forms, and homage to the one who possesses many bows.

Salutations ever to Sthāṇu, who is firm in his vows and possesses a beautiful bow; salutations indeed to the destroyer of Tripura and the slayer of Bhaga. Salutations to the Lord of the trees and the Lord of men.
Salutations to the Lord of Mothers and to the Lord of the Gaṇas; salutations eternally to the Lord of Waters and to the Lord of Sacrifices;
[salutations] to Pūṣan for the destruction of his teeth, and to the three-eyed giver of boons.
Salutations indeed to the blue-throated one, to the tawny one, and to the one with golden hair.
I shall proclaim to you the divine deeds of the wise Mahādeva, according to my knowledge and as I have heard them.
Neither gods, nor asuras in the world, nor gandharvas, nor rākṣasas—
though they have retreated into caves— find happiness when he is provoked,
for he was formerly prepared according to the rules by Dakṣa while he was performing a sacrifice.
Then Bhava, fearless, angrily pierced the sacrifice;
releasing an arrow from his bow, he let out a roar with a great sound. At that time, those gods found neither comfort nor peace.
When the sacrifice was suddenly disrupted and Maheśvara became enraged,
all the worlds were thrown into turmoil by the sound of his bowstring striking his palm;
O Pārtha, they fell under his power, and both gods and asuras collapsed.
All the waters were agitated and the earth trembled;
the mountains crumbled, the quarters of the sky were shattered, and the elephants were bewildered. Enveloped in darkness, the worlds became blind and lost their light.
Having struck down the splendor of all luminaries along with the sun,
they cried out, terrified by fear, and likewise performed rites for peace—
the seers who desire the welfare of all beings and themselves.
Śaṅkara, as if laughing, rushed toward Pūṣan and knocked out the teeth of him who was eating the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). Then the gods fled, trembling and bowing down before him.
And once again he aimed a blazing, sharpened arrow at the gods—
an arrow resembling smoke and sparks, like lightning amidst the clouds.
Seeing it, all the deities prostrated themselves before Maheśvara.
O King, out of fear, the thirty gods assigned a distinguished sacrificial portion to Rudra and sought refuge with him;
by that very act, despite his extreme wrath, the sacrifice was then restored.
The gods were vigilant against him, and even today they remain on guard. In ancient times, there were three cities belonging to the powerful Asuras in the sky:
one of iron, one of silver, and another great one of gold.
The iron [armor] belonged to Tārakākṣa, the silver to Kamalākṣa,
and that of Vidyunmālin was indeed made of supreme gold. Even Maghavan was not able to pierce them with any of his weapons.
Then all the immortals, being tormented, went for refuge to Rudra.
All those gods, together with Indra, spoke to that high-souled one:
"Indeed, these terrible inhabitants of Tripura have been granted boons by Brahmā."
Because they, arrogant due to the boons they have received, excessively oppress the world,
there is no one other than you, O Lord of the Gods of gods, who is able to slay the Daityas in any way whatsoever; O Mahādeva, you alone are the slayer of the enemies of the gods.
"O Rudra, the animals will become fierce in all their activities;
you shall strike down these Asuras, O Lord of the World. Having been addressed thus, he said "So be it," out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
Having made Śalya his arrowhead and Agni its shaft, and having placed Soma, the lord of the waters,
at the nock; having made the syllable *Oṃ* his bow and the *Sāvitrī* his bowstring, Maheśvara [prepared] the four Vedas as his horses and the essence of all the Vedas as his chariot.
Having appointed Prajāpati as the charioteer for that supreme chariot,
and having made Gandhamādana and Vindhya the two bamboo poles of the banner,
Śaṅkara, the Destroyer, fashioned the earth with its oceans and forests into a chariot.
Having made the lord of serpents Śeṣa his axle, the three-eyed one,
the god of gods who wields the Pināka bow, made the moon and sun his two wheels;
and Tryambaka made Elāpatra and Puṣpadanta his two linchpins.
Having made Mount Malaya the sacrificial post and Takṣaka the binding-cloth,
and having fashioned four parts for the yoke-harness, the powerful Śarva,
the Great Lord, then made the four Vedas his four horses.
Having fashioned the Upavedas into the bit, the Lord of the three worlds made Gāyatrī the reins and Sāvitrī the head-stall; Maheśvara made Oṃkāra the whip, and Brahmā himself the charioteer.
Making Mount Mandara the bow Gāṇḍīva and Vāsuki the string, making Viṣṇu the supreme arrow and Agni the shaft,
and then making Vāyu the two feathers and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, the nock;
Then, having made lightning his chariot-rein and Mount Meru his banner,
Śiva— the immovable one, the best among strikers— ascended that divine chariot composed of all the gods for the sake of slaying Tripura.
O Pārtha, the glorious Lord of incomparable prowess, the bringer of the end to the Asuras, being praised by the gods and by the ṛṣis rich in asceticism,
established his divine and matchless abode belonging to Maheśvara.
He stood there like a pillar for a thousand years;
when the three cities had indeed come together in the intermediate space,
he pierced them with that [spear] which had three joints and three points.
The Dānavas were unable even to look upon that arrow,
which was joined with the fire of time and endowed with Viṣṇu and Soma;
as it was burning the cities, the Goddess went forth to behold it.
The powerful Lord Śambhu, having given his command,

released [the fire] upon the cities; then, O illustrious one, those evil-minded Daityas, along with their sons and their followers, were reduced to ashes when the three cities were shattered in the past.
Having slain the Daityas, Mahādeva was honored by all the gods;
praised by the ṛṣis as well, he attained supreme joy. Then Brahmā, together with the gods led by Bṛhaspati, [approached him].
When the palace of Tripura had been shattered, they began to offer hymns of praise;
O Dhanañjaya, hear now another account of what occurred at the Goddess’s svayaṃvara. Having once again placed the five-crested child upon her lap, she herself—
Desiring to know who he was, Umā spoke thus to the gods:
"The Lord paralyzed the arm of the enraged Śakra, together with his thunderbolt, as he was about to strike with that very bolt out of malice."
Then the Blessed One, Śiva, the Lord of all worlds, laughed and quickly [acted].
Thereupon, his arm paralyzed, Śakra, surrounded by the hosts of gods,
swiftly went for refuge to the imperishable Lord Brahmā.
Having bowed their heads to him, they then spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"O Brahmin, there was some wonderful being on Pārvatī’s lap;
having seen it assuming the form of a child, we did not recognize it."
"Therefore, we wish to ask you about him by whom we have indeed been conquered— by that boy, who, without even fighting, effortlessly defeated us along with Indra himself.
Having heard those words of theirs, Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, [spoke].
Having meditated upon Śambhu and the boy of immeasurable splendor,
the Lord Brahmā spoke to Śakra and the other foremost gods;
for that Lord Hara is the master of the world of the moving and the unmoving.
"Therefore, there is nothing else superior to Maheśvara,
he of immeasurable splendor who was seen by you together with Umā;
for the sake of Pārvatī, that god assumed the form of a child."
"Come, all of you, together with me, take refuge in him alone;
for he is that Blessed One, the God, the Lord of all worlds, the Sovereign.
Having been addressed thus, the gods went to where the god Maheśvara was.
Then Brahmā, having seen that imperishable one in another form, [remained there]; yet all the gods, together with the Prajāpatis, did not recognize that Lord of the World,
who possessed a radiance like the rising sun.
Then Brahmā, having approached from there and beheld Maheśvara,
recognized that "this one is the most excellent," and the Grandfather paid him homage.
Brahmā said:
You are the sacrifice of this world; you are its refuge and its ultimate goal. You are Bhava, you are Mahādeva, you are the abode, the supreme state.
By you all this world, both the stationary and the moving, is pervaded.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Protector of the world, Master of the universe! Grant favor to Śakra, who is indeed afflicted by your wrath.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of the Lotus-born One, Maheśvara was then delighted;
becoming inclined toward grace, he let out a boisterous laugh.
Then those gods propitiated Umā and Rudra.
And the arm of the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrin) was restored once more to its natural state. The Blessed One, whose banner is the bull, accompanied by his consort,
the foremost of the thirty-three gods and the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, became gracious toward them.
He is indeed Rudra, he is Śiva, he is Agni, he is Śarva, and he is the omniscient one; he is Indra and Vāyu, he is the two Aśvins, and he is the lightning flashes;
he is Bhava, he is Parjanya, he is Mahādeva, and he is the sinless one.
He is the moon and he is Īśāna; he is the sun and he is Varuṇa.
He is time, he is the ender, death, and Yama; he is night and days, months and fortnights, the seasons, the two twilights, and the year.

He is the Ordainer and the Disposer, the soul of all, the performer of all actions; though bodiless, he sustains the bodies of all the deities. Praised by all the gods, that God exists both as one and as many.
In a hundred ways, in a thousand ways, and likewise in a hundred-thousand ways—those Brahmins who know the Veda understand that the God has two bodies:
one is terrible and the other is auspicious; yet these two bodies are further divided in many ways.
That which is his terrible body is fire, lightning, and the sun;
furthermore, the crescent moon, the waters, the luminaries, and the moon itself belong to him.
So too do the Vedāṅgas along with the Upaniṣads, and the Purāṇas that determine the nature of the supreme self.
That which is the supreme secret herein is indeed the god Maheśvara;
such is that Mahādeva, and furthermore, he is the blessed Unborn (Aja). For it is not possible for me to describe all the qualities of the Blessed One.
O son of Pāṇḍu, even in a thousand years,
he who is well-pleased and provides refuge liberates those who have sought his protection— even if they are seized by all the planets or possessed of every sin.

He bestows upon human beings long life, health, sovereignty, wealth, and abundant objects of desire; he likewise takes them away again. And his sovereignty is said to extend even over the gods, beginning with Indra.
He alone is the one who has manifested in this world as the source of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of human beings;
by virtue of his sovereignty over all desires, he is further called Īśvara,
and because he is the lord of great beings, he is called Maheśvara.
With many forms in manifold ways, he indeed pervades the entire world. That which is the mouth of this god remained in the ocean;
it is renowned as the Mare’s Mouth (*Vaḍavāmukha*), and it drinks the oblation consisting of water.
And this very god dwells eternally in cremation grounds; there people worship this Lord as Vīrasthāna. His forms are many, both blazing and terrible.
Whatever names humans in this world apply to him and proclaim among the people, many are these names here that correspond to his true nature;
they are derived from his greatness, his omnipresence, and likewise from his deeds.
In the Veda, the supreme Śatarudrīya hymn is recited for him; it is known by the name Anantarudra, a prayer of adoration to the Great-Souled One.
That god is the lord of all desires, both those that are divine and those that are human.
He is the all-pervading Lord, the God who encompasses the great universe. The Brahmins and the sages likewise call him the eldest of all beings;
for he is the first of the gods, and from his mouth fire was born.
Because he protects all creatures in every way, because he delights in them again,
and because he is their sovereign lord, he is therefore known as Paśupati. Since his linga remains established through perpetual celibacy (brahmacarya), [he is called Mahādeva].
The worlds worship him, and thus he is known as Maheśvara;
likewise, the ṛṣis, the gods, the gandharvas,
and the apsarases worship his linga, which stands erect.
Then the Blessed One was always addressed by the Brahmins as "the one whose liṅga is erect.
When he is thus worshipped, that Maheśvara rejoices;
Śaṃkara becomes happy, pleased, and truly delighted.
Whatever form of his exists manifoldly— established in the past, the future,
and the present, both stationary and moving— he is therefore remembered as Bahurūpa (the Multiform).
He remains blazing alone, or even consisting of eyes on every side.
Because he entered the worlds out of wrath, he is remembered as Śarva;
because his form is smoke-colored (dhūmra), he is called Dhūrjaṭi;
and because all the gods (viśve devāḥ) reside within him, he is therefore known as Viśvarūpa.
When the Lord of the World resorts to the three goddesses—
heaven, water, and earth— he is therefore known as Tryambaka;
for he constantly promotes all purposes in all undertakings.
Because he desires the welfare of human beings, he is therefore remembered as Śiva.
Whether he has a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, or consists of eyes on every side,
and because he protects the great universe, he is therefore remembered as Mahādeva.
Because he burns while standing upright, because he is established as the source of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*),
and because his *liṅga* is eternally fixed, he is therefore remembered as Sthāṇu.
Furthermore, those rays which illuminate the world of the sun and the moon—
Those hairs were designated as his; therefore, he is remembered as Vyomakeśa (Heavenly-Haired).
He is called the Best of Monkeys (Kapiśreṣṭha), and Dharma is said to be the Bull (Vṛṣa). That Blessed One, the God of Gods, is indeed celebrated as Vṛṣākapi.
Because he seizes Brahmā, Indra, Varuṇa, Yama, and even the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), he is therefore known as Hara. Due to his childhood, Maheśvara [was seized] by the Goddess with her eyes closed.
He created an eye on his forehead; therefore, he is called Tryakṣa (the Three-eyed).
Since he is the source of the past, the present, and the future—everything in its entirety—he is therefore Bhava, the originator of all that has been, is, and will be.
He who is situated unequally within bodies, yet remains equal toward all living beings here—
worship that Vāyu, who dwells within the bodies of those whose prāṇa and apāna are disturbed; he who would honor his physical form or worship his *liṅga* [is thereby honored].
One who constantly worships the *liṅga* attains great prosperity.
Half of Śiva’s body, from the thighs downward, belongs to Agni, while the other half belongs to Soma;
thus, Agni is said to be half of his self, and Soma is likewise said to be the other half.
His great, radiant, and luminous body is auspicious toward the gods;
his body among humans is called the blazing, terrible fire. With that auspicious body of his, he practices the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Because his most terrible form devours all beings,
and because he burns, because he is sharp, fierce, and majestic,
and because he consumes flesh, blood, and marrow, he is therefore called Rudra.
O Pārtha, this god who was seen by you in battle slaying your enemies with your assistance— the wielder of the Pināka bow, Mahādeva himself— was seen when you,
O sinless one, had vowed the slaughter of the King of Sindhu.
"That which was shown to you by Kṛṣṇa in a dream upon the summit of the king of mountains—
this indeed is the Blessed Lord, the God, who goes before you in battle;
he is the one by whom those weapons were given to you, with which the Dānavas were slain."
O Pārtha, this Śatarudriya of the God of gods, which is auspicious, conducive to fame, bestowing long life, meritorious, and recognized by the Vedas, has been explained to you;
it accomplishes all aims, is holy, and destroys all sins.
It pacifies all sins and removes all suffering and fear;
even a man of wicked conduct obtains the fruit of performing a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred *rājasūya* sacrifices.
He who always hears this fourfold hymn enjoys the fruit of giving away even a hundred million cows;
having conquered all his enemies, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.

This auspicious and divine account of the deeds of the Great-Souled One concerning battle— by constantly rising to recite or hear the Śatarudrīya, the man who listens with devotion or likewise proclaims it aloud, [attains the highest goal].
Whether by day or by night, he who is always devoted to the god Viśveśvara among men dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin; that man obtains his desired boons when Tryambaka is pleased.
"Go, O son of Kuntī, and fight; there shall be no defeat for you, since Janārdana stands by your side as both counselor and protector. Sañjaya said:
Having thus spoken to Arjuna on the battlefield, the son of Parāśara then departed, O best of the Bharatas, O subduer of enemies, just as he had come. Sañjaya said:
Having fought a most terrible battle for five days,
O King, that mighty Brāhmaṇa was slain and attained the world of Brahmā;
whatever fruit is obtained from studying the Veda, that same fruit is found in this Parvan as well.
The pure fame of fearless Kṣatriyas is proclaimed.
Whoever constantly recites or even hears this section is liberated from great sins and from terrible deeds committed.

A man who always recites this, which is endowed with all great purposes, or likewise listens to it, shall obtain victory in battle for the lion-like Pāṇḍava and Vṛṣṇi, as well as eternal auspiciousness.
Even one who has committed evil deeds is liberated from his karmas;
for a Brahmin, there is the constant attainment of sacrifice here,
and for Kṣatriyas, there is constant victory in battle.
The remaining two syllables grant one’s desired wishes; likewise, they always bestow beloved sons and grandsons. Having thus related all this to the king, Sañjaya, the Sūta, [spoke].
He set out for the camp indeed to witness the slaughter of Karṇa.
